Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

The Minor Collection

Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary to the Cariyāpiṭaka

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Cariyā [M 0.0001][V 0.0001][P 0.0001] sabbalokassa, hitā yassa mahesino;

Acinteyyānubhāvaṃ taṃ, vande lokagganāyakaṃ.

I venerate that Leader of the World, the Great Sage, whose conduct is for the welfare of all the world and whose power is inconceivable.

Vijjācaraṇasampannā, yena nīyanti lokato;

Vande tamuttamaṃ dhammaṃ, sammāsambuddhapūjitaṃ.

I venerate that supreme Dhamma, revered by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, by which those endowed with knowledge and conduct are led out from the world.

Sīlādiguṇasampanno, ṭhito maggaphalesu yo;

Vande ariyasaṅghaṃ taṃ, puññakkhettaṃ anuttaraṃ.

Endowed with virtues such as morality, established in the paths and fruits, I venerate that Noble Sangha, the unsurpassed field of merit.

Vandanājanitaṃ [V 0.0002] puññaṃ, iti yaṃ ratanattaye;

Hatantarāyo sabbattha, hutvāhaṃ tassa tejasā.

By the power of that merit generated by homage to the Triple Gem, may I be without obstacles everywhere.

Imasmiṃ bhaddakappasmiṃ, sambhatā yā sudukkarā;

Ukkaṃsapāramippattā, dānapāramitādayo.

In this auspicious aeon, those extremely difficult perfections, such as the perfection of generosity, were accumulated and brought to their highest culmination.

Tāsaṃ sambodhicariyānaṃ, ānubhāvavibhāvanaṃ;

Sakkesu nigrodhārāme, vasantena mahesinā.

A manifestation of the power of those practices for enlightenment, [was taught] by the Great Sage while dwelling in the Nigrodha Grove among the Sakyans,

Yaṃ dhammasenāpatino, sabbasāvakaketuno;

Lokanāthena cariyā-piṭakaṃ nāma desitaṃ.

the Cariyāpiṭaka by name, which was expounded by the Leader of the World to the Commander of the Dhamma, the standard-bearer of all disciples.

Yaṃ khuddakanikāyasmiṃ, saṅgāyiṃsu mahesayo;

Dhammasaṅgāhakā satthu, hetusampattidīpanaṃ.

Which the great sages, the compilers of the Dhamma, compiled in the Minor Collection, as an exposition of the Teacher's accomplishment of causes.

Tassa [M 0.0002] sambodhisambhāra-vibhāganayayogato;

Kiñcāpi dukkarā kātuṃ, atthasaṃvaṇṇanā mayā.

Though an exposition of its meaning is difficult for me to compose, in accordance with the method of analyzing the requisites for enlightenment,

Saha saṃvaṇṇanaṃ yasmā, dharate satthu sāsanaṃ;

Pubbācariyasīhānaṃ, tiṭṭhateva vinicchayo.

since the Teacher’s dispensation endures together with its commentary, and the judgment of the former lion-like teachers stands firm,

Tasmā taṃ avalambitvā, ogāhitvā ca sabbaso;

Jātakānupanissāya, porāṇaṭṭhakathānayaṃ.

therefore, relying on that and plunging completely into it, and depending on the Jātakas according to the method of the ancient commentaries,

Nissitaṃ [P 0.0002] vācanāmaggaṃ, suvisuddhamanākulaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, nipuṇatthavinicchayaṃ.

the well-established path of expression of the residents of the Mahāvihāra, which is very pure and unconfused, and their skillful ascertainment of meaning,

Nītaneyyatthabhedā ca, pāramī paridīpayaṃ;

Karissāmi taṃ cariyā-piṭakassatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

and illuminating the perfections and the distinctions between explicit and implicit meanings, I shall compose that commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka.

Iti [V 0.0003] ākaṅkhamānassa, saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitiṃ;

Vibhajantassa tassatthaṃ, nisāmayatha sādhavoti.

Thus, from me, who desires the long-standing of the true Dhamma and is analyzing its meaning, listen, O virtuous ones.

Tattha cariyāpiṭakanti kenaṭṭhena cariyāpiṭakaṃ? Atītāsu jātīsu satthu cariyānubhāvappakāsinī pariyattīti katvā, pariyattiattho hi ayaṃ piṭakasaddo, “mā piṭakasampadānenā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) viya. Atha vā yasmā sā pariyatti tasseva satthu purimajātīsu cariyānaṃ ānubhāvappakāsanena bhājanabhūtā, tasmāpi “cariyāpiṭaka”nti vuccati, bhājanatthopi hi piṭakasaddo niddiṭṭho “atha puriso āgaccheyya, kudālapiṭakaṃ ādāyā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.228; a. ni. 3.70) viya. Taṃ panetaṃ cariyāpiṭakaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ, suttantapiṭakaṃ, abhidhammapiṭakanti tīsu piṭakesu suttantapiṭakapariyāpannaṃ. Dīghanikāyo, majjhimanikāyo, saṃyuttanikāyo, aṅguttaranikāyo, khuddakanikāyoti pañcasu nikāyesu khuddakanikāyapariyāpannaṃ. Suttaṃ, geyyaṃ, veyyākaraṇaṃ, gāthā, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, jātakaṃ, abbhutadhammaṃ, vedallanti navasu sāsanaṅgesu gāthāsaṅgahaṃ.

Herein, in what sense is it the 'Cariyāpiṭaka'? Because it is the teaching that makes manifest the power of the Teacher's conduct in past lives, it is called 'Cariyāpiṭaka'. For this word 'piṭaka' has the meaning of 'teaching', as in such passages as 'not by mastering the teachings...' Or, because that teaching serves as a container for making manifest the power of the Teacher's conduct in former lives, it is therefore called 'Cariyāpiṭaka'. For the word 'piṭaka' is also shown to have the meaning of 'container', as in such passages as 'then a man might come, bringing a spade and a basket...'. This Cariyāpiṭaka, among the three Piṭakas—the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—is included in the Suttanta Piṭaka. Among the five Nikāyas—the Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya—it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine limbs of the dispensation—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—it is a collection of verses.

“Dvāsīti buddhato gaṇhiṃ, dvesahassāni bhikkhuto;

Caturāsīti sahassāni, ye me dhammā pavattino”ti. (theragā. 1027) –

Eighty-two thousand I received from the Buddha, two thousand from the monk; these eighty-four thousand teachings are those that are current for me.

Evaṃ [M 0.0003] dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena paṭiññātesu caturāsītiyā dhammakkhandhasahassesu katipayadhammakkhandhasaṅgahaṃ. Vaggato akittivaggo, hatthināgavaggo, yudhañjayavaggoti vaggattayasaṅgahaṃ. Cariyato akittivagge dasa, hatthināgavagge dasa, yudhañjayavagge pañcadasāti pañcatiṃsacariyāsaṅgahaṃ. Tīsu vaggesu akittivaggo ādi, cariyāsu akitticariyā. Tassāpi –

Thus, among the eighty-four thousand Dhamma-sections acknowledged by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, this is a collection of a few Dhamma-sections. By way of sections, it is a collection of three sections: the Akitti section, the Hatthināga section, and the Yudhañjaya section. By way of conducts, it is a collection of thirty-five conducts: ten in the Akitti section, ten in the Hatthināga section, and fifteen in the Yudhañjaya section. Among the three sections, the Akitti section is the first; among the conducts, the Akitti conduct is the first. And of that too—

“Kappe ca satasahasse, caturo ca asaṅkhiye;

Etthantare yaṃ caritaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ bodhipācana”nti. –

For one hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable periods, whatever conduct was practiced in that interval, all of that was for the maturing of enlightenment.

Ayaṃ gāthā ādi. Tassa ito pabhuti anukkamena atthasaṃvaṇṇanā hoti.

This verse is the beginning. From this point onwards, the exposition of its meaning proceeds in sequence.

Ganthārambhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the commencement of the treatise is concluded.

Nidānakathā

The Discourse on the Origins

Sā [V 0.0004] panāyaṃ atthasaṃvaṇṇanā yasmā dūrenidānaṃ, avidūrenidānaṃ, santikenidānanti imāni tīṇi nidānāni [P 0.0003] dassetvā vuccamānā suṇantehi samudāgamato paṭṭhāya suṭṭhu viññātā nāma hoti. Tasmā tesaṃ nidānānaṃ ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo.

Now, since this exposition of the meaning is well understood by its hearers from the outset when it is related after first showing these three origins—the distant origin, the not-so-distant origin, and the near origin—therefore, this division of those origins should be understood.

Dīpaṅkaradasabalassa pādamūlasmiñhi katābhinīhārassa mahābodhisattassa yāva tusitabhavane nibbatti, tāva pavatto kathāmaggo dūrenidānaṃ nāma. Tusitabhavanato paṭṭhāya yāva bodhimaṇḍe sabbaññutaññāṇappatti, tāva pavatto kathāmaggo avidūrenidānaṃ nāma. Mahābodhimaṇḍato pana paṭṭhāya yāva paccuppannavatthu, tāva pavatto kathāmaggo santikenidānaṃ nāma. Imesu tīsu nidānesu yasmā dūrenidānaavidūrenidānāni sabbasādhāraṇāni, tasmā tāni jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (jā. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā) vitthāritanayeneva vitthārato veditabbāni. Santikenidāne pana atthi visesoti tiṇṇampi nidānānaṃ ayamādito paṭṭhāya saṅkhepakathā.

Indeed, the narrative course that proceeded from the Great Bodhisatta's making of his aspiration at the feet of the Ten-Powered Buddha Dīpaṅkara up to his rebirth in the Tusita realm is called the Distant Origin. The narrative course that proceeded from the Tusita realm up to the attainment of omniscient knowledge at the Bodhimaṇḍa is called the Not-so-Distant Origin. The narrative course that proceeded from the Great Bodhimaṇḍa up to the present occasion is called the Proximate Origin. Among these three origins, since the Distant and Not-so-Distant Origins are common to all, they should be understood in detail according to the method by which they are elaborated in the Jātaka commentary. In the Proximate Origin, however, there is a distinction; therefore, this is the concise account of all three origins from the beginning.

Dīpaṅkarassa [M 0.0004] bhagavato pādamūle katābhinīhāro bodhisattabhūto lokanātho attano abhinīhārānurūpaṃ samattiṃsapāramiyo pūretvā, sabbaññutaññāṇasambhāraṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā, tusitabhavane nibbatto buddhabhāvāya uppattikālaṃ āgamayamāno, tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto sakyarājakule paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā anantena parihārena mahantena sirisobhaggena vaḍḍhamāno anukkamena yobbanaṃ patvā ekūnatiṃse vayasmiṃ katamahābhinikkhamano, chabbassāni mahāpadhānaṃ padahitvā, vesākhapuṇṇamāyaṃ bodhirukkhamūle nisinno sūriye anatthaṅgamiteyeva mārabalaṃ vidhamitvā purimayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussaritvā, majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhetvā, pacchimayāme diyaḍḍhakilesasahassaṃ khepetvā, anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhimabhisambujjhi.

The Lord of the World, who, having become a Bodhisatta and made his aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, fulfilled the thirty perfections in accordance with his aspiration and brought the accumulation for omniscient knowledge to its peak. Reborn in the Tusita realm, he awaited the time for his arising as a Buddha. Having dwelt there for the full lifespan, he passed away and took rebirth in the Sakyan royal family. Growing with boundless honor and great glory and beauty, he gradually reached youth. At the age of twenty-nine, he made the Great Renunciation. Practicing great striving for six years, on the full moon day of Vesākha, he sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Before the sun had set, he shattered the forces of Māra; in the first watch of the night, he recollected his past lives; in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye; and in the last watch, having destroyed the one and a half thousand defilements, he awakened to unsurpassable perfect enlightenment.

Tato tattheva sattasattāhe vītināmetvā, āsāḷhipuṇṇamāyaṃ bārāṇasiṃ gantvā isipatane migadāye aññāsikoṇḍaññappamukhā aṭṭhārasa brahmakoṭiyo dhammāmataṃ pāyento, dhammacakkaṃ (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13 ādayo; paṭi. ma. 2.30) pavattetvā, yasādike veneyye arahatte patiṭṭhāpetvā, te sabbeva saṭṭhi arahante lokānuggahāya vissajjetvā, uruvelaṃ gacchanto kappāsikavanasaṇḍe tiṃsa bhaddavaggiye sotāpattiphalādīsu patiṭṭhāpetvā, uruvelaṃ gantvā aḍḍhuḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassāni [P 0.0004] dassetvā uruvelakassapādayo sahassajaṭilaparivāre tebhātikajaṭile [V 0.0005] vinetvā, tehi parivuto rājagahanagarūpacāre laṭṭhivanuyyāne nisinno bimbisārappamukhe dvādasanahute brāhmaṇagahapatike sāsane otāretvā, magadharājena kārite veḷuvanavihāre viharati.

Having spent seven weeks there, he went to Bārāṇasī, to the Deer Park at Isipatana, on the full-moon day of Āsāḷhī. There, causing the eighteen crores of Brahmās led by Aññāsi Koṇḍañña to drink the nectar of the Dhamma, he turned the Wheel of Dhamma. Having established the trainees headed by Yasa in arahantship, he sent all those sixty arahants out for the welfare of the world. While traveling to Uruvelā, he established the thirty Bhaddavaggiyas in the fruits beginning with stream-entry at the Kappāsika forest grove. Upon reaching Uruvelā, he displayed three thousand five hundred miracles and tamed Uruvela Kassapa and his brothers, the three matted-hair ascetics with their thousand followers. Surrounded by them, he went to the vicinity of Rājagaha and, seated in the Laṭṭhivana grove, he brought twelve nahutas of brahmins and householders, led by King Bimbisāra, into the teaching. He then dwelled in the Veḷuvana Monastery, built by the King of Magadha.

Athevaṃ bhagavati veḷuvane viharante sāriputtamoggallānesu aggasāvakaṭṭhāne ṭhapitesu sāvakasannipāte jāte, suddhodanamahārājā “putto kira me chabbassāni dukkarakārikaṃ caritvā paramābhisambodhiṃ patvā pavattitavaradhammacakko rājagahaṃ nissāya veḷuvane viharatī”ti sutvā dasapurisasahassaparivāre, anukkamena dasa amacce pesesi “puttaṃ me idhānetvā dassethā”ti. Tesu rājagahaṃ gantvā satthu dhammadesanāya arahatte patiṭṭhitesu kāḷudāyittherena rañño adhippāye ārocite bhagavā vīsatisahassakhīṇāsavaparivuto rājagahato nikkhamitvā saṭṭhiyojanaṃ [M 0.0005] kapilavatthuṃ dvīhi māsehi sampāpuṇi. Sakyarājāno “amhākaṃ ñātiseṭṭhaṃ passissāmā”ti sannipatitvā nigrodhārāmaṃ bhagavato ca bhikkhusaṅghassa ca vasanayoggaṃ kāretvā, gandhapupphādihatthā paccuggamanaṃ katvā, satthāraṃ nigrodhārāmaṃ pavesesuṃ. Tatra bhagavā vīsatisahassakhīṇāsavaparivuto paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi. Sākiyā mānatthaddhā satthu paṇipātaṃ nākaṃsu. Bhagavā tesaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ oloketvā mānaṃ bhañjitvā te dhammadesanāya bhājane kātuṃ abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā tesaṃ sīse pādapaṃsuṃ okiramāno viya, kaṇḍambarukkhamūle katapāṭihāriyasadisaṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ akāsi. Rājā taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā “ayaṃ loke aggapuggalo”ti vandi. Raññā pana vandite te ṭhātuṃ nāma na sakkonti, sabbepi sākiyā vandiṃsu.

At that time, while the Blessed One was dwelling in the Veḷuvana, Sāriputta and Moggallāna having been established in the position of chief disciples, and an assembly of disciples having gathered, King Suddhodana heard: "My son, it is said, after practicing severe austerities for six years, attained supreme enlightenment, set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, and now dwells near Rājagaha in the Veḷuvana." Hearing this, he gradually sent ten ministers, each with a retinue of a thousand men, saying, "Bring my son here and show him to me." When they went to Rājagaha and, upon hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, were established in arahantship, the venerable Kāḷudāyi informed the Blessed One of the king's wish. The Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand who had destroyed the cankers, left Rājagaha and reached Kapilavatthu, a distance of sixty yojanas, in two months. The Sākyan kings, thinking, "We shall see our noblest relative," gathered and had the Nigrodhārāma prepared as a suitable dwelling for the Blessed One and the community of monks. Holding perfumes, flowers, and so on, they went forth to welcome him and led the Teacher into the Nigrodhārāma. There, the Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand who had destroyed the cankers, sat on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat. The Sākyans, stiff with pride, did not pay homage to the Teacher. Perceiving their disposition, the Blessed One, in order to break their pride and make them vessels for the Dhamma, attained the fourth jhāna that is the basis for supernormal powers. Emerging from it, he rose into the air and, as if scattering the dust from his feet on their heads, he performed the Twin Miracle, similar to the miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree. Seeing this marvel, the king bowed, saying, "This is the foremost person in the world!" When the king had bowed, the others could not remain standing—all the Sākyans bowed.

Tadā kira bhagavā yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karonto lokavivaraṇapāṭihāriyampi akāsi – yasmiṃ vattamāne manussā manussaloke yathāṭhitā yathānisinnāva cātumahārājikato paṭṭhāya yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanā sabbe deve tattha tattha attano bhavane kīḷante dibbānubhāvena jotante mahatiṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavante santāni samāpattisukhāni [P 0.0005] anubhavante aññamaññaṃ dhammaṃ sākacchante ca buddhānubhāvena attano maṃsacakkhunāva passanti. Tathā heṭṭhāpathaviyaṃ aṭṭhasu mahānirayesu, soḷasasu ca ussadanirayesu, lokantaraniraye cāti tattha tattha mahādukkhaṃ anubhavamāne satte passanti. Dasasahassilokadhātuyaṃ devā mahaccadevānubhāvena tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā acchariyabbhutacittajātā pañjalikā namassamānā payirupāsanti, buddhaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttā gāthāyo udāharantā thomenti apphoṭenti hasanti pītisomanassaṃ pavedenti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

At that time, it is said, the Blessed One, while performing the Twin Miracle, also performed the Miracle of Revealing the World. While this was happening, humans in the human world, just as they were standing or seated, could see with their own physical eyes, by the Buddha’s power, all the devas from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṭṭha realm, in their respective abodes—playing, shining with divine power, enjoying great divine prosperity, experiencing the tranquil bliss of meditative attainments, and discussing the Dhamma with one another. Likewise, below the earth, in the eight great hells, the sixteen subsidiary hells, and the Lokantara hell, they saw beings experiencing immense suffering. Throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system, devas of great divine power approached the Tathāgata, their minds filled with astonishment and wonder. With hands clasped in reverence, they paid homage and attended upon him. Reciting verses connected with the Buddha’s virtues, they praised him, applauded, laughed, and expressed their joy and gladness. This is what was meant by what was said:

“Bhummā [V 0.0006] mahārājikā tāvatiṃsā, yāmā ca devā tusitā ca nimmitā;

Paranimmitā yepi ca brahmakāyikā, ānanditā vipulamakaṃsu ghosa”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 1.6)

The earth-dwelling devas, the Mahārājikas, the Tāvatiṃsas, the Yāma devas, the Tusitas, and the Nimmitas; the Paranimmitas, and also those of the Brahmā group—rejoicing, they made a mighty sound.

Tadā [M 0.0006] hi dasabalo “atulaṃ attano buddhabalaṃ dassessāmī”ti mahākaruṇāya samussāhito ākāse dasasahassacakkavāḷasamāgame caṅkamaṃ māpetvā, dvādasayojanavitthate sabbaratanamaye caṅkame ṭhito yathāvuttaṃ devamanussanayanavihaṅgānaṃ ekanipātabhūtamacchariyaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ buddhānaṃ samādhiñāṇānubhāvadīpanaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā, puna tasmiṃ caṅkame caṅkamanto veneyyānaṃ ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ acinteyyānubhāvāya anopamāya buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then the Ten-Powered One, roused by great compassion with the thought, 'I will display my incomparable Buddha-power,' manifested a walking path in the sky spanning ten thousand world-systems. Standing on this twelve-yojana-wide walking path made entirely of precious gems, he displayed a miracle that was a wondrous, single focal point for the eyes of devas and humans, unshared by others, and a manifestation of the Buddhas’ power of concentration and knowledge. Then, while walking back and forth on that path, he taught the Dhamma in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained, with the inconceivable power and unparalleled grace of a Buddha. Therefore it is said:

“Na hete jānanti sadevamānusā, buddho ayaṃ kīdisako naruttamo;

Iddhibalaṃ paññābalañca kīdisaṃ, buddhabalaṃ lokahitassa kīdisaṃ.

For they do not know, humans together with devas, what kind of supreme person this Buddha is; of what sort is his psychic power and power of wisdom, of what sort is the Buddha's power for the welfare of the world.

“Na hete jānanti sadevamānusā, buddho ayaṃ edisako naruttamo;

Iddhibalaṃ paññābalañca edisaṃ, buddhabalaṃ lokahitassa edisaṃ.

For they do not know, humans together with devas, that this Buddha, the supreme person, is of such a kind; that his psychic power and power of wisdom are of such a kind; that the Buddha's power for the welfare of the world is of such a kind.

“Handāhaṃ dassayissāmi, buddhabalamanuttaraṃ;

Caṅkamaṃ māpayissāmi, nabhe ratanamaṇḍita”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 1.3-5);

“Come now, I shall display the unsurpassed power of a Buddha; I shall manifest a jewel-adorned walking path in the sky.”

Evaṃ tathāgate attano buddhānubhāvadīpanaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ [P 0.0006] dassetvā dhammaṃ desente āyasmā dhammasenāpati sāriputto rājagahe gijjhakūṭapabbate ṭhito dibbacakkhunā passitvā, tena buddhānubhāvasandassanena acchariyabbhutacittajāto “handāhaṃ bhiyyosomattāya buddhānubhāvaṃ lokassa pākaṭaṃ karissāmī”ti sañjātaparivitakko attano parivārabhūtānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ tamatthaṃ ārocetvā iddhiyā ākāsena tāvadeva āgantvā saparivāro bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalamañjaliṃ sirasi paggayha tathāgatassa mahābhinīhāraṃ pāramiparipūraṇañca pucchi. Bhagavā taṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā tattha sannipatitamanussānañceva dasasahassacakkavāḷadevabrahmānañca attano buddhānubhāvaṃ paridīpayanto buddhavaṃsaṃ desesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Thus, while the Tathāgata was teaching the Dhamma after displaying the miracle that manifests his own Buddha-power, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, standing on the Gijjhakūṭa mountain in Rājagaha, saw this with his divine eye. With a mind struck by wonder and astonishment at this display of the Buddha's power, he informed his retinue of five hundred bhikkhus of the matter. Then, by means of psychic power, he instantly came through the sky with his retinue, approached the Blessed One, and paid homage with the five-point prostration. Raising to his head the añjali gesture, made radiant by the joining of his ten fingernails, he inquired about the Tathāgata’s great aspiration and the fulfillment of the perfections. The Blessed One, making him a direct witness, and illuminating his own Buddha-power for the humans who had assembled there and for the devas and brahmās of the ten thousand world-systems, taught the Buddhavaṃsa. Therefore it is said:

“Sāriputto [M 0.0007][V 0.0007] mahāpañño, samādhijjhānakovido;

Paññāya pāramippatto, pucchati lokanāyakaṃ.

Sāriputta, of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna, having reached the perfection of wisdom, asks the Leader of the World:

“Kīdiso te mahāvīra, abhinīhāro naruttama;

Kamhi kāle tayā dhīra, patthitā bodhimuttamā.

“O Great Hero, supreme among men, what was your aspiration like? At what time, O steadfast one, did you aspire to the highest enlightenment?

“Dānaṃ sīlañca nekkhammaṃ, paññā vīriyañca kīdisaṃ;

Khanti saccamadhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettupekkhā ca kīdisā.

“What were your generosity, virtue, and renunciation like? Your wisdom and energy? What were your patience, truthfulness, and resolve like? Your loving-kindness and equanimity?

“Dasa pāramī tayā dhīra, kīdisī lokanāyaka;

Kathaṃ upapāramī puṇṇā, paramatthapāramī kathaṃ.

“O steadfast one, leader of the world, what were your ten perfections like? How were the intermediate perfections fulfilled, and how the ultimate perfections?”

“Tassa puṭṭho viyākāsi, karavīkamadhuragiro;

Nibbāpayanto hadayaṃ, hāsayanto sadevaka”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 1.74-78);

Being asked, he with a voice as sweet as the karavīka bird's explained, calming the heart and gladdening the world with its devas.

Evaṃ bhagavatā buddhavaṃse desite āyasmā dhammasenāpati “aho buddhānaṃ hetusampadā, aho samudāgamasampatti, aho mahābhinīhārasamijjhanā, dukkaraṃ vata bhagavatā kataṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ evaṃ pāramiyo pūrentena, evaṃvidhassa bodhisambhārasambharaṇassa anucchavikameva cetaṃ phalaṃ, yadidaṃ sabbaññutā balesu ca vasībhāvo evaṃmahiddhikatā evaṃmahānubhāvatā”ti buddhaguṇārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ pesesi. So anaññasādhāraṇaṃ bhagavato sīlaṃ samādhi paññā vimutti vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ hiriottappaṃ [P 0.0007] saddhāvīriyaṃ satisampajaññaṃ sīlavisuddhi diṭṭhivisuddhi samathavipassanā tīṇi kusalamūlāni tīṇi sucaritāni tayo sammāvitakkā tisso anavajjasaññāyo tisso dhātuyo cattāro satipaṭṭhānā cattāro sammappadhānā cattāro iddhipādā cattāro ariyamaggā cattāri ariyaphalāni catasso paṭisambhidā catuyoniparicchedakañāṇāni cattāro ariyavaṃsā cattāri vesārajjañāṇāni pañca padhāniyaṅgāni pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi pañcindriyāni pañca balāni pañca nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo pañca vimuttāyatanañāṇāni pañca vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā cha sāraṇīyā dhammā cha anussatiṭṭhānāni cha gāravā cha nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo cha satatavihārā cha anuttariyāni cha nibbedhabhāgiyā saññā cha abhiññā [M 0.0008] cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni satta aparihāniyā dhammā satta ariyadhanāni satta bojjhaṅgā satta sappurisadhammā satta niddasavatthūni satta saññā satta dakkhiṇeyyapuggaladesanā satta khīṇāsavabaladesanā [V 0.0008] aṭṭha paññāpaṭilābhahetudesanā aṭṭha sammattāni aṭṭha lokadhammātikkamā aṭṭha ārambhavatthūni aṭṭha akkhaṇadesanā aṭṭha mahāpurisavitakkā aṭṭha abhibhāyatanadesanā aṭṭha vimokkhā nava yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā nava pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni nava sattāvāsadesanā nava āghātappaṭivinayā nava paññā nava nānattadesanā nava anupubbavihārā dasa nāthakaraṇā dhammā dasa kasiṇāyatanāni dasa kusalakammapathā dasa sammattāni dasa ariyavāsā dasa asekkhā dhammā dasa ratanāni dasa tathāgatabalāni ekādasa mettānisaṃsā dvādasa dhammacakkākārā terasa dhutaṅgaguṇā cuddasa buddhañāṇāni pañcadasa vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā soḷasavidhā ānāpānassatī soḷasa aparampariyā dhammā aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā ekūnavīsati paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni catucattālīsa ñāṇavatthūni paññāsa udayabbayañāṇāni paropaṇṇāsa kusaladhammā sattasattati ñāṇavatthūni catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasamāpattisañcāritamahāvajirañāṇaṃ anantanayasamantapaṭṭhānapavicayapaccavekkhaṇadesanāñāṇāni tathā anantāsu lokadhātūsu anantānaṃ sattānaṃ āsayādivibhāvanañāṇāni cāti evamādike acinteyyānubhāve buddhaguṇe dhammanvayato anugacchanto anussaranto neva antaṃ, na pamāṇaṃ passi. Thero hi attanopi nāma guṇānaṃ antaṃ vā pamāṇaṃ vā āvajjento na [P 0.0008] passati, so bhagavato guṇānaṃ pamāṇaṃ kiṃ passissati? Yassa yassa hi paññā mahatī ñāṇaṃ visadaṃ, so so buddhaguṇe mahantato saddahati, iti thero bhagavato guṇānaṃ pamāṇaṃ vā paricchedaṃ vā apassanto “mādisassa nāma sāvakapāramiñāṇe ṭhitassa buddhaguṇā ñāṇena paricchindituṃ na sakkā, pageva itaresaṃ. Aho acinteyyā aparimeyyabhedā mahānubhāvā sabbaññuguṇā, kevalaṃ panete ekassa buddhañāṇasseva sabbaso gocarā, nāññesaṃ. Kathetuṃ pana sammāsambuddhehipi vitthārato na sakkāyevā”ti niṭṭhamagamāsi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Thus, when the Blessed One had taught the Buddhavaṃsa, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati reflected: "Ah, the perfection of causes for the Buddhas! Ah, the perfection of accumulation! Ah, the fulfillment of the great aspiration! Truly, the Blessed One has done what is difficult, fulfilling the perfections for such a long time. It is only fitting that such an accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment bears such fruit—namely, omniscience, mastery over the powers, such great might, and such great majesty!" He directed his knowledge toward the qualities of the Buddha. He reflected on the Blessed One’s unparalleled virtues: his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; his conscience and moral dread; his faith, energy, mindfulness, and clear comprehension; his purity of virtue and view; his serenity and insight; the three wholesome roots, the three good conducts, the three right thoughts, the three blameless perceptions, the three elements, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of spiritual power, the four noble paths, the four noble fruits, the four kinds of discrimination, the knowledges discerning the four modes of generation, the four noble lineages, the four kinds of confidence, the five factors for exertion, the five-factored right concentration, the five faculties, the five powers, the five elements of escape, the five spheres of liberation, the five factors for the maturation of liberation, the six principles of cordiality, the six recollections, the six grounds for respect, the six elements of escape, the six constant abodes, the six unsurpassed things, the six perceptions pertaining to penetration, the six super-knowledges, the six kinds of uncommon knowledge, the seven factors of non-decline, the seven noble treasures, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven qualities of a good person, the seven bases for description, the seven perceptions, the teaching on seven persons worthy of gifts, the teaching on the seven powers of one with taints destroyed, the teaching on the eight causes for gaining wisdom, the eight rightnesses, the eight transcendences of worldly conditions, the eight bases for effort, the teaching on the eight inopportune times, the eight thoughts of a great man, the teaching on the eight spheres of mastery, the eight liberations, the nine dhammas rooted in wise attention, the nine factors of exertion for purification, the teaching on the nine abodes of beings, the nine methods for dispelling resentment, the nine kinds of wisdom, the ninefold teaching of diversity, the nine progressive abidings, the ten acts that create protection, the ten kasiṇa spheres, the ten wholesome courses of action, the ten rightnesses, the ten noble abodes, the ten qualities of one beyond training, the ten jewel-like qualities, the ten powers of the Tathāgata, the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, the twelve aspects of the Dhamma-wheel, the thirteen ascetic practices, the fourteen kinds of Buddha-knowledge, the fifteen factors for the maturation of liberation, the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing, the sixteen successive dhammas, the eighteen exclusive qualities of the Buddha, the nineteen knowledges of reviewing, the forty-four bases of knowledge, the fifty knowledges of arising and passing away, the fifty-nine wholesome dhammas, the seventy-seven bases of knowledge, the great diamond-like knowledge pervading twenty-four trillion attainments, the knowledges for teaching, investigating, and reviewing the all-pervading conditional relations with its infinite methods, and the knowledge discerning the inclinations and so forth of infinite beings in infinite world-systems—and so forth. Tracing and recollecting such Buddha-qualities of inconceivable might in accordance with the Dhamma, he saw no end or measure to them. For even the elder himself, reflecting on his own virtues, could not perceive their limit or measure—how much less could he perceive the measure of the Blessed One’s virtues? Whoever possesses great wisdom and clear knowledge, they believe in the greatness of the Buddha’s qualities. Thus, the elder, seeing no measure or limit to the Blessed One’s virtues, concluded: "For one like me, whose knowledge is established in the perfection of a disciple, it is impossible to delimit the Buddha’s virtues by knowledge—how much more so for others? Ah, the inconceivable, immeasurable in their diversity, and majestic qualities of the Omniscient One! Indeed, these are entirely within the scope of a Buddha’s knowledge alone, not others’. Even the perfectly enlightened Buddhas cannot fully describe them in detail." For it has been said:

“Buddhopi [M 0.0009] buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ, kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare, vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.304; 3.141; udā. aṭṭha. 53);

Even a Buddha, praising another Buddha, speaking of nothing else for an entire eon, that eon, in the long, long interval, might come to an end, but the praise of the Tathāgata would never be exhausted.

Evaṃ buddhānaṃ guṇamahantataṃ nissāya uppannabalavapītisomanasso puna cintesi – “evarūpānaṃ nāma buddhaguṇānaṃ hetubhūtā buddhakārakā dhammā pāramiyo aho mahānubhāvā. Katamāsu nu kho jātīsu pāramitā paripācitā, kathaṃ vā paripākaṃ gatā, handāhaṃ imamatthaṃ pucchanto evampi samudāgamato paṭṭhāya buddhānubhāvaṃ imassa sadevakassa lokassa pākaṭataraṃ karissāmī”ti. So evaṃ cintetvā bhagavantaṃ imaṃ pañhaṃ apucchi – “katamāsu nu kho, bhante[V 0.0009], jātīsu ime buddhakārakā dhammā paripācitā, kathaṃ vā paripākaṃ gatā”ti? Athassa bhagavā tasmiṃ ratanacaṅkame tisandhipallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā yugandharapabbate bālasūriyo viya virocamāno nisinno “sāriputta, mayhaṃ buddhakārakā dhammā samādānato paṭṭhāya nirantaraṃ sakkaccakāritāya vīriyūpatthambhena ca sabbesu kappesu bhavato bhavaṃ jātito jātiṃ paripaccantāyeva ahesuṃ, imasmiṃ pana bhaddakappe imāsu jātīsu te paripakkā jātā”ti dassento “kappe ca satasahasse”tiādinā cariyāpiṭakaṃ buddhāpadāniyanti dutiyābhidhānaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ abhāsi. Apare pana “ratanacaṅkame caṅkamanto devātidevo devabrahmādīhi pūjiyamāno nigrodhārāme otaritvā vīsatisahassakhīṇāsavaparivuto [P 0.0009] paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinno bhagavā vuttanayeneva āyasmatā sāriputtena pucchito cariyāpiṭakaṃ desesī”ti vadanti. Ettāvatā dūrenidānaavidūrenidānāni saṅkhepato dassetvā cariyāpiṭakassa santikenidānaṃ vitthārato niddiṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ. Dūrenidānaṃ pana asaṅkhyeyyavibhāvanāyaṃ āvi bhavissatīti.

Thus, on account of the greatness of the Buddha’s virtues, with powerful joy and gladness having arisen, he thought further: “Indeed, the perfections—the qualities that make a Buddha, which are the cause of such Buddha-virtues—are of great power! In which births, pray, were the perfections matured, and how did they reach maturity? Come, I shall ask about this matter, and in this way, starting from this opportune occasion, I will make the Buddha’s power even more manifest to this world with its devas.” Having thought thus, he asked the Blessed One this question: “Venerable sir, in which births, pray, were these Buddha-making qualities matured, and how did they reach maturity?” Then, on that jeweled promenade, the Blessed One, having folded his legs into the three-sectioned posture, sat down, shining like the morning sun on Mount Yugandhara, and said: “Sāriputta, from the time of my undertaking, my Buddha-making qualities—through continuous and respectful practice, and with the support of energy—were ever ripening through all the aeons, from one existence to the next, from one birth to the next. In this fortunate aeon, however, they became mature in these births.” To show this, he delivered the discourse on conduct, the Cariyāpiṭaka, which has the second name Buddhāpadāniya, beginning with the words, “One hundred thousand aeons and…” Others, however, say: “While pacing on the jeweled promenade, the Blessed One, a deva surpassing devas, being worshipped by devas, Brahmās, and others, descended to the Nigrodhārāma, and surrounded by twenty thousand destroyers of the corruptions, sat down on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat. Being asked by the Venerable Sāriputta in the aforementioned way, he taught the Cariyāpiṭaka.” Thus it should be understood that, having shown the distant and non-distant origins in brief, the near origin of the Cariyāpiṭaka is set forth in detail. The distant origin, however, will become manifest in the exposition of the incalculable aeons.

1. Idāni “kappe ca satasahasse”tiādinayappavattāya cariyāpiṭakapāḷiyā atthasaṃvaṇṇanā hoti. Tatrāyaṃ [P 0.0010] kappa-saddo saupasaggo anupasaggo [M 0.0010] ca vitakkavidhānapaṭibhāgapaññattikālaparamāyusamaṇavohārasamantabhāvābhisaddahana- chedanaviniyogavinayakiriyālesantarakappataṇhādiṭṭhiasaṅkhyeyyakappamahākappādīsu dissati. Tathā hesa “nekkhammasaṅkappo abyāpādasaṅkappo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.137) vitakke āgato. “Cīvare vikappaṃ āpajjeyyā”tiādīsu (pārā. 642) vidhāne, adhikavidhānaṃ āpajjeyyāti attho. “Satthukappena vata kira, bho, sāvakena saddhiṃ mantayamānā na jānimhā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.260) paṭibhāge. Satthusadisenāti ayañhi tattha attho. “Idhāyasmā, kappo”tiādīsu (su. ni. 1098) paññattiyaṃ. “Yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) kāle. “Ākaṅkhamāno, ānanda, tathāgato kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.178; udā. 51) paramāyumhi. Āyukappo hi idha kappoti adhippeto. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjitu”ntiādīsu (cūḷava. 250) samaṇavohāre. “Kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ obhāsetvā”tiādīsu (khu. pā. 5.1; su. ni. maṅgalasutta) samantabhāve. “Saddhā saddahanā okappanā abhippasādo”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 12) abhisaddahane, saddhāyanti attho. “Alaṅkato kappitakesamassū”tiādīsu (vi. va. 1094; jā. 2.22.1368) chedane. “Evameva ito dinnaṃ, petānaṃ upakappatī”tiādīsu (khu. pā. 7.7; pe. va. 20) viniyoge. “Kappakatena akappakataṃ saṃsibbitaṃ [V 0.0010] hotī”tiādīsu (pāci. 371) vinayakiriyāyaṃ. “Atthi kappo nipajjituṃ, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”tiādīsu lese. “Āpāyiko nerayiko kappaṭṭho saṅghabhedako…pe… kappaṃ nirayamhi paccatī”ti (itivu. 18; cūḷava. 354; kathā. 657, 862) ca ādīsu antarakappe.

1. Now begins the commentary on the meaning of the Cariyāpiṭaka Pāḷi, which proceeds according to the method beginning, “And in a hundred thousand aeons…” Therein, this word “kappa,” both with and without a prefix, is seen in various senses, such as: thought, arrangement, likeness, designation, time, life-span, monastic usage, entirety, conviction, cutting, application, a Vinaya procedure, pretext, intermediate aeon, craving, views, incalculable aeon, and great aeon. For instance, it appears in the sense of thought in passages such as: “the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will.” It appears in the sense of arrangement in passages such as: “He should make a determination (vikappa) regarding a robe,” the meaning being that he should make a special arrangement. It appears in the sense of likeness in passages such as: “Sirs, it seems that while conversing with a disciple who is like the Teacher, we did not know.” For the meaning there is “similar to the Teacher.” It appears in the sense of designation in passages such as: “Here, Venerable Kappa.” It appears in the sense of time in passages such as: “where I constantly dwell.” It appears in the sense of life-span in passages such as: “Ānanda, if he so wished, the Tathāgata could remain for an aeon or for the remainder of an aeon.” For here “kappa” is intended to mean the life-aeon. It appears in the sense of monastic usage in passages such as: “Monks, I allow you to partake of fruit according to the five monastic proprieties.” It appears in the sense of entirety in passages such as: “illuminating the entire Jetavana.” It appears in the sense of conviction in passages such as: “faith, believing, commitment, confidence,” the meaning being “by faith.” It appears in the sense of cutting in passages such as: “adorned, with hair and beard cut.” It appears in the sense of application in passages such as: “In the same way, what is given from here is of benefit to the departed.” It appears in the sense of a Vinaya procedure in passages such as: “An unallowable cloth is sewn together with an allowable one.” It appears in the sense of pretext in passages such as: “There is a pretext for lying down; come, I shall lie down.” And it appears in the sense of intermediate aeon in passages such as: “A schismatic goes to the plane of misery, to hell, for an aeon… he is tormented in hell for an aeon.”

“Na kappayanti na purekkharonti, dhammāpi tesaṃ na paṭicchitāse;

Na [P 0.0011] brāhmaṇo sīlavatena neyyo, pāraṅgato na pacceti tādī”ti. –

“They form no concepts, they put nothing forward; no doctrines are adopted by them. A brahmin is not led by virtue and observances; such a one, having gone to the far shore, does not return.”

Ādīsu (su. ni. 809) taṇhādiṭṭhīsu. Tathā hi vuttaṃ niddese “kappāti uddānato dve kappā taṇhākappo diṭṭhikappo”ti (mahāni. 28). “Anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe”tiādīsu [M 0.0011] (dī. ni. 1.244; ma. ni. 1.68) asaṅkhyeyyakappe. “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, kappassa asaṅkhyeyyānī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.156) mahākappe. Idhāpi mahākappeyeva daṭṭhabbo (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.29; 3.275; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.1; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.128; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 5.evamiccādipāṭhavaṇṇanā).

It appears in the sense of craving and views in passages such as the preceding one. For thus it is said in the Niddesa: “‘Kappa,’ in summary, is of two kinds: the kappa of craving and the kappa of views.” It appears in the sense of an incalculable aeon in passages such as: “in many an aeon of contraction, in many an aeon of expansion.” It appears in the sense of a great aeon in passages such as: “Monks, there are these four incalculable periods of an aeon.” Here too, in the present context, it should be understood as a great aeon.

Tatrāyaṃ padasiddhi – kappīyatīti kappo, ettakāni vassānīti vā ettakāni vassasatānīti vā ettakāni vassasahassānīti vā ettakāni vassasatasahassānīti vā saṃvaccharavasena gaṇetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā kevalaṃ sāsaparāsiupamādīhi kappetabbo parikappetabbaparimāṇoti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

The derivation of the word is as follows: it is called a ‘kappa’ because it is reckoned (kappīyati). The meaning is that, because it is impossible to count in terms of years—as so many years, so many hundreds of years, so many thousands of years, or so many hundreds of thousands of years—it is a measure that can only be reckoned or calculated by means of similes, such as that of the heap of mustard seeds. For it has been said:

“Kīva dīgho nu kho, bhante, kappoti? Dīgho kho, bhikkhu, kappo, so na sukaro saṅkhātuṃ ‘ettakāni vassānī’ti vā ‘ettakāni vassasatānī’ti vā ‘ettakāni vassasahassānī’ti vā ‘ettakāni vassasatasahassānī’ti vā. Sakkā pana, bhante, upamaṃ kātunti? ‘Sakkā, bhikkhū’ti bhagavā avoca. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhu, yojanaṃ āyāmena yojanaṃ vitthārena yojanaṃ ubbedhena mahāsāsaparāsi. Tato vassasatassa vassasahassassa accayena ekamekaṃ sāsapaṃ uddhareyya, khippataraṃ kho so, bhikkhu, mahāsāsaparāsi iminā upakkamena parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyya, na tveva kappo, evaṃ dīgho kho, bhikkhu, kappo”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.128).

'How long, venerable sir, is an aeon?' 'Long, monk, is an aeon. It is not easy to calculate it as “so many years,” or “so many hundreds of years,” or “so many thousands of years,” or “so many hundreds of thousands of years.” But, venerable sir, is it possible to make a simile?' 'It is possible, monk,' the Blessed One said. 'Suppose, monk, there were a great heap of mustard seeds, one yojana in length, one yojana in width, and one yojana in height. From there, at the passing of every hundred years, one were to remove a single mustard seed. That great heap of mustard seeds, monk, would more quickly be exhausted and consumed by this endeavor, but not so the aeon. So long, monk, is an aeon'" (Saṃ. Ni. 2.128).

Svāyaṃ [V 0.0011] mahākappo saṃvaṭṭādivasena catuasaṅkhyeyyakappasaṅgaho. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

This great aeon is a collection of four incalculable aeons, by way of contraction and so forth. And this has been said:

“Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, kappassa asaṅkhyeyyāni. Katamāni cattāri? Saṃvaṭṭo, saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī, vivaṭṭo, vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī”ti (a. ni. 4.156).

"Monks, there are these four incalculable periods of an aeon. Which four? The contraction, the remaining contracted, the expansion, the remaining expanded" (A. Ni. 4.156).

Tattha tayo saṃvaṭṭā – tejosaṃvaṭṭo, āposaṃvaṭṭo, vāyosaṃvaṭṭoti. Tisso saṃvaṭṭasīmā – ābhassarā, subhakiṇhā, vehapphalāti. Yadā hi kappo tejena saṃvaṭṭati, ābhassarato heṭṭhā agginā ḍayhati. Yadā āpena saṃvaṭṭati, subhakiṇhato heṭṭhā udakena vilīyati. Yadā vāyunā saṃvaṭṭati, vehapphalato heṭṭhā vātena viddhaṃsati. Vitthārato pana koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaṃ vinassati, yaṃ buddhānaṃ [M 0.0012] āṇākkhettanti vuccati. Tesu tīsu saṃvaṭṭesu yathākkamaṃ kappavināsakamahāmeghato yāva jālāya vā udakassa vā vātassa vā upacchedo idaṃ ekaṃ [P 0.0012] asaṅkhyeyyaṃ saṃvaṭṭo nāma. Kappavināsakajālādipacchedato yāva koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaparipūrako sampattimahāmegho uṭṭhahati, idaṃ dutiyaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī nāma.

Herein, there are three kinds of contraction: contraction by fire, contraction by water, and contraction by wind. There are three limits of contraction: the Ābhassara realm, the Subhakiṇha realm, and the Vehapphala realm. For when the aeon contracts by fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is burned by fire. When it contracts by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water. When it contracts by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is destroyed by wind. In detail, a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems are destroyed, which is called the sphere of authority of the Buddhas. Among these three contractions, in sequence: from the great cloud that destroys the aeon up to the cessation of the flame, or the water, or the wind—this is one incalculable period, named 'contraction' (saṃvaṭṭa). From the cessation of the aeon-destroying flame and so forth up to the arising of the great cloud of accomplishment that fills a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems—this is the second incalculable period, named 'remaining contracted' (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī).

Sampattimahāmeghato yāva candimasūriyapātubhāvo, idaṃ tatiyaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ vivaṭṭo nāma. Candimasūriyapātubhāvato yāva puna kappavināsakamahāmegho, idaṃ catutthaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī nāma. Imesu catusaṭṭhiantarakappasaṅgahaṃ vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī. Tena samānakālaparicchedā vivaṭṭādayo veditabbā. “Vīsatiantarakappasaṅgaha”nti eke. Iti imāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni eko mahākappo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “svāyaṃ mahākappo saṃvaṭṭādivasena catuasaṅkhyeyyakappasaṅgaho”ti.

From the great cloud of accomplishment up to the appearance of the moon and sun, this is the third incalculable period, named 'expansion' (vivaṭṭa). From the appearance of the moon and sun up to when the great cloud that destroys the aeon arises again, this is the fourth incalculable period, named 'remaining expanded' (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī). The period of remaining expanded comprises sixty-four intermediate aeons. The expansion period and the others should be understood to have a duration equal to that. Some say, 'It is a collection of twenty intermediate aeons.' Thus, these four incalculable periods constitute one great aeon. Therefore it was said: 'This great aeon, by way of contraction and so forth, is a collection of four incalculable aeons.'

Kappeti ca accantasaṃyogavasena upayogabahuvacanaṃ. Satasahasseti kappasaddasambandhena cāyaṃ pulliṅganiddeso, idhāpi accantasaṃyogavaseneva bahuvacanaṃ. Samānādhikaraṇañhetaṃ padadvayaṃ. Caturo ca asaṅkhiyeti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kassa pana asaṅkhiyeti aññassa avuttattā kappassa ca vuttattā pakaraṇato kappānanti ayamattho viññāyateva. Na hi vuttaṃ vajjetvā avuttassa kassaci gahaṇaṃ yuttanti. Ca-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, mahākappānaṃ caturo asaṅkhyeyye satasahasse ca mahākappeti ayañhettha attho. Asaṅkhiyeti ettha saṅkhātuṃ na sakkāti asaṅkhiyā, gaṇanaṃ atikkantāti attho. “Asaṅkhyeyyanti eko gaṇanaviseso”ti eke. Te hi ekato paṭṭhāya mahābalakkhapariyosānāni ekūnasaṭṭhiṭṭhānāni vajjetvā dasamahābalakkhāni asaṅkhyeyyaṃ nāma, saṭṭhimaṭṭhānantaranti vadanti. Taṃ na yujjati, saṅkhyāṭhānantaraṃ nāma gaṇanaviseso, tassa asaṅkhyeyyabhāvābhāvato [V 0.0012] ekaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ asaṅkhyeyyañcāti viruddhametaṃ. Nanu ca asaṅkhyabhāvena asaṅkhyeyyattepi tassa catubbidhabhāvo na yujjatīti? No na yujjati. Catūsu ṭhānesu asaṅkhyeyyabhāvassa icchitattā. Tatrāyamādito paṭṭhāya vibhāvanā –

And in the word `kappe`, the plural is a plural of usage in the sense of continuous connection. In `satasahasse`, this is a masculine designation due to its connection with the word `kappa`, and here too the plural is used in the sense of continuous connection. These two words are in apposition. In `caturo ca asaṅkhiye`, the same method applies. But whose incalculables? Since nothing else is mentioned, and 'aeon' is mentioned, from the context the meaning 'of the aeons' is indeed understood. For it is not proper to take what is unstated while rejecting what is stated. The word `ca` has the meaning of combination: 'four incalculables of great aeons and a hundred thousand great aeons'—this is the meaning here. In `asaṅkhiya`, it means 'what cannot be counted'; the meaning is 'gone beyond calculation.' Some say: '“Incalculable” is a specific number.' They hold that starting from one, having excluded the fifty-nine places ending with the great balakkha, the ten great balakkhas are called 'incalculable,' and they call this the sixtieth place-interval. This is not correct. A numerical place-interval is a specific number; since it lacks the state of being incalculable, it is a contradiction for one place-interval to be a specific number and also incalculable. But surely, even if it is incalculable due to its uncountability, is its fourfold nature not unfitting? No, it is not unfitting. This is because the state of being incalculable is intended in four instances. Herein, this is the detailed explanation from the beginning:

Atīte kira ekasmiṃ kappe taṇhaṅkaro medhaṅkaro saraṇaṅkaro [P 0.0013] dīpaṅkaroti cattāro sammāsambuddhā anukkamena loke uppajjiṃsu. Tesu dīpaṅkarassa bhagavato kāle amaravatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi. Tattha [M 0.0013] sumedho nāma brāhmaṇo paṭivasati ubhato sujāto mātito ca pitito ca, saṃsuddhagahaṇiko yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā akkhitto anupakkuṭṭho jātivādena, abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato. So aññaṃ kammaṃ akatvā brāhmaṇasippameva uggaṇhi. Tassa daharakāleyeva mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. Athassa rāsivaḍḍhako amacco āyapotthakaṃ āharitvā suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādibharite sāragabbhe vivaritvā “ettakaṃ te, kumāra, mātusantakaṃ, ettakaṃ te pitusantakaṃ, ettakaṃ te ayyakapayyakāna”nti yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā dhanaṃ ācikkhitvā “etaṃ dhanaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti āha. Sumedhapaṇḍito cintesi – “imaṃ evaṃ bahuṃ dhanaṃ saṃharitvā mayhaṃ mātāpitādayo paralokaṃ gacchantā ekakahāpaṇampi gahetvā na gatā, mayā pana gahetvā gamanakāraṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So rañño ārocetvā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā mahājanassa dānaṃ datvā himavantappadesaṃ gantvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā sattāheneva aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattetvā samāpattivihārehi viharati.

In a past aeon, it is said that four Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas arose in the world in succession: Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara. Among them, during the time of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, there was a city named Amaravatī. There lived a brahmin named Sumedha, well-born on both his mother’s and father’s sides, of pure descent, unbroken and unblemished in lineage up to the seventh generation, handsome, pleasing to behold, gracious, and endowed with the highest perfection of beauty. Without engaging in any other work, he mastered only the brahminical arts. While he was still young, his parents passed away. Then, his steward brought the account book and, opening the treasury filled with gold, silver, gems, pearls, and other valuables, declared, “Young man, this much is your mother’s inheritance, this much your father’s, and this much belongs to your ancestors,” revealing wealth up to the seventh generation. He then instructed, “Manage this wealth.” The wise Sumedha reflected, “Though my parents and ancestors accumulated so much wealth, they departed for the next world without taking even a single coin. It is fitting, however, that I should find a way to take it with me when I go.” Having informed the king, he had a drum proclaimed throughout the city, gave his great wealth in alms to the people, and then went to the Himalayan region. There, he embraced the ascetic life and, within seven days, attained the eight meditative absorptions and the five higher knowledges. He dwelt there, abiding in the meditative attainments.

Tasmiñca kāle dīpaṅkaradasabalo paramābhisambodhiṃ patvā pavattitavaradhammacakko catūhi khīṇāsavasatasahassehi parivuto anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno rammavatīnagaraṃ nāma patvā tassa avidūre sudassanamahāvihāre paṭivasati. Rammavatīnagaravāsino “satthā kira amhākaṃ nagaraṃ patvā sudassanamahāvihāre paṭivasatī”ti sutvā gandhamālādihatthā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā ekamantaṃ nisinnā dhammadesanaṃ sutvā svātanāya nimantetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṃsu. Te punadivase mahādānaṃ sajjetvā nagaraṃ alaṅkaritvā dasabalassa āgamanamaggaṃ haṭṭhatuṭṭhā sodhenti.

At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, having attained supreme complete enlightenment and set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, was surrounded by four hundred thousand destroyers of the taints. Traveling gradually, he arrived at the city named Rammavatī and dwelled in the Sudassana Great Monastery not far from it. The citizens of Rammavatī, having heard, "The Teacher, it is said, has arrived in our city and is staying at the Sudassana Great Monastery," taking perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and honored him with perfumes, garlands, and the like. Sitting to one side, they listened to the Dhamma discourse, and inviting him for the next day's meal, they rose from their seats and departed. The next day, they prepared a great offering, adorned the city, and with joy and delight, cleared the path for the arrival of the Ten-Powered One.

Tasmiñca kāle sumedhatāpaso ākāsena gacchanto [P 0.0014] te haṭṭhatuṭṭhe manusse disvā “ambho, kassa tumhe imaṃ maggaṃ sodhethā”ti pucchi? Tehi “sammāsambuddhassa āgamanamaggaṃ sodhemā”ti vutte atītesu buddhesu katādhikārattā “buddho”ti vacanaṃ sutvā uppannapītisomanasso [V 0.0013] tāvadeva ākāsato oruyha “mayhampi okāsaṃ detha, ahampi sodhessāmī”ti [M 0.0014] tehi dassitaṃ okāsaṃ “kiñcāpi ahaṃ imaṃ iddhiyā sattaratanavicittaṃ katvā alaṅkarituṃ pahomi, ajja pana mayā kāyaveyyāvaccaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, kāyārahaṃ puññaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā tiṇakacavarādayo nīharitvā paṃsuṃ āharitvā samaṃ karonto sodheti. Aniṭṭhiteyeva pana tassa padesassa sodhane dīpaṅkaro bhagavā mahānubhāvānaṃ chaḷabhiññānaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ catūhi satasahassehi parivuto taṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji. Sumedhapaṇḍito “sammāsambuddho buddhasāvakā ca mā cikkhallaṃ akkamantū”ti attano vākacīrañca cammakhaṇḍañca jaṭākalāpañca pasāretvā sayañca yena bhagavā tena sīsaṃ katvā avakujjo nipajji. Evañca cintesi – “sacāhaṃ icchissāmi, imassa bhagavato sāvako hutvā ajjeva kilese ghātessāmi. Kiṃ mayhaṃ ekakeneva saṃsāramahoghato nittharaṇena? Yaṃnūnāhampi evarūpo sammāsambuddho hutvā sadevakaṃ lokaṃ saṃsāramahaṇṇavato tāreyya”nti. Iti so aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatamahābhinīhāravasena cittaṃ paṇidhesi. Atha bhagavā āgantvā tassa ussīsake ṭhatvā cittācāraṃ samijjhanabhāvañcassa ñatvā “ayaṃ ito kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake gotamo nāma sammāsambuddho bhavissatī”ti sabbaṃ imaṃ bhagavato pavattiṃ byākaritvā pakkāmi.

At that time, the ascetic Sumedha, traveling through the sky, saw those joyful and delighted people and asked, “Sirs, for whom are you clearing this path?” When they replied, “We are clearing the path for the arrival of the Perfectly Enlightened One,” he—due to his aspirations made under previous Buddhas—felt a surge of joy and happiness upon hearing the word “Buddha.” Immediately descending from the sky, he said, “Grant me a section too; I also will help clear the path.” When they had shown him a section, he thought, “Though I could use my psychic powers to adorn this place, making it resplendent with the seven kinds of jewels, today it is fitting for me to perform this service with my own body and earn merit thereby.” So, he removed grass, trash, and debris, brought soil, leveled the ground, and began clearing the path. While the clearing of his section was still unfinished, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara approached that path, surrounded by four hundred thousand destroyers of the taints, who were of great power and possessors of the six higher knowledges. The wise Sumedha thought, “Let not the Perfectly Enlightened One and his disciples tread on the mud,” and so he spread out his bark garment, his deerskin hide, and his matted locks, then lay face-down with his head toward the Blessed One, making a bridge of his body. He reflected thus: “If I wished, I could become a disciple of this Blessed One and destroy my defilements this very day. But what use is it for me alone to cross the great flood of saṃsāra? Surely, I should become a Perfectly Enlightened One just like him and ferry the world with its devas across the great ocean of saṃsāra.” Thus, by means of the great aspiration endowed with eight factors, he made his resolve. Then the Blessed One, arriving, stood at his head and, knowing the state of his mind and the certainty of his aspiration's fulfillment, declared, “This one, after four incalculable ages and a hundred thousand aeons from now, will become a Perfectly Enlightened One by the name of Gotama.” Having made this full prediction concerning the future Blessed One, he departed.

Tato aparepi koṇḍaññabhagavantaṃ ādiṃ katvā anukkamena uppannā yāva kassapadasabalapariyosānā sammāsambuddhā mahāsattaṃ “buddho bhavissatī”ti byākariṃsu. Iti amhākaṃ bodhisattassa pāramiyo pūrentasseva catuvīsati sammāsambuddhā uppannā. Yasmiṃ pana kappe dīpaṅkaradasabalo udapādi, tasmiṃ aññepi tayo buddhā ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ santike bodhisattassa byākaraṇaṃ nāhosi, tasmā te idha [P 0.0015] na gahitā. Porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tamhā kappā paṭṭhāya sabbabuddhe dassetuṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ –

Thereafter, other Perfectly Enlightened Ones who arose in succession, beginning with the Blessed One Koṇḍañña and ending with Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One, also prophesied to the Great Being, 'He will become a Buddha.' Thus, while our Bodhisatta was fulfilling his perfections, twenty-four Perfectly Enlightened Ones arose. Now, in the aeon in which Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, arose, there were also three other Buddhas. From them, the Bodhisatta did not receive a prophecy; therefore, they are not included here. However, in the ancient commentary, in order to show all the Buddhas from that aeon onwards, the following was said:

“Taṇhaṅkaro medhaṅkaro, athopi saraṇaṅkaro;

Dīpaṅkaro ca sambuddho, koṇḍañño dvipaduttamo.

Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, and also Saraṇaṅkara; Dīpaṅkara, the Enlightened One, and Koṇḍañña, the foremost of bipeds.

“Maṅgalo ca sumano ca, revato sobhito muni;

Anomadassī padumo, nārado padumuttaro.

Maṅgala and Sumana, Revata and Sobhita the Sage; Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, and Padumuttara.

“Sumedho [M 0.0015][V 0.0014] ca sujāto ca, piyadassī mahāyaso;

Atthadassī dhammadassī, siddhattho lokanāyako.

Sumedha and Sujāta, Piyadassī of great renown; Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, and Siddhattha, the leader of the world.

“Tisso phusso ca sambuddho, vipassī sikhi vessabhū;

Kakusandho koṇāgamano, kassapo cāpi nāyako.

Tissa and Phussa, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones; Vipassī, Sikhī, and Vessabhū; Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and also Kassapa, the Leader.

“Ete ahesuṃ sambuddhā, vītarāgā samāhitā;

Sataraṃsīva uppannā, mahātamavinodanā;

Jalitvā aggikkhandhāva, nibbutā te sasāvakā”ti. (jā. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā);

These were Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, free from passion and well-concentrated; arisen like the sun, they dispelled great darkness; having blazed like a mass of fire, they, with their disciples, attained final Nibbāna.

Tattha dīpaṅkaradasabalassa ca koṇḍaññadasabalassa ca antare mahākappānaṃ ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ buddhasuñño loko ahosi, tathā bhagavato koṇḍaññassa ca bhagavato maṅgalassa ca antare, tathā bhagavato sobhitassa ca bhagavato anomadassissa ca antare, tathā bhagavato nāradassa ca bhagavato padumuttarassa ca antare. Vuttañhetaṃ buddhavaṃse (bu. vaṃ. 28.3, 4, 6, 9) –

Therein, in the interval between Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, and Koṇḍañña, the Ten-Powered One, the world was void of Buddhas for one incalculable great aeon. Likewise, in the interval between the Blessed One Koṇḍañña and the Blessed One Maṅgala; likewise, in the interval between the Blessed One Sobhita and the Blessed One Anomadassī; and likewise, in the interval between the Blessed One Nārada and the Blessed One Padumuttara. For this has been stated in the Buddhavaṃsa:

“Dīpaṅkarassa bhagavato, koṇḍaññassa ca satthuno;

Etesaṃ antarā kappā, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyā.

Between the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara and the Teacher Koṇḍañña, the intervening aeons are incalculable by counting.

“Koṇḍaññassa aparena, maṅgalo nāma nāyako;

Tesampi antarā kappā, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyā.

After Koṇḍañña, there was a leader named Maṅgala; the aeons between them too were incalculable by counting.

“Sobhitassa aparena, anomadassī mahāyaso;

Tesampi antarā kappā, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyā.

After Sobhita, there was Anomadassī of great renown; the aeons between them too were incalculable by counting.

“Nāradassa bhagavato, padumuttarassa satthuno;

Tesampi antarā kappā, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyā”ti.

Between the Blessed One Nārada and the Teacher Padumuttara, the intervening aeons are incalculable by counting.

Evaṃ gaṇanātītatāya asaṅkhyeyyattepi catūsu ṭhānesu mahākappānaṃ gaṇanātikkamena “caturo ca asaṅkhiye”ti vuttaṃ, na saṅkhyāvisesenāti veditabbaṃ. Yasmā pana padumuttaradasabalassa ca sumedhadasabalassa ca antare tiṃsakappasahassāni, sujātadasabalassa ca piyadassīdasabalassa ca antare navasahassādhikānaṃ kappānaṃ saṭṭhisahassāni dvāsītuttarāni aṭṭha ca [V 0.0015] satāni, dhammadassīdasabalassa ca siddhatthadasabalassa ca antare vīsati kappā, siddhatthadasabalassa [P 0.0016] ca tissadasabalassa ca antare eko kappo[M 0.0016], bhagavato vipassissa ca bhagavato sikhissa ca antare saṭṭhi kappā, bhagavato ca vessabhussa bhagavato ca kakusandhassa antare tiṃsa kappā, iti padumuttaradasabalassa uppannakappato paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā tesaṃ tesaṃ buddhānaṃ uppannakappehi iminā ca bhaddakappena saddhiṃ satasahassamahākappā. Te sandhāya vuttaṃ “kappe ca satasahasse”ti. Imasmiṃ panatthe vitthāriyamāne sabbaṃ buddhavaṃsapāḷiṃ āharitvā saṃvaṇṇetabbaṃ hotīti ativitthārabhīrukassa mahājanassa cittaṃ anurakkhantā na vitthārayimha. Atthikehi buddhavaṃsato (bu. vaṃ. 1.1 ādayo) gahetabbo. Yopi cettha vattabbo kathāmaggo, sopi aṭṭhasāliniyā (dha. sa. aṭṭha. sumedhakathā) dhammasaṅgahavaṇṇanāya jātakaṭṭhakathāya (jā. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā) ca vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Thus, although they are incalculable because they are beyond counting, in four instances it is said 'four incalculables' due to the exceeding of the count of great aeons, and not as a specific number—this should be understood. Moreover, between the Ten-Powered One Padumuttara and the Ten-Powered One Sumedha, there were thirty thousand aeons. Between the Ten-Powered One Sujāta and the Ten-Powered One Piyadassī, there were sixty-nine thousand, eight hundred and eighty-two aeons. Between the Ten-Powered One Dhammadassī and the Ten-Powered One Siddhattha, there were twenty aeons. Between the Ten-Powered One Siddhattha and the Ten-Powered One Tissa, there was one aeon. Between the Blessed One Vipassī and the Blessed One Sikhī, there were sixty aeons. Between the Blessed One Vessabhū and the Blessed One Kakusandha, there were thirty aeons. Thus, from the aeon in which the Ten-Powered One Padumuttara arose, downwards, together with the aeons in which each of those Buddhas arose and with this Fortunate Aeon, there are one hundred thousand great aeons. It is in reference to these that it was said, 'and in one hundred thousand aeons.' If this matter were to be elaborated, the entire Buddhavaṃsa text would have to be brought forth and explained; but, out of concern for the minds of the great multitude who fear excessive detail, we have not elaborated. Those who are interested should ascertain this from the Buddhavaṃsa. Whatever expositional approach is stated herein should also be understood according to the method described in the Aṭṭhasālinī, the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, and in the Jātaka Commentary.

Etthantareti ettha antarasaddo –

Herein, regarding the phrase `etthantare`, the word `antara` is used as follows:

“Nadītīresu saṇṭhāne, sabhāsu rathiyāsu ca;

Janā saṅgamma mantenti, mañca tañca kimantara”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.228) –

On riverbanks, in public places, in assemblies, and on streets, people gather and discuss, 'What is this matter concerning me and you?'

Ādīsu kāraṇe āgato. “Addasā kho maṃ, bhante, aññatarā itthī vijjantarikāya bhājanaṃ dhovantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.149) khaṇe, vijjuniccharaṇakkhaṇeti attho. “Yassantarato na santi kopā”tiādīsu (udā. 20) citte. “Antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhi”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.285; mahāva. 11) vivare. “Na upajjhāyassa bhaṇamānassa antarantarā kathā opātetabbā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 66) vemajjhe. Idhāpi vemajjheyeva daṭṭhabbo (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.36), tasmā etasmiṃ antare vemajjheti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmiṃ mahākappe amhākaṃ bhagavā sumedhapaṇḍito hutvā dīpaṅkarassa bhagavato pādamūle –

In the preceding example and others, it appears in the sense of 'cause'. In such cases as, 'Indeed, venerable sir, a certain woman saw me washing a vessel during a flash of lightning' (Majjhima Nikāya 2.149), it appears in the sense of 'moment'; the meaning is 'the moment of the lightning flash'. In such cases as, 'For whom there are no angers from within' (Udāna 20), it appears in the sense of 'mind'. In such cases as, 'Between Gayā and the Bodhi tree' (Vinaya Mahāvagga 1.21.1), it appears in the sense of 'interval'. In such cases as, 'While the preceptor is speaking, one should not interject with speech in between' (Vinaya Mahāvagga 1.25.16), it appears in the sense of 'in the middle'. Here too, in the present context, it should be understood as 'in the middle'. Therefore, the meaning of `etasmiṃ antare` is 'in this interval'. This is what is meant: In that great aeon when our Blessed One, having become the wise Sumedha, at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara—

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59) –

Human existence, perfection of gender, the cause, seeing the Teacher; the going forth, accomplishment in special qualities, a sufficient foundation, and strong desire.

Evaṃ [V 0.0016] vuttehi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ mahābhinīhāraṃ akāsi, samattiṃsa pāramiyo pavicini samādiyi, sabbepi buddhakārake dhamme sampādetuṃ [M 0.0017] ārabhi, yamhi cetasmiṃ bhaddakappe sabbaso pūritapāramī hutvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhi. Imesaṃ dvinnaṃ mahākappānaṃ antare yathāvuttaparicchede kālaviseseti. Kathaṃ [P 0.0017] panetaṃ viññāyatīti? “Kappe ca satasahasse, caturo ca asaṅkhiye”ti idañhi mahākappānaṃ paricchedato aparicchedato ca saṅkhyādassanaṃ. Sā kho panāyaṃ saṅkhyā saṅkhyeyyassa ādipariyosānaggahaṇaṃ vinā na sambhavatīti yattha bodhisambhārānamārambho yattha ca te pariyositā tadubhayampi avadhibhāvena “etthantare”ti ettha atthato dassitanti viññāyati. Avadhi ca panāyaṃ abhividhivasena veditabbo, na mariyādāvasena, ārambhosānakappānaṃ ekadesena antogadhattā. Nanu ca nippadesena tesaṃ apariyādānato abhividhi ca idha na sambhavatīti? Na idamevaṃ tadekadesepi tabbohārato. Yo hi tadekadesabhūto kappo, so nippadesato pariyādinnoti.

Thus endowed with the eight qualities spoken of, he made the great aspiration, discerned and undertook the thirty perfections, and began to accomplish all the qualities that make one a Buddha. In that auspicious aeon, having completely fulfilled the perfections, he awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. This specifies the particular time within the interval of these two great aeons, according to the aforesaid definition. But how is this to be understood? It is understood by the passage: 'A hundred thousand aeons and four incalculables.' This indeed shows the calculation of the great aeons both as defined and undefined. This calculation, however, is not possible without grasping the beginning and end of what is to be counted. Thus it is understood that both the commencement of the requisites for enlightenment and their completion are shown in meaning here as boundaries by the phrase 'within this interval.' Moreover, this boundary should be understood as an inclusive limit, not an exclusive one, because the aeons of the beginning and the end are included by a portion. But surely, since they are not completely encompassed, an inclusive limit is not possible here? It is not so, because that designation is applied even to a part of one of them. For that aeon which constitutes a part of one of them is completely encompassed.

Yaṃ caritaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ bodhipācananti ettha caritanti cariyā, samattiṃsapāramisaṅgahā dānasīlādipaṭipatti, ñātatthacariyālokatthacariyābuddhatthacariyānaṃ tadantogadhattā. Tathā yā cimā aṭṭha cariyā, seyyathidaṃ – paṇidhisampannānaṃ catūsu iriyāpathesu iriyāpathacariyā, indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ ajjhattikāyatanesu āyatanacariyā, appamādavihārīnaṃ catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu saticariyā, adhicittamanuyuttānaṃ catūsu jhānesu samādhicariyā, buddhisampannānaṃ catūsu ariyasaccesu ñāṇacariyā, sammā paṭipannānaṃ catūsu ariyamaggesu maggacariyā, adhigataphalānaṃ catūsu sāmaññaphalesu patticariyā, tiṇṇaṃ buddhānaṃ sabbasattesu lokatthacariyāti. Tattha padesato dvinnaṃ bodhisattānaṃ paccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānañca lokatthacariyā, mahābodhisattānaṃ pana sammāsambuddhānañca nippadesato. Vuttañhetaṃ niddese (cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 121; paṭi. ma. 1.197) “cariyāti aṭṭha cariyāyo iriyāpathacariyā āyatanacariyā”ti vitthāro. “Adhimuccanto saddhāya carati, paggaṇhanto vīriyena carati, upaṭṭhahanto satiyā carati, avikkhipanto samādhinā carati, pajānanto paññāya carati, vijānanto viññāṇena carati, evampi paṭipannassa kusalā dhammā āyatantīti āyatanacariyāya carati, evampi paṭipanno visesamadhigacchatīti visesacariyāya caratī”ti yā [M 0.0018] imā aparāpi aṭṭha cariyā vuttā, tāsaṃ sabbāsaṃ pāramitāsveva samorodho veditabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “caritanti cariyā, samattiṃsapāramisaṅgahā [P 0.0018] dānasīlādipaṭipattī”ti. Hetucariyāya eva pana idhādhippetattā maggacariyāpatticariyānaṃ idha anavarodho veditabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbaṃ taṃ bodhipācana”nti.

Whatever the conduct, all of it is conducive to enlightenment. Here, 'conduct' means practice, which is the practice of giving, virtue, and so on, as included in the thirty perfections, because the conduct for the welfare of kinsmen, the conduct for the welfare of the world, and the conduct for the welfare of Buddhahood are included therein. Likewise, there are these eight kinds of conduct. That is to say: for those accomplished in aspiration, the conduct of deportment in the four postures; for those with guarded doors in the internal sense bases, the conduct of the sense bases; for those dwelling in heedfulness, the conduct of mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness; for those devoted to the higher mind, the conduct of concentration in the four jhānas; for those endowed with wisdom, the conduct of knowledge in the four noble truths; for those practicing rightly, the conduct of the path in the four noble paths; for those who have attained the fruit, the conduct of attainment in the four fruits of recluseship; for the three types of Buddhas, the conduct for the welfare of the world towards all beings. Among these, the conduct for the welfare of the world is partial for the two kinds of bodhisattas—paccekabuddhas and disciples of a Buddha—but it is complete for great bodhisattas and perfectly self-enlightened Buddhas. This is stated in the Niddesa: '“Practice” means the eight practices: the conduct of deportment, the conduct of the sense bases…'—the full detail is given there. 'One who is resolved practices with faith; one who is energetic practices with energy; one who is mindful practices with mindfulness; one who is undistracted practices with concentration; one who understands practices with wisdom; one who discerns practices with consciousness. For one so practicing, wholesome qualities extend; thus one practices with the conduct of the sense bases. One so practicing attains distinction; thus one practices with the conduct of distinction.' These other eight kinds of conduct that are mentioned should all be understood as being included within the perfections themselves. Therefore it was said: '“Conduct” means practice, which is the practice of giving, virtue, and so on, as included in the thirty perfections.' However, since only causal conduct is intended here, it should be understood that the conduct of the path and the conduct of attainment are not included. Therefore it was said: 'All of it is conducive to enlightenment.'

Tattha [V 0.0017] sabba-saddo sabbasabbaṃ āyatanasabbaṃ sakkāyasabbaṃ padesasabbanti catūsu atthesu dissati. Tathā hi “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthamāgacchantī”tiādīsu (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85) sabbasabbasmiṃ. “Sabbaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi taṃ suṇātha, kiñca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ cakkhuñceva rūpā ca…pe… mano ceva dhammā cā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.23) ettha āyatanasabbasmiṃ. “Sabbaṃ sabbato sañjānātī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.6) sakkāyasabbasmiṃ. “Sabbesampi vo, sāriputta, subhāsitaṃ pariyāyenā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.345) padesasabbasmiṃ. Idhāpi padesasabbasmiṃ eva veditabbo, bodhisambhārabhūtassa caritassa adhippetattā.

Here, the word 'all' is seen in four senses: the universal all, the all of the sense bases, the all of personality, and the partial all. For example, in passages such as, 'All phenomena in every way come into the range of the Blessed One, the Buddha’s, knowledge,' it is seen in the sense of the universal all. In, 'Bhikkhus, I will teach you the all. Listen to it. And what, bhikkhus, is the all? It is the eye and forms… the mind and mental objects,' it is in the sense of the all of the sense bases. In passages such as, 'One directly knows the all in every way,' it is in the sense of the all of personality. In passages such as, 'Sāriputta, what was well-spoken by all of you was so from a certain perspective,' it is in the sense of the partial all. Here too, it should be understood in the sense of the partial all, because what is intended is the conduct that constitutes the requisites for enlightenment.

Bodhīti rukkhopi ariyamaggopi nibbānampi sabbaññutaññāṇampi. “Bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddho”ti (mahāva. 1; udā. 1) ca “antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhi”nti (ma. ni. 1.285; mahāva. 11) ca āgataṭṭhāne bujjhati etthāti rukkho bodhi. “Bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇa”nti (cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 121) āgataṭṭhāne cattāri ariyasaccāni bujjhati etenāti ariyamaggo bodhi. “Patvāna bodhiṃ amataṃ asaṅkhata”nti āgataṭṭhāne bujjhati etasmiṃ nimittabhūteti nibbānaṃ bodhi. “Pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūrimedhaso”ti (dī. ni. 3.217) āgataṭṭhāne sabbe dhamme sabbākārena bujjhati etenāti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ bodhi. Idhāpi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Arahattamaggasabbaññutaññāṇāni vā idha bodhīti veditabbāni (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.11), mahābodhiyā adhippetattā bhagavato. Āsavakkhayañāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānañca āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ “mahābodhī”ti vuccati. Etthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yathāvuttakālaparicchede yaṃ mama dānāsīlādipaṭipattisaṅkhātaṃ caritaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ anavasesaṃ mahābodhiyā pācanaṃ sādhakaṃ nibbattakanti. Etena bodhisambhārānaṃ nirantarabhāvanaṃ dasseti. Atha vā [M 0.0019] sabbanti etthantare yathāvuttakālaparicchede yaṃ caritaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ sakalameva anavasesaṃ bodhisambhārabhūtameva. Etena sabbasambhārabhāvanaṃ dasseti.

The term 'Bodhi' refers to the tree, the noble path, Nibbāna, and the knowledge of omniscience. In passages such as, 'He first attained supreme enlightenment at the foot of the Bodhi tree,' and, 'between Gayā and the Bodhi tree,' the tree is called 'Bodhi' because 'one awakens there.' In the passage, 'Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths,' the noble path is called 'Bodhi' because 'one awakens to the four noble truths by means of it.' In, 'having attained Bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned,' Nibbāna is called 'Bodhi' because 'one awakens in relation to it as the object.' In, 'the one of excellent and vast wisdom attains Bodhi,' the knowledge of omniscience is called 'Bodhi' because 'one awakens to all phenomena in all their aspects by means of it.' Here, too, the knowledge of omniscience is intended. Alternatively, the path of Arahantship and the knowledge of omniscience are to be understood as 'Bodhi' here, since the great enlightenment of the Blessed One is intended. For the knowledge of omniscience is the proximate cause of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is the proximate cause of the knowledge of omniscience—this is called 'great enlightenment.' The concise meaning here is this: within the aforementioned period of time, all my conduct, consisting of practices such as giving and virtue, was entirely, without remainder, for the ripening, accomplishment, and production of great enlightenment. This indicates the uninterrupted cultivation of the requisites for enlightenment. Alternatively, regarding the word 'all' here: within the aforementioned period, all conduct that was practiced is entirely, completely, and without remainder, indeed the requisites for enlightenment. This indicates the cultivation of all the requisites.

Tasso hi bodhisambhāresu [P 0.0019] bhāvanā sabbasambhārabhāvanā nirantarabhāvanā cirakālabhāvanā sakkaccabhāvanā cāti. Tāsu “kappe ca satasahasse, caturo ca asaṅkhiye”ti iminā cirakālabhāvanā vuttā. Yo cettha accantasaṃyogo, tena paṭhame atthavikappe sabbaggahaṇena ca nirantarabhāvanā, dutiye atthavikappe sabbaṃ carita”nti iminā sabbasambhārabhāvanā, bodhipācana”nti [V 0.0018] iminā sakkaccabhāvanā vuttā hoti, yathā taṃ caritaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ pāceti evaṃbhūtabhāvadīpanato. Tathā hi taṃ “bodhipācana”nti vattabbataṃ arahati, na aññathāti. Kathaṃ panettha bodhicariyāya nirantarabhāvo veditabbo? Yadi cittanirantaratāya taṃ na yujjati, na hi mahābodhisattānaṃ mahābhinīhārato uddhaṃ bodhisambhārasambharaṇacittato aññaṃ cittaṃ nappavattatīti sakkā vattuṃ. Atha kiriyamayacittappavattiṃ sandhāya vucceyya, evampi na yujjati, na hi sabbāni tesaṃ kiriyamayacittāni bodhisambhārasambharaṇavaseneva pavattanti. Eteneva payoganirantaratāpi paṭikkhittāti daṭṭhabbā. Jātinirantaratāya pana nirantarabhāvanā veditabbā. Yassañhi jātiyaṃ mahābodhisattena mahāpaṇidhānaṃ nibbattitaṃ, tato paṭṭhāya yāva carimattabhāvā na sā nāma jāti upalabbhati, yā sabbena sabbaṃ bodhisambhārasambhatā na siyā antamaso dānapāramimattaṃ upādāya. Ayañhi niyatipatthitānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ dhammatā. Yāva ca te kammādīsu vasībhāvaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tāva sappadesampi sambhāresu payogamāpajjanti. Yadā pana sabbaso kammādīsu vasībhāvappattā honti, atha tato paṭṭhāya nippadesato eva bodhisambhāresu samīhanaṃ sātaccakiriyā ca sampajjati. Sakkaccakāritā pana sabbakālaṃ hoti, evaṃ yena yena bodhisattānaṃ tattha tattha yathādhippāyaṃ samijjhanaṃ sampajjatīti. Evametāya gāthāya bodhisambhāresu sabbasambhārabhāvanā cirakālabhāvanā nirantarabhāvanā sakkaccabhāvanā cāti catassopi bhāvanā pakāsitāti veditabbā.

For him, the cultivation of the requisites for enlightenment is fourfold: the cultivation of all requisites, uninterrupted cultivation, long-term cultivation, and respectful cultivation. Among these, by the words, 'for a hundred thousand eons and four incalculable aeons,' long-term cultivation is stated. And by the continuous connection implied herein, and by the inclusion of 'all' in the first interpretation of the meaning, uninterrupted cultivation is stated. In the second interpretation of the meaning, by 'all conduct was practiced,' the cultivation of all requisites is stated. By 'a ripening for enlightenment,' respectful cultivation is stated, because it reveals the state of being such that that conduct ripens perfect self-enlightenment. For thus it deserves to be called 'a ripening for enlightenment,' and not otherwise. How, here, is the uninterrupted nature of the Bodhisatta’s practice to be understood? If by uninterruptedness of mind, that is not suitable; for it cannot be said that for the Great Bodhisattas, after their great aspiration, no other thought arises apart from the thought of accumulating the requisites for enlightenment. If it were said with reference to the arising of functional consciousness, that too is not suitable; for not all their functional consciousnesses arise for the purpose of accumulating the requisites for enlightenment. By this reasoning, uninterruptedness of effort should also be understood as rejected. Rather, uninterrupted cultivation is to be understood as uninterruptedness of births.
