For from the birth in which the Great Bodhisatta made his great resolution, up to his final existence, no birth is found that is not in every way endowed with the requisites for enlightenment, at least to the extent of the perfection of giving. This, indeed, is the nature of Bodhisattas who aspire for the fixed course. And as long as they do not attain mastery over kamma and so on, they apply themselves to the requisites, even if only partially. But when they have in every way attained mastery over kamma and so on, then from that time onwards, their striving and constant action in the requisites for enlightenment are accomplished completely. Respectful action, however, occurs at all times; thus, for the Bodhisattas, in every case, success is achieved according to their wish. In this way, it should be understood that by this verse, all four kinds of cultivation regarding the requisites for enlightenment are shown: the cultivation of all requisites, long-term cultivation, uninterrupted cultivation, and respectful cultivation.

Tatra yasmā bodhisattacaritaṃ bodhisambhārā bodhicariyā aggayānaṃ pāramiyoti atthato ekaṃ, byañjanameva nānaṃ, yasmā ca parato vibhāgena [M 0.0020] vakkhamānānaṃ [P 0.0020] dānapāramiādīnaṃ caritanti idaṃ avisesavacanaṃ, tasmā sabbabodhisambhāresu kosallajananatthaṃ pāramiyo idha saṃvaṇṇetabbā. Tā parato pakiṇṇakakathāyaṃ sabbākārena saṃvaṇṇayissāma.

In this context, because 'the conduct of a Bodhisatta,' 'the requisites for enlightenment,' 'the practice for enlightenment,' and 'the perfections of the foremost ones' are one in meaning, with only the expressions differing; and because 'conduct' is a general term for the perfections of giving and so on, which will be spoken of in detail later; therefore, to generate skill in all the requisites for enlightenment, the perfections should be described here. We will describe them in all their aspects later in the miscellaneous section.

2. Iti bhagavā attano bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ caritaṃ ārambhato paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā mahābodhiyā paripācanamevāti avisesato dassetvā idāni tassa paramukkaṃsagamanena atisayato bodhiparipācanabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ imasmiṃ bhaddakappe katipayā pubbacariyā vibhāgato vibhāvento “atītakappe”tiādimāha.

2. Thus, the Blessed One, having first shown in a general way that his conduct in the Bodhisatta stage—from its beginning up to the very end—was entirely the ripening for great enlightenment, now, in order to show pre-eminently the state of the ripening for enlightenment through its attainment of the highest excellence, he spoke the verses beginning with, 'In a past eon,' clarifying in detail some of his former practices in this fortunate eon.

Tattha atītakappeti ito purime purimatare vā sabbasmiṃ atikkante yathāvuttaparicchede mahākappe, kappānaṃ satasahassādhikesu catūsu asaṅkhyeyyesūti attho. Caritanti ciṇṇaṃ dānādipaṭipattiṃ. Ṭhapayitvāti muñcitvā aggahetvā, avatvāti attho. Bhavābhaveti bhave ca abhave [V 0.0019] ca, “itibhavābhavakatha”nti (dī. ni. 1.17) ettha hi vuddhihāniyo bhavābhavāti vuttā. “Itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto”ti (udā. 20) ettha sampattivipattivuddhihānisassatucchedapuññapāpānibhavābhavāti adhippetāni. “Itibhavābhavahetu vā, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjatī”ti (a. ni. 4.9; itivu. 105) ettha pana paṇītapaṇītatarāni sappinavanītādibhesajjāni bhavābhavāti adhippetāni. Sampattibhavesu paṇītatarā paṇītatamā bhavābhavātipi vadanti eva, tasmā idhāpi so eva attho veditabbo, khuddake ceva mahante ca bhavasminti vuttaṃ hoti. Imamhi kappeti imasmiṃ bhaddakappe. Pavakkhissanti kathayissaṃ. Suṇohīti dhammasenāpatiṃ savane niyojeti. Meti mama santike, mama bhāsatoti attho.

Therein, atītakappe means: in a past eon, that is, in a former or even more former eon, in all that has passed, in a great eon with the aforementioned division, in the four incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand eons—this is the meaning. Caritaṃ means: the practiced conduct of giving and so forth. Ṭhapayitvā means: having set aside, having released, not having taken; or, not having spoken of—this is the meaning. Bhavābhave means: in existence and non-existence. For in the phrase itibhavābhavakathā (Dī. Ni. 1.17), growth and decline are called bhavābhava. In Itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto (Udā. 20), prosperity and decline, growth and decline, eternalism and annihilationism, and merit and demerit are intended as bhavābhava. And in Itibhavābhavahetu vā, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati (A. Ni. 4.9; Itivu. 105), fine and finer medicines such as ghee and fresh butter are intended as bhavābhava. In prosperous existences, they indeed also speak of finer and finest things as bhavābhava. Therefore, here too, that same meaning should be understood; it is said to mean in both small and great existences. Imamhi kappe means: in this Bhadda-kappa. Pavakkhissanti means: I will declare. Suṇohi means: He enjoins the General of the Dhamma to listen. Me means: in my presence, from me who is speaking—this is the meaning.

Nidānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Introductory Discourse is concluded.

1. Akittivaggo

1. The Chapter on Akitti

1. Akitticariyāvaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition on the Conduct of Akitti

3. Evaṃ [M 0.0021][V 0.0020] bhagavā āyasmato sāriputtattherassa sadevamanussāya ca parisāya attano pubbacariyāya savane ussāhaṃ janetvā idāni taṃ pubbacaritaṃ bhavantarapaṭicchannaṃ hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya paccakkhaṃ karonto “yadā ahaṃ brahāraññe”tiādimāha.

3. Thus the Blessed One, having generated enthusiasm in the Venerable Elder Sāriputta and in the assembly with its devas and humans for listening to His former conduct, now making that former conduct—which was concealed by intervening existences—as directly visible as an āmalaka fruit on the palm of the hand, spoke the verse beginning: “When I was in the great forest…”

Tattha yadāti yasmiṃ kāle. Brahāraññeti mahāaraññe, araññāniyaṃ, mahante vaneti attho. Suññeti janavivitte. Vipinakānaneti vipinabhūte kānane, padadvayenāpi tassa araññassa gahanabhāvameva dīpeti, sabbametaṃ kāradīpaṃ [P 0.0021] sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ajjhogāhetvāti anupavisitvā. Viharāmīti dibbabrahmaariyaāneñjavihārehi samuppāditasukhavisesena iriyāpathavihārena sarīradukkhaṃ vicchinditvā harāmi attabhāvaṃ pavattemi. Akitti nāma tāpasoti evaṃnāmako tāpaso hutvā yadā ahaṃ tasmiṃ araññe viharāmīti attho. Satthā tadā attano akittitāpasabhāvaṃ dhammasenāpatissa vadati. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā –

Therein, yadā means: at which time. Brahāraññe means: in a great forest, in a wilderness, that is, in a great wood. Suññe means: secluded from people. Vipinakānane means: in a forest that is a thicket; by this pair of words, the dense nature of that forest is shown. All this was said with reference to the island of Kāradīpa. Ajjhogāhetvā means: having entered into. Viharāmi means: having cut off bodily suffering by means of the abiding in the postures, with the special happiness produced by the divine, brahma, noble, and imperturbable abidings, I carry on, I maintain my individual existence. Akitti nāma tāpaso means: when I, having become an ascetic with this name, dwelt in that forest. The Teacher then tells the General of the Dhamma of His state as the ascetic Akitti. Herein, this is the sequential narrative:

Atīte kira imasmiṃyeva bhaddakappe bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte nāma rājini rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto asītikoṭivibhavassa brāhmaṇamahāsālassa kule nibbatti, “akittī”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassa padasā gamanakāle bhaginīpi jāyi. “Yasavatī”tissā nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So soḷasavassakāle takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggahetvā paccāgamāsi. Athassa mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. So tesaṃ petakiccāni kāretvā katipayadivasātikkamena ratanāvalokanaṃ āyuttakapurisehi kārayamāno “ettakaṃ mattikaṃ, ettakaṃ pettikaṃ, ettakaṃ pitāmaha”nti sutvā saṃviggamānaso hutvā “idaṃ dhanameva paññāyati, na dhanassa saṃhārakā, sabbe imaṃ dhanaṃ pahāyeva gatā, ahaṃ pana naṃ ādāya gamissāmī”ti rājānaṃ āpucchitvā bheriṃ carāpesi – “dhanena atthikā akittipaṇḍitassa gehaṃ āgacchantū”ti.

In the past, it is said, in this very Bhadda-kappa, while a king named Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the family of a brahmin of great wealth who possessed eighty crores. They gave him the name 'Akitti.' At the time when he could walk, a sister was also born. They gave her the name 'Yasavatī.' At the age of sixteen, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the sciences, and returned. Then his parents passed away. Having had their funeral rites performed, after a few days had passed, while having the treasures inspected by his appointed men, he heard it said: 'This much is the maternal inheritance, this much is the paternal, and this much is from the grandfather.' Hearing this, his mind was stirred with spiritual urgency, and he thought: 'Only this wealth is seen, not the accumulators of the wealth. All have departed, leaving this wealth behind. As for me, I shall take this and depart.' Having asked permission of the king, he had a drum beaten, proclaiming: 'Let those who have need of wealth come to the house of Akitti the wise!'

So [M 0.0022][V 0.0021] sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā dhane akhīyamāne “kiṃ me imāya dhanakīḷāya, atthikā gaṇhissantī”ti nivesanadvāraṃ vivaritvā hiraññasuvaṇṇādibharite sāragabbhe vivarāpetvā “dinnaṃyeva harantū”ti gehaṃ pahāya ñātiparivaṭṭassa paridevantassa bhaginiṃ gahetvā bārāṇasito nikkhamitvā [P 0.0022] nadiṃ uttaritvā dve tīṇi yojanāni gantvā pabbajitvā ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge paṇṇasālaṃ karitvā vasati. Yena pana dvārena tadā nikkhami, taṃ akittidvāraṃ nāma jātaṃ. Yena titthena nadiṃ otiṇṇo, taṃ akittititthaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Tassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ sutvā bahū manussā gāmanigamarājadhānivāsino tassa guṇehi ākaḍḍhiyamānahadayā anupabbajiṃsu. Mahāparivāro ahosi, mahālābhasakkāro nibbatti, buddhuppādo viya ahosi. Atha mahāsatto “ayaṃ lābhasakkāro mahā, parivāropi mahanto, kāyavivekamattampi idha na labhati, mayā ekākinā viharituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā paramappicchabhāvato vivekaninnatāya ca kassaci ajānāpetvā ekakova nikkhamitvā anupubbena damiḷaraṭṭhaṃ patvā kāvīrapaṭṭanasamīpe uyyāne viharanto jhānābhiññāyo nibbattesi. Tatrāpissa mahālābhasakkāro uppajji. So taṃ jigucchanto chaḍḍetvā ākāsena gantvā kāradīpe otari. Tadā kāradīpo ahidīpo nāma. So tattha mahantaṃ kārarukkhaṃ upanissāya paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Appicchatāya pana katthaci agantvā tassa rukkhassa phalakāle phalāni khādanto phale asati pattāni udakasittāni khādanto jhānasamāpattīhi vītināmesi.

He, having conducted a great giving for seven days, and with the wealth still unexhausted, thought: 'What use to me is this sport with wealth? Let those in need take it.' Opening the door of his residence and having the treasure chambers filled with gold, silver, and so forth, opened up, he declared: 'Let them carry away what has been given.' Abandoning his home while his circle of relatives lamented, he took his sister, departed from Bārāṇasī, crossed the river, and having gone two or three yojanas, he went forth. He made a leaf-hut in a delightful region and dwelt there. The gate by which he departed at that time came to be known as the Akitti Gate, and the ford by which he crossed the river came to be known as the Akitti Ford. Hearing of his going forth, many people dwelling in villages, towns, and the royal city, their hearts drawn by his virtues, went forth after him. A great retinue formed, and great gain and honor arose; it was like the arising of a Buddha. Then the Great Being thought: 'This gain and honor is great, and the retinue is also large. Not even mere bodily seclusion can be found here. It is right for me to dwell alone.' Having thus reflected, on account of his state of extreme contentment and his inclination to seclusion, without informing anyone, he departed all alone. Proceeding in due course, he reached the Damila country, and while dwelling in a park near Kāvīrapaṭṭana, he produced the meditative absorptions and the higher knowledges. There too, great gain and honor arose for him. Feeling revulsion for it, he abandoned it and, going through the air, he descended on the island of Kāradīpa. At that time, Kāradīpa was called Ahidīpa. There, relying on a large Kāra tree, he had a leaf-hut built and took up residence. Then, due to his contentment, without going anywhere, at the time when that tree was in fruit, he ate the fruits; when there were no fruits, eating leaves that had been boiled in water, he passed his time with the attainments of jhāna.

Tassa sīlatejena sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko “ko nu kho maṃ imamhā ṭhānā cāvetukāmo”ti āvajjento paṇḍitaṃ disvā “kimatthaṃ nu kho ayaṃ tāpaso evaṃ dukkaraṃ tapaṃ carati, sakkattaṃ nu kho pattheti, udāhu aññaṃ, vīmaṃsissāmi naṃ. Ayañhi suvisuddhakāyavacīmanosamācāro jīvite nirapekkho udakasittāni kārapattāni khādati, sace sakkattaṃ pattheti attano sittāni kārapattāni mayhaṃ dassati, no ce, na dassatī”ti brāhmaṇavaṇṇena tassa santikaṃ agamāsi[P 0.0023]. Bodhisattopi kārapattāni sedetvā “sītalībhūtāni khādissāmī”ti paṇṇasāladvāre nisīdi. Athassa purato sakko brāhmaṇarūpena [M 0.0023] bhikkhāya atthiko hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto taṃ disvā “lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata me, cirassaṃ vata me yācako diṭṭho”ti somanassappatto hutvā “ajja mama manorathaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dānaṃ dassāmī”ti pakkabhājaneneva ādāya gantvā dānapāramiṃ āvajjetvā attano asesetvāva tassa bhikkhābhājane pakkhipi. Sakko taṃ gahetvā thokaṃ gantvā antaradhāyi. Mahāsattopi tassa datvā puna pariyeṭṭhiṃ anāpajjitvā teneva pītisukhena vītināmesi.

By the power of his virtue, Sakka's Paṇḍukambala stone throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting, 'Who now wishes to dislodge me from this position?' saw the wise one and thought, 'For what purpose does this ascetic practice such severe austerity? Does he aspire to the state of Sakka, or to something else? I shall test him. For he is of utterly pure conduct in body, speech, and mind, indifferent to life, eating boiled Kāra leaves. If he aspires to the state of Sakka, he will not give me his boiled Kāra leaves; if not, he will give them.' Thus, in the guise of a brahmin, he approached him. The Bodhisatta, having boiled the Kāra leaves, sat at the door of his leaf-hut, thinking, 'I will eat them when they have cooled.' Then Sakka, in the form of a brahmin, stood before him as one in need of alms. The Great Being, seeing him, became filled with joy and thought, 'Ah, what a gain for me! What a great gain for me! After so long, I have seen a supplicant!' He resolved, 'Today, I will bring my heart's desire to fulfillment and give a gift.' Taking the leaves in the cooking pot itself and reflecting on the perfection of giving, he placed them all, leaving none for himself, into the brahmin's alms bowl. Sakka took them, went a short distance, and vanished. The Great Being, having given to him, did not go on a further search for food but passed the time with that very joy and happiness.

Dutiyadivase [V 0.0022] pana kārapattāni pacitvā “hiyyo dakkhiṇeyyaṃ alabhiṃ, ajja nu kho katha”nti paṇṇasāladvāre nisīdi. Sakkopi tatheva āgami. Mahāsatto punapi tatheva datvā vītināmesi. Tatiyadivase ca tatheva datvā “aho vata me lābhā, bahuṃ vata puññaṃ pasavāmi, sacāhaṃ dakkhiṇeyyaṃ labheyyaṃ, evameva māsampi dvemāsampi dānaṃ dadeyya”nti cintesi. Tīsupi divasesu “tena dānena na lābhasakkārasilokaṃ na cakkavattisampattiṃ na sakkasampattiṃ na brahmasampattiṃ na sāvakabodhiṃ na paccekabodhiṃ patthemi, api ca idaṃ me dānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇassa paccayo hotū”ti yathādhikāraṃ cittaṃ ṭhapesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

On the second day, having cooked the Kāra leaves, he sat at the door of his leaf-hut, thinking, 'Yesterday I found a worthy recipient; I wonder how it will be today?' Sakka came in the very same way. The Great Being again gave in the same manner and passed the time. And on the third day, having given likewise, he thought, 'Ah, what a gain for me! I am generating so much merit! If I could find a worthy recipient, I would give alms in this way for a month, or even two.' On all three days, he established his mind according to his aspiration, thinking, 'By this gift, I do not aspire to gain, honor, or fame, nor to the attainment of a universal monarch, nor to the state of Sakka, nor to the state of Brahmā, nor to the enlightenment of a disciple, nor to the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. Rather, may this gift of mine be a condition for the knowledge of omniscience!' Therefore, it was said:

4.

4.

“Tadā maṃ tapatejena, santatto tidivābhibhū;

Dhārento brāhmaṇavaṇṇaṃ, bhikkhāya maṃ upāgami.

Then, afflicted by the power of my austerity, the overlord of the celestial realm, assuming the guise of a brahmin, approached me for alms.

5.

5.

“Pavanā ābhataṃ paṇṇaṃ, atelañca aloṇikaṃ;

Mama dvāre ṭhitaṃ disvā, sakaṭāhena ākiriṃ.

The leaves brought from the forest, without oil and without salt; seeing him standing at my door, I poured them out, pot and all.

6.

6.

“Tassa datvānahaṃ paṇṇaṃ, nikujjitvāna bhājanaṃ;

Punesanaṃ jahitvāna, pāvisiṃ paṇṇasālakaṃ.

Having given him the leaves, I overturned my pot, and abandoning any further search, I entered my leaf-hut.

7.

7.

“Dutiyampi tatiyampi, upagañchi mamantikaṃ;

Akampito anolaggo, evamevamadāsahaṃ.

A second time and a third, he approached me; unshaken and unattached, I gave in the very same way.

8.

8.

“Na me tappaccayā atthi, sarīrasmiṃ vivaṇṇiyaṃ;

Pītisukhena ratiyā, vītināmemi taṃ divaṃ.

On account of that, there was no fading of my complexion; with joy, happiness, and delight, I passed that day.

9.

9.

“Yadi māsampi dvemāsaṃ, dakkhiṇeyyaṃ varaṃ labhe;

Akampito anolīno, dadeyyaṃ dānamuttamaṃ.

If for a month, or even two, I were to find an excellent recipient, unshaken and unhesitating, I would give the supreme gift.

10.

10.

“Na [M 0.0024][P 0.0024] tassa dānaṃ dadamāno, yasaṃ lābhañca patthayiṃ;

Sabbaññutaṃ patthayāno, tāni kammāni ācari”nti.

In giving that gift, I did not aspire for fame or gain; aspiring for omniscience, I performed those deeds.

Tattha tadāti yadā ahaṃ akittināmako tāpaso hutvā tasmiṃ dīpe kārāraññe viharāmi, tadā[V 0.0023]. Manti mama. Tapatejenāti sīlapāramitānubhāvena. Sīlañhi duccaritasaṃkilesassa tapanato “tapo”ti vuccati, nekkhammavīriyapāramitānubhāvena vā. Tāpi hi taṇhāsaṃkilesassa kosajjassa ca tapanato “tapo”ti vuccati, ukkaṃsagatā ca tā bodhisattassa imasmiṃ attabhāveti. Khantisaṃvarassa cāpi paramukkaṃsagamanato “khantipāramitānubhāvenā”tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭateva. “Khantī paramaṃ tapo”ti (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 184) hi vuttaṃ. Santattoti yathāvuttaguṇānubhāvajanitena dhammatāsiddhena paṇḍukambalasilāsanassa uṇhākārena santāpito. Tidivābhibhūti devalokādhipati, sakkoti attho. Paṇṇasālāya samīpe gahitampi kārapaṇṇaṃ paṇṇasālāya araññamajjhagatattā “pavanā ābhata”nti vuttaṃ.

Therein, tadā ('at that time') means: at the time when I was dwelling as an ascetic named Akitti in the Kāra forest on that island. Maṃ ('me') is used in the sense of mama ('of me'). Tapatejena ('by the power of austerity') means by the power of the perfection of virtue. For virtue, because it burns up the defilement of misconduct, is called tapa ('austerity'); or it means by the power of the perfections of renunciation and energy. For these too, because they burn up the defilement of craving and laziness, are called tapa. And these were brought to excellence by the Bodhisatta in this existence. And because of reaching the supreme excellence of patience and restraint, it is also correct to say 'by the power of the perfection of patience.' For it is said: 'Forbearance is the supreme austerity.' Santatto ('afflicted') means afflicted by the heat of the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, a heat which was produced by the power of the aforementioned qualities and established by natural law. Tidivābhibhū ('overlord of the celestial realm') means the lord of the deva world, that is, Sakka. Even though the Kāra leaves were gathered near the leaf-hut, because the leaf-hut was situated in the middle of the forest, they are said to be 'brought from the forest' (pavanā ābhataṃ).

Atelañca aloṇikanti deyyadhammassa anuḷārabhāvepi ajjhāsayasampattiyā dānadhammassa mahājutikabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Mama dvāreti mayhaṃ paṇṇasālāya dvāre. Sakaṭāhena ākirinti iminā attano kiñcipi asesetvā dinnabhāvaṃ dasseti.

Atelañca aloṇikaṃ ('without oil and without salt') is said to show the great splendor of the act of giving, which is due to the perfection of his intention, even though the object given was humble. Mama dvāre ('at my door') means at the door of my leaf-hut. By the phrase sakaṭāhena ākiriṃ ('I poured it out, pot and all'), he shows the fact that he gave without leaving anything at all for himself.

Punesanaṃ jahitvānāti “ekadivasaṃ dvikkhattuṃ ghāsesanaṃ na sallekha”nti cintetvā dānapītiyā titto viya hutvā tasmiṃ divase puna āhārapariyeṭṭhiṃ akatvā.

Punesanaṃ jahitvāna ('having abandoned any further search') means: having reflected, 'To search for food twice in one day is not in keeping with ascetic practice,' and being as if satiated by the joy of giving, he did not undertake a search for food again on that day.

Akampitoti sudūravikkhambhitattā macchariyena acalito dānajjhāsayato calanamattampi akārito. Anolaggoti lobhavasena īsakampi alaggo. Tatiyampīti pi-saddena dutiyampīti imaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Evamevamadāsahanti yathā paṭhamaṃ, evamevaṃ dutiyampi, tatiyampi adāsiṃ ahaṃ.

Akampito ('unshaken') means: unmoved by stinginess, as it was thoroughly suppressed, and not caused to waver even slightly from the intention to give. Anolaggo ('unattached') means: not clinging in the slightest way out of greed. In tatiyampi ('a third time also'), the particle pi ('also') includes dutiyampi ('a second time also'). Evamevamadāsahaṃ ('I gave in the very same way') means: just as on the first day, so too on the second and on the third day, I gave.

Na me tappaccayāti gāthāya vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti. Tattha tappaccayāti dānapaccayā tīsu divasesu chinnāhāratāya sarīrasmiṃ yena vevaṇṇiyena bhavitabbaṃ, tampi me sarīrasmiṃ vivaṇṇiyaṃ dānapaccayāyeva natthi[M 0.0025]. Kasmā? Dānavisayena pītisukhena dānavisayāya eva ca ratiyā. Vītināmemi taṃ divanti taṃ sakalaṃ timattadivasaṃ vītināmemi, na kevalañca tīṇi eva divasāni, atha kho māsadvimāsamattampi kālaṃ, evameva dātuṃ pahomīti dassetuṃ [P 0.0025] “yadi māsampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Anolīnoti alīnacitto, dāne asaṅkucitacittoti attho.

By the phrase 'Na me tappaccayā,' he clarifies the meaning already stated in the verse. Therein, 'tappaccayā' means: on account of giving. That discoloration which should have occurred in my body from having no food for three days—even that discoloration is not present in my body precisely because of giving. This is due to the joy and happiness with giving as its object, and indeed due to the delight in giving. 'Vītināmemi taṃ divaṃ' means: I pass that entire three-day period. And not only just three days, but rather, to show that 'I am able to give in this same way for a period of one or two months,' the words 'yadi māsampi,' etc., were spoken. 'Anolīno' means with an unsluggish mind; the meaning is with a mind unshrinking in giving.

Tassāti brāhmaṇarūpena āgatassa sakkassa. Yasanti kittiṃ, parivārasampattiṃ vā. Lābhañcāti devamanussesu cakkavattiādibhāvena laddhabbaṃ lābhaṃ vā na patthayiṃ. Atha kho sabbaññutaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ patthayāno ākaṅkhamāno tāni tīsu divasesu anekavāraṃ uppannāni dānamayāni [V 0.0024] puññakammāni dānassa vā parivārabhūtāni kāyasucaritādīni puññakammāni ācariṃ akāsinti.

'His' (tassa) refers to Sakka, who had come in the form of a brahmin. 'Fame' (yasaṃ) means renown or the attainment of a retinue. 'And gain' (lābhañca) refers to the gain obtainable among gods and humans, such as becoming a wheel-turning monarch; I did not desire that gain. Rather, desiring and aspiring for omniscience and perfect enlightenment, I performed and practiced those meritorious deeds—acts of giving and other meritorious deeds such as good bodily conduct, which are ancillary to giving—that arose many times over those three days.

Iti bhagavā tasmiṃ attabhāve attano sudukkaraṃ puññacaritamattameva idha mahātherassa pakāsesi. Jātakadesanāyaṃ pana catutthadivase sakkassa upasaṅkamitvā bodhisattassa ajjhāsayajānanaṃ varena upanimantanā bodhisattassa varasampaṭicchanasīsena dhammadesanā deyyadhammadakkhiṇeyyānaṃ puna sakkassa anāgamanassa ca ākaṅkhamānatā ca pakāsitā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Thus the Blessed One, in that existence, revealed to the great elder here only the matter of his own meritorious conduct, which was most difficult to perform. In the Jātaka discourse, however, the following are revealed: on the fourth day, Sakka's approach and his discernment of the Bodhisatta's intention; his invitation with a boon; the Dhamma discourse, headed by the Bodhisatta's acceptance of the boon, concerning things to be given and those worthy of receiving them; and also the aspiration for Sakka not to return. For it is said:

“Akittiṃ disvāna sammantaṃ, sakko bhūtapatī bravi;

Kiṃ patthayaṃ mahābrahme, eko sammasi ghammani.

Having seen Akitti, who was calm, Sakka, the lord of beings, spoke: 'What do you desire, great Brahma, that you strive alone in this hot, desolate place?'

“Dukkho punabbhavo sakka, sarīrassa ca bhedanaṃ;

Sammohamaraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, tasmā sammāmi, vāsava.

Painful is rebirth, O Sakka, and the breaking up of the body; painful is death with bewilderment; therefore, O Vāsava, I strive.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and excellent statement of yours, Kassapa, I grant you a boon, whatever you may wish for in your mind.

“Varañce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Yena putte ca dāre ca, dhanadhaññaṃ piyāni ca;

Laddhā narā na tappanti, so lobho na mayī vase.

If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings, may that greed not dwell in me, by which men, having obtained sons and wives, wealth and grain, and beloved things, are not satisfied.

Etasmiṃ te sulapite…pe… manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and excellent statement of yours... whatever you may wish for in your mind.

“Varañce [M 0.0026] me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Khettaṃ vatthuṃ hiraññañca, gavāssaṃ dāsaporisaṃ;

Yena jātena jīyanti, so doso na mayī vase.

If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings, may that ill-will not dwell in me, by which, once it has arisen, one's fields, property, gold, cattle, horses, and servants are ruined.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite…pe… manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and excellent statement of yours... whatever you may wish for in your mind.

“Varañce [V 0.0025] me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Bālaṃ na passe na suṇe, na ca bālena saṃvase;

Bālenallāpasallāpaṃ, na kare na ca rocaye.

If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may I not see a fool, nor hear one, nor associate with a fool; may I not engage in conversation with a fool, nor delight in it.

“Kiṃ [P 0.0026] nu te akaraṃ bālo, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa bālassa, dassanaṃ nābhikaṅkhasi.

What has the fool done to you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa. Why, Kassapa, do you not desire to see a fool?

“Anayaṃ nayati dummedho, adhurāyaṃ niyuñjati;

Dunnayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto pakuppati;

Vinayaṃ so na jānāti, sādhu tassa adassanaṃ.

The unwise one leads to ruin; he engages in what is not his burden. He is difficult to guide and given to sloth; when rightly spoken to, he becomes angry. He does not know discipline; not seeing him is good.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite…pe… manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and excellent statement of yours... whatever you may wish for in your mind.

“Varañce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Dhīraṃ passe suṇe dhīraṃ, dhīrena saha saṃvase;

Dhīrenallāpasallāpaṃ, taṃ kare tañca rocaye.

If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may I see the wise, hear the wise, and dwell with the wise; may I engage in conversation with the wise, and delight in it.

“Kiṃ nu te akaraṃ dhīro, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa dhīrassa, dassanaṃ abhikaṅkhasi.

What has the wise one done for you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa. Why, Kassapa, do you yearn to see the wise?

“Nayaṃ nayati medhāvī, adhurāyaṃ na yuñjati;

Sunayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto na kuppati;

Vinayaṃ so pajānāti, sādhu tena samāgamo.

The intelligent one leads along the right path; he does not engage in what is not his burden. He is easy to guide and is excellent; when rightly spoken to, he does not become angry. He understands discipline; association with him is good.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite…pe… manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and excellent statement of yours... whatever you may wish for in your mind.

“Varañce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Tato ratyā vivasāne, sūriyuggamanaṃ pati;

Dibbā bhakkhā pātubhaveyyuṃ, sīlavanto ca yācakā.

If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: then at the end of the night, toward the rising of the sun, may divine food appear, and virtuous supplicants as well.

“Dadato [V 0.0026] me na khīyetha, datvā nānutapeyyahaṃ;

Dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādeyyaṃ, etaṃ sakka varaṃ vare.

May what I have to give not be exhausted; having given, may I feel no regret; while giving, may I clarify my mind. This, O Sakka, is the boon I choose.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite…pe… manasicchasi.

“Varañce [M 0.0027] me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Na maṃ puna upeyyāsi, etaṃ sakka varaṃ vare.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and excellent statement of yours... whatever you may wish for in your mind. If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may you not approach me again—this, O Sakka, is the boon I choose.

“Bahūhi vatacariyāhi, narā ca atha nāriyo;

Dassanaṃ abhikaṅkhanti, kiṃ nu me dassane bhayaṃ.

Indeed, because of your many ascetic practices, men and also women desire to see you. What fear, then, is there for you in seeing me?

“Taṃ tādisaṃ devavaṇṇaṃ, sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ;

Disvā tapo pamajjeyyaṃ, etaṃ te dassane bhaya”nti. (jā. 1.13.83-103);

Seeing such a divine form as yours, endowed with all sensual pleasures, I might neglect my ascetic practice; this is the fear in seeing you.

Atha sakko “sādhu, bhante, na te ito paṭṭhāya santikaṃ āgamissāmī”ti taṃ abhivādetvā pakkāmi. Mahāsatto yāvajīvaṃ tattheva vasanto āyupariyosāne brahmaloke nibbatti.

Then Sakka said, 'Very well, venerable sir, from now on I shall not come into your presence,' and after paying homage to him, he departed. The Great Being, dwelling there for as long as he lived, was reborn in the Brahma world at the end of his life.

Anuruddhatthero tadā sakko ahosi, lokanātho akittipaṇḍito.

The Elder Anuruddha was Sakka at that time, and the Lord of the World was Akitti the Wise.

Tassa mahābhinikkhamanasadisaṃ nikkhantattā nekkhammapāramī. Suvisuddhasīlācāratāya sīlapāramī. Kāmavitakkādīnaṃ [P 0.0027] suṭṭhu vikkhambhitattā vīriyapāramī. Khantisaṃvarassa paramukkaṃsagamanato khantipāramī. Paṭiññānurūpaṃ paṭipattiyā saccapāramī. Sabbattha acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānena adhiṭṭhānapāramī. Sabbasattesu hitajjhāsayena mettāpāramī. Sattasaṅkhārakatavippakāresu majjhattabhāvappattiyā upekkhāpāramī. Tāsaṃ upakārānupakāre dhamme jānitvā anupakāre dhamme pahāya upakāradhammesu pavattāpanapurecarā sahajātā ca upāyakosallabhūtā atisallekhavuttisādhanī ca paññā paññāpāramīti imāpi dasa pāramiyo labbhanti.

Because his going forth was like the Great Renunciation, the perfection of renunciation is obtained. Through perfectly pure conduct in virtue, the perfection of virtue. By thoroughly suppressing sensual thoughts and the like, the perfection of energy. Because forbearance and restraint reached the highest excellence, the perfection of patience. By practicing in accordance with his promise, the perfection of truthfulness. Through unwavering undertaking and resolution in all things, the perfection of determination. With a disposition for the welfare of all beings, the perfection of loving-kindness. By attaining a state of neutrality towards the actions and alterations concerning beings and formations, the perfection of equanimity. Having known the helpful and unhelpful qualities among them, abandoning the unhelpful qualities, and being foremost in establishing the helpful qualities, wisdom—which is innate, endowed with skillful means, and conducive to an extremely austere life—is the perfection of wisdom. Thus, these ten perfections are also obtained.

Dānajjhāsayassa [V 0.0027] pana atiuḷārabhāvena dānamukhena desanā pavattā. Tasmā sabbattha samakā mahākaruṇā, dvepi puññañāṇasambhārā, kāyasucaritādīni tīṇi bodhisattasucaritāni, saccādhiṭṭhānādīni cattāri adhiṭṭhānāni, ussāhādayo catasso buddhabhūmiyo, saddhādayo pañca mahābodhiparipācanīyā dhammā, alobhajjhāsayādayo cha bodhisattānaṃ ajjhāsayā, tiṇṇo tāressāmītiādayo satta paṭiññā dhammā, appicchassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo mahicchassātiādayo (dī. ni. 3.358; a. ni. 8.30) aṭṭha mahāpurisavitakkā (dī. ni. 3.358), nava yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā, dānajjhāsayādayo dasa mahāpurisajjhāsayā, dānasīlādayo dasa puññakiriyavatthūnīti evamādayo ye anekasataanekasahassappabhedā bodhisambhārabhūtā [M 0.0028] mahābodhisattaguṇā. Te sabbepi yathārahaṃ idha niddhāretvā vattabbā.

Moreover, due to the exceedingly sublime disposition for generosity, the teaching proceeds with giving as its chief theme. Therefore, there are: great compassion that is impartial everywhere; the two accumulations of merit and wisdom; the three good conducts of a Bodhisatta, beginning with good bodily conduct; the four resolutions, beginning with the resolution of truth; the four grounds for Buddhahood, beginning with effort; the five qualities that ripen towards great enlightenment, beginning with faith; the six dispositions of Bodhisattas, beginning with the disposition of non-greed; the seven declarations, beginning with 'Having crossed over, I shall lead others across'; the eight thoughts of a great man, such as 'This Dhamma is for one with few wishes, not for one with many wishes'; the nine qualities rooted in wise consideration; the ten dispositions of a great man, beginning with the disposition for generosity; and the ten bases of meritorious action, beginning with giving and morality—these and other qualities of a great Bodhisatta, of many hundreds and thousands of kinds, which constitute the requisites for enlightenment. All of them should be specified and stated here as is appropriate.

Api cettha mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ mahantañca ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ pahāya mahābhinikkhamanasadisaṃ gehato nikkhamanaṃ, nikkhamitvā pabbajitassa bahujanasammatassa sato paramappicchabhāvena kulesu gaṇesu ca alaggatā, accantameva lābhasakkārasilokajigucchā, pavivekābhirati, kāyajīvitanirapekkho pariccāgo, anāhārasseva sato divasattayampi dānapītiyā parituṭṭhassa nibbikārasarīrayāpanaṃ, māsadvimāsamattampi kālaṃ yācake sati āhāraṃ tatheva datvā “dānagateneva pītisukhena sarīraṃ yāpessāmī”ti pariccāge anolīnavuttisādhako uḷāro dānajjhāsayo, dānaṃ datvā puna [P 0.0028] āhārapariyeṭṭhiyā akaraṇahetubhūtā paramasallekhavuttīti evamādayo mahāsattassa guṇānubhāvā veditabbā. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Furthermore, herein should be understood these and other qualities and powers of the great being: abandoning a great mass of wealth and a large circle of relatives, his departure from home was like the Great Renunciation; having gone forth and become an ascetic, though esteemed by many people, he remained unattached to families and groups due to his supreme contentment; he was utterly disgusted with gain, honor, and fame; he delighted in seclusion; his renunciation was without regard for body or life; though without food, he sustained his body for three days without alteration, being perfectly satisfied by the joy of giving; even for a period of one or two months, if a beggar were present, he would give food in the same way, possessing a sublime disposition for giving that accomplishes an unwavering practice in renunciation, thinking, 'I will sustain my body with the joy and happiness that comes from giving'; and after giving a gift, his life of supreme austerity was the cause for not seeking food again. Therefore it is said:

“Evaṃ acchariyā hete, abbhutā ca mahesino;

Mahākāruṇikā dhīrā, sabbalokekabandhavā.

“Thus, wonderful are these great seers, and marvelous; greatly compassionate, wise, the sole kinsmen of the entire world.

“Acinteyyānubhāvā ca, sadā saddhammagocarā;

Bodhisattā mahāsattā, sucisallekhavuttino.

“They are of inconceivable power, always resorting to the true Dhamma; Bodhisattas, great beings, of pure and austere conduct.

“Mahāvātasamuddhata-vīcimālo mahodadhi;

Api laṅgheyya velantaṃ, bodhisattā na dhammataṃ.

“The great ocean, with its garland of waves stirred up by a mighty wind, might even overstep its shore, but Bodhisattas never transgress the natural law of the Dhamma.

“Loke [V 0.0028] sañjātavaddhāpi, na te bhāvitabhāvino;

Limpanti lokadhammehi, toyena padumaṃ yathā.

“Though born and grown in the world, they, being of developed mind, are not stained by worldly conditions, just as a lotus is not by water.

“Yesaṃ ve attani sneho, nihīyati yathā yathā;

Sattesu karuṇāsneho, vaḍḍhateva tathā tathā.

“Indeed, as their affection for themselves diminishes, so their compassionate affection for beings grows ever more.

“Yathā cittaṃ vase hoti, na ca cittavasānugā;

Tathā kammaṃ vase hoti, na ca kammavasānugā.

“Just as their mind is under their control, and they do not follow the sway of the mind, so their action is under their control, and they do not follow the sway of action.

“Dosehi nābhibhūyanti, samugghātenti vā na te;

Carantā bodhipariyeṭṭhiṃ, purisājāniyā budhā.

“They are not overcome by defilements, nor do they eradicate them, as they, wise thoroughbreds among men, wander in quest of enlightenment.

“Tesu [M 0.0029] cittappasādopi, dukkhato parimocaye;

Pagevānukiriyā tesaṃ, dhammassa anudhammato”ti.

“Even serene confidence in them can free one from suffering; how much more so their practice in accordance with the Dhamma!”

Paramatthadīpaniyā cariyāpiṭakasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Paramatthadīpanī, the Commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka.

Akitticariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cariyā of the Sage Akitti is concluded.

2. Saṅkhabrāhmaṇacariyāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Cariyā of Saṅkha the Brahmin

11-12. Dutiyasmiṃ punāparanti puna aparaṃ, na kevalamidaṃ akitticariyameva, atha kho puna aparaṃ aññaṃ saṅkhacariyampi pavakkhissaṃ, suṇohīti adhippāyo. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Saṅkhasavhayoti saṅkhanāmo. Mahāsamuddaṃ taritukāmoti suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gantuṃ nāvāya mahāsamuddaṃ taritukāmo. Upagacchāmi paṭṭananti tāmalittipaṭṭanaṃ uddissa gacchāmi. Sayambhuñāṇena paccekabodhiyā adhigatattā sayameva bhūtanti sayambhuṃ. Kilesamārādīsu kenacipi na parājitanti aparājitaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ matthakaṃ madditvā ṭhitanti attho. Tattāya kaṭhinabhūmiyāti ghammasantāpena santattāya sakkharavālukānicitattā kharāya kakkhaḷāya bhūmiyā[P 0.0029].

11–12. In the second Cariyā, ‘punāparaṃ’ means ‘puna aparaṃ’ (again, another). The intention is: ‘It is not only this Cariyā of Akitti, but I will also explain another, different Cariyā, that of Saṅkha. Listen.’ This same method applies in the subsequent accounts as well. ‘Saṅkhasavhayo’ means named Saṅkha. ‘Mahāsamuddaṃ taritukāmo’ means desiring to cross the great ocean by boat to go to Suvaṇṇabhūmi. ‘Upagacchāmi paṭṭanaṃ’ means ‘I go, aiming for the port of Tāmalitti.’ ‘Sayambhuṃ’ means one who has become so by oneself, because of having attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha through self-existent knowledge. ‘Aparājitaṃ’ means not conquered by anything, such as the Māra of defilements; the meaning is ‘standing firm, having crushed the heads of the three Māras.’ ‘Tattāya kaṭhinabhūmiyā’ means on ground that is scorched by the heat of the sun, and is rough and hard because it is covered with gravel and sand.

13. Tanti taṃ paccekabuddhaṃ. Imamatthanti imaṃ idāni vakkhamānaṃ “idaṃ khetta”ntiādikaṃ [V 0.0029] atthaṃ. Vicintayinti tadā saṅkhabrāhmaṇabhūto cintesinti satthā vadati. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā –

13. ‘Taṃ’ means that Paccekabuddha. ‘Imam atthaṃ’ means this meaning, about to be spoken now, beginning with ‘this is the field.’ ‘Vicintayi’ (he reflected): the Teacher says, ‘At that time, being the brahmin Saṅkha, I reflected (cintesiṃ).’ Herein, this is the sequential narrative:

Atīte ayaṃ bārāṇasī moḷinī nāma ahosi. Moḷinīnagare brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto saṅkho nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā aḍḍho mahaddhano catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe attano nivesanadvāreti chasu ṭhānesu cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassāni vissajjento kapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattesi. So ekadivasaṃ cintesi – “ahaṃ gehe dhane khīṇe dānaṃ dātuṃ na sakkhissāmi, aparikkhīṇeyeva dhane nāvāya suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gantvā dhanaṃ āharissāmī”ti. So nāvaṃ bhaṇḍassa pūrāpetvā puttadāraṃ āmantetvā “yāvāhaṃ āgacchissāmi, tāva me dānaṃ anupacchindantā pavatteyyāthā”ti vatvā dāsakammakaraparivuto upāhanaṃ āruyha chattena dhāriyamānena paṭṭanagāmābhimukho pāyāsi.

In the past, this Bārāṇasī was named Moḷinī. While Brahmadatta was ruling in the city of Moḷinī, the Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Saṅkha, was rich and very wealthy. Having had six alms-halls built in six places—at the four city gates, in the city center, and at the entrance to his own residence—he daily dispensed great alms to the destitute, wayfarers, and others, giving away six hundred thousand. One day, he thought: 'When the wealth in my house is depleted, I will not be able to give alms. While the wealth is not yet depleted, I will go by ship to Suvaṇṇabhūmi and bring back wealth.' He had a ship filled with goods, summoned his wife and children, and said: 'Until I return, you should continue my alms-giving without interruption.' Then, surrounded by servants and workers, having put on his sandals and with a parasol being held over him, he set out toward the port-town.

Tasmiṃ [M 0.0030] khaṇe gandhamādane eko paccekabuddho sattāhaṃ nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā nirodhasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya lokaṃ volokento taṃ dhanāharaṇatthaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā “mahāpuriso dhanaṃ āharituṃ gacchati, bhavissati nu kho assa mahāsamudde antarāyo, no”ti āvajjetvā “bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “esa maṃ disvā chattañca upāhanañca mayhaṃ datvā upāhanadānanissandena samudde bhinnāya nāvāya patiṭṭhaṃ labhissati, karissāmissa anuggaha”nti ākāsena gantvā tassa avidūre otaritvā majjhanhikasamaye caṇḍavātātapena aṅgārasanthatasadisaṃ uṇhavālukaṃ maddanto tassa abhimukhaṃ āgañchi. So taṃ disvāva haṭṭhatuṭṭho “puññakkhettaṃ me āgataṃ, ajja mayā ettha bījaṃ ropetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintesi. Tena vuttaṃ “tamahaṃ paṭipathe disvā, imamatthaṃ vicintayi”ntiādi.

At that moment, on Mount Gandhamādana, a certain Paccekabuddha, having entered the attainment of cessation for seven days and having arisen from it, was surveying the world. Seeing that man going to bring back wealth, he reflected, 'This great man is going to bring back wealth. Will there be danger for him in the great ocean, or not?' Knowing that there would be, he thought, 'This man, upon seeing me, will give me his parasol and sandals. Through the result of the gift of sandals, when his ship is wrecked in the ocean, he will obtain a refuge. I shall render him assistance.' Having come through the sky, he descended not far from him. At midday, treading on the hot sand, which was like a layer of embers under a fierce wind and sun, he approached him. As soon as he saw him, the Bodhisatta was joyful and delighted, and thought, 'A field of merit has come to me. Today it is fitting for me to sow a seed herein.' Therefore it was said: 'Seeing him on the path, I reflected on this matter,' and so forth.

Tattha idaṃ khettantiādi cintitākāradassanaṃ. Khettanti [P 0.0030] khittaṃ bījaṃ mahapphalabhāvakaraṇena tāyatīti khettaṃ, pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇaviruhanabhūmi. Idha pana khettaṃ viyāti khettaṃ, aggadakkhiṇeyyo paccekabuddho. Tenevāha “puññakāmassa jantuno”ti.

Therein, the phrase beginning with 'this is a field' shows the manner of his thought. 'Field' (khettaṃ) is so called because it protects (tāyati) the sown (khittaṃ) seed by causing it to have great fruit; it is the ground where early and late crops grow. Here, however, it is a 'field' because it is like a field; it refers to the Paccekabuddha, the foremost one worthy of offerings. Therefore He said: 'for a being who desires merit.'

14. Mahāgamanti vipulaphalāgamaṃ, sassasampattidāyakanti attho. Bījaṃ na ropetīti bījaṃ na vapati.

14. 'Of great result' (mahāgamaṃ) means the source of abundant fruit; the meaning is 'giver of prosperity in crops'. 'Does not sow the seed' (bījaṃ na ropeti) means 'he does not plant the seed'.

15.

15.

Khettavaruttamanti khettavaresupi uttamaṃ. Sīlādiguṇasampannā hi visesato ariyasāvakā [V 0.0030] khettavarā, tatopi aggabhūto paccekabuddho khettavaruttamo. Kāranti sakkāraṃ. Yadi na karomīti sambandho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – idamīdisaṃ anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ labhitvā tattha pūjāsakkāraṃ yadi na karomi, puññena atthiko nāmāhaṃ na bhaveyyanti.

'The best of excellent fields' (khettavaruttamaṃ) means supreme even among excellent fields. For noble disciples endowed with virtues such as morality are especially excellent fields, but the Paccekabuddha, being foremost even among them, is the best of excellent fields. 'An act of reverence' (kāraṃ) means respect. The connection is: 'If I do not perform'. This is what is meant: 'Having obtained such an unsurpassed field of merit as this, if I do not pay homage and respect to him, then I would not be one who has need of merit.'

16-17. Yathā amaccotiādīnaṃ dvinnaṃ gāthānaṃ ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yathā nāma yo koci raññā muddādhikāre ṭhapito lañchanadharo amaccapuriso senāpati vā so antepure jane bahiddhā ca balakāyādīsu rañño yathānusiṭṭhaṃ na paṭipajjati na tesaṃ dhanadhaññaṃ deti, taṃ taṃ kattabbaṃ vattaṃ parihāpeti. So muddito parihāyati muddādhikāraladdhavibhavato [M 0.0031] paridhaṃsati, evameva ahampi puññakammassa rato laddhabbapuññaphalasaṅkhātaṃ puññakāmo dakkhiṇāya vipulaphalabhāvakaraṇena vipulaṃ disvāna taṃ dakkhiṇaṃ uḷāraṃ dakkhiṇeyyaṃ labhitvā tassa dānaṃ yadi na dadāmi puññato āyatiṃ puññaphalato ca paridhaṃsāmi. Tasmā idha mayā puññaṃ kātabbamevāti.

16-17. This is the summary meaning of the two verses beginning with 'Just as an official': Just as any seal-bearing minister or general appointed by the king to the office of the seal, if he does not act according to the king's instructions with regard to the people in the inner palace and those outside, the troops and so forth, does not give them wealth and grain, and neglects his various duties, he falls from his office of the seal and is ruined, losing the prosperity gained from it. Even so, I too, who delight in meritorious deeds and desire merit—which is designated as the fruit of merit to be obtained—having seen the vastness of this offering which brings an abundant result, and having obtained such a sublime recipient for that offering, if I do not give a gift to him, I will fall away from merit and from the future fruit of merit. Therefore, a meritorious deed must certainly be done by me in this case.

Evaṃ pana cintetvā mahāpuriso dūratova upāhanā orohitvā vegena upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “bhante, mayhaṃ anuggahatthāya imaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upagacchathā”ti vatvā tasmiṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upasaṅkamante tattha vālukaṃ ussāpetvā uttarāsaṅgaṃ paññāpetvā paccekabuddhe tattha nisinne vanditvā vāsitaparissāvitena udakena tassa pāde dhovitvā, gandhatelena makkhetvā, attano upāhanaṃ puñchitvā, gandhatelena makkhetvā, tassa pāde paṭimuñcitvā “bhante, imaṃ upāhanaṃ āruyha, imaṃ chattaṃ matthake katvā gacchathā”ti chattupāhanaṃ adāsi. Sopissa anuggahatthāya taṃ gahetvā pasādasaṃvaḍḍhanatthaṃ passantasseva vehāsaṃ uppatitvā gandhamādanaṃ agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Having reflected thus, the great man, taking off his sandals from afar, quickly approached, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sir, for my benefit, please approach the foot of this tree.' When the Paccekabuddha approached the foot of the tree, he prepared a seat of sand there, spread his upper robe, and when the Paccekabuddha was seated, he paid homage, washed his feet with scented and filtered water, anointed them with perfumed oil, wiped his own sandals, anointed them with perfumed oil, and put them on the Paccekabuddha's feet, saying, 'Venerable sir, please go, wearing these sandals and holding this parasol over your head.' Thus he gave the parasol and sandals. The Paccekabuddha, for his benefit, accepted them and, in order to increase his faith, rose into the air while he was still watching and departed to Mount Gandhamādana. Therefore it was said:

18.

18.

“Evāhaṃ [P 0.0031] cintayitvāna, orohitvā upāhanā;

Tassa pādāni vanditvā, adāsiṃ chattupāhana”nti.

Thus having reflected, I took off my sandals; having paid homage to his feet, I gave the parasol and sandals.

Bodhisatto taṃ disvā ativiya pasannacitto paṭṭanaṃ gantvā nāvaṃ abhiruhi. Athassa mahāsamuddaṃ tarantassa sattame divase nāvā vivaramadāsi. Udakaṃ ussiñcituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Mahājano maraṇabhayabhīto attano attano devatā namassitvā mahāviravaṃ viravi. Bodhisatto ekaṃ upaṭṭhākaṃ gahetvā sakalasarīraṃ telena makkhetvā sappinā saddhiṃ sakkharacuṇṇāni yāvadatthaṃ khāditvā tampi khādāpetvā tena saddhiṃ kūpakayaṭṭhimatthakaṃ āruyha “imāya disāya amhākaṃ nagara”nti disaṃ vavatthapetvā macchakacchapaparipanthato attānaṃ saccādhiṭṭhānena pamocento tena saddhiṃ usabhamattaṭṭhānaṃ atikkamitvā patitvā samuddaṃ tarituṃ ārabhi. Mahājano pana tattheva vināsaṃ [V 0.0031] pāpuṇi. Tassa tarantasseva satta divasā gatā. So tasmimpi kāle loṇodakena mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā uposathiko ahosiyeva.

Seeing him, the Bodhisatta, with an exceedingly delighted mind, went to the port and boarded a ship. Then, as he was crossing the great ocean, on the seventh day the ship sprung a leak. The people were unable to bail out the water. The great crowd, terrified by the fear of death, worshiped their respective deities and raised a great outcry. The Bodhisatta, taking one attendant, smeared his entire body with oil, ate as much as he desired of sugar powder together with ghee, and had the attendant eat as well. Together with him, he climbed to the top of the mast, determined the direction, thinking, 'Our city is in this direction,' and, intending to free himself from the danger of fish and turtles by an act of truth, he jumped with his companion, having gone beyond a distance of an usabha, and began to cross the ocean. The great crowd, however, perished right there. While he was crossing, seven days passed. Even at that time, rinsing his mouth with saltwater, he was indeed observing the Uposatha.

Tadā [M 0.0032] pana īdisānaṃ purisavisesānaṃ rakkhaṇatthāya catūhi lokapālehi ṭhapitā maṇimekhalā nāma devadhītā attano issariyena sattāhaṃ pamajjitvā sattame divase taṃ disvā “sacāyaṃ idha marissa, ativiya gārayhā abhavissa”nti saṃviggahadayā suvaṇṇapātiyā dibbabhojanassa pūretvā vegenāgantvā “brāhmaṇa, idaṃ dibbabhojanaṃ bhuñjā”ti āha. So taṃ ulloketvā “nāhaṃ bhuñjāmi, uposathikomhī”ti paṭikkhipitvā taṃ pucchanto –

At that time, a goddess named Maṇimekhalā, appointed by the four Lokapālas for the protection of such exceptional men, having been negligent in her sovereignty for seven days, on the seventh day saw him. With a heart struck with alarm, thinking, 'If this man were to die here, I would be greatly reproached,' she filled a golden bowl with divine food, came swiftly, and said, 'Brahmin, eat this divine food.' He, looking at her, refused, saying, 'I will not eat; I am observing the Uposatha,' and, wishing to question her, said:

“Yaṃ tvaṃ sukhenābhisamekkhase maṃ, bhuñjassu bhattaṃ iti maṃ vadesi;

Pucchāmi taṃ nāri mahānubhāve, devī nusi tvaṃ uda mānusī nū”ti. (jā. 1.10.42) –

You who look upon me with kindness, telling me, 'Partake of this food!' I ask you, O lady of great power, are you a goddess, or are you a human woman?

Āha. Sā tassa paṭivacanaṃ dentī –

She, giving a reply to him, said:

“Devī ahaṃ saṅkha mahānubhāvā, idhāgatā sāgaravārimajjhe;

Anukampikā no ca paduṭṭhacittā, taveva atthāya idhāgatāsmi.

I am a goddess, O Saṅkha, of great power, come here to the midst of the ocean's waters; compassionate and not of malevolent mind, I have come here for your benefit alone.

“Idhannapānaṃ sayanāsanañca, yānāni nānāvividhāni saṅkha;

Sabbassa [P 0.0032] tyāhaṃ paṭipādayāmi, yaṃ kiñci tuyhaṃ manasābhipatthita”nti. (jā. 1.10.43-44) –

Here, O Saṅkha, are food and drink, beds and seats, and various kinds of vehicles; I shall provide for you all that, whatever is wished for by your mind.

Imā gāthā abhāsi. Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “ayaṃ devadhītā samuddapiṭṭhe mayhaṃ ‘idañcidañca dammī’ti vadati, yañcesā mayhaṃ deti, tampi mama puññeneva, taṃ pana puññaṃ ayaṃ devadhītā jānāti nu kho, udāhu na jānāti, pucchissāmi tāva na”nti cintetvā pucchanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

She spoke these verses. Hearing this, the Great Being thought: 'This goddess, on the surface of the ocean, tells me, "I will give this and that." And whatever she gives me, she gives only because of my own merit. But does this goddess know of that merit, or does she not? First, I shall ask her.' Thinking thus, and wishing to ask, he spoke this verse:

“Yaṃ kiñci yiṭṭhañca hutañca mayhaṃ, sabbassa no issarā tvaṃ sugatte;

Sussoṇi subbhūru vilaggamajjhe, kissa me kammassa ayaṃ vipāko”ti. (jā. 1.10.45);

Whatever has been sacrificed and offered by me, O you of beautiful form, you are sovereign over it all. O you of beautiful hips, of lovely brows and thighs, and of slender waist, of what deed of mine is this the result?

Tattha [M 0.0033][V 0.0032] yiṭṭhanti dānavasena yajitaṃ. Hutanti āhunapāhunavasena dinnaṃ. Sabbassa no issarā tvanti amhākaṃ puññakammassa sabbassa tvaṃ issarā, “ayaṃ imassa vipāko, ayaṃ imassā”ti byākarituṃ samatthā. Sussoṇīti sundarajaghane. Subbhūrūti sundarehi bhamukehi ūrūhi ca samannāgate. Vilaggamajjheti vilaggatanumajjhe. Kissa meti mayā katakammesu katarakammassa ayaṃ vipāko, yenāhaṃ appatiṭṭhe mahāsamudde ajja patiṭṭhaṃ labhāmīti.

Therein, 'yiṭṭhaṃ' means sacrificed by way of giving. 'Hutaṃ' means given by way of offerings to guests. 'Sabbassa no issarā tvaṃ' means: you are sovereign over all our meritorious deeds, capable of explaining, 'This is the result of this deed, and this is the result of that.' 'Sussoṇī' means with beautiful hips. 'Subbhūrū' means endowed with beautiful eyebrows and thighs. 'Vilaggamajjhe' means with a slender waist. 'Kissa me...' means: 'Among the deeds done by me, of which deed is this the result, whereby I today find a footing in the great ocean where there is no footing?'

Taṃ sutvā devadhītā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo ‘yaṃ attanā kusalakammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ kammaṃ na jānātī’ti saññāya pucchati maññe, kathessāmi na”nti nāvābhiruhanadivase paccekabuddhassa chattupāhanadānapuññameva tassa kāraṇanti kathentī –

Hearing this, the goddess thought: 'This brahmin asks, I suppose, from the idea that he does not know the wholesome deed he himself has done. I shall tell him.' Then, explaining that the very merit from the gift of an umbrella and sandals to a Paccekabuddha on the day of boarding the ship was the cause, she said:

“Ghamme pathe brāhmaṇa ekabhikkhuṃ, ugghaṭṭapādaṃ tasitaṃ kilantaṃ;

Paṭipādayī saṅkha upāhanāni, sā dakkhiṇā kāmaduhā tavajjā”ti. (jā. 1.10.46) –

On a hot path in the heat, O brahmin, to a single monk with chafed feet, thirsty and weary, you, O Saṅkha, provided sandals. That offering today yields all your desires.

Gāthamāha.

She spoke the verse.

Tattha ekabhikkhunti ekaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ sandhāyāha. Ugghaṭṭapādanti uṇhavālukāya ghaṭṭapādaṃ, vibādhitapādanti [P 0.0033] attho. Tasitanti pipāsitaṃ. Paṭipādayīti paṭipādesi yojesi. Kāmaduhāti sabbakāmadāyikā.

Therein, 'ekabhikkhuṃ' is said referring to a Paccekabuddha. 'Ugghaṭṭapādaṃ' means feet chafed by hot sand; the meaning is afflicted feet. 'Tasitaṃ' means thirsty. 'Paṭipādayī' means you provided, you furnished. 'Kāmaduhā' means the giver of all desires.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “evarūpepi nāma appatiṭṭhe mahāsamudde mayā dinnaṃ chattupāhanadānaṃ mama sabbakāmadadaṃ jātaṃ aho sudinna”nti tuṭṭhacitto –

Hearing this, the Great Being, with a delighted mind, thought: 'Indeed, even in such a great ocean without footing, the gift of an umbrella and sandals given by me has become the giver of all my desires. Ah, how well it was given!'

“Sā hotu nāvā phalakūpapannā, anavassutā erakavātayuttā;

Aññassa yānassa na hettha bhūmi, ajjeva maṃ moḷiniṃ pāpayassū”ti. (jā. 1.10.47) –

Let there be a ship, endowed with planks and mast, watertight, and moved by a favorable wind. This is no place for any other vehicle. Convey me this very day to Moḷinī!

Gāthamāha.

He spoke the verse.

Tattha [M 0.0034][V 0.0033] phalakūpapannāti mahānāvatāya bahūhi phalakehi upetā. Udakappavesanābhāvena anavassutā. Sammā gahetvā gamanakavātena erakavātayuttā.

Therein, 'phalakūpapannā' means: being a great ship, it is endowed with many planks. 'Anavassutā' means not leaking, due to the absence of water entering. 'Erakavātayuttā' means endowed with a favorable wind for travel, having been set on a proper course.

Devadhītā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā dīghato aṭṭhausabhaṃ vitthārato catuusabhaṃ gambhīrato vīsatiyaṭṭhikaṃ sattaratanamayaṃ nāvaṃ māpetvā kūpaphiyārittayuttāni indanīlarajatasuvaṇṇamayādīni nimminitvā sattannaṃ ratanānaṃ pūretvā brāhmaṇaṃ āliṅgetvā nāvaṃ āropesi, upaṭṭhākaṃ panassa na olokesi. Brāhmaṇo attanā katakalyāṇato tassa pattiṃ adāsi, so anumodi. Atha devadhītā tampi āliṅgetvā nāvāya patiṭṭhāpetvā taṃ nāvaṃ moḷinīnagaraṃ netvā brāhmaṇassa ghare dhanaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva agamāsi. Tenāha bhagavā –

Hearing his words, the celestial maiden, delighted and joyful, created a boat measuring eight usabhas in length, four usabhas in width, and twenty yaṭṭhis in depth, made of the seven kinds of jewels. She fashioned its mast, yard, and oars from sapphire, silver, gold, and the like, filled it with the seven kinds of jewels, embraced the brahmin, and placed him aboard the boat. Yet, she paid no attention to his attendant. The brahmin gave him a share of the merit from the good deed he had done, and the attendant rejoiced. Then, the celestial maiden embraced him too, placed him on the boat, took that boat to the city of Moḷinī, deposited the wealth in the brahmin’s house, and returned to her own dwelling. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Sā tattha vittā sumanā patītā, nāvaṃ sucittaṃ abhinimminitvā;

Ādāya saṅkhaṃ purisena saddhiṃ, upānayī nagaraṃ sādhuramma”nti. (jā. 1.10.48);

There, pleased, joyful, and glad of heart, she, having created a beautifully adorned boat, took Saṅkha together with the man and brought them to the delightful city.

Mahāpurisassa hi cittasampattiyā paccekabuddhassa ca nirodhato vuṭṭhitabhāvena sattasu cetanāsu ādicetanā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyā atiuḷāraphalā ca jātā. Idampi tassa dānassa [P 0.0034] appamattaphalanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aparimāṇaphalañhi taṃ dānaṃ bodhisambhārabhūtaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

For the Great Being, due to the accomplishment of his mind and the Paccekabuddha's emergence from the attainment of cessation, the initial volition among the seven volitions became one to be experienced in this very life and of exceedingly great fruit. This too should be seen as a fruit of that gift that is not insignificant. For that gift, being a requisite for enlightenment, is of immeasurable fruit. Therefore, it is said:

19.

19.

“Tenevāhaṃ sataguṇato, sukhumālo sukhedhito;

Api ca dānaṃ paripūrento, evaṃ tassa adāsaha”nti.

Because of that, I was a hundredfold more delicate and nurtured in happiness. Moreover, while fulfilling the perfection of giving, thus I gave to him.

Tattha tenāti tato paccekabuddhato, sataguṇatoti sataguṇena ahaṃ tadā saṅkhabhūto sukhumālo, tasmā sukhedhito sukhasaṃvaḍḍho, api ca evaṃ santepi dānaṃ paripūrento, evaṃ mayhaṃ dānapāramī paripūretūti tassa paccekabuddhassa attano sarīradukkhaṃ anapekkhitvā chattupāhanaṃ adāsinti attano dānajjhāsayassa uḷārabhāvaṃ satthā pavedesi.

Therein, `tena` means 'from that Paccekabuddha.' `sataguṇato` means 'by a hundredfold.' At that time, I, being Saṅkha, was delicate and therefore nurtured in happiness, raised in comfort. Moreover, even while being so, fulfilling the perfection of giving, the Teacher proclaimed the greatness of his own inclination for giving, which was demonstrated by his disregarding his own bodily suffering with the thought, 'May my perfection of giving be fulfilled!'

Bodhisattopi [M 0.0035] yāvajīvaṃ amitadhanagehaṃ ajjhāvasanto bhiyyosomattāya dānāni datvā sīlāni rakkhitvā āyupariyosāne sapariso devanagaraṃ pūresi.

The Bodhisatta, too, for as long as he lived, dwelling in a house of immeasurable wealth, gave gifts ever more abundantly, observed the moral precepts, and at the end of his life, together with his retinue, filled the celestial city.

Tadā devadhītā uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, puriso ānandatthero, lokanātho saṅkhabrāhmaṇo.

At that time, the celestial maiden was Uppalavaṇṇā, the man was the Elder Ānanda, and the Lord of the World was the brahmin Saṅkha.

Tassa [V 0.0034] suvisuddhaniccasīlauposathasīlādivasena sīlapāramī dānasīlādīnaṃ paṭipakkhato nikkhantattā kusaladhammavasena nekkhammapāramī, dānādinipphādanatthaṃ abbhussahanavasena tathā mahāsamuddataraṇavāyāmavasena ca vīriyapāramī, tadatthaṃ adhivāsanakhantivasena khantipāramī, paṭiññānurūpappaṭipattiyā saccapāramī, sabbattha acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānavasena adhiṭṭhānapāramī, sabbasattesu hitajjhāsayavasena mettāpāramī, sattasaṅkhārakatavippakāresu majjhattabhāvappattiyā upekkhāpāramī, sabbapāramīnaṃ upakārānupakāre dhamme jānitvā anupakāre dhamme pahāya upakāradhammesu pavattāpanapurecarā sahajātā ca upāyakosallabhūtā paññā paññāpāramīti imāpi pāramiyo labbhanti.

For him, the perfection of virtue is attained by way of thoroughly pure and constant morality, such as the Uposatha precepts. The perfection of renunciation is attained by way of wholesome qualities, due to having departed from what is contrary to giving and virtue. The perfection of energy is attained by way of striving to accomplish giving and the like, and also by way of the effort to cross the great ocean. The perfection of patience is attained by way of endurance and forbearance for that purpose. The perfection of truthfulness is attained by practicing in accordance with his promise. The perfection of determination is attained by way of unshakeable resolve and undertaking in all things. The perfection of loving-kindness is attained by way of an intention for the welfare of all beings. The perfection of equanimity is attained by reaching a state of neutrality towards the actions and alterations of beings and conditioned things. Wisdom—which knows the helpful and unhelpful qualities for all perfections, abandons the unhelpful, and is a forerunner that initiates and is co-nascent with helpful qualities, being skill in means—is the perfection of wisdom. Thus, these perfections are also attained.

Dānajjhāsayassa pana atiuḷārabhāvena dānapāramīvasena desanā pavattā. Yasmā cettha dasa pāramiyo labbhanti, tasmā heṭṭhā vuttā mahākaruṇādayo bodhisattaguṇā idhāpi yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbā. Tathā attano bhogasukhaṃ anapekkhitvā mahākaruṇāya “dānapāramiṃ pūressāmī”ti dānasambhārasaṃharaṇatthaṃ samuddataraṇaṃ, tattha ca samuddapatitassapi uposathādhiṭṭhānaṃ, sīlakhaṇḍabhayena devadhītāyapi upagatāya āhārānāharaṇanti evamādayo mahāsattassa guṇā veditabbā. Idāni vakkhamānesu sesacaritesu imināva nayena guṇaniddhāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ[P 0.0035]. Tattha tattha visesamattameva vakkhāma. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Moreover, due to the exceedingly noble inclination for giving, the teaching proceeds by way of the perfection of giving. Since the ten perfections are obtained here, the previously mentioned qualities of the Bodhisatta—such as great compassion—should be determined here as appropriate. Thus, without regard for his own wealth and happiness, out of great compassion, thinking, "I shall fulfill the perfection of giving," the crossing of the ocean to accumulate the requisites for giving; and there, even when fallen into the ocean, his adherence to the Uposatha observance; out of fear of breaking his virtue, his refusal to take food even when a celestial maiden approached: such qualities of the Great Being should be understood. Now, in the remaining accounts of conduct to be discussed, the determination of qualities should be understood in this same way. We will mention only the particular distinctions in each case. Therefore, it is said:

“Evaṃ acchariyā hete, abbhutā ca mahesino…pe…;

Pagevānukiriyā tesaṃ, dhammassa anudhammato”ti.

Thus, these qualities of the great sage are wonderful and marvelous... What then to say of the practice that emulates them, in accordance with the Dhamma and its ancillary principles!

Saṅkhabrāhmaṇacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the conduct of Saṅkha the brahmin is concluded.

3. Kururājacariyāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Conduct of the Kuru King

20.

20.

Tatiye [M 0.0036] indapatthe puruttameti indapatthanāmake kururaṭṭhassa puravare uttamanagare. Rājāti dhammena samena catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi parisaṃ rañjetīti rājā. Kusale dasahupāgatoti kusalehi [V 0.0035] dasahi samannāgato, dānādīhi dasahi puññakiriyavatthūhi, dasahi kusalakammapathehi vā yuttoti attho.

In the third, `indapatthe puruttame` means in Indapattha, the excellent and foremost city of the Kuru country, named Indapattha. A king (`rājā`) is so called because he delights (`rañjeti`) his retinue with righteousness, impartiality, and the four bases of sympathy. `Kusale dasahupāgato` ('endowed with ten wholesome qualities') means possessed of ten wholesome qualities, that is, endowed with the ten bases for performing meritorious actions, such as generosity, or with the ten wholesome courses of action; this is the meaning.

21. Kaliṅgaraṭṭhavisayāti kaliṅgaraṭṭhasaṅkhātavisayā. Brāhmaṇā upagañchu manti kaliṅgarājena uyyojitā aṭṭha brāhmaṇā maṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu. Upasaṅkamitvā ca pana āyācuṃ maṃ hatthināganti hatthibhūtaṃ mahānāgaṃ maṃ āyāciṃsu. Dhaññanti dhanāyitabbasirisobhaggappattaṃ lakkhaṇasampannaṃ. Maṅgalasammatanti tāyayeva lakkhaṇasampattiyā maṅgalaṃ abhivuḍḍhikāraṇanti abhisammataṃ janehi.

21. `Kaliṅgaraṭṭhavisayā` means from the region known as the Kalinga country. `Brāhmaṇā upagañchu maṃ` ('brahmins approached me') means the eight brahmins sent by the king of Kalinga approached me. And having approached, `āyācuṃ maṃ hatthināgaṃ` ('they requested from me the elephant') means they requested from me the great elephant. `Dhaññaṃ` ('prosperous') means that which has attained the fortune and splendor worthy of being considered wealth, complete with auspicious marks. `Maṅgalasammataṃ` ('considered auspicious') means, due to that very completeness of auspicious marks, it was considered by people to be auspicious and a cause of growth.

22. Avuṭṭhikoti vassarahito. Dubbhikkhoti dullabhabhojano. Chātako mahāti mahatī jighacchābādhā vattatīti attho. Dadāhīti dehi. Nīlanti nīlavaṇṇaṃ. Añjanasavhayanti añjanasaddena avhātabbaṃ, añjananāmakanti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – amhākaṃ kaliṅgaraṭṭhaṃ avuṭṭhikaṃ, tena idāni mahādubbhikkhaṃ tattha mahantaṃ chātakabhayaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa vūpasamatthāya imaṃ añjanagirisaṅkāsaṃ tuyhaṃ añjananāmakaṃ maṅgalahatthiṃ dehi, imasmiñhi tattha nīte devo vassissati, tena taṃ sabbabhayaṃ vūpasammissatīti. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā –

22. 'Rainless' means devoid of rain. 'Famine' means scarcity of food. 'Great hunger' means a great affliction of hunger prevails; this is the meaning. 'Give' means give. 'Dark-hued' means of a dark color. 'Called Añjana' means to be summoned by the word Añjana, meaning named Añjana; this is the meaning. This is what was said: 'Our Kalinga country is rainless, and because of that, a great famine has now arisen there, a great fear of hunger. To pacify that, give this auspicious elephant of yours, named Añjana, resembling the Añjana mountain. For when this one is brought there, the god will send rain, and by that, all that fear will be pacified.' Herein is the sequential account:

Atīte kururaṭṭhe indapatthanagare bodhisatto kururājassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā anupubbena viññutaṃ patto, takkasilaṃ gantvā yogavihitāni sippāyatanāni vijjāṭṭhānāni ca uggahetvā paccāgato pitarā uparajje ṭhapito, aparabhāge pitu accayena rajjaṃ patvā dasa rājadhamme [P 0.0036] akopento dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi dhanañjayo nāma nāmena. So catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāreti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassaṃ dhanaṃ vissajjento sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā dānaṃ adāsi. Tassa dānajjhāsayatā dānābhirati sakalajambudīpaṃ patthari.

In the past, in the Kuru country, in the city of Indapatta, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the chief queen of the Kuru king. Gradually attaining discernment, he went to Takkasilā, mastered the various arts and sciences, and upon returning, was appointed viceroy by his father. Later, after his father's passing, he attained kingship. Not violating the ten royal virtues, he ruled righteously, his name being Dhanañjaya. He had six alms-halls established—at the four city gates, in the middle of the city, and at the entrance to his residence—and daily distributing six hundred thousand in wealth, he made the whole of Jambudīpa clamorous with appeals for alms. His disposition for generosity and delight in giving spread throughout the entire Jambudīpa.

Tasmiṃ [M 0.0037] kāle kaliṅgaraṭṭhe dubbhikkhabhayaṃ chātakabhayaṃ rogabhayanti tīṇi bhayāni uppajjiṃsu. Sakalaraṭṭhavāsino dantapuraṃ gantvā rājabhavanadvāre ukkuṭṭhimakaṃsu “devaṃ vassāpehi devā”ti. Rājā taṃ sutvā “kiṃkāraṇā ete viravantī”ti amacce pucchi. Amaccā rañño tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā porāṇakarājāno deve avassante kiṃ karontīti. “Devo vassatū”ti dānaṃ datvā uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya samādinnasīlā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā dabbasanthare sattāhaṃ nipajjantīti. Taṃ sutvā tathā akāsi. Devo na vassi, evaṃ rājā ahaṃ mayā kattabbakiccaṃ akāsiṃ, devo na vassati, kinti karomāti. Deva, indapatthanagare dhanañjayassa nāma kururājassa maṅgalahatthimhi ānīte devo vassissatīti[V 0.0036]. So rājā balavāhanasampanno duppasaho, kathamassa hatthiṃ ānessāmāti. Mahārāja, tena saddhiṃ yuddhakiccaṃ natthi, dānajjhāsayo so rājā dānābhirato yācito samāno alaṅkatasīsampi chinditvā pasādasampannāni akkhīnipi uppāṭetvā sakalarajjampi niyyātetvā dadeyya, hatthimhi vattabbameva natthi, avassaṃ yācito samāno dassatīti. Ke pana yācituṃ samatthāti? Brāhmaṇā, mahārājāti. Rājā aṭṭha brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā sakkārasammānaṃ katvā paribbayaṃ datvā hatthiyācanatthaṃ pesesi. Te sabbattha ekarattivāsena turitagamanaṃ gantvā katipāhaṃ nagaradvāre dānasālāsu bhuñjantā sarīraṃ santappetvā rañño dānaggaṃ āgamanapathe kālaṃ āgamayamānā pācīnadvāre aṭṭhaṃsu.

At that time, in the Kalinga country, three fears arose: the fear of famine, the fear of hunger, and the fear of disease. All the inhabitants of the country went to Dantapura and made a clamor at the palace gate, saying, "O king, make the god send rain, O lord!" Hearing this, the king asked his ministers, "For what reason are these people shouting?" The ministers explained the matter to the king. The king then asked what the ancient kings did when the god did not send rain. They replied, "Saying, 'May the god send rain,' they would give alms, observe the Uposatha, undertake the precepts, enter the state chamber, and lie on a grass mat for seven days." Hearing this, the king did likewise. But the god did not send rain. The king thought, "I have done what was to be done by me, yet the god does not send rain. What am I to do?" The ministers said, "O king, in the city of Indapatta, there is a Kuru king named Dhanañjaya. If his auspicious elephant is brought here, the god will send rain." The king said, "But that king is powerful, well-equipped with armies, and hard to subdue. How can we obtain his elephant?" They replied, "Great king, there is no need for battle with him. That king has a disposition for generosity and delights in giving. If asked, he would even cut off his own adorned head, pluck out his splendid eyes, or hand over his entire kingdom and give it away. There is no need to even speak of the elephant—if asked, he will surely give it." "But who is capable of asking for it?" "The brahmins, great king." The king summoned eight brahmins, honored and rewarded them, gave them provisions, and sent them to request the elephant. They traveled swiftly, staying only one night in each place, and after some days, having eaten in the alms-halls at the city gate and refreshed themselves, they stood at the eastern gate, awaiting the time of the king's arrival at the chief place of alms.

Bodhisattopi pātova nhātānulitto sabbālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍito alaṅkatavaravāraṇakhandhagato mahantena rājānubhāvena dānasālaṃ gantvā otaritvā sattaṭṭhajanānaṃ sahatthena dānaṃ datvā “imināva nīhārena dethā”ti vatvā hatthiṃ abhiruhitvā [P 0.0037] dakkhiṇadvāraṃ agamāsi. Brāhmaṇā pācīnadvāre ārakkhassa balavatāya okāsaṃ alabhitvā dakkhiṇadvāraṃ gantvā rājānaṃ āgacchantaṃ ullokayamānā dvārato nātidūre unnataṭṭhāne ṭhitā sampattaṃ rājānaṃ hatthe ukkhipitvā jayāpesuṃ. Rājā vajiraṅkusena vāraṇaṃ nivattetvā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā te brāhmaṇe “kiṃ icchathā”ti pucchi. Brāhmaṇā “kaliṅgaraṭṭhaṃ dubbhikkhabhayena chātakabhayena rogabhayena ca upaddutaṃ. So upaddavo imasmiṃ tava maṅgalahatthimhi nīte [M 0.0038] vūpasammissati. Tasmā imaṃ añjanavaṇṇaṃ nāgaṃ amhākaṃ dehī”ti āhaṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha “kaliṅgaraṭṭhavisayā…pe… añjanasavhaya”nti. Tassattho vutto eva.

The Bodhisatta, having bathed and anointed himself early in the morning, adorned with all his ornaments, and mounted on a magnificently decorated, choice elephant, went to the alms-hall with great royal splendor. After descending, he gave alms to seven or eight people with his own hand, saying, "Give in this very manner." Then, he mounted the elephant and proceeded to the southern gate. The brahmins, unable to find an opportunity at the eastern gate due to the strong guard, went to the southern gate. Standing on an elevated spot not far from the gate, watching for the king to approach, they raised their hands and acclaimed him with cries of victory when he arrived. The king, turning the elephant with his diamond goad, went to them and asked, "What do you desire?" The brahmins replied, "The Kalinga country is afflicted by the fear of famine, the fear of hunger, and the fear of disease. That affliction will be pacified when this auspicious elephant of yours is brought there. Therefore, give us this elephant, dark as kohl." Explaining this matter, the Teacher said: "From the Kalinga country..." and so on, up to "...named Añjana." The meaning of this has already been stated.

Atha bodhisatto “na metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yaṃ me yācakānaṃ manorathavighāto siyā, mayhañca samādānabhedo siyā”ti hatthikkhandhato otaritvā “sace analaṅkataṭṭhānaṃ atthi, alaṅkaritvā dassāmī”ti samantato oloketvā analaṅkataṭṭhānaṃ adisvā soṇḍāya naṃ gahetvā brāhmaṇānaṃ hatthesu ṭhapetvā ratanabhiṅgārena pupphagandhavāsitaṃ udakaṃ pātetvā adāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then the Bodhisatta, thinking, "It is not proper for me that the wish of a supplicant should be thwarted, nor that my own resolve should be broken," descended from the elephant's back. Looking all around, thinking, "If there is any unadorned spot, I shall adorn it and then give him," and seeing no such spot, he took the elephant by the trunk, placed the trunk in the hands of the brahmins, poured water scented with flowers and perfumes from a jeweled ewer, and gave him. For this reason, it was said:

23.

23.

“Na me yācakamanuppatte, paṭikkhepo anucchavo;

Mā me bhijji samādānaṃ, dassāmi vipulaṃ gajaṃ.

"For me, when a supplicant has approached, refusal is not suitable; may my resolve not be broken. I shall give the great elephant."

24.

24.

“Nāgaṃ gahetvā soṇḍāya, bhiṅgāre ratanāmaye;

Jalaṃ hatthe ākiritvā, brāhmaṇānaṃ adaṃ gaja”nti.

"Taking the great elephant by the trunk, and from a jeweled ewer pouring water upon the hand, I gave the elephant to the brahmins."

Tattha [V 0.0037] yācakamanuppatteti yācake anuppatte. Anucchavoti anucchaviko patirūpo. Mā me bhijji samādānanti sabbaññutaññāṇatthāya sabbassa yācakassa sabbaṃ anavajjaṃ icchitaṃ dadanto dānapāramiṃ pūressāmīti yaṃ mayhaṃ samādānaṃ, taṃ mā bhijji. Tasmā dassāmi vipulaṃ gajanti mahantaṃ imaṃ maṅgalahatthiṃ dassāmīti. Adanti adāsiṃ.

Herein, yācakamanuppatte means 'when supplicants have arrived.' Anucchavo means 'fitting, suitable.' Mā me bhijji samādānaṃ refers to the resolve: 'For the sake of the knowledge of omniscience, giving every faultless desired thing to every supplicant, I will fulfill the perfection of giving. May this, my resolve, not be broken.' Therefore, dassāmi vipulaṃ gajaṃ means, 'I shall give this great, auspicious elephant.' Adaṃ means 'I gave.'

25.

25.

Tasmiṃ pana hatthimhi dinne amaccā bodhisattaṃ etadavocuṃ – “kasmā, mahārāja, maṅgalahatthiṃ dadattha, nanu añño hatthī dātabbo, raññā nāma evarūpo opavayho maṅgalahatthī issariyaṃ abhivijayañca ākaṅkhantena na dātabbo”ti[P 0.0038]. Mahāsatto yaṃ maṃ yācakā yācanti, tadeva mayā dātabbaṃ, sace pana maṃ rajjaṃ yāceyyuṃ, rajjampi tesaṃ dadeyyaṃ, mayhaṃ rajjatopi jīvitatopi sabbaññutaññāṇameva piyataraṃ, tasmā taṃ hatthiṃ adāsinti āha. Tena vuttaṃ “tassa nāge padinnamhī”tiādi. Tattha tassāti tassa tena, tasmiṃ nāge hatthimhi dinne.

When that elephant was given, the ministers said this to the Bodhisatta: 'Great King, why did you give the auspicious elephant? Should not another elephant have been given? A king who desires sovereignty and conquest should not give away such a royal mount, an auspicious elephant.' The Great Being said: 'Whatever supplicants ask of me, that very thing must be given by me. If they should ask me for the kingdom, I would give them the kingdom as well. To me, the knowledge of omniscience is dearer than kingship and even life itself. Therefore, I gave that elephant.' Hence it is said: 'When that elephant was given,' and so forth. Herein, tassa means 'by him' (tena); the phrase means 'when that elephant, that bull elephant, was given'.

26. Maṅgalasampannanti maṅgalaguṇehi samannāgataṃ. Saṅgāmavijayuttamanti saṅgāmavijayā uttamaṃ, saṅgāmavijaye vā uttamaṃ padhānaṃ pavaraṃ nāgaṃ. Kiṃ te rajjaṃ [M 0.0039] karissatīti tasmiṃ nāge apagate tava rajjaṃ kiṃ karissati, rajjakiccaṃ na karissati, rajjampi apagatamevāti dasseti.

26. Maṅgalasampannaṃ means 'endowed with auspicious qualities.' Saṅgāmavijayuttamaṃ means 'supreme in victory in battle'; or, 'the supreme, chief, and excellent elephant in victory in battle.' Kiṃ te rajjaṃ karissati means: 'When that elephant is gone, what will your kingdom accomplish? It will not perform the functions of a kingdom; the kingdom itself will be lost'—thus it shows.

27. Rajjampi me dade sabbanti tiṭṭhatu nāgo tiracchānagato, idaṃ me sabbaṃ kururaṭṭhampi yācakānaṃ dadeyyaṃ. Sarīraṃ dajjamattanoti rajjepi vā kiṃ vattabbaṃ, attano sarīrampi yācakānaṃ dadeyyaṃ, sabbopi hi me ajjhattikabāhiro pariggaho lokahitatthameva mayā pariccatto. Yasmā sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ sabbaññutā ca dānapāramiṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbapāramiyo apūrentena na sakkā laddhuṃ, tasmā nāgaṃ adāsiṃ ahanti dasseti.

27. Rajjampi me dade sabbaṃ means: 'Let the elephant, a mere animal, be; I would give this entire Kuru kingdom of mine to supplicants.' Sarīraṃ dajjamattano means: 'What need is there to speak of the kingdom? I would give even my own body to supplicants. Indeed, all my possessions, both internal and external, have been relinquished by me solely for the welfare of the world. Because omniscience is dear to me, and omniscience cannot be attained by one who does not fulfill all the perfections, beginning with the perfection of giving, therefore I gave the elephant'—thus he shows.

Evampi tasmiṃ nāge ānīte kaliṅgaraṭṭhe devo na vassateva.
