Kaliṅgarājā “idānipi na vassati, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti pucchitvā “kururājā garudhamme rakkhati, tenassa raṭṭhe anvaddhamāsaṃ anudasāhaṃ devo vassati, rañño guṇānubhāvo esa, na imassa tiracchānagatassā”ti jānitvā “mayampi garudhamme rakkhissāma, gacchatha dhanañcayakorabyassa santike te suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhāpetvā ānethā”ti amacce pesesi. Garudhammā vuccanti pañca sīlāni, tāni bodhisatto suparisuddhāni katvā rakkhati, yathā ca bodhisatto. Evamassa mātā [V 0.0038] aggamahesī, kaniṭṭhabhātā uparājā, purohito brāhmaṇo, rajjuggāhako amacco, sārathi seṭṭhi, doṇamāpako dovāriko, nagarasobhinī vaṇṇadāsīti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Even after that elephant was brought to the Kalinga country, the rain still did not fall. The king of Kalinga, wondering, 'Even now it does not rain, what could be the reason?' inquired and learned: 'The king of Kuru protects the weighty principles; hence in his kingdom, it rains every half-month and every ten days. This is the power of the king’s virtue, not of this animal.' Realizing this, he said, 'We too shall protect the weighty principles. Go to Dhanañjayakorabya, have those principles inscribed on a golden plate, and bring it here.' He sent his ministers. The 'weighty principles' are said to be the five precepts. The Bodhisatta protected them, having made them utterly pure. And just as the Bodhisatta did, so did his mother, the chief queen, his younger brother the viceroy, the brahmin priest, the minister who held the measuring rope, the charioteer, the merchant, the grain measurer, the doorkeeper, and the city-beautifying courtesan. Hence it is said:

“Rājā mātā mahesī ca, uparājā purohito;

Rajjuggāho sārathī seṭṭhi, doṇo dovāriko tathā;

Gaṇikā te ekādasa, garudhamme patiṭṭhitā”ti.

"The king, the mother, and the chief queen, the viceroy, the priest, the rope-holder, the charioteer, the merchant, the grain measurer, and the doorkeeper, likewise the courtesan—these eleven were established in the weighty principles."

Te [P 0.0039] amaccā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Mahāsatto “mayhaṃ garudhamme kukkuccaṃ atthi, mātā pana me surakkhitaṃ rakkhati, tassā santike gaṇhathā”ti vatvā tehi “mahārāja, kukkuccaṃ nāma sikkhākāmassa sallekhavuttino hoti, detha no”ti yācito “pāṇo na hantabbo, adinnaṃ na ādātabbaṃ, kāmesumicchācāro na caritabbo, musā na bhaṇitabbaṃ, majjaṃ na pātabba”nti suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhāpetvā “evaṃ santepi mātu santike gaṇhathā”ti āha.

Those ministers approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and informed him of the matter. The Great Being said: 'I have a scruple concerning the weighty principles, but my mother protects them very well. Take them from her.' When they entreated him, saying, 'Great King, a scruple is something that occurs to one who desires the training and lives an austere life; give them to us,' he had the following written on a golden plate: 'A living being should not be killed; what is not given should not be taken; sexual misconduct should not be practiced; falsehood should not be spoken; intoxicants should not be consumed.' He then said: 'Even so, receive them from my mother.'

Dūtā [M 0.0040] rājānaṃ vanditvā tassā santikaṃ gantvā “devi, tumhe kira garudhammaṃ rakkhatha, taṃ no dethā”ti vadiṃsu. Bodhisattassa mātāpi tatheva attano kukkuccassa atthibhāvaṃ vatvāva tehi yācitā adāsi. Tathā mahesiādayopi. Te sabbesampi santike suvaṇṇapaṭṭe garudhamme likhāpetvā dantapuraṃ gantvā kaliṅgarañño datvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Sopi rājā tasmiṃ dhamme vattamāno pañca sīlāni pūresi. Tato sakalakaliṅgaraṭṭhe devo vassi. Tīṇi bhayāni vūpasantāni. Raṭṭhaṃ khemaṃ subhikkhaṃ ahosi. Bodhisatto yāvajīvaṃ dānādīni puññāni katvā sapariso saggapuraṃ pūresi.

The envoys, having paid homage to the king, went to her and said: 'Your Majesty, it is said that you protect the weighty principles; please give them to us.' The Bodhisatta’s mother, also stating that she had her own scruple, gave them when entreated. Likewise did the chief queen and the others. The envoys had the weighty principles inscribed on a golden plate after receiving them from all of them, and then went to Dantapura. They gave it to the king of Kalinga and reported the events. That king, abiding by that Dhamma, fulfilled the five precepts. Thereafter, rain fell throughout the entire kingdom of Kalinga. The three fears were allayed. The country became secure and prosperous. The Bodhisattva, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving for as long as he lived, filled the heavenly realm, together with his retinue.

Tadā gaṇikādayo uppalavaṇṇādayo ahesuṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

At that time, the courtesan and the others became Uppalavaṇṇā and the others. For this has been said:

“Gaṇikā uppalavaṇṇā, puṇṇo dovāriko tadā;

Rajjuggāho ca kaccāno, doṇamāpako ca kolito.

"The courtesan was Uppalavaṇṇā; Puṇṇa was the doorkeeper then; the rope-holder was Kaccāna; and the grain measurer was Kolita."

“Sāriputto tadā seṭṭhi, anuruddho ca sārathi;

Brāhmaṇo kassapo thero, uparājānandapaṇḍito.

"Sāriputta was the merchant then, and Anuruddha the charioteer; the brahmin was the Elder Kassapa, the viceroy was the wise Ānanda."

“Mahesī [V 0.0039] rāhulamātā, māyādevī janettikā;

Kururājā bodhisatto, evaṃ dhāretha jātaka”nti. (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.361 haṃsaghātakabhikkhuvatthu);

"The chief queen was Rāhula’s mother, the birth-mother was Māyādevī; the king of Kuru was the Bodhisatta. Thus should you remember the Jātaka."

Idhāpi nekkhammapāramiādayo sesadhammā ca vuttanayeneva niddhāretabbāti.

Here too, the perfection of renunciation and the other remaining principles should be determined in the same manner as has been stated.

Kururājacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Conduct of the King of Kuru is concluded.

4. Mahāsudassanacariyāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Conduct of Mahāsudassana

28. Catutthe [P 0.0040] kusāvatimhi nagareti kusāvatīnāmake nagare, yasmiṃ ṭhāne etarahi kusinārā niviṭṭhā. Mahīpatīti khattiyo, nāmena mahāsudassano nāma. Cakkavattīti cakkaratanaṃ vatteti catūhi vā sampatticakkehi vattati, tehi ca paraṃ pavatteti, parahitāya ca iriyāpathacakkānaṃ vatto etasmiṃ atthītipi cakkavattī. Atha vā catūhi acchariyadhammehi saṅgahavatthūhi ca samannāgatena, parehi anabhibhavanīyassa anatikkamanīyassa āṇāsaṅkhātassa cakkassa vatto etasmiṃ atthītipi cakkavattī. Pariṇāyakaratanapubbaṅgamena [M 0.0041] hatthiratanādipamukhena mahābalakāyena puññānubhāvanibbattena kāyabalena ca samannāgatattā mahabbalo. Yadā āsinti sambandho. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā –

28. In the fourth, in the city of Kusāvatī—that is, in the city named Kusāvatī, in the place where the present-day Kusinārā is situated. A great ruler means a noble warrior; by name, Mahāsudassana. A wheel-turning monarch is one who turns the wheel-treasure, or who functions with the four wheels of success and by these causes others to function, and in whom a cycle of conduct for the benefit of others exists—thus he is a wheel-turning monarch. Alternatively, he is a wheel-turning monarch because in him, who is endowed with the four wonderful qualities and the bases of sympathy, exists the turning of the wheel known as authority, which is unassailable and inviolable by others. He possessed great power because he was endowed with a great and powerful army, preceded by the advisor-treasure and headed by treasures such as the elephant-treasure, and with bodily strength born from the power of merit. 'When I was...'—this is the connection. Herein follows the sequential story:

Atīte kira mahāpuriso sudassanattabhāvato tatiye attabhāve gahapatikule nibbatto dharamānakassa buddhassa sāsane ekaṃ theraṃ araññavāsaṃ vasantaṃ attano kammena araññaṃ paviṭṭho rukkhamūle nisinnaṃ disvā “idha mayā ayyassa paṇṇasālaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā attano kammaṃ pahāya dabbasambhāraṃ chinditvā nivāsayoggaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ katvā dvāraṃ yojetvā kaṭṭhattharaṇaṃ katvā “karissati nu kho paribhogaṃ, na nu kho karissatī”ti ekamante nisīdi. Thero antogāmato āgantvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā kaṭṭhattharaṇe nisīdi. Mahāsattopi naṃ upasaṅkamitvā “phāsukā, bhante, paṇṇasālā”ti pucchi. Phāsukā, bhaddamukha, pabbajitasāruppāti. Vasissatha, bhante, idhāti? Āma, upāsakāti. So adhivāsanākāreneva “vasissatī”ti ñatvā “nibaddhaṃ mayhaṃ gharadvāraṃ āgantabba”nti paṭijānāpetvā niccaṃ attano [V 0.0040] ghareyeva bhattavissaggaṃ kārāpesi. So paṇṇasālāyaṃ kaṭasārakaṃ pattharitvā mañcapīṭhaṃ paññapesi, apassenaṃ nikkhipi, pādakaṭhalikaṃ ṭhapesi, pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇi, caṅkamaṃ katvā vālukaṃ okiri, parissayavinodanatthaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ kaṇṭakavatiyā parikkhipi, tathā pokkharaṇiṃ caṅkamañca. Tesaṃ antovatipariyante tālapantiyo ropesi. Evamādinā [P 0.0041] āvāsaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā therassa ticīvaraṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ samaṇaparikkhāraṃ adāsi. Therassa hi tadā bodhisattena ticīvarapiṇḍapātapattathālakaparissāvanadhamakaraṇaparibhogabhājanachattupāhanaudakatumbasūcikattara- yaṭṭhiārakaṇṭakapipphalinakhacchedanapadīpeyyādi pabbajitānaṃ paribhogajātaṃ adinnaṃ nāma nāhosi. So pañca sīlāni rakkhanto uposathaṃ karonto yāvajīvaṃ theraṃ upaṭṭhahi. Thero tattheva vasanto arahattaṃ patvā parinibbāyi.

In the past, it is said, the Great Being, in his third existence prior to his existence as Mahāsudassana, was reborn into a householder’s family during the dispensation of the living Buddha Kassapa. Having entered the forest on his own business, he saw an elder who was a forest-dweller seated at the foot of a tree. Thinking, 'It is fitting that I build a leaf-hut for the venerable one,' he set aside his own work, cut the building materials, and made a leaf-hut suitable for dwelling. He fitted a door, laid a wooden floor, and then, thinking, 'Will he make use of it, or will he not?' he sat to one side. The elder, having returned from the village, entered the leaf-hut and sat upon the wooden floor. The Great Being approached him and asked, 'Venerable sir, is the leaf-hut comfortable?' 'It is comfortable, good sir, and suitable for a renunciate.' 'Venerable sir, will you dwell here?' 'Yes, lay follower.' Understanding from his gesture of consent that he would dwell there, he had him promise, 'You must come regularly to my house door,' and arranged for a constant offering of food at his own house. In the leaf-hut, he spread a reed mat, prepared a bed and a seat, set up a leaning-board, and placed a foot-scraper. He dug a pond, made a walking path and scattered sand upon it. To ward off dangers, he enclosed the leaf-hut with a thorn fence, and likewise the pond and the walking path. At the inner edge of the fence, he planted rows of palm trees. Having thus completed the dwelling, beginning with the three robes, he gave the elder all the requisites of a monk. Indeed, at that time, there was nothing among the things used by renunciates that the Bodhisatta did not give to the elder, such as: the three robes, alms-food, bowl, dish, water-strainer, filtered water-pot, vessels for use, umbrella, sandals, water-gourd, needle, small knife, staff, awl, thorn-remover, long pepper, nail-cutter, and lamp. He, observing the five precepts and undertaking the Uposatha, attended to the elder for as long as he lived. The elder, dwelling there, attained Arahantship and passed into final Nibbāna.

29. Bodhisattopi yāvatāyukaṃ puññaṃ katvā devaloke nibbattitvā tato cuto manussalokaṃ āgacchanto kusāvatiyā rājadhāniyā nibbattitvā mahāsudassano nāma rājā ahosi cakkavattī. Tassissariyānubhāvo “bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano nāma ahosi khattiyo [M 0.0042] muddhāvasitto”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.242) nayena sutte āgato eva. Tassa kira caturāsīti nagarasahassāni kusāvatīrājadhānippamukhāni, caturāsīti pāsādasahassāni dhammapāsādappamukhāni, caturāsīti kūṭāgārasahassāni mahābyūhakūṭāgārappamukhāni, tāni sabbāni tassa therassa katāya ekissā paṇṇasālāya nissandena nibbattāni, caturāsīti pallaṅkasahassāni nāgasahassāni assasahassāni rathasahassāni tassa dinnassa mañcapīṭhassa, caturāsīti maṇisahassāni tassa dinnassa padīpassa, caturāsīti pokkharaṇisahassāni ekapokkharaṇiyā, caturāsīti itthisahassāni puttasahassāni gahapatisahassāni ca pattathālakādiparibhogārahassa pabbajitaparikkhāradānassa, caturāsīti dhenusahassāni pañcagorasadānassa, caturāsīti vatthakoṭṭhasahassāni nivāsanapārupanadānassa, caturāsīti thālipākasahassāni bhojanadānassa nissandena nibbattāni. So sattahi ratanehi catūhi iddhīhi ca samannāgato rājādhirājā hutvā sakalaṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ pathavimaṇḍalaṃ dhammena abhivijiya ajjhāvasanto anekasatesu ṭhānesu dānasālāyo kāretvā mahādānaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Divasassa tikkhattuṃ nagare bheriṃ carāpesi “yo yaṃ icchati, so dānasālāsu āgantvā taṃ gaṇhātū”ti. Tena vuttaṃ “tatthāhaṃ divase tikkhattuṃ, ghosāpemi tahiṃ tahi”ntiādi.

29. The Bodhisatta, too, having performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, was reborn in a celestial world. Passing away from there and coming to the human world, he was reborn in the royal city of Kusāvatī and became a wheel-turning king named Mahāsudassana. His majesty and power are described in the Sutta in the passage beginning: 'In the past, Ānanda, there was a king named Mahāsudassana, an anointed noble warrior...' (Dī. Ni. 2.242). It is said that he had eighty-four thousand cities with the royal city of Kusāvatī as the foremost; eighty-four thousand palaces with the Dhamma Palace as the foremost; and eighty-four thousand gabled chambers with the Great Array gabled chamber as the foremost—all these arose as the result of the single leaf-hut made for that elder. Eighty-four thousand couches, elephants, horses, and chariots arose as the result of his gift of a bed and seat. Eighty-four thousand jewels arose as the result of his gift of a lamp. Eighty-four thousand ponds arose from the one pond. Eighty-four thousand women, sons, and householders arose as the result of his gift of the requisites of a renunciate, such as bowls, dishes, and other items suitable for use. Eighty-four thousand milk-cows arose as the result of his gift of the five products of the cow. Eighty-four thousand storehouses of cloth arose as the result of his gift of garments for wearing and covering. Eighty-four thousand pots of cooked food arose as the result of his gift of food. Endowed with the seven treasures and the four spiritual powers, he became a king of kings. Having righteously conquered and ruling over the entire earth bounded by the ocean, he had alms-halls built in many hundreds of places and established great giving. Three times a day, he had a drum sounded throughout the city, proclaiming: 'Whoever desires anything, let them come to the alms-halls and receive it!' Therefore it was said: 'There, three times a day, I had the announcement made here and there...' and so on.

Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ nagare. “Tadāha”ntipi pāṭho, tassa tadā ahaṃ, mahāsudassanakāleti [V 0.0041] attho. Tahiṃ tahinti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne, tassa tassa pākārassa anto ca bahi cāti [P 0.0042] attho. Ko kiṃ icchatīti brāhmaṇādīsu yo koci satto annādīsu deyyadhammesu yaṃ kiñci icchati. Patthetīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Kassa kiṃ dīyatu dhananti anekavāraṃ pariyāyantarehi ca dānaghosanāya pavattitabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, etena dānapāramiyā sarūpaṃ dasseti. Deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakavikapparahitā hi bodhisattānaṃ dānapāramīti.

Herein, `tattha` means 'in that city'. 'Then I' is also a reading; its meaning is: 'at that time, I, during the time of Mahāsudassana'. `Tahiṃ tahiṃ` means 'in this and that place', that is, 'inside and outside of this and that rampart'. 'Who desires what?' means: whatever being among brahmins and others desires whatever gift among food and so on. `Pattheti` is a synonym for that. 'To whom should what wealth be given?' is stated repeatedly and in various ways to show that the proclamation of giving occurred, and by this, it shows the nature of the perfection of giving. For the perfection of giving of Bodhisattas is free from discrimination regarding the gift and the recipient.

30. Idāni dānaghosanāya tassa tassa deyyadhammassa anucchavikapuggalaparikittanaṃ dassetuṃ “ko chātako”tiādi vuttaṃ.

30. Now, to show the announcement of the suitable person for each and every gift by means of the proclamation of giving, the verse beginning 'Who is hungry?' was spoken.

Tattha [M 0.0043] chātakoti jighacchito. Tasitoti pipāsito. Ko mālaṃ ko vilepanantipi “icchatī”ti padaṃ ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Naggoti vatthavikalo, vatthena atthikoti adhippāyo. Paridahissatīti nivāsissati.

Herein, `chātako` means one who is hungry. `Tasito` means one who is thirsty. With the phrases 'Who a garland?' and 'Who an ointment?', the word `icchati` should be brought in and connected. `Naggo` means one who is deficient in clothes; the intention is 'one in need of a garment'. `Paridahissati` means 'will wear'.

31. Ko pathe chattamādetīti ko pathiko pathe magge attano vassavātātaparakkhaṇatthaṃ chattaṃ gaṇhāti, chattena atthikoti attho. Kopāhanā mudū subhāti dassanīyatāya subhā sukhasamphassatāya mudū upāhanā attano pādānaṃ cakkhūnañca rakkhaṇatthaṃ. Ko ādetīti ko tāhi atthikoti adhippāyo. Sāyañca pāto cāti ettha ca-saddena majjhanhike cāti āharitvā vattabbaṃ. “Divase tikkhattuṃ ghosāpemī”ti hi vuttaṃ.

31. 'Who on the path takes an umbrella?' means: who, a traveler on the path, on the road, takes an umbrella for the purpose of protecting oneself from rain, wind, and sun? The meaning is: 'one in need of an umbrella'. 'Who soft, beautiful sandals?' means: sandals that are beautiful due to being pleasant to see and soft due to having a pleasant touch, for the protection of one's own feet and eyes. 'Who takes them?' The intention is: 'who is in need of them?'. Here, in 'evening and morning', by the word `ca`, 'and at midday' should be brought in and stated. For it was said: 'I have it proclaimed three times a day'.

32. Na taṃ dasasu ṭhānesūti taṃ dānaṃ na dasasu ṭhānesu paṭiyattanti yojanā. Napi ṭhānasatesu vā paṭiyattaṃ, api ca kho anekasatesu ṭhānesu paṭiyattaṃ. Yācake dhananti yācake uddissa dhanaṃ paṭiyattaṃ upakkhaṭaṃ. Dvādasayojanāyāme hi nagare sattayojanavitthate sattasu pākārantaresu satta tālapantiparikkhepā, tāsu tālapantīsu caturāsīti pokkharaṇisahassāni pāṭiyekkaṃ pokkharaṇitīre mahādānaṃ paṭṭhapitaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

32. 'Not that in ten places'—the construction is: 'that gift was not prepared in ten places'. Nor was it prepared in a hundred places, but rather it was prepared in many hundreds of places. 'Wealth for beggars' means: wealth was prepared and set aside, having been designated for beggars. For in a city twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width, in the intervals between the seven ramparts, there were seven enclosures of rows of palm trees. Among those rows of palm trees, there were eighty-four thousand ponds, and at the bank of each and every pond, a great gift was established. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Paṭṭhapesi kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tāsaṃ pokkharaṇīnaṃ tīre evarūpaṃ dānaṃ annaṃ annatthikassa, pānaṃ pānatthikassa, vatthaṃ vatthatthikassa, yānaṃ yānatthikassa, sayanaṃ sayanatthikassa, itthiṃ itthitthikassa, hiraññaṃ hiraññatthikassa, suvaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇatthikassā”ti (dī. ni. 2.254).

'Indeed, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana established at the bank of those ponds a gift of this kind: food for one in need of food, drink for one in need of drink, clothing for one in need of clothing, a vehicle for one in need of a vehicle, a bed for one in need of a bed, a woman for one in need of a woman, silver for one in need of silver, and gold for one in need of gold' (DN 2.254).

33. Tatthāyaṃ [V 0.0042] dānassa pavattitākāro – mahāpuriso hi itthīnañca purisānañca anucchavike alaṅkāre kāretvā itthimattameva tattha paricāravasena sesañca sabbaṃ pariccāgavasena [P 0.0043] ṭhapetvā “rājā mahāsudassano dānaṃ deti, taṃ yathāsukhaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. Mahājanā pokkharaṇitīraṃ gantvā nhatvā vatthādīni nivāsetvā mahāsampattiṃ anubhavitvā yesaṃ tādisāni atthi, te pahāya gacchanti[M 0.0044]. Yesaṃ natthi, te gahetvā gacchanti. Ye hatthiyānādīsupi nisīditvā yathāsukhaṃ vicaritvā varasayanesupi sayitvā sampattiṃ anubhavitvā itthīhipi saddhiṃ sampattiṃ anubhavitvā sattavidharatanapasādhanāni pasādhetvā sampattiṃ anubhavitvā yaṃ yaṃ atthikā, taṃ taṃ gahetvā gacchanti, anatthikā ohāya gacchanti. Tampi dānaṃ uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya devasikaṃ dīyateva. Tadā jambudīpavāsīnaṃ aññaṃ kammaṃ natthi, dānaṃ paribhuñjantā sampattiṃ anubhavantā vicaranti. Na tassa dānassa kālaparicchedo ahosi. Rattiñcāpi divāpi yadā yadā atthikā āgacchanti, tadā tadā dīyateva. Evaṃ mahāpuriso yāvajīvaṃ sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Tena vuttaṃ “divā vā yadi vā rattiṃ, yadi eti vanibbako”tiādi.

33. Herein, this is the manner in which the giving occurred: the Great Being had suitable ornaments made for both women and men, and having established only the women there for the purpose of attendance and all the rest for the purpose of giving away, he had a drum beaten to announce: 'King Mahāsudassana is giving a gift; enjoy it as you please.' The great populace, going to the pond banks, bathed, put on clothing and other things, and experienced great prosperity. Those who had such things would leave them behind and go. Those who did not have them would take them and go. Some, having sat in elephant-carriages and other vehicles, having wandered about as they pleased, having slept on excellent beds, having experienced prosperity, having experienced prosperity together with women, having adorned themselves with the seven kinds of jewel-ornaments, and having experienced prosperity, would take whatever they were in need of and go; those not in need would leave it behind and go. And that gift was given daily, with diligence and effort. At that time, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa had no other work; they went about enjoying the gift and experiencing prosperity. There was no time limit for that gift. Whether by night or by day, whenever those in need came, it was given. Thus the Great Being, for as long as he lived, made the whole of Jambudīpa a place where no plows were needed and carried on this great giving. Therefore it was said: 'By day or by night, if a beggar comes,' and so on.

Tattha divā vā yadi vā rattiṃ, yadi etīti etenassa yathākālaṃ dānaṃ dasseti. Yācakānañhi lābhāsāya upasaṅkamanakālo eva bodhisattānaṃ dānassa kālo nāma. Vanibbakoti yācako. Laddhā yadicchakaṃ bhoganti etena yathābhirucitaṃ dānaṃ. Yo yo hi yācako yaṃ yaṃ deyyadhammaṃ icchati, tassa tassa taṃtadeva bodhisatto deti. Na tassa mahagghadullabhādibhāvaṃ attano uparodhaṃ cintesi. Pūrahatthova gacchatīti etena yāvadicchakaṃ dānaṃ dasseti, yattakañhi yācakā icchanti, tattakaṃ aparihāpetvāva mahāsatto deti uḷārajjhāsayatāya ca mahiddhikatāya ca.

Herein, by 'By day or by night, if one comes', it shows giving at any time. For, with Bodhisattas, the very time that beggars approach with the hope of gain is called the time for giving. `Vanibbako` means a beggar. By 'Having obtained desired possessions', it shows giving according to what is wished for. For whatever gift a beggar desires, the Bodhisatta gives that very thing to him. He does not consider its being costly or difficult to obtain as an obstacle to himself. By 'He departs with full hands', it shows giving as much as is desired. For however much the beggars desire, the Great Being gives that much without diminishing it, due to his noble disposition and great power.

34. “Yāvajīvika”nti etena dānassa kālapariyantābhāvaṃ dasseti. Samādānato paṭṭhāya hi mahāsattā yāvapāripūri vemajjhe na kālaparicchedaṃ karonti, bodhisambhārasambharaṇe saṅkocābhāvena antarantarā avosānāpattito maraṇenapi anupacchedo eva, tato parampi tatheva paṭipajjanato, “yāvajīvika”nti pana mahāsudassanacaritassa vasena vuttaṃ. Napāhaṃ dessaṃ dhanaṃ dammīti idaṃ dhanaṃ nāma mayhaṃ [P 0.0044] na dessaṃ amanāpanti evarūpaṃ mahādānaṃ dento gehato ca dhanaṃ nīharāpemi. Napi natthi nicayo mayīti mama samīpe dhananicayo dhanasaṅgaho nāpi natthi, sallekhavuttisamaṇo viya asaṅgahopi na homīti attho. Idaṃ yena ajjhāsayena tassidaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattitaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ.

34. “As long as life lasts”—by this is shown the absence of a time limit for the gift. Indeed, from the moment of their undertaking until its complete fulfillment, Great Beings do not set a time limit in the interim. Due to their lack of hesitation in accumulating the requisites for enlightenment, having attained a state of non-cessation in the intervals, there is no interruption even by death, because they practice in the very same way even after that. The phrase “as long as life lasts,” however, is spoken with reference to the conduct of Mahāsudassana. “I do not give wealth that I dislike” means: “This wealth is not disliked by me, not unpleasing.” While giving such a great gift, I have wealth brought out from the house. “Nor is there any accumulation for me” means: “In my presence there is no accumulation of wealth, no hoarding of wealth, nor does it exist; yet I am not without stores like an ascetic who practices austerity.” This is said to show the intention with which this great gift was set in motion by him.

35. Idāni [M 0.0045][V 0.0043] taṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathāpi āturo nāmā”tiādimāha. Tatthidaṃ upamāsaṃsandanena saddhiṃ atthadassanaṃ – yathā nāma āturo rogābhibhūto puriso rogato attānaṃ parimocetukāmo dhanena hiraññasuvaṇṇādinā vejjaṃ tikicchakaṃ tappetvā ārādhetvā yathāvidhi paṭipajjanto tato rogato vimuccati.

35. Now, to make this clear by means of a simile, he spoke the verse beginning, “Just as one who is afflicted…”. Therein, this is the explanation of the meaning together with the application of the simile: Just as a man who is afflicted and overcome by disease, wishing to free himself from that disease, having satisfied and pleased a physician, a healer, with wealth such as gold and silver, and practicing according to the prescribed method, is thereby freed from that disease.

36. Tatheva evameva ahampi aṭṭabhūtaṃ sakalalokaṃ kilesarogato sakalasaṃsāradukkharogato ca parimocetukāmo tassa tato parimocanassa ayaṃ sabbasāpateyyapariccāgo dānapāramiupāyoti jānamāno bujjhamāno asesato deyyadhammassa paṭiggāhakānañca vasena anavasesato mahādānassa vasena sattānaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ paripūretuṃ attano ca na mayhaṃ dānapāramī paripuṇṇā, tasmā ūnamananti pavattaṃ ūnaṃ manaṃ pūrayituṃ pavattayituṃ vanibbake yācake adāsiṃ taṃ dānaṃ evarūpaṃ mahādānaṃ dadāmi, tañca kho tasmiṃ dānadhamme tassa ca phale nirālayo anapekkho apaccāso kiñcipi apaccāsīsamāno kevalaṃ sambodhimanupattiyā sabbaññutaññāṇameva adhigantuṃ demīti.

36. Even so, I too, desiring to liberate the entire afflicted world from the disease of defilements and from the disease of the suffering of the entire cycle of existence—knowing and understanding that this relinquishment of all property is the means for the perfection of giving for their liberation from that—gave to mendicants and beggars in order to fulfill the aspirations of beings by means of a great gift, completely and without remainder with respect to both the object to be given and the recipients, and also for my own sake. Thinking, “My perfection of giving is not complete,” and therefore, to fulfill and set in motion a mind that was deficient, I give such a great gift. And I give it without attachment, without expectation, and without longing for that object of giving or for its fruit. Not longing for anything whatsoever, I give solely to attain supreme enlightenment, the knowledge of omniscience.

Evaṃ mahāsatto mahādānaṃ pavattento attano puññānubhāvanibbattaṃ dhammapāsādaṃ abhiruyha mahābyūhakūṭāgāradvāre eva kāmavitakkādayo nivattetvā tattha sovaṇṇamaye rājapallaṅke nisinno jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā tato nikkhamitvā sovaṇṇamayaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ pavisitvā tattha rajatamaye pallaṅke nisinno cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā caturāsīti vassasahassāni jhānasamāpattīhi vītināmetvā maraṇasamaye dassanāya upagatānaṃ subhaddādevīpamukhānaṃ caturāsītiyā itthāgārasahassānaṃ amaccapārisajjādīnañca –

Thus the Great Being, while setting in motion the great giving, ascended the Dhamma Palace that had arisen through the power of his own merit. At the very doorway of the great ornate gabled chamber, having turned back sensual thoughts and the like, and seated there on a golden royal couch, he produced the jhānas and higher knowledges. Then, emerging from there, he entered a golden gabled chamber, and seated there on a silver couch, he developed the four divine abidings. Having passed eighty-four thousand years in the attainments of jhāna, at the time of his death, to Queen Subhaddā and the eighty-four thousand women of the royal chambers, the ministers, attendants, and others who had come to see him, he said:

“Aniccā [P 0.0045] vata saṅkhārā, uppādavayadhammino;

Uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho”ti. (dī. ni. 2.221, 272; saṃ. ni. 1.186; 2.143) –

“Impermanent, alas, are formations, subject to arising and passing away. Having arisen, they cease; their pacification is bliss.”

Imāya gāthāya ovaditvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokaparāyano ahosi.

Having instructed them with this verse, at the end of his life, he became one bound for the Brahma-world.

Tadā subhaddādevī rāhulamātā ahosi, pariṇāyakaratanaṃ rāhulo, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, mahāsudassano pana lokanātho.

At that time, Queen Subhaddā was the mother of Rāhula; the jewel of a counselor was Rāhula; the remaining assembly became the Buddha’s assembly; and Mahāsudassana was the Lord of the World.

Idhāpi [M 0.0046][V 0.0044] dasa pāramiyo sarūpato labbhanti eva, dānajjhāsayassa pana uḷāratāya dānapāramī eva pāḷiyaṃ āgatā. Sesadhammā heṭṭhā vuttanayā eva. Tathā uḷāre sattaratanasamujjale catudīpissariyepi ṭhitassa tādisaṃ bhogasukhaṃ analaṅkaritvā kāmavitakkādayo dūrato vikkhambhetvā tathārūpe mahādāne pavattentasseva caturāsīti vassasahassāni samāpattīhi vītināmetvā aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammakathaṃ katvāpi vipassanāya anussukkanaṃ sabbattha anissaṅgatāti evamādayo guṇānubhāvā niddhāretabbāti.

Here too, the ten perfections are indeed found in their own form; however, due to the nobility of his disposition for giving, only the perfection of giving is mentioned in the Pāḷi. The remaining qualities are just as explained before. Furthermore, the following powers of virtue should be discerned: that even while established in noble sovereignty over the four continents, resplendent with the seven treasures, he did not indulge in such enjoyment of wealth; that he suppressed sensual thoughts and the like from afar; that while setting in motion such great giving, he spent eighty-four thousand years in meditative attainments; and that even after giving a Dhamma talk connected with impermanence and so on, there was his not being eager for insight and his non-attachment in all things.

Mahāsudassanacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Conduct of Mahāsudassana is concluded.

5. Mahāgovindacariyāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Conduct of Mahāgovinda

Pañcame sattarājapurohitoti sattabhūādīnaṃ sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ sabbakiccānusāsakapurohito. Pūjito naradevehīti tehi eva aññehi ca jambudīpe sabbeheva khattiyehi catupaccayapūjāya sakkārasammānena ca pūjito. Mahāgovindabrāhmaṇoti mahānubhāvatāya govindassābhisekena abhisittatāya ca “mahāgovindo”ti saṅkhaṃ gato brāhmaṇo, abhisittakālato paṭṭhāya hi bodhisattassa ayaṃ samaññā jātā, nāmena pana jotipālo nāma. Tassa kira jātadivase sabbāvudhāni jotiṃsu. Rājāpi paccūsasamaye attano maṅgalāvudhaṃ pajjalitaṃ disvā bhīto attano purohitaṃ bodhisattassa pitaraṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ pucchitvā “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, mayhaṃ putto jāto, tassānubhāvena na kevalaṃ rājageheyeva, sakalanagarepi āvudhāni pajjaliṃsu, na [P 0.0046] taṃ nissāya tuyhaṃ antarāyo atthi, sakalajambudīpe pana paññāya tena samo na bhavissati, tassetaṃ pubbanimitta”nti purohitena samassāsito tuṭṭhacitto “kumārassa khīramūlaṃ hotū”ti sahassaṃ datvā “vayappattakāle mayhaṃ dassethā”ti āha. So vuddhippatto aparabhāge alamatthadasso sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ sabbakiccānusāsako hutvā pabbajitvā ca satte diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikehi anatthehi pāletvā atthehi niyojesi. Iti jotitattā pālanasamatthatāya [M 0.0047] ca “jotipālo”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “nāmena jotipālo nāmā”ti (dī. ni. 2.304).

In the fifth, 'the chaplain of seven kings' means the chaplain who advised all seven kings, beginning with Sattabhū, in all their duties. 'Worshipped by kings' means he was honored by those very kings and all other khattiyas in Jambudīpa with the four requisites and with reverence and respect. 'The great brahmin Govinda' refers to the brahmin who became renowned as 'Mahāgovinda' due to his great majesty and his anointing with the Govinda consecration. From the time of his anointing, this designation was given to the Bodhisatta, though his personal name was Jotipāla. It is said that on the day of his birth, all weapons shone brightly. The king, too, seeing his own auspicious weapons blazing at dawn, became frightened. When the king’s chaplain—the Bodhisatta’s father—arrived for his morning audience, the king asked him about it. The chaplain reassured him, saying, 'Do not fear, great king. My son has been born. By his power, not only in the royal household but throughout the entire city, weapons have blazed. This is not a threat to you. Rather, it is a sign that in all of Jambudīpa, there will be none equal to him in wisdom.' Pleased and comforted, the king gave a thousand coins, saying, 'Let this be for the prince's sustenance. When he comes of age, bring him to me.' As he grew up, in due time, being capable of discerning what was beneficial, he became the advisor of the seven kings, guiding them in all matters. After renouncing the world, he protected the seven kings from harms pertaining to the present life and the life to come, and directed them toward what is beneficial. Thus, because he illumined and was capable of protecting, they gave him the name 'Jotipāla.' Hence it is said, 'by name, he was called Jotipāla' (Dī. Ni. 2.304).

Tattha bodhisatto disampatissa nāma rañño purohitassa govindabrāhmaṇassa putto hutvā attano pitu tassa ca rañño accayena tassa putto reṇu, sahāyā cassa sattabhū, brahmadatto, vessabhū[V 0.0045], bharato, dve ca dhataraṭṭhāti ime satta rājāno yathā aññamaññaṃ na vivadanti. Evaṃ rajje patiṭṭhāpetvā tesaṃ atthadhamme anusāsanto jambudīpatale sabbesaṃ rājūnaṃ aññesañca brāhmaṇānaṃ devanāgagahapatikānaṃ sakkato garukato mānito pūjito apacito uttamaṃ gāravaṭṭhānaṃ patto ahosi. Tassa atthadhammesu kusalatāya “mahāgovindo”tveva samaññā udapādi. Yathāha “govindo vata, bho brāhmaṇo, mahāgovindo vata, bho brāhmaṇo”ti (dī. ni. 2.305). Tena vuttaṃ –

There, the Bodhisatta was born as the son of Govinda the brahmin, the chaplain of King Disampati. After the passing of his father and that king, he established the king's son Reṇu and his friends—Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, Vessabhū, Bharata, and the two Dhataraṭṭhas—these seven kings in their kingdoms in such a way that they would not quarrel with one another. Advising them in matters of benefit and righteousness, he was honored, respected, esteemed, and revered by all the kings, other brahmins, devas, nāgas, and householders throughout the land of Jambudīpa, attaining the highest position of reverence. Due to his skill in matters of benefit and righteousness, the designation 'Mahāgovinda' arose for him. As it is said: 'Truly, Govinda, O brahmin, is Mahāgovinda, O brahmin!' (Dī. Ni. 2.305). Therefore, it was said:

37.

37.

“Punāparaṃ yadā homi, sattarājapurohito;

Pūjito naradevehi, mahāgovindabrāhmaṇo”ti.

Furthermore, when I was the brahmin Mahāgovinda, chaplain to seven kings, worshipped by kings,

Atha bodhisattassa puññānubhāvasamussāhitehi rājūhi tesaṃ anuyuttehi khattiyehi brāhmaṇagahapatikehi negamajānapadehi ca uparūpari upanīto samantato mahogho viya ajjhottharamāno aparimeyyo uḷāro lābhasakkāro uppajji, yathā taṃ aparimāṇāsu jātīsu upacitavipulapuññasañcayassa uḷārābhijātassa parisuddhasīlācārassa pesalassa pariyodātasabbasippassa sabbasattesu puttasadisamahākaruṇāvipphārasiniddhamuduhadayassa. So cintesi – “etarahi kho mayhaṃ mahālābhasakkāro, yaṃnūnāhaṃ iminā sabbasatte santappetvā dānapāramiṃ paripūreyya”nti. So nagarassa majjhe catūsu dvāresu attano nivesanadvāreti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ aparimitadhanapariccāgena mahādānaṃ [P 0.0047] pavattesi. Yaṃ yaṃ upāyanaṃ ānīyati, yañca attano atthāya abhisaṅkharīyati, sabbaṃ taṃ dānasālāsu eva pesesi. Evaṃ divase divase mahāpariccāgaṃ karontassa cassa cittassa titti vā santoso vā nāhosi, kuto pana saṅkoco. Dānaggañcassa lābhāsāya āgacchantehi deyyadhammaṃ gahetvā gacchantehi ca mahāsattassa ca guṇavisese kittayantehi mahājanakāyehi antonagaraṃ bahinagarañca [M 0.0048] samantato ekoghabhūtaṃ kappavuṭṭhānamahāvāyusaṅghaṭṭaparibbhamitaṃ viya mahāsamuddaṃ ekakolāhalaṃ ekaninnādaṃ ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, incited by the power of the Bodhisatta’s merit, kings, their attendant khattiyas, brahmins, householders, and people of the towns and countryside from all around brought him offerings in great abundance. An immeasurable and magnificent flood of gain and honor arose for him, overwhelming all, just as one would expect for one who had accumulated vast merit over countless births, was of noble birth, possessed pure conduct and gentle ways, was skilled in all arts, and whose heart was tender and soft, pervaded with great compassion for all beings as if they were his own children. He thought, 'Now I have great gain and honor. Let me satisfy all beings with this and perfect the pāramī of generosity.' So, in the middle of the city, at the four gates, and at the entrance to his own residence, he had six alms-halls built and began giving great gifts daily, offering immeasurable wealth. Whatever gifts were brought to him or prepared for his own use, he sent them all to the alms-halls. Day after day, as he made such great offerings, his mind knew no satiety or contentment—how much less any reluctance. By the great multitude of people who came seeking gifts, departed taking the things to be given, and praised the special virtues of the Great Being, the city, inside and out, became on all sides like a single flood, like the great ocean churned by a mighty wind at the end of the aeon—one great clamor, one great sound. Thus it is said:

38.

38.

“Tadāhaṃ sattarajjesu, yaṃ me āsi upāyanaṃ;

Tena demi mahādānaṃ, akkhobhaṃ sāgarūpama”nti.

Then, from the seven kingdoms, with whatever tribute came to me, I gave a great gift, unshakeable, like the ocean.

Tattha tadāhanti yadā sattarājapurohito mahāgovindabrāhmaṇo homi, tadā ahaṃ. Sattarajjesūti reṇuādīnaṃ sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ rajjesu. Akkhobhanti abbhantarehi ca bāhirehi ca paccatthikehi [V 0.0046] appaṭisedhanīyatāya kenaci akkhobhanīyaṃ. “Accubbha”ntipi pāṭho. Atipuṇṇadānajjhāsayassa deyyadhammassa ca uḷārabhāvena vipulabhāvena ca ativiya paripuṇṇanti attho. Sāgarūpamanti sāgarasadisaṃ, yathā sāgare udakaṃ sakalenapi lokena harantena khepetuṃ na sakkā, evaṃ tassa dānagge deyyadhammanti.

There, 'then I' refers to when I was the great brahmin Mahāgovinda, the royal chaplain of seven kings. 'In the seven kingdoms' means in the kingdoms of the seven kings, beginning with Reṇu. 'Unshakeable' means, being impossible to obstruct by any internal or external adversaries, it was unshakeable by anyone. There is also a variant reading: 'Accubbha.' It means 'exceedingly full' due to the intention of exceedingly abundant giving and the magnificence and vastness of the gifts to be given. 'Like the ocean' means like the ocean; just as the water in the ocean cannot be exhausted even if the whole world were to continually draw from it, so too the things to be given at his alms-hall could not be exhausted.

39. Osānagāthāya varaṃ dhananti uttamaṃ icchitaṃ vā dhanaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

39. In the concluding verse, 'best wealth' means supreme or desired wealth. The rest is as stated before.

Evaṃ mahāsatto paṭhamakappikamahāmegho viya mahāvassaṃ avibhāgena mahantaṃ dānavassaṃ vassāpento dānabyāvaṭo hutvāpi sesaṃ sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ atthadhamme appamatto anusāsati. Satta ca brāhmaṇamahāsāle vijjāsippaṃ sikkhāpeti, satta ca nhātakasatāni mante vāceti. Tassa aparena samayena evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato “sakkhi mahāgovindo brāhmaṇo brahmānaṃ passati, sakkhi mahāgovindo brāhmaṇo brahmunā sākaccheti sallapati mantetī”ti (dī. ni. 2.312). So cintesi – “etarahi kho mayhaṃ ayaṃ abhūto kittisaddo abbhuggato ‘brahmānaṃ passati, sakkhi mahāgovindo brāhmaṇo brahmunā sākaccheti sallapati mantetī’ti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ bhūtaṃ eva kareyya”nti. So “te satta rājāno satta ca brāhmaṇamahāsāle satta ca nhātakasatāni attano puttadārañca āpucchitvā brahmānaṃ [P 0.0048] passeyya”nti cittaṃ paṇidhāya vassike cattāro māse brahmavihārabhāvanamanuyuñji. Tassa cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya brahmā sanaṅkumāro purato pāturahosi. Taṃ disvā mahāpuriso pucchi –

Thus the great being, like the first great rain cloud of the aeon, causing a great rain of gifts to pour down impartially, though occupied with giving, diligently instructed those seven kings in what is beneficial and righteous. He had the seven great brahmin householders taught the arts and sciences, and he had the seven hundred initiated brahmins recite the sacred verses. After some time, this fair report arose concerning him: 'The great brahmin Mahāgovinda sees Brahmā face to face; the great brahmin Mahāgovinda converses, speaks, and consults with Brahmā.' He thought: 'Now this unfounded report has arisen about me: "He sees Brahmā... he converses, speaks, and consults with Brahmā." What if I were to make this true?' So, having taken leave of those seven kings, the seven great brahmin householders, the seven hundred initiated brahmins, and his own wife and children, he resolved, 'I shall see Brahmā,' and for the four months of the rainy season, he applied himself to the cultivation of the divine abodes. Then Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, knowing the thought in his mind with his own mind, appeared before him. Seeing him, the great man asked:

“Vaṇṇavā [M 0.0049] yasavā sirimā, ko nu tvamasi mārisa;

Ajānantā taṃ pucchāma, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ maya”nti. (dī. ni. 2.318);

“Of fair form, glorious, and majestic, who might you be, dear sir? Not knowing you, we ask; how may we know you?”

Tassa brahmā attānaṃ jānāpento –

To him Brahmā, making himself known, said:

“Maṃ ve kumāraṃ jānanti, brahmaloke sanantanaṃ;

Sabbe jānanti maṃ devā, evaṃ govinda jānāhī”ti. (dī. ni. 2.318) –

“They know me as the Youth, the Eternal, in the Brahmā-world. All the gods know me; thus, Govinda, know me.”

Vatvā tena –

When this was said, Govinda replied:

“Āsanaṃ [V 0.0047] udakaṃ pajjaṃ, madhusākañca brahmuno;

Agghe bhavantaṃ pucchāma, agghaṃ kurutu no bhava”nti. (dī. ni. 2.318) –

“A seat, water for the feet, and choice greens are ready for Brahmā. We invite you, venerable sir, to this offering of hospitality. May your reverence partake of this offering for us.”

Upanītaṃ atithisakkāraṃ anatthikopi brahmā tassa cittasampahaṃsanatthaṃ vissāsakaraṇatthañca sampaṭicchanto “paṭiggaṇhāma te agghaṃ, yaṃ, tvaṃ govinda, bhāsasī”ti. Vatvā okāsadānatthaṃ –

Though having no need for it, Brahmā, wishing to accept the hospitality offered to a guest for the sake of gladdening Govinda's mind and inspiring his confidence, said: 'We accept your offering of hospitality, Govinda, of which you speak.' Having said this, and in order to grant him an opportunity, he continued:

“Diṭṭhadhammahitatthāya, samparāyasukhāya ca;

Katāvakāso pucchassu, yaṃkiñci abhipatthita”nti. (dī. ni. 2.318) –

“For welfare in this present life, and for happiness in the life to come, an opportunity is made; ask whatever you desire.”

Okāsamakāsi.

He made an opportunity.

Atha naṃ mahāpuriso samparāyikaṃ eva atthaṃ –

Then the great man asked him about a matter concerning only the future life:

“Pucchāmi brahmānaṃ sanaṅkumāraṃ, kaṅkhī akaṅkhiṃ paravediyesu;

Katthaṭṭhito kimhi ca sikkhamāno, pappoti macco amataṃ brahmaloka”nti. (dī. ni. 2.319) –

“I ask Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, I who am doubtful ask the one without doubt about matters to be revealed by another: Established wherein, and training in what, does a mortal attain the deathless Brahmā-world?”

Pucchi.

He asked.

Tassa brahmā byākaronto –

To him Brahmā, explaining, said:

“Hitvā mamattaṃ manujesu brahme, ekodibhūto karuṇedhimutto;

Nirāmagandho virato methunasmā, etthaṭṭhito ettha ca sikkhamāno;

Pappoti macco amataṃ brahmaloka”nti. (dī. ni. 2.319) –

“Having abandoned the sense of ‘mine’ among humans, O brahmin, having become unified, intent on compassion, free from the stench of defilements, abstaining from sexual intercourse—established in this, and training in this, a mortal attains the deathless Brahmā-world.”

Brahmalokagāmimaggaṃ kathesi.

He spoke of the path leading to the Brahmā-world.

Tattha [M 0.0050][P 0.0049] maṃ ve kumāraṃ jānantīti ve ekaṃsena maṃ “kumāro”ti jānanti. Brahmaloketi seṭṭhaloke. Sanantananti ciratanaṃ porāṇaṃ. Evaṃ, govinda, jānāhīti, govinda, evaṃ maṃ dhārehi.

Herein, 'They know me indeed as the Youth' means they know me unequivocally as 'the Youth'. 'In the Brahmā-world' means in the highest world. 'The Eternal' means long-lasting, ancient. 'Thus, Govinda, know me' means, 'Govinda, thus bear me in mind.'

Āsananti [V 0.0048] idaṃ bhoto brahmuno nisīdanatthāya āsanaṃ paññattaṃ. Idaṃ udakaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ pādānaṃ dhovanatthaṃ pānīyaṃ pipāsaharaṇatthāya. Idaṃ pajjaṃ parissamavinodanatthaṃ pādabbhañjanatelaṃ. Idaṃ madhusākaṃ atakkaṃ aloṇikaṃ adhūpanaṃ udakena seditaṃ sākaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tadā hi bodhisattassa taṃ catumāsaṃ brahmacariyaṃ abhisallekhavuttiparamukkaṭṭhaṃ ahosi. Tassime sabbe agghe katvā pucchāma, tayidaṃ agghaṃ kurutu paṭiggaṇhātu no bhavaṃ idaṃ agghanti vuttaṃ hoti. Iti mahāpuriso brahmuno nesaṃ aparibhuñjanaṃ jānantopi vattasīse ṭhatvā attano āciṇṇaṃ atithipūjanaṃ dassento evamāha. Brahmāpissa adhippāyaṃ jānanto “paṭiggaṇhāma te agghaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ, govinda, bhāsasī”ti āha.

'A seat' means: this seat is prepared for the venerable Brahmā to sit upon. This water is for use: for washing the feet, and drinking water to quench thirst. This offering for the feet (`pajja`) is foot-anointing oil for dispelling weariness. He speaks of 'choice greens' (`madhusāka`) in reference to greens boiled in water, being without buttermilk, unsalted, and unspiced. For at that time, the Bodhisatta's four-month holy life was of the utmost supreme austerity. 'We invite you to accept this hospitality' means: 'Having made all these into an offering, we invite you. May the venerable one treat this as a worthy offering; may your reverence accept this from us as a worthy offering.' Thus the great man, though knowing that Brahmā would not partake of these things, stood firm in his duty and, demonstrating his customary veneration of guests, spoke thus. Brahmā too, knowing his intention, said: 'We accept your offering of hospitality, Govinda, of which you speak.'

Tattha tassa te āsane mayaṃ nisinnā nāma homa, pādodakena pādā dhotā nāma hontu, pānīyaṃ pītā nāma homa, pādabbhañjanena pādā makkhitā nāma hontu, udakasākampi paribhuttaṃ nāma hotūti attho.

Therein, the meaning is this: 'May we be counted as seated on that seat of yours; may our feet be counted as washed with water for the feet; may we be counted as having drunk the drinking water; may our feet be counted as anointed with foot-anointing oil; and may the greens boiled in water also be counted as consumed.'

Kaṅkhī akaṅkhiṃ paravediyesūti ahaṃ savicikiccho parena sayaṃ abhisaṅkhatattā parassa pākaṭesu paravediyesu pañhesu nibbicikicchaṃ.

The phrase 'A doubter asks one without doubt about matters to be revealed by another' means: I, who am full of doubt, ask one who is without doubt about questions that must be made known by another and are manifest to that other.

Hitvā mamattanti “idaṃ mama, idaṃ mamā”ti pavattanakaṃ upakaraṇataṇhaṃ cajitvā. Manujesūti sattesu. Brahmeti bodhisattaṃ ālapati. Ekodibhūtoti eko udeti pavattatīti ekodibhūto ekībhūto, ekena kāyavivekaṃ dasseti. Atha vā eko udetīti ekodi, samādhi. Taṃ bhūto pattoti ekodibhūto, upacārappanāsamādhīhi samāhitoti attho. Etaṃ ekodibhāvaṃ karuṇābrahmavihāravasena dassento “karuṇedhimutto”ti āha. Karuṇajjhāne adhimutto, taṃ jhānaṃ nibbattetvāti attho. Nirāmagandhoti kilesasaṅkhātavissagandharahito. Etthaṭṭhitoti etesu dhammesu ṭhito, ete dhamme sampādetvā. Ettha ca sikkhamānoti etesu dhammesu sikkhamāno[M 0.0051], etaṃ brahmavihārabhāvanaṃ bhāventoti attho. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana pāḷiyaṃ (dī. ni. 2.293 ādayo) āgatoyevāti.

“Having abandoned possessiveness” means having given up the craving for possessions that arises as “this is mine, this is my own.” “Among humans” means among beings. By “Brahmā,” he addresses the Bodhisatta. “Become one-pointed” means one arises, one proceeds; thus, one is one-pointed, unified. By this, it shows solitude of body. Alternatively, “one arises” means one-pointed, which is concentration. “Having become that” means having attained it; thus, one is one-pointed, meaning one is concentrated by means of access and absorption concentration. To show this state of one-pointedness by way of the divine abode of compassion, he said, “devoted to compassion.” This means one is devoted to the jhāna of compassion, having produced that jhāna. “Free from the raw smell” means devoid of the foul stench known as the defilements. “Established in this” means established in these states, having accomplished these states. “And training in this” means training in these states, that is, developing this meditation on the divine abodes. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation has come in the Pāli Canon (e.g., Dī. Ni. 2.293 ff.).

Atha mahāpuriso tassa brahmuno vacanaṃ sutvā āmagandhe jigucchanto “idānevāhaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti āha. Brahmāpi [P 0.0050] “sādhu, mahāpurisa, pabbajassu. Evaṃ sati mayhampi tava santike āgamanaṃ svāgamanameva bhavissati, tvaṃ, tāta, sakalajambudīpe aggapuriso paṭhamavaye ṭhito, evaṃ mahantaṃ nāma sampattiṃ issariyañca pahāya pabbajanaṃ nāma gandhahatthino ayobandhanaṃ chinditvā [V 0.0049] vanagamanaṃ viya atiuḷāraṃ, buddhatanti nāmesā”ti mahābodhisattassa daḷhīkammaṃ katvā brahmalokameva gato. Mahāsattopi “mama ito nikkhamitvā pabbajanaṃ nāma na yuttaṃ, ahaṃ rājakulānaṃ atthaṃ anusāsāmi, tasmā tesaṃ ārocetvā sace tepi pabbajanti sundarameva, no ce purohitaṭṭhānaṃ niyyātetvā pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā reṇussa tāva rañño ārocetvā tena bhiyyosomattāya kāmehi nimantiyamāno attano saṃvegahetuṃ ekantena pabbajitukāmatañcassa nivedetvā tena “yadi evaṃ ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti vutte “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā eteneva nayena sattabhūādayo cha khattiye, satta ca brāhmaṇamahāsāle, satta ca nhātakasatāni, attano bhariyāyo ca āpucchitvā sattāhamattameva tesaṃ cittānurakkhaṇatthaṃ ṭhatvā mahābhinikkhamanasadisaṃ nikkhamitvā pabbaji.

Then the great being, hearing the words of that Brahmā and feeling disgust for the raw smells of defilements, said, “Right now I will go forth.” Brahmā also said, “Good, great being, go forth. In that case, my coming to you will be a welcome arrival indeed. You are the foremost person in all of Jambudīpa, established in the prime of youth. To go forth, having abandoned such great prosperity and sovereignty, is exceedingly magnificent, like a royal elephant breaking its iron fetters and going to the forest. This is the tradition of the Buddhas.” Having thus strengthened the Great Bodhisatta’s resolve, he went to the Brahma-world. The great being also thought, “It is not proper for me to go forth after leaving from here. I instruct the royal families for their welfare. Therefore, I will inform them, and if they too go forth, that would be excellent. If not, I will hand over the position of chaplain and then go forth.” Having thought thus, he first informed King Reṇu. While being invited by the king with ever-increasing sensual pleasures, the Bodhisatta informed him of his own reason for spiritual urgency and his definite desire to go forth. When the king said, “If that is so, I too will go forth,” the great being agreed, saying, “Good.” In this same way, he took leave of the six khattiyas, including Sattabhū, the seven great brahmin landholders, the seven hundred brahmin graduates, and his own wives. After staying for just seven days for the sake of protecting their state of mind, he departed in a manner resembling the Great Renunciation and went forth.

Tassa te sattarājāno ādiṃ katvā sabbeva anupabbajiṃsu. Sā ahosi mahatī parisā. Anekayojanavitthārāya parisāya parivuto mahāpuriso dhammaṃ desento gāmanigamajanapadarājadhānīsu cārikaṃ carati, mahājanaṃ puññe patiṭṭhāpeti. Gatagataṭṭhāne buddhakolāhalaṃ viya hoti. Manussā “govindapaṇḍito kira āgacchatī”ti sutvā puretarameva maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā taṃ alaṅkārāpetvā paccuggantvā maṇḍapaṃ pavesetvā nānaggarasabhojanena patimānenti. Mahālābhasakkāro mahogho viya ajjhottharanto uppajji. Mahāpuriso mahājanaṃ puññe patiṭṭhāpesi sīlasampadāya indriyasaṃvare bhojane mattaññutāya jāgariyānuyoge kasiṇaparikamme jhānesu abhiññāsu aṭṭhasamāpattīsu brahmavihāresūti. Buddhuppādakālo viya ahosi.

Those seven kings and all the others went forth after him. It became a great assembly. Surrounded by an assembly that extended for many leagues, the great being wandered on tour through villages, towns, countrysides, and royal cities, teaching the Dhamma and establishing the great multitude in merit. In every place he went, it was like a Buddha-uproar. Hearing, “It is said that Govinda the Wise is coming,” people would prepare a pavilion beforehand, have it decorated, go out to meet him, lead him into the pavilion, and honor him with food of various excellent flavors. Great gain and honor arose, overwhelming him like a great flood. The great being established the great multitude in merit: in the accomplishment of virtue, in restraint of the sense faculties, in moderation in eating, in the practice of wakefulness, in the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, in the jhānas, in the higher knowledges, in the eight attainments, and in the divine abodes. It was as if it were the time of a Buddha’s appearance.

Bodhisatto [M 0.0052] yāvatāyukaṃ pāramiyo pūrento samāpattisukhena vītināmetvā āyupariyosāne brahmaloke nibbatti. Tassa taṃ brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ pavattittha. Tassa [P 0.0051] ye sāsanaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ ājāniṃsu, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ brahmalokaṃ upapajjiṃsu. Ye na ājāniṃsu, te appekacce paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjiṃsu. Appekacce nimmānaratīnaṃ…pe… tusitānaṃ yāmānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjiṃsu. Ye sabbanihīnā, te gandhabbakāyaṃ paripūresuṃ. Iti mahājano yebhuyyena brahmalokūpago saggūpago ca ahosi. Tasmā devabrahmalokā paripūriṃsu. Cattāro apāyā suññā viya ahesuṃ.

The Bodhisatta, fulfilling the perfections for as long as his life lasted, passed his time in the bliss of meditative attainments and, at the end of his life, arose in the Brahma-world. That holy life of his was successful, prosperous, widespread, known to many, and extensive; it was well-proclaimed among gods and humans and continued for a long, long time. Of those who understood his teaching in its entirety, they, with the breakup of the body, after death, were reborn in a good destination, the Brahma-world. Of those who did not understand it, some were reborn in the company of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas. Some were reborn in the company of the Nimmānaratī devas… and so on… the Tusita devas, the Yāma devas, the Tāvatiṃsa devas, and the Cātumahārājika devas. Those who were the very lowest filled the host of gandhabbas. Thus, the great multitude, for the most part, went to the Brahma-world or to heaven. Therefore, the deva and Brahma worlds became full, while the four states of woe were as if empty.

Idhāpi [V 0.0050] akittijātake (jā. 1.13.83 ādayo) viya bodhisambhāraniddhāraṇā veditabbā – tadā satta rājāno mahātherā ahesuṃ, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, mahāgovindo lokanātho. Tathā reṇuādīnaṃ sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ aññamaññāvirodhena yathā sakarajje patiṭṭhāpanaṃ, tathā mahati sattavidhe rajje tesaṃ atthadhammānusāsane appamādo, “brahmunāpi sākacchaṃ samāpajjatī”ti pavattasambhāvanaṃ yathābhūtaṃ kātuṃ cattāro māse paramukkaṃsagato brahmacariyavāso. Tena brahmuno attani samāpajjanaṃ, brahmuno ovāde ṭhatvā sattahi rājūhi sakalena ca lokena upanītaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya chaḍḍetvā aparimāṇāya khattiyabrāhmaṇādiparisāya anupabbajjānimittāya pabbajjāya anuṭṭhānaṃ, buddhānaṃ sāsanassa viya attano sāsanassa cirakālānuppabandhoti evamādayo guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Here too, as in the Akitti Jātaka, the determination of the requisites for enlightenment should be understood. At that time, the seven kings were great elders, the remaining assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Mahāgovinda was the Protector of the World. Likewise, the establishment of the seven kings, beginning with Reṇu, in their own kingdoms without mutual conflict; their diligence in instructing them in welfare and Dhamma in the great sevenfold kingdom; the holy life, which for four months reached the highest excellence in order to make real the possibility that 'he enters into discussion even with Brahmā'; Brahmā's personal appearance before him; standing firm in Brahmā's instruction, the discarding of the gain and honour brought by the seven kings and the entire world as if it were a lump of spittle; the undertaking of the going forth as a sign for the subsequent going forth of the immeasurable assembly of khattiyas, brahmins, and others; and the long-lasting continuity of his own teaching, like that of the Buddhas' teaching—these and similar virtues and powers should be elucidated.

Mahāgovindacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahāgovinda Cariya is concluded.

6. Nimirājacariyāvaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Cariya of King Nimi

40. Chaṭṭhe mithilāyaṃ puruttameti mithilānāmake videhānaṃ uttamanagare. Nimi nāma mahārājāti nemiṃ ghaṭento viya uppanno “nimī”ti laddhanāmo, mahantehi dānasīlādiguṇavisesehi mahatā ca [M 0.0053] rājānubhāvena samannāgatattā mahanto rājāti mahārājā. Paṇḍito kusalatthikoti attano ca paresañca puññatthiko.

40. In the sixth: 'In Mithilā, the foremost city' means in the excellent city of the Videhas named Mithilā. 'A great king named Nimi' means he received the name 'Nimi' because he was born as if joining a wheel's felly (nemi). He was a great king (mahārājā) because he was a great (mahanto) king (rājā), being endowed with great and special qualities such as generosity and virtue, and with great royal power. 'Wise, a seeker of the wholesome' means one who sought merit for himself and for others.

Atīte kira videharaṭṭhe mithilānagare amhākaṃ bodhisatto [P 0.0052] maghadevo nāma rājā ahosi. So caturāsīti vassasahassāni kumārakīḷaṃ kīḷitvā caturāsīti vassahassāni uparajjaṃ kāretvā caturāsīti vassasahassāni rajjaṃ kārento “yadā me sirasmiṃ palitāni passeyyāsi, tadā me āroceyyāsī”ti kappakassa vatvā aparabhāge tena palitāni disvā ārocite suvaṇṇasaṇḍāsena uddharāpetvā hatthe patiṭṭhāpetvā palitaṃ oloketvā “pātubhūto kho mayhaṃ devadūto”ti saṃvegajāto “idāni mayā pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā satasahassuṭṭhānakaṃ gāmavaraṃ kappakassa datvā jeṭṭhakumāraṃ pakkosāpetvā tassa –

In the past, it is said, in the kingdom of Videha, in the city of Mithilā, our Bodhisatta was a king named Maghadeva. He spent eighty-four thousand years in the play of a prince, eighty-four thousand years as a viceroy, and eighty-four thousand years ruling the kingdom. He said to his barber, 'When you see grey hairs on my head, you must inform me.' In a later time, when the barber saw grey hairs and informed him, he had them plucked out with golden tweezers and placed in his hand. Gazing at the grey hair, he was overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking, 'The divine messenger has indeed appeared to me. Now it is right for me to go forth.' He gave the barber a choice village worth a hundred thousand and had his eldest son summoned.

“Uttamaṅgaruhā mayhaṃ, ime jātā vayoharā;

Pātubhūtā devadūtā, pabbajjāsamayo mamā”ti. (jā. 1.1.9) –

'These hairs growing on my head have appeared, takers-away of youth; the divine messengers have manifested—it is the time for my going forth.'

Vatvā [V 0.0051] sādhukaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā yadipi attano aññānipi caturāsīti vassasahassāni āyu atthi, evaṃ santepi maccuno santike ṭhitaṃ viya attānaṃ maññamāno saṃviggahadayo pabbajjaṃ roceti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Having spoken thus and instructed him well in the matter of kingship, although he still had another eighty-four thousand years of life remaining, even so, considering himself as if standing in the presence of Death, with a heart stirred by urgency, he took delight in the going forth. Therefore it was said:

“Sirasmiṃ palitaṃ disvā, maghadevo disampati;

Saṃvegaṃ alabhī dhīro, pabbajjaṃ samarocayī”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.309);

"Seeing a grey hair upon his head, Maghadeva, lord of the land, the wise one, felt a sense of urgency, and took great delight in the going forth."

So puttaṃ “imināva nīhārena vatteyyāsi yathā mayā paṭipannaṃ, mā kho tvaṃ antimapuriso ahosī”ti ovaditvā nagarā nikkhamma bhikkhupabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā caturāsīti vassasahassāni jhānasamāpattīhi vītināmetvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokaparāyano ahosi. Puttopissa bahūni vassasahassāni dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā teneva upāyena pabbajitvā brahmalokaparāyano ahosi. Tathā tassa putto, tathā tassa puttoti evaṃ dvīhi ūnāni caturāsīti khattiyasahassāni sīse palitaṃ disvāva pabbajitāni. Atha bodhisatto brahmaloke ṭhitova “pavattati nu kho mayā manussaloke kataṃ kalyāṇaṃ na pavattatī”ti āvajjento addasa [M 0.0054] “ettakaṃ addhānaṃ pavattaṃ, idāni nappavattissatī”ti. So “na kho panāhaṃ mayhaṃ paveṇiyā ucchijjituṃ dassāmī”ti attano vaṃse jātarañño eva aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhitvā attano vaṃsassa nemiṃ ghaṭento viya nibbatto. Tena vuttaṃ “nemiṃ ghaṭento viya uppannoti [P 0.0053] nimīti laddhanāmo”ti.

He advised his son, 'You should conduct yourself in this very manner that I have practiced. Do not be the last man.' Then he departed from the city, went forth into the homeless life of a bhikkhu, and spent eighty-four thousand years passing the time with meditative absorptions and attainments. At the end of his life, he was bound for the Brahma-world. His son too, after ruling righteously for many thousands of years, went forth by that same method and was bound for the Brahma-world. Likewise his son, and his son's son—in this way, eighty-four thousand khattiyas less two went forth upon seeing a grey hair on their heads. Then the Bodhisatta, while abiding in the Brahma-world, reflected, 'Does the wholesome tradition I established in the human world continue or not?' He saw, 'It has continued for this long, but now it will not continue further.' Thinking, 'I will not allow my lineage to be cut off,' he took rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of a king born in his own lineage, being reborn as if joining the felly of his own lineage. Therefore it was said, 'He was born as if joining a felly, thus he received the name Nimi.'

Tassa hi nāmaggahaṇadivase pitarā ānītā lakkhaṇapāṭhakā. Lakkhaṇāni oloketvā “mahārāja, ayaṃ kumāro tumhākaṃ vaṃsaṃ paggaṇhāti, pitupitāmahehipi mahānubhāvo mahāpuñño”ti byākariṃsu. Taṃ sutvā rājā yathāvuttenatthena “nimī”tissa nāmaṃ akāsi, so daharakālato paṭṭhāya sīle uposathakamme ca yuttappayutto ahosi. Athassa pitā purimanayeneva palitaṃ disvā kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvā puttaṃ rajje samanusāsitvā nagarā nikkhamma pabbajitvā jhānāni nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyano ahosi.

Indeed, on the day of his naming ceremony, the interpreters of bodily marks who were brought by his father examined his marks and declared: 'Great King, this prince will uplift your lineage. He is of greater power and greater merit than his father and grandfathers.' Hearing this, the king, in accordance with the meaning of what was said, gave him the name 'Nimi'. From a young age, he was diligently devoted to virtue and the Uposatha observance. Then his father, in the same way as before, upon seeing a grey hair, gave a choice village to the barber, instructed his son in kingship, departed from the city, went forth, developed the meditative absorptions, and was bound for the Brahma-world.

Nimirājā pana dānajjhāsayatāya catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe cāti pañca dānasālāyo kāretvā mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Ekekāya dānasālāya satasahassaṃ satasahassaṃ katvā devasikaṃ pañcasatasahassāni pariccaji, pañca sīlāni rakkhi, pakkhadivasesu uposathakammaṃ samādiyi[V 0.0052], mahājanampi dānādīsu puññesu samādapesi, saggamaggaṃ ācikkhi, nirayabhayena tajjesi, pāpato nivāresi. Tassa ovāde ṭhatvā mahājano dānādīni puññāni katvā tato cuto devaloke nibbatti, devaloko paripūri, nirayo tuccho viya ahosi. Tadā pana attano dānajjhāsayassa uḷārabhāvaṃ savisesaṃ dānapāramiyā pūritabhāvañca pavedento satthā –

King Nimi, due to his inclination for generosity, had five alms-halls built—at the four city gates and in the middle of the city—and he established great almsgiving. At each alms-hall, having allocated one hundred thousand, he gave away five hundred thousand daily. He observed the five precepts, undertook the Uposatha observance on the fortnightly days, and also encouraged the great populace in meritorious deeds such as giving. He pointed out the path to heaven, admonished them with the fear of hell, and restrained them from evil. The great populace, abiding by his instruction, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and, after passing away from that state, were reborn in the deva world. The deva world became full, and hell became as if empty. At that time, the Teacher, making known the sublime and special nature of his own inclination for generosity and the fulfillment of the perfection of giving, said:

41.

41.

“Tadāhaṃ māpayitvāna, catussālaṃ catummukhaṃ;

Tattha dānaṃ pavattesiṃ, migapakkhinarādina”nti. – ādimāha;

“Then I, having caused a four-halled, four-entranced building to be constructed, established giving there for beasts, birds, humans, and others.”

Tattha tadāti tasmiṃ nimirājakāle. Māpayitvānāti kārāpetvā. Catussālanti catūsu disāsu sambandhasālaṃ. Catummukhanti catūsu disāsu catūhi dvārehi yuttaṃ. Dānasālāya hi mahantabhāvato deyyadhammassa yācakajanassa ca bahubhāvato na sakkā ekeneva dvārena [M 0.0055] dānadhammaṃ pariyantaṃ kātuṃ deyyadhammañca pariyosāpetunti sālāya catūsu disāsu cattāri mahādvārāni kārāpesi. Tattha dvārato paṭṭhāya yāva koṇā deyyadhammo rāsikato tiṭṭhati. Aruṇuggaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva pakatiyā saṃvesanakālo, tāva dānaṃ pavatteti. Itarasmimpi kāle anekasatā padīpā jhāyanti. Yadā yadā atthikā āgacchanti, tadā tadā dīyateva. Tañca dānaṃ na kapaṇaddhikavanibbakayācakānaññeva[P 0.0054], atha kho aḍḍhānaṃ mahābhogānampi upakappanavasena mahāsudassanadānasadisaṃ uḷāratarapaṇītatarānaṃ deyyadhammānaṃ pariccajanato sabbepi sakalajambudīpavāsino manussā paṭiggahesuñceva paribhuñjiṃsu ca. Sakalajambudīpañhi unnaṅgalaṃ katvā mahāpuriso tadā mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Yathā ca manussānaṃ, evaṃ migapakkhike ādiṃ katvā tiracchānagatānampi dānasālāya bahi ekamante tesaṃ upakappanavasena dānaṃ pavattesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “tattha dānaṃ pavattesiṃ, migapakkhinarādina”nti. Na kevalañca tiracchānānameva, petānampi divase divase pattiṃ dāpesi. Yathā ca ekissā dānasālāya, evaṃ pañcasupi dānasālāsu dānaṃ pavattittha. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “tadāhaṃ māpayitvāna, catussālaṃ catummukha”nti ekaṃ viya vuttaṃ, taṃ nagaramajjhe dānasālaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Therein, “tadā” means at that time of King Nimi. “Māpayitvāna” means having caused to be built. “Catussāla” means a hall connected in the four directions. “Catummukha” means endowed with four doors in the four directions. Indeed, due to the great size of the alms-hall and the abundance of both the gifts to be given and the people asking for them, it was not possible to complete the distribution of gifts and to exhaust the offerings through just one door. Therefore, he had four great doors built in the four directions of the hall. There, from the door up to the corner, the gifts to be given stood in heaps. Starting from the rising of the dawn until the usual time for retiring, he continuously gave gifts. Even at other times, many hundreds of lamps were burning. Whenever those in need came, gifts were invariably given. And that giving was not only for the wretched, the poor, beggars, and supplicants, but also for the wealthy and those with great riches, by way of providing for them, involving the relinquishing of excellent and superior gifts similar to the great giving of Mahāsudassana. Indeed, all the human inhabitants of the entire Jambudīpa both received and enjoyed them. The great being then established the great giving, having made the entire Jambudīpa like a house with its door-bolt removed. And just as for humans, so too, beginning with beasts and birds, he established giving outside the alms-hall in a separate area for those of the animal realm, by way of providing for them. Therefore, it is said: “There I established giving, for beasts, birds, humans, and others.” And not only to animals, but also to the departed spirits, he had a share of merit given day by day. Just as in one alms-hall, so too in all five alms-halls was giving established. In the Pāli text, however, when it says, “Then I, having caused a four-halled, four-entranced building to be constructed,” it is spoken of as if it were one, but this was said with reference to the alms-hall in the middle of the city.

42. Idāni tattha deyyadhammaṃ ekadesena dassento “acchādanañca sayanaṃ, annaṃ pānañca bhojana”nti āha.

42. Now, indicating a portion of the gifts given there, he said: “Clothing and bedding, food, drink, and nourishment.”

Tattha acchādananti khomasukhumādinānāvidhanivāsanapārupanaṃ. Sayananti mañcapallaṅkādiñceva gonakacittakādiñca anekavidhaṃ sayitabbakaṃ, āsanampi cettha sayanaggahaṇeneva [V 0.0053] gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Annaṃ pānañca bhojananti tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ yathābhirucitaṃ nānaggarasaṃ annañceva pānañca avasiṭṭhaṃ nānāvidhabhojanavikatiñca. Abbocchinnaṃ karitvānāti ārambhato paṭṭhāya yāva āyupariyosānā ahorattaṃ avicchinnaṃ katvā.

Herein, “clothing” means various kinds of lower and upper garments made of fine linen and so on. “Bedding” means various kinds of things to lie on, such as beds and couches, and also covers like woolen blankets with floral designs; it should be understood that seats are also included here under the term “bedding.” “Food, drink, and nourishment” means food of various excellent flavors, drink, and the remaining various kinds of prepared foods, according to the preference of those various beings. “Having made it uninterrupted” means having made it continuous, day and night, from the beginning right up to the end of life.

43-4. Idāni tassa dānassa sammāsambodhiṃ ārabbha dānapāramibhāvena pavattitabhāvaṃ dassento yathā tadā attano ajjhāsayo pavatto, taṃ upamāya dassetuṃ “yathāpi sevako”tiādimāha. Tassattho – yathā nāma sevakapuriso attano sāmikaṃ kālānukālaṃ sevanavasena [M 0.0056] upagato laddhabbadhanahetu kāyena vācāya manasā sabbathāpi kāyavacīmanokammehi yathā so ārādhito hoti, evaṃ ārādhanīyaṃ ārādhanameva esati gavesati, tathā ahampi bodhisattabhūto sadevakassa lokassa sāmibhūtaṃ anuttaraṃ buddhabhāvaṃ sevetukāmo tassa ārādhanatthaṃ sabbabhave sabbasmiṃ [P 0.0055] nibbattanibbattabhave dānapāramiparipūraṇavasena dānena sabbasatte santappetvā bodhisaṅkhātato ariyamaggañāṇato jātattā “bodhija”nti laddhanāmaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ parato sabbathā nānūpāyehi esissāmi gavesissāmi, taṃ uttamaṃ bodhiṃ sammāsambodhiṃ jīvitapariccāgādiṃ yaṃkiñci katvā icchāmi abhipatthemīti.

Now, to show that this giving occurred as the perfection of giving with perfect enlightenment as its object, and to illustrate with a simile how his own aspiration arose at that time, he spoke the verse beginning, “Just as a servant.” Its meaning is this: Just as a serving man, having approached his master from time to time through service, for the sake of the wages to be received, seeks and searches only for what is pleasing and for the act of pleasing, so that his master is pleased by his bodily, verbal, and mental actions in every way; so too, I, being a bodhisatta, desiring to attend upon the unsurpassed state of Buddhahood, the master of the world with its devas, for the purpose of pleasing the beings of the world, will, in every single birth, having satisfied all beings with gifts by way of fulfilling the perfection of giving, hereafter seek and search by all means and various methods for the all-knowing knowledge, which has obtained the name 'Bodhija' because it is born from the noble path-knowledge designated as 'bodhi.' I desire and intensely aspire for that supreme awakening, perfect enlightenment, having done whatever is necessary, such as sacrificing my life.

Evamidha dānajjhāsayassa uḷārabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ dānapāramivaseneva desanā katā. Jātakadesanāyaṃ panassa sīlapāramiādīnampi paripūraṇaṃ vibhāvitameva, tathā hissa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sīlādiguṇehi attānaṃ alaṅkaritvā mahājanaṃ tattha patiṭṭhapentassa ovāde ṭhatvā nibbattadevatā sudhammāyaṃ devasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā “aho amhākaṃ nimirājānaṃ nissāya mayaṃ imaṃ sampattiṃ pattā, evarūpāpi nāma anuppanne buddhe mahājanassa buddhakiccaṃ sādhayamānā acchariyamanussā loke uppajjantī”ti mahāpurisassa guṇe vaṇṇentā abhitthaviṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

Thus, here the teaching is given by way of the perfection of giving alone in order to show the sublime nature of the inclination for giving. In the Jātaka exposition, however, the fulfillment of his perfections of virtue and so on is also clearly explained. For, as was stated previously, while he was adorning himself with qualities such as virtue and establishing the great populace in them, the deities who were reborn after having stood firm in his instruction gathered in the Sudhammā divine assembly and extolled the great being, praising his qualities, saying: “Ah, it is by relying on our King Nimi that we have attained this prosperity! Indeed, even when a Buddha has not arisen, such wonderful humans arise in the world, accomplishing the work of a Buddha for the great populace!” Therefore, it was said:

“Accheraṃ vata lokasmiṃ, uppajjanti vicakkhaṇā;

Yadā ahu nimirājā, paṇḍito kusalatthiko”ti. (jā. 2.22.421) –

"Wonderful indeed in the world, the discerning arise; when King Nimi appeared, wise and seeking what is skillful."

Ādi.

Etc.

Taṃ sutvā sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbe devā bodhisattaṃ daṭṭhukāmā ahesuṃ. Athekadivasaṃ [V 0.0054] mahāpurisassa uposathikassa uparipāsādavaragatassa pacchimayāme pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi “dānaṃ nu kho varaṃ, udāhu brahmacariya”nti. So taṃ attano kaṅkhaṃ chindituṃ nāsakkhi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko taṃ kāraṇaṃ āvajjento bodhisattaṃ tathā vitakkentaṃ disvā “handassa vitakkaṃ chindissāmī”ti āgantvā purato ṭhito tena “kosi tva”nti puṭṭho attano devarājabhāvaṃ ārocetvā [M 0.0057] “kiṃ, mahārāja, cintesī”ti vutte tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Sakko brahmacariyameva uttamaṃ katvā dassento –

Hearing that, beginning with Sakka, lord of the devas, all the devas desired to see the Bodhisatta. Then one day, as the great being, who was observing the Uposatha, was seated cross-legged in the last watch of the night upon the upper terrace of the excellent palace, a reflection arose in his mind: "Is giving truly better, or is it the holy life?" He was unable to resolve this doubt of his. At that moment, Sakka's celestial abode showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting on the cause, saw the Bodhisatta pondering thus and thought, "Come, I shall resolve his doubt." Having approached, he stood before him. When asked by the king, "Who are you?" he revealed his identity as the king of the devas. When he then asked, "Great king, what are you pondering?" the king explained the matter. Sakka, demonstrating that the holy life is indeed supreme, said:

“Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visujjhati.

"By an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the khattiyas; by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; by the supreme, one is purified."

“Na [P 0.0056] hete sulabhā kāyā, yācayogena kenaci;

Ye kāye upapajjanti, anagārā tapassino”ti. (jā. 2.22.429-430) –

"These bodies are not easily obtained by any means of asking; those who are reborn in these bodies are homeless ascetics."

Āha.

He said.

Tattha puthutitthāyatanesu methunaviratimattaṃ hīnaṃ brahmacariyaṃ nāma, tena khattiyakule upapajjati. Jhānassa upacāramattaṃ majjhimaṃ nāma, tena devattaṃ upapajjati. Aṭṭhasamāpattinibbattanaṃ pana uttamaṃ nāma, tena brahmaloke nibbattati. Tañhi bāhirakā “nibbāna”nti kathenti. Tenāha “visujjhatī”ti. Sāsane pana parisuddhasīlassa bhikkhuno aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ patthentassa brahmacariyacetanā hīnatāya hīnaṃ nāma, tena yathāpatthite devaloke nibbattati. Parisuddhasīlassa aṭṭhasamāpattinibbattanaṃ majjhimaṃ nāma, tena brahmaloke nibbattati. Parisuddhasīlassa pana vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattappatti uttamaṃ nāma, tena visujjhatīti. Iti sakko “mahārāja, dānato brahmacariyavāsova sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena mahapphalo”ti vaṇṇesi. Kāyāti brahmagaṇā. Yācayogenāti yācanayuttena. “Yājayogenā”tipi pāḷi, yajanayuttena, dānayuttenāti attho. Tapassinoti tapanissitakā. Imāyapi gāthāya brahmacariyavāsasseva mahānubhāvataṃ dīpeti. Evañca pana vatvā “kiñcāpi, mahārāja, dānato brahmacariyameva mahapphalaṃ, dvepi panete mahāpurisakattabbāva[V 0.0055]. Dvīsupi appamatto hutvā dānañca dehi sīlañca rakkhāhī”ti vatvā taṃ ovaditvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

Therein, among the various external doctrines, the mere abstinence from sexual intercourse is called the inferior holy life; through that, one is reborn in a khattiya family. The mere attainment of access to jhāna is called the middling; through that, one attains the state of a deva. But the generation of the eight meditative attainments is called the supreme; through that, one is reborn in the Brahma-world. Indeed, outsiders declare that to be Nibbāna. Therefore, he said, "one is purified." In the Dispensation, however, for a monk of pure virtue who aspires to a certain class of devas, the intention for the holy life is called inferior due to its lowliness; through that, one is reborn in the desired deva-world. For one of pure virtue, the generation of the eight meditative attainments is called the middling; through that, one is reborn in the Brahma-world. But for one of pure virtue, the attainment of arahantship after developing insight is called the supreme; through that, one is purified. Thus Sakka praised it, saying, "Great king, the observance of the holy life is more fruitful than giving by a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times." 'Bodies' means the hosts of Brahma. 'By any means of asking' means connected with asking. There is also the reading 'by means of sacrifice,' which means connected with sacrifice, connected with giving. 'Ascetics' means those who rely on asceticism. By this verse also, he shows the great power of the observance of the holy life itself. And having said this, he advised him, "Although, great king, the holy life is indeed more fruitful than giving, both these things should be done by a great man. Being diligent in both, you should both give gifts and protect your virtue." Having thus admonished him, he went to his own abode.

Atha naṃ devagaṇo “mahārāja, kuhiṃ gatatthā”ti āha. Sakko “mithilāyaṃ nimirañño kaṅkha chinditu”nti tamatthaṃ pakāsetvā bodhisattassa guṇe vitthārato vaṇṇesi. Taṃ sutvā devā “mahārāja, mayhaṃ nimirājānaṃ daṭṭhukāmamhā, sādhu naṃ pakkosāpehī”ti vadiṃsu. Sakko “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā mātaliṃ āmantesi – “gaccha nimirājānaṃ vejayantaṃ āropetvā ānehī”ti[M 0.0058]. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā rathena gantvā tattha mahāsattaṃ āropetvā tena yācito yathākammaṃ pāpakammīnaṃ puññakammīnañca ṭhānāni ācikkhanto anukkamena devalokaṃ nesi[P 0.0057]. Devāpi kho “nimirājā āgato”ti sutvā dibbagandhavāsapupphahatthā yāva cittakūṭadvārakoṭṭhakā paccuggantvā mahāsattaṃ dibbagandhādīhi pūjentā sudhammaṃ devasabhaṃ ānayiṃsu.
