Rājā rathā otaritvā devasabhaṃ pavisitvā sakkena saddhiṃ ekāsane nisīditvā tena dibbehi kāmehi nimantiyamāno “alaṃ, mahārāja, mayhaṃ imehi yācitakūpamehi kāmehī”ti paṭikkhipitvā anekapariyāyena dhammaṃ desetvā manussagaṇanāya sattāhameva ṭhatvā “gacchāmahaṃ manussalokaṃ, tattha dānādīni puññāni karissāmī”ti āha. Sakko “nimirājānaṃ mithilaṃ nehī”ti mātaliṃ āṇāpesi. So taṃ vejayantarathaṃ āropetvā pācīnadisābhāgena mithilaṃ pāpuṇi. Mahājano dibbarathaṃ disvā rañño paccuggamanaṃ akāsi. Mātali sīhapañjare mahāsattaṃ otāretvā āpucchitvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Mahājanopi rājānaṃ parivāretvā “kīdiso, deva, devaloko”ti pucchi. Rājā devalokasampattiṃ vaṇṇetvā “tumhepi dānādīni puññāni karotha, evaṃ tasmiṃ devaloke uppajjissathā”ti dhammaṃ desesi. So aparabhāge pubbe vuttanayena palitaṃ disvā puttassa rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā kāme pahāya pabbajitvā cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Then the host of devas asked him, "Great king, where have you been?" Sakka, revealing the matter, said, "To resolve King Nimi's doubt in Mithilā," and he praised the Bodhisatta's virtues in detail. Hearing this, the devas said, "Great king, we wish to see King Nimi. It would be good if you would summon him." Sakka, agreeing, "So be it," addressed Mātali: "Go, place King Nimi upon the Vejayanta chariot and bring him here." Mātali, agreeing, "So be it," went by chariot, placed the Great Being upon it, and, being requested by him, explained the abodes of those who had done evil and those who had done merit according to their deeds, and in due course brought him to the deva-world. The devas, too, hearing, "King Nimi has arrived," went out to meet him as far as the gate-tower of Cittakūṭa, holding divine perfumes, scented powders, and flowers. Honoring the Great Being with divine perfumes and so forth, they brought him to Sudhammā, the assembly hall of the devas. The king, descending from the chariot, entered the assembly hall of the devas and sat on the same seat with Sakka. Being invited by him to enjoy divine sensual pleasures, he refused, saying, "Enough, great king, with these sensual pleasures, which are like borrowed goods to me." He then taught the Dhamma in many ways, and after staying for just seven days by human reckoning, he said, "I will go to the human world; there I will perform meritorious deeds such as giving." Sakka commanded Mātali, "Take King Nimi to Mithilā." He placed him upon the Vejayanta chariot and reached Mithilā by way of the eastern quarter. The populace, seeing the divine chariot, went out to meet the king. Mātali, having set the Great Being down at the lion-window, took his leave and went to his own abode. The populace, surrounding the king, asked, "Your Majesty, what is the deva-world like?" The king, praising the splendors of the deva-world, taught the Dhamma, saying, "You too should perform meritorious deeds such as giving; thus you will be reborn in that deva-world." In his later years, seeing a gray hair in the manner previously described, he had his son consecrated as king, forsook sensual pleasures, went forth into homelessness, and having developed the four divine abidings, he was bound for the Brahma-world.

Tadā sakko anuruddho ahosi. Mātali ānando. Caturāsīti rājasahassāni buddhaparisā. Nimirājā lokanātho.

At that time, Sakka was Anuruddha. Mātali was Ānanda. The eighty-four thousand kings were the Buddha's assembly. King Nimi was the Lord of the World.

Tassa idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva bodhisambhārā niddhāretabbā. Tathā brahmalokasampattiṃ pahāya pubbe attanā pavattitaṃ kalyāṇavattaṃ anuppabandhessāmīti mahākaruṇāya manussaloke nibbattanaṃ, uḷāro dānajjhāsayo, tadanurūpā dānādīsu paṭipatti, mahājanassa ca tattha patiṭṭhāpanaṃ, yāva devamanussānaṃ patthaṭayasatā, sakkassa devarājassa upasaṅkamane ativimhayatā, tena dibbasampattiyā nimantiyamānopi [V 0.0056] taṃ analaṅkaritvā puññasambhāraparibrūhanatthaṃ puna manussavāsūpagamanaṃ, lābhasampattīsu sabbattha alaggabhāvoti evamādayo guṇānubhāvā niddhāretabbāti.

Here too, his requisites for enlightenment should be ascertained in the same way as stated before. Likewise, these manifestations of his virtue should be ascertained: having abandoned the attainment of the Brahma world, his rebirth in the human world out of great compassion with the resolve, 'I will continue the virtuous conduct I previously initiated'; his noble disposition for giving and a corresponding practice in giving and other virtues; his establishing the great populace therein; the fact that he was longed for by gods and humans; the great wonder of his being approached by Sakka, king of the devas; though invited by him with divine prosperity, not indulging in it and returning again to a human dwelling for the sake of increasing his accumulation of merit; and his state of being unattached everywhere to gains and prosperity.

Nimirājacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Conduct of King Nimi is concluded.

7. Candakumāracariyāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Conduct of Prince Canda

45. Sattame [M 0.0059][P 0.0058] ekarājassa atrajoti ekarājassa nāma kāsirañño orasaputto. Nagare pupphavatiyāti pupphavatināmake nagare. Candasavhayoti candasaddena avhātabbo, candanāmoti attho.

45. In the seventh [Cariyā]: 'The son of Ekarāja' means he was the legitimate son of the king of Kāsi named Ekarāja. 'In the city of Pupphavatī' means in the city named Pupphavatī. 'Called Canda' means he was to be addressed by the word 'Canda'; the meaning is 'his name was Canda'.

Atīte kira ayaṃ bārāṇasī pupphavatī nāma ahosi. Tattha vasavattirañño putto ekarājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Bodhisatto tassa gotamiyā nāma aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. “Candakumāro”tissa nāmamakaṃsu. Tassa padasā gamanakāle aparopi putto uppanno, tassa “sūriyakumāro”ti nāmamakaṃsu. Tassa padasā gamanakāle ekā dhītā uppannā, “selā”tissā nāmamakaṃsu. Vemātikā ca nesaṃ bhaddaseno sūro cāti dve bhātaro ahesuṃ. Bodhisatto anupubbena vuddhippatto sippesu ca vijjāṭṭhānesu ca pāraṃ agamāsi. Tassa rājā anucchavikaṃ candaṃ nāma rājadhītaraṃ ānetvā uparajjaṃ adāsi. Bodhisattassa eko putto uppanno, tassa “vāsulo”ti nāmamakaṃsu. Tassa pana rañño khaṇḍahālo nāma purohito, taṃ rājā vinicchaye ṭhapesi. So lañjavittako hutvā lañjaṃ gahetvā assāmike sāmike karoti, sāmike ca assāmike karoti. Athekadivasaṃ aṭṭaparājito eko puriso vinicchayaṭṭhāne upakkosento nikkhamitvā rājūpaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantaṃ bodhisattaṃ disvā tassa pādesu nipatitvā “sāmi khaṇḍahālo vinicchaye vilopaṃ khādati, ahaṃ tena lañjaṃ gahetvā parājayaṃ pāpito”ti aṭṭassaramakāsi. Bodhisatto “mā bhāyī”ti taṃ assāsetvā vinicchayaṃ netvā sāmikameva sāmikaṃ akāsi. Mahājano mahāsaddena sādhukāramadāsi.

In the past, it is said, this city of Bārāṇasī was named Pupphavatī. There, the son of King Vasavatti, named Ekarājā, ruled the kingdom. The Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of his chief queen, named Gotamī. They named him 'Prince Canda.' When he began to walk, another son was born, and they named him 'Prince Sūriya.' When he, in turn, began to walk, a daughter was born, and they named her 'Selā.' They also had two half-brothers, Bhaddasena and Sūra. The Bodhisatta, growing up in due course, mastered the arts and sciences. The king brought a suitable princess named Candā for him and gave him the viceroyalty. A son was born to the Bodhisatta, and they named him 'Vāsula.' Now, that king had a chaplain named Khaṇḍahāla, whom the king appointed to judge legal cases. He became a taker of bribes and, having accepted them, would make non-owners into owners and owners into non-owners. Then one day, a man who had been defeated in a case came out of the courthouse shouting in protest. Seeing the Bodhisatta on his way to the king’s court, he fell at his feet and made his case, crying, 'My lord, Khaṇḍahāla devours justice in the court! Having taken a bribe, he had me defeated!' The Bodhisatta reassured him, saying, 'Do not be afraid,' took the case to the court, and made the rightful owner the owner once more. The great populace gave a loud shout of approval.

Rājā “bodhisattena kira aṭṭo suvinicchito”ti sutvā taṃ āmantetvā “tāta, ito paṭṭhāya [V 0.0057] tvameva aṭṭakaraṇe vinicchayaṃ vinicchināhī”ti vinicchayaṃ bodhisattassa adāsi. Khaṇḍahālassa āyo pacchijji. So tato paṭṭhāya bodhisatte āghātaṃ bandhitvā [P 0.0059] otārāpekkho vicari. So pana rājā mudhappasanno. So ekadivasaṃ supinantena devalokaṃ passitvā tattha gantukāmo hutvā “purohitaṃ [M 0.0060] brahmalokagāmimaggaṃ ācikkhā”ti āha. So “atidānaṃ dadanto sabbacatukkena yaññaṃ yajassū”ti vatvā raññā “kiṃ atidāna”nti puṭṭho “attano piyaputtā piyabhariyā piyadhītaro mahāvibhavaseṭṭhino maṅgalahatthiassādayoti ete cattāro cattāro katvā dvipadacatuppade yaññatthāya pariccajitvā tesaṃ galalohitena yajanaṃ atidānaṃ nāmā”ti saññāpesi. Iti so “saggamaggaṃ ācikkhissāmī”ti nirayamaggaṃ ācikkhi.

The king, hearing, 'It seems the Bodhisatta has judged the case well,' summoned him and said, 'Dear son, from this day forward, you alone must pass judgment in legal matters,' and so he handed over the adjudication of cases to the Bodhisatta. Khaṇḍahāla's income was cut off. From that time on, he bore a grudge against the Bodhisatta and went about seeking an opportunity to bring him down. Now, that king was credulous. One day, having seen the world of the devas in a dream and desiring to go there, he said to his chaplain, 'Teach me the path that leads to the Brahma world.' The chaplain said, 'Perform a sacrifice with every set of four while giving the ultimate gift.' When asked by the king, 'What is the ultimate gift?' he explained, 'It is called the ultimate gift to take four of each—your own dear sons, dear wives, dear daughters, and merchants of great wealth, as well as auspicious elephants, horses, and so on—and having given up these two-footed and four-footed beings for the sacrifice, to make an offering with the blood from their throats.' Thus, while claiming, 'I will teach the way to heaven,' he taught the way to hell.

Rājāpi tasmiṃ paṇḍitasaññī hutvā “tena vuttavidhi saggamaggo”ti saññāya taṃ paṭipajjitukāmo mahantaṃ yaññāvāṭaṃ kārāpetvā tattha bodhisattādike cattāro rājakumāre ādiṃ katvā khaṇḍahālena vuttaṃ sabbaṃ dvipadacatuppadaṃ yaññapasutaṭṭhāne nethāti āṇāpesi. Sabbañca yaññasambhāraṃ upakkhaṭaṃ ahosi. Taṃ sutvā mahājano mahantaṃ kolāhalaṃ akāsi. Rājā vippaṭisārī hutvā khaṇḍahālena upatthambhito punapi tathā taṃ āṇāpesi. Bodhisatto “khaṇḍahālena vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ alabhantena mayi āghātaṃ bandhitvā mameva maraṇaṃ icchantena mahājanassa anayabyasanaṃ uppādita”nti jānitvā nānāvidhehi upāyehi rājānaṃ tato duggahitaggāhato vivecetuṃ vāyamitvāpi nāsakkhi. Mahājano paridevi, mahantaṃ kāruññamakāsi. Mahājanassa paridevantasseva yaññāvāṭe sabbakammāni niṭṭhāpesi. Rājaputtaṃ netvā gīvāya nāmetvā nisīdāpesuṃ. Khaṇḍahālo suvaṇṇapātiṃ upanāmetvā khaggaṃ ādāya “tassa gīvaṃ chindissāmī”ti aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ disvā candā nāma rājaputtassa devī “aññaṃ me paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, attano saccabalena sāmikassa sotthiṃ karissāmī”ti añjaliṃ paggayha parisāya antare vicarantī “idaṃ ekanteneva pāpakammaṃ, yaṃ khaṇḍahālo saggamaggoti karoti. Iminā mayhaṃ saccavacanena mama sāmikassa sotthi hotu.

The king, perceiving the chaplain to be a wise man and thinking, 'The method he has described is the path to heaven,' desired to undertake it. He had a great sacrificial pit prepared and commanded, 'Lead the four royal princes, beginning with the Bodhisatta, and all the two-footed and four-footed creatures mentioned by Khaṇḍahāla, to the place of the sacrificial animals.' And all the requisites for the sacrifice were prepared. Hearing this, the great populace raised a mighty uproar. The king became remorseful, but being urged on by Khaṇḍahāla, he again gave the same command. The Bodhisatta, knowing, 'Because Khaṇḍahāla did not get the position of judge, he has conceived a grudge against me, and desiring my death, he has brought about this ruin and disaster for the great populace,' tried through various means to dissuade the king from that wrongly-held view, but he was unable. The great populace lamented, and a great sense of pity arose. Even as the people were lamenting, all the work at the sacrificial pit was completed. They brought the prince, bent his neck, and made him kneel. Khaṇḍahāla brought forth a golden bowl, took up a sword, and stood ready, thinking, 'I will cut off his neck.' Seeing this, the prince's consort, named Candā, thought, 'I have no other refuge. By the power of my own truth, I will bring about safety for my husband.' Raising her joined hands in reverence and moving about within the assembly, she declared: 'This is entirely an evil deed, which Khaṇḍahāla performs calling it the path to heaven. By this true statement of mine, may there be safety for my husband!'

“Yā devatā idha loke, sabbā tā saraṇaṃ gatā;

Anāthaṃ tāyatha mamaṃ, yathāhaṃ patimā siya”nti. –

“Whatever deities there are in this world, all have gone for refuge; protect me, who am helpless, so that I may have my husband.”

Saccakiriyamakāsi. Sakko [P 0.0060] devarājā tassā paridevanasaddaṃ sutvā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā jalitaṃ ayokūṭaṃ ādāya āgantvā rājānaṃ tāsetvā [M 0.0061] sabbe vissajjāpesi. Sakkopi tadā attano dibbarūpaṃ dassetvā sampajjalitaṃ sajotibhūtaṃ vajiraṃ paribbhamanto “are, pāparāja kāḷakaṇṇi, kadā tayā pāṇātipātena sugatigamanaṃ diṭṭhapubbaṃ, candakumāraṃ sabbañca imaṃ janaṃ bandhanato [V 0.0058] mocehi, no ce mocessasi, ettheva te imassa ca duṭṭhabrāhmaṇassa sīsaṃ phālessāmī”ti ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā rājā brāhmaṇo ca sīghaṃ sabbe bandhanā mocesuṃ.

She made an asseveration of truth. Sakka, the king of the devas, hearing the sound of her lamentation and understanding the matter, took a blazing iron hammer and came to threaten the king, causing him to release everyone. Then Sakka, revealing his divine form, stood in the sky, whirling a blazing, radiant thunderbolt, and said, “You there, wicked, wretched king! When have you ever seen a happy rebirth attained by taking life? Release Prince Canda and all these people from their bonds. If you do not release them, I will split your head and the head of this wicked brahmin right here!” Seeing this marvel, the king and the brahmin quickly released everyone from their bonds.

Atha mahājano ekakolāhalaṃ katvā sahasā yaññāvāṭaṃ ajjhottharitvā khaṇḍahālassa ekekaṃ leḍḍuppahāraṃ dento tattheva naṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā rājānampi māretuṃ ārabhi. Bodhisatto puretarameva pitaraṃ palissajitvā ṭhito māretuṃ na adāsi. Mahājano “jīvitaṃ tāvassa pāparañño dema, chattaṃ panassa na dassāma, nagare vāsaṃ vā na dassāma, taṃ caṇḍālaṃ katvā bahinagare vāsāpessāmā”ti rājavesaṃ hāretvā kāsāvaṃ nivāsāpetvā haliddipilotikāya sīsaṃ veṭhetvā caṇḍālaṃ katvā caṇḍālagāmaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Ye pana taṃ pasughātayaññaṃ yajiṃsu ceva yajāpesuñca anumodiṃsu ca, sabbe te nirayaparāyanā ahesuṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

Then the great crowd, making a single great uproar, suddenly overwhelmed the sacrificial enclosure and, striking Khaṇḍahāla one by one with clods of earth, brought about his death right there. They also began to kill the king. But the Bodhisatta, quickly embracing his father, stood his ground and did not allow him to be killed. The great crowd said, “For now, we will grant this wicked king his life, but we will not give him the royal umbrella, nor will we allow him to live in the city. We will make him an outcaste and have him live outside the city.” They stripped him of his royal attire, made him wear a dyed robe, wrapped his head in a turmeric-stained rag, and having made him an outcaste, sent him to an outcaste village. As for those who performed that animal-slaughtering sacrifice, caused it to be performed, or approved of it, all of them were destined for hell. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Sabbe patiṭṭhā nirayaṃ, yathā taṃ pāpakaṃ karitvāna;

Na hi pāpakammaṃ katvā, labbhā sugatiṃ ito gantu”nti. (jā. 2.22.1143);

“All of them were established in hell, as a result of having done that evil deed; for having done an evil deed, it is not possible to go from here to a happy destination.”

Atha sabbāpi rājaparisā nāgarā ceva jānapadā ca samāgantvā bodhisattaṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu. So dhammena rajjaṃ anusāsanto taṃ attano mahājanassa ca akāraṇeneva uppannaṃ anayabyasanaṃ anussaritvā saṃvegajāto puññakiriyāsu bhiyyosomattāya ussāhajāto mahādānaṃ pavattesi, sīlāni rakkhi, uposathakammaṃ samādiyi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then the entire royal assembly, together with the townspeople and country folk, gathered and consecrated the Bodhisatta in the kingdom. As he was ruling the kingdom righteously, he recollected that misfortune and disaster which had arisen without cause for himself and for the great populace. Filled with spiritual urgency, he became exceedingly diligent in meritorious deeds: he set in motion a great almsgiving, observed the moral precepts, and undertook the Uposatha observance. Therefore it was said:

46.

46.

“Tadāhaṃ yajanā mutto, nikkhanto yaññavāṭato;

Saṃvegaṃ janayitvāna, mahādānaṃ pavattayi”nti. – ādi;

“Then I, freed from the sacrifice, having emerged from the sacrificial enclosure, generated a sense of spiritual urgency and set in motion a great almsgiving.”

Tattha [M 0.0062][P 0.0061] yajanā muttoti khaṇḍahālena vihitayaññavidhito vuttanayena ghātetabbato mutto. Nikkhanto yaññavāṭatoti abhisekakaraṇatthāya ussāhajātena mahājanena saddhiṃ tato yaññabhūmito niggato. Saṃvegaṃ janayitvānāti evaṃ “bahuantarāyo lokasannivāso”ti ativiya saṃvegaṃ uppādetvā. Mahādānaṃ pavattayinti cha dānasālāyo kārāpetvā mahatā dhanapariccāgena vessantaradānasadisaṃ [V 0.0059] mahādānamadāsiṃ. Etena abhisekakaraṇato paṭṭhāya tassa mahādānassa pavattitabhāvaṃ dasseti.

Therein, freed from the sacrifice means freed from being killed according to the sacrificial rite arranged by Khaṇḍahāla, in the manner already described. Departed from the sacrificial enclosure means he went forth from that sacrificial ground together with the great populace, who were filled with enthusiasm for the purpose of performing the consecration. Having generated a sense of spiritual urgency means having aroused an extreme sense of spiritual urgency, thinking thus: “Living together in the world is fraught with many dangers!” I set in motion a great almsgiving means: having had six alms-halls built, with a great expenditure of wealth, I gave a great alms-giving similar to that of Vessantara. By this phrase, it shows that his great almsgiving was set in motion starting from the time of his consecration.

47. Dakkhiṇeyye adatvānāti dakkhiṇārahe puggale deyyadhammaṃ apariccajitvā. Api chappañca rattiyoti appekadā chapi pañcapi rattiyo attano pivanakhādanabhuñjanāni na karomīti dasseti.

47. Without giving to those worthy of offerings means without having given a suitable gift to a person worthy of offerings. Even for five or six nights shows that: “Sometimes for five or six nights, I do not partake of my own drinking, eating, or consuming.”

Tadā kira bodhisatto sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā mahāmegho viya abhivassanto mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Tattha kiñcāpi dānasālāsu annapānādiuḷāruḷārapaṇītapaṇītameva yācakānaṃ yathārucitaṃ divase divase dīyati, tathāpi attano sajjitaṃ āhāraṃ rājārahabhojanampi yācakānaṃ adatvā na bhuñjati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “nāhaṃ pivāmī”tiādi.

At that time, it is said, the Bodhisatta made the entire Jambudīpa as if its soil were turned up, and raining down like a great cloud, he set in motion a great almsgiving. There, although in the alms-halls food, drink, and other items of the most magnificent and exquisite kind were given daily to supplicants according to their wishes, nevertheless, he would not eat even the royal food prepared for himself without first giving it to the supplicants. It was with reference to this that it was said: ‘I do not drink,’ and so on.

48. Idāni tathā yācakānaṃ dāne kāraṇaṃ dassento upamaṃ tāva āharati “yathāpi vāṇijo nāmā”tiādinā. Tassattho – yathā nāma vāṇijo bhaṇḍaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā appena pābhatena bahuṃ bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇitvā vipulaṃ bhaṇḍasannicayaṃ katvā desakālaṃ jānanto yatthassa lābho udayo mahā hoti, tattha dese kāle vā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ harati upaneti vikkiṇāti.

48. Now, to show the reason for giving to supplicants in that way, he first introduces a simile, beginning with ‘Just as a merchant...’ and so on. Its meaning is this: Just as a merchant, having gone to a place of merchandise, sells much merchandise from a small initial stock, accumulates a vast store of goods, and, knowing the place and time where his profit and gain will be great, conveys, brings, and sells that merchandise in that place or at that time.

49. Sakabhuttāpīti sakabhuttatopi attanā paribhuttatopi. “Sakaparibhuttāpī”tipi pāṭho. Pareti parasmiṃ paṭiggāhakapuggale. Satabhāgoti anekasatabhāgo āyatiṃ bhavissati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā vāṇijena kītabhaṇḍaṃ tattheva avikkiṇitvā tathārūpe dese kāle ca vikkiṇiyamānaṃ bahuṃ udayaṃ vipulaṃ phalaṃ hoti, tatheva attano santakaṃ attanā anupabhuñjitvā parasmiṃ paṭiggāhakapuggale dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ anekasatabhāgo bhavissati, tasmā attanā [M 0.0063] abhuñjitvāpi parassa dātabbamevāti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “tiracchānagate dānaṃ datvā sataguṇā [P 0.0062] dakkhiṇā pāṭikaṅkhitabbā. Puthujjanadussīle dānaṃ datvā sahassaguṇā”ti (ma. ni. 3.379) vitthāro. Aparampi vuttaṃ “evaṃ ce, bhikkhave, sattā jāneyyuṃ dānasaṃvibhāgassa vipākaṃ, yathāhaṃ jānāmi, na adatvā bhuñjeyyuṃ, na ca nesaṃ maccheramalaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭheyya. Yopi nesaṃ assa carimo ālopo carimaṃ kabaḷaṃ, tatopi na asaṃvibhajitvā bhuñjeyyu”ntiādi (itivu. 26).

49. Than what is consumed by oneself means: than what is eaten by oneself, than what is enjoyed by oneself. There is also the reading sakaparibhuttāpi. To others means to another person who is a recipient. A hundredfold means it will become many hundredfold in the future. This is what is meant: Just as goods bought by a merchant, if not sold on the spot but sold at the right place and time, yield great profit and abundant fruit, so too, what belongs to oneself, if not enjoyed by oneself but given to a recipient, will become greatly fruitful, many hundredfold. Therefore, even if not consumed by oneself, it should indeed be given to others. For this was said by the Blessed One: ‘Having given a gift to an animal, a hundredfold offering may be expected. Having given a gift to an immoral ordinary person, a thousandfold...’ (MN 3.379), and so on in detail. Furthermore, it was said: ‘If, monks, beings knew the result of giving and sharing as I know it, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of stinginess overcome and pervade their minds. Even if it were their last morsel, their last mouthful, they would not eat it without having shared it...’ and so on (Itiv. 26).

50. Etamatthavasaṃ ñatvāti etaṃ dānassa mahapphalabhāvasaṅkhātañceva sammāsambodhiyā paccayabhāvasaṅkhātañca [V 0.0060] atthavasaṃ kāraṇaṃ jānitvā. Na paṭikkamāmi dānatoti dānapāramito īsakampi na nivattāmi abhikkamāmi eva. Kimatthaṃ? Sambodhimanupattiyāti sambodhiṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ anuppattiyā anuppattiyatthaṃ, adhigantunti attho.

50. 'Having known this significance' means: having known this reason, this significance, designated both as the state of great fruitfulness of giving and as the state of being a condition for perfect enlightenment. 'I do not turn back from giving' means: I do not retreat even slightly from the perfection of giving; I only go forward. For what purpose? 'For the attainment of enlightenment' means: for the attainment of enlightenment, the knowledge of omniscience; that is, for attaining it.

Tadā bodhisatto mahājanena pitari caṇḍālagāmaṃ pavesite dātabbayuttakaṃ paribbayaṃ dāpesi nivāsanāni pārupanāni ca. Sopi nagaraṃ pavisituṃ alabhanto bodhisatte uyyānakīḷādiatthaṃ bahigate upasaṅkamati, puttasaññāya pana na vandati, na añjalikammaṃ karoti, “ciraṃ jīva, sāmī”ti vadati. Bodhisattopi diṭṭhadivase atirekasammānaṃ karoti. So evaṃ dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā āyupariyosāne sapariso devalokaṃ pūresi.

At that time, when his father was made to enter the outcaste village by the great multitude, the Bodhisatta had suitable provisions given, as well as undergarments and outer garments. And he, unable to enter the city, approached the Bodhisatta when he had gone out for garden sports and the like. He did not, however, pay homage or make the gesture of reverence as to a son, but said, 'Long live, lord.' The Bodhisatta also showed him exceeding respect on the day he saw him. Thus, having ruled righteously, at the end of his life, he and his retinue filled the world of the devas.

Tadā khaṇḍahālo devadatto ahosi, gotamī devī mahāmāyā, candā rājadhītā rāhulamātā, vāsulo rāhulo, selā uppalavaṇṇā, sūro mahākassapo, bhaddaseno mahāmoggallāno, sūriyakumāro sāriputto, candarājā lokanātho.

At that time, Khaṇḍahāla was Devadatta, Queen Gotamī was Mahāmāyā, the princess Candā was Rāhula's mother, Vāsula was Rāhula, Selā was Uppalavaṇṇā, Sūra was Mahākassapa, Bhaddasena was Mahāmoggallāna, Prince Sūriya was Sāriputta, and King Canda was the Lord of the World.

Tassa idhāpi pubbe vuttanayeneva yathārahaṃ sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tadā khaṇḍahālassa kakkhaḷapharusabhāvaṃ jānantopi ajjhupekkhitvā dhammena samena aṭṭassa vinicchayo, attānaṃ māretukāmasseva khaṇḍahālassa tathā yaññavidhānaṃ jānitvāpi tassa upari cittappakopābhāvo, attano parisaṃ gahetvā pitu sattu bhavituṃ samatthopi “mādisassa nāma garūhi virodho na yutto”ti attānaṃ purisapasuṃ katvā ghātāpetukāmassa pitu āṇāyaṃ avaṭṭhānaṃ, kosiyā asiṃ gahetvā sīsaṃ [M 0.0064] chindituṃ upakkamante [P 0.0063] purohite attano pitari putte sabbasattesu ca mettāpharaṇena samacittatā, mahājane pitaraṃ māretuṃ upakkamante sayaṃ palissajitvā tassa jīvitadānañca, divase divase vessantaradānasadisaṃ mahādānaṃ dadatopi dānena atittabhāvo, mahājanena caṇḍālesu vāsāpitassa pitu dātabbayuttakaṃ datvā posanaṃ, mahājanaṃ puññakiriyāsu patiṭṭhāpananti evamādayo guṇānubhāvā niddhāretabbāti.

Here too, his remaining perfections should be determined as is appropriate, in the same way as previously described. That is: the determination of the case with law and impartiality, disregarding it though knowing the harsh and cruel nature of Khaṇḍahāla; the absence of mental agitation towards Khaṇḍahāla, even after knowing his sacrificial plan which was intended to kill him; though capable of becoming an enemy to his father by taking his own retinue, his standing firm in the command of his father who wished to have him killed, having made himself a human sacrificial animal, thinking, 'Opposition to elders is not fitting for one like me'; his equanimity through the pervasion of loving-kindness towards the chaplain who was endeavoring to cut off his head after taking a sword from its sheath, as well as towards his own father, his son, and all beings; and when the great multitude was endeavoring to kill his father, his protecting him and giving him the gift of life; his state of being insatiate with giving, even while giving great gifts daily like the gifts of Vessantara; his nourishing his father—who had been made to dwell among the outcastes by the great multitude—by giving him what was suitable to be given; and his establishing the great multitude in meritorious actions—these and other powerful virtues should be determined.

Candakumāracariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Conduct of Prince Canda is concluded.

8. Sivirājacariyāvaṇṇanā

8. The Exposition of the Conduct of King Sivi

51. Aṭṭhame [V 0.0061] ariṭṭhasavhaye nagareti ariṭṭhapuranāmake nagare. Sivi nāmāsi khattiyoti sivīti gottato evaṃnāmako rājā ahosi.

51. In the eighth story: 'In the city named Ariṭṭha' means in the city named Ariṭṭhapura. 'There was a khattiya named Sivi' means there was a king so-named from the Sivi clan.

Atīte kira siviraṭṭhe ariṭṭhapuranagare sivirāje rajjaṃ kārente mahāsatto tassa putto hutvā nibbatti. “Sivikumāro”tissa nāmamakaṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā uggahitasippo āgantvā pitu sippaṃ dassetvā uparajjaṃ labhitvā aparabhāge pitu accayena rājā hutvā agatigamanaṃ pahāya dasa rājadhamme akopetvā rajjaṃ kārento nagarassa catūsu dvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāreti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassapariccāgena mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Aṭṭhamīcātuddasīpannarasīsu sayaṃ dānasālaṃ gantvā dānaggaṃ oloketi.

In the past, it is said, when King Sivi was ruling in the city of Ariṭṭhapura in the Sivi kingdom, the Great Being was reborn as his son. They named him Prince Sivi. When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā, and having mastered the arts, he returned, displayed his skills to his father, obtained the viceroyalty, and in a later time, at his father’s passing, became king. Abandoning the paths of wrong conduct, he ruled without violating the ten royal virtues. He had six alms-halls established—at the four city gates, in the middle of the city, and at his palace gate—and daily he set in motion great giving with an expenditure of six hundred thousand. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, he would himself go to the alms-hall to inspect the distribution of gifts.

So ekadā puṇṇamadivase pātova samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisinno attanā dinnadānaṃ āvajjento bāhiravatthuṃ attanā adinnaṃ nāma adisvā “na me bāhirakadānaṃ tathā cittaṃ toseti, yathā ajjhattikadānaṃ, aho vata mama dānasālaṃ gatakāle koci yācako bāhiravatthuṃ ayācitvā [P 0.0064] ajjhattikameva yāceyya, sace hi me koci sarīre maṃsaṃ vā lohitaṃ vā sīsaṃ vā hadayamaṃsaṃ vā akkhīni vā upaḍḍhasarīraṃ vā sakalameva vā attabhāvaṃ dāsabhāvena yāceyya, taṃtadevassa [M 0.0065] adhippāyaṃ pūrento dātuṃ sakkomī”ti cintesi. Pāḷiyaṃ pana akkhīnaṃ eva vasena āgatā. Tena vuttaṃ –

One day, on the full-moon day, early in the morning, while seated on the royal throne under a raised white parasol, he was reflecting on the gifts he had given. Not seeing any external object that he had not given, he thought: 'An external gift does not please my mind as much as an internal gift. Oh, that when I go to the alms-hall some mendicant might not ask for an external object but would ask for something internal! For if someone were to ask me for the flesh of my body, or my blood, or my head, or the flesh of my heart, or my eyes, or half my body, or even my entire personal existence in servitude, I would be able to give it, fulfilling that very wish of his.' In the Pāḷi canon, however, the account is given only in terms of the eyes. Therefore, it was said:

“Nisajja pāsādavare, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā”.

Seated in the excellent palace, thus did I reflect at that time:

52.

52.

“Yaṃkiñci mānusaṃ dānaṃ, adinnaṃ me na vijjati;

Yopi yāceyya maṃ cakkhuṃ, dadeyyaṃ avikampito”ti.

Whatever human gift there is, none remains ungiven by me; should anyone ask me for my eye, I would give it, unwavering.

Tattha mānusaṃ dānanti pakatimanussehi dātabbadānaṃ annapānādi. Evaṃ pana mahāsattassa uḷāre dānajjhāsaye uppanne sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So tassa kāraṇaṃ āvajjento bodhisattassa ajjhāsayaṃ disvā “sivirājā ajja sampattayācakā cakkhūni ce yācanti, cakkhūni uppāṭetvā nesaṃ dassāmīti cintesī”ti sakko devaparisāya [V 0.0062] vatvā “so sakkhissati nu kho taṃ dātuṃ, udāhu noti vīmaṃsissāmi tāva na”nti bodhisatte soḷasahi gandhodakaghaṭehi nhatvā sabbālaṅkārehi paṭimaṇḍite alaṅkatahatthikkhandhavaragate dānaggaṃ gacchante jarājiṇṇo andhabrāhmaṇo viya hutvā tassa cakkhupathe ekasmiṃ unnatappadese ubho hatthe pasāretvā rājānaṃ jayāpetvā ṭhito bodhisattena tadabhimukhaṃ vāraṇaṃ pesetvā “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ icchasī”ti pucchito “tava dānajjhāsayaṃ nissāya samuggatena kittighosena sakalalokasannivāso nirantaraṃ phuṭo, ahañca andho, tasmā taṃ yācāmī”ti upacāravasena ekaṃ cakkhuṃ yāci. Tena vuttaṃ –

Therein, 'human giving' refers to the gift of food, drink, and the like, which is to be given by ordinary humans. However, when such a sublime inclination for generosity arose in the Great Being, Sakka’s Paṇḍukambala stone seat showed a sign of heat. Reflecting on the reason for this, Sakka saw the Bodhisatta’s resolve and said to the assembly of gods, 'King Sivi has thought, "Today, if beggars who have arrived should ask for my eyes, I will pluck out my eyes and give them to them."' To test whether he would indeed be capable of giving that, Sakka appeared as an old, decrepit, and blind brahmin while the Bodhisatta—having bathed with sixteen pots of fragrant water and been adorned with all ornaments—was proceeding to the alms hall, seated upon a magnificent adorned elephant. He stood on an elevated spot in the Bodhisatta’s line of sight, stretching out both hands and hailing the king. The Bodhisatta, having directed his elephant toward him, asked, 'Brahmin, what do you desire?' The brahmin replied, 'On account of your inclination for giving, the sound of your fame has arisen and continuously pervades the entire populace of the world. I am blind, and therefore I beg of you.' By way of polite speech, he requested one eye. Thus it was said—

53.

53.

“Mama saṅkappamaññāya, sakko devānamissaro;

Nisinno devaparisāya, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

“Knowing my resolve, Sakka, the lord of the gods, seated in the assembly of gods, spoke these words:”

54.

54.

“Nisajja pāsādavare, sivirājā mahiddhiko;

Cintento vividhaṃ dānaṃ, adeyyaṃ so na passati.

“Seated in the excellent palace, King Sivi, greatly powerful, pondering various gifts, saw nothing that could not be given.”

55.

55.

“Tathaṃ nu vitathaṃ netaṃ, handa vīmaṃsayāmi taṃ;

Muhuttaṃ āgameyyātha, yāva jānāmi taṃ manaṃ.

“Is this true or false? Come, I shall test him; wait a moment, until I know his mind.”

56.

56.

“Pavedhamāno palitasiro, valigatto jarāturo;

Andhavaṇṇova hutvāna, rājānaṃ upasaṅkami.

“Trembling, with gray hair, with a wrinkled body, afflicted by old age; having become like a blind person, he approached the king.”

57.

57.

“So [M 0.0066] tadā paggahetvāna, vāmaṃ dakkhiṇabāhu ca;

Sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ katvā, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

“Then, raising up his left and right arms, making a reverential salutation above his head, he spoke these words:”

58.

58.

“‘Yācāmi taṃ mahārāja, dhammika raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Tava dānaratā kitti, uggatā devamānuse.

“‘I beg of you, great king, righteous promoter of the realm; your fame for delighting in giving has arisen among gods and humans.”

59.

59.

“‘Ubhopi nettā nayanā, andhā upahatā mama;

Ekaṃ me nayanaṃ dehi, tvampi ekena yāpayā’”ti.

“‘Both my eyes, my organs of sight, are blind and damaged; give me one eye, and you too can sustain yourself with one.’”

Tattha cintento vividhaṃ dānanti attanā dinnaṃ vividhaṃ dānaṃ cintento, āvajjento dānaṃ vā attanā dinnaṃ vividhaṃ bāhiraṃ deyyadhammaṃ cintento. Adeyyaṃ so na passatīti bāhiraṃ viya ajjhattikavatthumpi adeyyaṃ dātuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ na passati, “cakkhūnipi uppāṭetvā dassāmī”ti cintesīti [V 0.0063] adhippāyo. Tathaṃ nu vitathaṃ netanti etaṃ ajjhattikavatthunopi [P 0.0065] adeyyassa adassanaṃ deyyabhāveneva dassanaṃ cintanaṃ saccaṃ nu kho, udāhu, asaccanti attho. So tadā paggahetvāna, vāmaṃ dakkhiṇabāhu cāti vāmabāhuṃ dakkhiṇabāhuñca tadā paggahetvā, ubho bāhū ukkhipitvāti attho. Raṭṭhavaḍḍhanāti raṭṭhavaḍḍhīkara. Tvampi ekena yāpayāti ekena cakkhunā samavisamaṃ passanto sakaṃ attabhāvaṃ tvaṃ yāpehi, ahampi bhavato laddhena ekena yāpemīti dasseti.

Therein, ‘pondering various gifts’ means pondering the various gifts he had given, or reflecting on the various external objects worthy of giving that he had bestowed. ‘He saw nothing that could not be given’ means that, just as with external things, he did not see even an internal object as unable to be given or impossible to give; the intention was, ‘I will even pluck out my eyes and give them.’ ‘Is this true or false?’ means whether this thought—this seeing of even internal objects not as unable to be given, but rather as fit to be given—is true or false. ‘Then, raising up his left and right arms’ means raising up his left arm and right arm at that time, that is, lifting both arms. ‘Promoter of the realm’ means one who causes the realm to prosper. ‘You too can sustain yourself with one’ indicates, ‘You sustain your own being, seeing both the even and uneven with one eye, and I too will sustain myself with the one received from you.’

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto tuṭṭhamānaso “idānevāhaṃ pāsāde nisinno evaṃ cintetvā āgato, ayañca me cittaṃ ñatvā viya cakkhuṃ yācati, aho vata me lābhā, ajja me manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇissati, adinnapubbaṃ vata dānaṃ dassāmī”ti ussāhajāto ahosi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Hearing this, the Great Being, with a joyful mind, thought: “Just now, seated in the palace, I came here reflecting thus, and this man, as if knowing my mind, asks for an eye. Oh, what a gain for me! Today my heart's desire will reach its culmination; I will give a gift never given before!” Thus he was filled with enthusiasm. To reveal this meaning, the Teacher said—

60.

60.

“Tassāhaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, haṭṭho saṃviggamānaso;

Katañjalī vedajāto, idaṃ vacanamabraviṃ.

“Hearing his words, delighted and with a mind stirred by spiritual emotion, with hands raised in reverence, and with rapture arisen, I spoke these words:”

61.

61.

“‘Idānāhaṃ cintayitvāna, pāsādato idhāgato;

Tvaṃ mama cittamaññāya, nettaṃ yācitumāgato.

“‘Just now, having reflected, I came here from the palace; you, understanding my mind, have come to ask for an eye.”

62.

62.

“‘Aho [M 0.0067] me mānasaṃ siddhaṃ, saṅkappo paripūrito;

Adinnapubbaṃ dānavaraṃ, ajja dassāmi yācake’”ti.

“‘Ah, my mind’s resolve is accomplished, my intention is fulfilled; today I will give the supreme gift, never given before, to the beggar.’”

Tattha tassāti tassa brāhmaṇarūpadharassa sakkassa. Haṭṭhoti tuṭṭho. Saṃviggamānasoti mama cittaṃ jānitvā viya iminā brāhmaṇena cakkhu yācitaṃ, ettakaṃ kālaṃ evaṃ acintetvā pamajjito vatamhīti saṃviggacitto. Vedajātoti jātapītipāmojjo. Abravinti abhāsiṃ. Mānasanti manasi bhavaṃ mānasaṃ, dānajjhāsayo, “cakkhuṃ dassāmī”ti uppannadānajjhāsayoti attho. Saṅkappoti manoratho. Paripūritoti paripuṇṇo.

Therein, ‘his’ means of that Sakka in the guise of a brahmin. ‘Delighted’ means joyful. ‘With a mind stirred by spiritual emotion’ means his mind was stirred with the thought, ‘This brahmin, as if knowing my mind, has asked for an eye. For so long, I have indeed been heedless, not having thought thus!’ ‘With rapture arisen’ means with joy and delight arisen. ‘I spoke’ means I said. ‘Mind’s resolve’ means that which is in the mind, the inclination for giving; the meaning is the inclination to give that arose with the thought, ‘I will give my eye.’ ‘Intention’ means the heart’s desire. ‘Fulfilled’ means complete.

Atha bodhisatto cintesi – “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo mama cittācāraṃ ñatvā viya duccajampi cakkhuṃ maṃ yācati, siyā nu kho kāyaci devatāya anusiṭṭho bhavissati, pucchissāmi tāva na”nti cintetvā taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ pucchi. Tenāha bhagavā jātakadesanāyaṃ –

Then the Bodhisatta thought: “This brahmin asks me for an eye, even though it is difficult to give, as if knowing my mind’s conduct. Could he have been instructed by some deity? I will first ask him.” Having reflected thus, he questioned the brahmin. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the Jātaka exposition—

“Kenānusiṭṭho [V 0.0064] idhamāgatosi, vanibbaka cakkhupathāni yācituṃ;

Suduccajaṃ [P 0.0066] yācasi uttamaṅgaṃ, yamāhu nettaṃ purisena duccaja”nti.(jā. 1.15.53);

“‘By whom instructed have you come here, O beggar, to ask for the paths of sight? You ask for a most excellent limb, very difficult to give up, which they say—the eye—is difficult for a man to give up.’”

Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇarūpadharo sakko āha –

Hearing that, Sakka in the guise of a brahmin said:

“Yamāhu devesu sujampatīti, maghavāti naṃ āhu manussaloke;

Tenānusiṭṭho idhamāgatosmi, vanibbako cakkhupathāni yācituṃ.

“‘Whom they call Sujampati among the gods, and Maghavā in the human world; instructed by him, I have come here, a beggar, to ask for the paths of sight.”

“Vanibbato mayhaṃ vaniṃ anuttaraṃ, dadāhi te cakkhupathāni yācito;

Dadāhi me cakkhupathaṃ anuttaraṃ, yamāhu nettaṃ purisena duccaja”nti. (jā. 1.15.54-55);

“‘Of me, a beggar, this is the supreme request; being asked, give your eyes. Give me the supreme path of sight, which they say—the eye—is difficult for a man to give up.’”

Mahāsatto āha –

The Great Being said:

“Yena atthena āgacchi, yamatthamabhipatthayaṃ;

Te te ijjhantu saṅkappā, labha cakkhūni brāhmaṇa.

For whatever purpose you have come, whatever goal you aspire to, may those intentions of yours be fulfilled. Receive the eyes, O brahmin.

“Ekaṃ [M 0.0068] te yācamānassa, ubhayāni dadāmahaṃ;

Sa cakkhumā gaccha janassa pekkhato,

Yadicchase tvaṃ tada te samijjhatū”ti. (jā. 1.15.56-57);

Though you ask for one, I give you both. Go, possessed of sight, as the people look on. Whatever you wish, may that be fulfilled for you.

Tattha vanibbakāti taṃ ālapati. Cakkhupathānīti dassanassa pathabhāvato cakkhūnamevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Yamāhūti yaṃ loke “duccaja”nti kathenti. Vanibbatoti yācantassa. Vaninti yācanaṃ. Te teti te tava tassa andhassa saṅkappā. Sa cakkhumāti so tvaṃ mama cakkhūhi cakkhumā hutvā. Tada te samijjhatūti yaṃ tvaṃ mama santikā icchasi, taṃ te samijjhatūti.

Therein, 'vanibbaka' is to address him. 'Cakkhupathāni' is a name for the eyes themselves, because they are the path of seeing. 'Yamāhu' refers to that which people in the world call 'difficult to give up'. 'Vanibbato' means 'of one who begs'. 'Vani' means 'begging'. 'Te te' means 'those intentions of yours, of that blind man'. 'Sa cakkhumā' means 'you, having become possessed of sight by my eyes'. 'Tada te samijjhatu' means 'whatever you desire from me, may that be fulfilled for you'.

Rājā ettakaṃ kathetvā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo sakkena anusiṭṭho idhāgatosmīti bhaṇati, nūna imassa iminā upāyena cakkhu sampajjissatī”ti ñatvā “idheva mayā cakkhūni uppāṭetvā dātuṃ asāruppa”nti cintetvā brāhmaṇaṃ ādāya antepuraṃ gantvā rājāsane nisīditvā sivakaṃ nāma vejjaṃ pakkosāpesi. Atha “amhākaṃ kira rājā akkhīni uppāṭetvā brāhmaṇassa dātukāmo”ti sakalanagare ekakolāhalaṃ [P 0.0067] ahosi. Atha naṃ rañño ñātisenāpatiādayo rājavallabhā [V 0.0065] amaccā pārisajjā nāgarā orodhā ca sabbe sannipatitvā nānāupāyehi nivāresuṃ. Rājāpi ne anuvāresi tenāha –

Having spoken thus, the king, knowing, 'This brahmin says he has come here instructed by Sakka; surely by this means his eyes will be restored,' reflected, 'It would not be fitting for me to pluck out my eyes and give them right here.' So, taking the brahmin, he went to the inner palace, sat on the royal throne, and had a physician named Sivaka summoned. Then, a great uproar arose throughout the city: 'Our king, it seems, desires to pluck out his eyes and give them to the brahmin!' At this, the king's relatives, generals, ministers, courtiers, citizens, and the women of the inner palace all gathered and tried to prevent him by various means. But the king did not heed them. Therefore, it was said:

“Mā no deva adā cakkhuṃ, mā no sabbe parākari;

Dhanaṃ dehi mahārāja, muttā veḷuriyā bahū.

O lord, do not give your eye! Do not cast all of us aside! Give wealth, O great king; there are many pearls and beryls.

“Yutte deva rathe dehi, ājānīye calaṅkate;

Nāge dehi mahārāja, hemakappanavāsase.

O lord, give yoked chariots; give adorned thoroughbreds. Give elephants, O great king, with golden coverings and apparel.

“Yathā taṃ sivayo sabbe, sayoggā sarathā sadā;

Samantā parikireyyuṃ, evaṃ dehi rathesabhā”ti. (jā. 1.15.58-60);

So that all the Sivis, with their conveyances and chariots, may ever surround you on all sides, give in such a way, O chief of charioteers.

Atha rājā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king spoke three verses:

“Yo ve dassanti vatvāna, adāne kurute mano;

Bhūmyaṃ so patitaṃ pāsaṃ, gīvāyaṃ paṭimuñcati.

Whoever, having said, 'I will give,' then sets his mind on not giving, fastens upon his own neck a noose fallen on the ground.

“Yo [M 0.0069] ve dassanti vatvāna, adāne kurute mano;

Pāpā pāpataro hoti, sampatto yamasādhanaṃ.

Whoever, having said, 'I will give,' then sets his mind on not giving, becomes more evil than the evil, having reached the domain of Yama.

“Yañhi yāce tañhi dade, yaṃ na yāce na taṃ dade;

Svāhaṃ tameva dassāmi, yaṃ maṃ yācati brāhmaṇo”ti. (jā. 1.15.61-63);

Indeed, what one is asked for, that one should give; what one is not asked for, that one should not give. I shall give that very thing which the brahmin asks of me.

Tattha mā no, devāti noti nipātamattaṃ. Deva, mā cakkhuṃ adāsi. Mā no sabbe parākarīti amhe sabbe mā pariccaji. Akkhīsu hi dinnesu tvaṃ rajjaṃ na karissasi, evaṃ tayā mayaṃ pariccattā nāma bhavissāmāti adhippāyena evamāhaṃsu. Parikireyyunti parivāreyyuṃ. Evaṃ dehīti yathā taṃ avikalacakkhuṃ sivayo ciraṃ parivāreyyuṃ, evaṃ dehi dhanamevassa dehi, mā akkhīni, akkhīsu hi dinnesu na taṃ sivayo parivāressantīti dasseti.

Therein, in 'mā no, deva,' 'no' is merely a particle. 'Deva, mā cakkhuṃ adāsi' means 'O lord, do not give the eye.' 'Mā no sabbe parākari' means 'do not abandon all of us.' They spoke with this intention: 'For if the eyes are given, you will not rule the kingdom, and thus we shall be as those abandoned by you.' 'Parikireyyuṃ' means 'they would surround.' 'Evaṃ dehi' shows: 'Give in such a way that the Sivis might long surround you, possessed of unimpaired eyes. Give him only wealth, not the eyes; for if the eyes are given, the Sivis will not surround you.'

Paṭimuñcatīti paṭipaveseti. Pāpā pāpataro hotīti lāmakā lāmakataro nāma hoti. Sampatto yamasādhananti yamassa āṇāpavattiṭṭhānaṃ ussadanirayaṃ esa patto nāma hoti. Yañhi yāceti [V 0.0066] yaṃ vatthuṃ yācako yācati, dāyakopi tadeva dadeyya, na ayācitaṃ, ayañca brāhmaṇo cakkhuṃ maṃ yācati, na muttādikaṃ dhanaṃ, taṃ dassāmīti vadati.

'Paṭimuñcati' means he goes back on his word. 'Pāpā pāpataro hoti' means he becomes more evil than the evil. 'Sampatto yamasādhanaṃ' means he is one who has reached the Ussada hell, the place where Yama's authority prevails. 'Yañhi yāce' means: 'Whatever thing a petitioner asks for, the giver should give that very thing, not what is unasked. And this brahmin asks me for my eyes, not for wealth such as pearls; that I will give,' he says.

Atha [P 0.0068] naṃ “āyuādīsu kiṃ patthetvā cakkhūni desi devā”ti pucchiṃsu. Mahāpuriso “nāhaṃ diṭṭhadhammikaṃ samparāyikaṃ vā sampattiṃ patthetvā demi, api ca bodhisattānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo porāṇakamaggo esa, yadidaṃ dānapāramipūraṇaṃ nāmā”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then they asked him: 'O lord, desiring what among things such as long life do you give your eyes?' The Great Being replied: 'I do not give desiring any attainment in this life or the next. Rather, this is the ancient path, repeatedly practiced by the Bodhisattas, namely, the fulfillment of the perfection of giving.' Therefore, it was said:

“Āyuṃ nu vaṇṇaṃ nu sukhaṃ balaṃ nu, kiṃ patthayāno nu janinda desi;

Kathañhi rājā sivinaṃ anuttaro, cakkhūni dajjā paralokahetu.

Is it long life, or beauty, or happiness, or strength—desiring what, O lord of men, do you give? How indeed could the king, unsurpassed among the Sivis, give his eyes for the sake of the next world?

“Na vāhametaṃ yasasā dadāmi, na puttamicche na dhanaṃ na raṭṭhaṃ;

Satañca dhammo carito purāṇo, icceva dāne ramate mano mamā”ti. (jā. 1.15.64-65);

I do not give this for the sake of fame, nor do I desire a son, nor wealth, nor a kingdom. But this is the ancient Dhamma practiced by the good, and for this very reason my mind delights in giving.

Tattha [M 0.0070] paralokahetūti, mahārāja, kathaṃ nāma tumhādiso paṇḍitapuriso sakkasampattisadisaṃ sandiṭṭhikaṃ issariyaṃ pahāya paralokahetu cakkhūni dadeyyāti.

Therein, 'paralokahetu' means: O great king, how could a wise man such as you, having abandoned a visible sovereignty comparable to the fortune of Sakka, give his eyes for the sake of the next world?

Na vāhanti na ve ahaṃ. Yasasāti dibbassa vā mānusassa vā issariyassa kāraṇā, apica sataṃ bodhisattānaṃ dhammo buddhakārako carito ācarito āciṇṇo purātano icceva iminā kāraṇena dāneyeva īdiso mama mano niratoti.

'Na vāhaṃ' means 'not indeed I.' 'Yasasā' means for the sake of divine or human sovereignty. Rather, it is the ancient Dhamma of the good Bodhisattas, the practice that leads to Buddhahood, which has been walked, followed, and repeatedly practiced. For this very reason, my mind is devoted to giving of this kind.

Evañca pana vatvā rājā amacce saññāpetvā sivakaṃ vejjaṃ āṇāpesi – “ehi, sivaka, mama ubhopi akkhīni imassa brāhmaṇassa dātuṃ sīghaṃ uppāṭetvā hatthe patiṭṭhapehī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ –

And having spoken thus, the king, having convinced his ministers, commanded the physician Sivaka: 'Come, Sivaka! So that I may give them to this brahmin, quickly pluck out both my eyes and place them in my hand.' Therefore, it was said:

63.

63.

“Ehi sivaka uṭṭhehi, mā dandhayi mā pavedhayi;

Ubhopi nayanaṃ dehi, uppāṭetvā vanibbake.

Come, Sivaka, arise! Do not delay, do not tremble. Having plucked out both eyes, give them to the beggar.

64.

64.

“Tato so codito mayhaṃ, sivako vacanaṃkaro;

Uddharitvāna pādāsi, tālamiñjaṃva yācake”ti.

Then Sivaka, urged by me and obedient to my word, having extracted them, gave them, as one would give a palm-fruit kernel to a petitioner.

Tattha [V 0.0067] uṭṭhehīti uṭṭhānavīriyaṃ karohi. Imasmiṃ mama cakkhudāne sahāyakiccaṃ karohīti dasseti. Mā dantayīti mā cirāyi. Ayañhi atidullabho cirakālaṃ patthito mayā uttamo dānakkhaṇo paṭiladdho, so mā virajjhīti adhippāyo. Mā pavedhayīti “amhākaṃ rañño cakkhūni uppāṭemī”ti cittutrāsavasena mā vedhayi sarīrakampaṃ mā āpajji. Ubhopi [P 0.0069] nayananti ubhopi nayane. Vanibbaketi yācakassa mayhanti mayā. Uddharitvāna pādāsīti so vejjo rañño akkhikūpato ubhopi akkhīni uppāṭetvā rañño hatthe adāsi.

Here, 'uṭṭhehi' means 'arouse energetic effort.' This shows, 'Perform the duty of an assistant in this gift of my eyes.' 'Mā dandhayi' means 'do not delay.' For this is an extremely rare and long-awaited supreme moment of giving that I have obtained; may it not be lost—this is the intention. 'Mā pavedhayi' means 'do not tremble,' meaning, 'do not be frightened by the thought, "I am plucking out the king's eyes," nor let your body shake.' 'Ubhopi nayanaṃ' refers to both eyes. 'Vanibbake' means 'to the beggar,' (given) by me. 'Uddharitvāna pādāsi' means that the physician, having plucked out both eyes from the king's eye sockets, gave them into the king's hands.

Dento ca na satthakena uddharitvā adāsi. So hi cintesi – “ayuttaṃ mādisassa susikkhitavejjassa rañño akkhīsu satthapātana”nti bhesajjāni ghaṃsetvā bhesajjacuṇṇena nīluppalaṃ paribhāvetvā dakkhiṇakkhiṃ upasiṅghāpesi, akkhi parivatti, dukkhā vedanā uppajji. So paribhāvetvā punapi upasiṅghāpesi, akkhi akkhikūpato mucci, balavatarā vedanā udapādi, tatiyavāre kharataraṃ paribhāvetvā upanāmesi, akkhi osadhabalena paribbhamitvā akkhikūpato nikkhamitvā nhārusuttakena olambamānaṃ aṭṭhāsi, adhimattā [M 0.0071] vedanā udapādi, lohitaṃ pagghari, nivatthasāṭakāpi lohitena temiṃsu. Orodhā ca amaccā ca rañño pādamūle patitvā “deva, akkhīni mā dehi, deva, akkhīni mā dehī”ti mahāparidevaṃ parideviṃsu.

And in giving, he did not extract them with a small knife. For he thought, 'It is not fitting for a well-trained physician like me to make an incision in the king's eyes.' Having ground medicines, he saturated a blue lotus with the medicinal powder and applied it to the right eye. The eye turned, and a painful sensation arose. He saturated it again and applied it once more; the eye came out of the eye socket, and a more intense pain arose. The third time, having saturated it more harshly, he brought it near; the eye, propelled by the power of the medicine, spun around, came out of the eye socket, and stood hanging by the nerve thread. Extremely intense pain arose, blood flowed, and even the garments worn were soaked with blood. The women of the inner palace and the ministers fell at the king's feet, wailing loudly, 'Your Majesty, do not give your eyes! Your Majesty, do not give your eyes!'

Rājā vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā “tāta, mā papañcaṃ karī”ti āha. So “sādhu, devā”ti vāmahatthena akkhiṃ dhāretvā dakkhiṇahatthena satthakaṃ ādāya akkhisuttakaṃ chinditvā akkhiṃ gahetvā mahāsattassa hatthe ṭhapesi. So vāmakkhinā dakkhiṇakkhiṃ oloketvā pariccāgapītiyā abhibhuyyamānaṃ dukkhavedanaṃ vedento “ehi, brāhmaṇā”ti brāhmaṇaṃ pakkosāpetvā “mama ito cakkhuto sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena samantacakkhumeva piyataraṃ, tassa me idaṃ akkhidānaṃ paccayo hotū”ti brāhmaṇassa akkhiṃ adāsi. So taṃ ukkhipitvā attano akkhimhi ṭhapesi, taṃ tassānubhāvena vikasitanīluppalaṃ viya hutvā upaṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto vāmakkhinā tassa taṃ akkhiṃ disvā “aho sudinnaṃ mayā akkhī”ti antosamuggatāya pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭasarīro hutvā aparampi adāsi. Sakkopi taṃ [P 0.0070] tatheva katvā rājanivesanā nikkhamitvā mahājanassa olokentasseva nagarā nikkhamitvā devalokameva gato.

The king, enduring the pain, said, 'Dear one, do not delay.' Saying, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' he (the physician) held the eye with his left hand, took a small knife with his right hand, cut the optic nerve, took the eye, and placed it in the Great Being's hand. He (the Great Being) looked at his right eye with his left eye and, enduring the painful sensation which was being overcome by the joy of giving, he had the brahmin summoned and said, 'Come, brahmin. To me, the all-seeing eye is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold dearer than this eye. May this gift of my eye be a condition for that.' He gave the eye to the brahmin. He (the brahmin) lifted it and placed it in his own eye socket. By his (Sakka's) power, it was established there like a fully blossomed blue lotus. The Great Being, seeing that eye with his left eye, thought, 'Ah, how well have I given the eye!' With his body continuously pervaded by the joy that arose from within, he gave the other one as well. Sakka, having done the same with that one, departed from the royal palace and, as the great assembly watched, left the city and went to the world of the devas.

Rañño nacirasseva akkhīni āvāṭabhāvaṃ appattāni kambalageṇḍukaṃ viya uggatena maṃsapiṇḍena pūretvā cittakammarūpassa viya ruhiṃsu, vedanā pacchijji. Atha mahāsatto katipāhaṃ pāsāde vasitvā “kiṃ andhassa rajjenāti amaccānaṃ rajjaṃ niyyātetvā uyyānaṃ gantvā pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ [V 0.0068] karissāmī”ti cintetvā amaccānaṃ tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “mukhadhovanādidāyako eko puriso mayhaṃ santike hotu, sarīrakiccaṭṭhānesupi me rajjukaṃ bandhathā”ti vatvā sivikāya gantvā pokkharaṇitīre rājapallaṅke nisīdi. Amaccāpi vanditvā paṭikkamiṃsu. Bodhisattopi attano dānaṃ āvajjesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakkassa āsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko taṃ disvā “mahārājassa varaṃ datvā cakkhuṃ paṭipākatikaṃ karissāmī”ti bodhisattassa samīpaṃ gantvā padasaddamakāsi. Mahāsattena ca “ko eso”ti vutte –

Before long, the king's eye sockets, without becoming hollow, filled with lumps of flesh that grew like woolen balls and healed over to look like the eyes of a painted image; the pain subsided. Then the Great Being, having stayed in the palace for a few days, thought, "What use is a kingdom to a blind man? I will entrust the kingdom to my ministers, go to the park, go forth into homelessness, and practice the ascetic life." He informed the ministers of this matter and said, "Let one man who attends to my face-washing and such remain by my side, and tie a rope for me even in places for attending to bodily functions." Then he went in a palanquin and sat on the royal couch by the lotus pond. The ministers, having paid their respects, departed. The Bodhisatta reflected on his own act of giving. At that moment, Sakka's throne showed signs of heat. Seeing this, Sakka thought, "I will grant the great king a boon and restore his vision to its natural state," and approached the Bodhisatta, making a sound with his foot. When the Great Being asked, "Who is that?"—

“Sakkohamasmi [M 0.0072] devindo, āgatosmi tavantike;

Varaṃ varassu rājīsi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasī”ti. (jā. 1.15.71) –

"I am Sakka, lord of the devas, I have come into your presence. Choose a boon, O royal sage, whatever you wish for in your mind."

Vatvā tena –

When he had said this—

“Pahūtaṃ me dhanaṃ sakka, balaṃ koso canappako;

Andhassa me sato dāni, maraṇaññeva ruccatī”ti. (jā. 1.15.72) –

"Abundant is my wealth, O Sakka, my army and treasury are not small; but now that I am blind, only death is pleasing to me."

Vutte atha naṃ sakko āha – “sivirāja, kiṃ pana tvaṃ maritukāmo hutvā maraṇaṃ rocesi, udāhu andhabhāvenā”ti. Andhabhāvena, devāti. “Mahārāja, dānaṃ nāma na kevalaṃ samparāyatthameva diyyati, diṭṭhadhammatthāyapi paccayo hoti, tasmā tava dānapuññameva nissāya saccakiriyaṃ karohi, tassa baleneva te cakkhu uppajjissatī”ti vutte “tena hi mayā mahādānaṃ sudinna”nti vatvā saccakiriyaṃ karonto –

When this was said, Sakka then asked him, "King of Sivi, do you desire death because you wish to die, or is it because of your blindness?" "Because of blindness, deva." "Great king, a gift is not given for the sake of the next life alone; it is also a condition for benefit in this very life. Therefore, relying on the merit of your gift, make a solemn declaration of truth. By its power, your eye will arise." When this was said, he replied, "In that case, a great gift has been well given by me," and making a solemn declaration of truth, he said—

“Ye [P 0.0071] maṃ yācitumāyanti, nānāgottā vanibbakā;

Yopi maṃ yācate tattha, sopi me manaso piyo;

Etena saccavajjena, cakkhu me upapajjathā”ti. (jā. 1.15.74) –

"The mendicants of various clans who come to beg from me; whoever begs from me there, he too is dear to my mind. By this utterance of truth, may my eye arise."

Āha.

He spoke.

Tattha ye manti ye maṃ yācitumāgacchanti, tesupi āgatesu yo imaṃ nāma dehīti vācaṃ nicchārento [V 0.0069] maṃ yācate, sopi me manaso piyo. Etenāti sace mayhaṃ sabbepi yācakā piyā, saccamevetaṃ mayā vuttaṃ, etena me saccavacanena ekaṃ cakkhu upapajjatha uppajjatūti.

Therein, 'ye maṃ' means 'those who come to beg from me.' Among those who have come, whoever begs from me, uttering the words, 'Give me this thing,' he too is dear to my mind. 'Etena' means: 'If all beggars are dear to me, and this has truly been spoken by me, then by this utterance of truth of mine, may one eye arise, may it be restored!'

Athassa vacanasamanantarameva paṭhamaṃ cakkhu udapādi. Tato dutiyassa uppajjanatthāya –

Then, immediately after his words, the first eye arose. Then, for the purpose of the second arising—

“Yaṃ maṃ so yācituṃ āgā, dehi cakkhunti brāhmaṇo;

Tassa cakkhūni pādāsiṃ, brāhmaṇassa vanibbato.

“That brahmin, a mendicant, came to me to beg, saying, ‘Give me your eye.’ I gave my eyes to that brahmin, the mendicant.”

“Bhiyyo maṃ āvisī pīti, somanassañcanappakaṃ;

Etena saccavajjena, dutiyaṃ me upapajjathā”ti. (jā. 1.15.75-76) –

“Greater still, joy pervaded me, and immeasurable happiness arose; by this utterance of truth, may my second eye arise.”

Āha.

He said.

Tattha yaṃ manti yo maṃ. Soti so cakkhuyācako brāhmaṇo. Āgāti āgato. Vanibbatoti yācantassa. Maṃ āvisīti brāhmaṇassa [M 0.0073] cakkhūni datvā andhakālepi tathārūpaṃ vedanaṃ agaṇetvā “aho sudinnaṃ me dāna”nti paccavekkhantaṃ maṃ bhiyyo atirekatarā pīti āvisi. Somanassañcanappakanti aparimāṇaṃ somanassaṃ uppajji. Etenāti sace tadā mama anappakaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppannaṃ, saccamevetaṃ mayā vuttaṃ, etena me saccavacanena dutiyampi cakkhu upapajjatūti.

Therein, ‘yaṃ maṃ’ means ‘who… me.’ ‘So’ means that brahmin who was a beggar for an eye. ‘Āgā’ means ‘he came.’ ‘Vanibbato’ means ‘of the one begging.’ ‘Maṃ āvisī’ means: after giving my eyes to the brahmin, even in the time of blindness, not taking into account such a feeling, as I reflected, ‘Ah, my gift was well given,’ an even greater joy pervaded me. ‘Somanassañcanappakaṃ’ means immeasurable happiness arose. ‘Etena’ means: ‘If at that time immeasurable joy and happiness arose in me, and this has truly been spoken by me, then by this utterance of truth, may a second eye also arise for me!’

Taṃkhaṇaññeva dutiyampi cakkhu udapādi. Tāni panassa cakkhūni neva pākatikāni, na dibbāni. Sakkabrāhmaṇassa hi dinnaṃ cakkhuṃ puna pākatikaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, upahatacakkhuno ca dibbacakkhu nāma nuppajjati, vuttanayena panassa ādimajjhapariyosānesu aviparītaṃ attano dānapītiṃ upādāya pītipharaṇavasena nibbattāni “saccapāramitācakkhūnī”ti vuttāni. Tena vuttaṃ –

At that very moment, a second eye also arose. But those eyes of his were neither natural nor divine. For it is not possible to make natural again the eye given to the Sakka-brahmin, and a divine eye does not arise for one whose eye has been destroyed. However, in accordance with the method described, they were produced by means of the suffusion of joy, on account of his joy in giving being undiminished in the beginning, middle, and end, and are called the ‘eyes of the perfection of truth.’ Thus it is said:

65.

65.

“Dadamānassa [P 0.0072] dentassa, dinnadānassa me sato;

Cittassa aññathā natthi, bodhiyāyeva kāraṇā”ti.

“For me, while preparing to give, while in the act of giving, and after having given the gift, there was no alteration of mind; it was for the sake of enlightenment alone.”

Tattha dadamānassāti cakkhūni dātuṃ vejjena uppāṭentassa. Dentassāti uppāṭitāni tāni sakkabrāhmaṇassa [V 0.0070] hatthe ṭhapentassa. Dinnadānassāti cakkhudānaṃ dinnavato. Cittassa aññathāti dānajjhāsayassa aññathābhāvo. Bodhiyāyeva kāraṇāti tañca sabbaññutaññāṇasseva hetūti attho.

Therein, ‘dadamānassa’ means of him who was having the eyes extracted by the physician in order to give them. ‘Dentassa’ means of him who was placing those extracted eyes in the hand of the Sakka-brahmin. ‘Dinnadānassa’ means of him who had given the gift of his eyes. ‘Cittassa aññathā’ means the mind’s being otherwise, that is, a change in the intention to give. ‘Bodhiyāyeva kāraṇā’ means that it is a cause for omniscience itself; this is the meaning.

66. Sabbaññutaññāṇassa sudullabhatāya evaṃ sudukkaraṃ mayā katanti na cakkhūnaṃ na attabhāvassapi appiyatāyāti dassento “na me dessā”ti osānagāthamāha. Tattha attā na me na dessiyoti paṭhamo na-kāro nipātamatto. Attā na me kujjhitabbo, na appiyoti attho. “Attānaṃ me na dessiya”ntipi pāṭho. Tassattho – me attānaṃ ahaṃ na dessiyaṃ na kujjheyyaṃ na kujjhituṃ arahāmi na so mayā kujjhitabboti. “Attāpi me na dessiyo”tipi paṭhanti. Adāsahanti adāsiṃ ahaṃ. “Adāsiha”ntipi pāṭho.

66. To show that he performed such a difficult act because omniscience is so very difficult to obtain, and not out of any dislike for his eyes or his own being, he spoke the concluding verse, “They are not hateful to me.” Therein, in the phrase ‘attā na me na dessiyo,’ the first ‘na’ is a mere particle. The meaning is: ‘The self is not to be resented by me; it is not unloved.’ There is also the reading ‘Attānaṃ me na dessiyaṃ.’ Its meaning is: ‘I should not resent my self; I should not be angry; I am not fit to be angry; it should not be resented by me.’ They also recite ‘Attāpi me na dessiyo.’ ‘Adāsahaṃ’ means ‘I gave.’ There is also the reading ‘Adāsihaṃ.’

Tadā pana bodhisattassa saccakiriyāya cakkhūsu uppannesu sakkānubhāvena sabbā rājaparisā sannipatitāva ahosi. Athassa sakko mahājanamajjhe ākāse ṭhatvā –

Then, when the eyes had arisen for the Bodhisatta through his act of truth, the entire royal assembly was gathered by the power of Sakka. Then Sakka, standing in the sky in the midst of the great crowd, said to him:

“Dhammena [M 0.0074] bhāsitā gāthā, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Etāni tava nettāni, dibbāni paṭidissare.

“Righteously were the verses spoken, O increaser of the Sivi realm; these divine eyes of yours now reappear.”

“Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiroselaṃ, samatiggayha pabbataṃ;

Samantā yojanasataṃ, dassanaṃ anubhontu te”ti. (jā. 1.15.77-78) –

“Beyond wall, beyond rock, surpassing the mountain, may your eyes experience sight for a hundred yojanas all around.”

Imāhi gāthāhi thutiṃ katvā devalokameva gato. Bodhisattopi mahājanaparivuto mahantena sakkārena nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājagehadvāre susajjite mahāmaṇḍape samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisinno cakkhupaṭilābhena tuṭṭhahaṭṭhapamuditānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ āgatānaṃ nāgarānaṃ jānapadānaṃ rājaparisāya ca dhammaṃ desento –

Having praised him with these verses, he went to the world of the devas. The Bodhisatta, surrounded by a great crowd, entered the city with great honor and, seated on the royal throne under a lofty white parasol in the well-adorned great pavilion at the royal palace gate, he taught the Dhamma to the citizens, countryfolk, and the royal assembly who had come to see him, joyful, elated, and delighted at the recovery of his sight:

“Ko nīdha vittaṃ na dadeyya yācito, api visiṭṭhaṃ supiyampi attano;

Tadiṅgha sabbe sivayo samāgatā, dibbāni nettāni mamajja passatha.

“Who here, when asked, would not give wealth, even a most excellent and beloved possession of one’s own? Come now, all you Sivis who are assembled, behold my divine eyes today!”

“Tirokuṭṭaṃ [P 0.0073] tiroselaṃ, samatiggayha pabbataṃ;

Samantā yojanasataṃ, dassanaṃ anubhonti me.

“Beyond wall, beyond rock, surpassing the mountain, my eyes experience sight for a hundred yojanas all around.”

“Na [V 0.0071] cāgamattā paramatthi kiñci, maccānaṃ idha jīvite;

Datvāna mānusaṃ cakkhuṃ, laddhaṃ me cakkhu amānusaṃ.

“There is nothing whatsoever higher than giving for mortals here in this life; having given a human eye, I have received a non-human eye.”

“Etampi disvā sivayo, detha dānāni bhuñjatha;

Datvā ca bhutvā ca yathānubhāvaṃ, aninditā saggamupetha ṭhāna”nti. (jā. 1.15.79-82) –

“Seeing this, O Sivis, give gifts and enjoy them. Having given and enjoyed according to your means, blameless, approach the heavenly state.”

Imā gāthā abhāsi. Tattha dhammena bhāsitāti, mahārāja, imā te gāthā dhammena sabhāveneva bhāsitā. Dibbānīti dibbānubhāvayuttāni. Paṭidissareti paṭidissanti. Tirokuṭṭanti parakuṭṭaṃ. Tiroselanti paraselaṃ. Samatiggayhāti atikkamitvā. Samantā dasadisā yojanasataṃ rūpadassanaṃ anubhontu sādhentu.

He spoke these verses. Therein, ‘dhammena bhāsitā’ means, ‘O great king, these verses of yours were spoken righteously, that is, by their very nature.’ ‘Dibbāni’ means ‘endowed with divine power.’ ‘Paṭidissare’ means ‘they are seen again.’ ‘Tirokuṭṭaṃ’ means ‘beyond the wall.’ ‘Tiroselaṃ’ means ‘beyond the rock.’ ‘Samatiggayha’ means ‘having surpassed.’ ‘Samantā… anubhontu’ means ‘may they experience and accomplish the seeing of forms in the ten directions for a hundred yojanas all around.’

Ko nīdhāti ko nu idha. Api visiṭṭhanti uttamampi samānaṃ. Na cāgamattāti cāgappamāṇato aññaṃ varaṃ nāma natthi. Idha jīviteti imasmiṃ [M 0.0075] jīvaloke. “Idha jīvata”ntipi paṭhanti. Imasmiṃ loke jīvamānānanti attho. Amānusanti dibbacakkhu mayā laddhaṃ, iminā kāraṇena veditabbametaṃ “cāgato uttamaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Etampi disvāti etaṃ mayā laddhaṃ dibbacakkhuṃ disvāpi.

‘Ko nīdha’ means ‘who indeed here?’ ‘Api visiṭṭhaṃ’ means ‘even being excellent.’ ‘Na cāgamattā’ means ‘there is nothing superior to the measure of giving.’ ‘Idha jīvite’ means ‘in this living world.’ They also read ‘idha jīvataṃ.’ The meaning is ‘for those living in this world.’ ‘Amānusaṃ’ means ‘a non-human eye was received by me; for this reason it should be understood that there is nothing superior to giving.’ ‘Etampi disvā’ means ‘having seen this divine eye received by me.’

Iti imāhi catūhi gāthāhi na kevalaṃ tasmiṃyeva khaṇe, atha kho anvaddhamāsampi uposathe mahājanaṃ sannipātetvā dhammaṃ desesi. Taṃ sutvā mahājano dānādīni puññāni katvā devalokaparāyano ahosi.

Thus, with these four verses, he taught the Dhamma not only at that very moment, but also every fortnight on the Uposatha day, having gathered a great assembly. Having heard that, the great multitude performed meritorious deeds such as giving and became destined for the world of the devas.

Tadā vejjo ānandatthero ahosi, sakko anuruddhatthero, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, sivirājā lokanātho.

At that time, Sakka was the Elder Anuruddha, the remaining assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and King Sivi was the Lord of the World.

Tassa idhāpi vuttanayeneva yathārahaṃ pāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā divase divase yathā adinnapubbaṃ bāhiradeyyadhammavatthu na hoti, evaṃ aparimitaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattentassa tena aparituṭṭhassa kathaṃ nu kho ahaṃ ajjhattikavatthukaṃ dānaṃ dadeyyaṃ, kadā nu kho maṃ koci āgantvā [P 0.0074] ajjhattikaṃ deyyadhammaṃ yāceyya, sace hi koci yācako me hadayamaṃsassa nāmaṃ gaṇheyya, kaṇayena naṃ nīharitvā pasannaudakato sanāḷaṃ padumaṃ uddharanto viya lohitabinduṃ paggharantaṃ [V 0.0072] hadayaṃ nīharitvā dassāmi. Sace sarīramaṃsassa nāmaṃ gaṇheyya, avalekhanena tālaguḷapaṭalaṃ uppāṭento viya sarīramaṃsaṃ uppāṭetvā dassāmi. Sace lohitassa nāmaṃ gaṇheyya, asinā vijjhitvā yantamukhe vā patitvā upanītaṃ bhājanaṃ pūretvā lohitaṃ dassāmi. Sace pana koci “gehe me kammaṃ nappavattati, tattha me dāsakammaṃ karohī”ti vadeyya, rājavesaṃ apanetvā tassa attānaṃ sāvetvā dāsakammaṃ karissāmi. Sace vā pana koci akkhīnaṃ nāmaṃ gaṇheyya, tālamiñjaṃ nīharanto viya akkhīni uppāṭetvā tassa dassāmīti evaṃ anaññasādhāraṇavasībhāvappattānaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃyeva āveṇikā uḷāratarā parivitakkuppatti, cakkhuyācakaṃ labhitvā amaccapārisajjādīhi nivāriyamānassāpi tesaṃ vacanaṃ anādiyitvā attano parivitakkānurūpaṃ paṭipattiyā ca paramā pītipaṭisaṃvedanā, tassā pītimanatāya avitathabhāvaṃ nissāya sakkassa purato saccakiriyākaraṇaṃ, tena ca attano cakkhūnaṃ paṭipākatikabhāvo, tesañca dibbānubhāvatāti evamādayo mahāsattassa guṇānubhāvā veditabbāti.

Here too, his perfections should be determined in the appropriate manner as previously described. Thus, day after day, as there was no external object of giving that had not been given before, while he was giving immeasurable great gifts, being dissatisfied with that, he thought: 'How might I give an internal gift? When will someone come to me to ask for an internal gift? If indeed any beggar were to ask for the flesh of my heart, I would take it out with a knife and give it, like drawing a lotus with its stalk from clear water, even as drops of blood trickle from it. If they were to ask for the flesh of my body, I would scrape off the flesh with a blade and give it, like peeling off a layer of palm fruit. If they were to ask for blood, I would pierce myself with a sword and, filling a vessel brought near with blood, I would give it. Or if someone were to say, “My work at home does not proceed, so do the work of a slave for me,” I would set aside my royal attire, announce myself to them, and perform the work of a slave. Or if someone were to ask for my eyes, I would pluck out my eyes and give them, like extracting the kernel of a palm fruit.' Thus, the arising of such an extraordinary and exceedingly lofty reflection is unique to the great bodhisattvas who have attained mastery. Upon finding a beggar asking for his eyes, even though being restrained by ministers and courtiers, he disregarded their words and acted in accordance with his own reflection, and through that practice experienced supreme joy. Relying on the unfailing nature of that joyful mind, he made a declaration of truth before Sakka. Thereby, his eyes were restored to their natural state, and they gained divine power. In this way, these and other virtues and powers of the great being are to be understood.

Sivirājacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Conduct of King Sivi is concluded.

9. Vessantaracariyāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Conduct of Vessantara

67. Navame [M 0.0076] yā me ahosi janikāti ettha meti vessantarabhūtaṃ attānaṃ sandhāya satthā vadati. Tenevāha – “phussatī nāma khattiyā”ti. Tadā hissa mātā “phussatī”ti evaṃnāmikā khattiyānī ahosi. Sā atītāsu jātīsūti sā tato anantarātītajātiyaṃ. Ekatthe hi etaṃ bahuvacanaṃ. Sakkassa mahesī piyā ahosīti sambandho. Atha vā yā me ahosi janikā imasmiṃ carimattabhāve, sā atītāsu jātīsu phussatī nāma, tattha atītāya jātiyā khattiyā, yatthāhaṃ tassā kucchimhi vessantaro [P 0.0075] hutvā nibbattiṃ, tato anantarātītāya sakkassa mahesī piyā ahosīti. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā –

67. In the ninth account, regarding the phrase 'She who was my mother,' the Teacher speaks referring to himself as having been Vessantara. Therefore, he said: 'A Khattiya named Phussatī.' At that time, his mother was a Khattiya lady named Phussatī. As for 'in past births,' this means in the immediately preceding past birth. Here, the plural is used in the sense of the singular. The connection is: 'She was the beloved chief queen of Sakka.' Alternatively: 'She who was my mother in this final existence, she in past births was named Phussatī, a Khattiya in that past birth where I, as Vessantara, was born in her womb; and in the birth immediately preceding that, she was the beloved chief queen of Sakka.' Here is the sequential account:

Ito hi ekanavute kappe vipassī nāma satthā loke udapādi. Tasmiṃ bandhumatīnagaraṃ upanissāya kheme migadāye viharante bandhumā rājā kenaci raññā pesitaṃ mahagghaṃ candanasāraṃ attano [V 0.0073] jeṭṭhadhītāya adāsi. Sā tena sukhumaṃ candanacuṇṇaṃ kāretvā samuggaṃ pūretvā vihāraṃ gantvā satthu suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ pūjetvā sesacuṇṇāni gandhakuṭiyaṃ vikiritvā “bhante, anāgate tumhādisassa buddhassa mātā bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Sā tato cutā tassā candanacuṇṇapūjāya phalena rattacandanaparipphositena viya sarīrena devesu ca manussesu ca saṃsarantī tāvatiṃsabhavane sakkassa devarañño aggamahesī hutvā nibbatti. Athassā āyupariyosāne pubbanimittesu uppannesu sakko devarājā tassā parikkhīṇāyukataṃ ñatvā tassā anukampāya “bhadde, phussati dasa te vare dammi, te gaṇhassū”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ –

For ninety-one aeons ago from this one, the Teacher named Vipassī arose in the world. While he was dwelling near the city of Bandhumatī in the Khema Deer Park, King Bandhumā gave a very precious piece of sandalwood, sent by another king, to his eldest daughter. She had it ground into fine sandalwood powder, filled a casket with it, went to the monastery, honored the Teacher’s golden-hued body, and scattered the remaining powder in the perfumed chamber. Then she made the aspiration: 'Venerable sir, in the future may I become the mother of a Buddha like you.' After passing away from that existence, as a result of her offering of sandalwood powder, she wandered among devas and humans with a body as if sprinkled with red sandalwood, until she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as the chief queen of Sakka, king of the devas. Then, at the end of her lifespan, when the preliminary signs appeared, Sakka, king of the devas, knowing that her life was exhausted, said to her out of compassion: 'Good lady, Phussatī, I give you ten boons. Accept them.' Therefore it was said:

68.

68.

“Tassā āyukkhayaṃ ñatvā, devindo etadabravi;

‘Dadāmi te dasa vare, vara bhadde yadicchasī’”ti.

Knowing her lifespan was ending, the lord of devas said this: 'I give you ten boons; choose, good lady, whatever you wish.'

Tattha varāti varassu varaṃ gaṇha. Bhadde, yadicchasīti, bhadde, phussati yaṃ icchasi yaṃ tava piyaṃ, taṃ dasahi koṭṭhāsehi “varaṃ varassu paṭiggaṇhāhī”ti vadati.

Therein, `vara` means 'choose' or 'take a boon.' As for 'Good lady, whatever you wish,' it means he says: 'Good lady Phussatī, whatever you desire, whatever is dear to you, that boon from among the ten portions, choose and accept.'

69. Punidamabravīti puna idaṃ sā attano cavanadhammataṃ ajānantī “kiṃ nu me aparādhatthī”tiādikaṃ abhāsi. Sā hi pamattā hutvā attano āyukkhayaṃ [M 0.0077] ajānantī ayaṃ “varaṃ gaṇhā”ti vadanto “katthaci mama uppajjanaṃ icchatī”ti ñatvā evamāha. Tattha aparādhatthīti aparādho atthi. Kiṃ nu dessā ahaṃ tavāti kiṃ kāraṇaṃ ahaṃ tava dessā kujjhitabbā appiyā jātā. Rammā cāvesi maṃ ṭhānāti ramaṇīyā imasmā ṭhānā cāvesi. Vātova dharaṇīruhanti yena balavā māluto viya rukkhaṃ ummūlento imamhā devalokā cāvetukāmosi kiṃ nu kāraṇanti taṃ pucchati.

69. Then she spoke again: not knowing her own nature of passing away, she said, 'What wrong is there on my part?' and so on. For she, being heedless and unaware that her lifespan was ending, and understanding that when he said, 'Accept a boon,' he wished for her to be reborn somewhere, spoke thus. Therein, 'What wrong is there on my part?' means 'Is there a fault?' 'Why am I hateful to you?' means 'For what reason have I become hateful, deserving of your anger, and unloved?' 'You make me fall from a delightful place' means 'You make me fall from this delightful place.' 'Like the wind, a tree' means she asks him: 'For what reason do you wish to make me fall from this deva world, just as a strong wind uproots a tree?'

70. Tassidanti tassā idaṃ. Na ceva te kataṃ pāpanti na ceva tayā kiñci pāpaṃ kataṃ yena te aparādho [P 0.0076] siyā. Na ca me tvaṃsi appiyāti mama tvaṃ na cāpi appiyā, yena dessā nāma mama appiyāti adhippāyo.

70. As for 'To her, this,' it means this was said to her. 'And you have done no evil' means 'No evil whatsoever has been done by you for which there might be a fault on your part.' 'Nor are you unloved by me' means 'You are not unloved by me either; the meaning is that you are not hateful to me.'

71. Idāni yena adhippāyena vare dātukāmo, taṃ dassento “ettakaṃyeva te āyu, cavanakālo bhavissatī”ti vatvā vare gaṇhāpento “paṭiggaṇha mayā dinne, vare dasa varuttame”ti āha.

71. Now, revealing the intention with which he wished to give the boons, he said, 'Your life is only this long; the time for your passing will come,' and, causing her to accept the boons, he said, 'Accept the ten supreme boons given by me.'

Tattha varuttameti varesu uttame aggavare.

Here, "supreme boon" means the highest and best of boons.

72. Dinnavarāti [V 0.0074] “vare dassāmī”ti paṭiññādānavasena dinnavarā. Tuṭṭhahaṭṭhāti icchitalābhaparitosena tuṭṭhā ceva tassa ca sikhāppattidassanena hāsavasena haṭṭhā ca. Pamoditāti balavapāmojjena pamuditā. Mamaṃ abbhantaraṃ katvāti tesu varesu maṃ abbhantaraṃ karitvā. Dasa vare varīti sā attano khīṇāyukabhāvaṃ ñatvā sakkena varadānatthaṃ katokāsā sakalajambudīpatalaṃ olokentī attano anucchavikaṃ sivirañño nivesanaṃ disvā tattha tassa aggamahesibhāvo nīlanettatā nīlabhamukatā phussatītināmaṃ guṇavisesayuttaputtapaṭilābho anunnatakucchibhāvo alambatthanatā apalitabhāvo sukhumacchavitā vajjhajanānaṃ mocanasamatthatā cāti ime dasa vare gaṇhi.

72. "One to whom boons were given": by virtue of the promise "I will give boons," she was one to whom boons were given. "Delighted and joyful": pleased by gaining what she desired and joyful with laughter upon seeing his crest. "Overjoyed": overjoyed with great delight. "Making me internal": making me central regarding those boons. Knowing that her lifespan was exhausted and having been given the opportunity by Sakka to be granted boons, she, surveying the entire surface of Jambudīpa and seeing the residence of King Sivi as suitable for her, chose these ten boons: becoming his chief queen, having dark eyes, dark eyebrows, the name Phussatī, obtaining a son endowed with special qualities, a non-protruding belly, non-sagging breasts, no gray hair, delicate skin, and the ability to free those condemned to death.

Iti sā dasa vare gahetvā tato cutā maddarañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. Jāyamānā ca sā candanacuṇṇaparipphositena viya sarīrena jātā. Tenassā nāmaggahaṇadivase “phussatī” tveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Sā mahantena parivārena vaḍḍhitvā soḷasavassakāle uttamarūpadharā [M 0.0078] ahosi. Atha naṃ jetuttaranagare sivimahārājā puttassa sañjayakumārassatthāya ānetvā setacchattaṃ ussāpetvā taṃ soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Thus, having taken those ten boons, she passed away from there and was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of King Madda. At birth, her body appeared as if sprinkled with sandalwood powder. Therefore, on the day of her naming ceremony, they gave her the name "Phussatī." She grew up surrounded by a great retinue and by the age of sixteen, she possessed supreme beauty.
