Then, King Sivi of Jetuttara city brought her for the sake of his son, Prince Sañjaya, raised a white parasol over her, made her the foremost among sixteen thousand women, and placed her in the position of chief queen. Hence it is said:

73.

73.

“Tato cutā sā phussatī, khattiye upapajjatha;

Jetuttaramhi nagare, sañjayena samāgamī”ti.

"Then, passing away from there, that Phussatī was reborn among the Khattiyas; in the city of Jetuttara, she was united with Sañjaya."

Sā sañjayarañño piyā ahosi manāpā. Atha sakko āvajjento “mayā phussatiyā dinnavaresu nava varā samiddhā”ti disvā “puttavaro na samiddho, tampissā samijjhāpessāmī”ti cintetvā bodhisattaṃ tadā tāvatiṃsadevaloke khīṇāyukaṃ disvā tassa santikaṃ gantvā “mārisa, tayā manussaloke [P 0.0077] sivisañjayarañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tassa ceva aññesañca cavanadhammānaṃ saṭṭhisahassānaṃ devaputtānaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Mahāsattopi tato cavitvā tatthuppanno. Sesā devaputtāpi saṭṭhisahassānaṃ amaccānaṃ gehesu nibbattiṃsu. Mahāsatte kucchigate phussatidevī catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāreti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassāni vissajjetvā dānaṃ dātuṃ dohaḷinī ahosi. Rājā tassā dohaḷaṃ sutvā nemittake brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā pucchitvā “mahārāja, deviyā kucchimhi dānābhirato uḷāro satto uppanno, dānena tittiṃ na pāpuṇissatī”ti sutvā tuṭṭhamānaso vuttappakāraṃ dānaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Samaṇabrāhmaṇajiṇṇāturakapaṇaddhikavanibbakayācake [V 0.0075] santappesi. Bodhisattassa paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāya rañño āyassa pamāṇaṃ nāhosi. Tassa puññānubhāvena sakalajambudīpe rājāno paṇṇākāraṃ pahiṇanti. Tena vuttaṃ –

She was dear and beloved to King Sañjaya. Then, Sakka, reflecting, saw, “Of the boons I gave to Phussatī, nine have been fulfilled,” and thought, “The boon of a son is not yet fulfilled; I shall cause that one to be fulfilled for her as well.” Having considered this, he saw the Bodhisatta in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven nearing the end of his life. Approaching him, he said, “Venerable sir, it is fitting for you to take rebirth in the human world, in the womb of the chief queen of King Sañjaya of the Sivis.” Having obtained the consent of the Bodhisatta and of sixty thousand other devas who were destined to pass away, Sakka returned to his own abode. The Great Being then passed away from there and was reborn in her womb. The remaining sixty thousand devas were also reborn in the households of sixty thousand ministers. When the Great Being was in her womb, Queen Phussatī developed a pregnancy craving to give alms. She had six alms-halls built—at the four city gates, in the middle of the city, and at the palace gate—and, distributing six hundred thousand daily, she had a craving to give gifts. When the king heard of her craving, he had soothsaying brahmins summoned and questioned them. Hearing them say, “Great king, a great being who delights in giving has been conceived in the queen’s womb; he will not attain satisfaction through giving,” he was pleased at heart and established the giving of gifts in the manner described. He satisfied ascetics, brahmins, the aged, the sick, the destitute, travellers, and beggars. From the time the Bodhisatta was conceived, there was no limit to the king’s revenue. Through the power of his merit, kings throughout all of Jambudīpa sent tribute. Therefore, it was said:

74.

74.

“Yadāhaṃ phussatiyā kucchiṃ, okkanto piyamātuyā;

Mama tejena me mātā, tadā dānaratā ahu.

“When I entered the womb of my dear mother Phussatī, then, by my power, my mother became devoted to giving.

75.

75.

“Adhane [M 0.0079] āture jiṇṇe, yācake addhike jane;

Samaṇe brāhmaṇe khīṇe, deti dānaṃ akiñcane”ti;

“To the poor, the sick, and the aged, to beggars and wayfaring folk; to ascetics, brahmins, the depleted, and those with nothing, she gives gifts.”

Tattha mama tejenāti mama dānajjhāsayānubhāvena. Khīṇeti bhogādīhi parikkhīṇe pārijuññappatte. Akiñcaneti apariggahe. Sabbattha visaye bhummaṃ. Adhanādayo hi dānadhammassa pavattiyā visayo.

Here, 'by my power' means by the power of my disposition for giving. 'Depleted' means exhausted of possessions and the like, having reached a state of utter ruin. 'Possessing nothing' means without any property. In all these terms, the locative case denotes the sphere of action, for the poor and the like are indeed the sphere for the practice of the virtue of giving.

Devī mahantena parihārena gabbhaṃ dhārentī dasamāse paripuṇṇe nagaraṃ daṭṭhukāmā hutvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā devanagaraṃ viya nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā deviṃ rathavaraṃ āropetvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ kāresi. Tassā vessavīthiyā majjhappattakāle kammajavātā caliṃsu. Amaccā rañño ārocesuṃ. So vessavīthiyaṃyevassā sūtigharaṃ kāretvā [P 0.0078] ārakkhaṃ gaṇhāpesi. Sā tattha puttaṃ vijāyi. Tenāha –

The queen, bearing the child with great care, when the ten months were complete, desiring to see the city, informed the king. The king, having adorned the city like a celestial city, placed the queen on a splendid chariot and had her circumambulate the city. When she had reached the middle of the merchants' street, labor pains arose. The ministers informed the king. He had a birthing house built right there in the merchants' street and arranged for protection. There, she gave birth to a son. Hence he said:

76.

76.

“Dasamāse dhārayitvāna, karonte puraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ;

Vessānaṃ vīthiyā majjhe, janesi phussatī mamaṃ.

“Having carried me for ten months, while they were circumambulating the city, in the middle of the merchants' street, Phussatī gave birth to me.

77. “Na mayhaṃ mattikaṃ nāmaṃ, nāpi pettikasambhavaṃ.

77. “My name is not one from my mother, nor is it one of paternal origin.

Jātettha vessavīthiyaṃ, tasmā vessantaro ahū”ti.

“I was born here in the merchants' street; therefore, I became Vessantara.”

Tattha karonte puraṃ padakkhiṇanti deviṃ gahetvā sañjayamahārāje nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ kurumāne. Vessānanti vāṇijānaṃ.

Here, 'while they were circumambulating the city' means while the great King Sañjaya, taking the queen with him, was circumambulating the city. 'Vessānaṃ' means 'of merchants'.

Na mattikaṃ nāmanti na mātuāgataṃ mātāmahādīnaṃ nāmaṃ. Pettikasambhavanti pitu idanti pettikaṃ[V 0.0076], sambhavati etasmāti sambhavo, taṃ pettikaṃ sambhavo etassāti pettikasambhavaṃ, nāmaṃ. Mātāpitusambandhavasena na katanti dasseti. Jātetthāti jāto ettha. “Jātomhī”tipi pāṭho. Tasmā vessantaro ahūti yasmā tadā vessavīthiyaṃ jāto, tasmā vessantaro nāma ahosi, vessantaroti nāmaṃ akaṃsūti attho.

'Not a maternal name' means not a name coming from the mother, such as from the maternal grandmother and so on. 'Of paternal origin' (pettikasambhavaṃ) is explained thus: 'of the father' (pitu) 'is this' (idaṃ), hence 'paternal' (pettikaṃ); 'it originates' (sambhavati) 'from this' (etasmā), hence 'origin' (sambhavo); 'for whom there is this paternal origin' is 'of paternal origin' (pettikasambhavaṃ). This shows that the name was not created based on a connection to his mother or father. 'Jātettha' means 'born here.' There is also the reading 'jātomhi' ('I was born'). 'Therefore, I became Vessantara' means: because he was born at that time in the merchants' street, therefore his name was Vessantara; the meaning is that they gave him the name Vessantara.

Mahāsatto mātu kucchito nikkhamanto visado hutvā akkhīni ummīletvāva nikkhami. Nikkhantamatte eva mātu hatthaṃ pasāretvā “amma, dānaṃ dassāmi, atthi kiñcī”ti āha. Athassa mātā “tāta, yathājjhāsayaṃ dānaṃ dehī”ti hatthasamīpe sahassatthavikaṃ ṭhapesi. Bodhisatto hi ummaṅgajātake [M 0.0080] (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) imasmiṃ jātake pacchimattabhāveti tīsu ṭhānesu jātamattova kathesi. Rājā mahāsattassa atidīghādidosavivajjitā madhurakhīrā catusaṭṭhidhātiyo upaṭṭhāpesi. Tena saddhiṃ jātānaṃ saṭṭhiyā dārakasahassānampi dhātiyo dāpesi. So saṭṭhidārakasahassehi saddhiṃ mahantena parivārena vaḍḍhati. Tassa rājā satasahassagghanakaṃ kumārapiḷandhanaṃ kārāpetvā adāsi. So catupañcavassikakāle taṃ omuñcitvā dhātīnaṃ datvā puna tāhi dīyamānaṃ na gaṇhāti. Taṃ [P 0.0079] sutvā rājā “mama puttena dinnaṃ sudinna”nti vatvā aparampi kāresi. Tampi deti. Dārakakāleyeva dhātīnaṃ navavāre piḷandhanaṃ adāsi.

The Great Being, emerging from his mother's womb, came forth unsullied, with his eyes already open. The very moment he emerged, he stretched out his hand toward his mother and said, “Mother, I wish to give alms; is there anything?” Then his mother, saying, “Dear one, give alms according to your inclination,” placed a purse containing a thousand coins near his hand. Indeed, the Bodhisatta spoke as soon as he was born in three instances: in the Ummaṅga Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.590 and others), in this Jātaka, and in his final existence. The king provided the Great Being with sixty-four wet nurses who were free from defects such as being too tall, and who had sweet milk. Nurses were also provided for the sixty thousand boys who were born at the same time as him. Thus, he grew up with a large retinue of sixty thousand boys. The king had a princely ornament made worth a hundred thousand and gave it to him. At the age of four or five years, he took it off and gave it to the wet nurses, and when they offered it back, he would not accept it. Hearing this, the king said, “What my son has given is well given,” and had another made. That too he gave away. Even in his childhood, he gave his ornaments to the wet nurses nine times.

Aṭṭhavassikakāle pana sayanapīṭhe nisinno cintesi – “ahaṃ bāhirakadānaṃ demi, na taṃ maṃ paritoseti, ajjhattikadānaṃ dātukāmomhi. Sace hi maṃ koci hadayaṃ yāceyya, hadayaṃ nīharitvā dadeyyaṃ. Sace akkhīni yāceyya, akkhīni uppāṭetvā dadeyyaṃ. Sace sakalasarīre maṃsaṃ rudhirampi vā yāceyya, sakalasarīrato maṃsaṃ chinditvā rudhirampi asinā vijjhitvā dadeyyaṃ. Athāpi koci ‘dāso me hohī’ti vadeyya, attānaṃ tassa sāvetvā dadeyya”nti. Tassevaṃ sabhāvaṃ sarasaṃ cintentassa catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalā ayaṃ mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā kampi. Sinerupabbatarājā onamitvā jetuttaranagarābhimukho aṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, at the age of eight, while sitting on his bed, he reflected: “I give external gifts, but that does not satisfy me; I wish to give internal gifts. If someone were to ask for my heart, I would take it out and give it. If someone asked for my eyes, I would pluck them out and give them. If someone asked for the flesh and blood of my entire body, I would cut the flesh from my whole body and give it, and piercing myself with a sword, I would give my blood. And if someone were to say, ‘Be my slave,’ I would declare myself his slave and give myself to him.” As he thus pondered his innate nature with such fervor, this great earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in thickness, trembled up to its watery boundaries. Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, bent down and stood facing the city of Jetuttara. Therefore it was said:

78.

78.

“Yadāhaṃ dārako homi, jātiyā aṭṭhavassiko;

Tadā nisajja pāsāde, dānaṃ dātuṃ vicintayiṃ.

“When I was a boy, eight years of age, seated in the palace, I reflected on the giving of gifts.

79.

79.

“Hadayaṃ [V 0.0077] dadeyyaṃ cakkhuṃ, maṃsampi rudhirampi ca;

Dadeyyaṃ kāyaṃ sāvetvā, yadi koci yācaye mamaṃ.

“I would give my heart and my eyes, my flesh and also my blood; I would give my body, having declared my servitude, if anyone were to ask it of me.

80.

80.

“Sabhāvaṃ cintayantassa, akampitamasaṇṭhitaṃ;

Akampi tattha pathavī, sineruvanavaṭaṃsakā”ti.

“As I contemplated my own nature, unshaken and unhesitating, the earth trembled there, and the mountains of Sineru with their forest garlands.”

Tattha sāvetvāti “ajja paṭṭhāya ahaṃ imassa dāso”ti dāsabhāvaṃ sāvetvā. Yadi koci yācaye mamanti koci maṃ yadi yāceyya. Sabhāvaṃ cintayantassāti aviparītaṃ attano yathābhūtaṃ sabhāvaṃ atittimaṃ [M 0.0081] yathājjhāsayaṃ cintentassa mama, mayi cintenteti attho. Akampitanti kampitarahitaṃ. Asaṇṭhitanti saṅkocarahitaṃ. Yena hi lobhādinā abodhisattānaṃ cakkhādidāne cittutrāsasaṅkhātaṃ kampitaṃ saṅkocasaṅkhātaṃ saṇṭhitañca siyā, tena vināti attho. Akampīti acali. Sineruvanavaṭaṃsakāti sinerumhi uṭṭhitanandanavanaphārusakavanamissakavanacittalatāvanādikappakataruvanaṃ sineruvanaṃ. Atha vā sineru ca jambudīpādīsu ramaṇīyavanañca sineruvanaṃ[P 0.0080], taṃ vanaṃ vaṭaṃsakaṃ etissāti sineruvanavaṭaṃsakā.

Herein, sāvetvā means having declared one's state of servitude, saying, “From this day forward, I am this person’s slave.” Yadi koci yācaye mamaṃ means if anyone should ask me. Sabhāvaṃ cintayantassa means while I was contemplating my own true, undistorted nature, my insatiable disposition, according to my inclination; this is the meaning. Akampitaṃ means free from trembling. Asaṇṭhitaṃ means free from shrinking. For, due to greed and the like, when non-Bodhisattas give gifts such as their eyes, there may be trembling, known as mental terror, and shrinking, known as contraction; the meaning is ‘without that.’ Akampi means it trembled. Sineruvanavaṭaṃsakā refers to the Sineru forest, which is the forest of celestial wishing-trees on Sineru, such as the Nandana, Phārusaka, Missaka, and Cittalatā forests. Alternatively, Sineru and the delightful forests in Jambudīpa and other places are the ‘Sineru forest’; that forest is a garland for her (i.e., for the perfection of giving), thus she is sineruvanavaṭaṃsakā.

Evañca pathavikampane vattamāne madhuragambhīradevo gajjanto khaṇikavassaṃ vassi, vijjulatā nicchariṃsu, mahāsamuddo ubbhijji, sakko devarājā apphoṭesi, mahābrahmā sādhukāramadāsi, yāva brahmalokā ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi. Mahāsatto soḷasavassakāleyeva sabbasippānaṃ nipphattiṃ pāpuṇi. Tassa pitā rajjaṃ dātukāmo mātarā saddhiṃ mantetvā maddarājakulato mātuladhītaraṃ maddiṃ nāma rājakaññaṃ ānetvā soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ aggamahesiṃ katvā mahāsattaṃ rajje abhisiñci. Mahāsatto rajje patiṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya devasikaṃ chasatasahassāni vissajjetvā mahādānaṃ pavattento anvaddhamāsaṃ dānaṃ oloketuṃ upasaṅkamati. Aparabhāge maddidevī puttaṃ vijāyi. Taṃ kañcanajālena sampaṭicchiṃsu, tenassa “jālikumāro”tveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassa padasā gamanakāle sā dhītaraṃ vijāyi. Taṃ kaṇhājinena sampaṭicchiṃsu, tenassā “kaṇhājinā”tveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

And so, while the earth was trembling, the storm god, thundering with a sweet and deep sound, sent down a momentary shower; flashes of lightning shot forth; the great ocean swelled up; Sakka, king of the gods, snapped his fingers in applause; Mahābrahmā gave a cry of approval; and a single great acclamation arose, reaching as far as the Brahma-world. The Great Being attained mastery in all the arts at the age of sixteen. His father, wishing to give him the kingdom, consulted with his mother, and brought the princess named Maddī, his maternal uncle’s daughter from the royal family of Madda. He made her the chief queen among sixteen thousand women and anointed the Great Being to the kingship. From the time he was established in the kingdom, the Great Being, dispensing six hundred thousand daily, maintained a great distribution of alms, and every half-month he would go to inspect the almsgiving. Later, Queen Maddī gave birth to a son. They received him in a golden net, for which reason they named him Jālikumāra. When he was old enough to walk on his own feet, she gave birth to a daughter. They received her in a black deerskin, for which reason they named her Kaṇhājinā. Therefore it was said:

81.

81.

“Anvaddhamāse pannarase, puṇṇamāse uposathe;

Paccayaṃ nāgamāruyha, dānaṃ dātuṃ upāgami”nti.

“Every half-month, on the fifteenth day, the full-moon Uposatha, mounting the elephant Paccaya, I went forth to give alms.”

Tattha anvaddhamāseti anuaddhamāse, addhamāse addhamāseti attho. Puṇṇamāseti puṇṇamāsiyaṃ, māsaparipūriyā [V 0.0078] candaparipūriyā ca samannāgate pannarase dānaṃ dātuṃ upāgaminti sambandho. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – paccayaṃ nāgamāruyha addhamāse addhamāse dānaṃ dātuṃ dānasālaṃ upāgamiṃ, evaṃ upagacchanto ca yadā ekasmiṃ pannarase puṇṇamāsiuposathe dānaṃ dātuṃ upāgamiṃ, tadā kaliṅgaraṭṭhavisayā brāhmaṇā upagañchu [M 0.0082] manti tattha paccayaṃ nāganti paccayanāmakaṃ maṅgalahatthiṃ. Bodhisattassa hi jātadivase ekā ākāsacārinī kareṇukā abhimaṅgalasammataṃ sabbasetahatthipotakaṃ ānetvā maṅgalahatthiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā pakkāmi. Tassa mahāsattaṃ [P 0.0081] paccayaṃ katvā laddhattā “paccayo”tveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Taṃ paccayanāmakaṃ opavayhaṃ hatthināgaṃ āruyha dānaṃ dātuṃ upāgaminti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Herein, ‘anvaddhamāse’ means ‘anuaddhamāse,’ that is, ‘every half-month.’ ‘Puṇṇamāse’ means ‘on the full moon day’; the connection is: ‘I went to give alms on the fifteenth day, endowed with the completion of the month and the completion of the moon.’ Herein, this is the construction: ‘Riding the elephant Paccaya, I went to the alms-hall to give alms every half-month. And as I was thus going, when I went to give alms on a certain fifteenth day, a full moon Uposatha day, then brahmins from the Kalinga country approached me.’ Herein, ‘paccayaṃ nāgaṃ’ refers to the auspicious elephant named Paccaya. For on the Bodhisatta’s day of birth, a sky-faring female elephant brought a completely white young elephant, considered highly auspicious, and having placed it in the station of the auspicious elephant, departed. Because it was obtained as a support (paccaya) for the Great Being, they gave it the name ‘Paccaya.’ Riding that lordly elephant named Paccaya, which was fit for riding, I went to give alms. Therefore, it was said:

82.

82.

“Kaliṅgaraṭṭhavisayā, brāhmaṇā upagañchu maṃ;

Ayācuṃ maṃ hatthināgaṃ, dhaññaṃ maṅgalasammataṃ.

“From the Kalinga country, brahmins approached me; They begged me for a lordly elephant, the auspiciously esteemed, prosperous one.

83.

83.

“Avuṭṭhiko janapado, dubbhikkho chātako mahā;

Dadāhi pavaraṃ nāgaṃ, sabbasetaṃ gajuttama”nti.

“The land is without rain, afflicted by famine, a great hunger. Give the excellent lordly elephant, the supreme elephant, all-white.”

Tattha “kaliṅgaraṭṭhavisayā”tiādigāthā heṭṭhā kururājacaritepi (cariyā. 1.21-22) āgatā eva, tasmā tāsaṃ attho kathāmaggo ca tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Idha pana maṅgalahatthino setattā “sabbasetaṃ gajuttama”nti vuttaṃ. Bodhisatto hatthikkhandhavaragato –

Herein, the verses beginning with ‘From the Kalinga country’ have already appeared below in the Kururāja-cariya (Cariyā. 1.21–22). Therefore, their meaning and the narrative path should be understood in the same way as stated there. Here, however, because the auspicious elephant is white, it is said, ‘the supreme all-white elephant.’ The Bodhisatta, being upon the excellent elephant's back—

84.

84.

“Dadāmi na vikampāmi, yaṃ maṃ yācanti brāhmaṇā;

Santaṃ nappaṭigūhāmi, dāne me ramate mano”ti. –

“I give and do not waver, whatever the brahmins ask of me; I do not conceal what exists, my mind delights in giving.”

Attano dānābhiratiṃ pavedento –

Making known his own delight in giving—

85.

85.

“Na me yācakamanuppatte, paṭikkhepo anucchavo;

Mā me bhijji samādānaṃ, dassāmi vipulaṃ gaja”nti. (cariyā. 1.23) –

“For me, when a petitioner has arrived, refusal is unseemly; Let not my resolve be broken, I shall give the great elephant.” (Cariyā. 1.23)

Paṭijānitvā hatthikkhandhato oruyha analaṅkataṭṭhānaṃ olokanatthaṃ anupariyāyitvā analaṅkataṭṭhānaṃ adisvā kusumamissagandhodakabharitaṃ suvaṇṇabhiṅgāraṃ gahetvā “bhonto ito ethā”ti [V 0.0079] alaṅkatarajatadāmasadisaṃ hatthisoṇḍaṃ tesaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā udakaṃ pātetvā alaṅkatavāraṇaṃ adāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Having made his promise, he descended from the elephant's back and circled around it to look for an unadorned spot. Seeing no unadorned spot, he took a golden pitcher filled with fragrant water mixed with flowers and saying, ‘Sirs, come here,’ he placed the elephant's trunk, which resembled an adorned silver chain, into their hands, poured the water, and gave the adorned elephant. Therefore, it was said:

86.

86.

“Nāgaṃ gahetvā soṇḍāya, bhiṅgāre ratanāmaye;

Jalaṃ hatthe ākiritvā, brāhmaṇānaṃ adaṃ gaja”nti. (cariyā. 1.24);

“Having taken the elephant by its trunk, with a jeweled pitcher, I sprinkled water on the brahmins' hands and gave the elephant.” (Cariyā. 1.24)

Tattha [M 0.0083] santanti vijjamānaṃ deyyadhammaṃ. Nappaṭigūhāmīti na paṭicchādemi. Yo hi attano santakaṃ “mayhameva hotū”ti cinteti, yācito vā paṭikkhipati, so yācakānaṃ abhimukhe ṭhitampi atthato paṭicchādeti nāma. Mahāsatto pana attano sīsaṃ ādiṃ katvā ajjhattikadānaṃ dātukāmova, kathaṃ bāhiraṃ paṭikkhipati, tasmā āha “santaṃ nappaṭigūhāmī”ti. Tenevāha “dāne me ramate mano”ti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

Herein, ‘santaṃ’ means an existing giftable item. ‘Nappaṭigūhāmi’ means ‘I do not conceal.’ For whoever thinks of their own possession, ‘May it be mine alone,’ or refuses when asked, is said to conceal it in effect, even while standing face-to-face with the petitioners. The Great Being, however, was desirous of giving even internal gifts, beginning with his own head—how could he refuse external ones? Therefore, he said, ‘I do not conceal what exists.’ For that very reason, he said, ‘My mind delights in giving.’ The rest has the meaning already stated below.

Tassa pana hatthino catūsu pādesu alaṅkārā cattāri satasahassāni [P 0.0082] agghanti, ubhosu passesu alaṅkārā dve satasahassāni, heṭṭhā udare kambalaṃ satasahassaṃ, piṭṭhiyaṃ muttājālaṃ maṇijālaṃ kañcanajālanti tīṇi jālāni tīṇi satasahassāni, ubho kaṇṇālaṅkārā dve satasahassāni, piṭṭhiyaṃ atthatakambalaṃ satasahassaṃ, kumbhālaṅkāro satasahassaṃ, tayo vaṭaṃsakā tīṇi satasahassāni, kaṇṇacūḷālaṅkāro satasahassaṃ, dvinnaṃ dantānaṃ alaṅkārā dve satasahassāni, soṇḍāya sovatthikālaṅkāro satasahassaṃ, naṅguṭṭhālaṅkāro satasahassaṃ, ārohaṇanisseṇi satasahassaṃ, bhuñjanakaṭāhaṃ satasahassaṃ, ṭhapetvā anagghabhaṇḍaṃ idaṃ tāva ettakaṃ catuvīsati satasahassāni agghati. Chattapiṇḍiyaṃ pana maṇi, cūḷāmaṇi, muttāhāre maṇi, aṅkuse maṇi, hatthikaṇṭhaveṭhanamuttāhāre maṇi, hatthikumbhe maṇīti imāni cha anagghāni, hatthīpi anaggho evāti hatthinā saddhiṃ satta anagghāni, tāni sabbāni brāhmaṇānaṃ adāsi. Tathā hatthino paricārakāni pañca kulasatāni hatthimeṇḍahatthigopakehi saddhiṃ adāsi. Saha dānena panassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva bhūmikampādayo ahesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

Now, regarding that elephant: the ornaments on its four feet were worth four hundred thousand, the ornaments on both sides two hundred thousand, the blanket beneath its belly one hundred thousand, on its back a net of pearls, a net of jewels, and a net of gold—these three nets were worth three hundred thousand, the ornaments on both ears two hundred thousand, the blanket spread on its back one hundred thousand, the ornament on its frontal globes one hundred thousand, the three crest ornaments three hundred thousand, the ear-pendant ornament one hundred thousand, the ornaments on its two tusks two hundred thousand, the svastika ornament on its trunk one hundred thousand, the ornament on its tail one hundred thousand, the mounting ladder one hundred thousand, and the feeding trough one hundred thousand. Excluding the priceless items, this much was worth twenty-four hundred thousand. However, the jewel on the parasol's knob, the crest-jewel, the jewel on the pearl necklace, the jewel on the goad, the jewel on the pearl necklace encircling its neck, and the jewel on its frontal globes—these six were priceless. The elephant, too, was priceless. Thus, together with the elephant, there were seven priceless things, all of which he gave to the brahmins. Likewise, he gave the five hundred families of the elephant’s attendants, together with the elephant trainers and elephant keepers. And with the giving of the gift, there occurred earthquakes and so forth, in the manner stated below. Therefore, it was said:

87.

87.

“Punāparaṃ dadantassa, sabbasetaṃ gajuttamaṃ;

Tadāpi pathavī kampi, sineruvanavaṭaṃsakā”ti.

“Furthermore, as I was giving the supreme, all-white elephant, then, too, the earth shook, along with Sineru and its forested crests.”

Jātakepi (jā. 2.22.1673) vuttaṃ –

And in the Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.1673) it was said:

“Tadāsi [V 0.0080] yaṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ, tadāsi lomahaṃsanaṃ;

Hatthināge padinnamhi, medanī sampakampathā”ti.

“Then there was terror, then there was the raising of the hairs; when the lordly elephant was given, the earth trembled violently.”

88. Tassa [M 0.0084] nāgassa dānenāti chahi anagghehi saddhiṃ catuvīsatisatasahassagghanikaalaṅkārabhaṇḍasahitassa tassa maṅgalahatthissa pariccāgena. Sivayoti sivirājakumārā ceva siviraṭṭhavāsino ca. “Sivayo”ti ca desanāsīsametaṃ. Tattha hi amaccā pārisajjā brāhmaṇagahapatikā negamajānapadā nāgarā sakalaraṭṭhavāsino ca sañjayamahārājaṃ phussatideviṃ maddideviñca ṭhapetvā sabbe eva. Kuddhāti devatāvattanena bodhisattassa kuddhā. Samāgatāti sannipatitā. Te [P 0.0083] kira brāhmaṇā hatthiṃ labhitvā taṃ abhiruhitvā mahādvārena pavisitvā nagaramajjhena pāyiṃsu. Mahājanena ca “ambho brāhmaṇā, amhākaṃ hatthī kuto abhiruḷho”ti vutte “vessantaramahārājena no hatthī dinno, ke tumhe”ti hatthavikārādīhi ghaṭṭentā agamaṃsu. Atha amacce ādiṃ katvā mahājanā rājadvāre sannipatitvā “raññā nāma brāhmaṇānaṃ dhanaṃ vā dhaññaṃ vā khettaṃ vā vatthu vā dāsidāsaparicārikā vā dātabbā siyā, kathañhi nāmāyaṃ vessantaramahārājā rājārahaṃ maṅgalahatthiṃ dassati, na idāni evaṃ rajjaṃ vināsetuṃ dassāmā”ti ujjhāyitvā sañjayamahārājassa tamatthaṃ ārocetvā tena anunīyamānā ananuyantā agamaṃsu. Kevalaṃ pana –

88. ‘By the gift of that elephant’ means by the donation of that auspicious elephant, together with six priceless items and ornamental goods worth two million four hundred thousand. ‘Sivayo’ means both the Sivi princes and the inhabitants of the Sivi kingdom. And ‘Sivayo’ is the heading of the discourse. There, indeed, all the ministers, courtiers, brahmins, householders, townspeople, country folk, citizens, and all the inhabitants of the entire kingdom, except for King Sañjaya, Queen Phussatī, and Queen Maddī, were gathered. ‘Angry’ means angry with the Bodhisatta due to the deception of the deities. ‘Gathered’ means assembled. It is said that those brahmins, having obtained the elephant, mounted it, and entering through the great gate, proceeded through the middle of the city. And when the great multitude asked, “Sirs, brahmins, how did you come to ride our elephant?” they replied, “King Vessantara gave us the elephant. Who are you?” and, pushing them aside with gestures of the elephant’s trunk and so forth, they went on. Then the great multitude, headed by the ministers, gathered at the king’s gate and complained, “A king should give wealth, grain, fields, property, male and female servants, or attendants to brahmins. But how could this King Vessantara give away the royal auspicious elephant? We will certainly not allow him to ruin the kingdom in this way now!” Having protested, they reported the matter to King Sañjaya, but though he tried to appease them, they would not be appeased and departed. However, only this was said:

“Mā naṃ daṇḍena satthena, na hi so bandhanāraho;

Pabbājehi ca naṃ raṭṭhā, vaṅke vasatu pabbate”ti. (jā. 2.22.1687) –

“Do not strike him with rod or sword, for he is not worthy of bonds; but expel him from the realm, let him dwell on Mount Vaṅka.”

Vadiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

They spoke. Hence it was said:

“Pabbājesuṃ sakā raṭṭhā, vaṅkaṃ gacchatu pabbata”nti.

“They banished him from their own kingdom, saying: ‘Let him go to Mount Vaṅka.’”

Tattha pabbājesunti rajjato bahi vāsatthāya ussukkamakaṃsu; –

Herein, ‘they banished’ means they strove for him to live outside the kingdom.

Rājāpi “mahā kho ayaṃ paṭipakkho, handa mama putto katipāhaṃ rajjato bahi vasatū”ti cintetvā –

The king, too, thinking: “This is indeed a great opposition; come, let my son dwell outside the kingdom for a few days,”—

“Eso [V 0.0081] ce sivīnaṃ chando, chandaṃ nappanudāmase;

Imaṃ so vasatu rattiṃ, kāme ca paribhuñjatu.

“If this is the wish of the Sivis, we shall not reject their wish. Let him dwell this night and enjoy sensual pleasures.

“Tato ratyā vivasāne, sūriyuggamanaṃ pati;

Samaggā sivayo hutvā, raṭṭhā pabbājayantu na”nti. (jā. 2.22.1688-1689) –

“Then, at the end of the night, at sunrise, let the Sivis, being united, banish him from the realm.”

Vatvā [M 0.0085] puttassa santike kattāraṃ pesesi “imaṃ pavattiṃ mama puttassa ārocehī”ti. So tathā akāsi.

Having spoken thus, he sent a messenger to his son, saying: “Report this matter to my son.” He did so.

Mahāsattopi taṃ sutvā –

The Great Being, too, hearing that,

“Kismiṃ me sivayo kuddhā, nāhaṃ passāmi dukkaṭaṃ;

Taṃ me katte viyācikkha, kasmā pabbājayanti ma”nti. (jā. 2.22.1701) –

“For what reason are the Sivis angry with me? I see no wrongdoing. Explain that to me, O messenger, why do they banish me?”

Kāraṇaṃ pucchi. Tena “tumhākaṃ hatthidānenā”ti vutte somanassappatto hutvā –

He asked the reason. When he was told, “Because of your gift of the elephant,” he became filled with joy and—

“Hadayaṃ cakkhumpahaṃ dajjaṃ, kiṃ me bāhirakaṃ dhanaṃ;

Hiraññaṃ vā suvaṇṇaṃ vā, muttā veḷuriyā maṇi.

“I would give my heart, my very eye; what is external wealth to me—gold or silver, pearls, beryl, or gems?

“Dakkhiṇaṃ [P 0.0084] vāpahaṃ bāhuṃ, disvā yācakamāgate;

Dadeyyaṃ na vikampeyyaṃ, dāne me ramate mano.

“Seeing a beggar come, I would give my right arm without wavering; my mind delights in giving.

“Kāmaṃ maṃ sivayo sabbe, pabbājentu hanantu vā;

Neva dānā viramissaṃ, kāmaṃ chindantu sattadhā”ti. (jā. 2.22.1703-1705) –

“Let all the Sivis banish me or kill me as they wish; I will never desist from giving. Let them cut me into seven pieces if they wish.”

Vatvā “nāgarā me ekadivasaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ okāsaṃ dentu, sve dānaṃ datvā tatiyadivase gamissāmī”ti vatvā kattāraṃ tesaṃ santike pesetvā “ahaṃ sve sattasatakaṃ nāma mahādānaṃ dassāmi[V 0.0082], sattahatthisatāni sattaassasatāni sattarathasatāni sattaitthisatāni sattadāsasatāni sattadāsisatāni sattadhenusatāni paṭiyādehi, nānappakārañca annapānādiṃ sabbaṃ dātabbayuttakaṃ upaṭṭhapehī”ti sabbakammikaṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpetvā ekakova maddideviyā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “bhadde maddi, anugāmikanidhiṃ nidahamānā, sīlavantesu dadeyyāsī”ti tampi dāne niyojetvā tassā attano gamanakāraṇaṃ ācikkhitvā “ahaṃ vanaṃ vasanatthāya gamissāmi, tvaṃ idheva anukkaṇṭhitā vasāhī”ti āha. Sā “nāhaṃ, mahārāja, tumhehi vinā ekadivasampi vasissāmī”ti āha.

Having said, “Let the townspeople grant me one day to give alms; having given alms tomorrow, I shall depart on the third day,” he sent a messenger to them. Then, having commanded his minister in charge of all works, “Tomorrow, I shall give the great donation called the Seven Hundreds. Prepare seven hundred elephants, seven hundred horses, seven hundred chariots, seven hundred women, seven hundred male servants, seven hundred female servants, and seven hundred milch cows. And prepare all kinds of food and drink, everything suitable for giving,” he went alone to Queen Maddī’s dwelling and said: “Fair Maddī, as you store up the treasure that will follow you, you should give to those of virtuous conduct.” Having thus encouraged her also in giving, he explained to her his reason for leaving, saying: “I am going to the forest to live; you must stay here without discontent.” She said: “Great king, I will not stay even a single day without you.”

Dutiyadivase sattasatakaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Tassa sattasatakaṃ dānaṃ dentasseva sāyaṃ ahosi. Alaṅkatarathena mātāpitūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “ahaṃ sve gamissāmī”ti te āpucchitvā akāmakānaṃ tesaṃ assumukhānaṃ rodantānaṃyeva vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tato nikkhamitvā [M 0.0086] taṃ divasaṃ attano nivesane vasitvā punadivase “gamissāmī”ti pāsādato otari. Maddidevī sassusasurehi nānānayehi yācitvā nivattiyamānāpi tesaṃ vacanaṃ anādiyitvā te vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā sesitthiyo apaloketvā dve putte ādāya vessantarassa paṭhamataraṃ gantvā rathe aṭṭhāsi.

On the second day, he initiated the great donation of the Seven Hundreds. While he was giving the donation of the Seven Hundreds, it became evening. Having gone to the dwelling place of his parents in a decorated chariot, he took leave of them, saying: “I will go tomorrow.” Though they were unwilling, with tearful faces, and weeping, he paid homage to them, circumambulated them, and departed from there. That day, he stayed in his own residence. On the next day, thinking, “I will go,” he descended from the palace. Queen Maddī, though begged in various ways by her father-in-law and mother-in-law to turn back, disregarded their words, paid homage to them, circumambulated them, and after taking leave of the other women, took her two sons and, going ahead of Vessantara, stood in the chariot.

Mahāpuriso rathaṃ abhiruhitvā rathe ṭhito mahājanaṃ āpucchitvā “appamattā dānādīni puññāni karothā”ti ovādamassa datvā nagarato nikkhami. Bodhisattassa mātā “putto me dānavittako dānaṃ detū”ti ābharaṇehi saddhiṃ sattaratanapūrāni sakaṭāni ubhosu passesu pesesi. Sopi attano kāyāruḷhameva ābharaṇabhaṇḍaṃ sampattayācakānaṃ [P 0.0085] aṭṭhārasa vāre datvā sesaṃ sabbamadāsi. Nagarā nikkhamitvāva nivattitvā oloketukāmo ahosi. Athassa puññānubhāvena rathappamāṇe ṭhāne mahāpathavī bhijjitvā parivattitvā rathaṃ nagarābhimukhaṃ akāsi. So mātāpitūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ olokesi. Tena kāruññena pathavikampo ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ “tesaṃ nicchubhamānāna”ntiādi.

The great man, having mounted the chariot and stood upon it, took leave of the great multitude, advising them: 'Be diligent in performing meritorious deeds such as giving,' and then departed from the city. The Bodhisatta's mother, thinking: 'Let my son, who is intent on giving, give alms,' sent carts filled with the seven treasures along with ornaments on both sides. He, too, gave the very ornaments worn on his person to the supplicants who had arrived eighteen times, and gave away all the rest. Just as he was leaving the city, he wished to turn back and look. Then, by the power of his merit, in a space the size of the chariot, the great earth split open, revolved, and turned the chariot to face the city. He gazed upon the dwelling place of his parents. Due to that compassion, an earthquake occurred. Therefore, it was said: 'Of them being driven out,' and so on.

89-90. Tattha nicchubhamānānanti tesu sivīsu nikkaḍḍhantesu, pabbājentesūti attho. Tesaṃ vā nikkhamantānaṃ. Mahādānaṃ pavattetunti sattasatakamahādānaṃ dātuṃ. Āyācissanti yāciṃ. Sāvayitvāti ghosāpetvā. Kaṇṇabherinti yugalamahābheriṃ. Dadāmahanti dadāmi ahaṃ.

89-90. Herein, nicchubhamānānanti means: while the Sivis were dragging them out, while they were banishing them—this is the meaning. Or, of them departing. Mahādānaṃ pavattetunti means: to give the great gift of seven hundred. Āyācissanti means: I asked. Sāvayitvāti means: having had it announced. Kaṇṇabherinti means: the pair of great drums. Dadāmahanti means: I give.

91. Athetthāti athevaṃ dāne dīyamāne etasmiṃ dānagge. Tumūloti ekakolāhalībhūto. Bheravoti [V 0.0083] bhayāvaho. Mahāsattañhi ṭhapetvā aññesaṃ so bhayaṃ janeti, tassa bhayajananākāraṃ dassetuṃ. “Dānenima”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Imaṃ vessantaramahārājānaṃ dānena hetunā sivayo raṭṭhato nīharanti pabbājenti, tathāpi puna ca evarūpaṃ dānaṃ deti ayanti.

91. Herein, athetthāti means: then, while this gift was being given, at this gift-pavilion. Tumūloti means: having become a single great commotion. Bheravoti means: fear-inspiring. For, excepting the Great Being, it generated fear in others. To show the manner in which it generated fear, it was said: 'Dānenimaṃ', and so on. 'Because of giving as the reason, the Sivis expel and banish this great king Vessantara from the kingdom; nevertheless, this one gives such a gift again'—thus.

92-94. Idāni taṃ dānaṃ dassetuṃ “hatthi”nti gāthamāha. Tattha gavanti dhenuṃ. Catuvāhiṃ rathaṃ datvāti vahantīti vāhino, assā, caturo ājaññasindhave [M 0.0087] rathañca brāhmaṇānaṃ datvāti attho. Mahāsatto hi tathā nagarato nikkhamanto sahajāte saṭṭhisahasse amacce sesajanañca assupuṇṇamukhaṃ anubaddhantaṃ nivattetvā rathaṃ pājento maddiṃ āha – “sace, bhadde, pacchato yācakā āgacchanti, upadhāreyyāsī”ti. Sā olokentī nisīdi. Athassa sattasatakamahādānaṃ gamanakāle katadānañca sampāpuṇituṃ asakkontā cattāro brāhmaṇā āgantvā “vessantaro kuhi”nti pucchitvā “dānaṃ datvā rathena gato”ti vutte “asse yācissāmā”ti anubandhiṃsu. Maddī te āgacchante disvā “yācakā, devā”ti ārocesi. Mahāsatto rathaṃ ṭhapesi. Te āgantvā asse yāciṃsu. Mahāsatto asse adāsi. Te te gahetvā gatā. Assesu [P 0.0086] pana dinnesu rathadhuraṃ ākāseyeva aṭṭhāsi. Atha cattāro devaputtā rohitamigavaṇṇenāgantvā rathadhuraṃ sampaṭicchitvā agamaṃsu. Mahāsatto tesaṃ devaputtabhāvaṃ ñatvā –

92-94. Now, to show that gift, he speaks the verse beginning with hatthi. Therein, gavanti means a milch-cow. Catuvāhiṃ rathaṃ datvāti means: having given a chariot and four excellent thoroughbred Sindhu horses, which are called vāhino because they pull (vahanti), to the brahmins. For when the Great Being was thus leaving the city, he turned back the sixty thousand ministers born with him and the remaining people who were following with tear-filled faces, and while driving the chariot, he said to Maddī: 'My dear, if any supplicants should come from behind, please take note.' She sat watching. Then, four brahmins who had been unable to obtain a share in the gifts given at the time of the great gift of seven hundred, came and asked, 'Where is Vessantara?' When told, 'Having given his gifts, he has departed by chariot,' they followed, thinking, 'We will ask for the horses.' Maddī, seeing them approaching, announced, 'Your Majesty, supplicants have come.' The Great Being stopped the chariot. They came and asked for the horses. The Great Being gave the horses. They took them and departed. When the horses were given, however, the chariot's yoke remained suspended in the air. Then four divine beings, having come in the guise of red deer, received the chariot's yoke and proceeded. The Great Being, knowing them to be divine beings—

“Iṅgha maddi nisāmehi, cittarūpaṃva dissati;

Migarohiccavaṇṇena, dakkhiṇassā vahanti ma”nti. (jā. 2.22.1864) –

Come, Maddī, behold! It appears like a wondrous form; in the guise of red deer, they pull me like well-trained horses.

Maddiyā āha.

He said to Maddī.

Tattha cittarūpaṃvāti acchariyarūpaṃ viya. Dakkhiṇassāti susikkhitaassā viya maṃ vahanti.

Herein, cittarūpaṃvāti means: like a wondrous form. Dakkhiṇassāti means: they carry me like well-trained horses.

Atha naṃ evaṃ gacchantaṃ aparo brāhmaṇo āgantvā rathaṃ yāci. Mahāsatto puttadāraṃ otāretvā rathaṃ adāsi. Rathe pana dinne devaputtā antaradhāyiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya pana sabbepi pattikāva ahesuṃ. Atha mahāsatto “maddi, tvaṃ kaṇhājinaṃ gaṇhāhi, ahaṃ jālikumāraṃ gaṇhāmī”ti ubhopi dve dārake aṅkenādāya aññamaññaṃ piyasallāpā paṭipathaṃ āgacchante manusse vaṅkapabbatassa maggaṃ pucchantā sayameva onatesu phalarukkhesu phalāni dārakānaṃ dadantā atthakāmāhi [V 0.0084] devatāhi maggassa saṅkhipitattā tadaheva cetaraṭṭhaṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “catuvāhiṃ rathaṃ datvā”tiādi.

Then, as he was thus proceeding, another brahmin came and asked for the chariot. The Great Being, having had his wife and children dismount, gave away the chariot. When the chariot was given, however, the divine beings vanished. From then on, they all went on foot. Then the Great Being said: 'Maddī, you take Kaṇhājinā, and I will take Prince Jāli.' Both of them, taking the two children onto their hips and engaging in pleasant conversation with one another, asking the people they met on the path the way to Mount Vaṅka, giving the children fruits from the fruit-bearing trees that bent down of their own accord, reached the Ceta kingdom that very day, as the path was shortened by deities who wished for their welfare. Therefore, it was said: 'Having given the four-horse chariot,' and so on.

Tattha ṭhatvā cātummahāpatheti attano gamanamaggena passato āgatena tena brāhmaṇena āgatamaggena ca vinivijjhitvā gataṭṭhānattā catukkasaṅkhāte [M 0.0088] catumahāpathe ṭhatvā tassa brāhmaṇassa rathaṃ datvā. Ekākiyoti amaccasevakādisahāyābhāvena ekako. Tenevāha “adutiyo”ti. Maddideviṃ idamabravīti maddideviṃ idaṃ abhāsi.

Therein, ṭhatvā cātummahāpathe means: because his own path of travel and the path by which that brahmin had come from the side intersected, he stood at the crossroads, so-called because of the fourfold intersection, and gave the chariot to that brahmin. Ekākiyoti means: alone, due to the absence of companions such as ministers and servants. For that reason, he said adutiyo ('without a second'). Maddideviṃ idamabravīti means: he spoke this to Queen Maddī.

96-99. Padumaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃvāti padumaṃ viya, puṇḍarīkaṃ viya ca. Kaṇhājinaggahīti kaṇhājinaṃ aggahesi. Abhijātāti jātisampannā. Visamaṃ samanti visamaṃ samañca bhūmippadesaṃ. Entīti āgacchanti. Anumagge paṭippatheti anumagge vā paṭipathe vāti vā-saddassa lopo daṭṭhabbo. Karuṇanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, karuṇāyitattanti attho. Dukkhaṃ te paṭivedentīti ime evaṃ sukhumālā padasā gacchanti, dūreva ito vaṅkapabbatoti te tadā amhesu kāruññavasena attanā dukkhaṃ paṭilabhanti, tathā attano [P 0.0087] uppannadukkhaṃ paṭivedenti vāti attho.

96-99. Padumaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃvāti means: like a lotus, and like a white lotus. Kaṇhājinaggahīti means: he took Kaṇhājinā. Abhijātāti means: of noble birth. Visamaṃ samanti means: an uneven and even region of ground. Entīti means: they come. Anumagge paṭippatheti means: along the path or on the path ahead; the elision of the particle vā should be understood. Karuṇanti is a neuter noun indicating a state; the meaning is a piteous utterance. Dukkhaṃ te paṭivedentīti means: 'These delicate ones are going on foot, and Mount Vaṅka is far from here'; thus, out of compassion for us, they themselves incur suffering, or they experience the suffering that has arisen for them—this is the meaning.

100-1. Pavaneti mahāvane. Phalineti phalavante. Ubbiddhāti uddhaṃ uggatā uccā. Upagacchanti dāraketi yathā phalāni dārakānaṃ hatthūpagayhakāni honti, evaṃ rukkhā sayameva sākhāhi onamitvā dārake upenti.

100-1. Pavaneti means: in the great forest. Phalineti means: fruit-bearing. Ubbiddhāti means: risen up high, lofty. Upagacchanti dāraketi means: just as fruits become graspable by the children's hands, so the trees, bending down their branches of their own accord, approach the children.

102. Acchariyanti accharāyoggaṃ, accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttaṃ. Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtanti abbhutaṃ. Lomānaṃ haṃsanasamatthatāya lomahaṃsanaṃ. Sāhukāranti sādhukāraṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Itthiratanabhāvena sabbehi aṅgehi avayavehi sobhatīti sabbaṅgasobhanā.

102. Regarding 'astonishing' (`acchariya`): it is fit for a finger-snap, fit to be marked by the snapping of a finger. Regarding 'unprecedentedly become' (`abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtaṃ`): it means marvelous (`abbhutaṃ`). It is 'hair-raising' (`lomahaṃsanaṃ`) because of its capacity to cause the hairs of the body to stand on end. Regarding 'acclamation' (`sāhukāra`): it means an utterance of 'well done' (`sādhukāra`), or this itself is the reading. She is 'radiant in every part' (`sabbaṅgasobhanā`) because, being a jewel among women, she is radiant with all her major and minor limbs.

103-4. Accheraṃ vatāti acchariyaṃ vata. Vessantarassa tejenāti vessantarassa puññānubhāvena. Saṅkhipiṃsu pathaṃ yakkhāti devatā mahāsattassa puññatejena coditā taṃ maggaṃ parikkhayaṃ pāpesuṃ, appakaṃ akaṃsu, taṃ pana dārakesu karuṇāya kataṃ viya katvā vuttaṃ “anukampāya dārake”ti. Jetuttaranagarato hi suvaṇṇagiritālo nāma pabbato pañca yojanāni, tato kontimārā nāma nadī pañca yojanāni, tato mārañjanāgiri nāma pabbato pañca yojanāni, tato daṇḍabrāhmaṇagāmo nāma pañca yojanāni, tato mātulanagaraṃ dasa [V 0.0085] yojanāni, iti taṃ raṭṭhaṃ jetuttaranagarato tiṃsa yojanāni hoti. Devatā [M 0.0089] bodhisattassa puññatejena coditā maggaṃ parikkhayaṃ pāpesuṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ ekāheneva atikkamiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “nikkhantadivaseneva, cetaraṭṭhamupāgamu”nti.

103-4. Regarding 'How marvelous indeed!' (`accheraṃ vata`): it means 'How wonderful indeed!' (`acchariyaṃ vata`). Regarding 'by the power of Vessantara' (`vessantarassa tejena`): it means by the majestic power of Vessantara's merit. Regarding 'the spirits shortened the path' (`saṅkhipiṃsu pathaṃ yakkhā`): the deities, urged on by the power of the Great Being's merit, brought that path to an end, that is, they made it short. This, however, was said as if it were done out of compassion for the children, hence the words 'out of compassion for the children.' Indeed, from the city of Jetuttara, the mountain named Suvaṇṇagiritāla is five yojanas away; from there, the river named Kontimārā is five yojanas; from there, the mountain named Mārañjanāgiri is five yojanas; from there, the brahmin village of Daṇḍa is five yojanas; and from there, the city of Mātula is ten yojanas. Thus, that country is thirty yojanas from the city of Jetuttara. The deities, urged on by the power of the Bodhisatta's merit, brought the road to an end. They traversed it all in a single day. Therefore it was said: 'On the very day they departed, they reached the Ceta country.'

Evaṃ mahāsatto sāyanhasamayaṃ cetaraṭṭhe mātulanagaraṃ patvā tassa nagarassa dvārasamīpe sālāyaṃ nisīdi. Athassa maddidevī pādesu rajaṃ puñchitvā pāde sambāhitvā “vessantarassa āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpessāmī”ti sālato nikkhamitvā tassa cakkhupathe sāladvāre aṭṭhāsi. Nagaraṃ pavisantiyo ca nikkhamantiyo ca itthiyo taṃ disvā parivāresuṃ. Mahājano tañca vessantarañca putte cassa tathā āgate disvā rājūnaṃ ācikkhi. Saṭṭhisahassā rājāno rodantā paridevantā tassa santikaṃ āgantvā maggaparissamaṃ vinodetvā [P 0.0088] tathā āgamanakāraṇaṃ pucchiṃsu.

Thus, the Great Being, arriving at the city of Mātula in the Ceta country in the evening, sat down in a hall near the city gate. Then Queen Maddī, having wiped the dust from his feet and massaged them, thought, 'I will make known Vessantara's arrival.' She stepped out of the hall and stood in the hall's doorway, within his line of sight. Women who were entering and leaving the city saw her and gathered around. The great crowd, seeing her, Vessantara, and his children arriving in such a state, informed the kings. Sixty thousand kings, weeping and lamenting, came into his presence, dispelled his fatigue from the journey, and asked the reason for his arrival.

Mahāsatto hatthidānaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ kathesi. Taṃ sutvā te attano rajjena nimantayiṃsu. Mahāpuriso “mayā tumhākaṃ rajjaṃ paṭiggahitameva hotu, rājā pana maṃ raṭṭhā pabbājeti, tasmā vaṅkapabbatameva gamissāmī”ti vatvā tehi nānappakāraṃ tattha vāsaṃ yāciyamānopi taṃ analaṅkaritvā tehi gahitārakkho taṃ rattiṃ sālāyameva vasitvā punadivase pātova nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā tehi parivuto nikkhamitvā pannarasayojanamaggaṃ gantvā vanadvāre ṭhatvā te nivattetvā purato pannarasayojanamaggaṃ tehi ācikkhitaniyāmeneva agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

The Great Being, beginning with the gift of the elephant, recounted everything. Hearing this, they offered him their own kingdom. The Great Man said, 'Let it be that I have accepted your kingdom, but the king has banished me from the country. Therefore, I will go to Vaṅka Mountain only.' And so, although they pleaded with him in various ways to stay there, he did not consent. With the protection they provided, he spent that night in the hall itself. The next day, early in the morning, after eating a meal of various supreme flavors, he departed, surrounded by them. He went for fifteen yojanas, stopped at the entrance to the forest, sent them back, and then proceeded for another fifteen yojanas along the very route they had indicated. Therefore it was said:

105.

105.

“Saṭṭhirājasahassāni, tadā vasanti mātule;

Sabbe pañjalikā hutvā, rodamānā upāgamuṃ.

"Sixty thousand kings dwelt at that time in Mātula; all, with hands clasped in reverence, approached him, weeping."

106.

106.

“Tattha vattetvā sallāpaṃ, cetehi cetaputtehi;

Te tato nikkhamitvāna, vaṅkaṃ agamu pabbata”nti.

"Having engaged in conversation there with the Cetas and the Ceta princes, the four of them departed from that place and went to the Vaṅka mountain."

Tattha tattha vattetvā sallāpanti tattha tehi rājūhi samāgamehi saddhiṃ paṭisammodamānā kathaṃ pavattetvā. Cetaputtehīti cetarājaputtehi. Te tato nikkhamitvānāti te rājāno tato vanadvāraṭṭhāne nivattetvā. Vaṅkaṃ agamu pabbatanti amhe cattāro janā vaṅkapabbataṃ uddissa agamamhā.

Regarding 'having engaged in conversation there' (`tattha vattetvā sallāpaṃ`): it means having exchanged pleasantries and held a conversation with those kings and their assembly. Regarding 'with the Ceta princes' (`cetaputtehi`): it means with the sons of the Ceta kings. Regarding 'they, having departed from that place' (`te tato nikkhamitvāna`): it means having sent those kings back from that place, the entrance to the forest. Regarding 'they went to the Vaṅka mountain' (`vaṅkaṃ agamu pabbataṃ`): this means, 'we four people went, heading for the Vaṅka mountain.'

Atha [M 0.0090] mahāsatto tehi ācikkhitamaggena gacchanto gandhamādanapabbataṃ patvā taṃ divasaṃ tattha [V 0.0086] vasitvā tato uttaradisābhimukho vepullapabbatapādena gantvā ketumatīnadītīre nisīditvā vanacarakena dinnaṃ madhumaṃsaṃ khāditvā tassa suvaṇṇasūciṃ datvā nhatvā pivitvā paṭippassaddhadaratho nadiṃ uttaritvā sānupabbatasikhare ṭhitassa nigrodhassa mūle thokaṃ nisīditvā uṭṭhāya gacchanto nālikapabbataṃ pariharanto mucalindasaraṃ gantvā saratīrena pubbuttarakaṇṇaṃ patvā ekapadikamaggeneva vanaghaṭaṃ pavisitvā taṃ atikkamma girividuggānaṃ nadīpabhavānaṃ purato caturassapokkharaṇiṃ pāpuṇi.

Then the Great Being, proceeding along the path indicated by them, reached the Gandhamādana mountain. Having stayed there for that day, he went from there facing north along the foot of the Vepulla mountain and sat on the bank of the Ketumatī river. He ate the honey and meat given by a forest-dweller, and giving him a golden pin, he bathed and drank. With his weariness allayed, he crossed the river. After sitting for a short while at the foot of a banyan tree standing on a mountain plateau's peak, he rose and, while journeying on, skirted the Nālika mountain and went to the Mucalinda lake. Reaching the northeastern corner by way of the lake shore, he entered a dense part of the forest by a single-file path. Having passed through it, he arrived at a square lotus pond in front of the inaccessible mountain regions from which rivers originate.

107. Tasmiṃ [P 0.0089] khaṇe sakko āvajjento “mahāsatto himavantaṃ paviṭṭho, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā vissakammaṃ pesesi – “gaccha vaṅkapabbatakucchimhi ramaṇīye ṭhāne assamapadaṃ māpehī”ti. So tattha dve paṇṇasālāyo dve caṅkame dve ca rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni māpetvā tesu tesu ṭhānesu nānāpupphavicitte rukkhe phalite rukkhe pupphagacche kadalivanādīni ca dassetvā sabbe pabbajitaparikkhāre paṭiyādetvā “yekeci pabbajitukāmā, te gaṇhantū”ti akkharāni likhitvā amanusse ca bheravasadde migapakkhino ca paṭikkamāpetvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

107. At that moment, Sakka, reflecting, thought, 'The Great Being has entered the Himālaya; it is fitting that he should obtain a dwelling place.' He sent Vissakamma, saying, 'Go and create a hermitage in a delightful spot in the hollow of the Vaṅka mountain.' So Vissakamma created there two leaf-huts, two walking paths, and two places for use by night and by day. In those various spots, he also manifested trees variegated with diverse flowers, fruit-bearing trees, flowering shrubs, groves of plantains, and so on. He prepared all the requisites of a renunciant and inscribed the words: 'Let whoever wishes to go forth take these.' Then, having caused the non-humans and the beasts and birds with terrifying cries to withdraw, he returned to his own abode.

Mahāsatto ekapadikamaggaṃ disvā “pabbajitānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti maddiñca putte ca tattheva ṭhapetvā assamapadaṃ pavisitvā akkharāni oloketvā “sakkena dinnosmī”ti paṇṇasāladvāraṃ vivaritvā paviṭṭho khaggañca dhanuñca apanetvā sāṭake omuñcitvā isivesaṃ gahetvā kattaradaṇḍaṃ ādāya nikkhamitvā paccekabuddhasadisena upasamena dārakānaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Maddidevīpi mahāsattaṃ disvā pādesu patitvā roditvā teneva saddhiṃ assamaṃ pavisitvā attano paṇṇasālaṃ gantvā isivesaṃ gaṇhi. Pacchā puttepi tāpasakumārake kariṃsu. Bodhisatto maddiṃ varaṃ yāci “mayaṃ ito paṭṭhāya pabbajitā nāma, itthī ca nāma brahmacariyassa malaṃ, mā dāni akāle mama santikaṃ āgacchā”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā mahāsattampi varaṃ yāci “deva, tumhe putte gahetvā idheva hotha, ahaṃ phalāphalaṃ āharissāmī”ti. Sā tato paṭṭhāya araññato phalāphalāni āharitvā tayo jane paṭijaggi. Iti cattāro khattiyā vaṅkapabbatakucchiyaṃ sattamāsamattaṃ vasiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “āmantayitvā devindo, vissakammaṃ mahiddhika”ntiādi.

The Great Being, seeing a single-footpath, thought, 'This will be a dwelling place for renunciants.' Leaving Maddī and the children there, he entered the hermitage grounds. Examining the letters, he realized, 'This has been given by Sakka,' and opened the door of the leaf hut. Entering, he removed his sword and bow, took off his garments, donned the attire of a hermit, took up a staff, and went out. With the calm demeanor of a Paccekabuddha, he approached the children. Maddīdevī, upon seeing the Great Being, fell at his feet and wept; then, entering the hermitage with him, she went to her own leaf hut and assumed the guise of a hermit. Later, they also made the children into young ascetics. The Bodhisatta asked Maddī for a boon: 'From now on, we are renunciates, and a woman is a defilement to the holy life. Do not come to me at an unseemly time.' She agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and in turn requested a boon from the Great Being: 'Lord, may you stay here with the children, and I will bring fruits.' From then on, she gathered fruits from the forest and looked after the three of them. Thus, the four Khattiyas lived in the Vaṅka mountain valley for about seven months. Hence it is said: 'Having summoned the lord of gods, the mighty Vissakamma,' and so on.

Tattha [M 0.0091] āmantayitvāti pakkosāpetvā. Mahiddhikanti mahatiyā deviddhiyā samannāgataṃ. Assamaṃ sukatanti assamapadaṃ sukataṃ katvā. Rammaṃ vessantarassa vasanānucchavikaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ. Sumāpayāti suṭṭhu māpaya. Āṇāpesīti vacanaseso. Sumāpayīti sammā māpesi.

Therein, `āmantayitvā` means 'having caused to be called.' `Mahiddhikaṃ` means 'endowed with great divine power.' `Assamaṃ sukataṃ` means 'having made the hermitage grounds well-prepared.' `Rammaṃ` refers to 'a delightful leaf hut suitable for Vessantara's dwelling.' `Sumāpaya` means 'make thoroughly.' `Āṇāpesi` is the remainder of the phrase. `Sumāpayī` means 'he made properly.'

111. Asuññoti [V 0.0087] yathā so assamo asuñño hoti, evaṃ tassa asuññabhāvakaraṇena [P 0.0090] asuñño homi. “Asuññe”ti vā pāṭho, mama vasaneneva asuññe assame dārake anurakkhanto vasāmi tattha tiṭṭhāmi. Bodhisattassa mettānubhāvena samantā tiyojane sabbe tiracchānāpi mettaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu.

111. Therein, `asuñño` (not empty) means that just as that hermitage is not empty, so by making it not empty, I become not empty. Alternatively, the reading is `asuññe` (in the not empty), meaning by my dwelling alone in the not empty hermitage, I dwell and remain there, protecting the children. By the power of the Bodhisatta's loving-kindness, all animals within three yojanas around also received loving-kindness.

Evaṃ tesu tattha vasantesu kaliṅgaraṭṭhavāsī jūjako nāma brāhmaṇo amittatāpanāya nāma bhariyāya “nāhaṃ te niccaṃ dhaññakoṭṭanaudakāharaṇayāgubhattapacanādīni kātuṃ sakkomi, paricārakaṃ me dāsaṃ vā dāsiṃ vā ānehī”ti vutte “kutohaṃ te bhoti duggato dāsaṃ vā dāsiṃ vā labhissāmī”ti vatvā tāya “esa vessantaro rājā vaṅkapabbate vasati. Tassa putte mayhaṃ paricārake yācitvā ānehī”ti vutte kilesavasena tassā paṭibaddhacittatāya tassā vacanaṃ atikkamituṃ asakkonto pātheyyaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā anukkamena jetuttaranagaraṃ patvā “kuhiṃ vessantaramahārājā”ti pucchi.

While they were living there, a brahmin named Jūjaka, a resident of the Kaliṅga country, was told by his wife, named Amittatāpanā: 'I cannot always perform for you the tasks of pounding grain, fetching water, cooking gruel and meals, and so on. Bring me a male or female servant to attend to me.' He replied, 'Where would I, a poor man, get a male or female servant for you, my dear?' She then said, 'That King Vessantara is living on Mount Vaṅka. Go and ask him for his children to be my attendants.' Unable to disregard her words, as his mind was bound to her by defilement, he had provisions prepared for the journey and gradually reached the city of Jetuttara. There he asked, 'Where is the great King Vessantara?'

Mahājano “imesaṃ yācakānaṃ atidānena amhākaṃ rājā raṭṭhā pabbājito, evaṃ amhākaṃ rājānaṃ nāsetvā punapi idheva āgacchatī”ti leḍḍudaṇḍādihattho upakkosanto brāhmaṇaṃ anubandhi. So devatāviggahito hutvā tato nikkhamitvā vaṅkapabbatagāmimaggaṃ abhiruḷho anukkamena vanadvāraṃ patvā mahāvanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā maggamūḷho hutvā vicaranto tehi rājūhi bodhisattassa ārakkhaṇatthāya ṭhapitena cetaputtena samāgañchi. Tena “kahaṃ, bho brāhmaṇa, gacchasī”ti puṭṭho “vessantaramahārājassa santika”nti vutte “addhā ayaṃ brāhmaṇo tassa putte vā deviṃ vā yācituṃ gacchatī”ti cintetvā “mā kho, tvaṃ brāhmaṇa, tattha gañchi, sace gacchasi, ettheva te sīsaṃ chinditvā mayhaṃ sunakhānaṃ ghāsaṃ karissāmī”ti tena santajjito maraṇabhayabhīto “ahamassa pitarā pesito dūto, ‘taṃ ānessāmī’ti āgato”ti musāvādaṃ abhāsi. Taṃ sutvā cetaputto tuṭṭhahaṭṭho brāhmaṇassa [M 0.0092] sakkārasammānaṃ katvā vaṅkapabbatagāmimaggaṃ ācikkhi. So tato paraṃ gacchanto antarāmagge accutena nāma tāpasena saddhiṃ samāgantvā tampi maggaṃ pucchitvā tenāpi magge ācikkhite tena ācikkhitasaññāya maggaṃ gacchanto anukkamena bodhisattassa assamapadaṭṭhānasamīpaṃ gantvā maddideviyā phalāphalatthaṃ [P 0.0091] gatakāle bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ubho dārake yāci. Tena vuttaṃ –

The people, holding clods and sticks, chased after the brahmin, shouting, 'It was because of excessive giving to beggars like this that our king was banished from the kingdom. After ruining our king, he now comes back here again!' But the brahmin, being misled by the devas, escaped from there and took the path leading to Mount Vaṅka. Gradually, he reached the edge of the forest and entered the great forest. Wandering lost, he encountered Cetaputta, who had been placed there by those kings to guard the Bodhisatta. When asked, 'Where are you going, brahmin?' he replied, 'To the presence of the great King Vessantara.' Cetaputta thought, 'Surely this brahmin is going to ask for his children or the queen.' He then threatened him, 'Do not go there, brahmin. If you do, I will cut off your head right here and feed it to my dogs!' Terrified by the fear of death, the brahmin lied, 'I am a messenger sent by his father; I have come to bring him back.' Hearing this, Cetaputta was delighted and pleased; he honored the brahmin and showed him the path leading to Mount Vaṅka. Going further from there, he met a hermit named Accuta on the way and also asked him for the path. Following the directions given by him, he gradually reached the vicinity of the Bodhisatta's hermitage. When Queen Maddī had gone to gather fruits, he approached the Bodhisatta and begged for both children. Thus it was said:

112.

112.

“Pavane vasamānassa, addhiko maṃ upāgami;

Ayāci puttake mayhaṃ, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho”ti.

While I was dwelling in the wilderness, a traveler approached me; he begged for my children, both Jāli and Kaṇhājinā.

Evaṃ [V 0.0088] brāhmaṇena dārakesu yācitesu mahāsatto “cirassaṃ vata me yācako adhigato, ajjāhaṃ anavasesato dānapāramiṃ pūressāmī”ti adhippāyena somanassajāto pasāritahatthe sahassatthavikaṃ ṭhapento viya brāhmaṇassa cittaṃ paritosento sakalañca taṃ pabbatakucchiṃ unnādento “dadāmi tava mayhaṃ puttake, api ca maddidevī pana pātova phalāphalatthāya vanaṃ gantvā sāyaṃ āgamissati, tāya āgatāya te puttake dassetvā tvañca mūlaphalāphalaṃ khāditvā ekarattiṃ vasitvā vigataparissamo pātova gamissasī”ti āha. Brāhmaṇo “kāmañcesa uḷārajjhāsayatāya puttake dadāti, mātā pana vacchagiddhā āgantvā dānassa antarāyampi kareyya, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ nippīḷetvā dārake gahetvā ajjeva gaccheyya”nti cintetvā “puttā ce te mayhaṃ dinnā, kiṃ dāni mātaraṃ dassetvā pesitehi, dārake gahetvā ajjeva gamissāmī”ti āha. “Sace, tvaṃ brāhmaṇa, rājaputtiṃ mātaraṃ daṭṭhuṃ na icchasi, ime dārake gahetvā jetuttaranagaraṃ gaccha, tattha sañjayamahārājā dārake gahetvā mahantaṃ te dhanaṃ dassati, tena dāsadāsiyo gaṇhissasi, sukhañca jīvissasi, aññathā ime sukhumālā rājadārakā, kiṃ te veyyāvaccaṃ karissantī”ti āha.

Thus, when the brahmin begged for the children, the Great Being, with the intention, 'After a long time, indeed, a petitioner has come to me; today I shall fulfill the perfection of giving without remainder,' became filled with joy. As if placing a bag of a thousand coins in the brahmin's outstretched hand, gladdening his heart and making the entire mountain hollow resound, he said: 'I give you my children. However, Queen Maddī has gone to the forest early in the morning for fruits and roots and will return in the evening. When she has returned, you may show her the children, and after you have eaten roots and fruits, you may stay for one night and depart early in the morning, free from fatigue.' The brahmin thought: 'Although he gives the children due to his noble disposition, their mother, being attached to her offspring, might return and obstruct the gift. What if I were to press him, take the children, and leave today itself?' Reflecting thus, he said: 'If the children have been given to me, what is the use of showing them to their mother now? I shall take the children and leave today.' 'If, O brahmin, you do not wish to see the princess their mother, then take these children and go to the city of Jetuttara. There, King Sañjaya will take the children and give you great wealth. With it, you may acquire male and female slaves and live happily. Otherwise, these are delicate royal children—what service can they render you?' he said.

Brāhmaṇo “evampi mayā na sakkā kātuṃ, rājadaṇḍato bhāyāmi, mayhameva gāmaṃ nessāmī”ti āha. Imaṃ tesaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ sutvā dārakā “pitā no kho amhe brāhmaṇassa dātukāmo”ti pakkamitvā pokkharaṇiṃ gantvā paduminigacche nilīyiṃsu. Brāhmaṇo te adisvāva “tvaṃ [M 0.0093] ‘dārake dadāmī’ti vatvā te apakkamāpesi, eso te sādhubhāvo”ti āha. Atha mahāsatto sahasāva uṭṭhahitvā dārake gavesanto paduminigacche nilīne disvā “etha, tātā, mā mayhaṃ dānapāramiyā antarāyaṃ akattha, mama dānajjhāsayaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetha, ayañca brāhmaṇo tumhe gahetvā tumhākaṃ ayyakassa sañjayamahārājassa santikaṃ gamissati[P 0.0092], tāta jāli, tvaṃ bhujisso hotukāmo brāhmaṇassa nikkhasahassaṃ datvā bhujisso bhaveyyāsi, kaṇhājine tvaṃ dāsasataṃ dāsisataṃ hatthisataṃ assasataṃ usabhasataṃ nikkhasatanti sabbasataṃ datvā bhujissā bhaveyyāsī”ti kumāre agghāpetvā samassāsetvā gahetvā assamapadaṃ gantvā kamaṇḍalunā udakaṃ gahetvā sabbaññutaññāṇassa paccayaṃ katvā brāhmaṇassa hatthe udakaṃ pātetvā ativiya pītisomanassajāto hutvā pathaviṃ unnādento piyaputtadānaṃ adāsi. Idhāpi pubbe vuttanayeneva pathavikampādayo ahesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

The brahmin said, 'Even so, I cannot do it. I fear punishment from the king. I will take them to my own village.' Hearing this conversation, the children thought, 'Our father indeed intends to give us to the brahmin.' They ran away and went to the lotus pond, hiding in a lotus thicket. Not seeing them, the brahmin said, 'You said, "I give the children," but you made them run away. Is this your integrity?' Then the Great Being rose quickly and searched for the children. Seeing them hidden in the lotus thicket, he said, 'Come, my dears. Do not hinder my perfection of giving. Bring my aspiration for generosity to its culmination. This brahmin will take you to your grandfather, King Sañjaya. Dear Jāli, if you wish to be free, give the brahmin a thousand nikkhas and you shall be free. Dear Kaṇhājinā, if you wish to be free, give a hundred male slaves, a hundred female slaves, a hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred bulls, and a hundred nikkhas—give a hundred of everything—and you shall be free.' Having thus set a price for the children and consoling them, he took them back to the hermitage. Taking water in his water pot, he made it a condition for omniscient knowledge and poured the water into the brahmin’s hands. Filled with immense joy and delight, he gave away his beloved children, making the earth resound. Here too, as previously described, earthquakes and other marvels occurred. Thus it is said—

113.

113.

“Yācakaṃ upagataṃ disvā, hāso me upapajjatha;

Ubho putte gahetvāna, adāsiṃ brāhmaṇe tadā.

Seeing a petitioner approaching, joy arose in me; taking both my children, I gave them to the brahmin then.

114.

114.

“Sake [V 0.0089] putte cajantassa, jūjake brāhmaṇe yadā;

Tadāpi pathavī kampi, sineruvanavaṭaṃsakā”ti.

When he was giving up his own children to the brahmin Jūjaka, even then the earth trembled, crowned with Sineru and its forests.

Atha brāhmaṇo dārake agantukāme latāya hatthesu bandhitvā ākaḍḍhi. Tesaṃ bandhaṭṭhāne chaviṃ chinditvā lohitaṃ pagghari. So latādaṇḍena paharanto ākaḍḍhi. Te pitaraṃ oloketvā.

Then the brahmin, as the children were unwilling to go, tied their hands with a creeper and dragged them. At the places where they were tied, their skin was cut and blood flowed. Striking them with the stalk of the creeper, he dragged them. They looked at their father.

“Ammā ca tāta nikkhantā, tvañca no tāta dassasi;

Mā no tvaṃ tāta adadā, yāva ammāpi etu no;

Tadāyaṃ brāhmaṇo kāmaṃ, vikkiṇātu hanātu vā”ti. (jā. 2.22.2126) –

"Mother, O father, has gone out, and you too, father, will give us away; do not give us away, father, until mother also comes to us; then this brahmin may do as he wishes, sell us or kill us."

Vatvā punapi ayaṃ evarūpo ghoradassano kurūrakammanto –

Having spoken, again this one, of such dreadful appearance and cruel deeds—

“Manusso udāhu yakkho, maṃsalohitabhojano;

Gāmā araññamāgamma, dhanaṃ taṃ tāta yācati;

Nīyamāne pisācena, kiṃ nu tāta udikkhasī”ti. (jā. 2.22.2130-2131) –

"Is he a human or a yakkha, a devourer of flesh and blood? Having come from a village to the forest, O father, he begs for that wealth. While we are being led away by a goblin, why, father, do you look on?"

Ādīni vadantā parideviṃsu. Tattha dhananti puttadhanaṃ.

Saying such things, they lamented. Therein, 'wealth' means the wealth that is one's children.

Jūjako [M 0.0094] dārake tathā paridevanteyeva pothentova gahetvā pakkāmi. Mahāsattassa dārakānaṃ karuṇaṃ paridevitena tassa ca brāhmaṇassa akāruññabhāvena balavasoko uppajji, vippaṭisāro ca udapādi. So taṅkhaṇaññeva bodhisattānaṃ paveṇiṃ anussari. “Sabbeva hi bodhisattā pañca mahāpariccāge pariccajitvā buddhā bhavissanti, ahampi [P 0.0093] tesaṃ abbhantaro, puttadānañca mahāpariccāgānaṃ aññataraṃ, tasmā vessantara dānaṃ datvā pacchānutāpo na te anucchaviko”ti attānaṃ paribhāsetvā “dinnakālato paṭṭhāya mama te na kiñci hontī”ti attānaṃ upatthambhetvā daḷhasamādānaṃ adhiṭṭhāya paṇṇasāladvāre pāsāṇaphalake kañcanapaṭimā viya nisīdi.

Jūjaka took the children, who were still crying and lamenting, beating them as he departed. Great sorrow arose in the Great Being because of the children's pitiable lamentation and the brahmin's lack of compassion, and remorse also arose. At that very moment, he recalled the tradition of the Bodhisattas. 'All Bodhisattas, having relinquished the five great relinquishments, will become Buddhas; I too am among them, and the gift of children is one of the great relinquishments. Therefore, Vessantara, regret after giving a gift is not appropriate for you.' Thus admonishing himself and supporting himself with the thought, 'From the moment of giving, they are nothing to me,' he sat firmly resolved on the stone slab at the door of the leaf hut, like a golden statue.

Atha maddidevī araññato phalāphalaṃ gahetvā nivattantī “mā mahāsattassa dānantarāyo hotū”ti [V 0.0090] vāḷamigarūpadharāhi devatāhi uparuddhamaggā tesu apagatesu cirena assamaṃ patvā “ajja me dussupinaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, dunnimittāni ca uppannāni, kiṃ nu kho bhavissatī”ti cintentī assamaṃ pavisitvā puttake apassantī bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “deva, na kho amhākaṃ puttake passāmi, kuhiṃ te gatā”ti āha. So tuṇhī ahosi. Sā puttake upadhārentī tahiṃ tahiṃ upadhāvitvā gavesantī adisvā punapi gantvā pucchi. Bodhisatto “kakkhaḷakathāya naṃ puttasokaṃ jahāpessāmī”ti cintetvā –

Then Queen Maddī, having gathered fruits from the forest, was returning. So that no obstacle might arise to the Great Being's gift, deities in the form of wild beasts blocked her path. When they had departed, she reached the hermitage after a long delay. Pondering, "Today I have seen a bad dream, and ill omens have appeared; what can be happening?" she entered the hermitage. Not seeing her children, she went to the Bodhisatta and said, "Your Majesty, I do not see our children. Where have they gone?" He remained silent. She, searching for her children, ran here and there seeking them, and not finding them, went and asked again. The Bodhisatta thought, "I shall make her abandon her grief for the children with harsh words," and said:

“Nūna maddī varārohā, rājaputtī yasassinī;

Pāto gatāsi uñchāya, kimidaṃ sāyamāgatā”ti. (jā. 2.22.2225) –

"Surely, Maddī, of noble form, a renowned princess; you went out at dawn for gleaning—why have you returned this evening?"

Vatvā tāya cirāyanakāraṇe kathite punapi dārake sandhāya na kiñci āha. Sā puttasokena te upadhārentī punapi vātavegena vanāni vicari. Tāya ekarattiyaṃ vicaritaṭṭhānaṃ pariggaṇhantaṃ pannarasayojanamattaṃ ahosi. Atha vibhātāya rattiyā mahāsattassa santikaṃ gantvā ṭhitā dārakānaṃ adassanena balavasokābhibhūtā tassa pādamūle chinnakadalī viya bhūmiyaṃ visaññī hutvā pati. So “matā”ti saññāya kampamāno uppannabalavasokopi satiṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā “jānissāmi tāva jīvati, na jīvatī”ti sattamāse kāyasaṃsaggaṃ anāpannapubbopi [M 0.0095] aññassa abhāvena tassā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā ūrūsu ṭhapetvā udakena paripphositvā urañca mukhañca hadayañca parimajji. Maddīpi kho thokaṃ vītināmetvā satiṃ paṭilabhitvā hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā “deva, dārakā te kuhiṃ gatā”ti pucchi. So āha – “devi, ekassa me brāhmaṇassa maṃ yācitvā āgatassa dāsatthāya dinnā”ti vatvā tāya “kasmā, deva, putte brāhmaṇassa [P 0.0094] datvā mama sabbarattiṃ paridevitvā vicarantiyā nācikkhī”ti vutte “paṭhamameva vutte tava cittadukkhaṃ bahu bhavissati, idāni pana sarīradukkhena tanukaṃ bhavissatī”ti vatvā –

After he had spoken, and she had told him the reason for her delay, he again said nothing concerning the children. She, with grief for her children, seeking them, again roamed the forests with the speed of the wind. The distance she traversed in a single night amounted to fifteen yojanas. Then, as the night gave way to dawn, she went to the Great Being and stood there. Overwhelmed by intense sorrow at not seeing the children, she fell unconscious at his feet, like a felled banana tree. Thinking, "She is dead," he trembled, and though intense sorrow arose in him, he re-established mindfulness, thinking, "Let me first find out whether she lives or not." Though for seven months he had not had any bodily contact with her, in the absence of anyone else he lifted her head, placed it on his lap, sprinkled her with water, and wiped her face, chest, and heart. After a short while, Maddī regained consciousness, and re-establishing her sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, she asked, "Your Majesty, where have the children gone?" He replied, "Queen, I have given them to a brahmin who came and begged me for them, to be his servants." When she said, "Your Majesty, why, having given the children to a brahmin, did you not tell me while I was lamenting and wandering the whole night?" he replied, "If I had told you at first, your mental suffering would have been great; but now, because of your physical suffering, it will be lessened."

“Maṃ passa maddi mā putte, mā bāḷhaṃ paridevasi;

Lacchāma putte jīvantā, arogā ca bhavāmase”ti. (jā. 2.22.2260) –

"Look at me, Maddī, do not grieve for the children, do not lament so intensely; we shall get our children back alive, and we shall be free from illness."

So samassāsetvā puna –

Having thus consoled her, he said again:

“Putte [V 0.0091] pasuñca dhaññañca, yañca aññaṃ ghare dhanaṃ;

Dajjā sappuriso dānaṃ, disvā yācakamāgataṃ;

Anumodāhi me maddi, puttake dānamuttama”nti. (jā. 2.22.2261) –

"A virtuous person, seeing a supplicant who has come, would give away children, cattle, grain, and whatever other wealth is in the home. Rejoice with me, Maddī, in this supreme gift of our children."

Vatvā attano puttadānaṃ taṃ anumodāpesi.

Having spoken thus, he caused her to rejoice in his gift of the children.

Sāpi –

And she:

“Anumodāmi te deva, puttake dānamuttamaṃ;

Datvā cittaṃ pasādehi, bhiyyo dānaṃ dado bhavā”ti. (jā. 2.22.2262) –

"I rejoice in your gift, O lord, the supreme offering of children. Having given, gladden your mind; may you be ever a giver of alms."

Vatvā anumodi.

Having spoken thus, she rejoiced.

Evaṃ tesu aññamaññaṃ sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ kathentesu sakko cintesi – “mahāpuriso hiyyo jūjakassa pathaviṃ unnādetvā dārake adāsi. Idāni naṃ koci hīnapuriso upasaṅkamitvā maddideviṃ yācitvā gahetvā gaccheyya, tato rājā nippaccayo bhaveyya, handāhaṃ brāhmaṇavaṇṇena naṃ upasaṅkamitvā maddiṃ yācitvā pāramikūṭaṃ gāhāpetvā kassaci avissajjiyaṃ katvā puna naṃ tasseva datvā āgamissāmī”ti. So sūriyuggamanavelāyaṃ brāhmaṇavaṇṇena tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ disvā mahāpuriso “atithi no āgato”ti pītisomanassajāto tena saddhiṃ madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā “brāhmaṇa, kenatthena idhāgatosī”ti [M 0.0096] pucchi. Atha naṃ sakko maddideviṃ yāci. Tena vuttaṃ –

While they were thus speaking words of mutual rejoicing, Sakka thought: "Yesterday the Great Being gave the children to Jūjaka, making the earth resound. Now some base person might approach him, ask for Queen Maddī, and take her away; then the king would be without support. Well then, I shall approach him in the guise of a brahmin, ask for Maddī, cause him to attain the pinnacle of the perfections, make her one who cannot be given to anyone else, and then, returning her to him, I shall depart." So, at sunrise, he went to him in the guise of a brahmin. Seeing him, the Great Being was filled with joy and gladness, thinking, "A guest has come to us." He exchanged pleasant greetings with him and asked, "Brahmin, for what purpose have you come here?" Then Sakka asked for Queen Maddī. Therefore it was said:

115.

115.

“Punadeva sakko oruyha, hutvā brāhmaṇasannibho;

Ayāci maṃ maddideviṃ, sīlavantiṃ patibbata”nti.

"Again Sakka descended and, having assumed the likeness of a brahmin, asked me for Queen Maddī, virtuous and devoted to her husband."

Tattha punadevāti dārake dinnadivasato pacchā eva. Tadanantaramevāti attho. Oruyhāti devalokato otaritvā. Brāhmaṇasannibhoti brāhmaṇasamānavaṇṇo.

Therein, "again" means it was just after the day the children were given; that is, immediately following. "Descended" means having come down from the world of the devas. "In the likeness of a brahmin" means having an appearance like a brahmin.

Atha [V 0.0092] mahāsatto “hiyyo me dvepi dārake brāhmaṇassa dinnā, ahampi araññe ekakova, kathaṃ te maddiṃ sīlavantiṃ [P 0.0095] patibbataṃ dassāmī”ti avatvāva pasāritahatthe anaggharatanaṃ ṭhapento viya asajjitvā abajjhitvā anolīnamānaso “ajja me dānapāramī matthakaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭho giriṃ unnādento viya –

Then the Great Being, without saying, "Yesterday I gave both my children to a brahmin, and I am alone in the forest; how can I give you Maddī, who is virtuous and devoted to her husband?", but rather, like one placing a priceless jewel into an outstretched hand, without attachment, without clinging, with an unhesitating mind, he rejoiced, thinking, "Today my perfection of giving will reach its summit!" and, as if making the mountain resound, he said:

“Dadāmi na vikampāmi, yaṃ maṃ yācasi brāhmaṇa;

Santaṃ nappaṭigūhāmi, dāne me ramatī mano”ti. (jā. 2.22.2278) –

"I give and do not waver, O brahmin, in what you ask of me; I do not conceal what I possess, for my mind delights in giving."

Vatvā sīghameva kamaṇḍalunā udakaṃ āharitvā brāhmaṇassa hatthe udakaṃ pātetvā bhariyamadāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Having said this, he quickly brought water in a water-pot, poured the water into the brahmin's hands, and gave his wife to him. Thus it was said:

116.

116.

“Maddiṃ hatthe gahetvāna, udakañjali pūriya;

Pasannamanasaṅkappo, tassa maddiṃ adāsaha”nti.

"Taking Maddī by the hand and filling the brahmin's cupped hands with water, with a mind of serene resolve, I gave Maddī to him."

Tattha udakañjalīti udakaṃ añjaliṃ, “udaka”nti ca karaṇatthe paccattavacanaṃ, udakena tassa brāhmaṇassa añjaliṃ pasāritahatthatalaṃ pūretvāti attho. Pasannamanasaṅkappoti “addhā iminā pariccāgena dānapāramiṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā sammāsambodhiṃ adhigamissāmī”ti upannasaddhāpasādena pasannacittasaṅkappo. Taṅkhaṇaññeva heṭṭhā vuttappakārāni sabbapāṭihāriyāni pāturahesuṃ. “Idānissa na dūre sammāsambodhī”ti devagaṇā brahmagaṇā ativiya pītisomanassajātā ahesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

Therein, `udakañjali` means water in the cupped hands. The word `udaka` is a nominative noun used in the instrumental sense; the meaning is: 'having filled the outstretched palm of that brahmin with water.' As for 'with a serene mental resolve,' it means his mental resolve was serene due to the faith and confidence that had arisen from the thought: 'Surely, by this act of relinquishment, having brought the perfection of giving to its pinnacle, I shall attain perfect supreme enlightenment.' At that very moment, all the portents of the kind previously described appeared. The hosts of devas and brahmās became exceedingly joyful and glad, thinking, 'Now, perfect supreme enlightenment is not far off for him.' Therefore, it was said:

117.

117.

“Maddiyā dīyamānāya, gagane devā pamoditā;

Tadāpi pathavī kampi, sineruvanavaṭaṃsakā”ti.

When Maddī was being given away, the devas in the sky rejoiced; then the earth trembled, with Sineru and its forest groves bowing down.

Tato [M 0.0097] pana dīyamānāya maddiyā deviyā ruṇṇaṃ vā dummukhaṃ vā bhākuṭimattaṃ vā nāhosi, evaṃ cassā ahosi “yaṃ devo icchati, taṃ karotū”ti.

Yet, as Queen Maddī was being given away, there was no weeping, nor a sad face, nor even a frown. Instead, this was her thought: 'Let my lord do as he wishes.'

“Komārī [V 0.0093] yassāhaṃ bhariyā, sāmiko mama issaro;

Yassicche tassa maṃ dajjā, vikkiṇeyya haneyya vā”ti. (jā. 2.22.2282) –

I am his wife from my youth; he is my husband, my master. To whomever he wishes, let him give me; let him sell me or even slay me.

Āha.

She said.

Mahāpurisopi “ambho, brāhmaṇa, maddito me sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena sabbaññutaññāṇameva piyataraṃ, idaṃ me dānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭivedhassa paccayo hotū”ti vatvā adāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

The Great Being also said, 'O brahmin, to me, the knowledge of omniscience is dearer by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold than Maddī. May this gift of mine be a condition for the realization of the knowledge of omniscience.' Having said this, he gave her away. Therefore, it is said:

118.

118.

“Jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ dhītaṃ, maddideviṃ patibbataṃ;

Cajamāno na cintesiṃ, bodhiyāyeva kāraṇā.

Jāli, my daughter Kaṇhājinā, and Queen Maddī, the devoted wife—giving them away, I did not hesitate, for the sake of enlightenment alone.

119.

119.

Na [P 0.0096] me dessā ubho puttā, maddidevī na dessiyā;

Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ, tasmā piye adāsaha”nti.

My two children were not hateful to me, nor was Queen Maddī hateful. Omniscience was dear to me; therefore, I gave away my dear ones.

Tattha cajamāno na cintesinti pariccajanto santāpavasena na cintesiṃ, vissaṭṭho hutvā pariccajinti attho.

Therein, 'giving them away, I did not hesitate' means: while relinquishing them, I did not hesitate out of distress. The meaning is that I relinquished them with a mind that had let go.
