Etthāha – kasmā panāyaṃ mahāpuriso attano puttadāre jātisampanne khattiye parassa dāsabhāvena pariccaji, na hi yesaṃ kesañcipi bhujissānaṃ abhujissabhāvakaraṇaṃ sādhudhammoti? Vuccate – anudhammabhāvato. Ayañhi buddhakārake dhamme anugatadhammatā, yadidaṃ sabbassa attaniyassa mamanti pariggahitavatthuno anavasesapariccāgo, na hi deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakavikapparahitaṃ dānapāramiṃ paripūretuṃ ussukkamāpannānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ mamanti pariggahitavatthuṃ yācantassa yācakassa na pariccajituṃ yuttaṃ, porāṇopi cāyamanudhammo. Sabbesañhi bodhisattānaṃ ayaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇadhammo kulavaṃso kulappaveṇī, yadidaṃ sabbassa pariccāgo. Tattha ca visesato piyataravatthupariccāgo, na hi keci bodhisattā vaṃsānugataṃ rajjissariyādidhanapariccāgaṃ, attano sīsanayanādiaṅgapariccāgaṃ, piyajīvitapariccāgaṃ, kulavaṃsapatiṭṭhāpakapiyaputtapariccāgaṃ, manāpacārinīpiyabhariyāpariccāganti [M 0.0098] ime pañca mahāpariccāge apariccajitvā buddhā nāma bhūtapubbā atthi. Tathā hi maṅgale bhagavati bodhisattabhūte [V 0.0094] bodhipariyesanaṃ caramāne ca carimattabhāvato tatiye attabhāve saputtadāre ekasmiṃ pabbate vasante kharadāṭhiko nāma yakkho mahāpurisassa dānajjhāsayataṃ sutvā brāhmaṇavaṇṇena upasaṅkamitvā mahāsattaṃ dve dārake yāci.

Here an objection is raised: Why did this Great Being give away his own wife and children—khattiyas of noble birth—to become the slaves of another? For surely, making free persons unfree is not the practice of the virtuous. The reply is: Because it is in accordance with the nature of the Dhamma. For this is the inherent nature that accords with the qualities that make a Buddha: namely, the complete relinquishment of all that is held as 'mine.' Indeed, for bodhisattas striving to fulfill the perfection of giving without making distinctions regarding the gift or the recipient, it is not proper to refuse a petitioner who asks for something held as one's own. This, moreover, is the ancient and concordant practice. For all bodhisattas, this is their habitual and well-practiced way, their lineage, their family tradition—that is, the relinquishment of everything. And within that, the relinquishment of what is most dear is especially significant. For no bodhisattas have ever become Buddhas without first making these five great relinquishments: the relinquishment of kingdom, sovereignty, and other wealth in accordance with their lineage; the relinquishment of their own limbs, such as their head and eyes; the relinquishment of their dear life; the relinquishment of a dear son who establishes the family lineage; and the relinquishment of a dear and pleasing wife. Thus, when the Blessed One Maṅgala was a bodhisatta practicing for the sake of enlightenment, in his third existence from his final one, while he was living on a mountain with his wife and children, a yakkha named Kharadāṭhika, having heard of the Great Being’s disposition for giving, approached the great bodhisatta in the guise of a brahmin and asked for his two children.

Mahāsatto “dadāmi brāhmaṇassa puttake”ti haṭṭhapahaṭṭho udakapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ kampento dvepi dārake adāsi. Yakkho caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ālambanaphalakaṃ nissāya ṭhito mahāsattassa passantasseva muḷālakalāpaṃ viya dve dārake khādi. Aggijālaṃ viya lohitadhāraṃ uggiramānaṃ yakkhassa mukhaṃ olokentassa mahāpurisassa “vañcesi vata maṃ yakkho”ti uppajjanakacittuppādassa okāsaṃ adentassa upāyakosallassa subhāvitattā atītadhammānaṃ [P 0.0097] appaṭisandhisabhāvato aniccādivasena saṅkhārānaṃ suparimadditabhāvato ca evaṃ ittaraṭṭhitikena pabhaṅgunā asārena saṅkhārakalāpena “pūritā vata me dānapāramī, mahantaṃ vata me atthaṃ sādhetvā idaṃ adhigata”nti somanassameva uppajji. So idaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe attano cittācāraṃ ñatvā “imassa nissandena anāgate imināva nīhārena sarīrato rasmiyo nikkhamantū”ti patthanamakāsi. Tassa taṃ patthanaṃ nissāya buddhabhūtassa sarīrappabhā niccameva dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā). Evaṃ aññepi bodhisattā attano piyataraṃ puttadāraṃ pariccajitvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhiṃsu.

The great bodhisatta, exceedingly joyful, declared, 'I give the children to the brahmin,' and making the earth tremble to its watery boundaries, he gave away both children. The yakkha, standing at the end of the walking path and leaning on a support plank, devoured the two children in the great bodhisatta's very sight as if they were a bundle of lotus roots. As the great bodhisatta looked at the yakkha's mouth spewing a stream of blood like a mass of flames, he gave no opportunity for a thought to arise such as, 'Alas, the yakkha has deceived me.' Due to his well-developed skill in means, the non-reconnecting nature of past phenomena, and his thorough mastery of conditioned phenomena in terms of impermanence and so forth, only gladness arose in him regarding this aggregate of formations that is so short-lived, fragile, and without substance, and he thought: 'Indeed, my perfection of giving has been fulfilled! Indeed, having accomplished a great purpose for me, this has been attained!' Recognizing this unique conduct of his own mind at that moment, he made an aspiration: 'As a result of this, in the future, may rays of light emanate from my body in this very same way.' On account of that aspiration, when he became a Buddha, the radiance from his body constantly pervaded the ten-thousand-world-system. In this way, other bodhisattas also, having relinquished their dearest children and wives, penetrated the knowledge of omniscience.

Api ca yathā nāma koci puriso kassaci santike gāmaṃ vā janapadaṃ vā keṇiyā gahetvā kammaṃ karonto attano antevāsikānaṃ vā pamādena pūtibhūtaṃ dhanaṃ dhāreyya, tamenaṃ so gāhāpetvā bandhanāgāraṃ paveseyya. Tassa evamassa “ahaṃ kho imassa rañño kammaṃ karonto ettakaṃ nāma dhanaṃ dhāremi, tenāhaṃ raññā bandhanāgāre pavesito, sacāhaṃ idheva homi, attānañca jīyeyya, puttadārakammakaraporisā ca me jīvikāpagatā mahantaṃ anayabyasanaṃ āpajjeyyuṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ rañño ārocetvā attano puttaṃ vā kaniṭṭhabhātaraṃ vā idha ṭhapetvā nikkhameyyaṃ[M 0.0099]. Evāhaṃ ito bandhanato mutto nacirasseva yathāmittaṃ yathāsandiṭṭhaṃ dhanaṃ saṃharitvā rañño datvā tampi bandhanato mocemi, appamattova hutvā uṭṭhānabalena attano sampattiṃ paṭipākatikaṃ karissāmī”ti. So tathā kareyya. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Furthermore, it is as if some man, having taken a village or a district on lease from a certain king, while carrying out his work, were to misappropriate, through his own or his apprentices' negligence, a certain amount of the king's revenue. That king would have him seized and put into prison. To him, this thought might occur: 'Indeed, while working for this king, I have misappropriated such-and-such an amount of wealth, and for that, I have been put in prison by the king. If I remain here, I myself shall perish, and my sons, wife, workers, and servants will be deprived of their livelihood and fall into great misfortune and ruin. What if I were to inform the king, place my own son or younger brother here as a surety, and depart? Thus freed from this bondage, I would, without delay, collect wealth from friends and acquaintances, give it to the king, and free him also from bondage. Then, being diligent, by the power of my effort, I shall restore my own prosperity to its original state.' And he would act accordingly. In this way is this illustration to be understood.

Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – rājā viya kammaṃ, bandhanāgāro viya saṃsāro, raññā bandhanāgāre ṭhapitapuriso viya kammavasena saṃsāracārake ṭhito mahāpuriso, tassa bandhanāgāre ṭhitapurisassa tattha puttassa vā bhātuno vā parādhīnabhāvakaraṇena tesaṃ attano ca dukkhappamocanaṃ [V 0.0095] viya mahāpurisassa attano puttādike paresaṃ datvā sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭilābhena sabbasattānaṃ vaṭṭadukkhappamocanaṃ, tassa vigatadukkhassa tehi saddhiṃ yathādhippetasampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhānaṃ viya mahāpurisassa arahattamaggena [P 0.0098] apagatavaṭṭadukkhassa buddhabhāvena dasabalādisabbaññutaññāṇasampattisamannāgamo attano vacanakārakānaṃ vijjattayādisampattisamannāgamo cāti evaṃ anavajjasabhāvo eva mahāpurisānaṃ puttadārapariccāgo. Eteneva nayena nesaṃ aṅgajīvitapariccāge yā codanā, sāpi visodhitāti veditabbāti.

Herein, this is the application of the simile: Kamma is like the king; saṃsāra is like the prison; the great being, established in the course of saṃsāra by the power of kamma, is like the man placed in the prison by the king. Just as that man in prison, by placing his son or brother under another's authority, brings about liberation from suffering for them and for himself, so too is the great being's liberation of all beings from the suffering of the cycle of existence by giving away his own children and others and attaining omniscient knowledge. Just as that man, freed from suffering, is established together with them in his desired prosperity, so too is the attainment of the state of a Buddha for the great being, for whom the suffering of the cycle has been removed by the path of Arahantship, endowed with the accomplishment of omniscient knowledge including the ten powers, and for those who follow his word, the endowment with accomplishments such as the three knowledges. Thus, the giving away of wife and children by great beings is indeed of a blameless nature. By this same method, it should be understood that any objection concerning their giving away of limbs and life is also cleared.

Evaṃ pana mahāsattena maddideviyā dinnāya sakko acchariyabbhutacittajāto hutvā –

Thus, when the Great Being had given Queen Maddī, Sakka, with a mind arisen of wonder and amazement, said:

“Sabbe jitā te paccūhā, ye dibbā ye ca mānusā;

Ninnāditā te pathavī, saddo te tidivaṃ gato. (jā. 2.22.2283-2284);

All obstacles have been conquered by you, both the divine and the human; the earth has been made to resound by you, your fame has gone to the triple heaven.

“Duddadaṃ dadamānānaṃ, dukkaraṃ kamma kubbataṃ;

Asanto nānukubbanti, sataṃ dhammo durannayo.

Giving what is difficult to give, doing a deed that is difficult to do—the unrighteous do not emulate this; the way of the good is difficult to follow.

“Tasmā satañca asataṃ, nānā hoti ito gati;

Asanto nirayaṃ yanti, santo saggaparāyanā”ti. (jā. 2.22.2286-2287) –

Therefore, from this world, the destinations of the good and the unrighteous are different; the unrighteous go to hell, while the good have heaven as their final resort.

Ādinā nayena mahāpurisassa dānānumodanavasena thutiṃ akāsi.

With such verses, he offered praise to the Great Being by way of rejoicing in his gift.

Tattha paccūhāti paccatthikā. Dibbāti dibbayasapaṭibāhakā. Mānusāti manussayasapaṭibāhakā. Ke pana teti? Macchariyadhammā, te sabbe puttadāraṃ dentena mahāsattena jitāti dasseti. Duddadanti puttadārādiduddadaṃ dadamānānaṃ [M 0.0100] tameva dukkaraṃ kubbataṃ tumhādisānaṃ kammaṃ aññe sāvakapaccekabodhisattā nānukubbanti, pageva asanto maccharino. Tasmā sataṃ dhammo durannayo sādhūnaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ paṭipattidhammo aññehi duranugamo.

Therein, 'obstacles' means adversaries. 'Divine' refers to those that obstruct divine glory. 'Human' refers to those that obstruct human glory. And what are these? They are the qualities of stinginess. It is shown that all of them are conquered by the Great Being who gives away his wife and children. 'Difficult to give' refers to giving what is difficult to give, such as children and wife. Regarding the deed of those like you who do what is difficult, other disciple-bodhisattas and paccekabodhisattas do not emulate it, how much less the unrighteous and stingy. Therefore, 'the way of the good is difficult to follow' means that the practice of the good, of the great Bodhisattas, is difficult for others to follow.

Evaṃ sakko mahāpurisassa anumodanavasena thutiṃ katvā maddideviṃ niyyātento –

Thus Sakka, having praised the Great Being by way of rejoicing, while restoring Queen Maddī, said:

“Dadāmi [V 0.0096] bhoto bhariyaṃ, maddiṃ sabbaṅgasobhanaṃ;

Tvañceva maddiyā channo, maddī ca patino tavā”ti. (jā. 2.22.2289) –

I give back to you, good sir, your wife, Maddī, beautiful in all her limbs. You are a fitting match for Maddī, and Maddī for you, her husband.

Vatvā taṃ maddiṃ paṭidatvā dibbattabhāvena jalanto taruṇasūriyo viya ākāse ṭhatvā attānaṃ ācikkhanto –

Having spoken thus and returned Maddī, shining in his divine form like the morning sun, he stood in the sky and, revealing himself, said:

“Sakkohamasmi [P 0.0099] devindo, āgatosmi tavantike;

Varaṃ varassu rājisi, vare aṭṭha dadāmi te”ti. (jā. 2.22.2292) –

I am Sakka, the lord of the devas; I have come into your presence. Choose your boons, O royal sage; eight boons I shall grant to you.

Vatvā varehi nimantesi. Mahāsattopi “pitā maṃ punadeva rajje patiṭṭhāpetu, vajjhappattaṃ vadhato moceyyaṃ, sabbasattānaṃ avassayo bhaveyyaṃ, paradāraṃ na gaccheyyaṃ, itthīnaṃ vasaṃ na gaccheyyaṃ, putto me dīghāyuko siyā, annapānādideyyadhammo bahuko siyā, tañca aparikkhayaṃ pasannacitto dadeyyaṃ, evaṃ mahādānāni pavattetvā devalokaṃ gantvā tato idhāgato sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇeyya”nti ime aṭṭha vare yāci. Sakko “nacirasseva pitā sañjayamahārājā idheva āgantvā taṃ gahetvā rajje patiṭṭhāpessati, itaro ca sabbo te manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇissati, mā cintayi, appamatto hohī”ti ovaditvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Bodhisatto ca maddidevī ca sammodamānā sakkadattiye assame vasiṃsu.

The Great Being then requested these eight boons: 'May my father establish me in the kingdom once more; may I be able to free from execution one who is condemned to death; may I be a reliable refuge for all beings; may I not approach another's wife; may my son be long-lived; may there be abundant items for giving, such as food and drink; may I give them with a serene mind, and may they be inexhaustible; and having performed great acts of giving, may I go to the deva world, and having passed from there and returned to this world, may I attain omniscience.' Sakka replied, 'Before long, your father, the great king Sañjaya, will come right here, take you, and establish you in the kingdom. And all your other wishes will reach their fulfillment. Do not be anxious; be diligent.' Having given this advice, he departed to his own abode. The Bodhisatta and Maddī-devī, rejoicing together, dwelt in the hermitage given by Sakka.

Jūjakepi kumāre gahetvā gacchante devatā ārakkhamakaṃsu. Divase divase ekā devadhītā rattibhāge āgantvā maddivaṇṇena kumāre paṭijaggi. So devatāviggahito hutvā “kaliṅgaraṭṭhaṃ gamissāmī”ti aḍḍhamāsena jetuttaranagarameva sampāpuṇi. Rājā vinicchaye nisinno brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ dārake rājaṅgaṇena gacchante disvā sañjānitvā brāhmaṇena [M 0.0101] saddhiṃ te pakkosāpetvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā bodhisattena kathitaniyāmeneva dhanaṃ datvā kumāre kiṇitvā nhāpetvā bhojetvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍite katvā rājā dārakaṃ phussatidevī dārikaṃ ucchaṅge katvā bodhisattassa rājaputtiyā ca pavattiṃ suṇiṃsu.

Even as Jūjaka was taking the children, the deities protected them. Each day, a celestial maiden would come at night and, in the guise of Maddī, care for the children. Though he, being led astray by the deities, intended, 'I will go to the kingdom of Kaliṅga,' within half a month he reached the city of Jetuttara itself. The king, seated in judgment, saw the children passing through the royal courtyard with the brahmin and, recognizing them, had them summoned along with the brahmin. Having heard the account, and following the very method spoken of by the Bodhisatta, he gave wealth and purchased the children. After having them bathed, fed, and adorned with all ornaments, the king placed the boy on his lap, and Queen Phussatī placed the girl on her lap, and they listened to the account of the Bodhisatta and the princess.

Taṃ sutvā rājā “bhūnahaccaṃ vata mayā kata”nti saṃviggamānaso tāvadeva dvādasaakkhobhanīparimāṇaṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā vaṅkapabbatābhimukho pāyāsi saddhiṃ phussatideviyā ceva [V 0.0097] dārakehi ca. Anukkamena gantvā puttena ca suṇisāya ca samāgañchi. Vessantaro piyaputte disvā sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto visaññī hutvā tattheva pati, tathā maddī mātāpitaro sahajātā saṭṭhisahassā ca amaccā. Taṃ kāruññaṃ passantesu ekopi sakabhāvena sandhāretuṃ [P 0.0100] nāsakkhi, sakalaṃ assamapadaṃ yugandharavātapamadditaṃ viya sālavanaṃ ahosi. Sakko devarājā tesaṃ visaññibhāvavinodanatthaṃ pokkharavassaṃ vassāpesi, temetukāmā tementi, pokkhare patitavassaṃ viya vinivattitvā udakaṃ gacchati. Sabbe saññaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Tadāpi pathavikampādayo heṭṭhā vuttappakārā acchariyā pāturahesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

Hearing this, the king, his heart struck with remorse, thought, 'Indeed, a great cruelty has been done by me!' At that very moment, he assembled an army of twelve akkhobhinīs and set out towards Vaṅka Mountain, together with Queen Phussatī and the children. Proceeding in due course, he was reunited with his son and daughter-in-law. Vessantara, upon seeing his beloved children, was unable to contain his grief and, becoming unconscious, fell right there. Likewise did Maddī, his mother and father, and the sixty thousand ministers. Among those witnessing such a pitiable scene, not even one was able to maintain composure. The entire hermitage became like a sāl forest crushed by a Yugandhara wind. Sakka, king of the gods, to dispel their state of unconsciousness, caused the lotus rain to fall. Those who wished to be wet were drenched, but for others, the water rolled off as it does from a lotus leaf. All regained consciousness. At that time also, the wonders described before, beginning with the trembling of the earth, appeared. Therefore it was said:

120.

120.

“Punāparaṃ brahāraññe, mātāpitusamāgame;

Karuṇaṃ paridevante, sallapante sukhaṃ dukhaṃ.

"Furthermore, in the great forest, at the reunion with his mother and father, they lamented piteously, conversing of their happiness and sorrow.

121.

121.

“Hirottappena garunā, ubhinnaṃ upasaṅkami;

Tadāpi pathavī kampi, sineruvanavaṭaṃsakā”ti.

"With solemn shame and moral dread, he approached them both; at that time also the earth trembled, and Sineru with its forests bowed down."

Tattha karuṇaṃ paridevanteti mātāpitaro ādiṃ katvā sabbasmiṃ āgatajane karuṇaṃ paridevamāne. Sallapante sukhaṃ dukhanti sukhadukkhaṃ pucchitvā paṭisanthāravasena ālāpasallāpaṃ karonte. Hirottappena garunā ubhinnanti ime sivīnaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā adūsakaṃ dhamme ṭhitaṃ maṃ pabbājayiṃsūti cittappakopaṃ akatvā ubhosu etesu mātāpitūsu dhammagāravasamussitena hirottappeneva yathārūpe upasaṅkami. Tena me dhammatejena tadāpi pathavī kampi.

Therein, 'lamenting piteously' means that, beginning with his mother and father, all the people who had come were lamenting piteously. 'Conversing of happiness and sorrow' means that they were engaging in conversation, asking about each other's well-being and sorrow by way of friendly inquiry. 'With solemn shame and moral dread, he approached them both' means that, without giving rise to anger at the thought, 'These parents of mine, heeding the words of the Sivi people, banished me, though I was blameless and established in the Dhamma,' he approached both these parents just as before, with shame and moral dread born of his reverence for the Dhamma. By that righteous power of mine, the earth trembled at that time also.

Atha [M 0.0102] sañjayamahārājā bodhisattaṃ khamāpetvā rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā taṅkhaṇaññeva kesamassukammādīni kārāpetvā nhāpetvā sabbābharaṇavibhūsitaṃ devarājānamiva virocamānaṃ saha maddideviyā rajje abhisiñcitvā tāvadeva ca tato paṭṭhāya dvādasaakkhobhanīparimāṇāya caturaṅginiyā senāya ca puttaṃ parivārayitvā vaṅkapabbatato yāva jetuttaranagarā saṭṭhiyojanamaggaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā dvīhi māsehi sukheneva nagaraṃ pavesesi. Mahājano uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedesi. Celukkhepādayo pavattiṃsu. Nagare ca nandibheriṃ carāpesuṃ. Antamaso biḷāre upādāya sabbesaṃ bandhane ṭhitānaṃ bandhanamokkho ahosi. So nagaraṃ paviṭṭhadivaseyeva paccūsakāle cintesi – “sve vibhātāya rattiyā mamāgatabhāvaṃ sutvā yācakā āgamissanti, tesāhaṃ kiṃ dassāmī”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakkassa āsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So āvajjento [P 0.0101] taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā [V 0.0098] tāvadeva rājanivesanassa purimavatthuṃ pacchimavatthuñca kaṭippamāṇaṃ pūrento ghanamegho viya sattaratanavassaṃ vassāpesi. Sakalanagare jaṇṇuppamāṇaṃ vassāpesīti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then the great king Sañjaya, having asked forgiveness of the Bodhisatta and handed over the kingdom to him, at that very moment had his hair and beard attended to. Having had him bathed and adorned with all ornaments so that he shone like the king of the gods, he anointed him to the kingship together with Queen Maddī. And right then, from that time onwards, surrounding his son with a fourfold army of twelve akkhobhinīs, and having the sixty-yojana road from Vaṅka Mountain to the city of Jetuttara decorated, he had him enter the city in great comfort over two months. The populace experienced immense joy and gladness. The tossing of cloths and other celebrations took place. They had the drum of rejoicing sounded throughout the city. All those in bondage were released, down to the very cats in their cages. On the very day he entered the city, at dawn, he thought: 'Tomorrow, when the night has brightened, mendicants will come, having heard of my return. What shall I give them?' At that moment, Sakka's throne showed signs of heat. He, reflecting, understood the reason and at once caused a rain of the seven treasures to fall like a dense cloud, filling the front and back grounds of the royal palace to the height of a man's waist. Throughout the entire city, he caused it to rain to the height of a man's knee. Therefore it was said:

122.

122.

“Punāparaṃ brahāraññā, nikkhamitvā sañātibhi;

Pavisāmi puraṃ rammaṃ, jetuttaraṃ puruttamaṃ.

"Furthermore, having departed from the great forest with my kinsmen, I enter the delightful city, Jetuttara, the best of cities.

123.

123.

“Ratanāni satta vassiṃsu, mahāmegho pavassatha;

Tadāpi pathavī kampi, sineruvanavaṭaṃsakā.

"The seven treasures rained down, a great cloud poured forth; at that time also the earth trembled, and Sineru with its forests bowed down.

124.

124.

“Acetanāyaṃ pathavī, aviññāya sukhaṃ dukhaṃ;

Sāpi dānabalā mayhaṃ, sattakkhattuṃ pakampathā”ti.

"This earth is without consciousness, not knowing pleasure or pain; yet even so, by the power of my giving, it trembled seven times."

Evaṃ sattaratanavasse vuṭṭhe punadivase mahāsatto “yesaṃ kulānaṃ purimapacchimavatthūsu vuṭṭhadhanaṃ, tesaññeva hotū”ti dāpetvā avasesaṃ āharāpetvā attano gehavatthusmiṃ dhanena saddhiṃ koṭṭhāgāresu okirāpetvā mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Acetanāyaṃ pathavīti cetanārahitā ayaṃ mahābhūtā pathavī, devatā pana cetanāsahitā. Aviññāya sukhaṃ dukhanti acetanattā eva sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ ajānitvā. Satipi sukhadukkhapaccayasaṃyoge [M 0.0103] taṃ nānubhavantī. Sāpi dānabalā mayhanti evaṃbhūtāpi sā mahāpathavī mama dānapuññānubhāvahetu. Sattakkhattuṃ pakampathāti aṭṭhavassikakāle hadayamaṃsādīnipi yācakānaṃ dadeyyanti dānajjhāsayuppāde maṅgalahatthidāne pabbājanakāle pavattitamahādāne puttadāne bhariyādāne vaṅkapabbate ñātisamāgame nagaraṃ paviṭṭhadivase ratanavassakāleti imesu ṭhānesu sattavāraṃ akampittha. Evaṃ ekasmiṃyeva attabhāve sattakkhattuṃ mahāpathavikampanādiacchariyapātubhāvahetubhūtāni yāvatāyukaṃ mahādānāni pavattetvā mahāsatto āyupariyosāne tusitapure uppajji. Tenāha bhagavā –

Thus, when the rain of seven jewels had fallen, on the following day, the Great Being, having decreed, 'May the wealth that has rained down upon the front and back grounds of these families belong to them alone,' had the remainder brought and scattered in his own palace grounds and storehouses along with his wealth, and then he held a great almsgiving. The phrase 'this earth is without consciousness' means this great element, the earth, is devoid of volition, whereas deities possess volition. The phrase 'not knowing pleasure and pain' means that due to being without consciousness, it does not know pleasure and pain. Even when conditions for pleasure and pain are present, it does not experience them. The phrase 'yet by the power of my giving' means that even such a great earth as this quaked on account of the power of my merit from giving. The phrase 'it trembled seven times' refers to the following: it quaked seven times across these nine occasions—when the aspiration to give arose, thinking, 'I shall give even my heart-flesh and so on to supplicants' when he was eight years old; at the giving of the state elephant; at the time of his banishment; at the great almsgiving he held; at the giving of his children; at the giving of his wife; at the reunion with his relatives on Mount Vaṅka; on the day he entered the city; and at the time of the rain of jewels. Thus, in that very same lifetime, having performed great acts of giving throughout his life—which were the cause for the manifestation of miracles such as the great earth trembling seven times—the Great Being, at the end of his lifespan, was reborn in the Tusita celestial realm. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Tato vessantaro rājā, dānaṃ datvāna khattiyo;

Kāyassa bhedā sappañño, saggaṃ so upapajjathā”ti. (jā. 2.22.2440);

"Then that wise King Vessantara, the Khattiya, having given gifts, upon the breaking up of the body, was reborn in heaven."

Tadā jūjako devadatto ahosi, amittatāpanā ciñcamāṇavikā[P 0.0102], cetaputto channo, accutatāpaso [V 0.0099] sāriputto, sakko anuruddho, maddī rāhulamātā, jālikumāro rāhulo, kaṇhājinā uppalavaṇṇā, mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, vessantaro rājā lokanātho.

At that time, Jūjaka was Devadatta; Amittatāpanā was Ciñcamāṇavikā; Cetaputta was Channa; the ascetic Accuta was Sāriputta; Sakka was Anuruddha; Maddī was Rāhula’s mother; Prince Jāli was Rāhula; Kaṇhājinā was Uppalavaṇṇā; the parents were the great royal family; the remaining assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and King Vessantara was myself, the Lord of the World.

Idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva yathārahaṃ sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā mahāsatte kucchigate mātu devasikaṃ chasatasahassāni vissajjetvā dānaṃ dātukāmatādohaḷo, tathā dīyamānepi dhanassa parikkhayābhāvo, jātakkhaṇe eva hatthaṃ pasāretvā “dānaṃ dassāmi, atthi kiñcī”ti vācānicchāraṇaṃ, catupañcavassikakāle attano alaṅkārassa dhātīnaṃ hatthagatassa puna aggahetukāmatā, aṭṭhavassikakāle hadayamaṃsādikassa attano sarīrāvayavassa dātukāmatāti evamādikā sattakkhattuṃ mahāpathavikampanādianekacchariyapātubhāvahetubhūtā idha mahāpurisassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbā. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Here too, the remaining perfections should be determined in the same manner as stated before, as is appropriate. For instance: when the Great Being was in his mother’s womb, she had a pregnancy craving to give away six hundred thousand daily; even when so much was being given, there was no depletion of wealth; at the very moment of his birth, he stretched out his hand and uttered the words, 'I shall give a gift, is there anything?'; at the age of four or five, he had no desire to take back his ornaments once they were in the hands of his nurses; at the age of eight, he desired to give away parts of his own body, such as his heart-flesh. In this way, the virtues and power of the Great Being, which were the cause for the manifestation of many miracles such as the great earth trembling seven times, should be elucidated here. Therefore it is said:

“Evaṃ acchariyā hete, abbhutā ca mahesino…pe…;

Tesu cittappasādopi, dukkhato parimocaye;

Pagevānukiriyā tesaṃ, dhammassa anudhammato”ti.

"Thus, wondrous and marvelous are these great seers...; Even serene confidence in them liberates one from suffering; How much more so the practice of acting in imitation of them, in conformity with the Dhamma."

Vessantaracariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Conduct of Vessantara is concluded.

10. Sasapaṇḍitacariyāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Conduct of the Wise Hare

125-6. Dasame [M 0.0104] yadā homi, sasakoti ahaṃ, sāriputta, bodhipariyesanaṃ caramāno yadā sasapaṇḍito homi. Bodhisattā hi kammavasippattāpi tādisānaṃ tiracchānānaṃ anuggaṇhanatthaṃ tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattanti. Pavanacārakoti mahāvanacārī. Dabbāditiṇāni rukkhagacchesu paṇṇāni yaṃkiñci sākaṃ rukkhato patitaphalāni ca bhakkho etassāti tiṇapaṇṇasākaphalabhakkho. Paraheṭhanavivajjitoti parapīḷāvirahito. Suttapoto cāti uddapoto ca. Ahaṃ tadāti yadāhaṃ sasako homi, tadā ete makkaṭādayo tayo sahāye ovadāmi.

In the tenth story, the phrase 'When I was a hare' means: when I, Sāriputta, was the Wise Hare while practicing for the sake of seeking enlightenment. For Bodhisattas, even when they have come under the sway of kamma, are reborn in the animal realm for the purpose of assisting such beings. 'A wanderer in the woods' means one who roams the great forest. 'One who eats grass, leaves, greens, and fruit' means one whose food is grass such as dabba grass, leaves from trees and bushes, any kind of greens, and fruit fallen from trees. 'Avoiding harm to others' means being free from afflicting others. 'And a young otter' refers to an otter. 'I then' means when I was the hare, I would advise those three companions, the monkey and the others.

127. Kiriye kalyāṇapāpaketi kusale ceva akusale ca kamme. Pāpānīti anusāsanākāradassanaṃ. Tattha pāpāni [P 0.0103] parivajjethāti pāṇātipāto…pe… micchādiṭṭhīti imāni pāpāni parivajjetha. Kalyāṇe abhinivissathāti dānaṃ sīlaṃ…pe… diṭṭhujukammanti idaṃ [V 0.0100] kalyāṇaṃ, imasmiṃ kalyāṇe attano kāyavācācittāni abhimukhabhāvena nivissatha, imaṃ kalyāṇapaṭipattiṃ paṭipajjathāti attho.

127. The phrase 'in action, good and evil' refers to skillful and unskillful deeds. The word 'evils' indicates the manner of instruction. Therein, 'you should avoid evils' means you should avoid these evils: killing living beings... and so on... up to wrong view. The phrase 'you should be devoted to the good' means: this is the good, namely, giving, virtue... and so on... up to the straightening of one's view. You should settle your body, speech, and mind upon this good with a direct inclination; you should undertake this good practice. This is the meaning.

Evaṃ mahāsatto tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattopi ñāṇasampannatāya kalyāṇamitto hutvā tesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ kālena kālaṃ upagatānaṃ ovādavasena dhammaṃ desesi. Te tassa ovādaṃ sampaṭicchitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā vasanti. Evaṃ kāle gacchante bodhisatto ākāsaṃ oloketvā candapāripūriṃ disvā “uposathakammaṃ karothā”ti ovadi. Tenāha –

Thus the Great Being, though reborn in the animal realm, on account of being endowed with wisdom, became a good friend and taught the Dhamma by way of instruction to those three beings who approached him from time to time. They, having accepted his instruction, entered their own dwelling places and resided there. As time was passing, the Bodhisatta, looking at the sky and seeing the fullness of the moon, advised them, 'You should perform the Uposatha observance.' Therefore, he said:

128.

128.

“Uposathamhi divase, candaṃ disvāna pūritaṃ;

Etesaṃ tattha ācikkhiṃ, divaso ajjuposatho.

On the Uposatha day, having seen the full moon, I announced to them then, 'Today is the Uposatha day.'

129.

129.

“Dānāni paṭiyādetha, dakkhiṇeyyassa dātave;

Datvā dānaṃ dakkhiṇeyye, upavassathuposatha”nti.

'Prepare gifts to be given to one worthy of offerings; having given a gift to one worthy of offerings, you should observe the Uposatha.'

Tattha candaṃ disvā na pūritanti juṇhapakkhacātuddasiyaṃ īsakaṃ aparipuṇṇabhāvena candaṃ na paripūritaṃ disvā tato vibhātāya rattiyā aruṇuggamanavelāyameva uposathamhi divase pannarase etesaṃ makkaṭādīnaṃ mayhaṃ [M 0.0105] sahāyānaṃ divaso ajjuposatho. Tasmā “dānāni paṭiyādethā”tiādinā tattha uposathadivase paṭipattividhānaṃ ācikkhinti yojetabbaṃ. Tattha dānānīti deyyadhamme. Paṭiyādethāti yathāsatti yathābalaṃ sajjetha. Dātaveti dātuṃ. Upavassathāti uposathakammaṃ karotha, uposathasīlāni rakkhatha, sīle patiṭṭhāya dinnadānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti, tasmā yācake sampatte tumhehi khāditabbāhārato datvā khādeyyāthāti dasseti.

Therein, 'having seen the moon not full' means: on the fourteenth day of the waxing fortnight, having seen the moon not completely full due to its slight incompleteness, then, when the night had dawned, at the very time of sunrise on the fifteenth, the Uposatha day, he thought: 'For these, the monkey and others, my companions, today is the Uposatha day. Therefore, prepare gifts.' By these and other words, the method of practice on the Uposatha day is explained therein and should be connected. Therein, 'gifts' means things to be given. 'Prepare' means to make ready according to one's ability and strength. 'To be given' means to give. 'Observe' means to perform the Uposatha act and keep the Uposatha precepts; a gift given while established in virtue is of great fruit. Therefore, it is shown that when supplicants arrive, you should give from the food that is to be eaten by you, and then you may eat.

Te “sādhū”ti bodhisattassa ovādaṃ sirasā sampaṭicchitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhahiṃsu. Tesu uddapoto pātova “gocaraṃ pariyesissāmī”ti nadītīraṃ gato. Atheko bāḷisiko satta rohitamacche uddharitvā valliyā āvuṇitvā nadītīre vālukāya paṭicchādetvā macche gaṇhanto nadiyā adho sotaṃ [P 0.0104] bhassi. Uddo macchagandhaṃ ghāyitvā vālukaṃ viyūhitvā macche disvā nīharitvā “atthi nu kho etesaṃ sāmiko”ti tikkhattuṃ ghosetvā sāmikaṃ apassanto valliyaṃ ḍaṃsitvā attano vasanagumbe ṭhapetvā “velāyameva khādissāmī”ti attano sīlaṃ āvajjento nipajji. Siṅgālopi gocaraṃ pariyesanto ekassa khettagopakassa kuṭiyaṃ dve maṃsasūlāni ekaṃ godhaṃ ekañca dadhivārakaṃ disvā “atthi nu kho etesaṃ sāmiko”ti tikkhattuṃ [V 0.0101] ghosetvā sāmikaṃ adisvā dadhivārakassa uggahaṇarajjukaṃ gīvāyaṃ pavesetvā maṃsasūle ca godhañca mukhena ḍaṃsitvā attano vasanagumbe ṭhapetvā “velāyameva khādissāmī”ti attano sīlaṃ āvajjento nipajji. Makkaṭopi vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā ambapiṇḍaṃ āharitvā attano vasanagumbe ṭhapetvā “velāyameva khādissāmī”ti attano sīlaṃ āvajjento nipajji. Tiṇṇampi “aho idha nūna yācako āgaccheyyā”ti cittaṃ uppajji. Tena vuttaṃ –

They said, 'Excellent,' and, accepting the Bodhisatta's advice with their heads, undertook the precepts of the Uposatha. Among them, the young otter went out early in the morning, thinking, 'I will search for food,' and went to the riverbank. Now, a certain fisherman had caught seven rohita fish, strung them on a vine, covered them with sand on the riverbank, and gone downstream. The otter, smelling the fish, cleared away the sand, saw the fish, and took them out. He called out three times, 'Is there an owner for these?' Seeing no owner, he bit the vine and placed the fish in his own dwelling-thicket, thinking, 'I will eat them at the proper time,' and lay down, reflecting on his virtue. The jackal, too, while searching for food, found in a field-watchman's hut two skewers of meat, one monitor lizard, and a pot of curd. He called out three times, 'Is there an owner for these?' Seeing no owner, he put the carrying-rope of the curd pot around his neck, took the skewers of meat and the monitor lizard in his mouth, placed them in his own dwelling-thicket, and lay down, thinking, 'I will eat them at the proper time,' reflecting on his virtue. The monkey, too, entered a forest grove, brought back a cluster of mangoes, placed it in his own dwelling-thicket, and lay down, thinking, 'I will eat it at the proper time,' reflecting on his virtue. In all three of them, the thought arose: 'Oh, if only a supplicant would come here!' Therefore, it was said:

130.

130.

“Te me sādhūti vatvāna, yathāsatti yathābalaṃ;

Dānāni paṭiyādetvā, dakkhiṇeyyaṃ gavesisu”nti.

Having said to me, 'Excellent!', according to their ability and strength, they prepared gifts and sought one worthy of offerings.

Bodhisatto pana “velāyameva nikkhamitvā dabbāditiṇāni khādissāmī”ti attano vasanagumbeyeva nisinno cintesi – “mama santikaṃ āgatānaṃ yācakānaṃ tiṇāni khādituṃ na sakkā, tilataṇḍulādayopi mayhaṃ [M 0.0106] natthi, sace me santikaṃ yācako āgamissati, ahaṃ tiṇena yāpemi, attano sarīramaṃsaṃ dassāmī”ti. Tenāha bhagavā –

The Bodhisatta, however, thinking, 'I will go out at the proper time and eat Dabba grass and other grasses,' sat in his own dwelling-thicket and reflected: 'Supplicants who come to me cannot eat grass. I have no sesame, rice, or the like. If a supplicant should come to me, I who sustain myself with grass shall give my own body's flesh.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:

131.

131.

“Ahaṃ nisajja cintesiṃ, dānaṃ dakkhiṇanucchavaṃ;

Yadihaṃ labhe dakkhiṇeyyaṃ, kiṃ me dānaṃ bhavissati.

Sitting, I pondered on a gift suitable for one worthy of offerings; if I should find one worthy of offerings, what gift would be mine?

132.

132.

“Na me atthi tilā muggā, māsā vā taṇḍulā ghataṃ;

Ahaṃ tiṇena yāpemi, na sakkā tiṇa dātave.

I have no sesame, beans, or other grains, nor rice, nor ghee. I sustain myself with grass; it is not possible to give grass as a gift.

133.

133.

“Yadi koci eti dakkhiṇeyyo, bhikkhāya mama santike;

Dajjāhaṃ sakamattānaṃ, na so tuccho gamissatī”ti.

If any worthy one comes to me for alms, I would give my own self; he shall not depart empty-handed.

Tattha [P 0.0105] dānaṃ dakkhiṇanucchavanti dakkhiṇābhāvena anucchavikaṃ dānaṃ dakkhiṇeyyassa dātabbaṃ deyyadhammaṃ cintesiṃ. Yadihaṃ labheti yadi ahaṃ kiñci dakkhiṇeyyaṃ ajja labheyyaṃ. Kiṃ me dānaṃ bhavissatīti kiṃ mama dātabbaṃ bhavissati. Na sakkā tiṇa dātaveti yadi dakkhiṇeyyassa dātuṃ tilamuggādikaṃ mayhaṃ natthi, yaṃ pana mama āhārabhūtaṃ, taṃ na sakkā tiṇaṃ dakkhiṇeyyassa dātuṃ. Dajjāhaṃ sakamattānanti kiṃ vā mayhaṃ etāya deyyadhammacintāya, nanu idameva mayhaṃ anavajjaṃ aparādhīnatāya sulabhaṃ paresañca paribhogārahaṃ sarīraṃ sace koci dakkhiṇeyyo [V 0.0102] mama santikaṃ āgacchati, tayidaṃ sakamattānaṃ tassa dajjāmahaṃ. Evaṃ sante na so tuccho mama santikaṃ āgato arittahattho hutvā gamissatīti.

Therein, 'a gift suitable for one worthy of offerings' means: I pondered a gift, a thing to be given, suitable for one worthy of offerings. 'If I should find' means: if today I should find some worthy recipient. 'What would my gift be?' means: what would be the thing to be given by me? 'It is not possible to give grass' means: I have no sesame, beans, or the like to give to a worthy recipient; as for the grass that is my food, it is not possible to give that to a worthy recipient. 'I would give my own self' means: what is the use of this thought about a thing to be given? Surely, this very body of mine is blameless, easily obtained without harming others, and fit for others' use. If some worthy one comes to me, I would give this very self of mine to him. This being so, he who has come to my presence will not depart empty, with unfilled hands.

Evaṃ mahāpurisassa yathābhūtasabhāvaṃ parivitakkentassa parivitakkānubhāvena sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So āvajjento imaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā “sasarājaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti paṭhamaṃ uddassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇavesena aṭṭhāsi. Tena “kimatthaṃ, brāhmaṇa, ṭhitosī”ti ca vutte sace kañci āhāraṃ labheyyaṃ, uposathiko hutvā samaṇadhammaṃ kareyyanti. So “sādhūti te āhāraṃ dassāmī”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ –

As the great being was thus reflecting on his true nature, through the power of his reflection, Sakka's Paṇḍukambala stone seat showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting and seeing this cause, thought, 'I will test the hare-king.' First, he went to the otter's dwelling place and stood there in the guise of a brahmin. When the otter asked, 'For what reason do you stand here, brahmin?', he replied, 'If I could obtain some food, I would observe the Uposatha and perform the duties of a recluse.' The otter said, 'Good, I will give you food.' Therefore, it was said:

“Satta me rohitā macchā, udakā thalamubbhatā;

Idaṃ brāhmaṇa me atthi, etaṃ bhutvā vane vasā”ti. (jā. 1.4.61);

Seven rohita fish are mine, brought up from the water to the land. This I have, O brahmin; having eaten this, dwell in the forest.

Brāhmaṇo [M 0.0107] “pageva tāva hotu, pacchā jānissāmī”ti tatheva siṅgālassa makkaṭassa ca santikaṃ gantvā tehipi attano vijjamānehi deyyadhammehi nimantito “pageva tāva hotu, pacchā jānissāmī”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ –

The brahmin said, 'Let it be for now; I will know later.' Then he went to the jackal and the monkey, and when he was invited by them also with the gifts they had available, he said, 'Let it be for now; I will know later.' Therefore, it was said:

“Dussa me khettapālassa, rattibhattaṃ apābhataṃ;

Maṃsasūlā ca dve godhā, ekañca dadhivārakaṃ;

Idaṃ brāhmaṇa me atthi, etaṃ bhutvā vane vasā”ti.

A field-guard forgot his evening meal which had been brought: two skewers of meat, a monitor lizard, and one pot of curd. This I have, O brahmin; eat this and dwell in the forest.

“Ambapakkaṃ dakaṃ sītaṃ, sītacchāyā manoramā;

Idaṃ brāhmaṇa me atthi, etaṃ bhutvā vane vasā”ti. (jā. 1.4.62-63);

“Ripe mangoes, cool water, a delightful cool shade; this I have, brahmin. Having eaten this, dwell in the forest.”

Tattha dussāti amussa. Rattibhattaṃ apābhatanti rattibhojanato apanītaṃ. Maṃsasūlā ca dve godhāti aṅgārapakkāni [P 0.0106] dve maṃsasūlāni ekā ca godhā. Dadhivārakanti dadhivārako.

Here, dussa means 'forgotten'. Rattibhattaṃ apābhataṃ means removed from the night meal. Maṃsasūlā ca dve godhā refers to two meat skewers roasted on coals and one monitor lizard. Dadhivārakaṃ means a curd container.

134. Atha brāhmaṇo sasapaṇḍitassa santikaṃ gato. Tenāpi “kimatthamāgatosī”ti vutte tathevāha. Tena vuttaṃ “mama saṅkappamaññāyā”tiādi.

134. Then the brahmin went to the wise hare. When asked by him, “For what reason have you come?” he replied as before. Therefore it was said: “Having understood my intention,” and so on.

Tattha [V 0.0103] mama saṅkappamaññāyāti pubbe vuttappakāraṃ parivitakkaṃ jānitvā. Brāhmaṇavaṇṇināti brāhmaṇarūpavatā attabhāvena. Āsayanti vasanagumbaṃ.

Here, mama saṅkappamaññāya means knowing the kind of thinking previously mentioned. Brāhmaṇavaṇṇinā means with a body in the form of a brahmin. Āsayaṃ refers to a dwelling-thicket.

135-7. Santuṭṭhoti samaṃ sabbabhāgeneva tuṭṭho. Ghāsahetūti āhārahetu. Adinnapubbanti yehi kehici abodhisattehi adinnapubbaṃ. Dānavaranti uttamadānaṃ. “Ajja dassāmi te aha”nti vatvā tuvaṃ sīlaguṇūpeto, ayuttaṃ te paraheṭhananti taṃ pāṇātipātato apanetvā idāni tassa paribhogayoggaṃ attānaṃ katvā dātuṃ “ehi aggiṃ padīpehī”tiādimāha.

135–7. Santuṭṭho means satisfied equally with every share. Ghāsahetu means for the sake of nourishment. Adinnapubbaṃ means never given before by any non-Bodhisattas. Dānavaraṃ means the supreme gift. Having said, “Today I will give to you,” and thinking, “You are endowed with virtuous qualities; it is not fitting for you to harm another,” thus preventing him from taking life, and now making himself fit to be consumed, the Great Being said, “Come, light the fire,” and so on.

Tattha ahaṃ pacissamattānanti tayā kate aṅgāragabbhe ahameva patitvā attānaṃ pacissaṃ. Pakkaṃ tvaṃ bhakkhayissasīti tathā pana pakkaṃ tvaṃ khādissasi.

Here, ahaṃ pacissamattānaṃ means that in the charcoal pit you have made, I myself will fall and cook myself. Pakkaṃ tvaṃ bhakkhayissasi means just so, you will eat me when I am cooked.

138-9. Nānākaṭṭhe [M 0.0108] samānayīti so brāhmaṇavesadhārī sakko nānādārūni samānento viya ahosi. Mahantaṃ akāsi citakaṃ, katvā aṅgāragabbhakanti vītaccikaṃ vigatadhūmaṃ aṅgārabharitabbhantaraṃ samantato jalamānaṃ mama sarīrassa nimujjanappahonakaṃ taṅkhaṇaññeva mahantaṃ citakaṃ akāsi, sahasā iddhiyā abhinimminīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “aggiṃ tattha padīpesi, yathā so khippaṃ mahābhave”ti.

138–9. Nānākaṭṭhe samānayī means that Sakka, wearing the guise of a brahmin, acted as if gathering various kinds of wood. Mahantaṃ akāsi citakaṃ, katvā aṅgāragabbhakaṃ means that through his psychic power, he instantly created a great pyre, a pit filled with glowing coals, without flame and smoke, burning fiercely all around, large enough to submerge my body. This is the meaning. Therefore, he said: “He lit the fire there, so that it would quickly become great.”

Tattha soti so aggikkhandho sīghaṃ mahanto yathā bhaveyya, tathā padīpesi. Phoṭetvā rajagate gatteti “sace lomantaresu pāṇakā atthi, te mā mariṃsū”ti paṃsugate mama gatte tikkhattuṃ vidhunitvā. Ekamantaṃ upāvisinti na tāva kaṭṭhāni ādittānīti tesaṃ ādīpanaṃ udikkhanto thokaṃ ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃ.

Here, so means that he lit it so that that mass of fire would quickly become great. Phoṭetvā rajagate gatte means having shaken my dust-covered body three times, thinking, “If there are any small creatures among my hairs, may they not die.” Ekamantaṃ upāvisiṃ means I sat for a short while to one side, observing the kindling of the firewood, thinking, “The firewood has not yet fully caught fire.”

140. Yadā mahākaṭṭhapuñjo, āditto dhamadhamāyatīti yadā pana so dārurāsi samantato āditto vāyuvegasamuddhaṭānaṃ jālasikhānaṃ vasena “dhamadhamā”ti evaṃ karoti. Taduppatitvā patati, majjhe jālasikhantareti tadā tasmiṃ kāle “mama sarīrassa jhāpanasamattho ayaṃ aṅgārarāsī”ti cintetvā uppatitvā ullaṅghitvā jālasikhānaṃ [P 0.0107] abbhantarabhūte tassa aṅgārarāsissa majjhe padumapuñje rājahaṃso viya pamuditacitto sakalasarīraṃ dānamukhe datvā patati.

140. “When the great pile of firewood, blazing, roared ‘dhamadhamā’” means when that heap of wood, fully ablaze all around, made such a sound due to the flames fanned by the force of the wind. “Then leaping up, he falls into the midst of the flames” means then at that time, thinking, “This heap of embers is capable of burning my body,” he leapt up and plunged into the midst of that heap of embers, within the flames, like a royal swan joyfully entering a cluster of lotuses, offering his entire body in the act of giving.

141-2. Paviṭṭhaṃ yassa kassacīti yathā ghammakāle sītalaṃ udakaṃ yena kenaci paviṭṭhaṃ tassa [V 0.0104] darathapariḷāhaṃ vūpasameti, assādaṃ pītiñca uppādeti. Tatheva jalitaṃ agginti evaṃ tathā pajjalitaṃ aṅgārarāsi tadā mama paviṭṭhassa usumamattampi nāhosi. Aññadatthu dānapītiyā sabbadarathapariḷāhavūpasamo eva ahosi. Cirassaṃ vata me chavicammādiko sabbo sarīrāvayavo dānamukhe juhitabbataṃ upagato abhipatthito manoratho matthakaṃ pattoti. Tena vuttaṃ –

141–2. At that time, for me who had entered that blazing mass of embers, there was not even a particle of heat. On the contrary, through the joy of giving, there was only the complete pacification of all distress and burning. My longed-for aspiration—that after a long time, indeed, every part of my body, including my outer skin and inner skin, should become fit to be offered in the act of giving—has reached its culmination. Therefore it was said:

143.

143.

“Chaviṃ cammaṃ maṃsaṃ nhāruṃ, aṭṭhiṃ hadayabandhanaṃ;

Kevalaṃ sakalaṃ kāyaṃ, brāhmaṇassa adāsaha”nti.

“Outer skin, inner skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and the heart’s binding—the entire, whole body—I gave to the brahmin.”

Tattha hadayabandhananti hadayamaṃsapesi. Tañhi hadayavatthuṃ bandhitvā viya ṭhitattā “hadayabandhana”nti vuttaṃ. Atha vā hadayabandhananti hadayañca bandhanañca, hadayamaṃsañceva [M 0.0109] taṃ bandhitvā viya ṭhitayakanamaṃsañcāti attho. Kevalaṃ sakalaṃ kāyanti anavasesaṃ sabbaṃ sarīraṃ.

Here, hadayabandhana refers to the mass of heart-flesh. Because it stands as if binding the heart-base, it is called ‘the heart’s binding.’ Alternatively, hadayabandhana means the heart and the binding; that is, the heart-flesh and the liver-flesh which stands as if binding it. Kevalaṃ sakalaṃ kāyaṃ means the entire body without remainder.

Evaṃ tasmiṃ aggimhi attano sarīre lomakūpamattampi uṇhaṃ kātuṃ asakkonto bodhisattopi himagabbhaṃ paviṭṭho viya hutvā brāhmaṇarūpadharaṃ sakkaṃ evamāha – “brāhmaṇa, tayā kato aggi atisītalo, kiṃ nāmeta”nti? Paṇḍita, nāhaṃ brāhmaṇo, sakkohamasmi, tava vīmaṃsanatthaṃ āgato evamakāsinti. “Sakka, tvaṃ tāva tiṭṭhatu, sakalopi ce loko maṃ dānena vīmaṃseyya, neva me adātukāmataṃ kathañcipi uppādeyya passetha na”nti bodhisatto sīhanādaṃ nadi.

Thus, when the fire was unable to produce even the warmth of a hair-pore on his body, the Bodhisatta, as if he had entered a chamber of snow, spoke to Sakka, who was disguised as a brahmin, saying: “Brahmin, the fire you have made is exceedingly cold; what is the reason for this?” Sakka replied: “Wise one, I am not a brahmin—I am Sakka. I came to test you and have acted thus.” The Bodhisatta roared a lion’s roar: “Sakka, you may stand aside. Even if the whole world were to test me in regard to giving, it could not in any way produce in me an unwillingness to give. Behold!”

Atha naṃ sakko “sasapaṇḍita, tava guṇā sakalakappampi pākaṭā hontū”ti pabbataṃ pīḷetvā pabbatarasaṃ ādāya candamaṇḍale sasalakkhaṇaṃ ālikhitvā bodhisattaṃ tasmiṃ [P 0.0108] vanasaṇḍe tattheva vanagumbe taruṇadabbatiṇapīṭhe nipajjāpetvā attano devalokameva gato. Tepi cattāro paṇḍitā samaggā sammodamānā niccasīlaṃ uposathasīlañca pūretvā yathārahaṃ puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gatā.

Then Sakka, thinking, “May your virtues, wise hare, be evident throughout the entire eon,” pressed the mountain, took the mountain’s essence, and drew the mark of the hare on the disk of the moon. He then caused the Bodhisatta to lie down there in that very grove, on a seat of young dabba grass in the forest thicket, and returned to his own celestial realm. Those four wise beings, united and rejoicing, fulfilled their constant morality and Uposatha precepts, performed meritorious deeds as they were able, and departed according to their kamma.

Tadā uddo āyasmā ānando ahosi, siṅgālo mahāmoggallāno, makkaṭo sāriputto, sasapaṇḍito pana lokanātho.

At that time, the otter was the Venerable Ānanda, the jackal was Mahāmoggallāna, the monkey was Sāriputta, and the wise hare was myself, the Protector of the World.

Tassa idhāpi sīlādipāramiyo heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbā. Tathā satipi tiracchānupapattiyaṃ kusalādidhamme kusalādito yathābhūtāvabodho, tesu aṇumattampi vajjaṃ bhayato disvā [V 0.0105] suṭṭhu akusalato oramaṇaṃ, sammadeva ca kusaladhammesu attano patiṭṭhāpanaṃ, paresañca “ime nāma pāpadhammā te evaṃ gahitā evaṃ parāmaṭṭhā evaṃgatikā bhavanti evaṃabhisamparāyā”ti ādīnavaṃ dassetvā tato viramaṇe niyojanaṃ, idaṃ dānaṃ nāma, idaṃ sīlaṃ nāma, idaṃ uposathakammaṃ nāma, ettha patiṭṭhitānaṃ devamanussasampattiyo hatthagatā evātiādinā puññakammesu ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā patiṭṭhāpanaṃ, attano sarīrajīvitanirapekkhaṃ, paresaṃ sattānaṃ anuggaṇhanaṃ, uḷāro ca dānajjhāsayoti evamādayo idha bodhisattassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbā. Tenetaṃ vuccati – “evaṃ acchariyā hete…pe… dhammassa anudhammato”ti.

Here too, his perfections of virtue and so forth should be determined as is appropriate, following the method previously stated. Likewise, even when reborn in the animal realm, there is knowledge of wholesome states and so forth as they truly are; seeing even an atom's worth of fault in them as a danger, one thoroughly refrains from the unwholesome; one rightly establishes oneself in wholesome states; and for others, one shows the danger, saying, “These are called evil qualities; those who grasp and cling to them in such a way will have such a destination and such a future existence,” and engages them in refraining from those qualities. By showing the benefits in meritorious deeds, saying, “This is called giving, this is called virtue, this is called the Uposatha observance; for those established in these, the prosperities of gods and humans are as if in their hands,” and so on, one establishes them therein. Disregard for one's own body and life, assisting other beings, and a sublime inclination for giving—such virtues and powers of the Bodhisatta should be made manifest here. Therefore it is said: “Thus, how wonderful are these…pe… in accordance with the Dhamma.”

Sasapaṇḍitacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the conduct of the Wise Hare is concluded.

Idāni [M 0.0110] “akittibrāhmaṇo”tiādinā yathāvutte dasapi cariyāvisese udānetvā nigameti. Tattha ahameva tadā āsiṃ, yo te dānavare adāti yo tāni uttamadānāni adāsi, so akittibrāhaṇādiko ahameva tadā tasmiṃ kāle ahosiṃ, na aññoti. Iti tesu attabhāvesu satipi sīlādipāramīnaṃ yathārahaṃ pūritabhāve attano pana tadā dānajjhāsayassa ativiya uḷārabhāvaṃ sandhāya dānapāramivaseneva desanaṃ āropesi. Ete dānaparikkhārā, ete dānassa pāramīti ye ime [P 0.0109] akittijātakādīsu (jā. 1.13.83 ādayo) anekākāravokārā mayā pavattitā deyyadhammapariccāgā mama sarīrāvayavaputtadārapariccāgā paramakoṭikā, kiñcāpi te karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitattā sabbaññutaññāṇameva uddissa pavattitattā dānassa paramukkaṃsagamanena dānapāramī eva, tathāpi mama dānassa paramatthapāramibhūtassa parikkharaṇatosantānassa paribhāvanāvasena abhisaṅkharaṇato ete dānaparikkhārā nāma. Yassa panete parikkhārā, taṃ dassetuṃ “jīvitaṃ yācake datvā, imaṃ pārami pūrayi”nti vuttaṃ. Ettha hi ṭhapetvā sasapaṇḍitacariyaṃ sesāsu navasu cariyāsu yathārahaṃ dānapāramidānaupapāramiyo veditabbā, sasapaṇḍitacariye (cariyā. 1.125 ādayo) pana dānaparamatthapāramī. Tena vuttaṃ –

Now, having brought forward the ten special conducts as previously stated, beginning with 'the Brahmin Akitti,' he concludes. Therein, 'I myself was he at that time, who gave those excellent gifts' means: he who gave those supreme gifts, that Brahmin Akitti and so on, was I myself at that time; it was not another. Thus, although in those existences the perfections of virtue and so forth were fulfilled as was appropriate, with reference to the exceedingly sublime nature of his own inclination for giving at that time, he presented the teaching solely in terms of the perfection of giving. 'These are the requisites of giving, these are the perfections of giving' means: those various kinds of relinquishments of possessions that I undertook in the Akitti Jātaka and others, and those supreme relinquishments of my own limbs, children, and wife—although these, being embraced by compassion and skill in means and having been undertaken with the sole aim of the knowledge of omniscience, are indeed the perfection of giving through having reached the highest excellence of giving, nevertheless, because they serve as requisites for my giving which has become the ultimate perfection, and because they are preparations by way of developing the continuity of perfections, they are called 'the requisites of giving.' And to show that for which these are the requisites, it was said: 'Having given my life to a petitioner, I fulfilled this perfection.' Here, setting aside the conduct of the Wise Hare, in the remaining nine conducts the perfection of giving and the secondary perfection of giving should be understood as is appropriate; but in the conduct of the Wise Hare, the giving is the ultimate perfection of giving. Therefore it is said:

“Bhikkhāya upagataṃ disvā, sakattānaṃ pariccajiṃ;

Dānena me samo natthi, esā me dānapāramī”ti. (cariyā. 1.tassuddāna);

“Having seen one who had come for alms, I sacrificed my own self; in giving, there is none equal to me—this is my perfection of giving.”

Kiñcāpi hi mahāpurisassa yathāvutte akittibrāhmaṇādikāle aññasmiñca mahājanakamahāsutasomādikāle [V 0.0106] dānapāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi, tathāpi ekanteneva sasapaṇḍitakāle dānapāramiyā paramatthapāramibhāvo vibhāvetabboti.

Although there is indeed no measure for the Great Being's states of having fulfilled the perfection of giving during the time of the Brahmin Akitti and others, as stated, and at other times such as those of Mahājanaka and Mahāsutasoma, nevertheless, it should be made manifest that at the time of the Wise Hare, the perfection of giving was exclusively the ultimate perfection.

Paramatthadīpaniyā cariyāpiṭakasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka,

Dasavidhacariyāsaṅgahassa visesato

especially of the compendium of the ten kinds of conduct,

Dānapāramivibhāvanassa

of the exposition of the perfection of giving,

Paṭhamavaggassa atthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the meaning of the first chapter is concluded.

2. Hatthināgavaggo

2. The Chapter of the Noble Elephant

1. Mātuposakacariyāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Conduct of Nourishing One's Mother

1. Dutiyavaggassa [M 0.0111][V 0.0107][P 0.0110] paṭhame kuñjaroti hatthī. Mātuposakoti andhāya jarājiṇṇāya mātuyā paṭijagganako. Mahiyāti bhūmiyaṃ. Guṇenāti sīlaguṇena, tadā mama sadiso natthi.

1. In the first [conduct] of the second chapter, 'kuñjaro' means elephant. 'Mātuposako' means one who attends to his blind and decrepit mother. 'Mahiyā' means on the earth. 'Guṇena' means by the virtue of morality; at that time, there was none equal to me.

Bodhisatto hi tadā himavantappadese hatthiyoniyaṃ nibbatti. So sabbaseto abhirūpo lakkhaṇasampanno mahāhatthī anekahatthisatasahassaparivāro ahosi. Mātā panassa andhā. So madhuraphalāphalāni hatthīnaṃ hatthesu datvā mātu peseti. Hatthino tassā adatvā sayaṃ khādanti. So pariggaṇhanto taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā “yūthaṃ pahāya mātarameva posessāmī”ti rattibhāge aññesaṃ hatthīnaṃ ajānantānaṃ mātaraṃ gahetvā caṇḍoraṇapabbatapādaṃ gantvā ekaṃ naḷiniṃ upanissāya ṭhitāya pabbataguhāya mātaraṃ ṭhapetvā posesi.

Indeed, at that time the Bodhisatta was reborn in the elephant womb in the region of the Himālaya. He was an all-white, beautiful, great elephant, endowed with the auspicious marks, and attended by many hundreds of thousands of elephants. His mother, however, was blind. He would place sweet fruits, both large and small, in the trunks of the elephants and send them to his mother. The elephants, however, would not give them to her but would eat them themselves. He, investigating the matter and understanding that situation, thought, 'Having abandoned the herd, I will nourish my mother alone.' So, in the night, unknown to the other elephants, he took his mother, went to the foot of Mount Caṇḍoraṇa, and placing his mother in a mountain cave situated near a lotus pond, he nourished her.

2-3. Pavane disvā vanacaroti eko vanacarako puriso tasmiṃ mahāvane vicaranto maṃ disvā. Rañño maṃ paṭivedayīti bārāṇasirañño maṃ ārocesi.

2-3. 'A forester having seen [me] in the wood' means: a certain man, a forest-dweller, saw me while wandering in that great forest. 'He informed the king about me' means: he informed the king of Bārāṇasī about me.

So hi maggamūḷho disaṃ vavatthapetuṃ asakkonto mahantena saddena paridevi. Bodhisattopi tassa saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ puriso anātho, na kho panetaṃ patirūpaṃ, yaṃ esa mayi ṭhite idha vinasseyyā”ti tassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ [P 0.0111] bhayena palāyantaṃ disvā “ambho purisa, natthi te maṃ nissāya bhayaṃ, mā palāyi, kasmā tvaṃ paridevanto vicarasī”ti pucchitvā “sāmi, ahaṃ maggamūḷho ajja me sattamo divaso”ti vutte “bho purisa, mā bhāyi, ahaṃ taṃ manussapathe ṭhapessāmī”ti taṃ attano piṭṭhiyaṃ nisīdāpetvā araññato nīharitvā nivatti. Sopi pāpo “nagaraṃ gantvā rañño ārocessāmī”ti rukkhasaññaṃ pabbatasaññañca karontova nikkhamitvā bārāṇasiṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ kāle rañño maṅgalahatthī mato[V 0.0108]. So puriso rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā mahāpurisassa attano diṭṭhabhāvaṃ ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ “tavānucchavo, mahārāja, gajo vasati kānane”tiādi.

Lost on the path and unable to determine the directions, he lamented with a great cry. Hearing his cry, the Bodhisatta thought, “This man is helpless. It is not fitting that he should perish here while I am present.” Approaching him, he saw the man fleeing in fear and asked, “Sir, you have nothing to fear from me. Do not flee. Why do you wander about lamenting?” When the man replied, “Lord, I am lost on the path; today is my seventh day,” the Bodhisatta said, “Do not fear, good man. I will place you on the path of men.” Seating him on his back, he led him out of the forest and turned back. But that wicked man, thinking, “I will go to the city and inform the king,” went out making note of trees and mountains, and came to Bārāṇasī. At that time, the king’s state elephant had died. The man approached the king and reported that he had seen the great being. Thus it was said: “O great king, an elephant worthy of you lives in the forest,” and so on.

Tattha [M 0.0112] tavānucchavoti tava opavayhaṃ kātuṃ anucchaviko yutto. Na tassa parikkhāyatthoti tassa gahaṇe gamanupacchedanatthaṃ samantato khaṇitabbaparikkhāya vā kareṇuyā kaṇṇapuṭena attānaṃ paṭicchādetvā khittapāsarajjuyā bandhitabbaāḷakasaṅkhātaālānena vā yattha paviṭṭho katthaci gantuṃ na sakkoti, tādisavañcanakāsuyā vā attho payojanaṃ natthi. Sahagahiteti gahaṇasamakālaṃ eva. Ehitīti āgamissati.

Herein, ‘worthy of you’ means suitable and fit to be your royal mount. ‘There is no need for any stratagem for him’ means that for his capture, there is no use or purpose for any stratagem to obstruct his movement, such as a trench dug all around, or a female elephant, or covering oneself with an ear-flap and throwing a rope-snare, or a tying-post known as an ‘āḷaka’, or a deceptive pit into which, having entered, he cannot go anywhere. ‘With the capture’ means at the very same time as the capture. ‘Come’ means he will come.

Rājā imaṃ maggadesakaṃ katvā araññaṃ gantvā “iminā vuttaṃ hatthināgaṃ ānehī”ti hatthācariyaṃ saha parivārena pesesi. So tena saddhiṃ gantvā bodhisattaṃ naḷiniṃ pavisitvā gocaraṃ gaṇhantaṃ passi. Tena vuttaṃ –

The king, making this man his guide, sent an elephant trainer with his retinue into the forest, saying, “Go and bring the great elephant spoken of by this man.” He went with them and saw the Bodhisatta entering a lotus pond and gathering food. Therefore, it was said:

4.

4.

“Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, rājāpi tuṭṭhamānaso;

Pesesi hatthidamakaṃ, chekācariyaṃ susikkhitaṃ.

“Hearing those words of his, the king, with a delighted mind, sent the elephant tamer, a skilled and well-trained master.”

5.

5.

“Gantvā so hatthidamako, addasa padumassare;

Bhisamuḷālaṃ uddharantaṃ, yāpanatthāya mātuyā”ti.

“Going there, that elephant tamer saw him in a lotus lake, pulling up lotus stalks and roots for the sustenance of his mother.”

Tattha chekācariyanti hatthibandhanādividhimhi kusalaṃ hatthācariyaṃ. Susikkhitanti hatthīnaṃ sikkhāpanavijjāya niṭṭhaṅgamanena suṭṭhu sikkhitaṃ.

Herein, ‘a skilled master’ means an elephant master skilled in the methods of capturing elephants and so forth. ‘Well-trained’ means thoroughly trained by having reached the culmination of the science of training elephants.

6. Viññāya me sīlaguṇanti “bhaddo ayaṃ hatthājānīyo na mando, na caṇḍo, na vomissasīlo vā”ti mama sīlaguṇaṃ jānitvā. Kathaṃ? Lakkhaṇaṃ [P 0.0112] upadhārayīti susikkhitahatthisippattā mama lakkhaṇaṃ samantato upadhāresi. Tena so ehi puttāti vatvāna, mama soṇḍāya aggahi.

6. ‘Having recognized my quality of virtue’ means having known my quality of virtue, thinking, “This thoroughbred elephant is excellent, not dull, not fierce, and not of a mixed disposition.” How so? ‘He observed the characteristics’ means that, due to his skill in the elephant craft, he thoroughly observed my characteristics from all sides. Therefore, saying, “Come, son,” he took hold of my trunk.

7. Bodhisatto hatthācariyaṃ disvā – “idaṃ bhayaṃ mayhaṃ etassa purisassa santikā uppannaṃ, ahaṃ kho pana mahābalo hatthisahassampi viddhaṃsetuṃ samattho, pahomi kujjhitvā saraṭṭhakaṃ senāvāhanaṃ nāsetuṃ, sace pana kujjhissāmi, sīlaṃ me bhijjissati, tasmā sattīhi koṭṭiyamānopi [V 0.0109] na kujjhissāmī”ti cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāya sīsaṃ onāmetvā niccalova aṭṭhāsi. Tenāha bhagavā “yaṃ me tadā pākatikaṃ, sarīrānugataṃ bala”ntiādi.

7. The Bodhisatta, seeing the elephant trainer, thought: “This danger has arisen for me from that man. I am of great strength, capable of destroying even a thousand elephants. If angered, I am able to destroy an army along with its kingdom. But if I were to become angry, my virtue would be broken. Therefore, even if I am pounded with spears, I will not become angry.” Having made this resolution, he lowered his head and stood perfectly still. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “That strength which was then my natural, bodily strength,” and so on.

Tattha [M 0.0113] pākatikanti sabhāvasiddhaṃ. Sarīrānugatanti sarīrameva anugataṃ kāyabalaṃ, na upāyakusalatāsaṅkhātañāṇānugatanti adhippāyo. Ajja nāgasahassānanti ajjakāle anekesaṃ hatthisahassānaṃ samuditānaṃ. Balena samasādisanti tesaṃ sarīrabalena samasamameva hutvā sadisaṃ, na upamāmattena. Maṅgalahatthikule hi tadā bodhisatto uppannoti.

Herein, ‘natural’ means established by its own nature. ‘Bodily’ means the physical strength that accompanies the body itself; the intention is that it is not the strength of wisdom, known as skill in means. ‘Of a thousand elephants today’ means of many thousands of elephants gathered at the present time. ‘Equal in strength’ means being exactly equal to their physical strength, not merely similar by way of comparison. For at that time, the Bodhisatta was born into the lineage of state elephants.

8. Yadihaṃ tesaṃ pakuppeyyanti maṃ gahaṇāya upagatānaṃ tesaṃ ahaṃ yadi kujjheyyaṃ, tesaṃ jīvitamaddane paṭibalo bhaveyyaṃ. Na kevalaṃ tesaññeva, atha kho yāva rajjampi mānusanti yato rajjato tesaṃ āgatānaṃ manussānaṃ sabbampi rajjaṃ pothetvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ kareyyaṃ.

8. ‘If I were to become angry at them’ means: if I were to become angry at those who have come to capture me, I would be capable of crushing their lives. Not only theirs, but also ‘even the human kingdom’ means I could smash and pulverize the entire kingdom from which those humans came.

9. Api cāhaṃ sīlarakkhāyāti evaṃ samatthopi ca ahaṃ attani patiṭṭhitāya sīlarakkhāya sīlaguttiyā gutto bandho viya. Na karomi citte aññathattanti tassa sīlassa aññathattabhūtaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ pothanādividhiṃ mayhaṃ citte na karomi, tattha cittampi na uppādemi. Pakkhipantaṃ mamāḷaketi ālānatthambhe pakkhipantaṃ, “disvāpī”ti vacanaseso. Kasmāti ce, sīlapāramipūriyā īdisesu ṭhānesu sīlaṃ akhaṇḍentassa me nacirasseva sīlapāramī paripūressatīti sīlapāramiparipūraṇatthaṃ tassa aññathattaṃ citte na karomīti yojanā.

9. ‘And I, for the sake of protecting my virtue’: though I am so capable, being established in the protection of virtue and guarded by my virtue, I am as if bound. ‘I do not create otherness in my mind’ means I do not create in my mind an act of striking those beings or the like, which would be a deviation from that virtue, nor do I even give rise to such a thought. ‘As they are putting me to the tying-post’ has the remainder of the phrase ‘even seeing them’ to be understood. If it is asked why, the connection is as follows: for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of virtue—since for me, who does not break my virtue in such situations, the perfection of virtue will be fulfilled before long—I do not create in my mind any deviation concerning that person.

10. “Yadi te ma”nti gāthāyapi sīlarakkhāya daḷhaṃ katvā sīlassa [P 0.0113] adhiṭṭhitabhāvameva dasseti. Tattha koṭṭeyyunti bhindeyyuṃ. Sīlakhaṇḍabhayā mamāti mama sīlassa khaṇḍanabhayena.

10. In the verse beginning ‘If they were to... me,’ it shows the very state of resolve in virtue, having made the protection of virtue firm. Therein, ‘they might pound’ means they might destroy. ‘Out of fear of my virtue being broken’ means: out of fear of the breaking of my virtue, I would not become angry.

Evaṃ pana cintetvā bodhisatte niccale ṭhite hatthācariyo padumasaraṃ otaritvā tassa lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā “ehi puttā”ti rajatadāmasadisāya soṇḍāya gahetvā sattame divase bārāṇasiṃ pāpuṇi. So antarāmagge vattamānova rañño sāsanaṃ pesesi. Rājā nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpesi. Hatthācariyo bodhisattaṃ katagandhaparibhaṇḍaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ hatthisālaṃ netvā vicitrasāṇiyā parikkhipāpetvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ ādāya gantvā bodhisattassa [V 0.0110] dāpesi. So “mātaraṃ vinā gocaraṃ na gaṇhissāmī”ti piṇḍaṃ na gaṇhi. Yācitopi aggahetvā –

Having thus reflected, while the Bodhisatta stood motionless, the elephant trainer descended into the lotus lake. Seeing the perfection of his marks, he said, 'Come, my son!' and taking him by his trunk, which was like a silver chain, he reached Bārāṇasī on the seventh day. While still on the way, he sent a message to the king. The king had the city adorned. The elephant trainer led the Bodhisatta, who had been anointed with perfumes and was well-adorned, to the elephant stable, had him surrounded with a colorful curtain, and informed the king. The king, taking food of various excellent flavors, went and had it offered to the Bodhisatta. But he did not take the lump of food, thinking, 'I will not take food without my mother.' Even when entreated, he did not accept it—

“Sā [M 0.0114] nūnasā kapaṇikā, andhā apariṇāyikā;

Khāṇuṃ pādena ghaṭṭeti, giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patī”ti. –

"Surely she, wretched, blind, and without a guide, now strikes her foot against a stump; she falls towards the rugged Caṇḍoraṇa mountain."

Āha. Taṃ sutvā rājā –

He spoke thus. Hearing that, the king said:

“Kā nu te sā mahānāga, andhā apariṇāyikā;

Khāṇuṃ pādena ghaṭṭeti, giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patī”ti. – pucchitvā –

"Who, pray, is she of yours, O great elephant, blind and without a guide, who strikes her foot against a stump and falls towards the rugged Caṇḍoraṇa mountain?" Having asked thus—

“Mātā me sā mahārāja, andhā apariṇāyikā;

Khāṇuṃ pādena ghaṭṭeti, giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patī”ti. –

"She is my mother, O great king, blind and without a guide; she strikes her foot against a stump and falls towards the rugged Caṇḍoraṇa mountain."

Vutte ajja sattamo divaso “mātā me gocaraṃ na labhitthā”ti vadato imassa gocaraṃ agaṇhantassa. Tasmā –

When this one, who was not taking food, said, 'Today is the seventh day; my mother will not have obtained food.' Therefore—

“Muñcathetaṃ mahānāgaṃ, yoyaṃ bharati mātaraṃ;

Sametu mātarā nāgo, saha sabbehi ñātibhī”ti. – vatvā muñcāpesi –

"Release this great elephant, who supports his mother; let the elephant be reunited with his mother, together with all his kinsmen." Having spoken thus, he had him released.

“Mutto ca bandhanā nāgo, muttadāmāya kuñjaro;

Muhuttaṃ assāsayitvā, agamā yena pabbato”ti.

Freed from bondage was the elephant, released from its tether was the great beast. Having rested for a moment, he went to where the mountain was.

Tattha kapaṇikāti varākā. Khāṇuṃ pādena ghaṭṭetīti andhatāya puttaviyogadukkhena ca paridevamānā tattha tattha rukkhakaḷiṅgare pādena ghaṭṭeti. Caṇḍoraṇaṃ patīti caṇḍoraṇapabbatābhimukhī, tasmiṃ pabbatapāde paribbhamamānāti attho. Agamā yena pabbatoti so hatthināgo [P 0.0114] bandhanā mutto thokaṃ vissamitvā rañño dasarājadhammagāthāhi dhammaṃ desetvā “appamatto hohi, mahārājā”ti ovādaṃ datvā mahājanena gandhamālādīhi pūjiyamāno nagarā nikkhamitvā tadaheva mātarā samāgantvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Sā tuṭṭhamānasā –

Therein, kapaṇikā means wretched. 'She strikes a stump with her foot' means: because of her blindness and the sorrow of separation from her son, lamenting, she strikes her foot against tree stumps here and there. 'She falls towards Caṇḍoraṇa' means: facing the Caṇḍoraṇa mountain, she wanders at the foot of that mountain. 'He went to where the mountain was' means: that great elephant, freed from bondage, rested for a short while and taught the Dhamma to the king with verses on the ten royal virtues. Having given the advice, 'Be diligent, O great king,' and being honored by the great multitude with perfumes, garlands, and so on, he departed from the city. That very day he was reunited with his mother and told her all that had occurred. She, with a joyful mind—

“Ciraṃ [V 0.0111] jīvatu so rājā, kāsīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhano;

Yo me puttaṃ pamocesi, sadā vuddhāpacāyika”nti. (jā. 1.11.12) –

"Long live that king, the prosperer of the Kāsī realm, who freed my son, he who is ever respectful to his elders."

Rañño anumodanaṃ akāsi. Rājā bodhisattassa guṇe pasīditvā naḷiniyā avidūre gāmaṃ māpetvā bodhisattassa mātu cassa nibaddhaṃ vattaṃ paṭṭhapesi[M 0.0115]. Aparabhāge bodhisatto mātari matāya tassā sarīraparihāraṃ katvā kuraṇḍakaassamapadaṃ nāma gato. Tasmiṃ pana ṭhāne himavantato otaritvā pañcasatā isayo vasiṃsu. Taṃ vattaṃ tesaṃ datvā rājā bodhisattassa samānarūpaṃ silāpaṭimaṃ kāretvā mahāsakkāraṃ pavattesi. Jambudīpavāsino anusaṃvaccharaṃ sannipatitvā hatthimahaṃ nāma kariṃsu.

The king, pleased with the Bodhisatta's virtues, had a village established not far from the lotus pond and set up a regular provision for the Bodhisatta's mother. In later times, when the Bodhisatta's mother died, he performed the funeral rites for her body and went to the hermitage named Kuraṇḍaka. Now, in that place dwelt five hundred seers who had descended from the Himālaya. The king, having given that provision to them, had a stone image of a similar form made and instituted a great festival of honor. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa, gathering annually, performed what was known as the Elephant Festival.

Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, hatthinī mahāmāyā, vanacarako devadatto, mātuposakahatthināgo lokanātho.

At that time, the king was Ānanda, the she-elephant was Mahāmāyā, the forester was Devadatta, and the great elephant who nourished his mother was the Lord of the World.

Idhāpi dānapāramiādayo yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbā. Sīlapāramī pana atisayavatīti sā eva desanaṃ āruḷhā. Tathā tiracchānayoniyaṃ uppannopi brahmapubbadevapubbācariyaāhuneyyādibhāvena sabbaññubuddhenapi pasatthabhāvānurūpaṃ mātuyā garucittaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā “mātā nāmesā puttassa bahūpakārā, tasmā mātupaṭṭhānaṃ nāma paṇḍitena paññatta”nti manasi katvā anekesaṃ hatthisahassānaṃ issarādhipati mahānubhāvo yūthapati hutvā tehi anuvattiyamāno ekakavihāre antarāyaṃ agaṇetvā yūthaṃ pahāya ekako hutvā upakārikhettaṃ pūjessāmīti mātuposanaṃ, maggamūḷhapurisaṃ disvā anukampāya taṃ gahetvā manussagocarasampāpanaṃ, tena ca katāparādhasahanaṃ[P 0.0115], hatthācariyappamukhānaṃ attānaṃ bandhituṃ āgatapurisānaṃ samatthopi samāno santāsanamattenapi tesaṃ pīḷanā bhavissati, mayhañca sīlassa khaṇḍādibhāvoti tathā akatvā sudantena opavayho viya sukheneva gahaṇūpagamanaṃ, mātaraṃ vinā na kañci ajjhoharissāmīti sattāhampi anāhāratā, imināpāhaṃ bandhāpitoti cittaṃ anuppādetvā rājānaṃ mettāya pharaṇaṃ, tassa ca nānānayehi dhammadesanāti evamādayo idha mahāpurisassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbā. Tena vuttaṃ – “evaṃ acchariyā ete, abbhutā ca mahesino…pe… dhammassa anudhammato”ti.

Here too, the perfections of giving and so on should be discerned as is appropriate. The perfection of virtue, however, is pre-eminent, and so it alone has been taken up in this discourse. Likewise, the following virtues and powers of the Great Being should be made manifest here: though born in the animal realm, he established a reverential mind towards his mother—in a manner befitting her praiseworthy state as acclaimed even by the All-Knowing Buddha, on account of her being like a former Brahmā, a former household deity, a former teacher, one worthy of offerings, and so on—and reflected, 'A mother is of great help to her son; therefore, the support of one's mother is prescribed by the wise.' Then, though he was the mighty and powerful lord and leader of a herd of many thousands of elephants and was followed by them, he disregarded the danger to his solitary life, forsook the herd, and became alone, thinking, 'I will honor this field of great benefit,' thus undertaking the nourishment of his mother. Seeing a man who had lost his way, out of compassion he took him and brought him to a region frequented by humans. He endured the offense committed against him by that man. Though he was capable of overpowering the men led by the elephant trainer who came to bind him, he did not do so, thinking, 'Even by merely threatening them, there would be affliction for them, and for me, a breaking of my virtue.' Instead, like a well-tamed royal elephant, he submitted to capture with ease. Resolving, 'Without my mother, I will not consume anything,' he remained without food for seven days. Without giving rise to the thought, 'I have been caused to be bound by this king,' he pervaded the king with loving-kindness. And he taught the Dhamma to him in various ways. Thus it is said: 'So wonderful are these, so marvelous are the qualities of the Great Sage... in accordance with the Dhamma and what follows from it.'

Mātuposakacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Conduct of Nourishing One's Mother is concluded.

2. Bhūridattacariyāvaṇṇanā

2. The Exposition on the Conduct of Bhūridatta

11. Dutiye [M 0.0116][V 0.0112] bhūridattoti bhūrisamadatto. Dattoti hi tadā bodhisattassa mātāpitūhi kataṃ nāmaṃ. Yasmā paneso nāgabhavane virūpakkhamahārājabhavane tāvatiṃsabhavane ca uppanne pañhe sammadeva vinicchināti, ekadivasañca virūpakkhamahārāje nāgaparisāya saddhiṃ tidasapuraṃ gantvā sakkaṃ parivāretvā nisinne devānamantare pañho samuṭṭhāsi. Taṃ koci kathetuṃ nāsakkhi. Sakkena pana anuññāto pallaṅkavaragato hutvā mahāsattova kathesi. Atha naṃ devarājā dibbagandhapupphehi pūjetvā “datta, tvaṃ pathavisamāya vipulāya paññāya samannāgato ito paṭṭhāya bhūridatto nāmā”ti āha. Bhūrīti hi pathaviyā nāmaṃ, tasmā bhūrisamatāya bhūte atthe ramatīti ca bhūrisaṅkhātāya mahatiyā paññāya samannāgatattā mahāsatto “bhūridatto”ti paññāyittha. Mahatiyā pana nāgiddhiyā samannāgatattā mahiddhiko cāti.

11. In the second Jātaka, 'Bhūridatta' means 'one who is given wisdom like the earth.' For 'Datta' was the name given to the Bodhisatta by his parents. Because he correctly resolved questions that arose in the Nāga realm, in the realm of Virūpakkha the great king, and in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, and one day, when Virūpakkha the great king, together with the assembly of Nāgas, had gone to the city of the thirty-three gods and was seated surrounding Sakka, a question arose among the gods, which no one could answer. But with Sakka’s permission, having taken a seat on a splendid couch, the Great Being himself explained it. Then the king of the gods honored him with divine fragrant flowers and said, 'Datta, you are endowed with wisdom as vast as the earth. Henceforth, you shall be called Bhūridatta.' For 'bhūrī' is a name for the earth; therefore, because his wisdom was like the earth, and because he delighted in the true meaning, and because he was endowed with great wisdom called 'bhūrī,' the Great Being became known as 'Bhūridatta.' Moreover, because he was endowed with great Nāga power, he was also called 'Mahiddhika' (the mighty one).

Atīte hi imasmiṃyeva kappe bārāṇasirañño putto pitarā raṭṭhato pabbājito vane vasanto aññatarāya nāgamāṇavikāya [P 0.0116] saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Tesaṃ saṃvāsamanvāya dve dārakā jāyiṃsu – putto ca dhītā ca. Puttassa “sāgarabrahmadatto”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu dhītāya “samuddajā”ti. So aparabhāge pitu accayena bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rajjaṃ kāresi. Atha dhataraṭṭho nāma nāgarājā pañcayojanasatike nāgabhavane nāgarajjaṃ kārento taṃ abhūtavādikena cittacūḷena nāma kacchapena “bārāṇasirājā attano dhītaraṃ tuyhaṃ dātukāmo, sā kho pana rājadhītā samuddajā nāma abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā cā”ti kathitaṃ sutvā dhataraṭṭho cattāro nāgamāṇavake pesetvā taṃ dātuṃ anicchantaṃ nāgavibhiṃsikāya bhiṃsāpetvā “dammī”ti vutte mahantaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pesetvā mahatiyā nāgiddhiyā mahantena parivārena tassa dhītaraṃ nāgabhavanaṃ netvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

In the past, in this very eon, the son of the king of Bārāṇasī, banished from the kingdom by his father, was living in the forest, where he cohabited with a certain Nāga maiden. As a result of their cohabitation, two children were born—a son and a daughter. They named the son 'Sāgarabrahmadatta' and the daughter 'Samuddajā.' Later, after his father’s death, he went to Bārāṇasī and ruled the kingdom. Then the Nāga king named Dhataraṭṭha, who was ruling over a Nāga realm five hundred yojanas in extent, heard from a deceitful turtle named Cittacūḷa: 'The king of Bārāṇasī wishes to give his daughter to you; that princess, named Samuddajā, is beautiful, lovely, and pleasing.' Upon hearing this, Dhataraṭṭha sent four Nāga youths. When the king was unwilling to give her, they terrified him with Nāga apparitions until he said, 'I will give her.' Then, sending a great tribute, Dhataraṭṭha, with great Nāga power and a large retinue, brought the king's daughter to the Nāga realm and established her in the position of chief queen.

Sā aparabhāge dhataraṭṭhaṃ paṭicca sudassano, datto, subhogo, ariṭṭhoti cattāro putte paṭilabhi.
