Tesu datto bodhisatto, so pubbe vuttanayeneva sakkena tuṭṭhacittena “bhūridatto”ti gahitanāmattā “bhūridatto”tveva [M 0.0117] paññāyittha. Atha nesaṃ pitā yojanasatikaṃ yojanasatikaṃ rajjaṃ bhājetvā adāsi. Mahanto yaso ahosi. Soḷasasoḷasanāgakaññāsahassāni parivārayiṃsu. Pitupi ekayojanasatameva rajjaṃ ahosi. Tayo puttā māse māse mātāpitaro passituṃ āgacchanti, bodhisatto pana anvaddhamāsaṃ āgacchati.

Later, by Dhataraṭṭha, she had four sons: Sudassana, Datta, Subhoga, and Ariṭṭha. Among them, Datta was the Bodhisatta. As previously mentioned, because the name 'Bhūridatta' had been given to him by Sakka, who was pleased in mind, he became known simply as 'Bhūridatta.' Then their father divided the kingdom, giving each a portion of one hundred yojanas. Their renown was great. Sixteen thousand Nāga maidens attended upon each of them. Their father's kingdom was also only one hundred yojanas. The three sons would come to see their parents every month, but the Bodhisatta came every half-month.

So [V 0.0113] ekadivasaṃ virūpakkhamahārājena saddhiṃ sakkassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gato vejayantapāsādaṃ sudhammadevasabhaṃ pāricchattakakoviḷāraṃ paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ devaccharāparivāraṃ atimanoharaṃ sakkasampattiṃ disvā “ettakamattampi nāgattabhāve ṭhitassa dullabhaṃ, kuto sammāsambodhī”ti nāgattabhāvaṃ jigucchitvā “nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā uposathavāsaṃ vasitvā sīlameva paggaṇhissāmi, taṃ bodhiparipācanaṃ hoti, imasmiṃ devaloke uppattikāraṇaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā mātāpitaro āha – “ammatātā, ahaṃ uposathakammaṃ karissāmī”ti. Tehi “idheva uposathaṃ upavasāhi, bahigatānaṃ nāgānaṃ mahantaṃ bhaya”nti [P 0.0117] vutte ekavāraṃ tathā katvā nāgakaññāhi upadduto punavāre mātāpitūnaṃ anārocetvā attano bhariyaṃ āmantetvā “bhadde, ahaṃ manussalokaṃ gantvā yamunātīre mahānigrodharukkho atthi tassa avidūre vammikamatthake bhoge ābhujitvā caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nipajjitvā “uposathakammaṃ karissāmī”ti nāgabhavanato nikkhamitvā tathā karoti. Tena vuttaṃ “virūpakkhena mahāraññā, devalokamagañchaha”ntiādi.

One day, he went with Virūpakkha, the great king, to attend upon Sakka. Seeing the exceedingly delightful splendor of Sakka—the Vejayanta Palace, the Sudhammā assembly hall of the gods, the Pāricchattaka coral tree, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, and the retinue of celestial nymphs—he thought, 'Even this much is difficult to obtain for one existing in the state of a Nāga, so how could I attain perfect supreme enlightenment?' Disgusted with his Nāga existence, he thought, 'I will go to the Nāga realm, undertake the Uposatha observance, and cultivate virtue itself. That will lead to the ripening of enlightenment and will be a cause for rebirth in this celestial world.' Having thus reflected, he went to the Nāga realm and said to his parents, 'Mother and father, I will perform the Uposatha observance.' When they said, 'Observe the Uposatha right here; there is great danger for Nāgas who go outside,' he did so once. But being disturbed by the Nāga maidens, the next time, without informing his parents, he addressed his wife, 'My dear, I will go to the human world. On the bank of the Yamunā river, there is a great banyan tree. Not far from it, on top of an anthill, I will coil my body, undertake the four-factored Uposatha, and lie down to perform the Uposatha observance.' Having left the Nāga realm, he did so. Therefore it was said: 'With Virūpakkha, the great king, I went to the celestial world,' and so on.

Tattha virūpakkhena mahāraññāti virūpakkhena nāma nāgādhipatimahārājena. Devalokanti tāvatiṃsadevalokaṃ. Agañchahanti agañchiṃ, upasaṅkamiṃ ahaṃ.

Therein, 'with Virūpakkha, the great king' means with the great king, the sovereign of the Nāgas, named Virūpakkha. 'The celestial world' means the Tāvatiṃsa celestial world. 'I went' means 'I went, I approached.'

12. Tatthāti tasmiṃ devaloke. Passiṃ tvāhanti addakkhiṃ ahaṃ tu-saddo nipātamatto. Ekantaṃ sukhasamappiteti ekantaṃ accantameva sukhena samaṅgībhūte. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “santi, bhikkhave, cha phassāyatanikā nāma saggā. Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, na sukaraṃ akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ yāva sukhā saggā”ti [M 0.0118] (ma. ni. 3.255) ca. Taṃsaggagamanatthāyāti tasmiṃ saggasmiṃ uppattivasena gamanatthāya. Sīlabbatanti sīlasaṅkhātaṃ vataṃ. Atha vā sīlabbatanti uposathasīlañceva “mama cammaṃ cammatthikā harantū”tiādinā attano sarīrāvayavapariccāgasamādiyanasaṅkhātaṃ vatañca.

12. 'Therein' means in that celestial world. 'I saw' means 'I beheld'; the word 'tu' is merely a particle. 'Completely endowed with happiness' means entirely and absolutely possessed of bliss. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, there are celestial realms known as the six spheres of contact. And, monks, it is not easy to convey by description how blissful those celestial realms are' (MN 149). 'For the purpose of going to that heaven' means for the sake of going to that heaven by way of rebirth. 'The vow of moral conduct' means the observance known as virtue. Alternatively, 'the vow of moral conduct' means both the Uposatha virtue and the vow known as the undertaking to relinquish one's own bodily parts, as in the saying, 'Let those who need my skin take it,' and so on.

13. Sarīrakiccanti mukhadhovanādisarīrapaṭijagganaṃ. Bhutvā yāpanamattakanti indriyāni nibbisevanāni kātuṃ sarīraṭṭhitimattakaṃ āhāraṃ āharitvā. Caturo aṅgeti cattāri aṅgāni. Adhiṭṭhāyāti adhiṭṭhahitvā. Semīti sayāmi.

13. 'Bodily duties' refers to attending to the body, such as washing the face and so forth. 'Having eaten just enough to sustain oneself' means having taken food only to the extent necessary for the body's maintenance, in order to make the senses tranquil. 'The four factors' means the four factors. 'Having resolved' means having resolved. 'I lie down' means I lie down.

14. Chaviyātiādi tesaṃ catunnaṃ aṅgānaṃ dassanaṃ. Tattha ca chavicammānaṃ vissajjanaṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, sesāni ekekameva, maṃsaggahaṇeneva cettha rudhirampi saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etenāti etehi[V 0.0114]. Harātu soti yassa etehi chaviādīhi karaṇīyaṃ atthi, tassa mayā dinnamevetaṃ. Sabbaṃ so haratūti attano attabhāve anapekkhapavāraṇaṃ pavāreti.

14. 'Skin and so forth' indicates those four factors. Therein, the relinquishing of the outer and inner skin is one factor; the remaining are each one. And it should be understood that here, by the inclusion of 'flesh', blood is also included. 'By these' means by these. 'Let him take' means: 'For whomever there is a need for these—skin and so forth—it is already given by me to him.' 'Let him take it all' is how he makes an invitation without regard for his own being.

Evaṃ [P 0.0118] mahāsattassa iminā niyāmeneva anvaddhamāsaṃ uposathakammaṃ karontassa dīgho addhā vītivatto. Evaṃ gacchante kāle ekadivasaṃ aññataro nesādabrāhmaṇo somadattena nāma attano puttena saha taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā aruṇuggamanasamaye nāgakaññāhi parivāriyamānaṃ mahāsattaṃ disvā tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Tāvadeva nāgakaññāyo pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā nāgabhavanameva gatā. Brāhmaṇo mahāsattaṃ pucchi – “ko nu kho tvaṃ, mārisa, devo vā yakkho vā nāgo vā”ti? Bodhisatto yathābhūtaṃ attānaṃ āvi katvā sacāyaṃ ito gaccheyya, idha me vāsaṃ mahājanassa pākaṭaṃ kareyya, tena me uposathavāsassa antarāyopi siyā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ ito imaṃ nāgabhavanaṃ netvā mahatiyā sampattiyā yojeyyaṃ. Evāyaṃ tattheva abhiramissati, tena me uposathakammaṃ addhaniyaṃ siyāti. Atha naṃ āha – “brāhmaṇa, mahantaṃ te yasaṃ dassāmi, ramaṇīyaṃ nāgabhavanaṃ, ehi tattha gacchāmā”ti. Sāmi, putto me atthi, tasmiṃ āgacchante āgamissāmīti. Gaccha, brāhmaṇa, puttaṃ ānehīti. Brāhmaṇo gantvā puttassa tamatthaṃ ārocetvā taṃ ānesi. Mahāsatto te ubhopi ādāya attano ānubhāvena nāgabhavanaṃ [M 0.0119] ānesi. Tesaṃ tattha dibbo attabhāvo pātubhavi. Atha tesaṃ mahāsatto dibbasampattiṃ datvā cattāri cattāri nāgakaññāsatāni adāsi. Te mahatiṃ sampattiṃ anubhaviṃsu.

Thus, for the Great Being who was performing the fortnightly Uposatha observance according to this very method, a long time passed. As time was going by, one day a certain hunter-brahmin, together with his son named Somadatta, arrived at that place. At the time of sunrise, seeing the Great Being surrounded by Nāga maidens, he approached him. At that very moment, the Nāga maidens plunged into the earth and went to the Nāga realm. The brahmin asked the Great Being: 'Who are you, sir? Are you a deva, a yakkha, or a Nāga?' The Bodhisatta, revealing himself as he truly was, thought: 'If this man should go from here, he would make my dwelling here known to the public. Because of that, there might be an obstacle to my Uposatha observance. What if I were to lead this man from here to the Nāga realm and establish him in great prosperity? Thus he would delight in that very place, and my Uposatha practice would be long-lasting.' Then he said to him: 'Brahmin, I will give you great renown. The Nāga realm is delightful; come, let us go there.' 'Sir, I have a son; when he comes, I will come.' 'Go, brahmin, bring your son.' The brahmin went, told his son of the matter, and brought him. The Great Being, taking them both, brought them to the Nāga realm by his own power. For them, a divine state of being appeared there. Then the Great Being, having given them divine prosperity, gave them four hundred Nāga maidens each. They experienced great prosperity.

Bodhisattopi appamatto uposathakammaṃ karoti. Anvaddhamāsaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā dhammakathaṃ kathetvā tato ca brāhmaṇassa santikaṃ gantvā ārogyaṃ pucchitvā “yena te attho, taṃ vadeyyāsī”ti āpucchitvā “anukkaṇṭhamāno abhiramā”ti vatvā somadattenapi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā attano nivesanaṃ gacchati. Brāhmaṇo saṃvaccharaṃ tattha vasitvā mandapuññatāya ukkaṇṭhitvā anicchamānampi puttaṃ gahetvā bodhisattaṃ āpucchitvā tena dīyamānaṃ bahuṃ dhanaṃ sabbakāmadadaṃ maṇiratanampi alakkhikatāya aggahetvā “manussalokaṃ gantvā pabbajissāmī”ti āha. Mahāsatto nāgamāṇavake āṇāpetvā taṃ saputtakaṃ manussalokaṃ pāpesi. Te ubhopi dibbābharaṇāni dibbavatthāni ca omuñcitvā nhāyituṃ [P 0.0119] ekaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ otariṃsu, tasmiṃ khaṇe tāni antaradhāyitvā nāgabhavanameva agamaṃsu. Atha paṭhamanivatthakāsāvapilotikāva sarīre paṭimuñci, dhanusarasattiyo gahetvā araññaṃ gantvā mige vadhitvā purimaniyāmeneva jīvikaṃ kappesuṃ.

The Bodhisatta, being diligent, performed the Uposatha observance. Every fortnight, he would go to attend upon his parents, give a Dhamma talk, and from there go to the brahmin to inquire about his well-being. Taking his leave by saying, 'You should speak of whatever you need,' and adding, 'Do not be discontented; take delight,' he would also exchange friendly greetings with Somadatta and then go to his own residence. The brahmin, having lived there for a year, grew discontented due to his lack of merit. Taking his son, who was unwilling, he took leave of the Bodhisatta. Due to his unworthiness, he did not accept the abundant wealth and the wish-fulfilling jewel that were being given, and said, 'I will go to the human world and go forth into homelessness.' The Great Being commanded the young Nāgas and had him sent to the human world with his son. Both of them took off their divine ornaments and garments and descended into a pond to bathe. At that moment, those things vanished and went back to the Nāga realm. Then, only the soiled bark-cloth garments they had first worn were fastened on their bodies. Taking up their bows, arrows, and spears, they went into the forest, killed deer, and made their living in the same way as before.

Tena [V 0.0115] ca samayena aññataro tāpaso supaṇṇarājato laddhaṃ alampāyanamantaṃ tassa anucchavikāni osadhāni mantūpacārañca attānaṃ upaṭṭhahantassa aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa adāsi. So “laddho me jīvikūpāyo”ti katipāhaṃ vasitvā tāpasaṃ āpucchitvā pakkamanto anupubbena yamunātīraṃ patvā taṃ mantaṃ sajjhāyanto mahāmaggena gacchati. Tadā bodhisattassa bhavanato tassa paricārikā nāgamāṇavikā taṃ sabbakāmadadaṃ maṇiratanaṃ ādāya yamunātīre vālukārāsimatthake ṭhapetvā tassobhāsena rattiyaṃ kīḷitvā aruṇuggamane tassa brāhmaṇassa mantasaddaṃ sutvā “supaṇṇo”ti saññāya bhayatajjitā maṇiratanaṃ aggahetvā pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā nāgabhavanaṃ agamaṃsu.

At that time, a certain ascetic gave the Alampāyana spell, which he had received from the Supaṇṇa king, along with the appropriate herbs and ritual procedure, to a certain brahmin who was attending upon him. Thinking, “I have obtained a means of livelihood,” the brahmin stayed for a few days, then took leave of the ascetic and departed. Gradually reaching the bank of the Yamunā, he recited the spell while traveling along the main road. Just then, the young Nāga maidens who were attendants from the Bodhisatta’s abode took the all-wish-fulfilling jewel and placed it atop a heap of sand on the Yamunā’s shore. After playing in its radiance throughout the night, at the rising of the sun they heard the sound of the brahmin's spell. Mistaking it for a Supaṇṇa, and terrified, they plunged into the earth without taking the jewel and returned to the Nāga abode.

Brāhmaṇo taṃ maṇiratanaṃ ādāya pāyāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe so nesādabrāhmaṇo puttena saddhiṃ migavadhāya araññaṃ gacchanto tassa hatthe [M 0.0120] taṃ maṇiratanaṃ disvā “idaṃ bhūridattassa sabbakāmadadaṃ maṇiratana”nti sañjānitvā taṃ gaṇhitukāmo tena saddhiṃ allāpasallāpaṃ katvā mantavādibhāvaṃ jānitvā evamāha – “sace me tvaṃ imaṃ maṇiratanaṃ dassasi, evāhaṃ te mahānubhāvaṃ nāgaṃ dassessāmi, yaṃ tvaṃ gahetvā gāmanigamarājadhāniyo caranto bahudhanaṃ lacchasī”ti. “Tena hi dassetvā gaṇhāhī”ti vutte taṃ ādāya bodhisattaṃ uposathakaraṇaṭṭhāne vammikamatthake bhoge ābhujitvā nipannaṃ avidūre ṭhito hatthaṃ pasāretvā dassesi.

The brahmin took that precious jewel and departed. At that moment, the hunter-brahmin, while going to the forest with his son to hunt deer, saw that jewel in his hand. Recognizing it as 'Bhūridatta’s all-wish-fulfilling jewel,' and desiring to take it, he engaged in conversation with him. Having learned that he was a spell-chanter, he said this: 'If you give me this jewel, I will show you a Nāga of great power. Capturing him and traveling through villages, towns, and royal cities, you will obtain great wealth.' When the other replied, 'In that case, show him and take it,' the hunter-brahmin took him and, standing not far away, stretched out his hand and showed him the Bodhisatta, who lay coiled up on top of an anthill in the place where he observed the Uposatha.

Mahāsatto taṃ nesādaṃ disvā “ayaṃ uposathassa me antarāyaṃ kareyyāti nāgabhavanaṃ netvā mahāsampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpitopi na icchi. Tato apakkamitvā sayaṃ gantukāmo mayā dīyamānampi maṇiratanaṃ gaṇhituṃ na icchi. Idāni pana ahiguṇḍikaṃ gahetvā āgacchati. Sacāhaṃ [P 0.0120] imassa mittadubbhino kujjheyyaṃ, sīlaṃ me khaṇḍaṃ bhavissati. Mayā kho pana paṭhamaṃyeva caturaṅgasamannāgato uposatho adhiṭṭhito, so yathādhiṭṭhitova hotu. Alampāyano maṃ chindatu vā mā vā, nevassa kujjhissāmī”ti cintetvā akkhīni nimmīletvā adhiṭṭhānapāramiṃ purecārikaṃ katvā bhogantare sīsaṃ pakkhipitvā niccalova hutvā nipajji. Nesādabrāhmaṇopi “bho alampāyana, imaṃ nāgaṃ gaṇha, maṇiṃ me dehī”ti āha. Alampāyano nāgaṃ disvā tuṭṭho maṇiṃ kismiñci agaṇetvā “gaṇha, brāhmaṇā”ti hatthe khipi. So tassa hatthato bhassitvā pathaviyaṃ patitamattova pathaviṃ pavisitvā nāgabhavanameva gato. Nesādabrāhmaṇo maṇiratanato bhūridattena saddhiṃ mittabhāvato ca parihāyitvā nippaccayova pakkanto.

The Great Being, seeing that hunter, thought: “This man might create an obstacle to my observance of the Uposatha. Even when taken to the nāga realm and established in great prosperity, he did not desire it. Then, departing from there, he himself desired to go, and did not wish to take even the jewel-gem being given by me. Now, however, he comes, having brought a snake-charmer. If I were to become angry at this betrayer of friendship, my virtue would be broken. But I have already undertaken the Uposatha endowed with the four factors, so let it remain as I have resolved. Whether Alampāyana cuts me or not, I will not be angry at him.” Having reflected thus, he closed his eyes, made his perfection of resolve foremost, placed his head between his coils, and lay down, completely still. The hunter-brahmin then said: “O Alampāyana, take this nāga and give me the gem!” Alampāyana, delighted upon seeing the nāga, did not value the gem at all and threw it into the brahmin's hand, saying: “Take it, brahmin!” The gem slipped from his hand and, as soon as it touched the ground, entered the earth and returned to the nāga realm. The hunter-brahmin, having lost both the jewel-gem and his friendship with Bhūridatta, departed with nothing.

15. Alampāyanopi mahānubhāvehi osadhehi attano sarīraṃ makkhetvā thokaṃ khāditvā kheḷaṃ [V 0.0116] attano kāyasmiṃ paribhāvetvā dibbamantaṃ jappanto bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā ākaḍḍhitvā sīse daḷhaṃ gaṇhanto mukhamassa vivaritvā osadhaṃ khāditvā mukhe sahakheḷaṃ osiñci. Sucijātiko mahāsatto sīlabhedabhayena akujjhitvā akkhīni na ummīlesi. Atha naṃ osadhamantabalena naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā heṭṭhā sīsaṃ katvā sañcāletvā gahitagocaraṃ chaḍḍāpetvā bhūmiyaṃ dīghaso nipajjāpetvā [M 0.0121] masūrakaṃ maddanto viya hatthehi parimaddi. Aṭṭhīni cuṇṇiyamānāni viya ahesuṃ.

15. Alampāyana, having anointed his own body with herbs of great power, chewed a little, recited over the saliva on his body, and, chanting a divine mantra, approached the Bodhisatta. He grabbed him by the tail, dragged him, and, holding his head firmly, forced open his mouth, chewed an herb, and poured it, together with saliva, into his mouth. The Great Being, who was of pure birth, out of fear that his virtue would be broken, did not become angry and did not open his eyes. Then, by the power of the herbs and the mantra, Alampāyana grabbed him by the tail, held him with his head hanging down, shook him, made him vomit the food he had taken, and laid him stretched out on the ground. He kneaded him with his hands as if crushing lentils. His bones were as if being ground to powder.

Puna naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā dussaṃ pothento viya pothesi. Mahāsatto evarūpaṃ [P 0.0121] dukkhaṃ anubhontopi neva kujjhittha. Aññadatthu attano sīlameva āvajjesi. Iti so mahāsattaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā vallīhi peḷaṃ sajjetvā mahāsattaṃ tattha pakkhipi. Sarīraṃ panassa mahantaṃ tattha na pavisati. Atha naṃ paṇhiyā koṭṭento pavesetvā peḷaṃ ādāya ekaṃ gāmaṃ gantvā gāmamajjhe otāretvā “nāgassa naccaṃ daṭṭhukāmā āgacchantū”ti saddamakāsi. Sakalagāmavāsino sannipatiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe alampāyano “nikkhama mahānāgā”ti āha. Mahāsatto cintesi – “ajja mayā parisaṃ tosentena kīḷituṃ vaṭṭati, evaṃ alampāyano bahudhanaṃ labhitvā tuṭṭho maṃ vissajjessati, yaṃ yaṃ esa maṃ kāreti, taṃ taṃ karissāmī”ti.

Again, grabbing him by the tail, he beat him as if beating a cloth. Though experiencing such suffering, the Great Being did not become angry at all. Instead, he only reflected on his own virtue. Thus, having weakened the Great Being, he prepared a basket with vines and put the Great Being in it. But his body was large and did not fit inside. Then, striking him with his heel, he forced him in, took the basket, and went to a village. Setting it down in the middle of the village, he made an announcement: “Let those who wish to see the nāga’s dance come!” All the villagers gathered. At that moment, Alampāyana said, “Come out, great nāga!” The Great Being thought: “Today it is fitting for me to perform, pleasing the assembly. In this way, Alampāyana will gain much wealth, be pleased, and will release me. Whatever he makes me do, that I shall do.”

Atha naṃ so peḷato nikkhamantaṃ “mahā hohī”ti āha, so mahā ahosi. “Khuddako vaṭṭo viphaṇo ekaphaṇo dviphaṇo yāva sahassaphaṇo ucco nīco dissamānakāyo adissamānakāyo dissamānaupaḍḍhakāyo nīlo pīto lohito odāto mañjiṭṭho hohi, dhūmaṃ vissajjehi, jālasikhaṃ udakañca vissajjehī”ti vutte tena vuttaṃ taṃ taṃ ākāraṃ nimminitvā naccaṃ dassesi. Taṃ disvā manussā acchariyabbhutacittajātā bahuṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇavatthālaṅkārādiṃ adaṃsu. Iti tasmiṃ gāme satasahassamattaṃ labhi. So kiñcāpi mahāsattaṃ gaṇhanto “sahassaṃ labhitvā taṃ vissajjessāmī”ti āha. Taṃ pana dhanaṃ labhitvā “gāmakepi tāva mayā ettakaṃ dhanaṃ laddhaṃ, nagare kira bahudhanaṃ labhissāmī”ti dhanalobhena na muñci.

Then, as he was coming out of the basket, Alampāyana said, “Become large!” and he became large. “Become small, round, with expanded hood, with one hood, with two hoods, up to a thousand hoods! Become tall, short, with a visible body, with an invisible body, with a half-visible body! Become blue, yellow, red, white, crimson! Release smoke, release a tongue of flame, and release water!” When this was said, he created each and every form as commanded and performed a dance. Seeing this, the people, their minds filled with wonder and amazement, gave much gold, silver, cloth, ornaments, and so on. Thus, in that village, he received about one hundred thousand. Although, when capturing the Great Being, he had said, “Having received a thousand, I will release you,” yet, having obtained that wealth, he thought, “If even in a small village I have received this much wealth, surely in the city I will receive much more!” Out of greed for wealth, he did not release him.

So tasmiṃ gāme kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā ratanamayaṃ peḷaṃ kāretvā tattha mahāsattaṃ pakkhipitvā sukhayānakaṃ āruyha mahantena parivārena [P 0.0122] gāmanigamarājadhānīsu taṃ kīḷāpetvā bārāṇasiṃ pāpuṇi, nāgarājassa madhulājaṃ deti, abaddhasattuñca deti. So gocaraṃ na gaṇhi avissajjanabhayena. Gocaraṃ agaṇhantampi ca naṃ cattāro nagaradvāre ādiṃ katvā tattha tattha māsamattaṃ kīḷāpesi. Tena vuttaṃ “saṃsito akataññunā”tiādi.

He established a household in that village, had a jewelled basket made, placed the Great Being inside it, mounted a comfortable vehicle, and with a large retinue, after making him perform in villages, market towns, and royal cities, he arrived at Bārāṇasī. He gave the nāga king sweet fried grain and also gave him flour cakes. But the nāga king did not take the food, out of fear of not being released. Even though he did not take the food, Alampāyana made him perform for about a month, starting at the four city gates and in various other places. Therefore it was said: “Bound by the ungrateful one,” and so on.

Tattha [M 0.0122][V 0.0117] saṃsitoti eso nāgo amukassa nigrodharukkhassa samīpe vammikamatthake sayitoti evaṃ ṭhānaṃ dassetvā kathito. Akataññunāti attanā kataṃ upakāraṃ ajānantena mittadubbhinā nesādabrāhmaṇenāti adhippāyo. Alampāyanoti alampāyanavijjāparijappanena “alampāyano”ti evaṃ laddhanāmo ahituṇḍikabrāhmaṇo. Mamaggahīti maṃ aggahesi. Kīḷeti maṃ tahiṃ tahinti tattha tattha gāmanigamarājadhānīsu attano jīvikatthaṃ maṃ kīḷāpeti.

Therein, `saṃsito` means he was pointed out by indicating his location, thus: “This nāga was lying on top of an anthill near such-and-such a banyan tree.” `Akataññunā` means by the hunter-brahmin, a betrayer of friendship, who does not recognize the help done by oneself—this is the meaning. `Alampāyano` means the snake-charmer brahmin who received the name “Alampāyana” by muttering the Alampāyana spell. `Mamaggahī` means “he seized me.” `Kīḷeti maṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ` means “he makes me perform in various villages, market towns, and royal cities for his own livelihood.”

17. Tiṇatopi lahuko mamāti attano jīvitapariccāgo tiṇasalākapariccāgatopi lahuko hutvā mama upaṭṭhātīti attho. Pathavīuppatanaṃ viyāti sīlavītikkamo pana catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalāya mahāpathaviyā parivattanaṃ viya tatopi taṃ bhāriyataraṃ hutvā mayhaṃ upaṭṭhātīti dasseti.

17. “Lighter than grass to me”: the meaning is that giving up my own life appears to me as being lighter even than giving up a blade of grass. “Like the upheaval of the earth”: this shows that a transgression of virtue, however, appears to me as being even heavier than the overturning of the great earth, which is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick.

18. Nirantaraṃ jātisatanti mama jātīnaṃ anekasatampi anekasatāsupi jātīsu nirantarameva sīlassa avītikkamanahetu. Mama jīvitaṃ cajeyyaṃ cajituṃ sakkomi. Neva sīlaṃ pabhindeyyanti sīlaṃ pana samādinnaṃ ekampi neva bhindeyyaṃ na vināseyyaṃ. Catuddīpāna hetūti cakkavattirajjasiriyāpi kāraṇāti dasseti.

18. "An unbroken succession of births" means that even in hundreds upon hundreds of my births, I never transgressed virtue. "I could give up my life" means I am capable of sacrificing it. "But never break my virtue" means that not even a single precept that I have undertaken would I violate or destroy. "For the sake of the four continents" shows that this is so even for the glory of a universal monarch.

19. Idāni yadatthaṃ attano jīvitampi pariccajitvā tadā sīlameva rakkhitaṃ, tāya ca sīlarakkhāya tathā anatthakārakesu nesādaalampāyanabrāhmaṇesu cittassa aññathattaṃ [P 0.0123] na kataṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “api cā”ti osānagāthamāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

19. Now, to show that for the sake of which he protected virtue, even sacrificing his own life, and that by that protection of virtue, no alteration of mind occurred towards the harmful Nesāda and Āḷampāyana brahmins, he spoke the concluding verse beginning, "Api ca." Its meaning is as stated previously.

Evaṃ pana mahāsatte ahituṇḍikahatthagate tassa mātā dussupinaṃ disvā puttañca tattha apassantī sokābhibhūtā ahosi. Athassā jeṭṭhaputto sudassano taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā subhogaṃ “himavantaṃ gantvā pañcasu mahānadīsu sattasu mahāsaresu bhūridattaṃ upadhāretvā ehī”ti pahiṇi. Kāṇāriṭṭhaṃ “devalokaṃ gantvā sace devatāhi dhammaṃ sotukāmāhi bhūridatto tattha nīto, tato naṃ ānehī”ti pahiṇi. Sayaṃ pana “manussaloke gavesissāmī”ti tāpasavesena nāgabhavanato [M 0.0123] nikkhami. Accimukhī nāmassa vemātikā bhaginī bodhisatte adhimattasinehā taṃ anubandhi. Taṃ maṇḍūkacchāpiṃ katvā jaṭantare pakkhipitvā mahāsattassa uposathakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbattha gavesanto anukkamena bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājadvāraṃ agamāsi. Tadā alampāyano rājaṅgaṇe mahājanassa majjhe rañño bhūridattassa kīḷaṃ dassetuṃ peḷaṃ vivaritvā “ehi mahānāgā”ti saññamadāsi.

Then, when the great being was in the snake charmer’s hand, his mother, having seen a bad dream and not seeing her son there, was overcome with grief. Hearing of this event, his eldest brother Sudassana sent Subhoga, saying: "Go to the Himalayas, investigate Bhūridatta in the five great rivers and seven great lakes, and return." He sent Kāṇāriṭṭha with the instruction: "Go to the deva world. If Bhūridatta has been taken there by devas who wish to hear the Dhamma, then bring him back." He himself, however, thinking, "I will search in the human world," left the nāga abode disguised as an ascetic. His half-sister, named Accimukhī, who had excessive affection for the Bodhisatta, followed him. Having transformed her into a small frog and placed her inside his matted hair, he began searching everywhere, starting from the place where the great being observed the Uposatha. In due course, he reached Bārāṇasī and went to the royal gate. At that time, in the royal courtyard amidst a large crowd, Āḷampāyana, to show Bhūridatta's performance to the king, opened the basket and gave the signal, saying, "Come forth, great nāga!"

Mahāsatto [V 0.0118] sīsaṃ nīharitvā olokento jeṭṭhabhātikaṃ disvā peḷato nikkhamma tadabhimukho pāyāsi. Mahājano bhīto paṭikkami. So gantvā taṃ abhivādetvā nivattitvā peḷameva pāvisi. Alampāyano “iminā ayaṃ tāpaso daṭṭho”ti saññāya “mā bhāyi, mā bhāyī”ti āha. Sudassano “ayaṃ nāgo mayhaṃ kiṃ karissati, mayā sadiso ahituṇḍiko nāma natthī”ti tena vādappaṭivādaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā “tvaṃ imaṃ nāgaṃ gahetvā gajjasi, ahaṃ taṃ imāya maṇḍūkacchāpiyā icchanto nāsayissāmī”ti bhaginiṃ pakkositvā hatthaṃ pasāresi. Sā tassa saddaṃ sutvā jaṭantare nipannā tikkhattuṃ maṇḍūkavassitaṃ vassitvā nikkhamitvā aṃsakūṭe nisīditvā uppatitvā tassa hatthatale tīṇi visabindūni pātetvā puna tassa jaṭantarameva pāvisi.

The great being, putting forth his head and looking around, saw his eldest brother. Emerging from the basket, he went towards him. The great crowd, frightened, retreated. He went, paid respects to him, and turning back, re-entered the basket. Āḷampāyana, thinking, "This ascetic has been bitten by this nāga," said to him, "Do not fear, do not fear!" Sudassana, instigating an argument with him, said, "What can this nāga do to me? There is no snake charmer equal to me. You boast, having captured this nāga, but I, if I wish, will destroy it with this small frog!" Calling his sister, he stretched out his hand. She, hearing his voice while lying in his matted hair, croaked three times like a frog, came out, sat on the tip of his shoulder, leapt up, and having dropped three drops of venom on the palm of his hand, re-entered his matted hair.

Sudassano visabinduṃ dassetvā “idaṃ binduṃ sace pathaviyaṃ pātessati, osadhitiṇavanappatayo sabbe nassissanti. Sace ākāse khipissati, sattavassāni devo na vassissati. Sace udake pātessati, yāvatā tattha udakajātā pāṇā sabbe mareyyu”nti [P 0.0124] vatvā rājānaṃ saddahāpetuṃ tayo āvāṭe khaṇāpetvā ekaṃ nānābhesajjānaṃ pūresi, dutiyaṃ gomayassa, tatiyaṃ dibbosadhānañceva pūretvā majjhe āvāṭe visabinduṃ pakkhipi. Taṅkhaṇaññeva dhūmāyitvā jālā uṭṭhahi. Sā gantvā gomayāvāṭaṃ gaṇhi. Tatopi jālā uṭṭhāya dibbosadhapuṇṇaṃ gahetvā dibbosadhāni jhāpetvā nibbāyi. Alampāyanaṃ tattha āvāṭassa avidūre ṭhitaṃ usumā pharitvā sarīracchaviṃ uppāṭetvā gatā. Setakuṭṭhī ahosi. So bhayatajjito “nāgarājānaṃ vissajjemī”ti tikkhattuṃ vācaṃ nicchāresi. Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto ratanapeḷāya nikkhamitvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ [M 0.0124] attabhāvaṃ māpetvā devalīḷāya ṭhito. Sudassano ca accimukhī ca tatheva aṭṭhaṃsu.

Sudassana showed the drop of poison and said, "If this drop is dropped on the earth, all medicinal herbs, grass, and trees will perish. If it is thrown into the sky, rain will not fall for seven years. If it is dropped into the water, all water-born creatures there will die." To convince the king, he had three pits dug. One he filled with various medicines, the second with cow dung, and the third with divine medicinal herbs. Then, he dropped the poison into the middle pit. Instantly, it smoked and flames arose. The flames went and caught the pit of cow dung. From there too, flames arose, caught the pit full of divine herbs, and after burning the divine herbs, were extinguished. The heat spread to Āḷampāyana, who was standing not far from the pit, and peeling off his skin, it departed. He became a white leper. Terrified by fear, he uttered three times the words, "I release the Nāga king!" Hearing this, the Bodhisatta emerged from the jeweled basket, created a form adorned with all ornaments, and stood with divine splendor. Sudassana and Accimukhī also stood in like manner.

Tato sudassano attano bhāgineyyabhāvaṃ rañño ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā te āliṅgitvā sīse cumbitvā antepuraṃ netvā mahantaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ katvā bhūridattena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto “tāta, evaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ taṃ alampāyano kathaṃ gaṇhī”ti pucchi. So sabbaṃ vitthārena kathetvā “mahārāja, raññā nāma iminā niyāmena rajjaṃ kāretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti mātulassa dhammaṃ desesi. Atha sudassano “mātula, mama mātā bhūridattaṃ apassantī kilamati, na sakkā amhehi idha papañcaṃ kātu”nti mātulaṃ āpucchitvā bhūridattaaccimukhīhi saddhiṃ nāgabhavanameva gato.

Then Sudassana informed the king that he was his nephew. Hearing this, the king embraced them, kissed their heads, led them into the inner palace, and paid them great honor and respect. While exchanging friendly greetings with Bhūridatta, he asked, "Dear one, how did Āḷampāyana capture one so mighty as you?" He explained everything in detail and then taught the Dhamma to his uncle, saying, "Great king, it is fitting for a king to rule according to this principle." Then Sudassana said, "Uncle, my mother is languishing from not seeing Bhūridatta. We cannot delay here." Taking leave of his uncle, he went with Bhūridatta and Accimukhī back to the nāga abode.

Atha [V 0.0119] tattha mahāpuriso gilānaseyyāya nipanno gilānapucchanatthaṃ āgatāya mahatiyā nāgaparisāya vede ca yaññe ca brāhmaṇe ca sambhāvetvā kāṇāriṭṭhe kathente taṃ vādaṃ bhinditvā nānānayehi dhammaṃ desetvā sīlasampadāya [P 0.0125] diṭṭhisampadāya ca patiṭṭhāpetvā yāvajīvaṃ sīlāni rakkhitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā āyupariyosāne saggapuraṃ pūresi.

Thereafter, the great being lay on his sickbed. When a great assembly of nāgas came to inquire about his illness, and while Kāṇāriṭṭha was speaking in praise of the Vedas, sacrifices, and brahmins, the great being refuted that doctrine. Having taught the Dhamma in various ways and established them in the accomplishment of virtue and the accomplishment of right view, he protected the precepts and performed the Uposatha observance for as long as he lived, and at the end of his life, he went to fill the city of heaven.

Tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ. Nesādabrāhmaṇo devadatto, somadatto ānando, accimukhī uppalavaṇṇā, sudassano sāriputto, subhogo mahāmoggallāno, kāṇāriṭṭho sunakkhatto, bhūridatto lokanātho.

At that time, the parents were of great royal families. The hunter-brahmin was Devadatta, Somadatta was Ānanda, Accimukhī was Uppalavaṇṇā, Sudassana was Sāriputta, Subhoga was Mahāmoggallāna, Kāṇāriṭṭha was Sunakkhatta, and Bhūridatta was the Lord of the World.

Tassa idhāpi sesapāramiyo heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva niddhāretabbā. Idhāpi yojanasatike attano nāgabhavanaṭṭhāne soḷasahi nāgakaññāsahassehi cittarūpaṃ viya paricāriyamāno devalokasampattisadise nāgalokissariye ṭhitopi issariyamadaṃ akatvā anvaddhamāsaṃ mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyanaṃ, sakalāya nāgaparisāya cātumahārājikaparisāya tāvatiṃsaparisāya ca samuṭṭhitapañhānaṃ taṃtaṃparisamajjhe kumudanālakalāpaṃ viya sunisitasatthena attano paññāsatthena tāvadeva pacchinditvā tesaṃ cittānukūladhammadesanā, vuttappakāraṃ bhogasampattiṃ pahāya attano sarīrajīvitanirapekkhaṃ caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ uposathādhiṭṭhānaṃ, tattha ca paṭiññāya visaṃvādanabhayena [M 0.0125] ahituṇḍikahatthagamanaṃ, tasmiñca mukhe visamissakheḷapātanaṃ naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā āviñchanaṃ kaḍḍhanaṃ bhūmiyaṃ ghaṃsanaṃ maddanaṃ pothananti evamādiṃ nānappakāravippakāraṃ karontepi evarūpaṃ mahādukkhaṃ anubhavatopi kujjhitvā olokanamattena taṃ chārikaṃ kātuṃ samatthassāpi sīlapāramiṃ āvajjitvā sīlakhaṇḍanabhayena īsakampi cittassa vikārābhāvo, dhanaṃ labhāpemīti vā tassa cittānuvattanaṃ, subhogena punānītassa akataññuno mittadubbhissa nesādabrāhmaṇassa sīlaṃ anadhiṭṭhahitvāpi akujjhanaṃ, kāṇāriṭṭhena kathitaṃ micchāvādaṃ bhinditvā anekapariyāyena dhammaṃ bhāsitvā nāgaparisāya sīlesu sammādiṭṭhiyañca patiṭṭhāpananti evamādayo bodhisattassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbā. Tenetaṃ [P 0.0126] vuccati – “evaṃ acchariyā hete…pe… dhammassa anudhammato”ti.

Here too, his remaining perfections are to be determined in the same way as explained previously. Here also, though dwelling in a state of Nāga kingship similar to the splendor of the deva realm—being attended like a painting by sixteen thousand Nāga maidens in his own Nāga palace a hundred leagues wide—he did not become intoxicated with sovereignty. Every half-month, he attended upon his parents and honored the elders in his family. In the midst of the entire Nāga assembly, as well as the assemblies of the Four Great Kings and the Tāvatiṃsa devas, he would instantly cut through the questions that arose with his sword of wisdom, just as one might sever a cluster of water-lily stalks with a well-sharpened sword, and he taught the Dhamma in a way agreeable to their minds. Renouncing the described wealth and luxury, indifferent to his own body and life, he undertook the observance of the Uposatha with its four factors. Then, fearing to break his promise, he fell into the hands of a snake-charmer. During this, venom-mixed spittle was spat into his mouth, he was seized by the tail, pulled and dragged, scraped on the ground, and crushed. Even while enduring such great suffering brought about by various kinds of abuse, he did not become angry. Though capable of reducing the offender to ashes with just a glance, he reflected on the Perfection of Virtue and, fearing the destruction of his virtue, did not allow the slightest disturbance in his mind. He complied with the charmer's wishes, thinking, 'I will let him gain wealth.' When the ungrateful, treacherous hunter-brahmin was brought back by Subhoga, he did not grow angry, even though he was not under the vow of virtue at that time. He refuted the false views spoken by Kāṇāriṭṭha, taught the Dhamma in many ways, and established the Nāga assembly in the moral precepts and in right view. These and other such demonstrations of the Bodhisatta's virtuous power are to be understood. Therefore, it is said: 'Thus, these are wonderful… and so on… in accordance with the Dhamma.'

Bhūridattacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Description of the Conduct of Bhūridatta is concluded.

3. Campeyyanāgacariyāvaṇṇanā

3. The Description of the Conduct of the Nāga King Campeyya.

20. Tatiye [V 0.0120] campeyyakoti aṅgamagadharaṭṭhānaṃ antare campā nāma nadī, tassā heṭṭhā nāgabhavanampi avidūrabhavattā campā nāma, tattha jāto nāgarājā campeyyako. Tadāpi dhammiko āsinti tasmiṃ campeyyanāgarājakālepi ahaṃ dhammacārī ahosiṃ.

20. In the third story, regarding 'Campeyya': between the realms of Aṅga and Magadha there is a river named Campā. Beneath it, the Nāga abode, being not far away, is also named Campā. The Nāga king born there is Campeyyaka. The line 'Even then, I was righteous' means: 'Even at that time when I was the Nāga king Campeyyaka, I was a practitioner of the Dhamma.'

Bodhisatto hi tadā campānāgabhavane nibbattitvā campeyyo nāma nāgarājā ahosi, mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo. So tattha nāgarajjaṃ kārento devarājabhogasampattisadisaissariyasampattiṃ anubhavanto pāramipūraṇassa anokāsabhāvato “kiṃ me imāya tiracchānayoniyā, uposathavāsaṃ vasitvā ito muccitvā sammadeva pāramiyo pūressāmī”ti tato paṭṭhāya attano pāsādeyeva uposathakammaṃ karoti. Alaṅkatanāgamāṇavikā tassa santikaṃ āgacchanti. So “idha me sīlassa antarāyo bhavissatī”ti pāsādato nikkhamitvā uyyāne nisīdati. Tatrāpi tā āgacchanti. So cintesi – “idha me sīlassa saṃkileso bhavissati, ito nāgabhavanato nikkhamitvā manussalokaṃ [M 0.0126] gantvā uposathavāsaṃ vasissāmī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya uposathadivasesu nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā ekassa paccantagāmassa avidūre maggasamīpe vammikamatthake “mama cammādīhi atthikā cammādīni gaṇhantu, kīḷāsappaṃ vā kātukāmā kīḷāsappaṃ karontū”ti sarīraṃ dānamukhe vissajjetvā bhoge [P 0.0127] ābhujitvā nipanno uposathavāsaṃ vasati cātuddasiyaṃ pañcadasiyañca, pāṭipade nāgabhavanaṃ gacchati. Tassevaṃ uposathaṃ karontassa dīgho addhā vītivatto.

Indeed, at that time, the Bodhisatta, having been reborn in the Nāga abode of Campā, became a Nāga king named Campeyya, of great power and majesty. While ruling the Nāga kingdom there and enjoying a sovereign splendor like that of the king of the devas, he reflected that it was not a suitable state for the fulfillment of the perfections, thinking: 'What use is this animal birth to me? By observing the Uposatha, I will free myself from this state and rightly fulfill the perfections.' From then on, he began to perform the Uposatha observance in his own palace. Adorned Nāga maidens would come to him. Thinking, 'Here, there will be an obstruction to my virtue,' he left the palace and sat in the garden. But they came there too. He thought, 'Here, my virtue will be defiled. I must leave this Nāga abode and go to the human world to observe the Uposatha.' From that day onward, on Uposatha days, he would leave the Nāga abode and go to the top of an anthill near a road, not far from a border village. Surrendering his body in an act of giving, he would lie down in coils and observe the Uposatha on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, thinking: 'Let those who need my skin and so on take my skin and so on. Or let those who wish to make me a play-snake do so.' On the first day of the next fortnight, he would return to the Nāga abode. A long time passed as he observed the Uposatha in this way.

Atha bodhisatto sumanāya nāma attano aggamahesiyā “deva, tvaṃ manussalokaṃ gantvā uposathaṃ upavasasi, so ca sāsaṅko sappaṭibhayo”ti vutto maṅgalapokkharaṇitīre ṭhatvā “sace maṃ, bhadde, koci paharitvā kilamessati, imissā pokkharaṇiyā udakaṃ āvilaṃ bhavissati. Sace supaṇṇo gaṇhissati, udakaṃ pakkuthissati. Sace ahituṇḍiko gaṇhissati, udakaṃ lohitavaṇṇaṃ bhavissatī”ti tīṇi nimittāni tassā ācikkhitvā cātuddasīuposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā tattha gantvā vammikamatthake nipajji sarīrasobhāya vammikaṃ sobhayamāno. Sarīrañhissa rajatadāmaṃ viya setaṃ ahosi, matthako rattakambalageṇḍuko viya, sarīraṃ naṅgalasīsappamāṇaṃ bhūridattakāle (jā. 2.22.784 ādayo) pana ūruppamāṇaṃ, saṅkhapālakāle (jā. 2.17.143 ādayo) ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ.

Then the Bodhisatta was addressed by his chief queen, named Sumanā: 'Your Majesty, you go to the human world to observe the Uposatha, but that world is perilous and fraught with danger.' Having been told this, he stood on the bank of the auspicious lotus pond and declared three signs to her: 'If, good lady, someone should strike and torment me, the water of this pond will become turbid. If a supaṇṇa should seize me, the water will boil. If a snake-charmer should capture me, the water will turn the color of blood.' Having explained these three signs to her, he undertook the fourteenth-day Uposatha, left the Nāga abode, and went there. He lay down on the top of the anthill, adorning the anthill with the splendor of his body. For his body was white like a silver chain, and his head was like a ball of red wool. His body was the size of a ploughshare. (In the time of Bhūridatta, however, it was the size of a thigh, and in the time of Saṅkhapāla, it was the size of a one-doṇa boat.)

Tadā [V 0.0121] eko bārāṇasimāṇavo takkasilaṃ gantvā alampāyanamantaṃ uggaṇhitvā tena maggena attano gāmaṃ gacchanto mahāsattaṃ disvā “kiṃ me tucchahatthena gāmaṃ gantuṃ, imaṃ nāgaṃ gahetvā gāmanigamarājadhānīsu kīḷāpento dhanaṃ uppādetvāva gamissāmī”ti cintetvā dibbosadhāni gahetvā dibbamantaṃ parivattetvā tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Dibbamantaṃ sutakālato paṭṭhāya mahāsattassa kaṇṇesu tattasalākāpavesanakālo viya ahosi, matthake sikharena abhimanthiyamāno viya. So “ko nu kho eso”ti bhogantarato sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā olokento ahituṇḍikaṃ disvā cintesi – “mama visaṃ uggatejaṃ, sacāhaṃ kujjhitvā [P 0.0128] nāsāvātaṃ vissajjessāmi, etassa sarīraṃ bhusamuṭṭhi viya vippakirissati, atha me sīlaṃ khaṇḍaṃ bhavissati, na naṃ olokessāmī”ti. So akkhīni nimmīletvā sīsaṃ bhogantare ṭhapesi. Ahituṇḍikabrāhmaṇo [M 0.0127] osadhaṃ khāditvā mantaṃ parivattetvā kheḷaṃ mahāsattassa sarīre osiñci. Osadhānañca mantassa ca ānubhāvena kheḷena phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāne phoṭānaṃ uṭṭhānakālo viya ahosi.

At that time, a certain young man from Bārāṇasī, having gone to Takkasilā and learned the Alampāyana spell, was returning to his own village by that road when he saw the Great Being. He thought, 'What use is it for me to go to the village empty-handed? I will capture this nāga, make him perform in villages, market towns, and royal cities, generate wealth, and only then will I go.' Thinking thus, he took divine herbs, recited a divine spell, and approached him. From the moment he heard the divine spell, it was as if a hot iron spike were being driven into the Great Being’s ears, and as if his head were being churned with a sharp point. He wondered, 'Who can this be?' Raising his head from within his coils and looking about, he saw the snake-charmer and reflected, 'My venom is of fierce power. If I become angry and release the breath from my nostrils, his body will be scattered like chaff-dust. But then my observance of virtue would be broken. I will not look at him.' Closing his eyes, he placed his head within his coils. The snake-charmer brahmin chewed an herb, recited the spell, and sprinkled his saliva on the Great Being’s body. Through the power of the herbs and the spell, wherever the saliva touched, it was as if blisters were rising.

Atha so naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā ākaḍḍhitvā dīghaso nipajjāpetvā ajapadena daṇḍena uppīḷetvā dubbalaṃ katvā sīsaṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā nippīḷesi. Mahāsatto mukhaṃ vivari. Athassa mukhe kheḷaṃ osiñcitvā osadhamantabalena dante bhindi. Mukhaṃ lohitassa pūri. Mahāsatto attano sīlabhedabhayena evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ adhivāsento akkhīni ummīletvā olokanamattampi nākāsi. Sopi “nāgarājānaṃ dubbalaṃ karissāmī”ti naṅguṭṭhato paṭṭhāya aṭṭhīni saṃcuṇṇayamāno viya sakalasarīraṃ madditvā paṭṭakaveṭhanaṃ nāma veṭhesi, tantamajjitaṃ nāma majji, naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā dussapothanaṃ nāma pothesi. Mahāsattassa sakalasarīraṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ ahosi, so mahāvedanaṃ adhivāsesi.

Then, seizing him by the tail, he dragged him out, made him lie down at full length, pressed down on him with a goat-foot-like stick, and having weakened him, he seized his head firmly and pressed down hard. The Great Being opened his mouth. Then, the man poured saliva into his mouth and, by the power of the herb and the spell, broke his fangs. His mouth filled with blood. The Great Being, enduring such suffering out of fear that his virtue would be broken, did not so much as open his eyes to look. That man, thinking, 'I will weaken the Nāga king,' massaged his entire body, starting from the tail, as if grinding his bones to powder. He coiled him in the manner called the 'cloth-wrap,' rubbed him in the manner called the 'sequential rub,' and, seizing him by the tail, beat him in the manner called the 'cloth-beating.' The Great Being's entire body became smeared with blood, yet he endured the great pain.

Athassa dubbalabhāvaṃ ñatvā vallīhi peḷaṃ karitvā tattha naṃ pakkhipitvā paccantagāmaṃ netvā mahājanassa majjhe kīḷāpesi. Nīlādīsu vaṇṇesu vaṭṭacaturassādīsu saṇṭhānesu aṇuṃthūlādīsu pamāṇesu yaṃ yaṃ brāhmaṇo icchati, mahāsatto taṃ tadeva katvā naccati, phaṇasatampi phaṇasahassampi karotiyeva. Mahājano pasīditvā bahudhanamadāsi. Ekadivasameva kahāpaṇasahassañceva sahassagghanike ca parikkhāre labhi. Brāhmaṇo [P 0.0129] āditova “sahassaṃ labhitvā vissajjessāmī”ti cintesi. Taṃ pana dhanaṃ labhitvā “paccantagāmeyeva tāva me ettakaṃ dhanaṃ laddhaṃ, rājarājamahāmattānaṃ dassite kīva bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhissāmī”ti sakaṭañca sukhayānakañca gahetvā sakaṭe parikkhāre ṭhapetvā sukhayānake nisinno “mahantena parivārena mahāsattaṃ [V 0.0122] gāmanigamarājadhānīsu kīḷāpento bārāṇasiyaṃ uggasenarañño santike kīḷāpetvā vissajjessāmī”ti agamāsi. So maṇḍūke māretvā nāgarañño deti. Nāgarājā “punappunaṃ maṃ nissāya māressatī”ti na khādati. Athassa madhulāje adāsi. Tepi “sacāhaṃ gocaraṃ gaṇhissāmi, antopeḷāyameva maraṇaṃ bhavissatī”ti na khādati.

Then, knowing his weakened state, he made a basket with vines, placed him inside it, and took him to a border village, where he made him perform in the midst of a great crowd. Whatever color—such as blue—whatever shape—such as round or square—whatever size—such as small or large—the brahmin desired, the Great Being would assume that very form and dance, even creating a hundred or a thousand hoods. The great crowd, being pleased, gave much wealth. In a single day, he received a thousand kahāpaṇas and requisites worth a thousand. From the very beginning, the brahmin had thought, 'Having received a thousand, I will release him.' But upon obtaining that wealth, he reflected, 'In a border village alone I have gained this much wealth; how much more will I obtain if I show him to kings and great ministers?' So he procured a cart and a comfortable vehicle, placed all the requisites in the cart, and, seated in the comfortable vehicle, he traveled with a great retinue, thinking, 'After making the Great Being perform in villages, market towns, and royal capitals, I will have him perform in the presence of King Uggasena of Bārāṇasī and then release him.' He would kill frogs and give them to the Nāga king. But the Nāga king, thinking, 'On my account, he will kill again and again,' did not eat. Then the man gave him sweet puffed rice. But he, thinking, 'If I take this food, I will die right here inside the basket,' did not eat that either.

21. Brāhmaṇo [M 0.0128] māsamattena bārāṇasiṃ patvā dvāragāmake taṃ kīḷāpento bahudhanaṃ labhi. Rājāpi naṃ pakkosāpetvā “amhākampi kīḷāpehī”ti āha. “Sādhu, deva, sve pannarase tumhākaṃ kīḷāpessāmī”ti āha. Rājā “sve nāgarājā rājaṅgaṇe naccissati, mahājano sannipatitvā passatū”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā punadivase rājaṅgaṇaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā brāhmaṇaṃ pakkosāpesi. So ratanapeḷāya mahāsattaṃ netvā vicittatthare peḷaṃ ṭhapetvā nisīdi. Rājāpi pāsādā oruyha mahājanaparivuto rājāsane nisīdi. Brāhmaṇo mahāsattaṃ nīharitvā naccāpesi. Mahāsatto tena cintitacintitākāraṃ dassesi. Mahājano sakabhāvena sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti. Celukkhepasahassāni pavattanti. Bodhisattassa upari ratanavassaṃ vassi. Tena vuttaṃ “tadāpi maṃ dhammacāri”ntiādi.

21. The brahmin reached Bārāṇasī in about a month and, making him perform in a gate-village, he received much wealth. The king had him summoned and said, 'Make him perform for us as well.' The brahmin replied, 'Very well, Your Majesty. Tomorrow, on the fifteenth day, I will make him perform for you.' The king had a drum beaten to announce, 'Tomorrow the Nāga king will dance in the royal courtyard; let the great populace assemble and watch.' The next day, he had the royal courtyard decorated and summoned the brahmin. The brahmin brought the Great Being in a jeweled basket, placed the basket on a splendid carpet, and sat down. The king, too, descended from his palace and, surrounded by a great crowd, sat on the royal throne. The brahmin took out the Great Being and made him dance. The Great Being displayed every form the brahmin thought of. The great crowd could not contain themselves. Thousands of cloths were thrown up in the air. A rain of jewels fell upon the Bodhisatta. For that reason, it was said: 'Even then, me, a practitioner of Dhamma...' and so on.

Tattha tadāpīti yadāhaṃ campeyyako nāgarājā homi, tadāpi. Dhammacārinti dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ [P 0.0130] eva carati, na aṇumattampi adhammanti dhammacārī. Upavuṭṭhauposathanti aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatassa ariyuposathasīlassa rakkhaṇavasena upavasitauposathaṃ. Rājadvāramhi kīḷatīti bārāṇasiyaṃ uggasenarañño gehadvāre kīḷāpeti.

Therein, 'even then' refers to: 'even at the time when I was the Nāga king Campeyya.' 'A practitioner of Dhamma' means: he practices only the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action and does not practice even a particle of what is not Dhamma; therefore, he is a practitioner of Dhamma. 'Having observed the Uposatha' refers to: the Uposatha observed by way of protecting the noble Uposatha virtue endowed with eight factors. 'He plays at the king’s gate' means: he makes him perform at the palace gate of King Uggasena in Bārāṇasī.

22. Yaṃ yaṃ so vaṇṇaṃ cintayīti so ahituṇḍikabrāhmaṇo “yaṃ yaṃ nīlādivaṇṇaṃ hotū”ti cintesi. Tena vuttaṃ “nīlaṃ va pītalohita”nti. Tattha nīlaṃ vāti vā-saddo aniyamattho, gāthāsukhatthaṃ rassaṃ katvā vutto, tena vāsaddena vuttāvasiṭṭhaṃ odātādivaṇṇavisesañceva vaṭṭādisaṇṭhānavisesañca aṇuṃthūlādipamāṇavisesañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa cittānuvattantoti tassa ahituṇḍikassa cittaṃ anuvattanto. Cintitasannibhoti tena cintitacintitākārena pekkhajanassa upaṭṭhahāmīti dasseti.

22. 'Whatever color he thought of' means that the snake-charmer brahmin thought, 'Let it be whatever color, such as blue.' Therefore, it was said, 'blue, or yellow, or red.' Therein, in the phrase 'nīlaṃ vā,' the word 'vā' has an indefinite meaning; for the sake of ease in reciting the verse, it is spoken with a short vowel. By that word 'vā,' it includes the remaining special colors such as white, special shapes such as round, and special sizes such as small and large. 'Conforming to his mind' means conforming to the mind of that snake-charmer. 'Appearing as imagined' means he shows, 'I appear to the onlookers in the very form imagined by him.'

23. Na kevalañca tena cintitākāradassanaṃ eva mayhaṃ ānubhāvo. Api ca thalaṃ kareyyamudakaṃ, udakampi thalaṃ kareti thalaṃ mahāpathaviṃ gahetvā udakaṃ, udakampi gahetvā pathaviṃ kātuṃ [V 0.0123] sakkuṇeyyaṃ evaṃ mahānubhāvo ca. Yadihaṃ tassa kuppeyyanti tassa ahituṇḍikassa ahaṃ yadi kujjheyyaṃ. Khaṇena chārikaṃ kareti kodhuppādakkhaṇe eva bhasmaṃ kareyyaṃ.

23. And my power is not merely the display of imagined forms. Moreover, I could make land into water, and water into land—taking the great earth and making it water, or taking water and making it earth—such is my great power. 'If I were to be angered at him' means if I were to become angry at that snake-charmer. 'In an instant, I could reduce him to ashes' means at the very moment anger arose, I could turn him to ashes.

24. Evaṃ [M 0.0129] bhagavā tadā attano uppajjanakānatthapaṭibāhane samatthataṃ dassetvā idāni yena adhippāyena taṃ paṭibāhanaṃ na kataṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “yadi cittavasī hessa”ntiādimāha.

24. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown his ability at that time to ward off the arising of his own disadvantage, now, to show the intention by which that warding off was not done, said, 'If I were a master of my mind,' and so on.

Tassattho – “ayaṃ ahituṇḍiko maṃ ativiya bādhati, na me ānubhāvaṃ jānāti, handassa me ānubhāvaṃ dassessāmī”ti kujjhitvā olokanamattenāpi yadi cittavasī abhavissaṃ, atha so bhusamuṭṭhi viya vippakirissati. Ahaṃ yathāsamādinnato parihāyissāmi sīlato. Tathā ca sati sīlena parihīnassa khaṇḍitasīlassa yvāyaṃ mayā dīpaṅkaradasabalassa pādamūlato paṭṭhāya abhipatthito[P 0.0131], uttamattho buddhabhāvo so na sijjhati.

Its meaning is: 'This snake-charmer greatly harasses me, not knowing my power. Come, I shall show him my power.' If, having become angry, by a mere glance I had yielded to the will of my mind, then he would have been scattered like a fistful of chaff. I would have fallen away from the virtue I had undertaken. And that being so, for me, being deficient in virtue, with virtue broken, that supreme goal of Buddhahood—which I have aspired to since the time of Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One—would not be achieved.

25. Kāmaṃ bhijjatuyaṃ kāyoti ayaṃ cātumahābhūtiko odanakummāsūpacayo aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammo kāyo kiñcāpi bhijjatu vinassatu, idheva imasmiṃ eva ṭhāne mahāvāte khittabhusamuṭṭhi viya vippakirīyatu, neva sīlaṃ pabhindeyyaṃ, vikirante bhusaṃ viyāti sīlaṃ pana uttamatthasiddhiyā hetubhūtaṃ imasmiṃ kaḷevare bhusamuṭṭhi viya vippakirantepi neva bhindeyyaṃ, kāyajīvitesu nirapekkho hutvā sīlapāramiṃyeva pūremīti cintetvā taṃ tādisaṃ dukkhaṃ tadā adhivāsesinti dasseti.

25. 'Let this body break apart' means: this body, composed of the four great elements, sustained by rice and gruel, and subject to impermanence, rubbing, crushing, breaking, and destruction—even if it should break apart and perish, even if it should be scattered right here in this very place like a handful of chaff thrown by a great wind, I will not break my virtue. 'Even as it is scattered like chaff' means: but virtue is the cause for achieving the highest goal; even if this body is scattered like a fistful of chaff, I will not break my virtue. Reflecting, 'Being indifferent to body and life, I will fulfill only the perfection of virtue,' he shows, 'I endured such suffering at that time.'

Atha mahāsattassa pana ahituṇḍikahatthagatassa māso paripūri, ettakaṃ kālaṃ nirāhārova ahosi. Sumanā “aticirāyati me sāmiko, ko nu kho pavattī”ti pokkharaṇiṃ olokentī lohitavaṇṇaṃ udakaṃ disvā “ahituṇḍikena gahito bhavissatī”ti ñatvā nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā vammikasantikaṃ gantvā mahāsattassa gahitaṭṭhānaṃ kilamitaṭṭhānañca disvā roditvā kanditvā paccantagāmaṃ gantvā pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rājadvāre ākāse rodamānā aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto naccantova ākāsaṃ ullokento taṃ disvā lajjito peḷaṃ pavisitvā nipajji.

Then a full month was completed for the Great Being while in the hands of the snake-charmer, and for that long he had been without food. Sumanā, thinking, 'My lord is taking too long, what can be the news?' looked at the pond. Seeing the water was the color of blood and realizing, 'He must have been captured by a snake-charmer,' she departed from the Nāga realm and went to the anthill. Seeing the place where the Great Being was captured and the place where he was tormented, she wept and lamented. Going to a border village, she inquired and heard that news. Then she went to Bārāṇasī and stood weeping in the sky at the king’s gate. The Great Being, while dancing, looked up at the sky, saw her, and, ashamed, entered the basket and lay down.

Rājā tassa peḷaṃ paviṭṭhakāle “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti ito cito ca olokento taṃ ākāse ṭhitaṃ disvā “kā nu tva”nti pucchitvā tassā nāgakaññābhāvaṃ sutvā “nissaṃsayaṃ kho nāgarājā imaṃ disvā [M 0.0130] lajjito peḷaṃ paviṭṭho, ayañca yathādassito iddhānubhāvo nāgarājasseva[V 0.0124], na ahituṇḍikassā”ti niṭṭhaṃ gantvā “evaṃ mahānubhāvo ayaṃ nāgarājā, kathaṃ nāma imassa hatthaṃ gato”ti pucchitvā “ayaṃ dhammacārī sīlavā nāgarājā, cātuddasīpannarasīsu uposathaṃ upavasanto attano sarīraṃ dānamukhe niyyātetvā mahāmaggasamīpe vammikamatthake nipajjati, tatthāyametena gahito, imassa devaccharāpaṭibhāgā anekasahassā itthiyo, devalokasampattisadisā nāgabhavanasampatti, ayaṃ mahiddhiko [P 0.0132] mahānubhāvo sakalapathaviṃ parivattetuṃ samattho, kevalaṃ ‘sīlaṃ me bhijjissatī’ti evarūpaṃ vippakāraṃ dukkhañca anubhotī”ti ca sutvā saṃvegappatto tāvadeva tassa ahituṇḍikassa brāhmaṇassa bahuṃ dhanaṃ mahantañca yasaṃ issariyañca datvā – “handa, bho, imaṃ nāgarājānaṃ vissajjehī”ti vissajjāpesi.

When the king saw him enter the basket, he wondered, 'What could be the reason?' Looking here and there, he saw her standing in the sky and asked, 'Who are you?' Hearing that she was a Nāga maiden, he concluded, 'Without doubt, the Nāga king saw her and, feeling ashamed, entered the basket. And this supernatural power that has been displayed belongs to the Nāga king himself, not to the snake-charmer.' Having come to this conclusion, he asked, 'How did such a mighty Nāga king fall into this man's hands?' He was told: 'This Nāga king is righteous in conduct and virtuous. On the fourteenth and fifteenth days, observing the Uposatha, he dedicates his body as a gift and lies atop an anthill near the main road. It was there that he was captured by this man. He has many thousands of wives comparable to celestial nymphs and a Nāga realm like the bliss of a deva world. He is of great psychic power and might, capable of overturning the entire earth. He endures such ill-treatment and suffering solely out of fear that "my virtue will be broken."' Hearing this, the king was struck with urgency and at that very moment gave that snake-charmer brahmin much wealth, great renown, and authority, saying, 'Come, sir, release this Nāga king,' and thus had him released.

Mahāsatto nāgavaṇṇaṃ antaradhāpetvā māṇavakavaṇṇena devakumāro viya aṭṭhāsi. Sumanāpi ākāsato otaritvā tassa santike aṭṭhāsi. Nāgarājā rañño añjaliṃ katvā “ehi, mahārāja, mayhaṃ nivesanaṃ passituṃ āgacchāhī”ti yāci. Tenāha bhagavā –

The Great Being, causing his Nāga form to disappear, stood in the form of a young man, like a divine youth. Sumanā also descended from the sky and stood near him. The Nāga king, making a reverential salutation to the king, entreated, 'Come, great king, please come to see my dwelling.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Mutto campeyyako nāgo, rājānaṃ etadabravi;

‘Namo te kāsirājatthu, namo te kāsivaḍḍhana;

Añjaliṃ te paggaṇhāmi, passeyyaṃ me nivesana”nti.

'Freed, the Campeyya Nāga addressed the king thus: 'Homage to you, O king of Kāsī; homage to you, O increaser of Kāsī. I raise my joined hands to you in reverence; pray, behold my dwelling.''

Atha rājā tassa nāgabhavanagamanaṃ anujāni. Mahāsatto taṃ saparisaṃ gahetvā nāgabhavanaṃ netvā attano issariyasampattiṃ dassetvā katipāhaṃ tattha vasāpetvā bheriṃ carāpesi – “sabbā rājaparisā yāvadicchakaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādikaṃ dhanaṃ gaṇhatū”ti. Rañño ca anekehi sakaṭasatehi dhanaṃ pesesi. “Mahārāja, raññā nāma dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, sīlaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ, dhammikā rakkhāvaraṇagutti sabbattha saṃvidahitabbā”ti dasahi rājadhammakathāhi ovaditvā vissajjesi. Rājā mahantena yasena nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā bārāṇasimeva gato. Tato paṭṭhāya kira jambudīpatale hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ jātaṃ. Mahāsatto sīlāni rakkhitvā anvaddhamāsaṃ uposathakammaṃ katvā sapariso saggapuraṃ pūresi.

Then the king gave him leave to go to the nāga realm. The Bodhisatta took him and his retinue, led them to the nāga realm, showed them his own sovereign wealth, and after having them stay there for some days, had a drum beaten to proclaim: “Let all the royal retinue take as much wealth as they desire, such as gold and silver.” He also sent wealth to the king by many hundreds of carts. Having advised him with the ten discourses on royal duties, saying, “Great king, a king should give gifts, guard virtue, and ensure that righteous protection, security, and guardianship are arranged everywhere,” he dismissed him. The king, with a great retinue, departed from the nāga realm and went to Bārāṇasī itself. From that time onward, it is said, gold and silver arose on the surface of Jambudīpa. The Bodhisatta, guarding his virtues and performing the Uposatha observance every fortnight, filled the celestial city along with his retinue.

Tadā ahituṇḍiko [M 0.0131] devadatto ahosi, sumanā rāhulamātā, uggaseno sāriputtatthero, campeyyako nāgarājā lokanātho.

At that time, the snake-charmer was Devadatta, Sumanā was Rāhulamātā, Uggasena was the Elder Sāriputta, and the Nāga king Campeyyaka was the Lord of the World.

Tassa [V 0.0125] idhāpi yathārahaṃ sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Idha bodhisattassa acchariyānubhāvā heṭṭhā vuttanayā evāti.

In this case also, his remaining perfections should be determined as is appropriate. Here, the wondrous powers of the Bodhisatta are just in the manner spoken of below.

Campeyyanāgacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Conduct of the Nāga King Campeyya is concluded.

4. Cūḷabodhicariyāvaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Conduct of Cūḷabodhi

26. Catutthe [P 0.0133] cūḷabodhīti mahābodhiparibbājakattabhāvaṃ upādāya idha “cūḷabodhī”ti samaññā āropitā, na pana imasmiṃ eva jātake (jā. 1.10.49 ādayo) attano jeṭṭhabhātikādino mahābodhissa sambhavatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Susīlavāti suṭṭhu sīlavā, sampannasīloti attho. Bhavaṃ disvāna bhayatoti kāmādibhavaṃ bhāyitabbabhāvena passitvā. Nekkhammanti ettha ca-saddassa lopo daṭṭhabbo, tena “disvānā”ti padaṃ ākaḍḍhīyati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – jātijarābyādhimaraṇaṃ apāyadukkhaṃ atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhanti imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ saṃvegavatthūnaṃ paccavekkhaṇena sabbampi kāmādibhedaṃ bhavaṃ saṃsārabhayato upaṭṭhahamānaṃ disvā nibbānaṃ tassa upāyabhūtā samathavipassanā tadupāyabhūtā ca pabbajjāti idaṃ tividhampi nekkhammaṃ anussavādisiddhena ñāṇacakkhunā tappaṭipakkhato disvā tāpasapabbajjūpagamanena anekādīnavākulā gahaṭṭhabhāvā abhinikkhamitvā gatoti.

26. In the fourth story, regarding 'Cūḷabodhi': the designation 'Cūḷabodhi' is applied here by reason of the state of being the Mahābodhi ascetic; it should be understood that this is not because, in this very Jātaka, he was the elder brother or the like of Mahābodhi. 'Susīlavā' means very virtuous, that is, endowed with perfect virtue. 'Bhavaṃ disvāna bhayato' means having seen existence, such as sensual existence, as something to be feared. Regarding 'nekkhammaṃ', the elision of the particle 'ca' should be noted here; by it, the word 'disvāna' is drawn in. This is what is meant: By reflecting on these eight grounds for spiritual urgency—namely, birth, aging, sickness, death, the suffering of the plane of misery, suffering in the past rooted in the cycle of existence, suffering in the future rooted in the cycle of existence, and suffering in the present rooted in the search for food—and having seen every kind of existence, such as sensual existence, presenting itself as the fear of saṃsāra; and having seen with the eye of wisdom, established through hearing and so forth, this threefold renunciation—namely, Nibbāna, serenity and insight meditation which are the means to it, and the going forth which is the means to them—as the opposite of that existence, he went forth from the household state, which is beset with many dangers, by undertaking the ascetic's going-forth.

27. Dutiyikāti porāṇadutiyikā, gihikāle pajāpatibhūtā. Kanakasannibhāti kañcanasannibhattacā. Vaṭṭe anapekkhāti saṃsāre nirālayā. Nekkhammaṃ abhinikkhamīti nekkhammatthāya gehato nikkhami, pabbajīti attho.

27. 'Dutiyikā' means the former companion, who was his wife in his lay life. 'Kanakasannibhā' means having skin like gold. 'Vaṭṭe anapekkhā' means without attachment to the cycle of existence, to saṃsāra. 'Nekkhammaṃ abhinikkhamī' means: for the sake of renunciation she went forth from home, that is, she renounced the world.

28. Ālayanti sattā etenāti ālayo, taṇhā, tadabhāvena nirālayā. Tato eva ñātīsu taṇhābandhanassa chinnattā chinnabandhu. Evaṃ gihibandhanābhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni pabbajitānampi kesañci yaṃ hoti bandhanaṃ[M 0.0132], tassāpi abhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “anapekkhā kule gaṇe”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha kuleti upaṭṭhākakule. Gaṇeti tāpasagaṇe, sesā brahmacārinoti vuccanti. Upāgamunti ubhopi mayaṃ upāgamimhā.

28. 'Ālaya' is that to which beings cling, thus it is craving (taṇhā). Through its absence, one is 'nirālayā' (without attachment). For that very reason, because the bond of craving towards relatives is severed, one is 'chinnabandhu' (one with severed ties). Having thus shown the absence of household bonds, now, to show the absence of that bond which exists even for some who have gone forth, it is said: “unconcerned with family or group.” Therein, 'kule' refers to supporting families. 'Gaṇe' refers to the group of ascetics; the others are called fellow practitioners of the holy life. 'Upāgamun' means 'we both approached'.

29. Tatthāti [V 0.0126] bārāṇasisāmante. Nipakāti paññavanto. Nirākuleti janasañcārarahitattā janehi anākule, appasaddeti migapakkhīnaṃ uṭṭhāpanato tesaṃ vassitasaddenāpi virahitattā appasadde. Rājuyyāne vasāmubhoti [P 0.0134] bārāṇasirañño uyyāne mayaṃ ubho janā tadā vasāma.

29. 'Tattha' means in the vicinity of Bārāṇasī. 'Nipakā' means wise. 'Nirākule' means undisturbed by people, as it was free from the movement of people. 'Appasadde' means with little sound, as it was free from the stirring of beasts and birds and even from the sound of their calls. 'Rājuyyāne vasāmubho' means: we two persons then dwelt in the royal park of the king of Bārāṇasī.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – atīte imasmiṃ eva bhaddakappe bodhisatto brahmalokato cavitvā aññatarasmiṃ kāsigāme ekassa mahāvibhavassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Tassa nāmaggahaṇasamaye “bodhikumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Vayappattakāle panassa takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā paccāgatassa anicchamānakasseva mātāpitaro samajātikaṃ kulakumārikaṃ ānesuṃ. Sāpi brahmalokacutāva uttamarūpadharā devaccharāpaṭibhāgā. Tesaṃ anicchamānānaṃ eva aññamaññaṃ āvāhavivāhaṃ kariṃsu. Ubhinnampi pana nesaṃ kilesamudācāro na bhūtapubbo, sārāgavasena aññamaññaṃ olokanampi nāhosi, kā pana kathā itarasaṃsagge. Evaṃ parisuddhasīlā ahesuṃ.

Herein, this is the sequential narrative: In the past, during this very fortunate aeon, the Bodhisatta passed away from the Brahma-world and was reborn as the son of a brahmin of great wealth in a certain village in Kāsi. At the time of his naming, they gave him the name ‘Bodhikumāra’. When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the sciences, and returned. Although he was unwilling, his parents brought him a maiden from a family of equal birth. She too had passed away from the Brahma-world, was a bearer of supreme beauty, and was like a celestial nymph. Though both were unwilling, their parents performed the marriage ceremony for them. But for both of them, there was never any defiled conduct; they never even looked at one another with lust—what then to say of other contact? Thus they were of perfectly pure virtue.

Aparabhāge mahāsatto mātāpitūsu kālaṃkatesu tesaṃ sarīrakiccaṃ katvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “bhadde, tvaṃ imaṃ asītikoṭidhanaṃ gahetvā sukhena jīvāhī”ti āha. “Tvaṃ pana ayyaputtā”ti? “Mayhaṃ dhanena kiccaṃ natthi, pabbajissāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana pabbajjā itthīnampi na vaṭṭatī”ti? “Vaṭṭati, bhadde”ti. “Tena hi mayhampi dhanena kiccaṃ natthi, ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti. Te ubhopi sabbaṃ vibhavaṃ pariccajitvā mahādānaṃ datvā nikkhamitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitvā uñchācariyāya phalāphalehi yāpentā pabbajjāsukheneva dasa saṃvaccharāni vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadacārikaṃ carantā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “rājuyyāne vasāmubho”ti.

Later, when his parents passed away, the Bodhisatta performed their funeral rites. Then, having summoned her, he said, “Good lady, take these eighty crores of wealth and live happily.” “But what of you, noble sir?” she asked. “I have no need for wealth; I shall go forth.” “But is the going-forth not fitting for women also?” “It is fitting, good lady.” “In that case, I too have no need for wealth; I also shall go forth.” Both of them, having given up all their wealth and given a great gift, departed and entered the forest. Having gone forth, they subsisted on gleanings and various fruits, dwelling for ten years in the happiness of the renunciate life. Then, for the purpose of partaking of salt and sour flavours, they wandered through the country and in due course reached Bārāṇasī, where they dwelt in the royal park. Therefore it was said: “we both dwelt in the royal park.”

30. Athekadivasaṃ [P 0.0135] rājā uyyānakīḷaṃ gato. Uyyānassa ekapasse pabbajjāsukhena vītināmentānaṃ tesaṃ samīpaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paramapāsādikaṃ uttamarūpadharaṃ [M 0.0133] paribbājikaṃ olokento kilesavasena paṭibaddhacitto hutvā bodhisattaṃ “ayaṃ te paribbājikā kiṃ hotī”ti pucchi. Tena “na ca kiñci hoti, kevalaṃ ekapabbajjāya pabbajitā, api ca kho pana gihikāle pādaparicārikā ahosī”ti vutte rājā “ayaṃ kiretassa na kiñci hoti, api ca kho panassa gihikāle pādaparicārikā ahosi, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ antepuraṃ paveseyyaṃ, tenevassa imissā [V 0.0127] paṭipattiṃ jānissāmī”ti andhabālo tattha attano paṭibaddhacittaṃ nivāretuṃ asakkonto aññataraṃ purisaṃ āṇāpesi “imaṃ paribbājikaṃ rājanivesanaṃ nehī”ti.

30. Then one day, the king went to the park for pleasure. Having gone to the vicinity of those who were passing their time in the happiness of renunciation on one side of the park, he beheld the female ascetic, who was exceedingly pleasing and possessed of supreme beauty. His mind becoming attached through the power of defilements, he asked the Bodhisatta, 'What is this female ascetic to you?' When he replied, 'She is nothing to me; she has merely gone forth into the same renunciation. However, in lay life, she was my foot attendant,' the king thought, 'It seems she is nothing to him, yet in lay life she was his foot attendant. What if I were to have her enter the inner palace? In that way, I will know his conduct towards her.' The utterly foolish one, unable to restrain his attached mind towards her, ordered a certain man, 'Take this female ascetic to the royal residence.'

So tassa paṭissuṇitvā “adhammo loke vattatī”tiādīni vatvā paridevamānaṃ eva taṃ ādāya pāyāsi. Bodhisatto tassā paridevanasaddaṃ sutvā ekavāraṃ oloketvā puna na olokesi. “Sace panāhaṃ vāressāmi, tesu cittaṃ padosetvā mayhaṃ sīlassa antarāyo bhavissatī”ti sīlapāramiṃyeva āvajjento nisīdi. Tena vuttaṃ “uyyānadassanaṃ gantvā, rājā addasa brāhmaṇi”ntiādi.

That man, having assented, said, 'Unrighteousness prevails in the world,' and so forth, and taking her even while she was lamenting, he departed. The Bodhisatta, hearing the sound of her lamentation, looked once and did not look again. Thinking, 'If I were to prevent this, my mind would become corrupted towards them, and there would be an obstacle to my virtue,' he remained seated, reflecting only on the perfection of virtue. Therefore it was said: 'Having gone to see the garden, the king saw the brahmin woman,' and so on.

Tattha tuyhesā kā kassa bhariyāti tuyhaṃ tava esā kā, kiṃ bhariyā, udāhu bhaginī vā samānā kassa aññassa bhariyā.

Herein, the phrase 'What is she to you? Whose wife is she?' means: What is she to you? Is she your wife, or perhaps your sister, or the wife of some other kinsman?

31. Na mayhaṃ bhariyā esāti kāmañcesā mayhaṃ gihikāle bhariyā ahosi, pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya na mayhaṃ bhariyā esā, nāpi ahaṃ etissā sāmiko, kevalaṃ pana sahadhammā ekasāsanī, ahampi paribbājako ayampi paribbājikāti samānadhammā paribbājakasāsanena ekasāsanī, sabrahmacārinīti attho.

31. As to 'She is not my wife': Though it is true she was my wife during my lay life, from the time of going forth, she is not my wife, nor am I her husband. We are merely companions in the Dhamma, under one teaching. I am a male ascetic and she is a female ascetic; thus, having a similar way of life under the teaching of the ascetics, we are under one teaching, fellow practitioners of the holy life. This is the meaning.

32. Tissā sārattagadhitoti kāmarāgena sāratto hutvā paṭibaddho. Gāhāpetvāna ceṭaketi ceṭakehi gaṇhāpetvā ceṭake vā attano rājapurise āṇāpetvā taṃ paribbājikaṃ gaṇhāpetvā. Nippīḷayanto balasāti taṃ anicchamānaṃ eva ākaḍḍhanaparikaḍḍhanādinā nippīḷayanto bādhento, tathāpi agacchantiṃ balasā balakkārena rājapurisehi gaṇhāpetvā attano antepuraṃ pavesesi.

32. As to 'Infatuated and greedy for her': this means being infatuated and attached through sensual passion. As to 'Having had the servants seize her': this means having her seized by servants, or, having ordered his own servants, the royal men, he had that female ascetic seized. As to 'Oppressing her by force': this means oppressing and harassing her, though she was unwilling, by means of pulling her back and forth; and as she would not come, he had her seized by his royal men through force and violence and made her enter his inner palace.

33. Odapattakiyāti udakapattaṃ āmasitvā gahitabhariyā odapattikā nāma, idaṃ vacanaṃ purāṇadutiyikābhāvena upalakkhaṇamattaṃ [P 0.0136] daṭṭhabbaṃ[M 0.0134], sā panassa brāhmaṇavivāhavasena mātāpitūhi sampaṭipāditā, “odapattakiyā”ti ca bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇe bhummaṃ. Sahajāti pabbajjājātivasena sahajātā, tenevāha “ekasāsanī”ti. “Ekasāsanī”ti ca idaṃ bhummatthe paccattaṃ, ekasāsaniyāti attho. Nayantiyāti nīyantiyā. Kopo me upapajjathāti ayaṃ te gihikāle bhariyā brāhmaṇī sīlavatī, pabbajitakāle ca sabrahmacārinībhāvato sahajātā bhaginī, sā tuyhaṃ purato balakkārena ākaḍḍhitvā nīyati. “Bodhibrāhmaṇa, kiṃ te purisabhāva”nti [V 0.0128] purisamānena ussāhito cirakālasayito vammikabilato kenaci purisena ghaṭṭito “susū”ti phaṇaṃ karonto āsiviso viya me cittato kopo sahasā vuṭṭhāsi.

33. As to `odapattakiyā`: a wife taken by touching a water vessel is called an `odapattikā`. This word should be understood as a mere designation for her status as his former wife. She had been given to him by her parents according to the Brahmin marriage custom. The word `odapattakiyā` is in the locative case in the sense of a locative absolute. As to `sahajātā`: born together in the sense of being born into the renunciate life. Therefore he said `ekasāsanī`. And this word `ekasāsanī` is in the nominative case with a locative sense, meaning `ekasāsaniyā` (while she was under the same teaching). As to `nayantiyā`: it means `nīyantiyā` (while she was being led away). As to 'Anger arose in me': 'This virtuous brahmin woman was your wife in lay life, and in the renunciate life, from being a fellow practitioner of the holy life, she is a sister born together with you. She is being dragged away by force from before you.' Roused by manly pride, as if being told, 'O Bodhi-brahmin, what of your manhood?', like a venomous serpent that has lain for a long time in an anthill hole, when struck by some man, makes its hood while hissing, so anger suddenly arose from my mind.

34-5. Sahakope samuppanneti kopuppattiyā saha, tassa uppattisamanantaramevāti attho. Sīlabbatamanussarinti attano sīlapāramiṃ āvajjesiṃ. Tattheva kopaṃ niggaṇhinti tasmiṃ eva āsane yathānisinnova taṃ kopaṃ nivāresiṃ. Nādāsiṃ vaḍḍhitūparīti tato ekavāruppattito upari uddhaṃ vaḍḍhituṃ na adāsiṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kope uppannamatte eva “nanu tvaṃ, bodhiparibbājaka, sabbapāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhitukāmo, tassa te kimidaṃ sīlamattepi upakkhalanaṃ, tayidaṃ gunnaṃ khuramattodake osīdantassa mahāsamuddassa paratīraṃ gaṇhitukāmatā viya hotī”ti attānaṃ paribhāsitvā paṭisaṅkhānabalena tasmiṃ eva khaṇe kopaṃ niggahetvā puna uppajjanavasenassa vaḍḍhituṃ na adāsinti. Tenevāha “yadi naṃ brāhmaṇi”ntiādi.

As to 'As soon as anger arose': this means together with the arising of anger, that is, immediately after its arising. As to 'I remembered my vow of virtue': I reflected on my own perfection of virtue. As to 'I suppressed the anger right there': I restrained that anger in that very seat, just as I was sitting. As to 'I did not let it grow further': I did not allow it to grow further, upwards from that single arising. This is what is meant: as soon as anger had arisen, I admonished myself, saying: 'O Bodhi the ascetic, are you not one who wishes to penetrate to omniscient knowledge after fulfilling all the perfections? For you, what is this stumbling even in the matter of mere virtue? This is like the desire of one who is sinking in water only as deep as a cow's hoof to grasp the further shore of the great ocean.' Having admonished myself thus, through the power of reflective understanding, I suppressed the anger in that very moment and did not allow it to grow by way of arising again. Therefore he said, 'If that brahmin woman...' and so on.

Tassattho – taṃ paribbājikaṃ brāhmaṇiṃ so rājā vā añño vā koci tiṇhāyapi nisitāya sattiyā koṭṭeyya, khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ yadi chindeyya, evaṃ santepi sīlaṃ attano sīlapāramiṃ neva bhindeyyaṃ. Kasmā? Bodhiyā eva kāraṇā, sabbattha akhaṇḍitasīleneva sakkā sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇituṃ, na itarenāti.

Its meaning is this: If that king or some other person were to strike that female ascetic, the brahmin woman, with a sharp, whetted spear, or if they were to cut her into pieces, even so, I would not break my virtue, my perfection of virtue. Why? For the sake of enlightenment itself. It is only with virtue that is unbroken in every respect that one can attain perfect enlightenment; it cannot be attained otherwise.

36. Na [M 0.0135] me sā brāhmaṇī dessāti sā brāhmaṇī jātiyā gottena kulappadesena ācārasampattiyā ciraparicayena pabbajjādiguṇasampattiyā cāti sabbappakārena [P 0.0137] na me dessā na appiyā, etissā mama appiyabhāvo koci natthi. Napi me balaṃ na vijjatīti mayhampi balaṃ na na vijjati, atthi eva. Ahaṃ nāgabalo thāmasampanno, icchamāno sahasā vuṭṭhahitvā taṃ ākaḍḍhante purise nippothetvā taṃ gahetvā yathicchitaṭṭhānaṃ gantuṃ samatthoti dasseti. Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhanti tato paribbājikato sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena sabbaññutaññāṇameva mayhaṃ piyaṃ. Tasmā sīlānurakkhissanti tena kāraṇena sīlameva anurakkhissaṃ.

36. 'She, the brahman woman, is not hateful to me' means: that brahman woman was not hateful or unpleasing to me in any way—by birth, clan, family lineage, accomplishment in conduct, long acquaintance, or accomplishment in the virtues of renunciation. I had no dislike for her whatsoever. 'Nor is it that I have no strength' means: it is not that I lack strength; I have it indeed. I possess the strength of an elephant, am endowed with might, and am capable, if I so wished, of rising up suddenly, striking down the men dragging her, seizing her, and going to whatever place I desire. 'Omniscience is dear to me' means: a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times dearer to me than that female wanderer is omniscient knowledge itself. Therefore, 'I will guard virtue': for that reason, I will guard virtue itself.

Atha so rājā uyyāne papañcaṃ akatvāva sīghataraṃ gantvā taṃ paribbājikaṃ pakkosāpetvā mahantena yasena nimantesi. Sā yasassa aguṇaṃ pabbajjāya guṇaṃ attano bodhisattassa ca mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya saṃvegena pabbajitabhāvañca kathesi.
