Rājā kenaci pariyāyena [V 0.0129] tassā manaṃ alabhanto cintesi – “ayaṃ paribbājikā sīlavatī kalyāṇadhammā, sopi paribbājako imāya ākaḍḍhitvā nīyamānāya na kiñci vippakāraṃ dassesi, sabbattha nirapekkhacitto, na kho pana metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yaṃ evarūpesu guṇavantesu vippakāro, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ paribbājikaṃ gahetvā uyyānaṃ gantvā imaṃ, tañca paribbājakaṃ khamāpeyya”nti? Evaṃ pana cintetvā “paribbājikaṃ uyyānaṃ ānethā”ti purise āṇāpetvā sayaṃ paṭhamataraṃ gantvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi – “bho pabbajita, kiṃ mayā tāya paribbājikāya nīyamānāya kopo te uppajjitthā”ti. Mahāsatto āha –

Then the king, without delay in the garden, returned very quickly, had that female wanderer summoned, and invited her with great honor. She spoke of the fault in honor and the virtue of renunciation, and of how she and the Bodhisatta had gone forth out of spiritual urgency, having abandoned a great mass of wealth. The king, being unable to win her heart by any means, thought: 'This female wanderer is virtuous and of noble character. That male wanderer, too, when she was being dragged away, showed no sign of agitation; his mind was unconcerned in all circumstances. It is indeed not proper for me to have committed this offense against such virtuous ones. What if I were to take this female wanderer to the garden and ask forgiveness of her and that male wanderer?' Having thought thus, he ordered his men, 'Bring the female wanderer to the garden,' and went ahead himself. Approaching the Bodhisatta, he asked, 'Venerable ascetic, did anger arise in you when that female wanderer was being led away by me?' The Great Being replied:

“Uppajji me na muccittha, na me muccittha jīvato;

Rajaṃva vipulā vuṭṭhi, khippameva nivārayi”nti. (jā. 1.10.52);

“It arose in me, but was not released; it was not released from me while I lived. Just as an abundant rain shower quickly settles the dust, so I restrained it.”

Taṃ sutvā rājā “kiṃ nu kho esa kopameva sandhāya vadati, udāhu aññaṃ kiñci sippādika”nti cintetvā puna pucchi –

Hearing this, the king thought, "Is he speaking with reference only to anger, or is there something else, such as a skill?" and asked again:

“Kiṃ [P 0.0138] te uppajji no mucci, kiṃ te no mucci jīvato;

Rajaṃva vipulā vuṭṭhi, katamaṃ taṃ nivārayī”ti. (jā. 1.10.53);

"What arose in you that was not released? What was not released from you while you lived? Like an abundant rain upon the dust, what was it that you restrained?"

Tattha [M 0.0136] uppajjīti ekavāraṃ uppajji, na puna uppajji. Na muccitthāti kāyavacīvikāruppādanavasena pana na muccittha, na naṃ bahi pavattituṃ vissajjesinti attho. Rajaṃva vipulā vuṭṭhīti yathā nāma gimhānaṃ pacchime māse uppannaṃ rajaṃ vipulā akālavuṭṭhidhārā ṭhānaso nivāreti, evaṃ taṃ vūpasamento nivārayiṃ, nivāresinti attho.

Therein, 'it arose' means it arose once; it did not arise again. 'It was not released' means it was not released by way of giving rise to bodily or verbal misconduct; the meaning is, 'I did not let it manifest outwardly.' 'Like an abundant rain upon the dust' means: just as a great, untimely downpour instantly suppresses the dust that has arisen in the last month of the hot season, even so, while pacifying it, I restrained it. This is the meaning.

Athassa mahāpuriso nānappakārena kodhe ādīnavaṃ pakāsento –

Then the Great Being, explaining in various ways the dangers of anger, said:

“Yamhi jāte na passati, ajāte sādhu passati;

So me uppajji no mucci, kodho dummedhagocaro.

“That in the arising of which one does not see, but in the non-arising of which one sees well—that anger, the resort of the unwise, arose in me but was not released.

“Yena jātena nandanti, amittā dukkhamesino;

So me uppajji no mucci, kodho dummedhagocaro.

“That by the arising of which enemies who wish for suffering rejoice—that anger, the resort of the unwise, arose in me but was not released.

“Yasmiñca [V 0.0130] jāyamānamhi, sadatthaṃ nāvabujjhati;

So me uppajji no mucci, kodho dummedhagocaro.

“And that in the arising of which one does not comprehend one's own welfare—that anger, the resort of the unwise, arose in me but was not released.

“Yenābhibhūto kusalaṃ jahāti, parakkare vipulañcāpi atthaṃ;

Sa bhīmaseno balavā pamaddī, kodho mahārājā na me amuccatha.

“That by which one, being overcome, abandons the wholesome and destroys even great welfare; that anger, with its terrifying army, powerful and crushing—O great king, was not released from me.

“Kaṭṭhasmiṃ manthamānasmiṃ, pāvako nāma jāyati;

Tameva kaṭṭhaṃ ḍahati, yasmā so jāyate gini.

“From the rubbing of a fire-stick, fire is born; that very fire then burns the stick from which it was born.

“Evaṃ mandassa posassa, bālassa avijānato;

Sārambhā jāyate kodho, sapi teneva ḍayhati.

“Even so, from agitation in a dull, foolish, and ignorant person, anger is born, and by that very anger is he burned.

“Aggīva tiṇakaṭṭhasmiṃ, kodho yassa pavaḍḍhati;

Nihīyati tassa yaso, kāḷapakkheva candimā.

“For whomsoever anger increases, like fire in grass and sticks, his glory diminishes, like the moon in the dark fortnight.

“Anindho dhūmaketūva, kodho yassūpasammati;

Āpūrati tassa yaso, sukkapakkheva candimā”ti. (jā. 1.10.54-61) –

“For whomsoever anger is pacified, like a fire without fuel, his glory increases, like the moon in the bright fortnight.”

Imāhi gāthāhi dhammaṃ desesi.

With these verses, he taught the Dhamma.

Tattha [M 0.0137] na passatīti attatthampi na passati, pageva paratthaṃ. Sādhu passatīti attatthaṃ paratthaṃ ubhayatthañca [P 0.0139] sammadeva passati. Dummedhagocaroti nippaññānaṃ visayabhūto, nippañño vā gocaro āhāro indhanaṃ etassāti dummedhagocaro. Dukkhamesinoti dukkhaṃ icchantā. Sadatthanti attano atthaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ. Parakkareti apaneyya vināseyya. Sabhīmasenoti so bhīmāya bhayajananiyā mahatiyā kilesasenāya samannāgato. Pamaddīti balavabhāvena satte pamaddanasīlo. Na me amuccathāti mama santikā mokkhaṃ na labhi, abbhantare eva damito, nibbisevano katoti attho. Khīraṃ viya vā muhuttaṃ dadhibhāvena cittena patiṭṭhahitthātipi attho.

Therein, 'one does not see' means one does not see one's own welfare, let alone another's. 'Sees well' means one sees one's own welfare, another's welfare, and the welfare of both, correctly. 'The resort of the unwise' means it is the domain of the unwise; or, it is that for which the unwise is the resort, the food, and the fuel. 'Seeking suffering' means desiring misery. 'One's own welfare' means one's own benefit and growth. 'Destroys' means one would remove or destroy. 'With its terrifying army' means it is endowed with a great, terrifying, fear-generating army of defilements. 'A crusher' means it has the nature of crushing beings by its power. 'Was not released from me' means it did not obtain release from me; the meaning is that it was subdued within, tamed, and rendered non-venomous. Or, as another meaning: just as milk does not for a moment become established as curd, so anger was not established in the mind.

Manthamānasminti araṇisahite mathiyamāne. “Mathamānasmi”ntipi pāṭho. Yasmāti yato kaṭṭhā[V 0.0131]. Ginīti aggi. Bālassa avijānatoti bālassa ajānantassa. Sārambhā jāyateti karaṇuttariyakaraṇalakkhaṇā sārambhā araṇimanthanato viya pāvako kodho jāyate. Sapi tenevāti sopi bālo teneva kodhena kaṭṭhaṃ viya agginā ḍayhati. Anindho dhūmaketūvāti anindhano aggi viya. Tassāti tassa adhivāsanakhantiyā samannāgatassa puggalassa sukkapakkhe cando viya laddho, yaso aparāparaṃ āpūratīti.

“Manthamānasminti” means, “when being churned with a fire-drill.” There is also the reading “mathamānasmiṃ.” “Yasmāti” means “from which wood.” “Ginīti” means fire. “Bālassa avijānato” means “of a fool, of one who does not know.” “Sārambhā jāyate” means: contention, which is characterized by acting excessively, arises; just as fire arises from churning the fire-sticks, so anger arises. “Sapi tenevāti” means: that fool is burned by that very anger, just as wood is burned by fire. “Anindho dhūmaketūvāti” means “like a fire without fuel.” “Tassāti” means: for that person endowed with patient forbearance, the fame that has been obtained increases successively, like the moon in the waxing fortnight.

Rājā mahāsattassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā mahāpurisaṃ paribbājikampi rājagehato āgataṃ khamāpetvā “tumhe pabbajjāsukhaṃ anubhavantā idheva uyyāne vasatha, ahaṃ vo dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā vanditvā pakkāmi. Te ubhopi tattheva vasiṃsu. Aparabhāge paribbājikā kālamakāsi. Bodhisatto himavantaṃ pavisitvā jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokaparāyano ahosi.

Having heard the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, the king asked for forgiveness from the great man and the female wanderer who had come from the royal household, and said, “You who are experiencing the bliss of the renunciate life, should dwell right here in this park. I will provide you with righteous protection, guarding, and security.” Having said this, he paid homage and departed. Both of them dwelled right there. In a later period, the female wanderer passed away. The Bodhisatta entered the Himālaya, brought forth the meditative absorptions and the higher knowledges, and at the end of his life, he was bound for the Brahma-world.

Tadā paribbājikā rāhulamātā ahosi, rājā ānandatthero, bodhiparibbājako lokanātho.

At that time, the female wanderer became Rāhula’s mother, the king became the Elder Ānanda, and the wandering ascetic Bodhi became the Lord of the World.

Tassa idhāpi yathārahaṃ sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ mahantañca ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ [P 0.0140] pahāya mahābhinikkhamanasadisaṃ gehato nikkhamanaṃ, tathā nikkhamitvā pabbajitassa bahujanasammatassa sato paramappicchatāya kulesu ca gaṇesu ca alaggatā, accantameva lābhasakkārajigucchāya [M 0.0138] pavivekābhirati, atisayavatī ca abhisallekhavutti, tathārūpāya sīlavatiyā kalyāṇadhammāya paribbājikāya ananuññātā attano purato balakkārena parāmasiyamānāya sīlapāramiṃ āvajjetvā vikārānāpatti, katāparādhe ca tasmiṃ rājini upagate hitacittataṃ mettacittataṃ upaṭṭhapetvā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikehi samanusāsananti evamādayo idha mahāpurisassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbā. Tenetaṃ vuccati “evaṃ acchariyā hete…pe… dhammassa anudhammato”ti.

Here too, his remaining perfections should be determined as is appropriate. Likewise, there is his departure from home, similar to the Great Renunciation, having abandoned a great mass of wealth and a large retinue of relatives. Also, having gone forth and become an ascetic esteemed by many people, there is his non-attachment to families and groups due to his having extremely few wishes; his delight in seclusion due to his utter disgust for gain and honor; and his exceedingly austere way of life. Also, when a virtuous female wanderer of good character was, without her consent, being forcibly handled in front of him, there is his not falling into a mental corruption, having reflected on the perfection of virtue. And when that king who had committed the offense approached, there is his instruction with teachings concerning the present life and the future, having established a mind of welfare and a mind of loving-kindness. These and other powerful virtues of the Great Being should be made manifest here. Therefore it is said: “Thus, wonderful are these… in accordance with the Dhamma.”

Cūḷabodhicariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷabodhi Cariyā is concluded.

5. Mahiṃsarājacariyāvaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Conduct of the Buffalo King

37. Pañcame [V 0.0132] mahiṃso pavanacārakoti mahāvanacārī vanamahiṃso yadā homīti yojanā. Pavaḍḍhakāyoti vayasampattiyā aṅgapaccaṅgānañca thūlabhāvena abhivaḍḍhakāyo. Balavāti mahābalo thāmasampanno. Mahantoti vipulasarīro. Hatthikalabhappamāṇo kira tadā bodhisattassa kāyo hoti. Bhīmadassanoti mahāsarīratāya vanamahiṃsajātitāya ca sīlaṃ ajānantānaṃ bhayaṃ jananato bhayānakadassano.

37. In the fifth, “mahiṃso pavanacārako” is to be connected as: “when I was a wild buffalo, a great forest-dweller.” “Pavaḍḍhakāyo” means: his body was fully developed due to reaching maturity and due to the thickness of his major and minor limbs. “Balavāti” means: of great strength, endowed with stamina. “Mahantoti” means: of vast body. It is said that at that time the Bodhisatta’s body was the size of a young elephant. “Bhīmadassano” means: of fearsome appearance, because he generated fear in those who did not know his virtue, on account of his great body and his being of the forest buffalo species.

38. Pabbhāreti olambakasilākucchiyaṃ. Dakāsayeti jalāsayasamīpe. Hotettha ṭhānanti ettha mahāvane yo koci padeso vanamahiṃsānaṃ tiṭṭhanaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tahiṃ tahinti tattha tattha.

38. “Pabbhāre” means in the hollow of an overhanging rock. “Dakāsaye” means near a reservoir. “Hotettha ṭhānanti” means: here in this great forest, whatever spot is a standing place for forest buffaloes. “Tahiṃ tahinti” means “in this or that place.”

39. Vicarantoti vihāraphāsukaṃ vīmaṃsituṃ vicaranto. Ṭhānaṃ addasa bhaddakanti evaṃ vicaranto tasmiṃ mahāraññe bhaddakaṃ mayhaṃ phāsukaṃ rukkhamūlaṭṭhānaṃ addakkhiṃ. Disvā ca taṃ ṭhānaṃ upagantvāna, tiṭṭhāmi ca sayāmi ca gocaraṃ gahetvā divā taṃ [P 0.0141] rukkhamūlaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā ṭhānasayanehi vītināmemīti dasseti.

39. “Vicarantoti” means “wandering” in order to investigate a comfortable dwelling. “Ṭhānaṃ addasa bhaddakanti” means: wandering thus in that great forest, “I saw a good, comfortable place for myself at the root of a tree.” And having seen that place and approached it, I both stand and lie down. This shows that, having taken his food, he goes to that place at the root of the tree during the day and passes the time by standing and lying down.

40. Tadā kira bodhisatto himavantappadese mahiṃsayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto thāmasampanno mahāsarīro hatthikalabhappamāṇo pabbatapādapabbhāragiriduggavanaghaṭādīsu [M 0.0139] vicaranto ekaṃ phāsukaṃ mahārukkhamūlaṃ disvā gocaraṃ gahetvā divā tattha vasati. Atheko lolamakkaṭo rukkhā otaritvā mahāsattassa piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhitvā uccārapassāvaṃ katvā siṅgesu gaṇhitvā olambanto naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā dolāyanto kīḷi. Bodhisatto khantimettānuddayasampadāya taṃ tassa anācāraṃ na manasākāsi. Makkaṭo punappunaṃ tatheva karoti. Tena vuttaṃ “athettha kapi māgantvā”tiādi.

40. It is said that at that time, the Bodhisatta was born in the buffalo womb in the region of the Himālaya. Having reached maturity, he was endowed with stamina, of great body, the size of a young elephant. While wandering among the foothills, mountain slopes, impassable mountains, forest thickets, and so on, he saw a comfortable place at the root of a great tree, and having gathered his food, he dwelled there during the day. Then a certain restless monkey descended from the tree, climbed onto the Great Being’s back, defecated and urinated, and played, grasping the horns and hanging down, grasping the tail and swinging. The Bodhisatta, through his endowment with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, paid no mind to that misconduct of his. The monkey did the very same thing again and again. Therefore it was said: “Then a certain monkey, having come there,” and so on.

Tattha kapi māgantvāti kapi āgantvā, ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Pāpoti lāmako. Anariyoti anaye iriyanena aye ca na iriyanena anariyo, nihīnācāroti attho. Lahūti lolo. Khandheti khandhappadese. Muttetīti passāvaṃ karoti. Ohadetīti karīsaṃ ossajjati. Tanti taṃ maṃ, tadā mahiṃsabhūtaṃ maṃ.

Therein, “kapi māgantvā” is “kapi āgantvā” (a monkey, having come); the letter “ma” is for euphonic connection. “Pāpo” means wicked. “Anariyo” (ignoble) means one who conducts oneself improperly and not properly; the meaning is “one of base conduct.” “Lahū” means restless. “Khandhe” refers to the shoulder region. “Mutteti” means he urinates. “Ohadeti” means he drops feces. “Taṃ” means “that me”—me who at that time was a buffalo.

41. Sakimpi [V 0.0133] divasanti ekadivasampi dūseti maṃ sabbakālampi. Tenāha “dūseti maṃ sabbakāla”nti. Na kevalañca dutiyatatiyacatutthadivasamattaṃ, atha kho sabbakālampi maṃ passāvādīhi dūseti. Yadā yadā muttādīni kātukāmo, tadā tadā mayhameva upari karotīti dasseti. Upaddutoti bādhito, tena siṅgesu olambanādinā muttādiasucimakkhaṇena tassa ca apaharaṇatthaṃ anekavāraṃ siṅgakoṭīhi vālaggena ca anekavāraṃ kaddamapaṃsumissakaṃ udakaṃ siñcitvā dhovanena ca nippīḷito homīti attho.

41. “Sakimpi divasanti” means he defiles me even for a single day, and also for all time. Therefore, he said: “He defiles me all the time.” It is not just for the second, third, or fourth day, but rather he defiles me with urine and so on all the time. This shows that whenever he wishes to urinate and so on, he does it right on top of me. “Upaddutoti” means afflicted. The meaning is: I am oppressed by that monkey hanging from my horns and so on, and by its smearing me with urine and other filth. And I am also oppressed by having to wash myself to remove it, repeatedly sprinkling water mixed with mud and dust and cleaning myself many times with the tips of my horns and the tip of my tail.

42. Yakkhoti tasmiṃ rukkhe adhivatthā devatā. Maṃ idamabravīti rukkhakkhandhe ṭhatvā “mahiṃsarāja, kasmā imassa duṭṭhamakkaṭassa avamānaṃ sahasī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsento nāsehetaṃ chavaṃ pāpaṃ [P 0.0142], siṅgehi ca khurehi cāti idaṃ vacanaṃ maṃ abhāsi.

42. "Yakkha" means the deity dwelling in that tree. "He said this to me" means: standing on the tree trunk, and to make this matter clear, the deity spoke to me, saying, "O king of buffaloes, why do you endure the contempt of this wicked monkey?" and spoke these words: "Destroy this evil corpse with your horns and hooves!"

43. Evaṃ vutte tadā yakkheti tadā tasmiṃ kāle tasmiṃ yakkhe evaṃ vutte sati. Ahaṃ taṃ idamabravinti ahaṃ taṃ yakkhaṃ idaṃ idāni vakkhamānaṃ abraviṃ abhāsiṃ. Kuṇapenāti kilesāsucipaggharaṇena sucijātikānaṃ sādhūnaṃ paramajigucchanīyatāya atiduggandhavāyanena ca kuṇapasadisatāya kuṇapena. Pāpenāti pāṇātipātapāpena. Anariyenāti anariyānaṃ [M 0.0140] asādhūnaṃ māgavikanesādādīnaṃ hīnapurisānaṃ dhammattā anariyena, kiṃ kena kāraṇena, tvaṃ devate maṃ makkhesi, ayuttaṃ tayā vuttaṃ maṃ pāpe niyojentiyāti dasseti.

43. "When this was said then by the yakkha" means: at that time, when this was said by that yakkha. "I said this to him" means: I spoke to that yakkha this which is now about to be said. "With a corpse" (kuṇapena) means: because it is like a corpse due to the oozing of the impurity of defilements, being utterly repulsive to the virtuous of pure nature, and because it spreads an extremely foul smell. "With evil" (pāpena) means: with the evil of taking life. "By what is ignoble" (anariyena) means: because it is the practice of the ignoble, the unvirtuous, base men such as hunters and fowlers. This shows the meaning: "For what reason, O deity, do you smear me? What you have said is improper, urging me to do evil."

44. Idāni tasmiṃ pāpadhamme ādīnavaṃ pakāsento “yadiha”ntiādimāha. Tassattho – bhadde devate, ahaṃ tassa yadi kujjheyyaṃ, tatopi lāmakataro bhaveyyaṃ. Yena hi adhammacaraṇena so bālamakkaṭo nihīno nāma jāto, sace panāhaṃ tatopi balavataraṃ pāpadhammaṃ careyyaṃ, nanu tena tato pāpataro bhaveyyaṃ, aṭṭhānañcetaṃ yadihaṃ idhalokaparalokaṃ taduttari ca jānitvā ṭhito ekanteneva parahitāya paṭipanno evarūpaṃ pāpadhammaṃ careyyanti. Kiñca bhiyyo – sīlañca me pabhijjeyyāti ahañceva kho pana evarūpaṃ pāpaṃ kareyyaṃ, mayhaṃ sīlapāramī khaṇḍitā siyā. Viññū ca garaheyyu manti paṇḍitā ca devamanussā maṃ garaheyyuṃ “passatha, bho, ayaṃ bodhisatto bodhipariyesanaṃ caramāno evarūpaṃ pāpaṃ akāsī”ti.

44. Now, revealing the danger in that evil quality, he says, "If I..." etc. The meaning is: "Good deity, if I were to be angry with him, I would be even more base than him. For by unrighteous conduct, that foolish monkey was born in a low state. But if I were to practice an even more powerful evil, would I not be even more evil than him? And it is impossible that I, knowing this world, the next world, and what is beyond, and being intent solely on the welfare of others, should practice such evil. Moreover, my virtue would be destroyed—indeed, if I were to do such evil, my perfection of virtue would be broken. And the wise would criticize me—the wise, both gods and humans, would criticize me, saying, 'Look, sirs, this Bodhisatta, while undertaking the quest for enlightenment, has done such an evil thing!'"

45. Hīḷitā jīvitā vāpīti vā-saddo avadhāraṇe. Evaṃ viññūhi hīḷitā garahitā jīvitāpi parisuddhena parisuddhasīlena hutvā mataṃ vā maraṇameva varaṃ uttamaṃ seyyo. Kyāhaṃ jīvitahetupi[V 0.0134], kāhāmi paraheṭhananti evaṃ jānanto ca ahaṃ mayhaṃ jīvitanimittampi parasattavihiṃsanaṃ kiṃ kāhāmi kiṃ karissāmi, etassa karaṇe kāraṇaṃ natthīti attho.

45. In "a life despised" (hīḷitā jīvitā vāpi), the particle 'vā' is for emphasis. Thus, death as one of pure virtue is indeed better, supreme, and superior to a life despised and censured by the wise. As for "Why should I, even for the sake of life, harm another?": this means, knowing this, why should I harm another being even for the sake of my own life? There is no reason to do this.

Ayaṃ pana aññepi maṃ viya maññamāno evaṃ [P 0.0143] anācāraṃ karissati, tato yesaṃ caṇḍamahiṃsānaṃ evaṃ karissati, te eva etaṃ vadhissanti, sā etassa aññehi māraṇā mayhaṃ dukkhato ca pāṇātipātato ca mutti bhavissatīti āha. Tena vuttaṃ –

"This monkey, however, thinking others are also like me, will misbehave in this way. Then, those fierce buffaloes towards whom he acts thus, they themselves will kill him. His being killed by others will be my release from suffering and from the act of taking life," he thought. Therefore it was said:

46.

46.

“Mamevāyaṃ maññamāno, aññepevaṃ karissati;

Teva tassa vadhissanti, sā me mutti bhavissatī”ti.

"Thinking others are just like me, he will act thus towards them as well; They will kill him, and that will be my release."

Tattha mamevāyanti maṃ viya ayaṃ. Aññepīti aññesampi. Sesaṃ vuttatthameva.

Therein, "thinking this one is me" means this monkey thinks others are like me. "Towards others also" means towards others as well. The rest has the meaning already stated.

47. Hīnamajjhimaukkaṭṭheti [M 0.0141] hīne ca majjhime ca ukkaṭṭhe ca nimittabhūte. Sahanto avamānitanti vibhāgaṃ akatvā tehi pavattitaṃ avamānaṃ paribhavaṃ sahanto khamanto. Evaṃ labhati sappaññoti evaṃ hīnādīsu vibhāgaṃ akatvā khantimettānuddayaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā tadaparādhaṃ sahanto sīlādipāramiyo brūhetvā manasā yathāpatthitaṃ yathicchitaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ labhati paṭivijjhati, tassa taṃ na dūreti.

47. "Low, middling, and excellent" means: with regard to beings who are low, middling, and excellent. "Enduring contempt" means: enduring and tolerating the contempt and scorn instigated by them without making a distinction. "Thus a wise person obtains" means: in this way, without making a distinction regarding the low, etc., by establishing patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, and enduring their offense, by cultivating the perfections of virtue and so on, with his mind, he obtains and penetrates the omniscient knowledge as he has resolved and as he desires; for him, that is not far.

Evaṃ mahāsatto attano ajjhāsayaṃ pakāsento devatāya dhammaṃ desesi. So katipāhaccayena aññattha gato. Añño caṇḍamahiṃso nivāsaphāsutāya taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā aṭṭhāsi. Duṭṭhamakkaṭo “so eva aya”nti saññāya tassa piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhitvā tatheva anācāraṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ so vidhunanto bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā siṅgena hadaye vijjhitvā pādehi madditvā sañcuṇṇesi.

Thus, the Great Being, revealing his own disposition, taught the Dhamma to the deity. After a few days, he went elsewhere. Another fierce buffalo, for the sake of a comfortable dwelling, went to that place and stood there. The wicked monkey, perceiving, ‘This is the same one,’ climbed onto its back and behaved indecently as before. Then, shaking him off, the buffalo threw him to the ground, pierced his heart with its horn, trampled him with its feet, and crushed him to pieces.

Tadā sīlavā mahiṃsarājā lokanātho.

At that time, the virtuous buffalo king was the Protector of the World.

Tassa idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva yathārahaṃ sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā hatthināga- (cariyā. 2.1 ādayo) bhūridatta- (cariyā. 2.11 ādayo) campeyyanāgarāja- (cariyā. 2.20 ādayo) cariyāsu viya idha mahāsattassa guṇānubhāvā veditabbā.

Here too, his remaining perfections should be determined appropriately, in the manner explained below. Similarly, just as in the conduct stories of Hatthināga, Bhūridatta, and the Nāga King Campeyya, here too the virtues and powers of the Great Being should be understood.

Mahiṃsarājacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Conduct of the Buffalo King is concluded.

6. Rurumigarājacariyāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Conduct of the Ruru Deer King

48. Chaṭṭhe [V 0.0135][P 0.0144] sutattakanakasannibhoti yathā suṭṭhu apagatasabbakāḷako hoti, evaṃ aggimhi pakkhipitvā sutattakanakasannibho. Migarājā ruru nāmāti jātisiddhena nāmena ruru nāma migarājā, jātito ruru, migānañca rājāti attho. Paramasīlasamāhitoti uttamasīlasamāhito, visuddhasīlo ceva samāhitacitto ca, visuddhasīle vā sammā āhitacittoti evamettha attho veditabbo.

48. In the sixth story, "like gold thoroughly heated" (sutattakanakasannibho) means: just as gold becomes completely free of all impurities when placed in a fire, so too was he like gold thoroughly heated. "The deer king named Ruru" (miga-rājā ruru nāma) means: by his birth-given name, he was the deer king named Ruru; by species, a Ruru deer, and also the king of deer—this is the meaning. "Of supreme virtue and composure" (paramasīlasamāhito) means: endowed with the highest virtue; that is, both pure in virtue and composed in mind, or alternatively, one whose mind is rightly established in pure virtue—thus the meaning should be understood here.

Tadā bodhisatto rurumigayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Tassa sarīracchavi suṭṭhu tāpetvā majjitakañcanapaṭṭavaṇṇo ahosi, hatthapādā lākhārasaparikammakatā viya, naṅguṭṭhaṃ camarīnaṅguṭṭhaṃ viya, siṅgāni rajatadāmavaṇṇāni akkhīni sumajjitamaṇiguḷikā [M 0.0142] viya, mukhaṃ odahitvā ṭhapitarattakambalageṇḍukā viya. So janasaṃsaggaṃ pahāya vivekavāsaṃ vasitukāmo parivāraṃ chaḍḍetvā ekakova gaṅgānivattane ramaṇīye sālamissake supupphitapavane vasati. Tena vuttaṃ –

At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the species of the Ruru deer. The skin of his body was the color of a well-burnished plate of gold; his fore- and hind-feet were as if finely worked with lac; his tail was like that of a chowrie; his horns had the color of silver garlands; his eyes were like well-polished jewel orbs; and his mouth was like a ball of red wool placed with its opening closed. Desiring to abandon the company of others and dwell in seclusion, he left his retinue and lived entirely alone in a delightful, well-flowered forest interspersed with sal trees, at a bend in the Ganges. Therefore, it was said:

49.

49.

“Ramme padese ramaṇīye, vivitte amanussake;

Tattha vāsaṃ upagañchiṃ, gaṅgākūle manorame”ti.

‘In a delightful and charming place, secluded and uninhabited, there I took up my dwelling, on the lovely bank of the Ganges.’

Tattha ramme padeseti muttātalasadisavālukācuṇṇapaṇḍarehi bhūmibhāgehi siniddhaharitatiṇasañcaritehi vanatthalehi cittattharaṇehi viya nānāvaṇṇavicittehi silātalehi maṇikkhandhanimmalasalilehi jalāsayehi ca samannāgatattā yebhuyyena ca indagopakavaṇṇāya rattāya sukhasamphassāya tiṇajātiyā sañchannattā ramme araññappadese. Rammaṇīyeti pupphaphalapallavālaṅkatavipulasākhāvinaddhehi nānāvidhadijagaṇūpakūjitehi vividhatarulatāvanavirājitehi yebhuyyena ambasālavanasaṇḍamaṇḍitehi vanagahanehi upasobhitattā tattha paviṭṭhassa janassa ratijananaṭṭhena ramaṇīye. Vuttampi cetaṃ rurumigarājajātake –

Therein, ‘in a delightful place’ means in a delightful forest region, because it was endowed with areas of ground white with fine sand like a surface of pearls; with forest glades covered in smooth, green grass; with stone slabs of various hues, variegated like a patterned carpet; and with reservoirs of water as clear as a jewel column; and because it was mostly covered with a species of grass that was red, the color of the indagopaka insect, and pleasant to the touch. ‘Charming’ means charming in the sense of generating delight for a person who entered it, because it was beautified by forest thickets, adorned with groves of mango and sal trees, resplendent with various trees and creepers, and resounding with the calls of diverse flocks of birds whose wide branches were festooned with flowers, fruits, and new shoots. And this was also said in the Jātaka of the Ruru Deer King:

“Etasmiṃ [P 0.0145] vanasaṇḍasmiṃ, ambā sālā ca pupphitā;

Indagopakasañchanno, ettheso tiṭṭhate migo”ti. (jā. 1.13.119);

‘In this forest grove, mango and sal trees are in bloom; the ground is veiled in the red of the indagopaka, and here this deer dwells.’

Vivitteti janavāsavirahena suññe. Amanussaketi sañcaraṇamanussānampi tattha abhāvena manussarahite[V 0.0136]. Manorameti yathāvuttaguṇasampattiyā visesato pavivekakāmānaṃ mano rametīti manorame.

‘Secluded’ means empty, due to the absence of human habitation. ‘Uninhabited’ means devoid of humans, because of the absence there of even wandering people. ‘Lovely’ means it delights the mind—`mano rameti`—especially of those who desire solitude, due to its possession of the aforementioned qualities; hence, `manorame`.

50. Atha uparigaṅgāyāti ettha athāti adhikāre nipāto, tena mayi tattha tathā vasante idaṃ adhikārantaraṃ uppannanti dīpeti. Uparigaṅgāyāti gaṅgāya nadiyā uparisote. Dhanikehi paripīḷitoti iṇaṃ gahetvā taṃ dātuṃ asakkonto iṇāyikehi codiyamāno.

50. Regarding ‘Then, on the upper Ganges’: here, `atha` is a particle indicating a new topic. It shows: ‘While I was dwelling there in that way, this other matter arose.’ ‘On the upper Ganges’ means in the upper stream of the river Ganges. ‘Harassed by creditors’ means being pressed by his creditors, as he was unable to repay the debt he had taken.

Eko kira bārāṇasiseṭṭhi attano puttaṃ “ayaṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhanto kilamissatī”ti kiñci sippaṃ na uggaṇhāpesi. Gītavāditanaccakhādanabhojanato uddhaṃ na kiñci aññāsi. Taṃ vayappattaṃ patirūpena dārena saṃyojetvā dhanaṃ niyyātetvā mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. So tesaṃ accayena [M 0.0143] itthidhuttasurādhuttādiparivuto nānābyasanamukhehi sabbaṃ dhanaṃ viddhaṃsetvā tattha tattha iṇaṃ ādāya tampi dātuṃ asakkonto dhanikehi codiyamāno “kiṃ mayhaṃ jīvitena, tenevamhi attabhāvena añño viya jāto, maraṇaṃ me seyyo”ti cintetvā iṇāyike āha – “tumhākaṃ iṇapaṇṇāni gahetvā āgacchatha, gaṅgātīre me nihitaṃ kulasantakaṃ dhanaṃ atthi, taṃ vo dassāmī”ti. Te tena saddhiṃ agamaṃsu. So “idha dhanaṃ, ettha dhana”nti nidhiṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhanto viya “evaṃ me iṇamokkho bhavissatī”ti palāyitvā gaṅgāyaṃ pati. So caṇḍasotena vuyhanto kāruññaravaṃ ravi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha uparigaṅgāyā”tiādi.

It is said that a certain merchant of Benares, thinking, ‘This son of mine will become weary if he learns a craft,’ did not have him learn any craft at all. He knew nothing beyond singing, playing music, dancing, eating, and drinking. When his son came of age, his parents joined him in a suitable marriage, handed over their wealth, and passed away. After their passing, he, surrounded by profligates, drunkards, and the like, squandered all his wealth through various means of ruin. Having taken loans here and there and being unable to repay them, he was pressed by his creditors. He thought, ‘What is this life to me? In this very existence, I have become like a stranger. Death is better for me.’ He then told his creditors, ‘Take your debt certificates and come. By the bank of the Ganges, there is ancestral wealth of mine that is buried. I will give it to you.’ They went with him. As if pointing out the location of the treasure, saying, ‘The wealth is here, the wealth is there,’ he thought, ‘In this way, I will be free from debt,’ and running away, he fell into the Ganges. Being swept away by the fierce current, he cried out piteously. Therefore, it was said: ‘Then, on the upper Ganges…,’ and so on.

Tattha jīvāmi vā marāmi vāti imasmiṃ gaṅgāsote patito jīvāmi vā marāmi vā, jīvitaṃ vā me ettha hotu maraṇaṃ vā, ubhayathāpi iṇāyikapīḷā na hotīti adhippāyo.

Therein, ‘Whether I live or die’ has this meaning: ‘Having fallen into this current of the Ganges, whether I live or whether I die, whether life or death be my lot here, in either case there is no torment from creditors.’

51. Majjhe gaṅgāya [P 0.0146] gacchatīti so puriso rattindivaṃ gaṅgāya vuyhamāno jīvitapemassa vijjamānattā maraṇaṃ appatto maraṇabhayatajjito hutvā karuṇaṃ ravaṃ ravanto gaṅgāya majjhe mahodakena gacchati.

51. ‘He goes in the middle of the Ganges’ means: that man, being swept along by the Ganges day and night, had not yet met his death because a remnant of his life-span remained. Terrified by the fear of death, he went along in the middle of the Ganges in the great flood, crying out a piteous cry.

52. Atha mahāpuriso aḍḍharattasamaye tassa taṃ karuṇaṃ paridevantassa paridevitasaddaṃ sutvā “manussasaddo sūyati, mā mayi idha dharante maratu, jīvitamassa dassāmī”ti cintetvā sayanagumbā vuṭṭhāya nadītīraṃ gantvā “ambho purisa, mā bhāyi, jīvitaṃ te dassāmī”ti vatvā assāsetvā sotaṃ chindanto gantvā taṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ āropetvā tīraṃ pāpetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ netvā parissamaṃ vinodetvā phalāphalāni datvā dvīhatīhaccayena taṃ āha – “ambho purisa[V 0.0137], ahaṃ taṃ bārāṇasigāmimaggaṃ pāpessāmi, tvaṃ ‘asukaṭṭhāne nāma kañcanamigo vasatī’ti mā kassaci ārocehī”ti. So “sādhu, sāmī”ti sampaṭicchi. Mahāsatto taṃ attano piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā bārāṇasimagge otāretvā nivatti. Tena vuttaṃ – “tassāhaṃ saddaṃ sutvāna, karuṇaṃ paridevato”tiādi.

52. Then the Great Being, at midnight, hearing the sound of that man lamenting piteously, thought: ‘A human voice is heard. While I am here, let him not die. I will give him his life.’ Rising from his resting-thicket, he went to the riverbank and, after reassuring the man by saying, ‘O man, do not be afraid; I will give you your life,’ he cut across the current, went to him, and placing him on his back, brought him to the bank. He led him to his own dwelling place, relieved his exhaustion, and gave him various fruits. After two or three days had passed, he said to him, ‘O man, I will take you to the road to Benares, but you must not tell anyone, “A golden deer lives in such-and-such a place.”’ The man agreed, saying, ‘Very well, master.’ The Great Being placed the man on his back, set him down on the road to Benares, and returned. Therefore, it was said: ‘Hearing his voice, as he was piteously lamenting…,’ and so on.

Tattha kosi tvaṃ naroti tvaṃ ko manusso asi, kuto idha vuyhamāno āgatosīti attho.

Therein, ‘Who are you, O man?’ means: ‘What man are you? From where have you come, being swept along to this place?’

53. Attano [M 0.0144] karaṇanti attano kiriyaṃ. Dhanikehi bhītoti iṇāyikehi ubbiggo. Tasitoti utrasto.

53. ‘By my own doing’ means by my own action. ‘Afraid of creditors’ means distressed by lenders. ‘Frightened’ means terrified.

54. Tassa katvāna kāruññaṃ, cajitvā mama jīvitanti kāruññaṃ katvā mahākaruṇāya samussāhito mama jīvitaṃ tassa purisassa pariccajitvā. Pavisitvā nīhariṃ tassāti nadiṃ pavisitvā sotaṃ chindanto ujukameva gantvā mama piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā tato taṃ nīhariṃ. Tassāti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. “Tatthā”tipi pāḷi, tattha nadiyanti attho. Andhakāramhi rattiyāti rattiyā andhakārasamaye, kāḷapakkharattiyanti attho.

54. 'Having shown him compassion, having given up my life' means: urged on by great compassion, I gave up my life for that man. 'Having entered, I brought him out' means: having entered the river, cutting through the current and going straight, I placed him upon my back and brought him out from there. The word 'tassa' is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative. 'Tatthā' is also a reading in the text, meaning 'there in the river.' 'In the darkness of night' means at the dark time of the night, that is, the night of the dark fortnight.

55. Assatthakālamaññāyāti parissamaṃ apanetvā phalāphalāni datvā dvīhatīhaccayena kilamathassa [P 0.0147] vigatakālaṃ jānitvā. Ekaṃ taṃ varaṃ yācāmīti ahaṃ taṃ ekaṃ varaṃ yācāmi, mayhaṃ ekaṃ varaṃ dehīti attho. Kiṃ taṃ varanti ce? Āha – mā maṃ kassaci pāvadāti “asukaṭṭhāne suvaṇṇamigo vasatī”ti kassaci rañño vā rājamahāmattassa vā maṃ mā pāvada.

55. 'Recognizing the time of his recovery' means: having removed his fatigue by giving him fruits, and knowing after two or three days that the time of his exhaustion had passed. 'I ask you for one boon' means: 'I ask you for one boon; give me one boon.' If it is asked, 'What is that boon?' He said, 'Do not speak of me to anyone,' meaning: 'Do not tell any king or great royal minister, "A golden deer lives in such-and-such a place."

Atha tasmiṃ purise bārāṇasiṃ paviṭṭhadivaseyeva so rājā “ahaṃ, deva, suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ migaṃ mayhaṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ supinena addasaṃ, ahañhi saccasupinā, addhā so vijjati, tasmā kañcanamigassa dhammaṃ sotukāmā labhissāmi ce jīvissāmi, no ce me jīvitaṃ natthī”ti aggamahesiyā vutto taṃ assāsetvā “sace manussaloke atthi, labhissasī”ti vatvā brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā “suvaṇṇamigā nāma hontī”ti pucchitvā “āma, deva, hontī”ti sutvā sahassatthavikaṃ suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭake ṭhapetvā taṃ hatthikkhandhaṃ āropetvā nagare bheriṃ carāpesi – “yo suvaṇṇamigaṃ [V 0.0138] ācikkhissati, tassa hatthinā saddhiṃ imaṃ dassāmī”ti. Tato uttarimpi dātukāmo hutvā –

Then, on the very day that man entered Bārāṇasī, the king was told this by his chief queen: 'Your Majesty, I saw in a dream a golden-colored deer teaching me the Dhamma. My dream is true; he surely exists. Therefore, if I get to hear the Dhamma from the golden deer, I shall live; if not, I shall not live.' The king comforted her, saying, 'If such a one exists in the world of humans, you shall get him.' Then, having summoned the brahmins and asked, 'Do golden deer exist?' and having heard them say, 'Yes, Your Majesty, they do,' he had a purse of a thousand coins placed in a golden basket, set it upon an elephant's back, and had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: 'Whoever points out the golden deer, to him I will give this, together with the elephant.' Then, desiring to give even more...

“Tassa gāmavaraṃ dammi, nāriyo ca alaṅkatā;

Yo metaṃ migamakkhāti, migānaṃ migamuttama”nti. (jā. 1.13.117) –

I shall give him a choice village, and women finely adorned; whoever points out to me this deer, the best among deer.

Gāthaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhāpetvā sakalanagare vācāpesi. Atha so seṭṭhiputto taṃ gāthaṃ sutvā rājapurisānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “rañño evarūpaṃ migaṃ [M 0.0145] ācikkhissāmi, maṃ rājānaṃ dassethā”ti āha. Rājapurisā taṃ rañño santikaṃ netvā tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā “saccaṃ, bho, addasā”ti pucchi. So “saccaṃ, deva, mayā saddhiṃ āgacchatu, ahaṃ taṃ dassessāmī”ti āha. Rājā tameva purisaṃ maggadesakaṃ katvā mahantena parivārena taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā tena mittadubbhinā purisena dassitaṃ padesaṃ [P 0.0148] āvudhahatthe purise samantatova parivāretvā “ukkuṭṭhiṃ karothā”ti vatvā sayaṃ katipayehi janehi saddhiṃ ekamante aṭṭhāsi. Sopi puriso avidūre aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto saddaṃ sutvā “mahato balakāyassa saddo, addhā tamhā me purisā bhayena uppannena bhavitabba”nti ñatvā uṭṭhāya sakalaparisaṃ oloketvā “rañño ṭhitaṭṭhāneyeva me sotthi bhavissatī”ti rājābhimukho pāyāsi. Rājā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “nāgabalo avattharanto āgaccheyyā”ti saraṃ sannayhitvā “imaṃ migaṃ santāsetvā sace palāyati, vijjhitvā dubbalaṃ katvā gaṇhissāmī”ti bodhisattābhimukho ahosi. Mahāsatto –

Having had the verse inscribed on a golden plaque, he had it read aloud throughout the entire city. Then that merchant’s son, hearing the verse, went to the king’s men and said, 'I will point out such a deer to the king; show me to the king.' The king’s men took him to the king and reported the matter. The king asked, 'Is it true, sir, that you have seen him?' He replied, 'It is true, Your Majesty. Let the king come with me, and I will show him.' The king, making that very man his guide, went to that place with a large retinue. At the spot pointed out by that friend-betraying man, he had it surrounded on all sides by men with weapons in hand. He said, 'Make a great shout!' and stood aside himself with a few men. That man also stood not far away. The Great Being, hearing the sound, knew, 'This is the sound of a great host; surely, a danger has arisen for me from that man.' Rising and surveying the entire assembly, he thought, 'My safety will be right where the king is standing,' and he went towards the king. The king, seeing him approaching, thought, 'He might charge with the strength of an elephant,' and fitting an arrow to his bow, he thought, 'I will frighten this deer, and if he flees, I will shoot him, weaken him, and capture him.' He thus faced the Bodhisatta. The Great Being—

“Āgamehi mahārāja, mā maṃ vijjhi rathesabha;

Ko nu te idamakkhāsi, ettheso tiṭṭhate migo”ti. (jā. 1.13.121) –

'Wait, great king! Do not shoot me, O lord of the realm! Who was it that told you, "This deer stands here"?'

Gāthaṃ abhāsi. Rājā tassa madhurakathāya bajjhitvā saraṃ paṭisaṃharitvā gāravena aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsattopi rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ akāsi. Mahājanopi sabbāvudhāni apanetvā āgantvā rājānaṃ parivāresi. Tena vuttaṃ –

He spoke this verse. The king, captivated by his sweet speech, withdrew his arrow and stood respectfully. The Great Being, in turn, approached the king and made a pleasant and friendly greeting. The great crowd also, laying aside all their weapons, came and surrounded the king. Therefore it was said:

56.

56.

“Nagaraṃ gantvāna ācikkhi, pucchito dhanahetuko;

Rājānaṃ so gahetvāna, upagañchi mamantika”nti.

'Having gone to the city, he informed on me for the sake of wealth; then, taking the king with him, he came into my presence.'

Tassattho [V 0.0139] – yo mittadubbhī pāpapuriso jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā tathā mayā pāṇasaṃsayato mocito bārāṇasinagaraṃ gantvā attanā laddhabbadhananimittaṃ rañño maṃ ācikkhi, ācikkhitvā so rañño gāhāpetuṃ maggadesako hutvā rājānaṃ gahetvā mama santikamupāgamīti.

Its meaning is this: That wicked man, a betrayer of a friend, was freed by me from peril to his life, even as I gave up my own life for him. He then went to the city of Bārāṇasī and, for the sake of the wealth he was to obtain, informed the king about me. Having informed him, he became a guide in order to have me seized, and taking the king, he came into my presence.

Mahāsatto suvaṇṇakiṅkiṇikaṃ cālento viya madhurassarena rājānaṃ puna pucchi – “ko nu te idamakkhāsi, ettheso [P 0.0149] tiṭṭhate migo”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe so pāpapuriso thokaṃ paṭikkamitvā sotapathe aṭṭhāsi[M 0.0146]. Rājā “iminā me tvaṃ dassito”ti taṃ purisaṃ niddisi. Tato bodhisatto –

The Great Being, with a sweet voice like the ringing of a golden bell, asked the king again: 'Who was it that told you, "This deer stands here"?' At that moment, that wicked man stepped back a little and stood within earshot. The king pointed to that man, saying, 'It was by this man that you were pointed out to me.' Then the Bodhisatta—

“Saccaṃ kireva māhaṃsu, narā ekacciyā idha;

Kaṭṭhaṃ niplavitaṃ seyyo, na tvevekacciyo naro”ti. (jā. 1.13.123) –

'Truly indeed have some men here spoken a truth: "Better to pull a floating log from the water, than a certain kind of man."

Gāthamāha. Taṃ sutvā rājā saṃvegajāto –

He spoke this verse. Hearing it, the king was struck with profound emotion and said:

“Kiṃ nu ruru garahasi migānaṃ, kiṃ pakkhīnaṃ kiṃ pana mānusānaṃ;

Bhayañhi maṃ vindatinapparūpaṃ, sutvāna taṃ mānusiṃ bhāsamāna”nti. (jā. 1.13.124) –

'Is it the deer you reproach, O Ruru? Or the birds? Or is it humans? For a fear of no small measure comes upon me, hearing you speak with a human voice.'

Gāthamāha. Tato mahāpuriso “mahārāja, na migaṃ na pakkhiṃ garahāmi, manussaṃ pana garahāmī”ti dassento –

The king spoke this verse. Then the Great Being, explaining, 'Great king, I do not reproach the deer, nor do I reproach the birds; it is a human, however, that I reproach,' said:

“Yamuddhariṃ vāhane vuyhamānaṃ, mahodake salile sīghasote;

Tatonidānaṃ bhayamāgataṃ mama, dukkho have rāja asabbhi saṅgamo”ti. (jā. 1.13.125) –

Whom I rescued as he was being carried away by the current, in the great water, in the swift-flowing stream; for that reason, fear has come to me. Truly, O king, association with the wicked is painful.

Āha.

He said.

Tattha niplavitanti uddharitaṃ, ekacciyoti ekacco mittadubbhī pāpapuriso udake patantopi [V 0.0140] uttārito natveva seyyo. Kaṭṭhañhi nānappakārena upakārāya saṃvattati, mittadubbhī pana vināsāya, tasmā tato kaṭṭhameva varataranti. Migānanti rurumigarāja, migānaṃ kiṃ aññataraṃ garahasi, udāhu pakkhīnaṃ manussānanti pucchati. Bhayañhi maṃ vindatinapparūpanti mahantaṃ bhayaṃ maṃ paṭilabhati, attano santakaṃ viya karotīti attho.

Therein, `niplavitaṃ` means rescued. As for `ekacciyo`: a certain wicked person, a betrayer of friends, is better off even while falling into the water; being rescued is by no means better. For wood is indeed useful in various ways, but a betrayer of friends leads to destruction; therefore, rescuing wood is far better than rescuing him. As for `migānaṃ`: the king asks, 'O Ruru deer king, do you censure a certain one among the deer, or among the birds, or among humans?' As for `bhayañhi maṃ vindati napparūpaṃ`, the meaning is: 'Great fear befalls me; it makes me as if its own possession.'

Vāhaneti patitapatite vahituṃ samatthe gaṅgāvahe. Mahodake [P 0.0150] salileti mahodakībhūte salile. Ubhayenāpi gaṅgāvahassa bahūdakataṃ dasseti. Tato nidānanti, mahārāja, yo mayhaṃ tayā dassito puriso, eso mayā gaṅgāya vuyhamāno aḍḍharattasamaye karuṇaṃ paridevanto tato uttārito, tatonidānaṃ idaṃ mayhaṃ bhayamāgataṃ, asappurisehi samāgamo nāma dukkhoti.

As for `vāhane`: in the Ganges current, capable of carrying away whatever falls into it. As for `mahodake salile`: in the water that has become a great flood. By both phrases, he shows the great quantity of water in the Ganges current. As for `tato nidānaṃ`: 'Great king, the man you pointed out to me, I rescued him from the Ganges as he was being swept away at midnight, lamenting piteously. For that reason, this fear has come to me. Association with the wicked is indeed suffering.'

Taṃ [M 0.0147] sutvā rājā tassa kujjhitvā “evaṃ bahūpakārassa nāma guṇaṃ na jānāti, dukkhaṃ uppādeti, vijjhitvā naṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessāmī”ti saraṃ sannayhi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Hearing this, the king became angry with him and thought, 'Indeed, he does not recognize the virtue of one who has done so much good, and causes suffering! I will pierce him and bring about his death!' He then strung an arrow. Thus it is said:

57.

57.

“Yāvatā karaṇaṃ sabbaṃ, rañño ārocitaṃ mayā;

Rājā sutvāna vacanaṃ, usuṃ tassa pakappayi;

Idheva ghātayissāmi, mittadubbhiṃ anariya”nti.

Whatever deed was done, all of it I have reported to the king. The king, having heard my words, prepared an arrow on his account, thinking: 'Right here I will slay this ignoble betrayer of friends!'

Tattha yāvatā karaṇanti yaṃ tassa mayā kataṃ upakārakaraṇaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ. Pakappayīti sannayhi. Mittadubbhinti attano mittesu upakārīsu dubbhanasīlaṃ.

Therein, 'yāvatā karaṇaṃ' refers to all that helpful assistance done by me for him. 'Pakappayi' means he prepared or strung the bow. 'Mittadubbhi' means one who has a disposition to betray one's own friends and benefactors.

Tato mahāsatto “esa bālo maṃ nissāya mā nassī”ti cintetvā “mahārāja, vadho nāmesa bālassa vā paṇḍitassa vā na sādhūhi pasaṃsito, aññadatthu garahito eva, tasmā mā imaṃ ghātehi, ayaṃ yathāruci gacchatu, yañceva tassa ‘dassāmī’ti tayā paṭiññātaṃ, tampi ahāpetvāva dehī”ti āha. “Ahañca te yaṃ icchitaṃ, taṃ karissāmi, attānaṃ tuyhaṃ dammī”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then the great being thought, 'May this fool not perish on my account,' and said, 'O great king, killing is not praised by the good, whether of a fool or a wise man—indeed, it is always censured. Therefore, do not kill him. Let him go as he pleases. And whatever you have promised to him, give it without fail.' He also said, 'I will do whatever you desire, and I give myself to you.' Thus it was said:

58.

58.

“Tamahaṃ anurakkhanto, nimminiṃ mama attanā;

Tiṭṭhateso mahārāja, kāmakāro bhavāmi te”ti.

Protecting him, I offered myself in exchange. Let him be, O great king; I shall be one who does your will.

Tattha nimmininti taṃ mittadubbhiṃ pāpapuggalaṃ anurakkhanto mama attano attabhāvena taṃ parivattesiṃ[V 0.0141], attānaṃ rañño niyyātetvā rājahatthato pattaṃ tassa maraṇaṃ nivāresinti attho. Tiṭṭhatesotiādi vinimayākāradassanaṃ[P 0.0151].

Therein, as for `nimminiṃ`, the meaning is: protecting that evil person, that betrayer of friends, I exchanged him for my own being; having surrendered myself to the king, I prevented his death which was to come from the king's hand. The phrase beginning with `tiṭṭhatu eso` shows the manner of the exchange.

59. Idāni yadatthaṃ so attavinimayo kato, taṃ dassetuṃ osānagāthamāha. Tassattho – tadā maṃ nissāya taṃ mittadubbhiṃ purisaṃ tasmiṃ raññe jīvitā voropetukāme ahaṃ attānaṃ rañño pariccajanto mama sīlameva anurakkhiṃ, jīvitaṃ pana nārakkhiṃ. Yaṃ panāhameva attano jīvitanirapekkhaṃ sīlavā āsiṃ, taṃ sammāsambodhiyā eva kāraṇāti.

59. Now, to show for what purpose that self-exchange was made, he speaks the concluding verse. Its meaning is this: At that time, when that king, on my account, desired to deprive that treacherous man of life, I, giving up myself to the king, protected my virtue alone, but I did not protect my life. That I was virtuous, disregarding my own life, was for the sake of perfect enlightenment alone.

Atha rājā bodhisattena attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā tassa purisassa maraṇe nivārente tuṭṭhamānaso “gaccha, bho, migarājassa anuggahena mama hatthato [M 0.0148] maraṇā mutto”ti vatvā yathāpaṭiññāya tañcassa dhanaṃ dāpesi. Mahāsattassa yathāruciyāva anujānitvā taṃ nagaraṃ netvā nagarañca bodhisattañca alaṅkārāpetvā deviyā dhammaṃ desāpesi. Mahāsatto deviṃ ādiṃ katvā rañño ca rājaparisāya ca madhurāya manussabhāsāya dhammaṃ desetvā rājānaṃ dasahi rājadhammehi ovaditvā mahājanaṃ anusāsitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā migagaṇaparivuto vāsaṃ kappesi. Rājāpi mahāsattassa ovāde ṭhatvā sabbasattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā dānādīni puññāni katvā sugatiparāyano ahosi.

Then the king, pleased that the Bodhisatta, having sacrificed his own life, had prevented that man's death, said, 'Go, sir, released from death from my hand through the grace of the deer king.' Keeping his promise, he had that wealth given to him. Having granted the Great Being's wish, he brought him to the city and had the city and the Bodhisatta adorned. He had the Bodhisatta teach the Dhamma to the queen. The Great Being, beginning with the queen, taught the Dhamma to the king and his court in sweet human speech. Having admonished the king with the ten royal duties and instructed the multitude, he entered the forest and dwelt surrounded by a herd of deer. The king, too, abiding by the Great Being's advice, granted safety to all beings, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and was destined for a happy realm.

Tadā seṭṭhiputto devadatto ahosi, rājā ānando, rurumigarājā lokanātho.

At that time, the merchant's son was Devadatta, the king was Ānanda, and the Ruru deer king was the Lord of the World.

Tassa idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva yathārahaṃ sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā idhāpi pavivekārāmatāya janasaṃsaggaṃ anicchato yūthaṃ pahāya ekakavihāro, aḍḍharattasamaye nadiyā vuyhamānassa karuṇaṃ paridevantassa purisassa aṭṭassaraṃ sutvā sayitaṭṭhānato vuṭṭhāya nadītīraṃ gantvā mahāgaṅgāya mahati udakoghe vattamāne attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā otaritvā sotaṃ pacchinditvā taṃ purisaṃ attano piṭṭhiyaṃ āropetvā tīraṃ pāpetvā samassāsetvā phalāphalādīni datvā parissamavinodanaṃ, puna taṃ attano piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā araññato nīharitvā mahāmagge otāraṇaṃ, saraṃ sannayhitvā vijjhissāmīti abhimukhe ṭhitassa rañño nibbhayena hutvā paṭimukhameva gantvā paṭhamataraṃ manussabhāsāya ālapitvā madhurapaṭisanthārakaraṇaṃ, mittadubbhī pāpapurisaṃ [P 0.0152] hantukāmaṃ rājānaṃ dhammakathaṃ katvā punapi attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā maraṇato pamocanaṃ, tassa ca rañño yathāpaṭiññaṃ dhanadāpanaṃ, raññā attano vare dīyamāne tena sabbasattānaṃ abhayadāpanaṃ, rājānañca deviñca pamukhaṃ katvā mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā dānādīsu [V 0.0142] puññesu tesaṃ patiṭṭhāpanaṃ, laddhābhayānaṃ migānaṃ ovādaṃ datvā manussānaṃ sassakhādanato nivāraṇaṃ, paṇṇasaññāya ca tassa yāvajjakālā thāvarakaraṇanti evamādayo mahāsattassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Here too, the remaining perfections should be determined in the same way as previously described, according to their suitability. Likewise, here too, the qualities and power of the Great Being should be made manifest—such as his delight in solitude and his disinterest in socializing, abandoning the herd to dwell alone; hearing the pitiful cries of a man being swept away by the river at midnight, rising from his resting place, going to the riverbank, and seeing the great Ganges in full flood, he sacrificed his own life, plunged in, cut through the current, placed the man on his back, brought him to shore, comforted him, gave him fruits and other provisions to relieve his exhaustion, and then, carrying him again on his back, brought him out of the forest and set him down on the main road; when the king stood before him, having nocked an arrow and intending to shoot, he went fearlessly directly towards him, and first addressed him in human speech with a sweet welcome; when the king desired to kill the wicked man, the betrayer of a friend, he preached the Dhamma to him and again risked his own life to free him from death; causing the king to give wealth as promised; when the king offered him a boon, causing him to grant safety to all beings; teaching the Dhamma to the great assembly headed by the king and queen, establishing them in meritorious deeds such as giving; advising the deer who had gained safety to refrain from eating people’s crops; and by the sign of a leaf, making that protection permanent even to this day—such and similar are the qualities and powers of the Great Being that should be made manifest.

Rurumigarājacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Conduct of the Ruru Deer King is concluded.

7. Mātaṅgacariyāvaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Conduct of Mātaṅga

60. Sattame [M 0.0149] jaṭiloti jaṭāvanto, jaṭābandhakesoti attho. Uggatāpanoti manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ tāpanato niggaṇhanato tapasaṅkhātaṃ uggatāpanaṃ etassāti uggatāpano, ghoratapo paramadhitindriyoti attho. Atha vā nānappakāre diṭṭhadhammikādibhede anatthe uggiraṇato bahi chaḍḍāpanato ghorabhīmabhayānakaṭṭhena vā “uggā”ti laddhanāme kilese vīriyātapena santāpanato ugge tāpetīti uggatāpano. Mātaṅgo nāma nāmenāti nāmena mātaṅgo nāma. Mātaṅgakule nibbattiyā jātiyā āgataṃ hissa etaṃ nāmaṃ. Sīlavāti sīlasampanno suparisuddhasīlo. Susamāhitoti upacārappanāsamādhīhi suṭṭhu samāhito, jhānasamāpattilābhīti attho.

60. In the seventh story, 'Jaṭila' means one who has matted hair; that is, one who binds his hair in matted locks. 'Uggatāpana' means one whose asceticism is an 'uggatāpana,' that is, the tormenting and restraining of the six sense faculties, including the mind; therefore, he is called 'Uggatāpana,' meaning one of fierce austerity and supreme control over his faculties. Alternatively, he is 'Uggatāpano' because he burns away the 'fierce' (ugge) defilements with the heat of his energy. The defilements are called 'fierce' because they cause the disgorging and casting out of various unprofitable things, such as those pertaining to this life, or because they are terrible, dreadful, and frightening. 'Mātaṅgo nāma' means named Mātaṅga; this name came to him from his birth in the Mātaṅga clan. 'Sīlavā' means endowed with virtue, one of perfectly purified moral conduct. 'Susamāhito' means well-composed through both access and attainment concentration; that is, an attainer of meditative absorptions.

Tadā hi bodhisatto caṇḍālayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā rūpena duddasiko bahinagare caṇḍālagāme vasati. “Mātaṅgapaṇḍito”ti pakāsanāmo. Athekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ nagare nakkhatte ghosite yebhuyyena nāgarā nakkhattaṃ kīḷanti. Aññatarāpi brāhmaṇamahāsālakaññā soḷasapannarasavassuddesikā devakaññā viya rūpena dassanīyā pāsādikā “attano [P 0.0153] vibhavānurūpaṃ nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti pahūtakhajjabhojjādīni sakaṭesu āropetvā sabbasetaṃ vaḷavārathamāruyha mahatā parivārena uyyānabhūmiṃ gacchati. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā nāmesā, sā kira dussaṇṭhitaṃ rūpaṃ “avamaṅgala”nti taṃ daṭṭhuṃ na icchati, tenassā “diṭṭhamaṅgalikā”tveva samaññā udapādi.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in an outcaste womb and lived in an outcaste village outside the city, repulsive in appearance. He was known by the renowned name 'Mātaṅga the Wise.' Now one day, when a festival was announced in that city, most of the citizens were celebrating the festival. A certain wealthy brahmin maiden, about fifteen or sixteen years of age, as lovely and pleasing in form as a celestial nymph, thought, 'I will enjoy the festival in a manner befitting my station.' Having loaded abundant food and drink onto carts, she mounted a chariot drawn by all-white mares and set out for the pleasure grove with a large retinue. Her name was Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, for it is said she did not wish to see an unsightly form, considering it 'inauspicious'; hence the designation 'Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā' arose for her.

Tadā bodhisatto kālasseva uṭṭhāya paṭapilotikaṃ nivāsetvā jajjaritamukhabhāgaṃ veṇudaṇḍaṃ gahetvā bhājanahattho nagaraṃ pavisati manusse disvā dūratova tesaṃ dūrīkaraṇatthaṃ tena veṇudaṇḍena saññaṃ karonto. Atha diṭṭhamaṅgalikā “ussaratha ussarathā”ti ussāraṇaṃ karontehi attano purisehi nīyamānā nagaradvāramajjhe mātaṅgaṃ disvā “ko eso”ti āha. “Ayye, mātaṅgacaṇḍālo”ti [V 0.0143] ca vutte “īdisaṃ disvā gatānaṃ kuto vuḍḍhī”ti yānaṃ nivattāpesi. Manussā “yaṃ mayaṃ uyyānaṃ gantvā bahuṃ khajjabhojjādiṃ labheyyāma, tassa no mātaṅgena [M 0.0150] antarāyo kato”ti kupitā “gaṇhatha, caṇḍāla”nti leḍḍūhi paharitvā visaññībhūtaṃ pātetvā agamaṃsu.

Then the Bodhisatta rose early in the morning, put on his tattered rags, took a worn-out bamboo staff, and entered the city with a bowl in hand. Seeing people, he made a sign with the bamboo staff from afar to make them keep their distance. Then, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, being led by her attendants who were clearing the way, crying, 'Make way, make way!' saw the outcaste in the middle of the city gate and asked, 'Who is that?' When told, 'My lady, it is Mātaṅga the outcaste,' she said, 'What prosperity can there be for those who go forth after seeing such a sight?' and had her carriage turned back. The people, angry that 'Mātaṅga has created an obstacle to our obtaining much food and delicacies by going to the park,' shouted, 'Seize the outcaste!' They struck him with clods of earth, knocked him unconscious to the ground, and went away.

So na cireneva satiṃ paṭilabhitvā vuṭṭhāya manusse pucchi – “kiṃ, ayyā, dvāraṃ nāma sabbasādhāraṇaṃ, udāhu brāhmaṇānaṃ eva kata”nti? “Sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇa”nti. “Evaṃ sabbasādhāraṇadvāre ekamantaṃ apakkamantaṃ maṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya manussā imaṃ anayabyasanaṃ pāpesu”nti rathikāya manussānaṃ ārocetvā “handāhaṃ imissā mānaṃ bhindissāmī”ti tassā nivesanadvāraṃ gantvā “ahaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ aladdhā na vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti nipajji. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya pitā “gharadvāre mātaṅgo nipanno”ti sutvā “tassa kākaṇikaṃ detha, telena sarīraṃ makkhetvā gacchatū”ti āha. So “diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ aladdhā na uṭṭhahissāmi”cceva āha. Tato brāhmaṇena – “dve kākaṇike detha, māsakaṃ pādaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ dve tīṇi yāva kahāpaṇasataṃ kahāpaṇasahassaṃ dethā”ti vuttepi na sampaṭicchati eva. Evaṃ tesaṃ mantentānaṃ eva sūriyo atthaṅgato.

Before long, he regained his senses, stood up, and asked the people, 'Sirs, is the city gate common to all, or was it made only for brahmins?' 'It is common to all,' they replied. 'In that case, while I was stepping aside at this common gate, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s people brought this disaster upon me.' Having informed the people in the street, he thought, 'Come now, I will break her pride.' He went to the door of her house and lay down, declaring, 'I will not get up until I obtain Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.' When Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s father heard, 'An outcaste is lying at the house door,' he said, 'Give him a small coin, anoint his body with oil, and let him go.' But he only said, 'I will not rise until I obtain Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.' Then, even when the brahmin said, 'Give him two small coins, a māsaka, a pāda, a kahāpaṇa, two, three, up to a hundred kahāpaṇas, a thousand kahāpaṇas,' he still would not accept. As they were deliberating thus, the sun set.

Atha diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya mātā pāsādā oruyha sāṇipākāraṃ parikkhipāpetvā tassa santikaṃ gantvā “tāta, mātaṅga[P 0.0154], diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya aparādhaṃ khama, dve sahassāni gaṇhāhi yāva satasahassaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vuttepi na sampaṭicchi, nipajji eva. Tassevaṃ cha divase nipajjitvā sattame divase sampatte samantā sāmantagharā paṭivisakagharā ca manussā uṭṭhahitvā “tumhe mātaṅgaṃ vā uṭṭhāpetha, dārikaṃ vā detha, mā amhe nāsayitthā”ti āhaṃsu. Tadā kira ayaṃ tasmiṃ dese desadhammo “yassa gharadvāre evaṃ nipajjitvā caṇḍālo marati, tena gharena saddhiṃ sattasattagharavāsino caṇḍālā hontī”ti.

Then, the mother of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā descended from the palace, had a cloth enclosure placed around him, approached him, and said, "Dear Mātaṅga, forgive the offense of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. Take two thousand; take up to a hundred thousand." But even when spoken to thus, he did not accept and simply lay there. After he had lain thus for six days, when the seventh day arrived, the people from the surrounding vassal houses and neighboring houses rose up and said, "Either make Mātaṅga rise or give the girl. Do not ruin us." At that time, it is said, the local custom in that region was: "If an outcaste dies lying at someone’s door, then that household, along with the residents of seven times seven houses, becomes outcastes."

Tato diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya mātāpitaro diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ paṭapilotikaṃ nivāsāpetvā caṇḍālānucchavikaṃ parikkhāraṃ datvā paridevamānaṃ eva tassa santikaṃ netvā “handa, dāni dārikaṃ uṭṭhāya gaṇhāhī”ti adaṃsu. Sā passe ṭhatvā “uṭṭhāhī”ti āha. So “ahaṃ ativiya kilanto, hatthe gahetvā maṃ uṭṭhāpehī”ti āha. Sā tathā akāsi. Mātaṅgo “mayaṃ antonagare vasituṃ na labhāma, ehi, bahinagare caṇḍālagāmaṃ gamissāmā”ti taṃ apassāya attano gehaṃ agamāsi. “Tassā piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhitvā”ti jātakabhāṇakā vadanti.

Then, the parents of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, having dressed her in rags and given her the equipment befitting an outcaste, brought her weeping to him and gave her, saying, "Come now, rise up and take the girl." She stood nearby and said, "Rise up." He replied, "I am very tired; take me by the hand and help me up." She did so. Mātaṅga said, "We are not permitted to live inside the city. Come, let us go to the outcaste village outside the city." Taking her with him, he went to his own house. The Jātaka reciters say, "Having climbed onto her back."

Evaṃ [M 0.0151][V 0.0144] pana gehaṃ gantvā jātisambhedavītikkamaṃ akatvāva katipāhaṃ gehe vasitvā balaṃ gahetvā cintesi – “ahaṃ imaṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālakaññaṃ mayhaṃ caṇḍālagehe vāsāpesiṃ, handa, dāni taṃ lābhaggayasaggappattaṃ karissāmī”ti. So araññaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitvā sattāhabbhantareyeva aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañcābhiññāyo nibbattetvā iddhiyā caṇḍālagāmadvāre otaritvā gehadvāre ṭhito diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ pakkosāpetvā “sāmi, kissa maṃ anāthaṃ katvā pabbajitosī”ti paridevamānaṃ “tvaṃ, bhadde, mā cintayi, tava porāṇakayasato idāni mahantataraṃ yasaṃ karissāmi, tvaṃ pana ‘mahābrahmā me sāmiko[P 0.0155], na mātaṅgo, so brahmalokaṃ gato, ito sattame divase puṇṇamāya candamaṇḍalaṃ bhinditvā āgamissatī’ti parisāsu vadeyyāsī”ti vatvā himavantameva gato.

Having gone to the house in this way, without transgressing the bond of birth, he stayed in the house for a few days, gathered strength, and thought: "I have made this daughter of a wealthy brahmin dwell in my outcaste house. Now, I will make her attain the highest gain and glory." Entering the forest, he went forth and within seven days, he developed the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges. Descending by psychic power at the gate of the outcaste village, he stood at the door of the house and had Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā summoned. As she lamented, saying, "Master, why have you made me helpless and gone forth?" he said, "Dear one, do not worry. I will now bring you greater glory than your former glory. But you must say in the assemblies, 'My master is the Great Brahmā, not Mātaṅga. He has gone to the Brahmā world and will return on the seventh day from now, on the full moon, breaking through the moon's disk.'" Having said this, he went to the Himālaya.

Diṭṭhamaṅgalikāpi bārāṇasiyaṃ mahājanamajjhe tesu tesu ṭhānesu tathā kathesi. Atha puṇṇamadivase bodhisatto candamaṇḍalassa gaganamajjhe ṭhitakāle brahmattabhāvaṃ māpetvā candamaṇḍalaṃ bhinditvā dvādasayojanikaṃ bārāṇasiṃ sakalaṃ kāsiraṭṭhañca ekobhāsaṃ katvā ākāsato otaritvā bārāṇasiyā upari tikkhattuṃ paribbhamitvā mahājanena gandhamālādīhi pūjiyamāno caṇḍālagāmābhimukho ahosi. Brahmabhattā sannipatitvā taṃ caṇḍālagāmakaṃ gantvā diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya gehaṃ suddhavatthagandhamālādīhi devavimānaṃ viya alaṅkariṃsu. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā ca tadā utunī hoti. Mahāsatto tattha gantvā diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ aṅguṭṭhena nābhiyaṃ parāmasitvā “bhadde, gabbho te patiṭṭhito, tvaṃ puttaṃ vijāyissasi, tvampi puttopi te lābhaggayasaggappattā bhavissatha, tava sīsadhovanaudakaṃ sakalajambudīpe rājūnaṃ abhisekodakaṃ bhavissati, nhānodakaṃ pana te amatodakaṃ bhavissati, ye naṃ sīse āsiñcissanti, te sabbarogehi muccissanti, kāḷakaṇṇiyā ca parimuccissanti, tava pādapiṭṭhe sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā vandantā sahassaṃ dassanti, kathāsavanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā vandantā sataṃ dassanti, cakkhupathe ṭhatvā vandantā ekekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ datvā vandissanti, appamattā hohī”ti taṃ ovaditvā gehā nikkhamma mahājanassa passantasseva candamaṇḍalaṃ pāvisi.

Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā spoke thus in various places in Bārāṇasī amidst the great crowd. Then, on the full moon day, at the time when the moon's disk was in the middle of the sky, the Bodhisatta, having created the form of a Brahmā, broke through the moon's disk and illuminated the entire twelve-yojana Bārāṇasī and the whole Kāsi country with a single radiance. Descending from the sky, he circled above Bārāṇasī three times and, being worshipped by the great crowd with perfumes and garlands, headed toward the outcaste village. The devotees of Brahmā gathered and went to that outcaste village, adorning Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s house with pure clothes, perfumes, and garlands like a divine mansion. At that time, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā was in her fertile period. The Great Being went there and, touching Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s navel with his thumb, said: "Good lady, a conception is established in you. You will give birth to a son, and both you and your son will attain the highest gain and glory. The water from washing your head will become the consecration water for all the kings in Jambudīpa. The water from your bath will become the water of immortality. Those who sprinkle it on their heads will be freed from all diseases and released from misfortune. Those who bow, placing their heads upon your feet, will give a thousand. Those who bow while standing in a place where they can hear you speak will give a hundred. Those who bow while standing within sight will give one kahāpaṇa each. Be heedful!" Having advised her thus, he left the house and, while the great crowd watched, entered the moon's disk.

Brahmabhattā [M 0.0152] sannipatitvā diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ mahantena [P 0.0156] sakkārena nagaraṃ pavesetvā mahantena sirisobhaggena tattha vasāpesuṃ. Devavimānasadisañcassā nivesanaṃ kāresuṃ. Tattha netvā uḷāraṃ lābhasakkāraṃ upanāmesuṃ. Puttalābhādi sabbo bodhisattena vuttasadisova ahosi. Soḷasasahassā brāhmaṇā diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya puttena saha nibaddhaṃ bhuñjanti, sahassamattā naṃ parivārenti, anekasahassānaṃ dānaṃ dīyati. Atha mahāsatto “ayaṃ aṭṭhāne abhippasanno, handassa [V 0.0145] dakkhiṇeyye jānāpessāmī”ti bhikkhāya caranto tassā gehaṃ gantvā tena saddhiṃ sallapitvā agamāsi. Atha kumāro gāthamāha –

The devotees of Brahmā gathered together and, with great honor, led Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā into the city, establishing her there with great splendor and prosperity. They built a dwelling for her like a divine mansion. Having brought her there, they presented her with abundant gain and honor. The acquisition of a son and all else was just as the Bodhisatta had foretold. Sixteen thousand brahmins constantly ate with her son, while about a thousand attended upon him, and gifts were given to many thousands. Then the Great Being thought, "This one is pleased with an improper object; well then, I shall make her know those who are worthy of offerings." So, while wandering for alms, he went to her house, conversed with the son, and departed. Then the boy spoke a verse:

“Kuto nu āgacchasi dummavāsī, otallako paṃsupisācakova;

Saṅkāracoḷaṃ paṭimuñca kaṇṭhe, ko re tuvaṃ hosi adakkhiṇeyyo”ti. (jā. 1.15.1);

"From where do you come, O foul-smelling one, contemptible, like a dust-demon? A rag from a dust-heap is tied on your neck. Who are you, wretch, unworthy of offerings?"

Tena vuttaṃ anācāraṃ asahamānā devatā tassa tesañca soḷasasahassānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ mukhaṃ viparivattesuṃ. Taṃ disvā diṭṭhamaṅgalikā mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Bodhisatto “tassa anācāraṃ asahantehi yakkhehi so vippakāro kato, api ca kho pana imaṃ ucchiṭṭhapiṇḍakaṃ tesaṃ mukhe āsiñcitvā taṃ vippakāraṃ vūpasamehī”ti āha. Sāpi tathā katvā taṃ vūpasamesi. Atha diṭṭhamaṅgalikā puttaṃ āha – “tāta, imasmiṃ loke dakkhiṇeyyā nāma mātaṅgapaṇḍitasadisā bhavanti, na ime brāhmaṇā viya jātimattena, mantasajjhāyanamattena vā mānatthaddhā”ti vatvā ye tadā sīlādiguṇavisesayuttā jhānasamāpattilābhino ceva paccekabuddhā ca, tatthevassa pasādaṃ uppādesīti.

The deities, unable to endure the misconduct spoken by him, turned upside down the mouths of that brahmin and his sixteen thousand brahmins. Seeing this, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā approached the Great Being and reported the matter. The Bodhisatta said, "That harm was done by yakkhas who could not endure his misconduct. Nevertheless, sprinkle this leftover lump of food into their mouths and pacify this harm." She did so and thus pacified it. Then Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā said to her son, "Dear one, in this world, those worthy of offerings are like the wise Mātaṅga, not like these brahmins who are arrogant merely due to birth or the recitation of mantras." Having said this, she inspired faith in him right there toward those who were endowed with special qualities such as morality, those who had attained jhāna and other spiritual attainments, and the Paccekabuddhas.

Tadā vettavatīnagare jātimanto nāma eko brāhmaṇo pabbajitvāpi jātiṃ nissāya mahantaṃ mānamakāsi. Mahāsatto “tassa mānaṃ bhindissāmī”ti taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā tassāsanne uparisote vāsaṃ kappesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

At that time, in the city of Vettavatī, there was a brahmin named Jātimanta who, even after having gone forth, still took great pride in his birth and was very arrogant. The Great Being, intending to break his arrogance, went to that place and took up residence near him, upstream. Thus it is said:

61.

61.

“Ahañca brāhmaṇo eko, gaṅgākūle vasāmubho;

Ahaṃ vasāmi upari, heṭṭhā vasati brāhmaṇo”ti.

"I am one brahmin, and on the bank of the Ganges we both dwell; I dwell upstream, the brahmin dwells downstream."

Atha [M 0.0153][P 0.0157] mahāsatto ekadivasaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā “idaṃ jātimantassa jaṭāsu laggatū”ti adhiṭṭhāya nadiyaṃ pātesi. Taṃ tassa udakaṃ ācamentassa jaṭāsu laggi, so taṃ disvā “nassa vasalā”ti vatvā “kutoyaṃ kāḷakaṇṇī āgato, upadhāressāmi na”nti uddhaṃsotaṃ gacchanto mahāsattaṃ disvā “kiṃjātikosī”ti pucchi. “Caṇḍālosmī”ti. “Tayā nadiyaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ pātita”nti? “Āma, mayā”ti. “Nassa, vasala, caṇḍāla, kāḷakaṇṇi, mā idha vasi, heṭṭhāsote vasā”ti vatvā heṭṭhāsote vasantenapi pātite dantakaṭṭhe paṭisotaṃ āgantvā [V 0.0146] jaṭāsu laggante “nassa, vasala, sace idha vasissasi, sattame divase sattadhā te muddhā phalissatī”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then the Great Being, one day after chewing a toothstick, made a resolution, "May this cling to Jātimanta's matted locks," and threw it into the river. As the brahmin was rinsing his mouth with water, it stuck in his matted locks. Seeing this, he said, "Perish, you outcaste!" and thinking, "From where has this ill-omened one come? I shall investigate him," he went upstream. Seeing the Great Being, he asked, "Of what caste are you?" "I am a Caṇḍāla." "Did you throw the toothstick into the river?" "Yes, I did." "Perish, you outcaste, you Caṇḍāla, you ill-omened one! Do not live here—live downstream!" he said. But even when the Bodhisatta was living downstream, a toothstick he threw went against the current and clung to the brahmin's matted locks. The brahmin said, "Perish, you outcaste! If you continue to live here, on the seventh day your head will split into seven pieces!" Thus it was said:

62.

62.

“Vicaranto anukūlamhi, uddhaṃ me assamaddasa;

Tattha maṃ paribhāsetvā, abhisapi muddhaphālana”nti.

"While wandering along the bank, he saw my hermitage upstream. There, after reviling me, he cursed me with the splitting of my head."

Tattha vicaranto anukūlamhīti ucchiṭṭhadantakaṭṭhe attano jaṭāsu lagge tassa āgamanagavesanavasena gaṅgāya tīre anuvicaranto. Uddhaṃ me assamaddasāti attano vasanaṭṭhānato uparisote mama assamaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ addakkhi. Tattha maṃ paribhāsetvāti mama assamaṃ āgantvā jātiṃ sutvā tatova paṭikkamitvā savanūpacāre ṭhatvā “nassa, vasala caṇḍāla, kāḷakaṇṇi mā idha vasī”tiādīni vatvā bhayena santajjetvā. Abhisapi muddhaphālananti “sace jīvitukāmosi, ettova sīghaṃ palāyassū”ti vatvā “sace na pakkamissati, ito te sattame divase sattadhā muddhā phalatū”ti me abhisapaṃ adāsi.

Here, 'while wandering along the bank' means that with the discarded toothstick clinging to his own matted locks, he wandered along the shore of the Ganges searching for its source. 'He saw my hermitage upstream' means that from his own dwelling place, he saw my leaf-hut further upstream. 'There, after reviling me' means that upon coming to my hermitage, hearing my caste, turning back from there, and standing within earshot, he said, 'Perish, you outcaste, you Caṇḍāla, you ill-omened one! Do not stay here!' and so on, intimidating me with threats. 'He cursed me with the splitting of my head' means that after saying, 'If you wish to live, flee quickly from here!' he pronounced this curse upon me: 'If you do not depart, on the seventh day from now, may your head split into seven pieces!'

Kiṃ pana tassa abhisapena muddhā phalatīti? Na phalati, kuhako pana so, evamayaṃ maraṇabhayatajjito sudūraṃ pakkamissatīti saññāya santāsanatthaṃ tathā āha.

But does a head split because of his curse? No, it does not. He was, however, a deceiver, and he spoke thus for the purpose of intimidation, thinking, 'Threatened by the fear of death, this one will flee far away.'

63. Yadihaṃ tassa pakuppeyyanti tassa mānatthaddhassa kūṭajaṭilassa ahaṃ yadi kujjheyyaṃ. Yadi sīlaṃ na gopayeti sīlaṃ yadi na rakkheyyaṃ, idaṃ sīlaṃ nāma jīvitanirapekkhaṃ sammadeva rakkhitabbanti yadi na cinteyyanti attho. Oloketvānahaṃ tassa, kareyyaṃ chārikaṃ viyāti sacāhaṃ tadā tassa appatīto abhavissaṃ[P 0.0158]. Mama cittācāraṃ ñatvā mayi abhippasannā devatā khaṇeneva taṃ bhasmamuṭṭhiṃ viya viddhaṃseyyunti adhippāyo. Satthā pana [M 0.0154] tadā attano appatītabhāve sati devatāhi sādhetabbaṃ tassa anatthaṃ attanā kattabbaṃ viya katvā desesi “kareyyaṃ chārikaṃ viyā”ti.

63. 'If I were to become angry with him' means: if I were to become angry with that arrogant and deceitful matted-hair ascetic. 'If I were not to guard my virtue' means: if I were not to protect my virtue, if I were not to think, 'This virtue must be rightly guarded even without regard for one's life.' 'Having looked upon him, I would reduce him to ashes' means: if I had been displeased with him at that time. The intention is that the deities, knowing the conduct of my mind and being especially pleased with me, would have instantly scattered him like a handful of ashes. The Teacher, however, at that time, spoke as if the harm to that ascetic, which would be accomplished by the deities if he were displeased, was to be done by himself, saying, 'I would reduce him to ashes.'

Vitaṇḍavādī panāha – “bodhisattova taṃ jaṭilaṃ icchamāno iddhiyā chārikaṃ kareyya, evañhi sati imissā pāḷiyā attho ujukameva nīto hotī”ti. So evamassa vacanīyo – “tvaṃ iddhiyā parūpaghātaṃ vadasi, iddhi nāmesā adhiṭṭhānā iddhi, vikubbanā iddhi, manomayā iddhi, ñāṇavipphārā iddhi, samādhivipphārā iddhi, ariyā iddhi, kammavipākajā iddhi, puññavato iddhi, vijjāmayā iddhi, tattha tattha sammāpayogappaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena [V 0.0147] iddhīti dasavidhā. Tattha “kataraṃ iddhiṃ vadesī”ti? “Bhāvanāmaya”nti. “Kiṃ pana bhāvanāmayāya parūpaghātakammaṃ hotī”ti? Āma, ekacce ācariyā “ekavāraṃ hotī”ti vadanti, yathā hi paraṃ paharitukāmena udakabharite ghaṭe khitte paropi paharīyati, ghaṭopi bhijjati, evameva bhāvanāmayāya iddhiyā ekavāraṃ parūpaghātakammaṃ hoti, tato paṭṭhāya pana sā nassati.

A debater, however, says: "The Bodhisatta himself, if he wished, could have reduced that matted-hair ascetic to ashes through psychic power. For if so, the meaning of this Pāli passage would be straightforwardly understood." To him, it should be said: "You speak of harming another through psychic power. But psychic power is of ten kinds: the psychic power of determination, the psychic power of transformation, the mind-made power, the power of pervasive knowledge, the power of pervasive concentration, the noble power, the power resulting from kamma, the power of the meritorious, the power based on knowledge, and the power that succeeds due to right application in various circumstances. Among these, which psychic power do you mean?" "The power born of meditation," he says. "But can an act of harming another be done with the power born of meditation?" "Yes, some teachers say it can be done once. For just as when someone, wishing to strike another, throws a pot full of water, the other person is struck and the pot is also broken; in the same way, an act of harming another can be done once with the power born of meditation, but from that point on, that power is lost."

Atha so “bhāvanāmayāya iddhiyā neva ekavāraṃ na dvevāraṃ parūpaghātakammaṃ hotī”ti vatvā pucchitabbo “kiṃ bhāvanāmayā iddhi kusalā akusalā abyākatā, sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dukkhāya vedanāya sampayuttā adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā, savitakkasavicārā avitakkavicāramattā avitakkaavicārā, kāmāvacarā rūpāvacarā arūpāvacarā”ti? Jānanto “bhāvanāmayā iddhi kusalā abyākatā vā adukkhamasukhavedaniyā avitakkaavicārā rūpāvacarā cā”ti vakkhati. So vattabbo “pāṇātipātacetanā kusalādīsu kataraṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ bhajatī”ti? Jānanto vakkhati “pāṇātipātacetanā akusalāva dukkhavedanāva savitakkasavicārāva kāmāvacarāvā”ti. Evaṃ sante “tava pañho neva kusalattikena sameti, na vedanāttikena na vitakkattikena na bhūmantarenā”ti pāḷiyā virodhaṃ [P 0.0159] dassetvā saññāpetabbo. Yadi pana so “puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, idhekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā iddhimā cetovasippatto aññissā kucchigataṃ gabbhaṃ pāpakena manasānupekkhitā hoti ‘aho vata yaṃ taṃ kucchigataṃ gabbhaṃ na sotthinā abhinikkhameyyā’ti. Evampi, bhikkhave, kulumpassa upaghāto hotī”ti [M 0.0155] saṅgītiṃ anāruḷhaṃ kulumpasuttaṃ udāhareyya. Tassāpi “tvaṃ atthaṃ na jānāsi. Iddhimā cetovasippattoti hi ettha na bhāvanāmayā iddhi adhippetā, āthabbanikā iddhi adhippetā. Sā hi ettha labbhamānā labbhatīti bhāvanāmayāya iddhiyā parūpaghāto na sambhavatiyevā”ti saññāpetabbo. No ce saññattiṃ upeti, kammaṃ katvā uyyojetabbo. Tasmā yathāvuttanayenevettha gāthāya attho veditabbo.

Then, having said, 'With the power born of meditation, the act of harming others does not occur even once or twice,' he should be asked: 'Is the power born of meditation wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
