Is it associated with pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling? Is it with initial and sustained thought, without initial thought but with sustained thought alone, or without both initial and sustained thought? Does it belong to the sensuous sphere, the form sphere, or the formless sphere?' Knowing, he would say, 'The power born of meditation is wholesome or indeterminate, associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, without initial and sustained thought, and belonging to the form sphere.' He should be counter-questioned: 'The intention of killing living beings—into which category does it fall among the wholesome, etc.?' Knowing, he would say, 'The intention of killing living beings is only unwholesome, only associated with painful feeling, only with initial and sustained thought, and only belonging to the sensuous sphere.' This being so, he should be made to understand by showing the contradiction with the Pāli text: 'Your proposition does not accord with the triad of wholesome states, nor with the triad of feelings, nor with the triad of thoughts, nor with the different planes of existence.' But if he were to cite the Kulumpa Sutta, which was not included in the canonical recitation, saying, 'Furthermore, monks, here some ascetic or brahmin who is powerful and has mastery of mind, regards the fetus in another’s womb with a malevolent mind, thinking, “Oh, may that fetus in the womb not emerge safely!” In this way, monks, there is harm to the fetus,' he should also be made to understand by saying: 'You do not understand the meaning. Here, “powerful and has mastery of mind” does not mean the power born of meditation; it means the power of sorcery. For that is obtainable and is what is found here; thus, with the power born of meditation, harming others is simply not possible.' If he does not come to an understanding, a formal act should be performed and he should be expelled. Therefore, the meaning of the verse here should be understood according to the method already stated.

Tathā pana tena abhisapito mahāsatto “sacāhaṃ etassa kujjhissāmi, sīlaṃ me arakkhitaṃ bhavissati, upāyenevassa mānaṃ bhindissāmi, sā cassa rakkhā bhavissatī”ti sattame divase sūriyuggamanaṃ vāresi. Manussā sūriyassa anuggamanena ubbāḷhā jātimantatāpasaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, tumhe sūriyassa uggantuṃ na dethā”ti pucchiṃsu. So “na metaṃ kammaṃ, gaṅgātīre pana eko caṇḍālatāpaso vasati, tassetaṃ kammaṃ siyā”ti āha[V 0.0148]. Manussā mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, tumhe sūriyassa uggantuṃ na dethā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Āmāvuso”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Tumhākaṃ kulūpakatāpaso maṃ niraparādhaṃ abhisapi, tasmiṃ āgantvā khamāpanatthaṃ mama pādesu patite sūriyaṃ vissajjessāmī”ti. Te gantvā taṃ ākaḍḍhantā ānetvā mahāsattassa pādamūle nipajjāpetvā khamāpetvā “sūriyaṃ vissajjetha, bhante”ti āhaṃsu. “Na sakkā vissajjetuṃ, sacāhaṃ vissajjessāmi, imassa sattadhā muddhā phalissatī”ti. “Atha, bhante, kiṃ karomā”ti. Mahāsatto “mattikāpiṇḍaṃ āharathā”ti āharāpetvā “imaṃ tāpasassa sīse ṭhapetvā tāpasaṃ otāretvā udake ṭhapetha, yadā sūriyo dissati, tadā tāpaso udake nimujjatū”ti vatvā sūriyaṃ vissajjesi. Sūriyarasmīhi phuṭṭhamatteva mattikāpiṇḍo sattadhā bhijji. Tāpaso udake nimujji. Tena vuttaṃ –

But when the Great Being was cursed by him, he thought: 'If I become angry with him, my virtue will be unprotected. I must break his pride by some means, and that will be his protection.' On the seventh day, he prevented the sun from rising. The people, distressed by the sun's failure to rise, approached the high-caste ascetic and asked, 'Venerable sir, are you not allowing the sun to rise?' He replied, 'This is not my doing. But there is an outcaste ascetic living on the banks of the Ganges—perhaps this is his doing.' The people then approached the Great Being and asked, 'Venerable sir, are you not allowing the sun to rise?' 'Yes, friends.' 'Why?' 'Your family’s attendant ascetic cursed me without cause. When he comes and falls at my feet to ask for forgiveness, I will release the sun.' They went, dragged him along, brought him, made him prostrate at the feet of the Great Being, and after making him ask for forgiveness, said, 'Venerable sir, release the sun.' 'It cannot be released. If I release it, his head will split into seven pieces.' 'Then, venerable sir, what should we do?' The Great Being said, 'Bring a lump of clay.' They brought it, and he said, 'Place this on the ascetic's head, lower the ascetic into the water, and when the sun appears, let the ascetic sink beneath the water.' Then he released the sun. As soon as the sun's rays touched the lump of clay, it split into seven pieces. The ascetic sank beneath the water. Therefore, it is said:

64.

64.

“Yaṃ [P 0.0160] so tadā maṃ abhisapi, kupito duṭṭhamānaso;

Tasseva matthake nipati, yogena taṃ pamocayi”nti.

That curse he hurled at me then, in anger, with a hateful mind—that very curse fell upon his own head, and by my skillful means I released him.

Tattha yaṃ so tadā maṃ abhisapīti so jātimantajaṭilo yaṃ muddhaphālanaṃ sandhāya tadā maṃ abhisapi, mayhaṃ sapaṃ adāsi. Tasseva matthake [M 0.0156] nipatīti taṃ mayhaṃ upari tena icchitaṃ tasseva pana upari nipati nipatanabhāvena aṭṭhāsi. Evañhetaṃ hoti yathā taṃ appaduṭṭhassa padussato. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “yo appaduṭṭhassa narassa dussati…pe… paṭivātaṃva khitto”ti (dha. pa. 125; su. ni. 667; jā. 1.5.94). Yogena taṃ pamocayinti taṃ tassa bhāsitaṃ matthakaphālanaṃ upāyena tato pamocesiṃ, taṃ vā jaṭilaṃ tato pamocesiṃ, yena upāyena taṃ na hoti, tathā akāsinti attho.

Here, 'the curse he cast upon me then' refers to the high-caste matted-hair ascetic who, intending to split my head, cursed me and gave me that curse. 'That very curse fell upon his own head' means what he wished for me fell upon himself and stood ready to fall upon him. Thus it is for one who offends the inoffensive. As the Blessed One has said: 'Whoever harms an innocent man... like dust thrown against the wind.' (Dhammapada 125; Sutta Nipāta 667; Jātaka 1.5.94). 'By my skillful means I freed him' means: by a skillful method I freed him from the splitting of his head, brought about by his own words; or I freed that matted-hair ascetic from that fate, acting in such a way that it would not happen—this is the meaning.

Yañhi tena pāramitāparibhāvanasamiddhāhi nānāsamāpattivihāraparipūritāhi sīladiṭṭhisampadāhi susaṅkhatasantāne mahākaruṇādhivāse mahāsatte ariyūpavādakammaṃ abhisapasaṅkhātaṃ pharusavacanaṃ payuttaṃ, taṃ mahāsattassa khettavisesabhāvato tassa ca ajjhāsayapharusatāya diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ hutvā sace so mahāsattaṃ na khamāpesi, sattame divase vipaccanasabhāvaṃ jātaṃ, khamāpite pana mahāsatte payogasampattipaṭibāhitattā avipākadhammataṃ āpajji ahosikammabhāvato. Ayañhi ariyūpavādapāpassa diṭṭhadhammavedanīyassa ca dhammatā. Tattha yaṃ sattame divase bodhisattena sūriyuggamananivāraṇaṃ kataṃ, ayamettha yogoti adhippeto upāyo. Tena hi ubbāḷhā manussā bodhisattassa santike tāpasaṃ ānetvā khamāpesuṃ. Sopi ca mahāsattassa [V 0.0149] guṇe jānitvā tasmiṃ cittaṃ pasādesīti veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ panassa matthake mattikāpiṇḍassa ṭhapanaṃ, tassa ca sattadhā phālanaṃ kataṃ, taṃ manussānaṃ cittānurakkhaṇatthaṃ, aññathā hi ime pabbajitāpi samānā cittassa vase vattanti, na pana cittaṃ attano vase vattāpentīti mahāsattampi [P 0.0161] tena sadisaṃ katvā gaṇheyyuṃ. Tadassa nesaṃ dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyāti.

For when harsh words, in the nature of a curse, were uttered by that one as the kamma of reviling a noble one against the Great Being—whose mental continuum was well-composed through the accomplishment of cultivating the perfections, who was fulfilled by abiding in various meditative attainments, and who was endowed with virtue and right view, a dwelling place of great compassion—that kamma, due to the special nature of the Great Being as a field of merit and the harshness of that one's intention, became experienceable in this very life. Had he not asked for the Great Being's forgiveness, it would have naturally ripened on the seventh day. But since the Great Being was asked for forgiveness, its successful application was obstructed, and it became a kamma without result, becoming ineffective. For such is the nature of the evil of reviling a noble one and of kamma experienceable in this very life. Herein, what was done by the Bodhisatta on the seventh day, the prevention of the sun's rising, is the intended means, called 'yoga'. For by that, the distressed people brought the ascetic to the Bodhisatta and had him ask for forgiveness. And it should be understood that he, having come to know the virtues of the Great Being, gained faith in him. As for the placing of a lump of clay on his head and its splitting into seven pieces, that was done to protect the minds of the people. Otherwise, they might think, 'These men, though they are renunciants, act under the sway of their minds and do not bring their minds under their own sway,' and thus they would consider the Great Being to be like that one. That would be for their long-term harm and suffering.

65. Idāni yadatthaṃ tadā tasmiṃ tāpase cittaṃ adūsetvā suparisuddhaṃ sīlameva rakkhitaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “anurakkhiṃ mama sīla”nti osānagāthamāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

65. Now, to show the purpose for which, at that time, without corrupting his mind towards that ascetic, his perfectly pure virtue was guarded, he speaks the concluding verse: "I guarded my virtue." This meaning has already been explained above.

Tadā maṇḍabyo udeno, mātaṅgo lokanātho.

Then Maṇḍabya was Udena, and Mātaṅga was the Lord of the World.

Idhāpi sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā nihīnajātikassa sato yathādhippāyaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya mānaniggaho, pabbajitvā “diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya avassayo [M 0.0157] bhavissāmī”ti uppannacitto araññaṃ gantvā pabbajitvā sattadivasabbhantareyeva yathādhippāyaṃ jhānābhiññānibbattanaṃ, tato āgantvā diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya lābhaggayasaggappattiyā upāyasampādanaṃ, maṇḍabyakumārassa mānaniggaho, jātimantatāpasassa mānaniggaho, tassa ca ajānantasseva bhāvino jīvitantarāyassa apanayanaṃ, mahāparādhassāpi tassa akujjhitvā attano sīlānurakkhaṇaṃ, acchariyabbhutapāṭihāriyakaraṇanti evamādayo mahāsattassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbā.

Here too, the remaining perfections should be determined. Likewise, the humbling of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā by him who was of low birth, according to his wish; having gone forth, the arising of the thought, 'I will be a refuge for Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā'; his going to the forest, ordaining, and within seven days producing the jhānas and higher knowledges as desired; then returning and providing the means for Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā to attain the highest gain and honor; the humbling of Prince Maṇḍabya; the humbling of the high-born ascetic; the removal of the impending danger to that one's life, of which he was unaware; his not becoming angry at that one's great offense but protecting his own virtue; and the performance of marvelous and astonishing miracles—in such ways the qualities and powers of the Great Being should be elucidated.

Mātaṅgacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Conduct of Mātaṅga is concluded.

8. Dhammadevaputtacariyāvaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Conduct of the Deva-son Dhamma

66. Aṭṭhame mahāpakkhoti mahāparivāro. Mahiddhikoti mahatiyā deviddhiyā samannāgato. Dhammo nāma mahāyakkhoti nāmena dhammo nāma mahānubhāvo devaputto. Sabbalokānukampakoti vibhāgaṃ akatvā mahākaruṇāya sabbalokaṃ anuggaṇhanako.

66. In the eighth verse, 'Mahāpakkha' means 'having a great retinue'. 'Mahiddhika' means 'endowed with great divine power'. 'Dhammo nāma mahāyakkho' means 'a powerful deva-son named Dhamma'. 'Sabbalokānukampaka' means 'one who compassionately supports the entire world without making distinctions, with great compassion'.

Mahāsatto hi tadā kāmāvacaradevaloke dhammo nāma devaputto hutvā nibbatti. So dibbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito [V 0.0150] dibbarathamabhiruyha accharāgaṇaparivuto manussesu sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā attano attano gharadvāresu sukhakathāya [P 0.0162] nisinnesu puṇṇamuposathadivase gāmanigamarājadhānīsu ākāse ṭhatvā “pāṇātipātādīhi dasahi akusalakammapathehi viramitvā tividhasucaritadhammaṃ pūretha, matteyyā petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino bhavatha, saggaparāyanā hutvā mahantaṃ yasaṃ anubhavissathā”ti manusse dasakusalakammapathe samādapento jambudīpaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karoti. Tena vuttaṃ –

At that time, the Great Being was reborn as a deva-son named Dhamma in the sense-sphere heaven. Adorned with divine ornaments, riding a divine chariot, and surrounded by a host of nymphs, he would, on the full-moon Uposatha day, stand in the sky above villages, market towns, and royal capitals, after humans had finished their evening meal and were seated at their doorsteps engaged in pleasant conversation. He would exhort the people in the ten wholesome courses of action, saying: "Abstain from the ten unwholesome courses of action beginning with taking life. Fulfill the threefold virtuous conduct. Be one who reveres your mother, reveres your father, is respectful to ascetics, respectful to brahmins, and honors the elders in your family. By making heaven your destination, you will experience great glory." Thus, exhorting the people in the ten wholesome courses of action, he would circumambulate Jambudīpa, keeping it to his right. Therefore it is said:

67.

67.

“Dasakusalakammapathe, samādapento mahājanaṃ;

Carāmi gāmanigamaṃ, samitto saparijjano”ti.

"Exhorting the great multitude in the ten wholesome courses of action, I wander through village and town, with my friends and retinue."

Tattha samittoti dhammikehi dhammavādīhi sahāyehi sasahāyo.

Therein, 'samitto' means with friends who are righteous and speak the Dhamma.

Tena [M 0.0158] ca samayena adhammo nāmeko devaputto kāmāvacaradevaloke nibbatti. “So pāṇaṃ hanatha, adinnaṃ ādiyathā”tiādinā nayena satte akusalakammapathe samādapento mahatiyā parisāya parivuto jambudīpaṃ vāmaṃ karoti. Tena vuttaṃ –

And at that time, a certain deva-son named Adhamma was reborn in the sense-sphere heaven. Encouraging beings in the unwholesome courses of action, saying, "Take life, take what is not given," and so on, he would circumambulate Jambudīpa, keeping it to his left, surrounded by a large retinue. Thus it was said:

68.

68.

“Pāpo kadariyo yakkho, dīpento dasa pāpake;

Sopettha mahiyā carati, samitto saparijjano”ti.

"The wicked, miserly yakkha, expounding the ten evils, also wanders here on earth, with his friends and retinue."

Tattha pāpoti pāpadhammehi samannāgato. Kadariyoti thaddhamaccharī. Yakkhoti devaputto. Dīpento dasa pāpaketi sabbaloke gocaraṃ nāma sattānaṃ upabhogaparibhogāya jātaṃ. Tasmā satte vadhitvā yaṃkiñci katvā ca attā pīṇetabbo, indriyāni santappetabbānītiādinā nayena pāṇātipātādike dasa lāmakadhamme kattabbe katvā pakāsento. Sopetthāti sopi adhammo devaputto imasmiṃ jambudīpe. Mahiyāti bhūmiyā āsanne, manussānaṃ dassanasavanūpacāreti attho.

Therein, 'pāpo' means endowed with evil qualities. 'Kadariyo' means stubborn and miserly. 'Yakkho' means a deva-son. 'Dīpento dasa pāpake' means proclaiming the ten base qualities, beginning with taking life, as things that ought to be done, in this way: 'The sphere of the whole world has arisen for the use and enjoyment of beings. Therefore, by killing beings and doing whatever one wishes, oneself should be gratified and the senses satisfied.' 'Sopettha' means: that deva-son Adhamma is also in this Jambudīpa. 'Mahiyā' means near the earth; the meaning is, within the range of human sight and hearing.

69. Tattha ye sattā sādhukammikā dhammagaruno, te dhammaṃ devaputtaṃ tathā āgacchantameva disvā āsanā vuṭṭhāya gandhamālādīhi pūjentā yāva cakkhupathasamatikkamanā tāva abhitthavanti[P 0.0163], pañjalikā namassamānā tiṭṭhanti, tassa vacanaṃ sutvā appamattā sakkaccaṃ puññāni karonti. Ye pana sattā pāpasamācārā kurūrakammantā, te adhammassa vacanaṃ sutvā abbhanumodanti[V 0.0151], bhiyyosomattāya pāpāni samācaranti. Evaṃ te tadā aññamaññassa ujuvipaccanīkavādā ceva ujuvipaccanīkakiriyā ca hutvā loke vicaranti. Tenāha bhagavā “dhammavādī adhammo ca, ubho paccanikā maya”nti.

69. There, those beings who perform good deeds and respect the Dhamma, upon seeing the deva-son Dhamma approaching in such a manner, rise from their seats, honor him with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and praise him until he passes beyond their sight. They stand with joined palms paying homage, and having heard his words, they diligently and earnestly perform meritorious deeds. But those beings who are of evil conduct and cruel actions, upon hearing Adhamma's words, rejoice and commit even more evil deeds. Thus, at that time, they wander in the world with directly opposing views and directly opposing actions. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'The speaker of Dhamma and Adhamma, we are both opponents.'

Evaṃ pana gacchante kāle athekadivasaṃ tesaṃ rathā ākāse sammukhā ahesuṃ. Atha nesaṃ parisā “tumhe kassa, tumhe kassā”ti pucchitvā “mayaṃ dhammassa, mayaṃ adhammassā”ti vatvā maggā okkamitvā dvidhā jātā. Dhammassa pana adhammassa ca rathā abhimukhā hutvā īsāya īsaṃ āhacca aṭṭhaṃsu. “Tava rathaṃ okkamāpetvā mayhaṃ maggaṃ dehi, tava rathaṃ okkamāpetvā mayhaṃ maggaṃ dehī”ti aññamaññaṃ maggadāpanatthaṃ vivādaṃ akaṃsu. Parisā [M 0.0159] ca nesaṃ āvudhāni abhiharitvā yuddhasajjā ahesuṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

As time passed in this way, one day their chariots appeared in the sky facing each other. Then their retinues asked, 'Whose are you? Whose are you?' and replied, 'We are of Dhamma, we are of Adhamma,' and stepping aside from the path, they divided into two. The chariots of Dhamma and Adhamma faced each other and stopped, shaft touching shaft. 'Make your chariot yield and give way to me,' 'Make your chariot yield and give way to me,' they argued with each other to give way. Their retinues brought weapons and prepared for battle. Regarding this, it is said:

“Dhure dhuraṃ ghaṭṭayantā, samimhā paṭipathe ubho”.

"Striking pole against pole, we both met on the opposing path."

70.

70.

“Kalaho vattatī bhesmā, kalyāṇapāpakassa ca;

Maggā okkamanatthāya, mahāyuddho upaṭṭhito”ti.

"A dreadful conflict arises between the good and the evil; for the sake of yielding the path, a great battle is at hand."

Tattha dhure dhuranti ekassa rathīsāya itarassa rathīsaṃ ghaṭṭayantā. Samimhāti samāgatā sammukhībhūtā. Puna ubhoti vacanaṃ ubhopi mayaṃ aññamaññassa paccanīkā hutvā loke vicarantā ekadivasaṃ paṭimukhaṃ āgacchantā dvīsu parisāsu ubhosu passesu maggato okkantāsu saha rathena mayaṃ ubho eva samāgatāti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhesmāti bhayajanako. Kalyāṇapāpakassa cāti kalyāṇassa ca pāpakassa ca. Mahāyuddho upaṭṭhitoti mahāsaṅgāmo [P 0.0164] paccupaṭṭhito āsi.

Here, 'dhure dhuraṃ' means 'the chariot-pole of one striking the chariot-pole of the other'. 'Samimhā' means 'having come together, we were face to face'. Again, the word 'both' (ubho) is said to show that 'we both, being opponents to each other and wandering in the world, came face to face one day, and when both retinues on both sides had stepped aside from the path, we both met together with our chariots.' 'Bhesmā' means 'fear-generating'. 'Kalyāṇapāpakassa ca' means 'of the good and also of the evil'. 'Mahāyuddho upaṭṭhito' means 'a great battle had arisen'.

Aññamaññassa hi parisāya ca yujjhitukāmatā jātā. Tattha hi dhammo adhammaṃ āha – “samma, tvaṃ adhammo, ahaṃ dhammo, maggo mayhaṃ anucchaviko, tava rathaṃ okkamāpetvā mayhaṃ maggaṃ dehī”ti. Itaro “ahaṃ daḷhayāno balavā asantāsī, tasmā maggaṃ na demi, yuddhaṃ pana karissāmi, yo yuddhe jinissati, tassa maggo hotū”ti āha. Tenevāha –

Indeed, in the retinues of both, a desire to fight arose. There, Dhamma said to Adhamma: 'Friend, you are Adhamma, I am Dhamma. The path is fitting for me. Make your chariot yield and give me the path.' The other replied: 'I am firmly mounted, strong, and fearless. Therefore, I will not give way. Instead, I will fight. Whoever wins the battle, the path shall be his.' Thus he said—

“Yasokaro [V 0.0152] puññakarohamasmi, sadātthuto samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ;

Maggāraho devamanussapūjito, dhammo ahaṃ dehi adhamma maggaṃ.

"I am the maker of fame, the maker of merit, always praised by ascetics and brahmins; worthy of the path, revered by gods and humans. I am the Dhamma; give way, Adhamma."

“Adhammayānaṃ daḷhamāruhitvā, asantasanto balavāhamasmi;

Sa kissa hetumhi tavajja dajjaṃ, maggaṃ ahaṃ dhamma adinnapubbaṃ.

"Having firmly mounted the vehicle of Adhamma, fearless and strong am I. For what reason should I give you the path today, O Dhamma, a path never before given?"

“Dhammo [M 0.0160] have pāturahosi pubbe, pacchā adhammo udapādi loke;

Jeṭṭho ca seṭṭho ca sanantano ca, uyyāhi jeṭṭhassa kaniṭṭha maggā.

"The Dhamma truly appeared formerly; later, Adhamma arose in the world. I am the eldest, the best, and the most ancient; O younger one, depart from the path for the elder."

“Na yācanāya napi pātirūpā, na arahatā tehaṃ dadeyya maggaṃ;

Yuddhañca no hotu ubhinnamajja, yuddhamhi yo jessati tassa maggo.

"Not by entreaty, nor by seemly speech, nor by your worthiness would I give you the path. Let there be battle between us two today; to the one who conquers in battle belongs the path."

“Sabbā disā anuvisaṭohamasmi, mahabbalo amitayaso atulyo;

Guṇehi sabbehi upetarūpo, dhammo adhamma tvaṃ kathaṃ vijessasi.

"I have pervaded all directions; I am mighty, of boundless fame, without equal, and endowed with all virtues. O Adhamma, how will you conquer the Dhamma?"

“Lohena ve haññati jātarūpaṃ, na jātarūpena hananti lohaṃ;

Sace adhammo hañchati dhammamajja, ayo suvaṇṇaṃ viya dassaneyyaṃ.

"Gold is indeed beaten with iron, not iron with gold. If Adhamma should strike Dhamma today, it would be like iron beating beautiful gold."

“Sace [P 0.0165] tuvaṃ yuddhabalo adhamma, na tuyhaṃ vuḍḍhā ca garū ca atthi;

Maggañca te dammi piyāppiyena, vācā duruttānipi te khamāmī”ti. (jā. 1.11.26-32);

"If you are strong in battle, O Adhamma, you have no elders or revered teachers; I give you the path, whether you be dear or not dear, and I endure even your harsh words."

Imā hi tesaṃ vacanapaṭivacanakathā.

This, indeed, was their exchange of words and counter-words.

Tattha yasokaroti dhamme niyojanavasena devamanussānaṃ yasadāyako. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Sadātthutoti sadā thuto niccappasattho. Sa kissa hetumhi tavajja dajjanti somhi ahaṃ adhammo adhammayānarathaṃ abhiruḷho abhīto balavā, kiṃkāraṇā ajja, bho dhamma, kassaci adinnapubbaṃ maggaṃ tuyhaṃ dammi. Pāturahosīti paṭhamakappikakāle imasmiṃ loke dasakusalakammapathadhammo pubbe pāturahosi, pacchā adhammo. Jeṭṭho cāti pure nibbattabhāvena ahaṃ jeṭṭho ca seṭṭho ca porāṇako ca, tvaṃ pana kaniṭṭho, tasmā “maggā uyyāhī”ti vadati.

There, 'yasokaro' means 'the giver of fame to gods and humans by means of applying them to the Dhamma'. The same applies to the second phrase. 'Sadātthuto' means 'always praised, constantly extolled'. The phrase 'Sa kissa hetumhi tavajja dajjaṃ' means: 'I am Adhamma, mounted on the vehicle of Adhamma, fearless and strong. For what reason today, O Dhamma, should I give you a path never given to anyone?' 'Pāturahosi' means: 'in the first age of the world, the Dhamma of the tenfold path of wholesome action appeared first in this world; Adhamma came afterward'. 'Jeṭṭho ca' means: 'because of having arisen first, I am the elder, the foremost, and the ancient one, while you are the younger. Therefore, he says, "Depart from the path!"'

Napi [M 0.0161][V 0.0153] pātirūpāti ahañhi bhoto neva yācanāya na paṭirūpavacanena na maggārahatāya maggaṃ dadeyyaṃ. Anuvisaṭoti ahaṃ catasso disā catasso anudisāti sabbā disā attano guṇena patthaṭo paññāto. Lohenāti ayomuṭṭhikena. Hañchatīti hanissati. Yuddhabalo adhammāti sace tuvaṃ yuddhabalo asi adhamma. Vuḍḍhā ca garū cāti yadi tuyhaṃ ime vuḍḍhā ime garū paṇḍitāti etaṃ natthi. Piyāppiyenāti piyena viya appiyena, appiyenapi dadanto (jā. aṭṭha. 4.11.32) piyena viya te maggaṃ dadāmīti attho.

'Napi pātirūpā' means 'I would not give you the path either by entreaty, or by seemly speech, or by worthiness for the path.' 'Anuvisaṭo' means 'I have spread through all directions—the four cardinal and four intermediate directions—and am renowned by my own virtue.' 'Lohena' means 'with an iron hammer.' 'Hañchati' means 'he will strike.' 'Yuddhabalo adhamma' means 'if you are strong in battle, O Adhamma.' 'Vuḍḍhā ca garū ca' means 'that you have elders and revered teachers who are wise—this is not so.' 'Piyāppiyena' means 'as if to one dear or one not dear'; the meaning is 'even when giving to one not dear, I give you the path as if to a dear one' (Jā. aṭṭha. 4.11.32).

71. Mahāsatto hi tadā cintesi – “sacāhaṃ imaṃ pāpapuggalaṃ sabbalokassa ahitāya paṭipannaṃ evaṃ mayā vilomaggāhaṃ gahetvā ṭhitaṃ accharaṃ paharitvā ‘anācāra mā idha tiṭṭha, sīghaṃ paṭikkama vinassā’ti vadeyyaṃ, so taṅkhaṇaññeva mama dhammatejena bhusamuṭṭhi viya vikireyya, na kho pana metaṃ patirūpaṃ, svāhaṃ sabbalokaṃ [P 0.0166] anukampanto ‘lokatthacariyaṃ matthakaṃ pāpessāmī’ti paṭipajjāmi, ayaṃ kho pana pāpo āyatiṃ mahādukkhabhāgī, svāyaṃ mayā visesato anukampitabbo, tasmāssa maggaṃ dassāmi, evaṃ me sīlaṃ suvisuddhaṃ akhaṇḍitaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Evaṃ pana cintetvā bodhisatte “sace tuvaṃ yuddhabalo”ti gāthaṃ vatvā thokaṃ maggato okkantamatte eva adhammo rathe ṭhātuṃ asakkonto avaṃsiro pathaviyaṃ patitvā pathaviyā vivare dinne gantvā avīcimhi eva nibbatti. Tena vuttaṃ “yadihaṃ tassa kuppeyya”ntiādi.

71. The Great Being then reflected: “If I were to adopt a hostile stance towards this wicked person, who acts for the harm of the whole world, and, standing firm, strike him in an instant, saying, ‘O miscreant, do not stay here, depart quickly and perish,’ he would at that very moment scatter like a handful of chaff by the power of my Dhamma. But that would not be fitting for me. I, having compassion for the whole world, undertake the practice to bring the welfare of the world to its summit. This wicked one, however, is destined for great suffering in the future, so he should be shown special compassion by me. Therefore, I will show him the path. Thus, my virtue will remain perfectly pure and unbroken.” Having reflected thus, the Bodhisatta spoke the verse, “If you are strong in battle,” and as soon as the Bodhisatta had stepped slightly off the path, the unrighteous one, unable to remain standing in the chariot, fell headfirst to the ground. A fissure having been given by the earth, he went and was reborn in Avīci. Hence it is said, “If I were to be angry with him,” and so on.

Tattha yadihaṃ tassa kuppeyyanti tassa adhammassa yadi ahaṃ kujjheyyaṃ. Yadi bhinde tapoguṇanti tenevassa kujjhanena mayhaṃ tapoguṇaṃ sīlasaṃvaraṃ yadi vināseyyaṃ. Sahaparijanaṃ tassāti saparijanaṃ taṃ adhammaṃ. Rajabhūtanti rajamiva bhūtaṃ, rajabhāvaṃ pattaṃ ahaṃ kareyyaṃ.

Herein, “If I were to be angry with him” means ‘if I were to be angry with that unrighteous one.’ “If I were to destroy my ascetic virtue” means ‘by that very anger, I would destroy my ascetic virtue, my moral restraint.’ “With his retinue” means ‘that unrighteous one along with his retinue.’ “Reduced to dust” means ‘become like dust, having attained the state of dust, I would make him so.’

72. Apicāhanti ettha ahanti nipātamattaṃ. Sīlarakkhāyāti sīlarakkhaṇatthaṃ. Nibbāpetvānāti paṭikacceva khantimettānuddayassa upaṭṭhāpitattā tasmiṃ adhamme uppajjanakakodhassa anuppādaneneva dosapariḷāhavūpasamanena mānasaṃ vūpasametvā. Saha janenokkamitvāti mayhaṃ parijanena saddhiṃ maggā okkamitvā tassa pāpassa adhammassa ahaṃ maggaṃ adāsiṃ.

72. In “Apicāhaṃ,” the word “ahaṃ” is merely a particle. “Sīlarakkhāya” means ‘for the purpose of guarding virtue.’ “Having extinguished” means ‘because patience, loving-kindness, and compassion had been established beforehand, by the very non-arising of anger towards that unrighteous one and by calming the fever of hatred, I pacified my mind.’ “Having stepped aside with my people” means ‘having stepped aside from the path with my retinue, I gave way to that wicked, unrighteous one.’

73. Saha [M 0.0162] pathato okkanteti vuttanayena cittassa vūpasamaṃ katvā “maggaṃ te dammī”ti ca vatvā thokaṃ maggato saha okkamanena. Pāpayakkhassāti adhammadevaputtassa. Tāvadeti taṅkhaṇaṃ [V 0.0154] eva mahāpathavī vivaramadāsi. Jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “maggañca te dammī”ti gāthāya kathitakkhaṇeyevāti vuttaṃ.

73. “Saha pathato okkante” means ‘having calmed his mind in the manner described, and saying, “I will give you the path,” by stepping aside a short distance from the path together.’ “Pāpayakkhassa” means ‘of the unrighteous devaputta.’ “Tāvade” means ‘at that very moment the great earth gave an opening.’ In the Jātaka commentary, however, it is said that this happened at the very moment the verse “and I will give you the path” was spoken.

Evaṃ tasmiṃ bhūmiyaṃ patite catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalā sakalaṃ varāvaraṃ dhārentīpi mahāpathavī “nāhamimaṃ pāpapurisaṃ dhāremī”ti kathentī viya tena ṭhitaṭṭhāne dvidhā bhijji. Mahāsatto pana tasmiṃ nipatitvā avīcimhi nibbatte rathadhure yathāṭhitova saparijano mahatā devānubhāvena gamanamaggeneva gantvā attano bhavanaṃ pāvisi. Tenāha bhagavā –

Thus, when he fell upon the earth, the great earth—two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, bearing all things, high and low—as if saying, “I will not bear this wicked man,” split in two at the place where he stood. But when that one had fallen and was reborn in Avīci, the Great Being, standing just as he was at the chariot’s yoke, together with his retinue, by great divine power, proceeded along the path of his journey and entered his own dwelling. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Khantībalo [P 0.0167] yuddhabalaṃ vijetvā, hantvā adhammaṃ nihanitva bhūmyā;

Pāyāsi vitto abhiruyha sandanaṃ, maggeneva atibalo saccanikkamo”ti. (jā. 1.11.34);

“With patience as his strength, conquering the force of battle,

Having slain the unrighteous one, striking him down to the earth;

Pleased, mounting his chariot, he departed by that very path,

Exceedingly strong, steadfast in truth.” (Jā. 1.11.34)

Tadā adhammo devadatto ahosi, tassa parisā devadattaparisā, dhammo lokanātho, tassa parisā buddhaparisā.

At that time, the unrighteous one was Devadatta, and his retinue was the retinue of Devadatta. Dhamma was the Lord of the World, and his retinue was the Buddha’s retinue.

Idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sesapāramiyo yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbā. Tathā idhāpi dibbehi āyuvaṇṇayasasukhaādhipateyyehi dibbeheva uḷārehi kāmaguṇehi samappitassa samaṅgībhūtassa anekasahassasaṅkhāhi accharāhi sabbakālaṃ paricāriyamānassa mahati pamādaṭṭhāne ṭhitassa sato īsakampi pamādaṃ anāpajjitvā “lokatthacariyaṃ matthakaṃ pāpessāmī”ti māse māse puṇṇamiyaṃ dhammaṃ dīpento saparijano manussapathe vicaritvā mahākaruṇāya sabbasatte adhammato vivecetvā dhamme niyojanaṃ, adhammena samāgatopi tena kataṃ anācāraṃ agaṇetvā tattha cittaṃ akopetvā khantimettānuddayameva paccupaṭṭhapetvā akhaṇḍaṃ suvisuddhañca katvā attano sīlassa rakkhaṇanti evamādayo mahāsattassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Here too, in the manner previously explained, the remaining perfections should be determined accordingly. Likewise, here too, the qualities and power of the Great Being should be made manifest, such as these: although endowed with divine life, beauty, glory, happiness, and sovereignty, furnished and possessed of the most excellent divine sensual pleasures, waited upon at all times by many thousands of nymphs, and being in a situation conducive to great heedlessness, he did not fall into even the slightest heedlessness; resolving, “I will bring the practice for the welfare of the world to its summit,” he traveled the path of humans with his retinue, explaining the Dhamma month after month on the full moon day; through great compassion, he separated all beings from unrighteousness and established them in the Dhamma; even when encountering the unrighteous one, he disregarded the misconduct done by him, did not become angered in his mind on that account, but established patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, thereby protecting his own virtue, keeping it unbroken and perfectly pure.

Dhammadevaputtacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Conduct of the Dhamma-devaputta is concluded.

9. Alīnasattucariyāvaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition on the Conduct of Alīnasattu

74. Navame [M 0.0163] pañcālaraṭṭheti evaṃnāmake janapade. Nagaravare, kapilāyanti “kapilā”ti evaṃladdhanāme [V 0.0155] uttamanagare. “Nagaravare”ti vatvā puna “puruttame”ti vacanaṃ tasmiṃ kāle jambudīpe sabbanagarānaṃ tassa nagarassa agganagarabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Jayaddiso nāmāti raññā attano paccatthike jite jāto, attano vā paccāmittabhūtaṃ yakkhinīsaṅkhātaṃ jayaddisaṃ jitoti evaṃladdhanāmo. Sīlaguṇamupāgatoti ācārasīlañceva ussāhasampattiyādirājaguṇañca [P 0.0168] upāgato, tena samannāgatoti attho.

74. In the ninth: ‘In the Pañcāla country’ means in the land so named. ‘In the excellent city, Kapilā’ means in the supreme city that had received the name ‘Kapilā.’ Having said ‘in the excellent city,’ the word ‘best of towns’ is stated again to show that at that time in Jambudīpa, that city was the chief among all cities. ‘Named Jayaddisa’ means he was so named because he was born when the king had conquered his enemies, or because he himself had conquered his adversary, the yakkha known as Jayaddisa. ‘Possessed of the quality of virtue’ means he had attained both virtuous conduct and royal qualities such as the accomplishment of energy; that is the meaning of ‘endowed with them.’

75. Tassa raññoti jayaddisarājassa, ahaṃ putto ahosinti vacanaseso. Sutadhammoti yāvatā rājaputtena sotabbadhammo nāma, tassa sabbassa sutattā sutadhammo, bahussutoti attho. Atha vā sutadhammoti vissutadhammo, dhammacariyāya samacariyāya pakāso paññāto, loke patthaṭakittidhammoti attho. Alīnasattoti evaṃnāmo. Guṇavāti uḷārehi mahāpurisaguṇehi samannāgato. Anurakkhaparijano sadāti saddhādiguṇavisesayogato catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi sammadeva saṅgahaṇato ca sabbakālaṃ sambhattaparivārajano.

75. Of that king: that is, of King Jayaddisa; 'I was his son' is the rest of the sentence. Sutadhammo: because he had heard all the teachings that should be heard by a prince, he was Sutadhammo; the meaning is 'very learned.' Alternatively, Sutadhammo means one whose virtue is renowned; he was manifest and renowned for his righteous practice and equitable conduct; the meaning is that his virtuous reputation was spread throughout the world. Alīnasatta was his name. Guṇavā: endowed with the sublime qualities of a great man. Anurakkhaparijano sadā: his retinue was always devoted to him because he possessed special qualities such as faith and because he always properly supported them with the four bases of beneficence.

76. Pitā me migavaṃ gantvā, porisādaṃ upāgamīti mayhaṃ pitā jayaddisarājā migavaṃ caranto araññamajjhaṃ gantvā porisādaṃ manussakhādakaṃ yakkhiniputtaṃ upagañchi, tena samāgami.

76. My father went hunting and encountered a man-eater: this means my father, King Jayaddisa, while roaming on a hunt, went into the middle of the forest and encountered a man-eater, a devourer of humans, the son of a yakkhinī; he met with him.

Jayaddisarājā kira ekadivasaṃ “migavaṃ gamissāmī”ti tadanurūpena mahatā parivārena kapilanagarato nikkhami. Taṃ nikkhantamattameva takkasilāvāsī nando nāma brāhmaṇo catasso satārahā gāthā nāma kathetuṃ ādāya upasaṅkamitvā attano āgamanakāraṇaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā “nivattitvā suṇissāmī”ti tassa vasanagehaṃ paribbayañca dāpetvā araññaṃ paviṭṭho “yassa passena migo palāyati, tasseva so gīvā”ti vatvā mige pariyesanto vicarati. Atheko pasadamigo mahājanassa padasaddena āsayato nikkhamitvā rañño abhimukho gantvā [M 0.0164] palāyi. Amaccā parihāsaṃ kariṃsu. Rājā taṃ anubandhitvā tiyojanamatthake taṃ parikkhīṇajavaṃ ṭhitaṃ vijjhitvā pātesi. Patitaṃ khaggena dvidhā katvā anatthikopi “maṃsena migaṃ gahetuṃ nāsakkhī”ti vacanamocanatthaṃ kāje katvā āgacchanto ekassa nigrodhassa mūle dabbatiṇesu nisīditvā thokaṃ vissamitvā [P 0.0169] gantuṃ ārabhi.

It is said that one day King Jayaddisa, thinking, 'I will go hunting,' left the city of Kapilā with a large retinue suited to the occasion. Just as he was departing, a brahmin from Takkasilā named Nanda approached, bringing four verses worth a hundred each to recite, and he informed the king of his reason for coming. The king said, 'I will listen when I return,' and after arranging for his lodging and expenses, he entered the forest. He declared, 'Whichever one's side the deer flees past, its neck belongs to him,' and went about searching for game. Then a swift deer, startled by the sound of the large party's footsteps, came out of its lair, ran towards the king, and then fled. The ministers made jokes. The king pursued it and, after three yojanas, shot and felled it as it stood with its speed exhausted. He cut the fallen deer in two with his sword and, though he had no need of it, he made a carrying pole and came back carrying the meat in order to be free from the taunt: 'He was unable to secure the deer with its meat.' As he was returning, he sat down at the foot of a banyan tree on some dabba grass to rest for a short while before starting out again.

Tena ca samayena tasseva rañño jeṭṭhabhātā jātadivase eva ekāya yakkhiniyā khādituṃ gahito ārakkhamanussehi anubaddhāya tāya niddhamanamaggena gacchantiyā ure ṭhapito mātusaññāya [V 0.0156] mukhena thanaggahaṇena puttasinehaṃ uppādetvā saṃvaḍḍhiyamāno tadāhāropayogitāya manussamaṃsaṃ khādanto anukkamena vuddhippatto attānaṃ antaradhāpanatthaṃ yakkhiniyā dinnaosadhamūlānubhāvena antarahito hutvā manussamaṃsaṃ khāditvā jīvanto tāya yakkhiniyā matāya taṃ osadhamūlaṃ attano pamādena nāsetvā dissamānarūpova manussamaṃsaṃ khādanto naggo ubbiggavirūpadassano rājapurisehi passitvā anubaddho palāyitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā tassa nigrodhassa mūle vāsaṃ kappento rājānaṃ disvā “bhakkhosi me”ti hatthe aggahesi. Tena vuttaṃ “so me pitumaggahesi, bhakkhosi mama mā calī”tiādi.

Now at that time, on the very day of his birth, the king’s elder brother had been seized by a yakkhinī to be devoured. As she was fleeing along a sewer tunnel, pursued by the guards, she placed the baby on her breast. Because he perceived her as his mother and took her breast in his mouth, he aroused motherly affection in her, and so he was raised by her. Being used to her diet, he ate human flesh and gradually grew up. To conceal himself, he would become invisible by the power of a medicinal root given to him by the yakkhinī. He lived by eating human flesh, but when that yakkhinī died, he lost the medicinal root through his own negligence. Now visible again, he continued to eat human flesh. Naked and of a frightening, ugly appearance, he was spotted by the king's men and pursued, but he fled and entered the forest. Making his dwelling at the foot of that banyan tree, he saw the king and seized him by the hand, saying, 'You are my food!' Hence it was said: 'He seized my father, saying, "You are my food, do not move,"' and so on.

Tattha so me pitumaggahesīti so porisādo mama pitaraṃ jayaddisarājānaṃ attano nisinnarukkhasamīpamāgataṃ “mama bhakkho tvaṃ āgatosi, hatthaparipphandanādivasena mā cali, calantampi ahaṃ taṃ khādissāmī”ti hatthe aggahesi.

Therein, he seized my father means: that man-eater seized my father, King Jayaddisa, who had come near the tree where he sat, by the hand, saying, 'You have come as my food; do not move by shaking your hands or the like; even if you do move, I will devour you.'

77. Tassāti tassa yakkhiniputtassa. Tasitavedhitoti cittutrāsena tasito sarīraparikampena vedhito. Ūrukkhambhoti ubhinnaṃ ūrūnaṃ thaddhabhāvo, yena so tato palāyituṃ nāsakkhi.

77. His: this means, of that yakkhinī's son. Frightened and trembling: this means frightened by mental terror and trembling with a quaking of the body. Paralysis of the thighs: this means the stiffness of both thighs, on account of which he was unable to flee from there.

Migavaṃ gahetvā muñcassūti ettha migavanti migavavasena laddhattā taṃ migamaṃsaṃ “migava”nti āha, imaṃ migamaṃsaṃ gahetvā maṃ muñcassūti attho. So hi rājā naṃ yakkhiniputtaṃ disvā bhīto ūrukkhambhaṃ patvā khāṇuko viya aṭṭhāsi. So vegena gantvā taṃ hatthe gahetvā “bhakkhosi me āgatosī”ti āha. Atha naṃ rājā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā “sace āhāratthiko, imaṃ te maṃsaṃ dadāmi, taṃ gahetvā khāda, maṃ muñcāhī”ti āha[M 0.0165]. Taṃ sutvā porisādo “kimidaṃ mayhameva santakaṃ [P 0.0170] datvā mayā vohāraṃ karosi, nanu imaṃ maṃsañca tvañca mama hatthagatakālato paṭṭhāya mayhameva santakaṃ, tasmā taṃ paṭhamaṃ khāditvā pacchā maṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti āha.

Take the game and release me: here, 'game' refers to the deer's flesh because it was obtained through hunting; thus it is called 'game.' The meaning is, 'Take this deer meat and release me.' For the king, upon seeing the yakkhinī's son, was struck with fear, his thighs became paralyzed, and he stood like a tree stump. The man-eater quickly approached, seized him by the hand, and said, 'You have come as my food.' Then the king, re-establishing his mindfulness, said, 'If you are in need of food, I give you this meat. Take it and eat it, and release me.' Hearing this, the man-eater replied, 'Why do you bargain with me by giving me what is already mine? Surely, from the moment this meat and you fell into my hands, both belong to me. Therefore, I will devour you first and eat the meat afterwards.'

Atha rājā “maṃsanikkayenāyaṃ na maṃ muñcati, mayā ca migavaṃ āgacchantena tassa brāhmaṇassa ‘āgantvā te dhanaṃ dassāmī’ti paṭiññā katā. Sacāyaṃ yakkho anujānissati, saccaṃ anurakkhanto gehaṃ gantvā taṃ paṭiññaṃ mocetvā puna imassa yakkhassa bhattatthaṃ āgaccheyya”nti cintetvā tassa tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā porisādo “sace tvaṃ saccaṃ anurakkhanto gantukāmosi, gantvā tassa brāhmaṇassa dātabbaṃ dhanaṃ datvā saccaṃ anurakkhanto sīghaṃ [V 0.0157] puna āgaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā rājānaṃ vissajjesi. So tena vissaṭṭho “tvaṃ mā cintayi, ahaṃ pātova āgamissāmī”ti vatvā magganimittāni sallakkhento attano balakāyaṃ upagantvā tena parivuto nagaraṃ pavisitvā nandabrāhmaṇaṃ pakkosāpetvā mahārahe āsane nisīdāpetvā tā gāthā sutvā cattāri sahassāni datvā yānaṃ āropetvā “imaṃ takkasilameva nethā”ti manusse datvā brāhmaṇaṃ uyyojetvā dutiyadivase porisādassa santikaṃ gantukāmo puttaṃ rajje patiṭṭhapetuṃ anusāsaniñca dento tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then the king thought: 'This one will not release me for the price of meat, but when I came hunting I made a promise to that brahmin, "When I return, I will give you wealth." If this yakkha permits, preserving my truthfulness, I will go home, fulfill that promise, and then return to be this yakkha's meal.' Having considered this, he told him the matter. Hearing this, the man-eater said: 'If you wish to go, preserving your truthfulness, then go, give the brahmin the wealth that is to be given, and then, preserving your truthfulness, return quickly.' With these words, he released the king. Having been released by him, the king said, 'Do not worry, I will return in the morning.' Marking the landmarks along the way, he went to his army and, surrounded by them, entered the city. He had the brahmin Nanda summoned, had him seated on a magnificent seat, and after hearing those verses, he gave him four thousand. Having him mount a vehicle, he gave him an escort, saying, 'Take him all the way to Takkasilā,' and sent the brahmin off. On the next day, intending to go to the man-eater, he established his son in the kingdom, gave him instructions, and informed him of the matter. Thus it was said:

78.

78.

“Migavaṃ gahetvā muñcassu, katvā āgamanaṃ puna;

Brāhmaṇassa dhanaṃ datvā, pitā āmantayī mamaṃ.

Having said, 'Having captured your prey, release me,' and having promised to return, and having given wealth to the brahmin, my father addressed me.

79.

79.

“Rajjaṃ putta paṭipajja, mā pamajji puraṃ idaṃ;

Kataṃ me porisādena, mama āgamanaṃ punā”ti.

'Son, take up the kingdom; do not be heedless regarding this city. An agreement for my return has been made by me with the man-eater.'

Tattha āgamanaṃ punāti puna āgamanaṃ paṭiññātassa porisādassa saṅgaraṃ katvā. Brāhmaṇassa dhanaṃ datvāti takkasilato āgatassa nandanāmassa brāhmaṇassa tā gāthā sutvā catusahassaparimāṇaṃ dhanaṃ datvā. Pitā āmantayī mamanti mama pitā jayaddisarājā maṃ āmantesi.

Therein, to return again means: having made an agreement to return again to the man-eater to whom he had made a promise. Having given wealth to the brahmin means: having given wealth amounting to four thousand to the brahmin named Nanda who came from Takkasilā, after hearing those verses. My father addressed me means: my father, King Jayaddisa, addressed me.

Kathaṃ [M 0.0166] āmantesīti ce? Āha “rajja”ntiādi. Tassattho – putta, tvaṃ imaṃ kulasantakaṃ rajjaṃ paṭipajja, yathāhaṃ dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāremi, evaṃ tvampi chattaṃ ussāpetvā rajjaṃ kārehi. Tvaṃ idaṃ puraṃ rakkhanto rajjañca kārento mā pamādamāpajji, asukasmiṃ [P 0.0171] ṭhāne nigrodharukkhamūle porisādena yakkhena katametaṃ mayā saṅgaraṃ mama puna tassa santikaṃ āgamanaṃ uddissa, kevalaṃ tassa brāhmaṇassa dhanadānatthaṃ idhāgato saccaṃ anurakkhanto, tasmā tatthāhaṃ gamissāmīti.

If it is asked, 'How did he address him?' He said, 'Son,' etc. The meaning is: 'Son, you should take up this ancestral kingdom. Just as I rule the kingdom righteously and justly, so you too, having raised the royal parasol, should rule. While protecting this city and ruling the kingdom, do not become heedless. At such-and-such a place, at the foot of a banyan tree, this agreement concerning my return to him was made by me with the yakkha, the man-eater. I came here, preserving my truthfulness, solely for the purpose of giving wealth to that brahmin. Therefore, I will go there.'

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “mā kho tvaṃ, mahārāja, tattha agamāsi, ahaṃ tattha gamissāmi. Sace pana tvaṃ, tāta, gamissasiyeva, ahampi tayā saddhiṃ gamissāmiyevā”ti. “Evaṃ sante mayaṃ ubhopi na bhavissāma, tasmā ahameva tattha gamissāmī”ti nānappakārena vārentaṃ rājānaṃ saññāpetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā pitu atthāya attānaṃ pariccajitvā sotthibhāvāya pitari sāsitavādaṃ payuñjamāne mātubhaginibhariyāsu ca saccakiriyaṃ karontīsu āvudhaṃ gahetvā nagarato [V 0.0158] nikkhamitvā assupuṇṇamukhaṃ mahājanaṃ anubandhantaṃ āpucchitvā pitarā akkhātanayena yakkhavāsamaggaṃ paṭipajji. Yakkhiniputtopi “khattiyā nāma bahumāyā, ko jānāti kiṃ bhavissatī”ti rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā rañño āgamanaṃ olokento nisinno kumāraṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “pitaraṃ nivattetvā putto āgato bhavissati, natthi me bhaya”nti otaritvā tassa piṭṭhiṃ dassetvāva nisīdi. Mahāsatto āgantvā tassa purato aṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Hearing that, the Great Being said: “Do not go there, Great King. I will go there. But if you insist on going, dear father, then I too will go with you.” “In that case, neither of us will survive. Therefore, I myself will go there.” Having in various ways persuaded the king, who was trying to prevent him, he paid homage to his parents and, for his father’s sake, gave up his own person. While his father was uttering words of instruction for his well-being, and his mother, sister, and wives were making an asseveration of truth for his welfare, he took up his weapon and left the city. Bidding farewell to the great crowd that followed him with tear-filled faces, he took the path to the yakkha’s dwelling as indicated by his father. The yakkhinī’s son, thinking, “Khattiyas are very deceitful; who knows what will happen?” had climbed a tree and was sitting there watching for the king’s arrival. Seeing the prince approaching, he thought: “The son must have sent his father back and come himself. I have nothing to fear.” He descended, turned his back to him, and sat down. The Great Being approached and stood before him. It was in reference to this that it was said:

80.

80.

“Mātāpitū ca vanditvā, nimminitvāna attanā;

Nikkhipitvā dhanuṃ khaggaṃ, porisādaṃ upāgami”nti.

“Having paid homage to mother and father, and having offered himself, he laid aside his bow and sword and approached the man-eater.”

81. Sasatthahatthūpagatanti sasatthahatthaṃ upagataṃ āvudhapāṇiṃ maṃ attano santikaṃ upagataṃ disvā. Kadāci so tasissatīti so yakkho api taseyya. Tena bhijjissati sīlanti tena tassa tāsuppādanena mayhaṃ sīlaṃ vinassati saṃkilissati. Paritāsaṃ kate mayīti mayi tassa paritāsaṃ kate sati.

81. Having approached with weapon in hand means: seeing me approaching his presence with a weapon in hand. He might become frightened: that yakkha might become frightened. By that my virtue would be broken: by my causing him that fear, my virtue would be destroyed, would be defiled. When I have caused terror: when I have caused terror in him.

82. Sīlakhaṇḍabhayā mayhaṃ, tassa dessaṃ na byāharinti yathā ca sīlabhedabhayena nihitasattho tassa santikaṃ agamāsi, evaṃ mayhaṃ sīlakhaṇḍabhayā [M 0.0167] eva tassa porisādassa dessaṃ aniṭṭhampi na byāhariṃ, kevalaṃ pana mettacittena hitavādī idaṃ idāni vakkhamānaṃ vacanaṃ abhāsiṃ.

82. From fear of a break in my virtue, I spoke no hateful word to him: just as, from fear of a breach of virtue, I approached his presence having laid down my weapon, so too, from fear of a break in my virtue, I did not speak a hateful or disagreeable word to that man-eater. But solely with a mind of loving-kindness, speaking for his welfare, I spoke these words that are now about to be stated.

Mahāsatto [P 0.0172] ca gantvā purato ṭhito. Yakkhiniputto taṃ vīmaṃsitukāmo “kosi tvaṃ, kuto āgato, kiṃ maṃ na jānāsi ‘luddo manussamaṃsakhādako’ti, kasmā ca idhāgatosī”ti pucchi. Kumāro “ahaṃ jayaddisarañño putto, tvaṃ porisādakoti jānāmi, pitu jīvitaṃ rakkhituṃ idhāgato, tasmā taṃ muñca, maṃ khādā”ti āha. Puna yakkhiniputto mukhākāreneva “taṃ tassa puttoti ahaṃ jānāmi, dukkaraṃ pana tayā kataṃ evaṃ āgacchantenā”ti āha. Kumāro “na idaṃ dukkaraṃ, yaṃ pitu atthe jīvitapariccajanaṃ, mātāpituhetu hi evarūpaṃ puññaṃ katvā ekanteneva sagge pamodati, ahañca ‘amaraṇadhammo nāma koci satto natthī’ti jānāmi, attanā ca kiñci kataṃ pāpaṃ nāma na sarāmi, tasmā maraṇatopi me bhayaṃ natthi, idaṃ sarīraṃ mayā te nissaṭṭhaṃ, aggiṃ jāletvā khādā”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ –

The Great Being went and stood before him. The yakkhinī’s son, wishing to test him, asked: “Who are you? Where have you come from? Do you not know that I am a cruel man-eater? Why have you come here?” The prince replied: “I am the son of King Jayaddisa. I know you are a man-eater. I have come here to protect my father’s life. Therefore, release him and eat me.” Again, the yakkhinī’s son said, as if by his facial expression alone: “I know you are his son. But what you have done in coming here like this is a difficult thing.” The prince replied: “This is not difficult—to give up one’s life for one’s father’s sake. For by doing such a meritorious deed for the sake of one’s parents, one surely rejoices in heaven. And I know that there is no being whatsoever who is not subject to death. I do not recall having done any evil myself, so I have no fear even of death. This body I have relinquished to you. Kindle a fire and eat it.” It was in reference to this that it was said:

83.

83.

“Ujjālehi mahāaggiṃ, papatissāmi rukkhato;

Tvaṃ pakkakālamaññāya, bhakkhaya maṃ pitāmahā”ti.

“Kindle a great fire; I will fall from the tree. When you know it is cooked, devour me, O grandfather.”

Taṃ [V 0.0159] sutvā yakkhiniputto “na sakkā imassa maṃsaṃ khādituṃ, upāyena imaṃ palāpessāmī”ti cintetvā “tena hi araññaṃ pavisitvā sāradārūni āharitvā niddhūme aṅgāre karohi, tattha te maṃsaṃ pacitvā khādissāmī”ti āha. Mahāsatto tathā katvā tassa ārocesi. So taṃ olokento “ayaṃ purisasīho maraṇatopi bhayaṃ natthi, evaṃ nibbhayo nāma na mayā diṭṭhapubbo”ti lomahaṃsajāto kumāraṃ olokesi. Kumāro kissa maṃ olokesi, na yathāvuttaṃ karosīti. Yakkhiniputto mahāsattaṃ “sattadhā tassa muddhā phaleyya, yo taṃ khādeyyā”ti āha. “Sace maṃ na khāditukāmosi, atha kasmā aggiṃ kāresī”ti? “Tava pariggaṇhanattha”nti. “Tvaṃ idāni maṃ kathaṃ pariggaṇhissasi, svāhaṃ tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattopi sakkassa devarañño attānaṃ pariggaṇhituṃ na adāsi”nti imamatthaṃ dassento –

Hearing that, the yakkhinī’s son thought: “It is not possible to eat this one’s flesh. I will make him run away by a stratagem.” He said: “Well then, go into the forest, bring back heartwood, and make smokeless embers. There I will cook your flesh and eat it.” The Great Being did so and informed him. As he watched him, the yakkhinī’s son, his hair standing on end, gazed at the prince, thinking: “This lion among men has no fear even of death. I have never before seen such fearlessness!” The prince asked: “Why are you looking at me? Why do you not do as you said?” The yakkhinī’s son said to the Great Being: “May the head of anyone who would eat you split into seven pieces!” “If you do not wish to eat me, why did you have me make the fire?” “To take you under my protection.” “How will you take me under your protection now? Even when I was born in an animal womb, I did not allow myself to be taken under the protection of Sakka, king of the devas.” To show this, he said:

“Idañhi [M 0.0168][P 0.0173] so brāhmaṇaṃ maññamāno, saso avāsesi sake sarīre;

Teneva so candimā devaputto, sasatthuto kāmaduhajja yakkhā”ti.(jā. 1.16.93) –

“Thinking him to be a brahmin, the hare made him dwell in his own body. For that reason, O yakkha who today grants wishes, the moon-god is praised with the name ‘hare.’”

Gāthamāha.

He spoke the verse:

Tattha saso avāsesi sake sarīreti attano sarīrahetu imaṃ sarīraṃ khāditvā idha vasāti evaṃ sake sarīre attano sarīraṃ dento taṃ brāhmaṇarūpaṃ sakkaṃ tattha vāsesi. Sasatthutoti “sasī”ti evaṃ sasasaddena thuto. Kāmaduhoti kāmavaḍḍhano. Yakkhāti deva.

Here, ‘the hare made him dwell in his own body’ means: thinking, “Let him dwell here after eating this body for his body’s sake,” he gave his own body and thus made Sakka in the form of a brahmin dwell there. ‘Praised with the name ‘hare’’ means: praised with the word “sasa,” as in “sasī” (the moon). ‘Grants wishes’ means: increaser of desires. ‘Yakkha’ means: a deva.

Evaṃ mahāsatto cande sasalakkhaṇaṃ kappaṭṭhiyaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ sakkhiṃ katvā attano sakkenapi pariggaṇhituṃ asakkuṇeyyataṃ abhāsi. Taṃ sutvā porisādo acchariyabbhutacittajāto –

Thus the Great Being, having made the aeon-long miracle of the mark of the hare on the moon his witness, declared that he could not be taken under protection even by Sakka. Hearing this, the man-eater, his mind filled with wonder and amazement, said:

“Cando yathā rāhumukhā pamutto, virocate pannaraseva bhāṇumā;

Evaṃ tuvaṃ porisādā pamutto, viroca kapile mahānubhāva;

Āmodayaṃ pitaraṃ mātarañca, sabbo ca te nandatu ñātipakkho”ti. (jā. 1.16.94) –

“Just as the luminous moon, freed from Rāhu’s mouth, shines on the fifteenth day, so you, freed from the man-eater, shine forth, O mighty one of Kapila! Delighting your father and mother, may your whole host of kinsmen rejoice.”

Gāthaṃ vatvā “gaccha mahāvīrā”ti kumāraṃ vissajjesi. Sopi taṃ nibbisevanaṃ katvā pañca sīlāni [V 0.0160] datvā “yakkho nu kho esa, no”ti vīmaṃsanto “yakkhānaṃ akkhīni rattāni honti animisāni ca, chāyā ca na paññāyati, asambhīto hoti, na imassa tathā. Tasmā nāyaṃ yakkho manusso eso, mayhaṃ kira pitu tayo bhātaro yakkhiniyā gahitā, tesu tāya dve khāditā bhavissanti, eko puttasinehena paṭijaggito bhavissati. Iminā tena bhavitabba”nti nayaggāhena anumānena sabbaññutaññāṇena viya aviparītato niṭṭhaṃ gantvā “mayhaṃ pitu ācikkhitvā rajje patiṭṭhāpessāmī”ti cintetvā “na tvaṃ yakkho, pitu me jeṭṭhabhātikosi, ehi mayā saddhiṃ gantvā kulasantakaṃ rajjaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti āha. Tena [M 0.0169] vuttaṃ “tvaṃ pitāmahā”ti, tvaṃ mama mahāpitāti [P 0.0174] attho. Itarena “nāhaṃ manusso”ti vutte tena saddhātabbassa dibbacakkhukatāpasassa santikaṃ nesi. Tāpasena “kiṃ karontā pitā puttā araññe vicarathā”ti pitubhāve kathite porisādo saddahitvā “gaccha, tāta, tvaṃ, na me rajjena attho, pabbajissāmaha”nti tāpasassa santike isipabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Tena vuttaṃ –

Having recited the verse, he dismissed the prince, saying, “Go, great hero.” The prince, in turn, having instructed him against evil and established him in the five precepts, investigated whether he was a yakkha or not, thinking: “The eyes of yakkhas are red and unblinking, their shadow is not visible, and they are fearless; but this is not so with him. Therefore, he is not a yakkha but a human. It is said that my father’s three brothers were seized by a yakkhinī; two of them she must have eaten, but one she must have raised out of love for a son. This must be he.” Having come to this unerring conclusion by means of inference and reasoning, as if with the knowledge of omniscience, he thought, “I will inform my father and establish him in the kingdom.” Then he said: “You are not a yakkha; you are my father’s eldest brother. Come with me and take up the ancestral kingdom.” This is why he said, “O grandfather,” meaning, “You are my great-father (father’s elder brother).” When the other said, “I am not a human,” he led him to a trustworthy ascetic who possessed the divine eye. When the ascetic explained his relationship as the prince's uncle, the man-eater believed it and said: “Go, dear one. I have no need for the kingdom; I will go forth.” He then undertook the going forth of a sage in the presence of the ascetic. It was in reference to this that it was said:

84.

84.

“Iti sīlavataṃ hetu, nārakkhiṃ mama jīvitaṃ;

Pabbājesiṃ cahaṃ tassa, sadā pāṇātipātika”nti.

“Thus for the sake of the virtuous, I did not guard my own life; and I caused him to go forth, who was ever a destroyer of life.”

Tattha sīlavataṃ hetūti sīlavantānaṃ mama pitūnaṃ hetu. Atha vā sīlavataṃ hetūti sīlavatahetu, mayhaṃ sīlavatasamādānanimittaṃ tassa abhijjanatthaṃ. Tassāti taṃ porisādaṃ.

Here, ‘for the sake of the virtuous’ means: for the sake of my virtuous fathers. Or, ‘for the sake of the virtuous’ means: for the sake of my own virtue, on account of my undertaking the virtuous observances, so that he would not be destroyed. ‘Him’ means: that man-eater.

Atha mahāsatto attano mahāpitaraṃ pabbajitaṃ vanditvā nagarassa samīpaṃ gantvā “kumāro kira āgato”ti sutvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhena raññā nāgarehi negamajānapadehi ca paccuggato rājānaṃ vanditvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā taṅkhaṇaññeva bheriṃ carāpetvā mahantena parivārena tassa santikaṃ gantvā “ehi, bhātika, rajjaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti āha. “Alaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi mayhaṃ uyyāne vasā”ti. “Na āgacchāmī”ti. Rājā tassa assamassa avidūre gāmaṃ nivesetvā bhikkhaṃ paṭṭhapesi. So cūḷakammāsadammanigamo nāma jāto.

Then the Great Being, having paid homage to his great-father who had gone forth, went near the city. Hearing, “The prince has returned!” the king, joyful and delighted, went out to meet him with the city-dwellers, townsfolk, and country people. The prince paid homage to the king and related the whole story. Hearing it, the king immediately had a drum beaten and went to his brother with a great retinue, saying: “Come, dear brother, take the kingdom.” “Enough, Great King.” “Then live in my park.” “I will not come.” The king had a village established not far from his hermitage and arranged for his almsfood. It came to be known as the Market Town of the Taming of the Lesser Kammāsadamma.

Tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, tāpaso sāriputto, porisādo aṅgulimālo, kaniṭṭhā uppalavaṇṇā, aggamahesī rāhulamātā, alīnasattukumāro lokanātho.

At that time, the parents were members of the great royal family, the ascetic was Sāriputta, the man-eater was Aṅgulimāla, the younger sister was Uppalavaṇṇā, the chief queen was Rāhula’s mother, and the prince of unwearied energy was the Lord of the World.

Tassa idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva yathārahaṃ sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā pitarā nivāriyamāno attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā pitu jīvitarakkhaṇatthaṃ “porisādassa santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti [V 0.0161] nicchayo, tassa ca santāsapariharaṇatthaṃ nihitasatthassa gamanaṃ, “attano sīlakhaṇḍanaṃ mā hotū”ti tena piyavācāya samudācāro, tena ca nānānayehi pariggaṇhiyamānassa maraṇasantāsābhāvo, pitu atthe mayhaṃ sarīraṃ saphalaṃ karissāmīti haṭṭhatuṭṭhabhāvo, sakkenāpi pariggaṇhituṃ asakkuṇeyyassa sasajātiyampi pariccāgatthaṃ [P 0.0175] attano jīvitanirapekkhabhāvassa jānanaṃ, tena [M 0.0170] samāgamepi ossaṭṭhepi cittassa vikārābhāvo, tassa ca manussabhāvamahāpitubhāvānaṃ aviparītato jānanaṃ, ñātamatte ca taṃ kulasantake rajje patiṭṭhāpetukāmatā, dhammadesanāya saṃvejetvā sīlesu patiṭṭhāpananti. Evamādayo idha bodhisattassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Here too, the remaining perfections should be determined appropriately, in the way explained above. Thus: his resolve, though restrained by his father, to sacrifice his own life to protect his father’s by going to Porisāda; his going with weapons laid aside to allay the other's fear; his courteous conduct with kind words, thinking, “Let there be no breach of my virtue”; his lack of fear of death even when being seized by various means; his joy and delight, thinking, “I will make my body fruitful for my father’s sake”; his knowledge of his own indifference to life for the sake of renouncing even his own kind, which even Sakka could not grasp; the absence of any change of mind even when he was caught and then released; his undistorted understanding of the other's human state and his status as a great-father; and, on merely knowing this, his desire to establish him in the kingdom belonging to his lineage, and then to stir him with a Dhamma talk and establish him in the moral precepts. In such ways the qualities and power of the Bodhisatta should be elucidated here.

Alīnasattucariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the Explanation of the Conduct of Alīnasattu.

10. Saṅkhapālacariyāvaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Conduct of Saṅkhapāla

85. Dasame saṅkhapālotiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – devabhogasampattisadisāya mahatiyā nāgiddhiyā samannāgatattā mahiddhiko. Heṭṭhā dve, upari dveti catasso dāṭhā āvudhā etassāti dāṭhāvudho. Uggatejavisatāya ghoraviso. Nāgayonisiddhāhi dvīhi jivhāhi samannāgatoti dvijivho. Mahānubhāvānampi urena gamanato “uragā”ti laddhanāmānaṃ nāgānaṃ adhipatibhāvato uragādhibhū.

85. In the tenth, regarding 'Saṅkhapāla,' etc., this is the brief meaning: He was of great might (mahiddhika) because he was endowed with great nāga power similar to the fortune of the devas. He has four fangs as weapons, two below and two above, thus he is 'one with fangs for weapons' (dāṭhāvudha). Because of his poison of fierce potency, he is 'one of dreadful venom' (ghoravisa). Endowed with two tongues perfected in the nāga-womb, he is 'two-tongued' (dvijivha). Because he was the lord of the nāgas—who are called 'breast-goers' (uraga) because they go on their chests, despite their great power—he was the 'lord of the breast-goers' (uragādhibhū).

86. Dvinnaṃ maggānaṃ vinivijjhitvā sandhibhāvena gataṭṭhānasaṅkhāte catuppathe. Aparāparaṃ mahājanasañcaraṇaṭṭhānabhūte mahāmagge. Tato eva mahājanasamākiṇṇabhāvena nānājanasamākule. Idāni vakkhamānānaṃ catunnaṃ aṅgānaṃ vasena caturo aṅge. Adhiṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhahitvā, citte ṭhapetvā. Yadāhaṃ saṅkhapālo nāma yathāvuttarūpo nāgarājā homi, tadā heṭṭhā vuttappakāre ṭhāne vāsaṃ uposathavāsavasena nivāsaṃ akappayiṃ kappesiṃ.

86. At a crossroads (catuppathe): at a place known as the junction where two paths meet. On the great road (mahāmagge): a place where great crowds of people repeatedly traveled. Thronged with various folk (nānājanasamākule): because it was crowded with many people. The four factors (caturo aṅge): by way of the four factors about to be mentioned. Having resolved (adhiṭṭhāya): having made a determination, having established it in the mind. When I was the nāga king named Saṅkhapāla, of the kind described above, then I took up my dwelling (akappayiṃ), that is, I made my residence in the place described above for the purpose of observing the uposatha.

Mahāsatto hi dānasīlādipuññapasuto hutvā bodhipariyesanavasena aparāparaṃ devamanussagatīsu saṃsaranto kadāci devabhogasadisasampattike nāgabhavane nibbattitvā saṅkhapālo nāma nāgarājā ahosi mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo. So gacchante kāle tāya sampattiyā vippaṭisārī hutvā manussayoniṃ patthento uposathavāsaṃ vasi. Athassa nāgabhavane [P 0.0176] vasantassa uposathavāso [V 0.0162] na sampajjati, sīlaṃ saṃkilissati, tena so nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā kaṇhavaṇṇāya nadiyā avidūre mahāmaggassa ca ekapadikamaggassa ca antare ekaṃ vammikaṃ parikkhipitvā [M 0.0171] uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya cātuddasapannarasesu samādinnasīlo “mama cammādīni atthikā gaṇhantū”ti attānaṃ dānamukhe vissajjetvā nipajjati, pāṭipade nāgabhavanaṃ gacchati. Tena vuttaṃ “punāparaṃ yadā homi, saṅkhapālo”tiādi. Tassattho vutto eva.

The Great Being, being devoted to merit such as giving and moral virtue, and seeking enlightenment, was wandering through the successive rounds of rebirth in the divine and human destinations. On one occasion, he was reborn in the nāga world, which possesses a fortune like that of the devas, and he became a nāga king named Saṅkhapāla, of great might and great power. As time passed, he became dissatisfied with that fortune and, aspiring for a human birth, he undertook the uposatha observance. But while he was dwelling in the nāga world, his uposatha observance did not succeed and his virtue became defiled. Therefore he left the nāga world and, not far from the Kaṇhavaṇṇā river, between the highway and a footpath, he coiled himself around an anthill, undertook the uposatha, and on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the fortnight, having taken upon himself the precepts, he lay down, having offered himself at the portal of the gift with the thought: “Let those who have need of my skin, etc., take it.” On the first day of the next fortnight, he would return to the nāga world. Therefore it was said: “And further, when I was Saṅkhapāla…,” etc. Its meaning has already been stated.

87. Yaṃ panettha chaviyā cammenātiādikaṃ “caturo aṅge adhiṭṭhāyā”ti vuttaṃ caturaṅgādhiṭṭhānadassanaṃ. Chavicammāni hi idha ekamaṅgaṃ. Evaṃ uposathavāsaṃ vasantassa mahāsattassa dīgho addhā vītivatto.

87. Herein, the words 'my skin, my hide,' etc., show the fourfold resolution spoken of as 'having resolved on the four factors.' For here, the skin and the hide are one factor. In this way, a long time passed for the Great Being as he was observing the uposatha.

Athekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ tathā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā nipanne soḷasa bhojaputtā “maṃsaṃ āharissāmā”ti āvudhahatthā araññe carantā kiñci alabhitvā nikkhamantā taṃ vammikamatthake nipannaṃ disvā “mayaṃ ajja godhāpotakampi na labhimhā, imaṃ nāgarājānaṃ vadhitvā khādissāmā”ti cintetvā “mahā kho panesa gayhamāno palāyeyyāti yathānipannakaṃyeva naṃ bhogesu sūlehi vijjhitvā dubbalaṃ katvā gaṇhissāmā”ti sūlāni ādāya upasaṅkamiṃsu. Bodhisattassāpi sarīraṃ mahantaṃ ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitasumanapupphadāmaṃ viya jiñjukaphalasadisehi akkhīhi jayasumanapupphasadisena ca sīsena samannāgataṃ ativiya sobhati. So tesaṃ soḷasannaṃ janānaṃ padasaddena bhogantarato sīsaṃ nīharitvā rattakkhīni ummīletvā te sūlahatthe [P 0.0177] āgacchante disvā “ajja mayhaṃ manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti attānaṃ dānamukhe niyyātetvā “ime mama sarīraṃ sattīhi koṭṭetvā chiddāvachiddaṃ karonte na olokessāmī”ti attano sīlakhaṇḍabhayena daḷhaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā sīsaṃ bhogantare eva pavesetvā nipajji.

Then one day, while he was lying there having undertaken the precepts in this way, sixteen Bhoja youths, who were wandering in the forest with weapons in hand, thinking, “We will get some meat,” left without finding anything. They saw him lying on top of the anthill and thought: “Today we have not even gotten a young iguana. We will kill this nāga king and eat him.” Then they thought: “But this is a great being; if we try to seize him, he might escape. We will pierce him with stakes right where he lies in his coils, weaken him, and then capture him.” Taking up their stakes, they approached. The Bodhisatta’s body was huge, the size of a boat that holds one doṇa, and it was extremely beautiful, like a garland of sumana flowers laid out in a circle, endowed with eyes like jiñjuka fruits and a head like a jayasumana flower. Hearing the footsteps of those sixteen men, he raised his head from between his coils, opened his red eyes, and saw them approaching with stakes in hand. He thought, “Today my heart’s desire will be fulfilled,” and entrusting himself to the portal of the gift, he made a firm resolution out of fear that his virtue might be broken: “I will not look at them while they are striking my body with their spears and riddling it with holes.” He then inserted his head back inside his coils and lay down.

Atha naṃ te upagantvā naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā ākaḍḍhantā bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā tikhiṇasūlehi aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vijjhitvā sakaṇṭakā kāḷavettayaṭṭhiyo pahāramukhehi pavesetvā aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu kājehi ādāya mahāmaggaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu. Mahāsatto sūlehi vijjhanato paṭṭhāya ekaṭṭhānepi akkhīni ummīletvā te na olokesi. Tassa aṭṭhahi kājehi ādāya nīyamānassa sīsaṃ olambitvā bhūmiṃ paharati[M 0.0172]. Atha naṃ “sīsamassa olambatī”ti mahāmagge nipajjāpetvā sukhumena sūlena nāsāpuṭe vijjhitvā rajjukaṃ pavesetvā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā kājakoṭiyaṃ laggetvā punapi ukkhipitvā maggaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then they approached him, seized him by the tail, dragged him down, and threw him on the ground. They pierced him in eight places with sharp stakes, and after inserting thorny black rattan canes into the mouths of the wounds, they took him up on eight carrying-poles and set out on the highway. From the moment he was pierced by the stakes, the Great Being did not once open his eyes to look at them. As he was being carried along on the eight carrying-poles, his head hung down and hit the ground. Then, saying, “His head is hanging down,” they laid him down on the highway, pierced his nostrils with a fine spike, passed a cord through, lifted his head, and tied it to the end of a carrying-pole. Then they lifted him up again and proceeded along the road. Therefore it was said:

88.

88.

“Addasaṃsu [V 0.0163] bhojaputtā, kharā luddā akāruṇā;

Upagañchuṃ mamaṃ tattha, daṇḍamuggarapāṇino.

“The Bhoja youths then saw me there, harsh, cruel, and merciless; they came up to me right there, with sticks and clubs in their hands.

89.

89.

“Nāsāya vinivijjhitvā, naṅguṭṭhe piṭṭhikaṇṭake;

Kāje āropayitvāna, bhojaputtā hariṃsu ma”nti.

“Having pierced me through the nose, in the tail, and along the spine, the Bhoja youths hoisted me on poles and then they carried me away.”

Tattha bhojaputtāti luddaputtā. Kharāti kakkhaḷā, pharusakāyavacīkammantā. Luddāti dāruṇā, ghoramānasā. Akāruṇāti nikkaruṇā. Daṇḍamuggarapāṇinoti caturassadaṇḍahatthā. Nāsāya vinivijjhitvāti rajjukaṃ pavesetuṃ sukhumena sūlena nāsāpuṭe vijjhitvā. Naṅguṭṭhe piṭṭhikaṇṭaketi naṅguṭṭhappadese tattha tattha piṭṭhikaṇṭakasamīpe ca vinivijjhitvāti sambandho. Kāje āropayitvānāti aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vinivijjhitvā baddhesu aṭṭhasu vettalatāmaṇḍalesu [P 0.0178] ekekasmiṃ ovijjhitaṃ ekekaṃ kājaṃ dve dve bhojaputtā attano attano khandhaṃ āropetvā.

Herein, Bhoja youths (bhojaputtā) means sons of hunters. Harsh (kharā) means rough, with harsh actions of body and speech. Cruel (luddā) means savage, with fierce minds. Merciless (akāruṇā) means without compassion. With sticks and clubs in their hands (daṇḍamuggarapāṇino) means with four-cornered clubs in their hands. Having pierced through the nose (nāsāya vinivijjhitvā) means having pierced the nostrils with a fine spike in order to insert a cord. In the tail and along the spine (naṅguṭṭhe piṭṭhikaṇṭake): the connection is 'having pierced him here and there in the region of the tail and near the spine.' Hoisted me on poles (kāje āropayitvāna) means: having pierced him in eight places and bound him with eight loops of rattan cane, two Bhoja youths each hoisted one carrying-pole, which was passed through one loop, onto their own shoulders.

90. Sasāgarantaṃ pathavinti samuddapariyantaṃ mahāpathaviṃ. Sakānanaṃ sapabbatanti saddhiṃ kānanehi pabbatehi cāti sakānanaṃ sapabbatañca. Nāsāvātena jhāpayeti sacāhaṃ icchamāno icchanto kujjhitvā nāsāvātaṃ vissajjeyyaṃ, samuddapariyantaṃ sakānanaṃ sapabbataṃ imaṃ mahāpathaviṃ jhāpeyyaṃ, saha nāsāvātavissajjanena chārikaṃ kareyyaṃ, etādiso tadā mayhaṃ ānubhāvo.

90. The earth with its ocean bounds (sasāgarantaṃ pathaviṃ) means the great earth that ends at the ocean. With its forests and mountains (sakānanaṃ sapabbataṃ) means together with its forests and its mountains. I could burn with the blast from my nose (nāsāvātena jhāpaye): if I wished, I could become angry and release the blast from my nose, and I could burn up this great earth with its ocean bounds, with its forests and mountains. I could reduce it to ashes just by releasing the blast from my nose. Such was my power then.

91. Evaṃ santepi sūlehi vinivijjhante, koṭṭayantepi sattibhi. Bhojaputte na kuppāmīti dubbalabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ vettalatāpavesanatthañca sāradārūhi tacchetvā katehi tikhiṇasūlehi aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vijjhantepi dubbalabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ tikhiṇāhi sattīhi tahiṃ tahiṃ koṭṭayantepi bhojaputtānaṃ luddānaṃ na kuppāmi. Esā me sīlapāramīti evaṃ mahānubhāvassa tathā adhiṭṭhahantassa yā me mayhaṃ sīlakhaṇḍabhayena tesaṃ [M 0.0173] akujjhanā, esā ekanteneva jīvitanirapekkhabhāvena pavattā mayhaṃ sīlapāramī, sīlavasena paramatthapāramīti attho.

91. Even when they pierced me with stakes, even when they struck me with spears, I was not angry at the Bhoja youths: even when they were piercing me in eight places with sharp stakes hewn from hardwood in order to weaken me and to insert the rattan canes, and even when they were striking me here and there with sharp spears to weaken me, I was not angry at the cruel Bhoja youths. This is my perfection of virtue: for one of such great power who has undertaken such a resolve, that non-anger of mine towards them, which arose from fear of breaking my virtue, this is my perfection of virtue, which proceeded from a complete indifference to life. The meaning is that it is the perfection of virtue in the ultimate sense.

Tathā pana bodhisatte tehi nīyamāne mithilanagaravāsī āḷāro nāma kuṭumbiko pañcasakaṭasatāni ādāya sukhayānake nisīditvā gacchanto te bhojaputte mahāsattaṃ harante disvā kāruññaṃ uppādetvā te ludde pucchi – “kissāyaṃ nāgo nīyati, netvā cimaṃ kiṃ karissathā”ti? Te “imassa nāgassa maṃsaṃ sāduñca muduñca thūlañca pacitvā khādissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Atha so tesaṃ soḷasavāhagoṇe pasataṃ pasataṃ suvaṇṇamāsake sabbesaṃ nivāsanapārupanāni [V 0.0164] bhariyānampi tesaṃ vatthābharaṇāni datvā “sammā, ayaṃ mahānubhāvo nāgarājā, attano sīlaguṇena tumhākaṃ na dubbhi, imaṃ kilamantehi bahuṃ tumhehi apuññaṃ pasutaṃ, vissajjethā”ti āha. Te “ayaṃ amhākaṃ manāpo bhakkho, bahū ca no uragā bhuttapubbā, tathāpi tava vacanaṃ amhehi pūjetabbaṃ, tasmā [P 0.0179] imaṃ nāgaṃ vissajjessāmā”ti vissajjetvā mahāsattaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā attano kakkhaḷatāya tā kaṇṭakācitā āvutā kāḷavettalatā koṭiyaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhituṃ ārabhiṃsu.

Then, while the Bodhisatta was being led away, a householder named Āḷāra, a resident of Mithilā, was traveling in a comfortable carriage with five hundred carts. Seeing those Bhoja-lads carrying the Great Being, compassion arose in him and he asked those cruel men: “Why is this nāga being led away? What will you do with him after taking him?” They replied: “We will cook and eat the flesh of this nāga, for it is delicious, tender, and substantial.” Then that man gave them sixteen draught oxen, heaps of gold coins, garments for all, and even clothes and ornaments for their wives, saying: “Sirs, this is a mighty nāga king. By his own virtue, he has done you no harm. By tormenting him, you have accumulated much demerit. Release him!” They replied: “This is a pleasing food for us, and we have eaten many serpents before. Still, we must honor your words, so we will release this nāga.” Having released him, they laid the Great Being down on the ground. Then, out of their own cruelty, they took hold of the tip of the black rattan vine covered with thorns that had been threaded through him and began to pull it out.

Atha so nāgarājānaṃ kilamantaṃ disvā akilamentova asinā latā chinditvā dārakānaṃ kaṇṇavedhato paṭiharaṇaniyāmena adukkhāpento saṇikaṃ nīhari. Tasmiṃ kāle te bhojaputtā yaṃ bandhanaṃ tassa natthuto pavesetvā paṭimukkaṃ, taṃ bandhanaṃ saṇikaṃ mocayiṃsu. Mahāsatto muhuttaṃ pācīnābhimukho gantvā assupuṇṇehi nettehi āḷāraṃ olokesi. Luddā thokaṃ gantvā “urago dubbalo, matakāle gahetvāva naṃ gamissāmā”ti nilīyiṃsu. Āḷāro mahāsattassa añjaliṃ paggayha “gaccheva kho tvaṃ, mahānāga, mā taṃ luddā puna gahesu”nti vadanto thokaṃ taṃ nāgaṃ anugantvā nivatti.

Then, seeing the nāga king exhausted, without causing him further distress, he cut the vine with his sword and gently drew it out without causing pain, in the manner of removing an earring from a child's pierced ear. At that time, the Bhoja-lads gently loosened the bond they had inserted and tied through his nostril. The Great Being went eastward for a moment, then looked back at Āḷāra with tear-filled eyes. The cruel men, having gone a short distance, hid themselves, thinking: “The serpent is weak; we will seize him at the moment of death.” Āḷāra, raising his hands in reverential salutation, said: “Go now, great nāga, may the cruel men not capture you again.” After following the nāga a short way, he turned back.

Bodhisatto nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā tattha papañcaṃ akatvā mahantena parivārena nikkhamitvā āḷāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā nāgabhavanassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā taṃ tattha netvā tīhi kaññāsatehi saddhiṃ mahantamassa yasaṃ datvā dibbehi kāmehi santappesi. Āḷāro nāgabhavane ekavassaṃ vasitvā dibbe [M 0.0174] kāme paribhuñjitvā “icchāmahaṃ, samma, pabbajitu”nti nāgarājassa kathetvā pabbajitaparikkhāre gahetvā tato nikkhamitvā himavantappadesaṃ gantvā pabbajitvā tattha ciraṃ vasitvā aparabhāge cārikaṃ caranto bārāṇasiṃ patvā bārāṇasiraññā samāgato tena ācārasampattiṃ nissāya pasannena “tvaṃ uḷārabhogā maññe kulā pabbajito, kena nu kho kāraṇena pabbajitosī”ti puṭṭho attano pabbajjākāraṇaṃ kathento luddānaṃ hatthato bodhisattassa vissajjāpanaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ rañño ācikkhitvā –

The Bodhisatta went to the nāga world and, without delay, departed with a great retinue. He approached Āḷāra, described the splendor of the nāga world, and then led him there. He bestowed upon him great glory along with three hundred maidens and satisfied him with divine sensual pleasures. Āḷāra lived in the nāga world for one year enjoying divine sensual pleasures, then said to the nāga king: “Friend, I wish to go forth.” Having told the nāga king, he took the requisites for one who has gone forth and departed from there. He went to the Himalayan region, went forth, and lived there for a long time. Later, while wandering on tour, he arrived at Benares and met the king of Benares. Pleased by his accomplishment in conduct, the king asked: “You seem to have gone forth from a family of great wealth. For what reason have you gone forth?” Āḷāra explained the reason for his going forth, recounting the entire story to the king, beginning with securing the Bodhisatta’s release from the hands of the cruel men.

“Diṭṭhā mayā mānusakāpi kāmā, asassatā vipariṇāmadhammā;

Ādīnavaṃ [P 0.0180] kāmaguṇesu disvā, saddhāyahaṃ pabbajitomhi, rāja.

“I have seen human sensual pleasures, impermanent and subject to change; having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, I went forth in faith, O king.

“Dumapphalānīva [V 0.0165] patanti māṇavā, daharā ca vuddhā ca sarīrabhedā;

Etampi disvā pabbajitomhi rāja, apaṇṇakaṃ sāmaññameva seyyo”ti. (jā. 2.17.191-192) –

“Like fruits from a tree, mortals fall, both young and old, at the breakup of the body. Seeing this too, O king, I have gone forth; the ascetic life is certainly the best.”

Imāhi gāthāhi dhammaṃ desesi.

With these verses, he taught the Dhamma.

Taṃ sutvā rājā –

Having heard that, the king said:

“Addhā have sevitabbā sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Nāgañca sutvāna tavañcaḷāra, kāhāmi puññāni anappakānī”ti. (jā. 2.17.193) –
