“Truly, one should associate with the wise, the learned who reflect on many matters; having heard of the Nāga and of you, Āḷāra, I will perform abundant meritorious deeds.”

Āha.

He said.

Athassa tāpaso –

Then the ascetic said to him:

“Addhā have sevitabbā sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Nāgañca sutvāna mamañca rāja, karohi puññāni anappakānī”ti. (jā. 2.17.194) –

“Truly, one should associate with the wise, the learned who reflect on many matters; having heard of the Nāga and of me, O king, perform abundant meritorious deeds.”

Evaṃ [M 0.0175] dhammaṃ desetvā tattheva cattāro vassānamāse vasitvā puna himavantaṃ gantvā yāvajīvaṃ cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi. Bodhisattopi yāvajīvaṃ uposathavāsaṃ vasitvā saggapuraṃ pūresi. Sopi rājā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Having taught the Dhamma in this way, he dwelt there for the four months of the rains, then returned to the Himalayas. For the rest of his life he developed the four divine abodes and was reborn in the Brahma-world. The Bodhisatta, too, observed the Uposatha for the rest of his life and went to fill the heavenly city. That king, too, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, passed away according to his kamma.

Tadā āḷāro sāriputtatthero ahosi, bārāṇasirājā ānandatthero, saṅkhapālanāgarājā lokanātho.

At that time, Āḷāra was the Elder Sāriputta, the king of Benares was the Elder Ānanda, and the nāga king Saṅkhapāla was the Protector of the World.

Tassa sarīrapariccāgo dānapāramī, tathārūpenapi visatejena samannāgatassa tathārūpāyapi pīḷāya sati sīlassa abhinnatā sīlapāramī, devabhogasampattisadisaṃ bhogaṃ pahāya nāgabhavanato nikkhamitvā samaṇadhammakaraṇaṃ nekkhammapāramī, “dānādiatthaṃ idañcidañca kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti [V 0.0166] saṃvidahanaṃ paññāpāramī, kāmavitakkavinodanaṃ adhivāsanavīriyañca vīriyapāramī, adhivāsanakhanti khantipāramī, saccasamādānaṃ saccapāramī, acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānaṃ [P 0.0181] adhiṭṭhānapāramī, bhojaputte upādāya sabbasattesu mettānuddayabhāvo mettāpāramī, vedanāya sattasaṅkhārakatavippakāresu ca majjhattabhāvo upekkhāpāramīti evaṃ dasa pāramiyo labbhanti. Sīlapāramī pana atisayavatīti katvā sā eva desanaṃ āruḷhā. Tathā idha bodhisattassa guṇānubhāvā “yojanasatike nāgabhavanaṭṭhāne”tiādinā bhūridattacariyāyaṃ (cariyā. 2.11 ādayo) vuttanayeneva yathārahaṃ vibhāvetabbāti.

His giving up of his body is the perfection of giving. Though he was endowed with such venomous power, the unbrokenness of his virtue even when subject to such affliction is the perfection of virtue. Having abandoned wealth comparable to divine fortune and left the nāga world to undertake the ascetic’s life is the perfection of renunciation. The planning, “It is proper to do this and that for the sake of giving, etc.,” is the perfection of wisdom. The dispelling of sensual thoughts and the energy in enduring is the perfection of energy. The patience in enduring is the perfection of patience. The undertaking of truth is the perfection of truth. The determination of unshakable undertaking is the perfection of determination. The state of loving-kindness and compassion towards all beings, including the Bhoja lads, is the perfection of loving-kindness. The state of equanimity towards feeling and towards the various results produced by beings and volitional formations is the perfection of equanimity. In this way the ten perfections are found. However, because the perfection of virtue is pre-eminent, it is this that has entered the discourse. Similarly here, on account of the Bodhisatta’s powerful virtue, this should be explained as appropriate in the way stated in the Bhūridatta-cariyā, beginning “in the nāga realm a hundred yojanas in extent.”

Saṅkhapālacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Conduct of Saṅkhapāla is finished.

Eteti ye hatthināgacariyādayo imasmiṃ vagge niddiṭṭhā anantaragāthāya ca “hatthināgo bhūridatto”tiādinā uddānavasena saṅgahetvā dassitā nava cariyā, te sabbe visesato sīlapāramipūraṇavasena pavattiyā sīlaṃ balaṃ etesanti sīlabalā. Sīlassa paramatthapāramibhūtassa parikkharaṇato santānassa ca paribhāvanāvasena abhisaṅkharaṇato parikkhārā. Ukkaṃsagatāya sīlaparamatthapāramiyā asampuṇṇattā padeso etesaṃ atthi, na nippadesoti padesikā sappadesā. Kasmāti ce? Āha “jīvitaṃ parirakkhitvā, sīlāni anurakkhisa”nti, yasmā etesu hatthināgacariyādīsu (cariyā. 2.1 ādayo) ahaṃ attano jīvitaṃ ekadesena [M 0.0176] parirakkhitvāva sīlāni anurakkhiṃ, jīvitaṃ na sabbathā pariccajiṃ, ekanteneva pana saṅkhapālassa me sato sabbakālampi jīvitaṃ yassa kassaci niyyattaṃ, saṅkhapālanāgarājassa pana me mahānubhāvassa uggavisatejassa sato samānassa sabbakālampi tehi luddehi samāgame tato pubbepi pacchāpi sato evaṃ puggalavibhāgaṃ akatvā yassa kassaci sīlānurakkhaṇatthameva jīvitaṃ ekaṃseneva niyyattaṃ nīyātitaṃ dānamukhe nissaṭṭhaṃ, tasmā sā sīlapāramīti yasmā cetadevaṃ, tasmā tena kāraṇena sā paramatthapāramibhāvaṃ pattā mayhaṃ sīlapāramīti dassetīti.

These nine modes of conduct—the Hatthināga-cariyā and others—which were indicated in this chapter and shown collected together in the summary verse that immediately follows, beginning “The elephant-king, Bhūridatta,” all proceed by way of fulfilling the perfection of virtue in particular. Thus, virtue is their strength, and they are called ‘those whose strength is virtue’ (sīlabalā). Because they are accessories for the ultimate perfection of virtue and because they are preparations by way of developing the mental continuum, they are called ‘accessories’ (parikkhārā). Because of the incompleteness of the ultimate perfection of virtue that has reached its peak, they have a part but are not part-less; thus they are called ‘partial’ (padesikā) or ‘having a part’ (sappadesā). Why so? He says: “Having protected my life, I guarded my virtues.” For in these modes of conduct, such as the Hatthināga-cariyā, I guarded my virtues only while protecting my life to some extent; I did not give up my life completely. But when I was Saṅkhapāla, my life was at all times completely dedicated to anyone whatsoever. When I was the nāga king Saṅkhapāla, of great power and fierce venomous energy, my life was at all times—both before and after my encounter with those cruel men—without making any distinction of persons, completely dedicated, handed over, and released by way of a gift to anyone whatsoever, solely for the sake of protecting virtue. Therefore, that is the ultimate perfection. Since this is so, for that reason he shows: ‘That perfection of virtue of mine has attained the state of an ultimate perfection.’”

Paramatthadīpaniyā cariyāpiṭakasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Paramatthadīpanī, the Commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka,

Dasavidhacariyāsaṅgahassa visesato

in the special section on the Collection of the Ten Kinds of Conduct,

Sīlapāramivibhāvanassa

the Elucidation of the Perfection of Virtue,

Dutiyavaggassa atthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the Explanation of the Meaning of the Second Chapter is finished.

3. Yudhañjayavaggo

3. The Yudhañjaya Chapter

1. Yudhañjayacariyāvaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition on the Conduct of Yudhañjaya

1. Tatiyavaggassa [M 0.0177][V 0.0167][P 0.0182] paṭhame amitayasoti aparimitaparivāravibhavo. Rājaputto yudhañjayoti rammanagare sabbadattassa nāma rañño putto nāmena yudhañjayo nāma.

1. In the first verse of the third chapter, ‘one of limitless glory’ means one with a boundless retinue and splendor. ‘The prince Yudhañjaya’ means the prince named Yudhañjaya, the son of the king named Sabbadatta in the city of Rammanagara.

Ayañhi bārāṇasī udayajātake (jā. 1.11.37 ādayo) surundhananagaraṃ nāma jātā. Cūḷasutasomajātake (jā. 2.17.195 ādayo) sudassanaṃ nāma, soṇanandajātake (jā. 2.20.92 ādayo) brahmavaḍḍhanaṃ nāma, khaṇḍahālajātake(jā. 2.22.982 ādayo) pupphavatī nāma, imasmiṃ pana yudhañjayajātake (jā. 1.11.73 ādayo) rammanagaraṃ nāma ahosi, evamassa kadāci nāmaṃ parivattati. Tena vuttaṃ – “rājaputtoti rammanagare sabbadattassa nāma rañño putto”ti. Tassa pana rañño puttasahassaṃ ahosi. Bodhisatto jeṭṭhaputto, tassa rājā uparajjaṃ adāsi. So heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva divase divase mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Evaṃ gacchante kāle bodhisatto ekadivasaṃ pātova rathavaraṃ abhiruhitvā mahantena sirivibhavena uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchanto rukkhaggatiṇaggasākhaggamakkaṭakasuttajālādīsu muttājālākārena lagge ussāvabindū disvā “samma sārathi, kiṃ nāmeta”nti pucchitvā “ete, deva, himasamaye patanakaussāvabindū nāmā”ti sutvā divasabhāgaṃ uyyāne kīḷitvā sāyanhakāle paccāgacchanto te adisvā “samma sārathi, kahaṃ te ussāvabindū, na te idāni passāmī”ti pucchitvā “deva, sūriye uggacchante [P 0.0183] sabbe bhijjitvā vilayaṃ gacchantī”ti sutvā “yathā ime uppajjitvā bhijjanti, evaṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitasaṅkhārāpi tiṇagge ussāvabindusadisāva, tasmā mayā byādhijarāmaraṇehi apīḷiteneva mātāpitaro āpucchitvā pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ussāvabindumeva ārammaṇaṃ katvā āditte viya tayo bhave passanto attano gehaṃ āgantvā alaṅkatapaṭiyattāya vinicchayasālāya nisinnassa pitu santikameva gantvā pitaraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito pabbajjaṃ yāci. Tena vuttaṃ –

This Bārāṇasī was named Surundhananagara in the Udayajātaka, Sudassana in the Cūḷasutasomajātaka, Brahmavaḍḍhana in the Soṇanandajātaka, and Pupphavatī in the Khaṇḍahālajātaka. But in this Yudhañjayajātaka, it was named Rammanagara. Thus its name changed from time to time. Therefore it was said: ‘The prince in the city of Rammanagara, the son of the king named Sabbadatta.’ That king had a thousand sons. The Bodhisatta was the eldest son, and the king gave him the position of viceroy. In the way previously described, he gave great alms day after day. As time passed, one day the Bodhisattva, having mounted a splendid chariot early in the morning, was going to the park for amusement with great splendor and magnificence. Seeing dewdrops clinging like strings of pearls to the tips of trees, the tips of grass, the tips of branches, spiderwebs, and the like, he asked: ‘Friend charioteer, what is this?’ Having heard, ‘Sire, these are called dewdrops, which fall during the cold season,’ he played in the park for the day. Returning in the evening and not seeing them, he asked: ‘Friend charioteer, where are those dewdrops? I do not see them now.’ Having heard, ‘Sire, when the sun rises, they all break up and vanish,’ he thought: ‘Just as these arise and break up, so the life-formations of these beings are like dewdrops on a blade of grass. Therefore, before I am afflicted by sickness, old age, and death, I should ask leave of my mother and father and go forth.’ Taking the dewdrops themselves as his object, seeing the three planes of existence as if ablaze, he returned to his own house. He went to his father, who was seated in the adorned and prepared hall of justice, paid homage to him, and, standing to one side, requested to go forth. Therefore it was said:

“Ussāvabinduṃ [M 0.0178][V 0.0168] sūriyātape, patitaṃ disvāna saṃvijiṃ.

“Having seen a dewdrop dissipated in the sun’s heat, I was stirred.

2.

2.

“Taññevādhipatiṃ katvā, saṃvegamanubrūhayiṃ;

Mātāpitū ca vanditvā, pabbajjamanuyācaha”nti.

“Having made that my governing principle, I cultivated a sense of urgency; and having venerated my mother and father, I requested the going forth.”

Tattha sūriyātapeti sūriyātapahetu, sūriyarasmisamphassanimittaṃ. “Sūriyātapenā”tipi pāṭho. Patitaṃ disvānāti vinaṭṭhaṃ passitvā, pubbe rukkhaggādīsu muttājālādiākārena laggaṃ hutvā dissamānaṃ sūriyarasmisamphassena vinaṭṭhaṃ paññācakkhunā oloketvā. Saṃvijinti yathā etāni, evaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitānipi lahuṃ lahuṃ bhijjamānasabhāvānīti aniccatāmanasikāravasena saṃvegamāpajjiṃ.

Herein, sūriyātape means on account of the sun’s heat, as a result of contact with the sun’s rays. There is also the reading sūriyātapena. Patitaṃ disvāna means having seen it perished; that is, having observed with the eye of wisdom how what was formerly seen clinging to the tips of trees and so on in the form of a net of pearls had perished by contact with the sun’s rays. Saṃvijiṃ means: I experienced a sense of spiritual urgency by means of attention to impermanence, thinking: ‘Just as these are, so too the lives of beings have a nature that quickly and easily breaks apart.’

Taññevādhipatiṃ katvā, saṃvegamanubrūhayinti taññeva ussāvabindūnaṃ aniccataṃ adhipatiṃ mukhaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā tatheva sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ ittaraṭṭhitikataṃ parittakālataṃ manasikaronto ekavāraṃ uppannaṃ saṃvegaṃ punappunaṃ uppādanena anuvaḍḍhesiṃ. Pabbajjamanuyācahanti “tiṇagge ussāvabindū viya na ciraṭṭhitike sattānaṃ jīvite mayā byādhijarāmaraṇehi anabhibhūteneva pabbajitvā yattha etāni na santi, taṃ amataṃ mahānibbānaṃ gavesitabba”nti cintetvā mātāpitaro upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “pabbajjaṃ me anujānāthā”ti te ahaṃ pabbajjaṃ yāciṃ. Evaṃ mahāsattena pabbajjāya yācitāya sakalanagare mahantaṃ kolāhalamahosi – “uparājā kira yudhañjayo pabbajitukāmo”ti[P 0.0184].

Taññevādhipatiṃ katvā, saṃvegam anubrūhayiṃ means: having made that very impermanence of the dewdrops the sovereign, the principal, the forerunner, and the leader, and in the same way attending to the transient nature and brief duration of all formations, I augmented the sense of urgency that had arisen once by arousing it again and again. Pabbajjam anuyācahaṃ means: I requested the going forth, thinking: ‘The life of beings is not long-lasting, like dewdrops on a blade of grass. Before I am overcome by sickness, old age, and death, I must go forth and seek the deathless, great Nibbāna, where these things do not exist.’ Having approached my mother and father and paid homage to them, I requested of them the going forth, saying: ‘Grant me permission for the going forth.’ When the Great Being thus requested the going forth, a great uproar arose in the entire city: ‘The viceroy Yudhañjaya, it seems, desires to go forth!’

Tena ca samayena kāsiraṭṭhavāsino rājānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ āgantvā rammake paṭivasanti. Te sabbepi sannipatiṃsu. Iti sapariso rājā negamā ceva jānapadā ca bodhisattassa mātā devī ca sabbe ca orodhā mahāsattaṃ “mā kho tvaṃ, tāta kumāra, pabbajī”ti nivāresuṃ. Tattha rājā “sace te kāmehi ūnaṃ, ahaṃ te paripūrayāmi, ajjeva rajjaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti āha. Tassa mahāsatto –

At that time, inhabitants of the Kāsī country who had come to see the king were residing in Rammaka. They all assembled. Then the king with his retinue, the townsfolk and the countryfolk, the Bodhisatta’s mother the queen, and all the women of the royal harem tried to dissuade the Great Being, saying: ‘Dear Prince, do not go forth!’ Thereupon the king said: ‘If you are lacking in sensual pleasures, I will provide them for you. Take over the kingdom this very day!’ To him the Great Being said:

“Mā maṃ deva nivārehi, pabbajantaṃ rathesabha;

Māhaṃ kāmehi sammatto, jarāya vasamanvagū”ti. (jā. 1.11.77) –

“Do not prevent me from going forth, O Sire, bull among chariot-warriors; lest, intoxicated with sensual pleasures, I fall under the sway of old age.”

Attano [M 0.0179] pabbajjāchandameva vatvā taṃ sutvā saddhiṃ orodhehi mātuyā karuṇaṃ paridevantiyā –

Having thus stated his own wish to go forth, he spoke to his mother, who, upon hearing this, was lamenting piteously along with the women of the harem:

“Ussāvova [V 0.0169] tiṇaggamhi, sūriyuggamanaṃ pati;

Evamāyu manussānaṃ, mā maṃ amma nivārayā”ti. (jā. 1.11.79) –

“Like a dewdrop on a blade of grass at the sun’s rising, such is the lifespan of humans. Do not prevent me, mother.”

Attano pabbajjākāraṇaṃ kathetvā nānappakāraṃ tehi yāciyamānopi abhisaṃvaḍḍhamānasaṃvegattā anosakkitamānaso piyatare mahati ñātiparivaṭṭe uḷāre rājissariye ca nirapekkhacitto pabbaji. Tena vuttaṃ –

Having thus stated the reason for his going forth, though he was implored by them in various ways, because his sense of spiritual urgency was ever increasing, his mind did not waver. With a mind detached, he went forth, indifferent to his very dear, great circle of relatives and to his lofty royal sovereignty. Therefore it was said:

3.

3.

“Yācanti maṃ pañjalikā, sanegamā saraṭṭhakā;

Ajjeva putta paṭipajja, iddhaṃ phītaṃ mahāmahiṃ.

“With hands raised in homage they entreat me, the townsfolk and the countryfolk together: ‘Son, this very day take up this great earth, prosperous and thriving.’

4.

4.

“Sarājake sahorodhe, sanegame saraṭṭhake;

Karuṇaṃ paridevante, anapekkho pariccaji”nti.

“While the king with his harem, the townsfolk and the countryfolk, were all lamenting piteously, unconcerned, I renounced them.”

Tattha pañjalikāti paggahitaañjalikā. Sanegamā saraṭṭhakāti negamehi ceva raṭṭhavāsīhi ca saddhiṃ sabbe rājapurisā “mā kho, tvaṃ deva, pabbajī”ti maṃ yācanti. Mātāpitaro pana ajjeva putta paṭipajja, gāmanigamarājadhāniabhivuddhiyā vepullappattiyā ca, iddhaṃ vibhavasārasampattiyā sassādinipphattiyā ca, phītaṃ imaṃ mahāmahiṃ anusāsa, chattaṃ ussāpetvā rajjaṃ kārehīti yācanti. Evaṃ pana saha raññāti sarājake, tathā sahorodhe sanegame saraṭṭhake mahājane yathā suṇantānampi pageva passantānaṃ mahantaṃ kāruññaṃ hoti, evaṃ karuṇaṃ paridevante tattha tattha anapekkho alaggacitto “ahaṃ tadā pabbaji”nti dasseti.

Herein, pañjalikā means with hands raised in the gesture of reverence. Sanegamā saraṭṭhakā means that all the royal retainers together with the townsfolk and the countryfolk entreat me, saying: ‘Sire, do not go forth!’ My parents, however, entreat me, saying: ‘Son, this very day take up and rule this great earth, which is prosperous (iddhaṃ) because of its attainment of abundant wealth and resources and its successful harvests, and thriving (phītaṃ) because of the growth and expansion of its villages, towns, and capital city. Raise the white parasol and exercise sovereignty!’ Then, sarājake means along with the king. Similarly for sahorodhe, sanegame, and saraṭṭhake. He shows: ‘While the great populace was lamenting so piteously that great compassion arose even in those who merely heard them, to say nothing of those who saw them, I was unconcerned (anapekkho), my mind unattached (alaggacitto) to this or that, and I went forth at that time.’

5-6. Idāni [P 0.0185] yadatthaṃ cakkavattisirisadisaṃ rajjasiriṃ piyatare ñātibandhave pahāya siniddhaṃ pariggahaparijanaṃ lokābhimataṃ mahantaṃ yasañca nirapekkho pariccajinti dassetuṃ dve gāthā abhāsi.

Now he spoke two verses to show for what reason he, being unconcerned, renounced the glory of kingship comparable to the splendor of a wheel-turning monarch, his very dear relatives and kinsmen, his affectionate dependents and attendants, and the great fame esteemed by the world.

Tattha kevalanti anavasesaṃ itthāgāraṃ samuddapariyantañca pathaviṃ pabbajjādhippāyena cajamāno evaṃ me sammāsambodhi sakkā adhigantunti bodhiyāyeva kāraṇā na kiñci cintesiṃ, na tattha īsakaṃ laggaṃ janesinti attho. Tasmāti yasmā mātāpitaro tañca mahāyasaṃ rajjañca me na dessaṃ[M 0.0180], piyameva, tato pana sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena sabbaññutaññāṇameva mayhaṃ piyataraṃ, tasmā mātādīhi saddhiṃ rajjaṃ ahaṃ tadā pariccajinti.

Herein, kevalaṃ means entirely: renouncing the women's quarters without remainder and the earth bounded by the ocean with the intention of going forth, for the sake of awakening alone I thought of nothing else, thinking, ‘In this way, perfect self-enlightenment can be attained by me.’ The meaning is: I did not generate even the slightest attachment to it. Tasmā means: since my parents and that great, glorious kingship were not hateful to me, but were indeed dear, yet the knowledge of omniscience was a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times dearer to me, therefore I renounced the kingdom along with my mother and the others at that time.

Tadetaṃ [V 0.0170] sabbaṃ pariccajitvā pabbajjāya mahāsatte nikkhamante tassa kaniṭṭhabhātā yudhiṭṭhilakumāro nāma pitaraṃ vanditvā pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā bodhisattaṃ anubandhi. Te ubhopi nagarā nikkhamma mahājanaṃ nivattetvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā manorame ṭhāne assamapadaṃ katvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā vanamūlaphalādīhi yāvajīvaṃ yāpetvā brahmalokaparāyanā ahesuṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

Having renounced all this, when the Great Being was departing for the going forth, his younger brother, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila, after paying homage to their father and getting his permission for the going forth, followed the Bodhisatta. Both of them left the city, turned back the great crowd, and entered the Himalayas. Having made a hermitage in a delightful spot, they went forth with the going forth of seers. They produced the meditative absorptions and the direct knowledges, sustained themselves for life on wild roots and fruits, and had the Brahma-world as their destination. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Ubho kumārā pabbajitā, yudhañjayo yudhiṭṭhilo;

Pahāya mātāpitaro, saṅgaṃ chetvāna maccuno”ti. (jā. 1.11.83);

“Both princes went forth, Yudhañjaya and Yudhiṭṭhila; having left their mother and father, having cut off the attachment of Death.”

Tattha saṅgaṃ chetvāna maccunoti maccumārassa sahakārikāraṇabhūtattā santakaṃ rāgadosamohasaṅgaṃ vikkhambhanavasena chinditvā ubhopi pabbajitāti.

Herein, saṅgaṃ chetvāna maccuno means: having cut off, by way of suppression, the attachment consisting of lust, hatred, and delusion, which is one’s own property and the cooperating cause of Māra the Death-bringer, both of them went forth.

Tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, yudhiṭṭhilakumāro ānandatthero, yudhañjayo lokanātho.

At that time the mother and father were of the great royal family, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila was the Elder Ānanda, and Yudhañjaya was the Protector of the World.

Tassa pabbajjato pubbe pavattitamahādānāni ceva rajjādipariccāgo ca dānapāramī, kāyavacīsaṃvaro sīlapāramī, pabbajjā ca jhānādhigamo ca nekkhammapāramī, aniccato manasikāraṃ ādiṃ katvā abhiññādhigamapariyosānā paññā dānādīnaṃ upakārānupakāradhammapariggaṇhanapaññā ca paññāpāramī, sabbattha tadatthasādhanaṃ vīriyaṃ vīriyapāramī[P 0.0186], ñāṇakhanti adhivāsanakhanti ca khantipāramī, paṭiññāya avisaṃvādanaṃ saccapāramī, sabbattha acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānapāramī, sabbasattesu hitacittatāya mettābrahmavihāravasena ca mettāpāramī, sattasaṅkhārakatavippakāraupekkhanavasena upekkhābrahmavihāravasena ca upekkhāpāramīti dasa pāramiyo labbhanti. Visesato pana nekkhammapāramīti veditabbā. Tathā akitticariyāyaṃ viya idhāpi mahāpurisassa acchariyaguṇā yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbā. Tena vuccati “evaṃ acchariyā hete, abbhutā ca mahesino…pe… dhammassa anudhammato”ti.

Before his renunciation, the great gifts he gave and the relinquishment of kingship and other possessions were the perfection of generosity; restraint in body and speech was the perfection of virtue; his renunciation and attainment of jhāna were the perfection of renunciation; beginning with contemplation of impermanence and ending with the attainment of the higher knowledges, and the wisdom that discerns the helpful and harmful aspects of generosity and other virtues, was the perfection of wisdom; the effort that accomplishes the purpose in all things was the perfection of energy; patience in respect to knowledge and patient endurance were the perfection of patience; not deceiving in what was promised was the perfection of truthfulness; unshakable resolution and determination in all things was the perfection of determination; a mind of goodwill toward all beings, by way of the divine abiding of loving-kindness, was the perfection of loving-kindness; equanimity toward the various actions of beings and formations, by way of the divine abiding of equanimity, was the perfection of equanimity. Thus, the ten perfections are obtained. In particular, it should be understood as the perfection of renunciation. Just as in the case of Akitti’s conduct, here too the marvelous qualities of the great being should be ascertained as is proper. Therefore, it is said: “So marvelous are these, and so wonderful, the qualities of the great sage… in accordance with the Dhamma.”

Yudhañjayacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Conduct of Yudhañjaya is concluded.

2. Somanassacariyāvaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Conduct of Somanassa

7. Dutiye [M 0.0181][V 0.0171] indapatthe puruttameti evaṃnāmake nagaravare. Kāmitoti mātāpituādīhi “aho vata eko putto uppajjeyyā”ti evaṃ cirakāle patthito. Dayitoti piyāyito. Somanassoti vissutoti “somanasso”ti evaṃ pakāsanāmo.

7. In the second story: in Indapattha, the best of cities, so named. `Kāmita` means desired for a long time by his parents and others, who wished, “Oh, if only a son would be born!” `Dayita` means beloved. `Somanassa` means renowned; thus his proclaimed name was “Somanassa.”

8. Sīlavāti dasakusalakammapathasīlena ceva ācārasīlena ca samannāgato. Guṇasampannoti saddhābāhusaccādiguṇehi upeto, paripuṇṇo vā. Kalyāṇapaṭibhānavāti taṃtaṃitikattabbasādhanena upāyakosallasaṅkhātena ca sundarena paṭibhānena samannāgato. Vuḍḍhāpacāyīti mātāpitaro kule jeṭṭhāti evaṃ ye jātivuḍḍhā, ye ca sīlādiguṇehi vuḍḍhā, tesaṃ apacāyanasīlo. Hirīmāti pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇāya hiriyā samannāgato. Saṅgahesu ca kovidoti dānapiyavacanaatthacariyāsamānattatāsaṅkhātehi catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi yathārahaṃ sattānaṃ saṅgaṇhanesu kusalo. Evarūpo reṇussa nāma kururājassa putto somanassoti vissuto yadā homīti sambandho.

8. `Sīlavā` (virtuous) means endowed with the virtue of the tenfold path of wholesome kamma and the virtue of good conduct. `Guṇasampanna` (full of virtues) means possessing qualities such as faith, great learning, and so on, or being complete in them. `Kalyāṇapaṭibhānavā` (endowed with fine intelligence) means endowed with a beautiful intelligence characterized by skill in means for accomplishing what is appropriate. `Vuḍḍhāpacāyī` (reverential toward elders) means having the habit of honoring those who are senior by birth—such as one's mother, father, and the eldest in the family—and those who are senior by virtue of qualities such as virtue. `Hirīmā` (conscientious) means endowed with the moral shame that has the characteristic of abhorring evil. `Saṅgahesu ca kovido` (skilled in the means of beneficence) means being adept in the four bases of beneficence—generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality—as appropriate for gathering beings. The connection is to the words: 'When I was such a one, the son of King Reṇu of the Kurus, renowned as Somanassa.'

9. Tassa rañño patikaroti tena kururājena pati abhikkhaṇaṃ upakattabbabhāvena patikaro vallabho. Kuhakatāpasoti asantaguṇasambhāvanalakkhaṇena kohaññena [P 0.0187] jīvitakappanako eko tāpaso, tassa rañño sakkātabbo ahosi. Ārāmanti phalārāmaṃ, yattha eḷālukalābukumbhaṇḍatipusādivalliphalāni ceva taṇḍuleyyakādisākañca ropīyati. Mālāvacchanti jātiatimuttakādipupphagacchaṃ, tena pupphārāmaṃ dasseti. Ettha ca ārāmaṃ katvā tattha mālāvacchañca yathāvuttaphalavacchañca ropetvā tato laddhadhanaṃ saṃharitvā ṭhapento jīvatīti attho veditabbo.

9. `A favorite of that king`: this means he was a favorite (`vallabho`) of that Kuru king, one who had to be constantly attended to. `A deceitful ascetic` means an ascetic who maintained his livelihood through deceit, characterized by pretending to possess virtues he did not have; he was to be honored by the king. `Ārāma` means a fruit park where vining fruits such as cucumbers, gourds, and pumpkins, as well as greens like taṇḍuleyyaka, were planted. `Mālāvaccham` means a thicket of flowers such as jasmine and atimuttaka; by this, it indicates a flower park. Here, it should be understood that he lived by establishing a park and planting in it both a flower thicket and the aforesaid fruit thicket, then gathering and storing the wealth obtained from them.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – tadā mahārakkhito nāma tāpaso pañcasatatāpasaparivāro himavante vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadacārikaṃ caranto indapatthanagaraṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā sapariso piṇḍāya [M 0.0182] caranto rājadvāraṃ pāpuṇi. Rājā isigaṇaṃ disvā iriyāpathe pasanno alaṅkatamahātale nisīdāpetvā paṇītenāhārena parivisitvā “bhante, imaṃ vassārattaṃ mama uyyāneyeva vasathā”ti vatvā tehi saddhiṃ uyyānaṃ gantvā vasanaṭṭhānāni kāretvā pabbajitaparikkhāre datvā nikkhami. Tato paṭṭhāya sabbepi te rājanivesane bhuñjanti.

Here is the sequential account: At that time, an ascetic named Mahārakkhita, with a retinue of five hundred ascetics, was dwelling in the Himalayas. Wandering on tour through the countryside to obtain salt and sour things, he arrived at the city of Indapattha and stayed in the royal park. While going for alms with his retinue, he reached the king’s gate. The king, pleased by their deportment, had them seated on a grand, ornamented terrace, served them with excellent food, and said, “Venerable sirs, please dwell in my park for this rainy season.” Then, he went with them to the park, had lodgings prepared, provided them with the requisites of a renunciate, and departed. From then on, they all ate in the royal palace.

Rājā [V 0.0172] pana aputtako putte pattheti, puttā nuppajjanti. Vassārattaccayena mahārakkhito “himavantaṃ gamissāmā”ti rājānaṃ āpucchitvā raññā katasakkārasammāno nikkhamitvā antarāmagge majjhanhikasamaye maggā okkamma ekassa sandacchāyassa rukkhassa heṭṭhā sapariso nisīdi. Tāpasā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “rājā aputtako, sādhu vatassa sace rājaputtaṃ labheyyā”ti. Mahārakkhito taṃ kathaṃ sutvā “bhavissati nu kho rañño putto, udāhu no”ti upadhārento “bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “mā tumhe cintayittha, ajja paccūsakāle eko [P 0.0188] devaputto cavitvā rañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattissatī”ti āha.

The king, however, was childless and longed for sons, but no sons were born to him. At the end of the rainy season, Mahārakkhita took leave of the king, saying, “We will go to the Himalayas.” Having been honored and respected by the king, he departed. On the way, at midday, he and his retinue stepped off the road and sat beneath a densely shady tree. The ascetics started a conversation: “The king is childless—it would be good if he could obtain a prince!” Hearing this conversation, Mahārakkhita reflected, “Will the king have a son, or not?” Knowing that he would, he said, “Do not worry. Today at dawn, a divine being will pass away and be reborn in the womb of the king's chief queen.”

Taṃ sutvā eko kūṭajaṭilo “idāni rājakulūpako bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā tāpasānaṃ gamanakāle gilānālayaṃ katvā nipajjitvā “ehi gacchāmā”ti vutte “na sakkomī”ti āha. Mahārakkhito tassa nipannakāraṇaṃ ñatvā “yadā sakkosi, tadā āgaccheyyāsī”ti isigaṇaṃ ādāya himavantameva gato. Kuhako nivattitvā vegena gantvā rājadvāre ṭhatvā “mahārakkhitassa upaṭṭhākatāpaso āgato”ti rañño ārocāpetvā raññā vegena pakkosāpito pāsādaṃ abhiruyha paññatte āsane nisīdi. Rājā taṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno isīnaṃ ārogyaṃ pucchitvā “bhante, atikhippaṃ nivattittha, kenatthena āgatatthā”ti āha.

Hearing that, a fraudulent matted-hair ascetic thought, “Now I will become an associate of the royal family.” When the ascetics were leaving, he made a pretense of being sick, lay down, and when told, “Come, let us go,” he replied, “I am unable.” Mahārakkhita, knowing the reason for his lying down, said, “When you are able, then you may come,” and taking the group of seers, went straight to the Himalayas. The charlatan turned back, hurried to the king's gate, stood there, and had it announced to the king, “The attendant ascetic of Mahārakkhita has arrived.” Having been quickly summoned by the king, he ascended to the palace and sat on the prepared seat. The king paid homage to him, sat to one side, inquired about the health of the seers, and said, “Venerable sir, you have returned very quickly. For what reason have you come?”

Mahārāja, isigaṇo sukhanisinno “sādhu vatassa sace rañño vaṃsānurakkhako putto uppajjeyyā”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Ahaṃ taṃ kathaṃ sutvā “bhavissati nu kho rañño putto, udāhu no”ti dibbacakkhunā olokento “mahiddhiko devaputto cavitvā aggamahesiyā sudhammāya kucchimhi nibbattissatī”ti disvā “ajānantā gabbhaṃ nāseyyuṃ, ācikkhissāmi [M 0.0183] tāva na”nti tumhākaṃ kathanatthāya āgato, kathitaṃ vo mayā, gacchāmaha”nti. Rājā “bhante, na sakkā gantu”nti haṭṭhatuṭṭho pasannacitto kuhakatāpasaṃ uyyānaṃ netvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ saṃvidahitvā adāsi. So tato paṭṭhāya rājakule bhuñjanto vasati, “dibbacakkhuko”tvevassa nāmaṃ ahosi.

“Great king, the group of seers, seated comfortably, initiated a discussion: ‘Indeed, it would be good if a son were born to the king to preserve the lineage.’ Having heard that discussion, I thought, ‘Will the king have a son, or not?’ and looked with the divine eye. I saw that a mighty divine being, having passed away, would be reborn in the womb of the chief queen Sudhammā. Thinking, ‘Those who do not know might destroy the embryo, so I must inform him,’ I came to tell you. I have told you; now I shall go.” The king, delighted, gratified, and with a pleased mind, said, “Venerable sir, you cannot go,” and, taking the deceitful ascetic to the park, he had a dwelling place arranged and gave it to him. From then on, he dwelt there, eating in the royal household, and he acquired the name “Dibbacakkhuka,” the One with the Divine Eye.

Tadā bodhisatto tāvatiṃsabhavanato cavitvā tattha paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, jātassa ca nāmaggahaṇadivase “somanasso”ti [P 0.0189] nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So kumāraparihārena vaḍḍhati. Kuhakatāpasopi uyyānassa ekapasse nānappakāraṃ sūpeyyasākañca phalavalliādayo ca ropetvā paṇṇikānaṃ hatthe vikkiṇanto dhanaṃ saṃharati. Atha bodhisattassa sattavassikakāle rañño paccanto [V 0.0173] kupito. So “tāta, dibbacakkhutāpase mā pamajjā”ti kumāraṃ paṭicchāpetvā paccantaṃ vūpasametuṃ gato.

Then the Bodhisatta passed away from the Tāvatiṃsa realm and took rebirth there. On the day of his naming ceremony, they named him “Somanassa.” He grew up with the care befitting a prince. The deceitful ascetic, for his part, planted various kinds of vegetables for curry, fruit vines, and so on, on one side of the park, and sold them through female greengrocers, accumulating wealth. When the Bodhisatta was seven years old, the king's border region rose in revolt. The king entrusted the prince to the ascetic, saying to his son, “My son, do not be negligent toward the ascetic with the divine eye,” and went to pacify the border region.

10-13. Athekadivasaṃ kumāro “jaṭilaṃ passissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gantvā kūṭajaṭilaṃ ekaṃ gandhikakāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā ubhohi hatthehi dve ghaṭe gahetvā sākavatthusmiṃ udakaṃ siñcantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ kūṭajaṭilo attano samaṇadhammaṃ akatvā paṇṇikakammaṃ karotī”ti ñatvā “kiṃ karosi paṇṇikagahapatikā”ti taṃ lajjāpetvā avanditvā eva nikkhami.

Then one day, the prince thought, “I will see the matted-hair ascetic,” and went to the park. There, he saw the deceitful ascetic wearing one dyed-ochre robe as a lower garment and another as an upper garment, holding two pots in both hands, and sprinkling water on the vegetable plot. Knowing, “This deceitful ascetic is not practicing his duties as a recluse but is doing the work of a greengrocer,” he shamed him by saying, “What are you doing, you greengrocer-householder?” and left without paying homage.

Kūṭajaṭilo “ayaṃ idāneva evarūpo, pacchā ‘ko jānāti kiṃ karissatī’ti idāneva naṃ nāsetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā rañño āgamanakāle pāsāṇaphalakaṃ ekamantaṃ khipitvā pānīyaghaṭaṃ bhinditvā paṇṇasālāya tiṇāni vikiritvā sarīraṃ telena makkhetvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā sasīsaṃ pārupitvā mahādukkhappatto viya mañce nipajji. Rājā āgantvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā nivesanaṃ apavisitvāva “mama sāmikaṃ dibbacakkhukaṃ passissāmī”ti paṇṇasāladvāraṃ gantvā taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti anto pavisitvā taṃ nipannakaṃ disvā pāde parimajjanto pucchi – “kena, tvaṃ bhante, evaṃ viheṭhito, kamajja yamalokaṃ nemi, taṃ me sīghaṃ ācikkhā”ti.

The fraudulent matted-hair ascetic thought: “He is like this even now; later, who knows what he will do? It is fitting to destroy him right now.” So thinking, at the time of the king’s arrival, he threw a stone slab to one side, broke the water pot, scattered grass in the leaf-hut, smeared his body with oil, entered the leaf-hut, covered himself from head to foot, and lay down on the bed as if afflicted by great suffering. The king arrived, circumambulated the city, and without entering his own residence, he went to the door of the leaf-hut, thinking: “I will see my master, the one with the divine eye.” Seeing the disarray, he wondered: “What can this be?” Entering, he saw him lying down, and stroking his feet, he asked: “Venerable sir, by whom have you been harassed like this? Whom shall I send to the world of Yama today? Tell me quickly!”

Taṃ [M 0.0184] sutvā kūṭajaṭilo nitthunanto uṭṭhāya diṭṭho, [P 0.0190] mahārāja, tvaṃ me, passitvā tayi vissāsena ahaṃ imaṃ vippakāraṃ patto, tava puttenamhi evaṃ viheṭhitoti. Taṃ sutvā rājā coraghātake āṇāpesi – “gacchatha kumārassa sīsaṃ chinditvā sarīrañcassa khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā rathiyā rathiyaṃ vikirathā”ti. Te mātarā alaṅkaritvā attano aṅke nisīdāpitaṃ kumāraṃ ākaḍḍhiṃsu – “raññā te vadho āṇatto”ti. Kumāro maraṇabhayatajjito mātu aṅkato vuṭṭhāya – “rañño maṃ dassetha, santi rājakiccānī”ti āha. Te kumārassa vacanaṃ sutvā māretuṃ avisahantā goṇaṃ viya rajjuyā parikaḍḍhantā netvā rañño dassesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “tamahaṃ disvāna kuhaka”ntiādi.

Hearing that, the fraudulent matted-hair ascetic, groaning, got up and said: “Great king, you see me. It is because I trusted you that I have met with this disaster; I have been harassed in this way by your son.” Hearing this, the king ordered the executioners: “Go, cut off the prince’s head, and after cutting his body to pieces, scatter them on every street.” The executioners dragged away the prince, who had been adorned by his mother and seated on her lap, saying: “The king has ordered your execution.” Terrified by the fear of death, the prince rose from his mother’s lap and said: “Show me to the king; there are royal matters to attend to.” Hearing the prince’s words, unable to bring themselves to kill him, they dragged him with a rope like an ox and presented him to the king. Therefore it was said: “Having seen that fraudulent one,” and so on.

Tattha thusarāsiṃva ataṇḍulanti taṇḍulakaṇehi virahitaṃ thusarāsiṃ viya, dumaṃva rukkhaṃ viya, anto mahāsusiraṃ. Kadaliṃva asārakaṃ sīlādisārarahitaṃ tāpasaṃ ahaṃ disvā natthi imassa sataṃ sādhūnaṃ jhānādidhammo. Kasmā? Sāmaññā samaṇabhāvā sīlamattatopi apagato parihīno [V 0.0174] ayaṃ, tathā hi ayaṃ hirīsukkadhammajahito pajahitahirisaṅkhātasukkadhammo. Jīvitavuttikāraṇāti “kevalaṃ jīvitasseva hetu ayaṃ tāpasaliṅgena caratī”ti cintesinti dasseti. Parantihīti paranto paccanto nivāsabhūto etesaṃ atthīti parantino, sīmantarikavāsino. Tehi parantīhi aṭavikehi paccantadeso khobhito ahosi. Taṃ paccantakopaṃ nisedhetuṃ vūpasametuṃ gacchanto mama pitā kururājā “tāta somanassakumāra, mayhaṃ sāmikaṃ uggatāpanaṃ ghoratapaṃ paramasantindriyaṃ jaṭilaṃ mā pamajji. So hi amhākaṃ sabbakāmadado, tasmā yadicchakaṃ cittaruciyaṃ tassa cittānukūlaṃ pavattehi anuvattehī”ti tadā maṃ anusāsīti dasseti.

Herein, 'like a heap of chaff without rice grains' means like a heap of chaff devoid of rice grains; 'like a tree' means like a tree that is very hollow inside. 'Like a plantain without substance' means, having seen an ascetic devoid of the substance of virtue and so on, I thought: “This one does not possess the qualities of the good, such as jhāna. Why? Because he has fallen away, declined, even from the mere virtue of the ascetic state. For he has abandoned the white quality of conscience; that is, he has discarded the white quality called conscience.” 'For the sake of livelihood' shows that I thought: “This one wanders about in the guise of an ascetic merely for the sake of his livelihood.” 'By borderers': those for whom the borderland is their dwelling place are borderers, that is, dwellers on the frontier. The border region had been agitated by those borderers, the forest-dwellers. While going to suppress and pacify that border uprising, my father, the king of the Kurus, instructed me: “Dear Somanassakumāra, do not be negligent toward my master, the matted-hair ascetic of fierce austerity, of terrible asceticism, with supremely tranquil faculties. For he is the giver of all our wishes. Therefore, act according to his will, conform to his mind, just as you wish.” This shows that he instructed me thus at that time.

14. Tamahaṃ gantvānupaṭṭhānanti pitu vacanaṃ anatikkanto taṃ kūṭatāpasaṃ upaṭṭhānatthaṃ gantvā taṃ sākavatthusmiṃ udakaṃ āsiñcantaṃ disvā “paṇṇiko aya”nti ca ñatvā kacci te, gahapati, kusalanti, gahapati, [P 0.0191] te sarīrassa kacci kusalaṃ kusalameva, tathā hi sākavatthusmiṃ udakaṃ āsiñcasi. Kiṃ vā tava hiraññaṃ vā suvaṇṇaṃ vā āharīyatu, tathā hi paṇṇikavuttiṃ anutiṭṭhasīti idaṃ vacanaṃ abhāsiṃ.

14. 'I went to attend on him' means: not transgressing my father's word, I went for the purpose of attending on that fraudulent ascetic. Seeing him sprinkling water on a teak tree and knowing, “This is a vegetable-seller,” I spoke these words: “I hope you are well, householder? Householder, I hope your body is well? It must be well indeed, for you are sprinkling water on a teak tree. Or should bullion or gold be brought for you, since you are practicing the livelihood of a vegetable-seller?”

15. Tena [M 0.0185] so kupito āsīti tena mayā vuttagahapativādena so mānanissito mānaṃ allīno kuhako mayhaṃ kupito kuddho ahosi. Kuddho ca samāno “ghātāpemi tuvaṃ ajja, raṭṭhā pabbājayāmi vā”ti āha.

15. 'By that he was angered' means: because of that address “householder” spoken by me, that fraudulent one, who was reliant on conceit and clinging to conceit, became angry and enraged with me. And being enraged, he said: “Today I will have you killed, or I will have you banished from the kingdom!”

Tattha tuvaṃ ajjāti, tvaṃ ajja, idāniyeva rañño āgatakāleti attho.

Herein, 'you today' means: you today, that is, right now at the time of the king’s arrival. This is the meaning.

16. Nisedhayitvā paccantanti paccantaṃ vūpasametvā nagaraṃ apaviṭṭho taṅkhaṇaññeva uyyānaṃ gantvā kuhakaṃ kuhakatāpasaṃ kacci te, bhante, khamanīyaṃ, sammāno te pavattitoti kumārena te sammāno pavattito ahosi.

16. 'Having suppressed the border' means: having pacified the border, he entered the city. At that very moment, he went to the park and asked the fraudulent one, the fraudulent ascetic: “Venerable sir, are you getting by? Is honor being shown to you?” That is, was honor shown to you by the prince?

17. Kumāro yathā nāsiyoti yathā kumāro nāsiyo nāsetabbo ghātāpetabbo, tathā so pāpo tassa rañño ācikkhi. Āṇāpesīti mayhaṃ sāmike imasmiṃ dibbacakkhutāpase sati kiṃ mama na nipphajjati, tasmā puttena me attho natthi, tatopi ayameva seyyoti cintetvā āṇāpesi.

17. 'So that the prince would be destroyed' means: that evil one told the king in such a way that the prince would be destroyed, that he should be caused to be killed. 'He commanded': he commanded, thinking: “When my master, this ascetic with the divine eye, is here, what cannot be accomplished for me? Therefore, I have no need for a son; this one is better than him.”

18. Kinti[V 0.0175]? Sīsaṃ tattheva chinditvāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne taṃ kumāraṃ passatha, tattheva tassa sīsaṃ chinditvā sarīrañcassa katvāna catukhaṇḍikaṃ caturo khaṇḍe katvā rathiyā rathiyaṃ nīyantā vīthito vīthiṃ vikkhipantā dassetha. Kasmā? Sā gati jaṭilahīḷitāti yehi ayaṃ jaṭilo hīḷito, tesaṃ jaṭilahīḷitānaṃ sā gati sā nipphatti so vipākoti. Jaṭilahīḷitāti vā jaṭilahīḷanahetu sā tassa nipphattīti evañcettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

18. How so? 'Having cut off his head right there' means: wherever you see that prince, cut off his head right there; and having made his body into four pieces—into four parts—display it by carrying it from street to street and scattering it from lane to lane. Why? 'That is the destiny of one who scorns a matted-hair ascetic' means: for those by whom this matted-hair ascetic was scorned, that is their destiny, that their outcome, that their result. Or, 'of one who scorns a matted-hair ascetic' means: that is his outcome because of scorning the matted-hair ascetic. Thus the meaning should be understood here.

19. Tatthāti tassa rañño āṇāyaṃ, tasmiṃ vā tāpasassa paribhave. Kāraṇikāti ghātakā, coraghātakāti attho. Caṇḍāti kurūrā. Luddāti sudāruṇā. Akāruṇāti tasseva vevacanaṃ kataṃ. “Akaruṇā”tipi pāḷi, nikkaruṇāti attho. Mātu aṅke nisinnassāti mama mātu sudhammāya deviyā ucchaṅge nisinnassa. “Nisinnassā”ti anādare sāmivacanaṃ. Ākaḍḍhitvā nayanti manti mātarā alaṅkaritvā attano aṅke [M 0.0186] nisīdāpitaṃ [P 0.0192] maṃ rājāṇāya te coraghātakā goṇaṃ viya rajjuyā ākaḍḍhitvā āghātanaṃ nayanti. Kumāre pana nīyamāne dāsigaṇaparivutā saddhiṃ orodhehi sudhammā devī nāgarāpi “mayaṃ niraparādhaṃ kumāraṃ māretuṃ na dassāmā”ti tena saddhiṃyeva agamaṃsu.

19. 'Therein' means: in that command of the king, or in that contempt for the ascetic. 'The agents' means the killers, that is, the executioners of thieves. 'Fierce' means cruel. 'Savage' means very harsh. 'Uncompassionate' is a synonym for the same. There is also the reading 'akaruṇā', meaning merciless. 'Of him seated on his mother's lap' means: of me, seated on the lap of my mother, Queen Sudhammā. 'Of him seated' is a genitive of disregard. 'They drag me away and lead me' means: after my mother had adorned me and seated me on her lap, those executioners, by the king's command, drag me with a rope like an ox and lead me to the execution ground. But as the prince was being led away, Queen Sudhammā, surrounded by a retinue of slave girls along with the women of the harem, and the townspeople too, went along with him, thinking: “We will not allow the innocent prince to be killed.”

20. Bandhataṃ gāḷhabandhananti gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhantānaṃ tesaṃ kāraṇikapurisānaṃ. Rājakiriyāni atthi meti mayā rañño vattabbāni rājakiccāni atthi. Tasmā rañño dassetha maṃ khippanti tesaṃ ahaṃ evaṃ vacanaṃ avacaṃ.

20. 'Of them binding with a tight bond' means: of those executioners who were binding with a tight bond. 'I have royal business' means: there are royal matters that must be told by me to the king. 'Therefore show me to the king quickly': I spoke these words to them.

21. Rañño dassayiṃsu, pāpassa pāpasevinoti attanā pāpasīlassa lāmakācārassa kūṭatāpasassa sevanato pāpasevino rañño maṃ dassayiṃsu. Disvāna taṃ saññāpesinti taṃ mama pitaraṃ kururājānaṃ passitvā “kasmā maṃ, deva, mārāpesī”ti vatvā tena “kasmā ca pana tvaṃ mayhaṃ sāmikaṃ dibbacakkhutāpasaṃ gahapativādena samudācari. Idañcidañca vippakāraṃ karī”ti vutte “deva, gahapatiññeva ‘gahapatī’ti vadantassa ko mayhaṃ doso”ti vatvā tassa nānāvidhāni mālāvacchāni ropetvā pupphapaṇṇaphalāphalādīnaṃ vikkiṇanaṃ hatthato cassa tāni devasikaṃ vikkiṇantehi mālākārapaṇṇikehi saddahāpetvā “mālāvatthupaṇṇavatthūni upadhārethā”ti vatvā paṇṇasālañcassa pavisitvā pupphādivikkiyaladdhaṃ kahāpaṇakabhaṇḍikaṃ attano purisehi nīharāpetvā rājānaṃ saññāpesiṃ tassa kūṭatāpasabhāvaṃ jānāpesiṃ. Mamañca vasamānayinti tena saññāpanena “saccaṃ kho pana kumāro vadati, ayaṃ kūṭatāpaso pubbe appiccho viya hutvā idāni [V 0.0176] mahāpariggaho jāto”ti yathā tasmiṃ nibbinno mama vase vattati, evaṃ rājānaṃ mama vasamānesiṃ.

21. They showed me to the king, an associate of evil means: they showed me to the king, who was an associate of evil because he himself associated with a fraudulent ascetic of evil virtue and base conduct. Having seen him, I convinced him means: having seen my father, the king of the Kurus, I said, “Why, sire, did you have me ordered to be killed?” When he said, “But why did you address my master, the ascetic with the divine eye, with the term ‘householder’ and cause this and that disaster?” I replied, “Sire, what fault is mine for calling a householder ‘householder’?” Then, having had various kinds of flower beds and vegetable plots planted for him, and having had the gardeners and vegetable-sellers who sold the produce daily confirm this, and saying, “Please examine the plots for flowers and vegetables,” and having entered his leaf-hut and had my men bring out the bag of coins obtained from the sale of flowers and so on, I convinced the king, making him know the fraudulent nature of that ascetic. And I brought him under my control means: by that act of convincing, I brought the king under my control, so that, being disenchanted with that ascetic, he would act under my influence, thinking: “Indeed, the prince speaks the truth. This fraudulent ascetic, who formerly seemed to have few wishes, has now become one with great possessions.”

Tato mahāsatto “evarūpassa bālassa rañño santike vasanato himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajituṃ yutta”nti cintetvā rājānaṃ āpucchi – “na me, mahārāja, idha vāsena attho, anujānātha maṃ pabbajissāmī”ti. Rājā “tāta, mayā anupadhāretvāva te vadho āṇatto, khama mayhaṃ aparādha”nti mahāsattaṃ khamāpetvā “ajjeva imaṃ rajjaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti āha. Kumāro “deva, kimatthi mānusakesu [P 0.0193] bhogesu, ahaṃ pubbe dīgharattaṃ [M 0.0187] dibbabhogasampattiyo anubhaviṃ, na tatthāpi me saṅgo, pabbajissāmevāhaṃ, na tādisassa bālassa paraneyyabuddhino santike vasāmī”ti vatvā taṃ ovadanto –

Then the Great Being thought: “It is better to enter the Himalayas and go forth than to live near such a foolish king.” So he took leave of the king, saying: “Great King, there is no purpose in my living here. Permit me, I will go forth.” The king said: “My dear, without proper investigation I ordered your execution. Forgive my offense.” Having asked for the Great Being’s forgiveness, he said: “Take over this kingdom this very day.” The prince replied: “Your Majesty, what is the use of human enjoyments? In the past I enjoyed the divine fortune of enjoyments for a long time, but I had no attachment even to them. I will certainly go forth; I will not live near such a foolish person whose intelligence is led by others.” Advising him, he said:

“Anisamma kataṃ kammaṃ, anavatthāya cintitaṃ;

Bhesajjasseva vebhaṅgo, vipāko hoti pāpako.

“A deed done without investigation, a thought not well-defined, is like a medicine that has gone wrong: its result is evil.

“Nisamma ca kataṃ kammaṃ, sammāvatthāya cintitaṃ;

Bhesajjasseva sampatti, vipāko hoti bhadrako.

“But a deed done with investigation, a thought rightly defined, is like a medicine that is successful: its result is excellent.

“Alaso gihī kāmabhogī na sādhu, asaññato pabbajito na sādhu;

Rājā na sādhu anisammakārī, yo paṇḍito kodhano taṃ na sādhu.

“A lazy householder enjoying sensual pleasures is not good; an unrestrained one who has gone forth is not good; a king who acts without investigation is not good; and a wise person who is angry is not good.

“Nisamma khattiyo kayirā, nānisamma disampati;

Nisammakārino rāja, yaso kitti ca vaḍḍhati.

“A khattiya should act with investigation; a lord of the land should not act without investigation. O king, for one who acts with investigation, fame and renown increase.

“Nisamma daṇḍaṃ paṇayeyya issaro, vegā kataṃ tappati bhūmipāla;

Sammāpaṇīdhī ca narassa atthā, anānutappā te bhavanti pacchā.

“A ruler should impose punishment with investigation; the lord of the land repents what is done in haste. But a person’s aims that are rightly resolved do not lead to remorse afterwards.

“Anānutappāni hi ye karonti, vibhajja kammāyatanāni loke;

Viññuppasatthāni sukhudrayāni, bhavanti buddhānumatāni tāni.

“Indeed, the deeds that one performs in the world after having distinguished the grounds of action do not lead to later remorse; they are praised by the wise, have a happy outcome, and are approved by the enlightened.

“Āgacchuṃ [V 0.0177] dovārikā khaggabandhā, kāsāviyā hantu mamaṃ janinda;

Mātuñca aṅkasmimahaṃ nisinno, ākaḍḍhito sahasā tehi deva.

“Gatekeepers came with swords girded on, clad in ochre robes, to kill me, O lord of men. While I was sitting on my mother’s lap, O sire, I was dragged away by them with force.

“Kaṭukañhi [M 0.0188] sambādhaṃ sukicchaṃ patto, madhurampiyaṃ jīvitaṃ laddha rāja;

Kicchenahaṃ ajja vadhā pamutto, pabbajjamevābhimanohamasmī”ti. (jā. 1.15.227-234) –

“I have met with bitter, oppressive, and difficult peril, but have gained a sweet and dear life, O king. Today I have been freed from execution with difficulty; my mind is set only on going forth.”

Imāhi gāthāhi dhammaṃ desesi.

With these verses, he taught the Dhamma.

Tattha [P 0.0194] anisammāti anupadhāretvā. Anavatthāyāti avavatthapetvā. Vebhaṅgoti vipatti. Vipākoti nipphatti. Asaññatoti asaṃvuto dussīlo. Paṇayeyyāti paṭṭhapeyya. Vegāti vegena sahasā. Sammāpaṇīdhī cāti sammāpaṇidhinā, yoniso ṭhapitena cittena katā narassa atthā pacchā anānutappā bhavantīti attho. Vibhajjāti imāni kātuṃ yuttāni, imāni ayuttānīti evaṃ paññāya vibhajitvā. Kammāyatanānīti kammāni. Buddhānumatānīti paṇḍitehi anumatāni anavajjāni honti. Kaṭukanti dukkhaṃ asātaṃ, sambādhaṃ sukicchaṃ maraṇabhayaṃ pattomhi. Laddhāti attano ñāṇabalena jīvitaṃ labhitvā. Pabbajjamevābhimanoti pabbajjābhimukhacitto evāhamasmi.

Herein, anisamma means without investigating. Anavatthāya means without having determined. Vebhaṅgo means failure. Vipāko means outcome. Asaññato means unrestrained, immoral. Paṇayeyya means one should apply. Vegā means with haste, by force. As to sammāpaṇīdhī ca, the meaning is that a person’s aims achieved with a rightly directed mind, that is, a mind wisely established, do not lead to remorse afterwards. Vibhajja means having distinguished with wisdom thus: “These are fit to be done, these are unfit.” Kammāyatanāni means actions. Buddhānumatāni means they are approved by the wise, they are blameless. Kaṭukaṃ means painful, disagreeable; I have met with the fear of death, which is oppressive and difficult. Laddhā means having gained life by the power of his own knowledge. Pabbajjamevābhimano means I am one whose mind is facing toward going forth.

Evaṃ mahāsattena dhamme desite rājā deviṃ āmantesi – “devi, tvaṃ puttaṃ nivattehī”ti. Devīpi kumārassa pabbajjameva rocesi. Mahāsatto mātāpitaro vanditvā “sace mayhaṃ doso atthi, taṃ khamathā”ti khamāpetvā mahājanaṃ āpucchitvā himavantābhimukho agamāsi. Gate ca pana mahāsatte mahājano kūṭajaṭilaṃ pothetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Bodhisattopi sanāgarehi amaccapārisajjādīhi rājapurisehi assumukhehi anubandhiyamāno te nivattesi. Manussesu nivattesu manussavaṇṇenāgantvā devatāhi nīto satta pabbatarājiyo atikkamitvā himavante vissakammunā nimmitāya paṇṇasālāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Tena vuttaṃ –

When the Great Being had thus taught the Dhamma, the king addressed the queen: “My queen, you must turn our son back.” But the queen too approved of the prince’s going forth. The Great Being paid homage to his mother and father, asked for their forgiveness, saying, “If I have any fault, please forgive it,” took leave of the great assembly, and went facing the Himalayas. But after the Great Being had gone, the great crowd beat the fraudulent matted-hair ascetic and brought him to the end of his life. The Bodhisatta, though followed by weeping citizens, ministers, assembly members, and royal officials, turned them back. When the humans had turned back, deities came in human form and led him past seven mountain ranges to a leaf-hut in the Himalayas created by Vissakamma, where he went forth with the going-forth of a seer. Thus it was said:

22.

22.

“So maṃ tattha khamāpesi, mahārajjaṃ adāsi me;

Sohaṃ tamaṃ dālayitvā, pabbajiṃ anagāriya”nti.

“He asked me for forgiveness there, and he gave me the great kingdom; but I, having rent asunder that darkness, went forth into the homeless life.”

Tattha [V 0.0178] tamaṃ dālayitvāti kāmādīnavadassanassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ sammohatamaṃ vidhamitvā. Pabbajinti upāgacchiṃ. Anagāriyanti pabbajjaṃ.

Herein, having rent asunder that darkness means having dispelled the darkness of delusion, which is the opponent of seeing the danger in sensual pleasures. I went forth means I approached. The homeless life means the state of one who has gone forth.

23. Idāni [M 0.0189] yadatthaṃ tadā taṃ rājissariyaṃ pariccattaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “na me dessa”nti osānagāthamāha. Tassattho vuttanayova.

23. Now, to show for what reason he then relinquished that royal sovereignty, he speaks the concluding verse beginning “It was not hateful to me.” Its meaning is in the way already stated.

Evaṃ pana mahāsatte pabbajite yāva soḷasavassakālā rājakule [P 0.0195] paricārikavesena devatāyeva naṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu. So tattha jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Now, after the Great Being had thus gone forth, for a period of sixteen years deities in the guise of attendants served in the royal family. He, having there produced the jhānas and direct knowledges, became one bound for the Brahma world.

Tadā kuhako devadatto ahosi, mātā mahāmāyā, mahārakkhitatāpaso sāriputtatthero, somanassakumāro lokanātho.

At that time the fraudulent ascetic was Devadatta; the mother was Mahāmāyā; the ascetic Mahārakkhita was the Elder Sāriputta; and Prince Somanassa was the Protector of the World.

Tassa yudhañjayacariyāyaṃ (cariyā. 3.1 ādayo) vuttanayeneva dasa pāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Idhāpi nekkhammapāramī atisayavatīti sā eva desanaṃ āruḷhā. Tathā sattavassikakāle eva rājakiccesu samatthatā, tassa tāpasassa kūṭajaṭilabhāvapariggaṇhanaṃ, tena payuttena raññā vadhe āṇatte santāsābhāvo, rañño santikaṃ gantvā nānānayehi tassa sadosataṃ attano ca niraparādhataṃ mahājanassa majjhe pakāsetvā rañño ca paraneyyabuddhitaṃ bālabhāvañca paṭṭhapetvā tena khamāpitepi tassa santike vāsato rajjissariyato ca saṃvegamāpajjitvā nānappakāraṃ yāciyamānenapi hatthagataṃ rajjasiriṃ kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya chaḍḍetvā katthaci alaggacittena hutvā pabbajanaṃ, pabbajitvā pavivekārāmena hutvā nacirasseva appakasirena jhānābhiññānibbattananti evamādayo mahāsattassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

His ten perfections should be deduced in the same way as stated in the Cariya on Yudhañjaya. Here, too, the perfection of renunciation is pre-eminent, and so it is this that has been taken up in the teaching. Likewise, the following qualities and powers of the Great Being should be elucidated: his competence in royal duties even at the age of seven; his recognition of that ascetic’s state as a fraudulent matted-hair ascetic; his lack of terror when the king, instigated by that ascetic, ordered his execution; his going to the king and, in the midst of the great assembly, proclaiming by various methods that ascetic’s faultiness and his own innocence, and establishing the king’s susceptibility to being led by others and his foolishness; and then, even when asked for forgiveness by the king, feeling a sense of spiritual urgency regarding living near him and regarding royal sovereignty; and though begged in various ways, casting away the royal fortune that had come into his hands like a glob of phlegm and going forth with a mind unattached to anything; and having gone forth, delighting in seclusion and before long, with little trouble, producing the jhānas and direct knowledges.

Somanassacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Cariya on Somanassa is finished.

3. Ayogharacariyāvaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Ayoghara Conduct

24. Tatiye ayogharamhi saṃvaḍḍhoti amanussaupaddavaparivajjanatthaṃ caturassasālavasena kate mahati sabbaayomaye gehe saṃvaḍḍho. Nāmenāsi ayogharoti ayoghare jātasaṃvaḍḍhabhāveneva “ayogharakumāro”ti nāmena pākaṭo ahosi.

24. In the third, He grew up in an iron house means: he grew up in a large, all-iron house, built in the style of a quadrangular hall for the purpose of avoiding danger from non-humans. His name was Ayoghara means: he became known by the name 'Prince Ayoghara' simply because he was born and raised in an iron house.

25-6. Tadā [M 0.0190][V 0.0179] hi kāsirañño aggamahesiyā purimattabhāve sapatti “tava jātaṃ jātaṃ pajaṃ khādeyya”nti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā [P 0.0196] yakkhiniyoniyaṃ nibbattā okāsaṃ labhitvā tassā vijātakāle dve vāre putte khādi. Tatiyavāre pana bodhisatto tassā kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Rājā “deviyā jātaṃ jātaṃ pajaṃ ekā yakkhinī khādati, kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti manussehi sammantetvā “amanussā nāma ayogharassa bhāyanti, ayogharaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutte kammāre āṇāpetvā thambhe ādiṃ katvā ayomayeheva sabbagehasambhārehi caturassasālaṃ mahantaṃ ayogharaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā paripakkagabbhaṃ deviṃ tattha vāsesi. Sā tattha dhaññapuññalakkhaṇaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. “Ayogharakumāro”tvevassa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Taṃ dhātīnaṃ datvā mahantaṃ ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahitvā rājā deviṃ antepuraṃ ānesi. Yakkhinīpi udakavāraṃ gantvā vessavaṇassa udakaṃ vahantī jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā.

For at that time, a rival of the chief queen of the king of Kāsi in a former existence had made an aspiration, 'May I devour each child you bear!' Having been reborn as a yakkhinī, she found the opportunity and on two occasions devoured the queen’s sons at birth. But the third time, the Bodhisatta took conception in her womb. The king, realizing that a yakkhinī was devouring each child born to the queen, consulted with his men, asking, 'What should be done?' When they said, 'Non-humans, it is said, fear an iron house; it is proper to build an iron house,' the king ordered smiths to construct a large quadrangular hall made entirely of iron, beginning with the pillars and including all the house-furnishings. When the queen’s pregnancy was mature, he had her dwell there. There she gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of fortune and merit. They gave him the name 'Prince Ayoghara.' Entrusting him to nurses and arranging for strong protection, the king brought the queen back to the inner palace. The yakkhinī, too, when it was her turn to carry water for Vessavaṇa, reached the end of her life.

Mahāsatto ayoghareyeva vaḍḍhitvā viññutaṃ patto, tattheva sabbasippāni uggaṇhi. Rājā puttaṃ soḷasavassuddesikaṃ viditvā “rajjamassa dassāmī”ti amacce āṇāpesi – “puttaṃ me ānethā”ti. Te “sādhu, devā”ti nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ maṅgalavāraṇaṃ ādāya tattha gantvā kumāraṃ alaṅkaritvā hatthikkhandhe nisīdāpetvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ kāretvā rañño dassesuṃ. Mahāsatto rājānaṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Rājā tassa sarīrasobhaṃ oloketvā balavasinehena taṃ āliṅgitvā “ajjeva me puttaṃ abhisiñcathā”ti amacce āṇāpesi. Mahāsatto pitaraṃ vanditvā “na mayhaṃ rajjena attho, ahaṃ pabbajissāmi, pabbajjaṃ me anujānāthā”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ “dukkhena jīvito laddho”tiādi.

The Great Being grew up in the iron house itself and reached discernment, mastering all the arts right there. When the king learned that his son was about sixteen years of age, he thought, 'I will give him the kingdom,' and ordered his ministers: 'Bring my son.' They replied, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' and, having had the city decorated, they took a splendidly adorned auspicious elephant and went there. They adorned the prince, seated him on the elephant’s back, had him circumambulate the city, and presented him to the king. The Great Being paid homage to the king and stood by. The king, seeing the beauty of his son’s body, embraced him with strong affection and ordered his ministers: 'Anoint my son this very day!' The Great Being paid homage to his father and said: 'I have no need for the kingdom. I will go forth. Please grant me permission to go forth.' Thus it was said: 'With difficulty was my life obtained,' and so on.

Tattha dukkhenāti, tāta, tava bhātikā dve ekāya yakkhiniyā khāditā, tuyhaṃ pana tato amanussabhayato nivāraṇatthaṃ katena dukkhena mahatā āyāsena jīvito laddho. Saṃpīḷe patipositoti nānāvidhāya amanussarakkhāya [P 0.0197] sambādhe ayoghare vijāyanakālato paṭṭhāya yāva soḷasavassuppattiyā sambādhe saṃvaḍḍhitoti attho. Ajjeva, putta, paṭipajja, kevalaṃ vasudhaṃ imanti kañcanamālālaṅkatassa setacchattassa heṭṭhā ratanarāsimhi ṭhapetvā tīhi saṅkhehi abhisiñciyamāno [M 0.0191] imaṃ kulasantakaṃ kevalaṃ sakalaṃ samuddapariyantaṃ tatoyeva saha raṭṭhehīti saraṭṭhakaṃ saha nigamehi mahāgāmehīti sanigamaṃ aparimitena parivārajanena saddhiṃ sajanaṃ imaṃ vasudhaṃ mahāpathaviṃ ajjeva, putta, paṭipajja, rajjaṃ kārehīti attho. Vanditvā khattiyaṃ. Añjaliṃ paggahetvāna, idaṃ vacanamabravinti khattiyaṃ kāsirājānaṃ mama pitaraṃ vanditvā tassa añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā idaṃ vacanaṃ abhāsiṃ.

Herein, with difficulty means: 'Dear son, your two brothers were devoured by a yakkhinī, but your life was obtained with great difficulty and exertion, undertaken to protect you from the danger of that non-human.' Nurtured in confinement means: you were raised in confinement from the time of your birth in the cramped iron house, amidst various protections against non-humans, until you reached the age of sixteen. This very day, son, take up this entire earth means: 'Being placed on a heap of jewels under a white parasol adorned with a golden garland, and being anointed with three conches, this very day, son, take up and rule this great earth, this entire ancestral domain bounded by the ocean, together with its people, its districts, its towns, and its great villages, along with an immeasurable retinue.' Having paid homage to the khattiya, and having raised my hands in anjali, I spoke this word means: 'Having paid homage to the khattiya, the king of Kāsi, my father, and having raised my hands in an anjali to him, I spoke this word.'

27. Ye [V 0.0180] keci mahiyā sattāti imissā mahāpathaviyā ye keci sattā nāma. Hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhimāti lāmakā ceva uttamā ca, ubhinnaṃ vemajjhe bhavattā majjhimā ca. Sake geheti sabbe te sake gehe. Sakañātibhīti sakehi ñātīhi sammodamānā vissaṭṭhā anukkaṇṭhitā yathāvibhavaṃ vaḍḍhanti.

27. Whatever beings are on the earth means: whatever beings there are on this great earth. Low, superior, and middling means: the base, the excellent, and the middling, who are between the two. In their own homes means: all of them are in their own homes. With their own kinsmen means: rejoicing with their own relatives, they are at ease, untroubled, and prosper according to their means.

28. Idaṃ loke uttariyanti idaṃ pana imasmiṃ loke asadisaṃ, mayhaṃ eva āveṇikaṃ. Kiṃ pana taṃ saṃpīḷe mama posananti sambādhe mama saṃvaḍḍhanaṃ. Tathā hi ayogharamhi saṃvaḍḍho, appabhe candasūriyeti candasūriyānaṃ pabhārahite ayoghare saṃvaḍḍhomhīti saṃvaḍḍho amhi.

28. This is superior in the world means: this, however, is unparalleled in this world, unique to me. What is that? My nourishment in confinement means: my being raised in confinement. For I was raised in an iron house, with little light from sun and moon means: I was raised in an iron house devoid of the light of the sun and moon.

29. Pūtikuṇapasampuṇṇāti pūtigandhanānappakārakuṇapasampuṇṇā gūthanirayasadisā. Mātu kucchito jīvitasaṃsaye vattamāne kathaṃ muccitvā nikkhamitvā. Tato ghoratareti tatopi gabbhavāsato dāruṇatare, avissaṭṭhavāsena dukkhe. Pakkhittayoghareti pakkhitto ayoghare, bandhanāgāre ṭhapito viya ahosinti dasseti.

29. Filled with putrid corpses means: like a hell of excrement, filled with various kinds of foul-smelling corpses. From the mother’s womb: having somehow escaped and emerged from the mother's womb while my life was in peril. Then into one more dreadful means: into suffering more terrible even than dwelling in the womb, because of the confinement. Cast into an iron house shows: I was cast into an iron house, as if placed in a prison.

30. Yadihanti ettha yadīti nipātamattaṃ. Tādisanti yādisaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ, tādisaṃ paramadāruṇaṃ dukkhaṃ patvā ahaṃ rajjesu yadi rajjāmi yadi ramissāmi, evaṃ sante pāpānaṃ lāmakānaṃ nihīnapurisānaṃ uttamo nihīnatamo siyaṃ[P 0.0198].

30. Herein, in the phrase If I, the word if is a mere particle. Such: having experienced such extremely terrible suffering as was described before, if I were to delight in kingdoms, if I were to take pleasure in them, then I would be the foremost of the evil, the base, the inferior—the most inferior of all.

31. Ukkaṇṭhitomhi kāyenāti aparimuttagabbhavāsādinā pūtikāyena ukkaṇṭhito nibbinno amhi. Rajjenamhi anatthikoti rajjenapi anatthiko amhi. Yakkhiniyā hatthato muttopi hi nāhaṃ ajarāmaro, kiṃ [M 0.0192] me rajjena, rajjañhi nāma sabbesaṃ anatthānaṃ sannipātaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha ṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya dunnikkhamaṃ hoti, tasmā taṃ anupagantvā nibbutiṃ pariyesissaṃ, yattha maṃ maccu na maddiyeti yattha ṭhitaṃ maṃ mahāseno maccurājā na maddiye na otthareyya na abhibhaveyya, taṃ nibbutiṃ amatamahānibbānaṃ pariyesissāmīti.

31. I am dismayed by this body means: I am dismayed and disgusted with this foul body, which is not free from dwelling in the womb and so on. I have no need for a kingdom means: I have no need for a kingdom. For even though I am freed from the hand of the yakkhinī, I am not ageless and deathless. What use is a kingdom to me? A kingdom is the meeting place of all calamities. From the time one is established in it, it is difficult to escape. Therefore, without taking it up, I will seek peace. Where death cannot crush me means: a place where, once I am established, the King of Death with his great army cannot crush, overwhelm, or overpower me. I will seek that peace, the deathless great Nibbāna.

32. Evāhaṃ cintayitvānāti evaṃ iminā vuttappakārena nānappakāraṃ saṃsāre ādīnavaṃ paccavekkhaṇena nibbāne ānisaṃsadassanena ca yoniso cintetvā. Viravante mahājaneti mayā vippayogadukkhāsahanena viravante paridevante mātāpituppamukhe mahante jane. Nāgova bandhanaṃ chetvāti yathā nāma mahābalo hatthināgo dubbalataraṃ rajjubandhanaṃ sukheneva chindati, evameva ñātisaṅgādibhedassa [V 0.0181] tasmiṃ jane taṇhābandhanassa chindanena bandhanaṃ chetvā kānanasaṅkhātaṃ mahāvanaṃ pabbajjūpagamanavasena pāvisiṃ. Osānagāthā vuttatthā eva.

32. Having thought thus means: having reflected wisely in this aforesaid manner, in various ways, by contemplating the danger in saṃsāra and by seeing the benefit in Nibbāna. The great folk wailing means: the great folk headed by my mother and father, who were wailing and lamenting, unable to bear the pain of separation from me. Like a nāga breaking its bond means: just as a mighty elephant-nāga easily breaks a weak rope-bond, so too, by severing the bond of craving for those people—the bond of attachment to kinsmen and so on—I broke my bonds and entered the great forest called the wilderness by going forth. The meaning of the concluding verse has already been stated.

Tattha ca mahāsatto attano pabbajjādhippāyaṃ jānitvā “tāta, kiṃkāraṇā pabbajasī”ti raññā vutto “deva, ahaṃ mātukucchimhi dasa māse gūthaniraye viya vasitvā mātu kucchito nikkhanto yakkhiniyā bhayena soḷasavassāni bandhanāgāre vasanto bahi oloketumpi na labhiṃ, ussadaniraye pakkhitto viya ahosiṃ, yakkhinito muttopi ajarāmaro na homi, maccu nāmesa na sakkā kenaci jinituṃ, bhave ukkaṇṭhitomhi, yāva me byādhijarāmaraṇāni nāgacchanti, tāvadeva pabbajitvā dhammaṃ carissāmi, alaṃ me rajjena, anujānāhi maṃ, deva, pabbajitu”nti vatvā –

Then the Great Being, having made known his intention to go forth, was asked by the king, 'Dear son, for what reason are you going forth?' He replied: 'Your Majesty, after dwelling for ten months in my mother’s womb as if in a hell of filth, I emerged from her womb. Then, for sixteen years, living in a prison out of fear of the yakkhinī, I was not able to look outside, as if I had been cast into an Ussada hell. Even though freed from the yakkhinī, I am not ageless and deathless. Death, it is said, cannot be conquered by anyone. I am dismayed by existence. Before sickness, aging, and death come upon me, I will go forth and live the good life. Enough of this kingdom for me! Grant me permission, Your Majesty, to go forth.' Having spoken thus, he said:

“Yamekarattiṃ [P 0.0199] paṭhamaṃ, gabbhe vasati māṇavo;

Abbhuṭṭhitova so yāti, sa gacchaṃ na nivattatī”ti. (jā. 1.15.363) –

'From the first night the young man dwells in the womb, he has already set out; he goes on and does not turn back.' (Jā. 1.15.363)

Ādinā catuvīsatiyā gāthāhi pitu dhammaṃ desetvā “mahārāja, tumhākaṃ rajjaṃ tumhākameva hotu, na mayhaṃ iminā attho, tumhehi saddhiṃ kathenteyeva byādhijarāmaraṇāni āgaccheyyuṃ, tiṭṭhatha tumhe”ti vatvā ayadāmaṃ chinditvā mattahatthī viya, kañcanapañjaraṃ bhinditvā sīhapotako viya, kāme pahāya mātāpitaro vanditvā nikkhami. Athassa pitā “ayaṃ nāma kumāro pabbajitukāmo, kimaṅgaṃ panāhaṃ, mamāpi rajjena attho natthī”ti [M 0.0193] rajjaṃ pahāya tena saddhiṃ eva nikkhami. Tasmiṃ nikkhamante devīpi amaccāpi brāhmaṇagahapatikādayopīti sakalanagaravāsino bhoge chaḍḍetvā nikkhamiṃsu. Samāgamo mahā ahosi, parisā dvādasayojanikā jātā, te ādāya mahāsatto himavantaṃ pāvisi.

Having taught the Dhamma to his father with twenty-four verses beginning with this one, he said: 'Great king, let your kingdom be yours alone. I have no need of it. Even while I am speaking with you, sickness, aging, and death might come. You may stay.' So saying, like an elephant in rut breaking its iron chain, like a lion cub bursting from a golden cage, he abandoned sensual pleasures, paid homage to his mother and father, and went forth. Then his father thought: 'This prince wishes to go forth. What then of me? I too have no need for the kingdom.' Abandoning the kingdom, he went forth together with him. When he went forth, the queen, the ministers, the brahmins and householders, and so on—all the inhabitants of the city—abandoned their possessions and went forth. There was a great congregation; the assembly stretched for twelve yojanas. Taking them with him, the Great Being entered the Himalayas.

Sakko devarājā tassa nikkhantabhāvaṃ ñatvā vissakammaṃ pesetvā dvādasayojanāyāmaṃ sattayojanavitthāraṃ assamapadaṃ kāresi, sabbe ca pabbajitaparikkhāre paṭiyādāpesi. Idha mahāsattassa pabbajjā ca ovādadānañca brahmalokaparāyanatā ca parisāya sammā paṭipatti ca sabbā mahāgovindacariyāyaṃ (cariyā. 1.37 ādayo) vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Sakka, king of the devas, knowing of his renunciation, sent Vissakamma to construct a hermitage twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width, and he had all the requisites for one who has gone forth prepared. Here, the Great Being's renunciation, his giving of advice, his passing on to the Brahma-world, and the assembly's right practice—all this should be understood in the same way as it was stated in the Mahāgovinda Cariyā (Cariyā. 1.37ff.).

Tadā [V 0.0182] mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, parisā buddhaparisā, ayogharapaṇḍito lokanātho.

At that time the mother and father were the great royal families, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and the Ayoghara Paṇḍita was the Protector of the World.

Tassa sesapāraminiddhāraṇā ānubhāvavibhāvanā ca heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbāti.

His determination of the remaining perfections and the manifestation of their power should be understood in the same way as stated above.

Ayogharacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ayoghara Cariyā is finished.

4. Bhisacariyāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Cariyā of the Lotus Stalks

34.

34.

Catutthe [P 0.0200] yadā homi, kāsīnaṃ puravaruttameti “kāsī”ti bahuvacanavasena laddhavohārassa raṭṭhassa nagaravare bārāṇasiyaṃ yasmiṃ kāle jātasaṃvaḍḍho hutvā vasāmīti attho. Bhaginī ca bhātaro satta, nibbattā sottiye kuleti upakañcanādayo cha ahañcāti bhātaro satta sabbakaniṭṭhā kañcanadevī nāma bhaginī cāti sabbe mayaṃ aṭṭha janā mantajjhenaniratatāya sottiye uditodite mahati brāhmaṇakule tadā nibbattā jātāti attho.

Regarding 'In the fourth, when I was in the best of cities of the Kāsīs': the meaning is that at that time I was living in Bārāṇasī, the excellent city of the country designated by the plural 'Kāsī,' having been born and raised there. Regarding 'A sister and seven brothers, born in the Sottiya clan': the meaning is that the six brothers beginning with Upakañcana and myself made seven brothers, and there was a sister named Kañcanadevī, who was the youngest of all. All eight of us were devoted to the study of sacred texts and were born at that time in the great and eminent brahmin clan of the Sottiyas.

35.

35.

Bodhisatto hi tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ asītikoṭivibhavassa brāhmaṇamahāsālassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Tassa “kañcanakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Athassa padasā vicaraṇakāle aparo putto vijāyi. “Upakañcanakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya mahāsattaṃ “mahākañcanakumāro”ti [M 0.0194] samudācaranti. Evaṃ paṭipāṭiyā satta puttā ahesuṃ. Sabbakaniṭṭhā pana ekā dhītā. Tassā “kañcanadevī”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Mahāsatto vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggahetvā paccāgañchi.

For at that time the Bodhisatta was born in Bārāṇasī as the son of a brahmin of great wealth who possessed a fortune of eighty crores. They gave him the name Kañcanakumāra. Then, when he was old enough to walk, another son was born. They gave him the name Upakañcanakumāra. From then on, they addressed the Great Being as Mahākañcanakumāra. Thus in succession there were seven sons. The youngest of all, however, was one daughter. They gave her the name Kañcanadevī. When the Great Being came of age, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and returned.

Atha naṃ mātāpitaro gharāvāsena bandhitukāmā “attano samānajātikulato te dārikaṃ ānessāmā”ti vadiṃsu. So “amma, tāta, na mayhaṃ gharāvāsena attho. Mayhañhi sabbo lokasannivāso āditto viya sappaṭibhayo, bandhanāgāraṃ viya palibuddhanaṃ, ukkārabhūmi viya jiguccho hutvā upaṭṭhāti, na me cittaṃ kāmesu rajjati, aññe vo puttā atthi, te [P 0.0201] gharāvāsena nimantethā”ti vatvā punappunaṃ yācitopi sahāyehi yācāpitopi na icchi, atha naṃ [V 0.0183] sahāyā “samma, kiṃ pana tvaṃ patthayanto kāme paribhuñjituṃ na icchasī”ti pucchiṃsu. So tesaṃ attano nekkhammajjhāsayaṃ ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ “etesaṃ pubbajo āsi”ntiādi.

Then his parents, wishing to bind him to the household life, said, 'We will bring a girl for you from a family of birth equal to your own.' He replied: 'Mother, father, I have no use for the household life. To me, all worldly existence appears as if ablaze and fraught with peril, like a prison of confinement, like a disgusting refuse heap. My mind does not delight in sensual pleasures. You have other sons; invite them to the household life.' Though they pleaded with him repeatedly and had his friends urge him, he did not consent. Then his friends asked him: 'Friend, what do you aspire to, that you do not wish to enjoy sensual pleasures?' He revealed to them his inclination for renunciation. Hence it was said: 'I was the eldest of these,' and so on.

Tattha etesaṃ pubbajo āsinti etesaṃ upakañcanakādīnaṃ sattannaṃ jeṭṭhabhātiko ahaṃ tadā ahosiṃ. Hirīsukkamupāgatoti sukkavipākattā santānassa visodhanato ca sukkaṃ pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇaṃ hiriṃ bhusaṃ āgato, ativiya pāpaṃ jigucchanto āsinti attho. Bhavaṃ disvāna bhayato, nekkhammābhirato ahanti kāmabhavādīnaṃ vasena sabbaṃ bhavaṃ pakkhandituṃ āgacchantaṃ caṇḍahatthiṃ viya, hiṃsituṃ āgacchantaṃ ukkhittāsikaṃ vadhakaṃ viya, sīhaṃ viya, yakkhaṃ viya, rakkhasaṃ viya, ghoravisaṃ viya, āsivisaṃ viya, ādittaṃ aṅgāraṃ viya, sappaṭibhayaṃ bhayānakabhāvato passitvā tato muccanatthañca pabbajjābhirato pabbajitvā “kathaṃ nu kho dhammacariyaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ pūreyyaṃ, jhānasamāpattiyo ca nibbatteyya”nti pabbajjākusaladhammapaṭhamajjhānādiabhirato tadā ahaṃ āsinti attho.

Herein, 'I was their eldest brother' means: At that time I was the eldest brother of those seven beginning with Upakañcanaka. 'Possessed of the pure quality of shame' means: Because it is the fruit of pure kamma and because it purifies the mental continuum, he was deeply possessed of shame (hiri), which is pure and is characterized by revulsion towards evil; the meaning is that he intensely loathed evil. 'Seeing existence as fearful, I delighted in renunciation' means: Seeing all existence—in terms of the sensual-sphere existence and so on—as perilous and terrifying, like a charging wild elephant, like a slayer with uplifted sword coming to kill, like a lion, a yakkha, a rāksasa, a dreadful poison, a venomous serpent, or like blazing coals, and for the sake of release from that, he delighted in renunciation. Having gone forth, he thought: 'How might I fulfill the righteous life and right practice, and generate the meditative attainments?' The meaning is: at that time I was one who delighted in the wholesome states connected with renunciation, such as the first jhāna.

36. Pahitāti mātāpitūhi pesitā. Ekamānasāti samānajjhāsayā pubbe mayā ekacchandā manāpacārino mātāpitūhi pahitattā pana mama paṭikkūlaṃ amanāpaṃ vadantā.
