Kāmehi maṃ nimantentīti mahāpitūhi vā ekamānasā kāmehi maṃ nimantenti. Kulavaṃsaṃ dhārehīti gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapento attano kulavaṃsaṃ dhārehi patiṭṭhapehīti kāmehi maṃ nimantesunti attho.

36. 'Sent' means: sent by my mother and father. 'Of one mind' means: of the same disposition. Though previously they were of one accord with me and acted in a pleasing way, now, having been sent by my parents, they spoke what was repulsive and displeasing to me. 'They invite me with sensual pleasures' means: being of one mind with my parents, they invite me to sensual pleasures. 'Uphold the family lineage' means: they invite me to sensual pleasures, saying, 'By establishing a household, uphold and found your own family lineage.' This is the meaning.

37. Yaṃ [M 0.0195] tesaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanti tesaṃ mama piyasahāyānaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Gihidhamme sukhāvahanti gihibhāve sati gahaṭṭhabhāve ṭhitassa purisassa ñāyānugatattā diṭṭhadhammikassa samparāyikassa ca sukhassa āvahanato sukhāvahaṃ. Taṃ me ahosi kaṭhinanti taṃ tesaṃ mayhaṃ sahāyānaṃ mātāpitūnañca vacanaṃ ekanteneva nekkhammābhiratattā amanāpabhāvena me kaṭhinaṃ pharusaṃ divasaṃ santattaphālasadisaṃ ubhopi kaṇṇe jhāpentaṃ viya [P 0.0202] ahosi.

37. 'Whatever word they spoke' means: whatever word was spoken by those dear friends of mine. 'Bringing happiness in the household life' means: because it brings happiness both in this present life and in the life to come for a person who stands in the householder's state and follows the right method, it is 'happiness-bringing.' 'That was harsh to me' means: that word of my friends and parents, because of my exclusive delight in renunciation, was harsh and rough to me on account of its unpleasantness; it was as if it were burning both my ears like a ploughshare heated all day.

38. Te maṃ tadā ukkhipantanti te mayhaṃ sahāyā mātāpitūhi attano ca upanimantanavasena anekavāraṃ upanīyamāne kāme uddhamuddhaṃ khipantaṃ chaḍḍentaṃ paṭikkhipantaṃ maṃ pucchiṃsu. Patthitaṃ mamāti ito visuddhataraṃ kiṃ nu kho iminā patthitanti mayā abhipatthitaṃ mama taṃ patthanaṃ pucchiṃsu – “kiṃ tvaṃ patthayase, samma, yadi kāme na bhuñjasī”ti.

38. 'They then questioned me' means: those friends of mine questioned me as I was flinging away, casting off, and rejecting the sensual pleasures that were repeatedly brought before me by way of invitation from my parents and from themselves. 'My aspiration' means: they asked about that aspiration of mine, thinking, 'What indeed, purer than this, is aspired to by him?' They asked: 'Friend, what do you aspire to, if you do not enjoy sensual pleasures?'

39. Atthakāmoti [V 0.0184] attano atthakāmo, pāpabhīrūti attho. “Attakāmo”tipi pāḷi. Hitesinanti mayhaṃ hitesīnaṃ piyasahāyānaṃ. Keci “atthakāmahitesina”nti paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ.

39. 'Desiring my welfare' means: desiring my own welfare; the meaning is 'one who fears evil.' There is also the reading 'attakāmo' (desiring one's own self-interest). 'To the well-wishers' refers to my dear friends who wished me well. Some read this as a compound, 'atthakāmahitesinaṃ,' but that is not a good reading.

40. Pitu mātu ca sāvayunti te mayhaṃ sahāyā anivattanīyaṃ mama pabbajjāchandaṃ viditvā pabbajitukāmatādīpakaṃ mayhaṃ vacanaṃ pitu mātu ca sāvesuṃ. “Yagghe, ammatātā, jānātha, ekanteneva mahākañcanakumāro pabbajissati, na so sakkā kenaci upāyena kāmesu upanetu”nti avocuṃ. Mātāpitā evamāhūti tadā mayhaṃ mātāpitaro mama sahāyehi vuttaṃ mama vacanaṃ sutvā evamāhaṃsu – “sabbeva pabbajāma, bho”ti, yadi mahākañcanakumārassa nekkhammaṃ abhirucitaṃ, yaṃ tassa abhirucitaṃ, tadamhākampi abhirucitameva, tasmā sabbeva pabbajāma, bhoti. “Bho”ti tesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ ālapanaṃ. “Pabbajāma kho”tipi pāṭho, pabbajāma evāti attho. Mahāsattassa hi pabbajjāchandaṃ viditvā upakañcanādayo cha bhātaro bhaginī ca kañcanadevī pabbajitukāmāva ahesuṃ, tena tepi mātāpitūhi gharāvāsena nimantiyamānā na icchiṃsuyeva. Tasmā evamāhaṃsu “sabbeva pabbajāma, bho”ti.

40. 'They informed my father and mother' means: those friends of mine, having known that my desire for renunciation was irreversible, reported my words indicating my wish to go forth to my father and mother. They said: 'Pray, mother and father, know that Mahākañcanakumāra will definitely go forth; it is not possible by any means to lead him back to sensual pleasures.' 'The parents said thus' means: then my parents, having heard from my friends the words I had spoken, said this: 'Then let us all go forth, sirs!' That is: 'If renunciation is agreeable to Mahākañcanakumāra, then what is agreeable to him is agreeable to us too. Therefore let us all go forth, sirs!' 'Sirs' (bho) is a term of address for those brahmins. There is also the reading 'pabbajāma kho,' which means 'we will indeed go forth.' For when they learned of the Great Being's desire for renunciation, the six brothers beginning with Upakañcana and his sister Kañcanadevī also became desirous of going forth. Therefore, though invited by their parents to the household life, they too did not consent. Thus they said: 'Then let us all go forth, sirs!'

Evañca [M 0.0196] pana vatvā mahāsattaṃ mātāpitaro pakkositvā attanopi adhippāyaṃ tassa ācikkhitvā “tāta, yadi pabbajitukāmosi, asītikoṭidhanaṃ tava santakaṃ yathāsukhaṃ vissajjehī”ti āhaṃsu. Atha naṃ mahāpuriso kapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ vissajjetvā mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā himavantaṃ pāvisi. Tena saddhiṃ mātāpitaro cha bhātaro ca bhaginī ca eko dāso ekā dāsī eko ca sahāyo gharāvāsaṃ pahāya agamaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

And having spoken thus, the parents summoned the Great Being, explained their own intention to him, and said: 'Dear son, if you wish to go forth, give away the eighty crores of wealth that belongs to you as you please.' Then the Great Man gave it away to the poor, travelers, and others, made the great renunciation, and entered the Himālaya. Together with him went his parents, six brothers, a sister, one male servant, one female servant, and one friend, having abandoned the household life. Therefore it was said:

41.

41.

“Ubho [P 0.0203] mātā pitā mayhaṃ, bhaginī ca satta bhātaro;

Amitadhanaṃ chaḍḍayitvā, pavisimhā mahāvana”nti.

"Both my mother and my father, a sister and seven brothers—having abandoned our immeasurable wealth, we entered the great forest."

Jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (jā. aṭṭha. 4.14.77 bhisajātakavaṇṇanā) pana “mātāpitūsu kālaṃkatesu tesaṃ kattabbakiccaṃ katvā mahāsatto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamī”ti vuttaṃ.

But in the Jātaka Commentary (Jā-a 4.14.77, commentary on the Bhisa Jātaka), it is said: 'After his parents had passed away, the Great Being performed the funeral rites for them and made the great renunciation.'

Evaṃ himavantaṃ pavisitvā ca te bodhisattappamukhā ekaṃ padumasaraṃ nissāya ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge assamaṃ katvā pabbajitvā vanamūlaphalāhārā yāpayiṃsu. Tesu upakañcanādayo aṭṭha janā vārena phalāphalaṃ āharitvā ekasmiṃ pāsāṇaphalake attano itaresañca koṭṭhāse katvā ghaṇṭisaññaṃ [V 0.0185] datvā attano koṭṭhāsaṃ ādāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisanti. Sesāpi ghaṇṭisaññāya paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā attano attano pāpuṇanakoṭṭhāsaṃ ādāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paribhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti.

Having thus entered the Himalayas, those ascetics, with the Bodhisatta as their chief, established a hermitage in a delightful region near a lotus pond. Having gone forth, they sustained themselves on roots and fruits from the forest. Among them, eight people including Upakañcana would take turns gathering fruits. They would divide them on a stone slab into portions for themselves and for the others, and after giving a signal with a bell, they would take their own portions and enter their dwellings. The others too, on the signal of the bell, would come out of their leaf-huts, take their respective portions, go to their dwellings, consume them, and practice the duties of recluses.

Aparabhāge bhisāni āharitvā tatheva khādanti. Tattha te ghoratapā paramadhitindriyā kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontā vihariṃsu. Atha nesaṃ sīlatejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi. Sakko taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “ime isayo vīmaṃsissāmī”ti attano ānubhāvena mahāsattassa koṭṭhāse tayo divase antaradhāpesi. Mahāsatto paṭhamadivase koṭṭhāsaṃ adisvā “mama koṭṭhāso pamuṭṭho bhavissatī”ti cintesi. Dutiyadivase “mama dosena bhavitabbaṃ, paṇāmanavasena mama koṭṭhāsaṃ na ṭhapitaṃ maññe”ti cintesi. Tatiyadivase “taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā khamāpessāmī”ti sāyanhasamaye ghaṇṭisaññaṃ datvā tāya saññāya sabbesu sannipatitesu tamatthaṃ ārocetvā tīsupi divasesu [M 0.0197] tehi jeṭṭhakoṭṭhāsassa ṭhapitabhāvaṃ sutvā “tumhehi mayhaṃ koṭṭhāso ṭhapito, mayā pana na laddho, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti [P 0.0204] āha. Taṃ sutvā sabbeva saṃvegappattā ahesuṃ.

Subsequently, they would bring lotus roots and eat them in the same way. There they dwelt, ascetics of fierce austerity with supreme control over their faculties, practicing the preliminary kasina meditation. Then, by the power of their virtue, Sakka's celestial palace trembled. Knowing the reason, Sakka thought, 'I will test these sages,' and by his power, he made the Great Being's portion disappear for three days. On the first day, not seeing his portion, the Great Being thought, 'My portion must have been forgotten.' On the second day, he thought, 'It must be due to some fault of mine; I think they did not set my portion aside as a rebuke.' On the third day, thinking, 'I will find out the reason and ask for forgiveness,' he gave the bell signal in the evening. When all had gathered at the signal, he explained the matter. When he heard from them that the eldest's portion had been set aside on all three days, he said, 'You set aside my portion, but I did not receive it. What could be the reason?' Hearing this, they were all struck with agitation.

Tasmiṃ assame rukkhadevatāpi attano bhavanato otaritvā tesaṃ santike nisīdi. Manussānaṃ hatthato palāyitvā araññaṃ paviṭṭho eko vāraṇo ahituṇḍikahatthato palāyitvā mutto sappakīḷāpanako eko vānaro ca tehi isīhi kataparicayā tadā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Sakkopi “isigaṇaṃ pariggaṇhissāmī”ti adissamānakāyo tattheva aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiñca khaṇe bodhisattassa kaniṭṭho upakañcanatāpaso uṭṭhāya bodhisattaṃ vanditvā sesānaṃ apacitiṃ dassetvā “ahaṃ saññaṃ paṭṭhapetvā attānaññeva sodhetuṃ labhāmī”ti pucchitvā “āma, labhasī”ti vutte isigaṇamajjhe ṭhatvā sapathaṃ karonto –

At that hermitage, a tree deity also descended from her mansion and sat near them. An elephant that had fled from human hands and entered the forest, and a monkey that had been a snake-charmer's plaything and had escaped from the snake-charmer's hands—both of whom were acquainted with those sages—approached and stood to one side. Sakka, too, thinking, 'I will test this group of sages,' stood there invisible. At that moment, the Bodhisatta's youngest brother, the ascetic Upakañcana, rose, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, showed respect to the others, and asked: 'May I establish a sign to clear myself?' When he was told, 'Yes, you may,' he stood in the midst of the assembly of sages and made an oath:

“Assaṃ gavaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ, bhariyañca so idha labhataṃ manāpaṃ;

Puttehi dārehi samaṅgi hotu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsī”ti. (jā. 1.14.78) –

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he obtain horses, cattle, silver, and gold, and here a pleasing wife. May he be endowed with sons and wives!'

Imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi. Imañhi so “yattakāni piyavatthūni honti, tehi vippayoge tattakāni dukkhāni uppajjantī”ti vatthukāme garahanto āha.

He spoke this verse. For he said this while censuring sensual pleasures, on the grounds that 'however many dear things there are, just as many sorrows arise from separation from them.'

Taṃ [V 0.0186] sutvā isigaṇo “mārisa, mā kathaya, atibhāriyo te sapatho”ti kaṇṇe pidahi. Bodhisattopi “atibhāriyo te sapatho, na, tvaṃ tāta, gaṇhasi, tava pattāsane nisīdā”ti āha. Sesāpi sapathaṃ karontā yathākkamaṃ –

Hearing this, the group of sages said, 'Sir, do not speak, your oath is too heavy,' and covered their ears. The Bodhisatta also said, 'Your oath is too heavy, dear one, do not take it. Sit on your assigned seat.' The rest, in turn, made their oaths:

“Mālañca so kāsikacandanañca, dhāretu puttassa bahū bhavantu;

Kāmesu [P 0.0205] tibbaṃ kurutaṃ apekkhaṃ, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he wear garlands and Kasi sandalwood, and may he have many sons! May he develop intense longing for sensual pleasures!'

“Pahūtadhañño [M 0.0198] kasimā yasassī, putte gihī dhanimā sabbakāme;

Vayaṃ apassaṃ gharamāvasātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he be rich in grain, a famous farmer, a householder with sons, wealthy in all sensual pleasures! May he dwell at home, not seeing his own decline.'

“So khattiyo hotu pasayhakārī, rājābhirājā balavā yasassī;

Sacāturantaṃ mahimāvasātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he be a warrior, an oppressor, a king of kings, powerful and renowned! May he rule the entire earth to its four oceans!'

“So brāhmaṇo hotu avītarāgo, muhuttanakkhattapathesu yutto;

Pūjetu naṃ raṭṭhapatī yasassī, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he be a brahmin with unabated passion, devoted to astrology and auspicious moments! May the famous ruler of the land honor him!'

“Ajjhāyakaṃ sabbasamantavedaṃ, tapassinaṃ maññatu sabbaloko;

Pūjentu naṃ jānapadā samecca, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may the whole world consider him a scholar who has mastered all the Vedas and their supplements, and an ascetic! May the country folk gather and honor him!'

“Catussadaṃ gāmavaraṃ samiddhaṃ, dinnañhi so bhuñjatu vāsavena;

Avītarāgo maraṇaṃ upetu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he enjoy an excellent, prosperous village abounding in four things, as if given by Vāsava! May he meet his death with passion unallayed!'

“So gāmaṇī hotu sahāyamajjhe, naccehi gītehi pamodamāno;

So rājato byasanamālattha kiñci, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he be a village headman among his companions, delighting in dance and song! May he never suffer any misfortune from the king!'

“Taṃ ekarājā pathaviṃ vijetvā, itthīsahassassa ṭhapetu agge;

Sīmantinīnaṃ pavarā bhavātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yā ahāsi.

'She who stole your lotus roots, O brahmin—may a sole monarch, having conquered the earth, place her at the head of a thousand women! May she become the foremost among women!'

“Isīnañhi [M 0.0199] sā sabbasamāgatānaṃ, bhuñjeyya sāduṃ avikampamānā;

Carātu [P 0.0206] lābhena vikatthamānā, bhisāni te brāhaṇa yā ahāsi.

'She who stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may she eat delicious food unperturbed in the midst of all the assembled sages! May she wander about, boasting of her gain!'

“Āvāsiko [V 0.0187] hotu mahāvihāre, navakammiko hotu gajaṅgalāyaṃ;

Ālokasandhiṃ divasaṃ karotu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he be a resident monk in a great monastery, in charge of new construction at Gajaṅgala! May he spend a whole day making a single window opening!'

“So bajjhataṃ pāsasatehi chamhi, rammā vanā nīyatu rājadhāniṃ;

Tuttehi so haññatu pācanehi, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he be bound in six places with hundreds of snares! May he be led from the delightful forest to the capital city! May he be struck with goads and prods!'

“Alakkamālī tipukaṇṇapiṭṭho, laṭṭhīhato sappamukhaṃ upetu;

Sakacchabandho visikhaṃ carātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsī”ti. (jā. 1.14.79-90) –

'Whoever stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, may he, wearing a garland of `alakka` flowers and with tin ornaments on his ears, be beaten with a stick and approach a snake's mouth! Bound with a loincloth, may he wander the streets!'

Imā gāthāyo avocuṃ.

They spoke these verses.

Tattha tibbanti vatthukāmakilesakāmesu bahalaṃ apekkhaṃ karotu. Kasimāti sampannakasikammo. Putte gihī dhanimā sabbakāmeti putte labhatu, gihī hotu, sattavidhena dhanena dhanimā hotu, rūpādibhede sabbakāme labhatu. Vayaṃ apassanti mahallakakālepi apabbajitvā attano vayaṃ apassanto pañcakāmaguṇasamiddhaṃ gharameva āvasatu. Rājābhirājāti rājūnaṃ antare atirājā. Avītarāgoti purohitaṭṭhānataṇhāya sataṇho. Tapassinanti tapasīlaṃ, sīlasampannoti naṃ maññatu. Catussadanti ākiṇṇamanussatāya manussehi pahūtadhaññatāya dhaññena sulabhadārutāya dārūhi sampannodakatāya udakenāti catūhi ussannaṃ. Vāsavenāti vāsavena dinnaṃ viya acalaṃ, vāsavato laddhavarānubhāveneva rājānaṃ ārādhetvā tena dinnantipi attho. Avītarāgoti avigatarāgo kaddame sūkaro viya kāmapaṅke nimuggova hotu.

Herein, a farmer means: one accomplished in the work of farming. With sons, a householder, wealthy in all sensual pleasures means: may he obtain sons, be a householder, be wealthy with the seven kinds of wealth, and obtain all sensual pleasures, such as forms and so on. Not seeing his decline means: even in old age, without having gone forth, not seeing his own decline, may he dwell right in a home replete with the five strands of sensual pleasure. A king of kings means: a king superior among kings. With passion unallayed means: having craving, with craving for the position of royal chaplain. An ascetic means: ascetic virtue; may the world think of him as endowed with virtue. Abounding in four things means: abounding in four things, namely: with people, because it is crowded with people; with grain, because of its abundance of grain; with timber, because timber is easily obtained; and with water, because it is endowed with water. By Vāsava means: unshakable, as if given by Vāsava. Or the meaning is also: given by the king after having pleased him by the power of a boon received from Vāsava. With passion unallayed means: with passion not departed, may he be immersed in the bog of sensual pleasure just like a pig in the mud.

Gāmaṇīti [M 0.0200] gāmajeṭṭhako. Tanti taṃ itthiṃ. Ekarājāti aggarājā. Itthīsahassassāti vacanamaṭṭhatāya vuttaṃ. Soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne [P 0.0207] ṭhapetūti attho. Sīmantinīnanti sīmantadharānaṃ, itthīnanti attho. Sabbasamāgatānanti sabbesaṃ sannipatitānaṃ majjhe nisīditvā. Avikampamānāti anosakkamānā sādurasaṃ bhuñjatūti attho. Carātu lābhena vikatthamānāti lābhahetu siṅgāravesaṃ gahetvā lābhaṃ uppādetuṃ caratu. Āvāsikoti āvāsajagganako. Gajaṅgalāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tattha kira dabbasambhārā sulabhā. Ālokasandhiṃ divasanti ekadivasena ekameva vātapānaṃ karotu. So kira devaputto kassapabuddhakāle gajaṅgalanagaraṃ nissāya [V 0.0188] yojanike mahāvihāre āvāsiko saṅghatthero hutvā jiṇṇe vihāre navakammāni karontova mahādukkhaṃ anubhavi, taṃ sandhāyāha.

Headman means village chief. Her refers to that woman. Sole monarch means chief king. Of a thousand women is said for rhetorical effect; the meaning is, 'May he place her in the chief position among sixteen thousand women.' Of women means of those who wear a parting in their hair; that is, of women. Of all assembled means sitting in the midst of all who have gathered. Unperturbed means: not shrinking back, may she eat the delicious food. May she wander boasting of her gain means: for the sake of gain, having adopted an alluring guise, may she wander about to generate gain. Resident means the caretaker of the residence. At Gajaṅgala refers to the city of that name. There, it seems, materials and supplies were easy to get. A window-opening a day means: may he make only one window in a single day. It is said that this devaputta, in the time of the Buddha Kassapa, had been the resident elder of the Sangha in a great monastery one yojana in extent near the city of Gajaṅgala. While undertaking new construction on the old monastery, he experienced great suffering. It is with reference to this that he spoke.

Pāsasatehīti bahūhi pāsehi. Chamhīti catūsu pādesu gīvāya kaṭibhāge cāti chasu ṭhānesu. Tuttehīti dvikaṇṭakāhi dīghalaṭṭhīhi. Pācanehīti rassapācanehi, aṅkusakehi vā. Alakkamālīti ahituṇḍikena kaṇṭhe parikkhipitvā ṭhapitāya alakkamālāya samannāgato. Tipukaṇṇapiṭṭhoti tipupiḷandhanena piḷandhitapiṭṭhikaṇṇo kaṇṇapiṭṭho. Laṭṭhihatoti sappakīḷāpanaṃ sikkhāpayamāno laṭṭhiyā hato hutvā. Sabbaṃ te kāmabhogaṃ gharāvāsaṃ attanā attanā anubhūtadukkhañca jigucchantā tathā tathā sapathaṃ karontā evamāhaṃsu.

With hundreds of snares means with many snares. In six means in six places: on the four feet, the neck, and the waist. With goads means with long sticks having two prongs. With prods means with short prods, or with hooks. Wearing an `alakka` garland means endowed with a garland of `alakka` placed around the neck by a snake-charmer. With `tipukaṇṇapiṭṭha` means with the back of the ears adorned with a tin ornament. Beaten with a stick means being beaten with a stick while being taught snake-charming. All of them, despising sensual enjoyment, the household life, and the suffering they had personally experienced, made their oaths in this and that way and spoke thus.

Atha bodhisatto “sabbehi imehi sapatho kato, mayāpi kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sapathaṃ karonto –

Then the Bodhisatta thought, 'An oath has been made by all these; it is proper for me to make one too,' and, making an oath, he said:

“Yo ve anaṭṭhaṃva naṭṭhanti cāha, kāmeva so labhataṃ bhuñjatañca;

Agāramajjhe maraṇaṃ upetu, yo vā bhonto saṅkati kañci devā”ti. (jā. 1.14.91) –

“Whoever declares as lost what is not lost, may he obtain and enjoy sensual pleasures, and may he meet death in the midst of his house; and also, sirs, whichever of you gods suspects anyone!”

Imaṃ gāthamāha.

He spoke this verse.

Tattha bhontoti bhavanto. Saṅkatīti āsaṅkati. Kañcīti aññataraṃ.

Herein, `bhonto` means sirs. `Saṅkati` means suspects. `Kañci` means anyone.

Atha [M 0.0201] sakko “sabbepime kāmesu nirapekkhā”ti jānitvā saṃviggamānaso na imesu kenacipi bhisāni nītāni, nāpi tayā anaṭṭhaṃ naṭṭhanti vuttaṃ, apica ahaṃ tumhe vīmaṃsitukāmo antaradhāpesinti dassento –

Then Sakka, knowing, “All these are indifferent to sensual pleasures,” and with a mind struck by urgency, in order to show that “the lotus roots were not taken by any of these, nor was it said by you that what is not lost is lost, but rather I, wishing to test you, made them disappear,” said:

“Vīmaṃsamāno [P 0.0208] isino bhisāni, tīre gahetvāna thale nidhesiṃ;

Suddhā apāpā isayo vasanti, etāni te brahmacārī bhisānī”ti. (jā. 1.14.95) –

“Investigating the sages’ lotus roots, I took them and placed them on the dry land of the bank. Pure and sinless are the sages who dwell here—these are your lotus roots, O holy man.”

Osānagāthamāha.

He spoke the concluding verse.

Taṃ [V 0.0189] sutvā bodhisatto –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said:

“Na te naṭā no pana kīḷaneyyā, na bandhavā no pana te sahāyā;

Kismiṃ vupatthambha sahassanetta, isīhi tvaṃ kīḷasi devarājā”ti. (jā. 1.14.96) –

“They are neither your dancers nor your playthings, neither your relatives nor your companions. Relying on what, O Thousand-Eyed One, do you sport with the sages, O King of Gods?”

Sakkaṃ tajjesi.

He rebuked Sakka.

Atha naṃ sakko –

Then Sakka said to him:

“Ācariyo mesi pitā ca mayhaṃ, esā patiṭṭhā khalitassa brahme;

Ekāparādhaṃ khama bhūripañña, na paṇḍitā kodhabalā bhavantī”ti. (jā. 1.14.97) –

“You are my teacher and my father; you are a refuge for one who has stumbled, O Brahma. Forgive this single offense, O one of vast wisdom, for the wise are not those whose strength is anger.”

Khamāpesi.

He asked for forgiveness.

Mahāsatto sakkassa devarañño khamitvā sayaṃ isigaṇaṃ khamāpento –

The Great Being, having forgiven Sakka, the king of the gods, and causing the assembly of sages to forgive him as well, said:

“Suvāsitaṃ isinaṃ ekarattaṃ, yaṃ vāsavaṃ bhūtapatiddasāma;

Sabbeva bhonto sumanā bhavantu, yaṃ brāhmaṇo paccupādī bhisānī”ti. (jā. 1.14.98) –

“The sages’ one-night stay was well-spent, for we have seen Vāsava, the lord of beings. May all you sirs be glad of heart, since the brahmin has gotten back the lotus roots.”

Āha.

He said.

Tattha [M 0.0202] na te naṭāti, devarāja, mayaṃ tava naṭā vā kīḷitabbayuttakā vā na homa. Nāpi tava ñātakā, sahāyā hassaṃ kātabbā. Atha tvaṃ kismiṃ vupatthambhāti kiṃ upatthambhakaṃ katvā, kiṃ nissāya isīhi saddhiṃ kīḷasīti attho. Esā patiṭṭhāti esā tava pādacchāyā ajja mama khalitassa aparādhassa patiṭṭhā hotu. Suvāsitanti āyasmantānaṃ isīnaṃ ekarattimpi imasmiṃ araññe vasitaṃ suvasitameva. Kiṃkāraṇā? Yaṃ vāsavaṃ bhūtapatiṃ addasāma. Sace hi mayaṃ nagare avasimhā, na imaṃ addasāma. Bhontoti bhavanto. Sabbepi sumanā bhavantu tussantu, sakkassa devarañño khamantu, kiṃkāraṇā? Yaṃ brāhmaṇo paccupādī bhisāni [V 0.0190] yasmā tumhākaṃ ācariyo bhisāni alabhīti. Sakko [P 0.0209] isigaṇaṃ vanditvā devalokaṃ gato. Isigaṇopi jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Herein, `na te naṭā` means: “O king of gods, we are not your dancers or your playthings. Nor are we your relatives or companions with whom to make jokes.” `Atha tvaṃ kismiṃ vupatthambha` means: “Relying on what, depending on what, do you sport with the sages?” This is the meaning. `Esā patiṭṭhā` means: “May this shadow of your feet today become a refuge for my stumbling and offense.” `Suvāsitaṃ` means: “The dwelling for even a single night in this forest by the venerable sages was indeed well-dwelt.” For what reason? “Because we have seen Vāsava, the lord of beings. For if we had dwelt in the city, we would not have seen him.” `Bhonto` means sirs. “May all be glad of heart, may they be pleased, may they forgive Sakka, the king of the gods.” For what reason? `Yaṃ brāhmaṇo paccupādī bhisāni` means: “Because your teacher has obtained the lotus roots.” Sakka, having paid homage to the assembly of sages, went to the deva world. The assembly of sages too, having developed the jhānas and supernormal knowledges, went to the Brahma-world.

Tadā upakañcanādayo cha bhātaro sāriputtamoggallānamahākassapaanuruddhapuṇṇaānandattherā, bhaginī uppalavaṇṇā, dāsī khujjuttarā, dāso citto gahapati, rukkhadevatā sātāgiro, vāraṇo pālileyyanāgo, vānaro madhuvāsiṭṭho, sakko kāḷudāyī, mahākañcanatāpaso lokanātho.

At that time, the six brothers, Upakañcana and the others, were Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, Anuruddha, Puṇṇa, and Ānanda, the Elders; the sister was Uppalavaṇṇā; the female servant was Khujjuttarā; the male servant was Citta the householder; the tree deity was Sātāgiri; the elephant was the nāga Pālileyya; the monkey was Madhuvāsiṭṭha; Sakka was Kāḷudāyī; and the great ascetic Mahākañcana was the Lord of the World.

Tassa idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva dasa pāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā accantameva kāmesu anapekkhatādayo guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Here too, in his case, the ten perfections should be determined in the same way as stated before. Likewise, the powerful qualities such as complete indifference to sensual pleasures should be elucidated.

Bhisacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Bhisa Cariya is finished.

5. Soṇapaṇḍitacariyāvaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Cariya of Soṇa the Wise

42. Pañcame nagare brahmavaḍḍhaneti brahmavaḍḍhananāmake nagare. Kulavareti aggakule. Seṭṭheti pāsaṃsatame. Mahāsāleti mahāsāre. Ajāyahanti ajāyiṃ ahaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tasmiṃ kāle “brahmavaḍḍhana”nti laddhanāme bārāṇasinagare yadā homi bhavāmi paṭivasāmi, tadā abhijātasampattiyā uditoditabhāvena agge vijjāvatasampattiyā seṭṭhe asītikoṭivibhavatāya mahāsāle brāhmaṇakule ahaṃ uppajjinti.

42. In the fifth Cariya: `In the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana` means in the city named Brahmavaḍḍhana. `In an excellent family` means in a foremost family. `Best` means most praiseworthy. `Of great substance` means very wealthy. `I was born` means I was born. This is what is said: At that time, when I was dwelling in the city of Bārāṇasī, which was then named Brahmavaḍḍhana, I was born into a brahmin family that was foremost on account of its noble birth and prosperity, best on account of its accomplishment in knowledge, and of great substance on account of its wealth of eighty crores.

Tadā [M 0.0203] hi mahāsatto brahmalokato cavitvā brahmavaḍḍhananagare asītikoṭivibhavassa aññatarassa brāhmaṇamahāsālassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “soṇakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassa padasā gamanakāle aññopi satto brahmalokā cavitvā bodhisattassa mātuyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa jātassa “nandakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tesaṃ uggahitavedānaṃ sabbasippanipphattippattānaṃ vayappattānaṃ rūpasampadaṃ disvā tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā mātāpitaro “gharabandhanena bandhissāmā”ti paṭhamaṃ soṇakumāraṃ āhaṃsu – “tāta, te patirūpakulato dārikaṃ [P 0.0210] ānessāma, tvaṃ kuṭumbaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti.

Then the Great Being, having passed away from the Brahma-world, was reborn as the son of a certain brahmin of great substance, possessing eighty crores of wealth, in the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana. On his naming day, they named him “Soṇakumāra.” At the time when he was able to walk, another being, having passed away from the Brahma-world, took conception in the womb of the Bodhisatta’s mother. When he was born, they named him “Nandakumāra.” Seeing their mastery of the Vedas, their accomplishment in all arts, and their beauty upon reaching maturity, their pleased and joyful parents thought, “We shall bind them with the bonds of household life.” First, they said to Soṇakumāra: “Dear son, we will bring you a suitable girl from a worthy family; you must undertake the household life.”

Mahāsatto [V 0.0191] “alaṃ mayhaṃ gharāvāsena, ahaṃ yāvajīvaṃ tumhe paṭijaggitvā tumhākaṃ accayena pabbajissāmī”ti āha. Mahāsattassa hi tadā tayopi bhavā ādittaṃ agāraṃ viya aṅgārakāsu viya ca upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Visesato panesa nekkhammajjhāsayo nekkhammādhimutto ahosi. Tassa adhippāyaṃ ajānantā te punappunaṃ kathentāpi tassa cittaṃ alabhitvā nandakumāraṃ āmantetvā “tāta, tena hi tvaṃ kuṭumbaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti vatvā tenāpi “nāhaṃ mama bhātarā chaḍḍitakheḷaṃ sīsena ukkhipāmi, ahampi tumhākaṃ accayena bhātarā saddhiṃ pabbajissāmī”ti vutte “ime evaṃ taruṇā kāme jahanti, kimaṅgaṃ pana mayanti sabbeva pabbajissāmā”ti cintetvā “tāta, kiṃ vo amhākaṃ accayena pabbajjāya, sabbe saheva pabbajāmā”ti vatvā ñātīnaṃ dātabbayuttakaṃ datvā dāsajanaṃ bhujissaṃ katvā rañño ārocetvā sabbaṃ dhanaṃ vissajjetvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā cattāropi janā brahmavaḍḍhananagarā nikkhamitvā himavantappadese padumapuṇḍarīkamaṇḍitaṃ mahāsaraṃ nissāya ramaṇīye vanasaṇḍe assamaṃ māpetvā pabbajitvā tattha vasiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

The Great Being said, “Enough of household life for me. I will take care of you as long as you live, and after your passing, I will go forth.” For the Great Being at that time, the three kinds of existence appeared like a burning house and a pit of embers. Especially, his disposition was for renunciation, and he was intent on renunciation. Not understanding his intention, they repeatedly spoke to him but could not sway his mind. Then, summoning Nandakumāra, they said, “Dear son, in that case, you manage the household.” But he too replied, “I will not lift with my head the spittle discarded by my brother. After your passing, I too will go forth with my brother.” Hearing this, they thought, “These young ones abandon sensual pleasures so easily—what then of us? Let us all go forth.” So they said, “Dear son, why wait for our passing to go forth? Let us all go forth together.” After distributing to their relatives what was due to them and freeing their servants, they informed the king, gave away all their wealth, and held a great almsgiving. Then, all four left the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana and, reaching a delightful forest grove near a great lake adorned with red and white lotuses in the Himalayan region, built a hermitage, went forth, and dwelt there. Thus it is said:

43.

43.

“Tadāpi lokaṃ disvāna, andhībhūtaṃ tamotthaṭaṃ;

Cittaṃ bhavato patikuṭati, tuttavegahataṃ viya.

“Even then, seeing the world become blind, shrouded in darkness, my mind recoiled from existence, like something struck by the force of a goad.

44.

44.

“Disvāna vividhaṃ pāpaṃ, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā;

Kadāhaṃ gehā nikkhamma, pavisissāmi kānanaṃ.

“Having seen manifold evil, thus I thought at that time: ‘When shall I, having gone forth from home, enter the forest?’

45.

45.

“Tadāpi maṃ nimantiṃsu, kāmabhogehi ñātayo;

Tesampi chandamācikkhiṃ, mā nimantetha tehi maṃ.

“Even then my relatives invited me with sensual enjoyments; but I declared my intention to them: ‘Do not invite me with those.’

46.

46.

“Yo [M 0.0204] me kaniṭṭhako bhātā, nando nāmāsi paṇḍito;

Sopi maṃ anusikkhanto, pabbajjaṃ samarocayi.

“My younger brother, named Nanda, who was wise, he too, following my example, found delight in the going forth.

47.

47.

“Ahaṃ [P 0.0211] soṇo ca nando ca, ubho mātāpitā mama;

Tadāpi bhoge chaḍḍetvā, pāvisimhā mahāvana”nti.

“I, Soṇa, and Nanda, and both my mother and father—even then, having abandoned our wealth, we entered the great forest.”

Tattha tadāpīti yadā ahaṃ brahmavaḍḍhananagare soṇo nāma brāhmaṇakumāro ahosiṃ, tadāpi. Lokaṃ disvānāti sakalampi sattalokaṃ paññācakkhunā passitvā. Andhībhūtanti paññācakkhuvirahena [V 0.0192] andhajātaṃ andhabhāvaṃ pattaṃ. Tamotthaṭanti avijjandhakārena abhibhūtaṃ. Cittaṃ bhavato patikuṭatīti jātiādisaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena kāmādibhavato mama cittaṃ saṅkuṭati sannilīyati na visarati. Tuttavegahataṃ viyāti tuttaṃ vuccati ayokaṇṭakasīso dīghadaṇḍo, yo patodoti vuccati. Tena vegasā abhihato yathā hatthājānīyo saṃvegappatto hoti, evaṃ mama cittaṃ tadā kāmādīnavapaccavekkhaṇena saṃvegappattanti dasseti.

Herein, `even then` means: when I was the brahmin youth named Soṇa in the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana. `Having seen the world` means: having seen the entire world of beings with the eye of wisdom. `Become blind` means: having become blind, having reached a state of blindness, through the absence of the eye of wisdom. `Shrouded in darkness` means: overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance. `My mind recoils from existence` means: by reflecting on the grounds for spiritual urgency such as birth, my mind shrinks back from existence based on sensual pleasures and so on; it contracts, it does not expand. `Like something struck by the force of a goad` means: a `tutta` is a long staff with an iron point, which is called a goad. Just as a thoroughbred elephant, when struck forcefully with it, becomes agitated, so too my mind at that time became agitated by reflecting on the danger in sensual pleasures and so on. This is what is shown.

Disvāna vividhaṃ pāpanti gehaṃ āvasantehi gharāvāsanimittaṃ chandadosādivasena karīyamānaṃ nānāvidhaṃ pāṇātipātādipāpakammañceva tannimittañca nesaṃ lāmakabhāvaṃ passitvā. Evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadāti “kadā nu kho ahaṃ mahāhatthī viya ayabandhanaṃ gharabandhanaṃ chinditvā gehato nikkhamanavasena vanaṃ pavisissāmī”ti evaṃ tadā soṇakumārakāle cintesiṃ ahaṃ. Tadāpi maṃ nimantiṃsūti na kevalaṃ ayogharapaṇḍitādikāleyeva, atha kho tadāpi tasmiṃ soṇakumārakālepi maṃ mātāpituādayo ñātayo kāmabhogino kāmajjhāsayā “ehi, tāta, imaṃ asītikoṭidhanaṃ vibhavaṃ paṭipajja, kulavaṃsaṃ patiṭṭhāpehī”ti uḷārehi bhogehi nimantayiṃsu. Tesampi chandamācikkhinti tesampi mama ñātīnaṃ tehi kāmabhogehi mā maṃ nimantayitthāti attano chandampi ācikkhiṃ, pabbajjāya ninnajjhāsayampi kathesiṃ, yathājjhāsayaṃ paṭipajjathāti adhippāyo.

“Having seen manifold evil”: This refers to seeing the various unwholesome actions such as killing, and their causes, committed by householders dwelling in a home on account of desire, hatred, and so on, and recognizing their base nature. “Thus I thought then”: This means I pondered: “When will I, like a great elephant breaking its iron fetters, shatter the fetter of the home and enter the forest by going forth from household life?” Even then they invited me—not only during the time of the Ayoghara Paṇḍita, but even then, during my youth as Soṇa, my relatives, led by my parents, who were enjoyers of sensual pleasures and inclined toward them, urged me with lavish riches, saying: “Come, dear one, take possession of this wealth of eighty crores and establish the family lineage.” “I declared my wish to them”: This means I expressed my own wish to those relatives, saying, “Do not invite me with those sensual pleasures,” and I spoke of my inclination toward going forth, the meaning being: “You should proceed according to your own disposition.”

Sopi maṃ anu sikkhantoti “ime kāmā nāma appassādā bahudukkhā bahūpāyāsā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.234; 2.43-45; pāci.417) nayena nānappakāraṃ kāmesu ādīnavaṃ paccavekkhitvā yathāhaṃ sīlādīni sikkhanto pabbajjaṃ rocesiṃ. Sopi nandapaṇḍito [M 0.0205] tatheva tassa nekkhammena maṃ anusikkhanto pabbajjaṃ samarocayīti. Ahaṃ soṇo ca nando cāti tasmiṃ kāle soṇanāmako ahaṃ mayhaṃ kaniṭṭhabhātā nando cāti. Ubho mātāpitā [P 0.0212] mamāti “ime nāma puttakā evaṃ taruṇakālepi kāme jahanti, kimaṅgaṃ pana maya”nti uppannasaṃvegā mātāpitaro ca. Bhoge chaḍḍetvāti asītikoṭivibhavasamiddhe mahā bhoge anapekkhacittā kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya pariccajitvā mayaṃ cattāropi janā himavantappadese mahāvanaṃ nekkhammajjhāsayena pavisimhāti attho.

“He too, training in imitation of me”: Having reflected in various ways on the danger in sensual pleasures—in the manner of “These sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, much suffering, and much despair,” and so on—just as I, training in virtue and so forth, came to approve of the going forth, so too the wise Nanda, following my example in renunciation, came to approve of the going forth. “I, Soṇa, and Nanda”: At that time, I was named Soṇa, and Nanda was my younger brother. “Both my mother and father”: And our parents too, in whom a sense of spiritual urgency arose, thinking: “These sons of ours are renouncing sensual pleasures even at such a young age—what then of us?” “Having forsaken wealth”: Having forsaken great riches amounting to eighty crores, with unattached minds, casting them away like a lump of phlegm, we four persons entered the great forest in the Himalayan region with an intention for renunciation. That is the meaning.

Pavisitvā ca te tattha ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge assamaṃ māpetvā tāpasapabbajjāya pabbajitvā tattha vasiṃsu. Te ubhopi bhātaro mātāpitaro paṭijaggiṃsu. Tesu nandapaṇḍito “mayā ābhataphalāphalāneva mātāpitaro khādāpessāmī”ti hiyyo ca purimagocaragahitaṭṭhānato ca [V 0.0193] yāni tāni avasesāni phalāphalāni pātova ānetvā mātāpitaro khādāpeti. Te tāni khāditvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā uposathikā honti. Soṇapaṇḍito pana dūraṃ gantvā madhuramadhurāni supakkāni āharitvā upanāmeti. Atha naṃ te “tāta, kaniṭṭhena ābhatāni mayaṃ khāditvā uposathikā jātā, idāni no attho natthī”ti vadanti. Iti tassa phalāphalāni paribhogaṃ na labhanti vinassanti, punadivasādīsupi tathevāti, evaṃ so pañcābhiññatāya dūrampi gantvā āharati, te pana na khādanti.

Having entered, they had a hermitage built in a delightful stretch of land there, went forth into the ascetic life, and dwelt there. Both brothers attended to their parents. Among them, the wise Nanda thought, “I will have my parents eat only the fruits and wild roots that I have brought.” So in the morning he would bring the fruits and roots that remained from the foraging ground of the previous day and feed them to his parents. Having eaten them and rinsed their mouths, they would undertake the Uposatha observance. But the wise Soṇa would go far away and bring back very sweet, fully ripe fruits and offer them. Then they would say to him: “Dear son, we have eaten what your younger brother brought and have undertaken the Uposatha; now we have no need for these.” Thus his fruits and roots were not consumed but went to waste; and it was the same on the following days. In this way, although he would go far with his five higher knowledges and bring them back, they would not eat them.

Atha mahāsatto cintesi – “mātāpitaro sukhumālā, nando ca yāni tāni apakkāni duppakkāni phalāphalāni āharitvā khādāpeti, evaṃ sante ime na ciraṃ pavattissanti, vāressāmi na”nti. Atha naṃ āmantetvā “nanda, ito paṭṭhāya phalāphalaṃ āharitvā mamāgamanaṃ patimānehi, ubho ekatova khādāpessāmā”ti āha. Evaṃ vuttepi attano puññaṃ paccāsīsanto na tassa vacanamakāsi. Mahāsatto taṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ “na tvaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ karosi, ahaṃ jeṭṭho, mātāpitaro ca mameva bhāro, ahameva ne paṭijaggissāmi, tvaṃ [P 0.0213] ito aññattha yāhī”ti tassa accharaṃ pahari.

Then the Great Being thought: “My parents are delicate, and Nanda brings unripe and poorly ripened fruits and roots for them to eat. This being so, they will not last long. I must stop him.” Then he addressed him, saying: “Nanda, from now on, bring the fruits and roots and wait for my arrival. We will both feed them together.” But even when this was said, Nanda, desiring his own merit, did not do as he said. When he came to attend on them, the Great Being rebuked him with a snap of his fingers, saying: “You do not follow the words of the wise. I am the elder, and our parents are my responsibility. I alone will attend to them. You go elsewhere from here!”

So tena paṇāmito tattha ṭhātuṃ asakkonto taṃ vanditvā mātāpitūnaṃ tamatthaṃ ārocetvā attano paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā kasiṇaṃ [M 0.0206] oloketvā taṃdivasameva aṭṭha ca samāpattiyo pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattetvā cintesi – “kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ sinerupādato ratanavālukaṃ āharitvā mama bhātu paṇṇasālāpariveṇaṃ ākiritvā khamāpessāmi, udāhu anotattato udakaṃ āharitvā khamāpessāmi? Atha vā me bhātā devatāvasena khameyya, cattāro mahārājāno sakkañca devarājānaṃ ānetvā khamāpessāmi, evaṃ pana na sobhissati, ayaṃ kho manojo brahmavaḍḍhanarājā sakalajambudīpe aggarājā, taṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbe rājāno ānetvā khamāpessāmi, evaṃ sante mama bhātu guṇo sakalajambudīpaṃ avattharitvā gamissati, cando viya sūriyo viya ca paññāyissatī”ti.

Having been dismissed by him and being unable to remain there, he paid homage to him, informed his parents of the matter, entered his own leaf-hut, gazed at a kasiṇa device, and on that very day produced the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges. He then reflected: "Should I bring jewel-sand from the foot of Mount Sineru, scatter it around my brother's leaf-hut compound, and ask his forgiveness? Or should I bring water from Lake Anotatta and ask his forgiveness? Or perhaps my brother might forgive me on account of the deities; should I bring the Four Great Kings and Sakka, king of the devas, and ask his forgiveness? But that would not be proper. This King Brahmavaḍḍhana of Manoja is the chief king in all of Jambudīpa. I will bring him first and then all the other kings and ask for forgiveness. When this is done, my brother's virtue will spread throughout all of Jambudīpa and he will become as famous as the moon and the sun."

So tāvadeva iddhiyā gantvā brahmavaḍḍhananagare tassa rañño nivesanadvāre otaritvā “eko tāpaso tumhe daṭṭhukāmo”ti rañño ārocāpetvā tena katokāso tassa santikaṃ gantvā “ahaṃ attano balena sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ gahetvā tava dassāmī”ti. “Kathaṃ pana tumhe, bhante, sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ gahetvā dassathā”ti? “Mahārāja, kassaci vadhacchedaṃ akatvā attano iddhiyāva gahetvā dassāmī”ti mahatiyā senāya saddhiṃ taṃ ādāya kosalaraṭṭhaṃ [V 0.0194] gantvā nagarassa avidūre khandhāvāraṃ nivesetvā “yuddhaṃ vā no detu, vase vā vattatū”ti kosalarañño dūtaṃ pāhesi. Tena kujjhitvā yuddhasajjena hutvā nikkhantena saddhiṃ yuddhe āraddhe attano iddhānubhāvena yathā dvinnaṃ senānaṃ pīḷanaṃ na hoti, evaṃ katvā yathā ca kosalarājā tassa vase vattati, evaṃ vacanapaṭivacanaharaṇehi saṃvidahi. Etenupāyena sakalajambudīpe rājāno tassa vase vattāpesi.

He went at once by psychic power to the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana, descended at the gate of that king's palace, and had it announced to the king: "An ascetic wishes to see you." Having been given an opportunity by him, he went into his presence and said: "By my own power I will take the kingship of all Jambudīpa and give it to you." "But how, venerable sir, will you take the kingship of all Jambudīpa and give it to me?" "Great king, without causing the death or injury of anyone, I will take it by my own psychic power and give it to you." Taking the king with a great army, he went to the kingdom of Kosala, set up camp not far from the city, and sent a messenger to the king of Kosala, saying: "Either give us battle or come under our sway." When that king, angered, came out prepared for battle, and the battle commenced, he, by his psychic power, acted so that there was no affliction to either of the two armies, and he arranged by an exchange of messages that the king of Kosala would come under his sway. By this means he made all the kings in Jambudīpa come under his sway.

So tena parituṭṭho nandapaṇḍitaṃ āha – “bhante, tumhehi yathā mayhaṃ paṭiññātaṃ, tathā kataṃ, bahūpakārā me tumhe, kimahaṃ [P 0.0214] tumhākaṃ karissāmi, ahañhi te sakalajambudīpe upaḍḍharajjampi dātuṃ icchāmi, kimaṅgaṃ pana hatthiassarathamaṇimuttāpavāḷarajatasuvaṇṇadāsidāsaparijanapariccheda”nti? Taṃ sutvā nandapaṇḍito “na me te, mahārāja, rajjena attho, nāpi hatthiyānādīhi, api ca kho te raṭṭhe asukasmiṃ nāma assame mama mātāpitaro pabbajitvā vasanti. Tyāhaṃ upaṭṭhahanto ekasmiṃ [M 0.0207] aparādhe mama jeṭṭhabhātikena soṇapaṇḍitena nāma mahesinā paṇāmito, svāhaṃ taṃ ādāya tassa santikaṃ gantvā khamāpessāmi, tassa me tvaṃ khamāpane sahāyo hohī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā catuvīsatiakkhobhanī parimāṇāya senāya parivuto ekasatarājūhi saddhiṃ nandapaṇḍitaṃ purakkhatvā taṃ assamapadaṃ patvā caturaṅgulappadesaṃ muñcitvā ākāse ṭhitena kājena anotattato udakaṃ āharitvā pānīyaṃ paṭisāmetvā pariveṇaṃ sammajjitvā mātāpitūnaṃ āsannappadese nisinnaṃ jhānaratisamappitaṃ mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā nandapaṇḍito naṃ khamāpesi. Mahāsatto nandapaṇḍitaṃ mātaraṃ paṭicchāpetvā attanā yāvajīvaṃ pitaraṃ paṭijaggi. Tesaṃ pana rājūnaṃ –

Greatly pleased with him, the king said to the wise Nanda: "Venerable sir, you have done for me as you promised. You have been a great help to me. What can I do for you? I am willing to give you even half the kingdom in all of Jambudīpa, to say nothing of elephants, horses, chariots, gems, pearls, coral, silver, gold, male and female slaves, and attendants." Hearing this, the wise Nanda said: "Great king, I have no use for a kingdom, nor for elephants, chariots, and so on. But in your country, in a certain hermitage, my parents have gone forth and are dwelling. While I was attending on them, on one occasion when I was at fault, I was dismissed by my elder brother, the great sage named the wise Soṇa. I will take you with me, go to him, and ask his forgiveness. You must be my helper in asking for this forgiveness." The king agreed, saying, "Good." Surrounded by an army of twenty-four akkhobhinīs and accompanied by one hundred and one other kings, with the wise Nanda at their head, he arrived at the hermitage site. Leaving a space of four finger-breadths, with his body poised in the air, he brought water from Lake Anotatta, prepared drinking water, swept the compound, and approached the Great Being, who was seated near his parents, absorbed in the bliss of jhāna; and he asked his forgiveness. The Great Being entrusted their mother to the wise Nanda, while he himself attended on their father for the rest of his life. As for those kings—

“Ānando ca pamodo ca, sadā hasitakīḷitaṃ;

Mātaraṃ paricaritvāna, labbhametaṃ vijānatā.

Delight and joy, constant laughter and play: this is obtained by a wise person who has served his mother.

“Ānando ca pamodo ca, sadā hasitakīḷitaṃ;

Pitaraṃ paricaritvāna, labbhametaṃ vijānato.

Delight and joy, constant laughter and play: this is obtained by a wise person who has served his father.

“Dānañca peyyavajjañca, atthacariyā ca yā idha;

Samānattatā ca dhammesu, tattha tattha yathārahaṃ;

Ete kho saṅgahā loke, rathassāṇīva yāyato.

Generosity, endearing speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality in all things, in each case as is proper: these are the means of unification in the world, like the linchpin of a moving chariot.

“Ete [V 0.0195] ca saṅgahā nāssu, na mātā puttakāraṇā;

Labhetha mānaṃ pūjaṃ vā, pitā vā puttakāraṇā.

If these means of unification did not exist, neither a mother nor a father would receive honor or veneration on account of their child.

“Yasmā ca saṅgahā ete, sammapekkhanti paṇḍitā;

Tasmā mahattaṃ papponti, pāsaṃsā ca bhavanti te.

And because the wise give due consideration to these means of unification, they therefore attain greatness and become worthy of praise.

“Brahmāti mātāpitaro, pubbācariyāti vuccare;

Āhuneyyā ca puttānaṃ, pajāya anukampakā.

Parents are called Brahmā and first teachers; they are worthy of offerings from their children, compassionate to their offspring.

“Tasmā hi ne namasseyya, sakkareyya ca paṇḍito;

Annena [P 0.0215] atha pānena, vatthena sayanena ca;

Ucchādanena nhāpanena, pādānaṃ dhovanena ca.

Therefore a wise person should pay them homage and honor them with food and drink, with clothing and bedding, with anointing and bathing, and with washing their feet.

“Tāya naṃ pāricariyāya, mātāpitūsu paṇḍitā;

Idheva naṃ pasaṃsanti, pecca sagge pamodatī”ti. (jā. 2.20.176-183) –

For that service to his mother and father, the wise praise him right here in this world; and after death, he rejoices in heaven.

Buddhalīḷāya [M 0.0208] dhammaṃ desesi, taṃ sutvā sabbepi te rājāno sabalakāyā pasīdiṃsu. Atha ne pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā “dānādīsu appamattā hothā”ti ovaditvā vissajjesi. Te sabbepi dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā āyupariyosāne devanagaraṃ pūrayiṃsu. Bodhisatto “ito paṭṭhāya mātaraṃ paṭijaggāhī”ti mātaraṃ nandapaṇḍitaṃ paṭicchāpetvā attanā yāvajīvaṃ pitaraṃ paṭijaggi. Te ubhopi āyupariyosāne brahmalokaparāyanā ahesuṃ.

He taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, and on hearing it, all those kings along with their armies gained faith. Then, having established them in the five precepts, he advised them, “Be heedful in giving and so forth,” and dismissed them. All of them ruled righteously and, at the end of their lives, filled the city of the devas. The Bodhisatta, having entrusted his mother to Nanda the Wise with the instruction, “From now on, you are to care for mother,” personally attended to his father for the rest of his life. Both of them, at the end of their lives, were destined for the Brahma-world.

Tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni, nandapaṇḍito ānandatthero, manojo rājā sāriputtatthero, ekasatarājāno asītimahātherā ceva aññataratherā ca, catuvīsatiakkhobhanīparisā buddhaparisā, soṇapaṇḍito lokanātho.

At that time, the parents were the great royal family; Nanda the Wise was the Venerable Ānanda; King Manoja was the Venerable Sāriputta; the one hundred and one kings were the eighty great elders and certain other elders; the retinue of twenty-four akkhobhaṇīs was the Buddha’s retinue; and Soṇa the Wise was the Lord of the World.

Tassa kiñcāpi sātisayā nekkhammapāramī, tathāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sesapāramiyo ca niddhāretabbā. Tathā accantameva kāmesu anapekkhatā, mātāpitūsu tibbo sagāravasappatissabhāvo[V 0.0196], mātāpituupaṭṭhānena atitti, satipi nesaṃ upaṭṭhāne sabbakālaṃ samāpattivihārehi vītināmananti evamādayo mahāsattassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Although his perfection of renunciation was pre-eminent, the remaining perfections should be determined in the way stated below. Likewise, his utter non-concern for sensual pleasures, his intense respect and reverence towards his parents, his insatiability in serving his parents, and his spending all his time dwelling in meditative attainments even while attending to them—these and other such qualities and powers of the Great Being are to be elucidated.

Soṇapaṇḍitacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Conduct of Soṇa the Wise is finished.

Nekkhammapāramī niṭṭhitā.

The Perfection of Renunciation is completed.

6. Temiyacariyāvaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Conduct of Temiya

48. Chaṭṭhe kāsirājassa atrajoti kāsirañño atrajo putto yadā homi, tadā mūgapakkhoti nāmena, temiyoti vadanti manti temiyoti nāmena mūgapakkhavatādhiṭṭhānena “mūgapakkho”ti mātāpitaro ādiṃ katvā sabbeva maṃ vadantīti sambandho. Mahāsattassa hi jātadivase sakalakāsiraṭṭhe [P 0.0216] devo vassi, yasmā ca so rañño ceva amaccādīnañca hadayaṃ uḷārena pītisinehena temayamāno uppanno, tasmā “temiyakumāro”ti nāmaṃ ahosi.

48. In the sixth, 'son of the king of Kāsi' means: when I was the son, the offspring, of the king of Kāsi. 'Mūgapakkha by name, they call me Temiya': the connection is that because of my resolution to be mute and crippled, my parents and everyone else called me 'Mūgapakkha.' For on the day the Great Being was born, rain fell throughout the entire kingdom of Kāsi, and because he was born moistening the hearts of the king, his ministers, and others with abundant joy and affection, his name became 'Prince Temiya'.

49. Soḷasitthisahassānanti [M 0.0209] soḷasannaṃ kāsirañño itthāgārasahassānaṃ. Na vijjati pumoti putto na labbhati. Na kevalañca putto eva, dhītāpissa natthi eva. Ahorattānaṃ accayena, nibbatto ahamekakoti aputtakasseva tassa rañño bahūnaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ atītattā anekesaṃ ahorattānaṃ apagamanena sakkadattiyo ahamekakova bodhipariyesanaṃ caramāno, tadā tassa putto hutvā uppannoti satthā vadati.

49. 'Sixteen thousand women' means the sixteen thousand women in the harem of the king of Kāsi. 'No male exists' means no son was obtained. And not only no son, but there was also no daughter. 'After the passing of days and nights, I alone was born': the Teacher says that since that king was childless and many years had passed, after the passing of many days and nights, he alone, a gift from Sakka, was born as the king's son while he was pursuing the quest for enlightenment.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ kāsirājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa soḷasasahassā itthiyo ahesuṃ. Tāsu ekāpi puttaṃ vā dhītaraṃ vā na labhati. Nāgarā “amhākaṃ rañño vaṃsānurakkhako ekopi putto natthī”ti vippaṭisārī jātā sannipatitvā rājānaṃ “puttaṃ patthehī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā soḷasasahassā itthiyo “puttaṃ patthethā”ti āṇāpesi. Tā candādīnaṃ upaṭṭhānādīni katvā patthentiyopi na labhiṃsu. Aggamahesī panassa maddarājadhītā candādevī nāma sīlasampannā ahosi. Rājā “tvampi puttaṃ patthehī”ti āha. Sā puṇṇamadivase uposathikā hutvā attano sīlaṃ āvajjetvā “sacāhaṃ akhaṇḍasīlā, iminā me saccena putto uppajjatū”ti saccakiriyamakāsi. Tassā sīlatejena sakkassa āsanaṃ [V 0.0197] uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “candādeviyā puttapaṭilābhassa upāyaṃ karissāmī”ti tassā anucchavikaṃ puttaṃ upadhārento bodhisattaṃ tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbattitvā tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cavitvā uparidevaloke uppajjitukāmaṃ disvā tassa santikaṃ gantvā “samma, tayi manussaloke uppanne pāramiyo ca te pūressanti, mahājanassa ca vuḍḍhi bhavissati, ayaṃ kāsirañño candā nāma aggamahesī puttaṃ pattheti, tassā [P 0.0217] kucchiyaṃ uppajjāhī”ti āha.

Here is the story in sequence. In the past, a king of Kāsi was ruling in Bārāṇasī. He had sixteen thousand wives, but not one of them bore him a son or a daughter. The townspeople became distressed, thinking, “Our king has no son to preserve the lineage.” They assembled and told the king: “You should pray for a son!” The king commanded his sixteen thousand wives: “You must pray for a son!” Though they performed services to the moon and other deities, they did not obtain a son. Now his chief queen, Candādevī, the daughter of the king of Madda, was endowed with virtue. The king said to her: “You, too, should pray for a son.” On the full-moon observance day, having undertaken the Uposatha, she reflected on her own virtue and made an asseveration of truth: “If my virtue is unbroken, by this truth may a son be born to me!” By the power of her virtue, Sakka’s throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting, understood the reason and thought: “I will find a way for Queen Candā to obtain a son.” Looking for a son suitable for her, he saw the Bodhisatta, who had been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm and, having lived out his lifespan there, had passed away and was about to be reborn in a higher deva world. He approached him and said: “Friend, if you are reborn in the human world your perfections will be fulfilled and the great populace will prosper. Candā, the chief queen of the king of Kāsi, is praying for a son. Be reborn in her womb!”

So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā tassā kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa sahāyā pañcasatā devaputtā khīṇāyukā devalokā cavitvā tasseva rañño amaccabhariyānaṃ kucchīsu paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Devī gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā gabbhaparihāraṃ dāpesi. Sā paripuṇṇagabbhā dhaññapuññalakkhaṇasampannaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Taṃdivasameva amaccagehesu [M 0.0210] pañcakumārasatāni vijāyiṃsu. Ubhayampi sutvā rājā “mama puttassa parivārā ete”ti pañcannaṃ dārakasatānaṃ pañcadhātisatāni pesetvā kumārapasādhanāni ca pesesi. Mahāsattassa pana atidīghādidosavivajjitā alambatthanā madhurathaññā catusaṭṭhidhātiyo datvā mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā candādeviyāpi varaṃ adāsi. Sā gahitakaṃ katvā ṭhapesi. Dārako mahatā parivārena vaḍḍhati. Atha naṃ ekamāsikaṃ alaṅkaritvā rañño santikaṃ ānayiṃsu. Rājā piyaputtaṃ oloketvā āliṅgitvā aṅke nisīdāpetvā ramayamāno nisīdi.

Saying, “Very well,” he agreed and took conception in her womb. His five hundred devaputta companions, their lifespans exhausted, passed away from the deva world and took conception in the wombs of that same king’s ministers’ wives. The queen, realizing that she had conceived, informed the king. The king provided for the protection of the embryo. When her womb was mature, she gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of fortune and merit. On that very day, five hundred boys were born in the ministers’ houses. Hearing of both events, the king said, “These are my son’s retinue,” and he sent five hundred nurses for the five hundred boys, along with princely adornments. For the Great Being, however, he provided sixty-four nurses who were free from such faults as being too tall, whose breasts were not pendulous, and who had sweet milk. Having bestowed great honor, he also granted a boon to Queen Candā. She accepted it and held it in reserve. The boy grew up with a great retinue. When he was one month old, they adorned him and brought him to the king. The king looked at his dear son, embraced him, placed him on his lap, and sat there enjoying his company.

50. Tasmiṃ khaṇe cattāro corā ānītā. Rājā tesu ekassa sakaṇṭakāhi kasāhi pahārasahassaṃ āṇāpesi, ekassa saṅkhalikāya bandhitvā bandhanāgārappavesanaṃ, ekassa sarīre sattippahāradānaṃ, ekassa sūlāropanaṃ. Mahāsatto pitu kathaṃ sutvā saṃvegappatto hutvā “aho mama pitā rajjaṃ nissāya bhāriyaṃ nirayagāmikammaṃ karotī”ti cintesi. Punadivase naṃ setacchattassa heṭṭhā alaṅkatasirisayane nipajjāpesuṃ.

50. At that moment, four thieves were brought before him. The king ordered a thousand lashes with thorny whips for one of them, for another imprisonment in chains, for another piercing with a spear, and for another impalement on a stake. On hearing his father’s words, the Great Being was overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency and thought: “Alas, on account of his kingship my father is performing heavy kamma that leads to hell!” The next day, they laid him down on an adorned, splendid couch beneath a white parasol.

So thokaṃ niddāyitvā paṭibuddho akkhīni ummīletvā setacchattaṃ olokento mahantaṃ sirivibhavaṃ passi. Athassa pakatiyāpi saṃvegappattassa atirekataraṃ bhayaṃ uppajji. So “kuto nu kho ahaṃ imaṃ rājagehaṃ āgato”ti upadhārento jātissarañāṇena devalokato āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā tato paraṃ olokento ussadaniraye pakkabhāvaṃ [P 0.0218] passi. Tato paraṃ olokento tasmiṃyeva nagare rājabhāvaṃ passi. Atha so “ahaṃ vīsativassāni rajjaṃ kāretvā [V 0.0198] asītivassasahassāni ussadaniraye pacciṃ, idāni punapi imasmiṃ coragehe nibbattosmi, pitāpi me hiyyo catūsu coresu ānītesu tathārūpaṃ pharusaṃ nirayasaṃvattanikaṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Na me iminā aviditavipulānatthāvahena rajjena attho, kathaṃ nu kho imamhā coragehā mucceyya”nti cintento nipajji. Atha naṃ ekā devadhītā “tāta temiyakumāra, mā bhāyi, tīṇi aṅgāni adhiṭṭhahitvā tava sotthi bhavissatī”ti samassāsesi. Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto rajjasaṅkhātā [M 0.0211] anatthato muccitukāmo soḷasasaṃvaccharāni tīṇi aṅgāni acalādhiṭṭhānavasena adhiṭṭhahi. Tena vuttaṃ “kicchāladdhaṃ piyaṃ putta”ntiādi.

After sleeping for a little while, he awoke, opened his eyes, and, gazing at the white parasol, he saw the great royal splendor. Then, for him who was by nature already possessed of spiritual urgency, an even greater fear arose. Reflecting, “From where have I come to this royal palace?” he recollected his past lives with his special knowledge and knew that he had come from the deva world. Looking beyond that, he saw that he had been boiled in the Ussada hell. Looking beyond that, he saw that he had been a king in this very city. Then he thought: “Having reigned for twenty years, I was boiled in the Ussada hell for eighty thousand years. Now I have been reborn again in this thieves’ den. And yesterday, when four thieves were brought before him, my father spoke such harsh words that lead to hell. I have no use for this kingship, which brings vast and unforeseen calamity. How can I escape from this thieves’ den?” Thinking thus, he lay down. Then a certain devadhītā comforted him, saying: “Dear Prince Temiya, do not be afraid. If you resolve upon three things, you will be safe.” Hearing this, the Great Being, wishing to be free from the calamity called kingship, for sixteen years resolved upon three things with an unshakable determination. Thus it was said: “A beloved son obtained with difficulty,” and so on.

Tattha kicchāladdhanti kicchena kasirena cirakālapatthanāya laddhaṃ. Abhijātanti jātisampannaṃ. Kāyajutiyā ceva ñāṇajutiyā ca samannāgatattā jutindharaṃ. Setacchattaṃ dhārayitvāna, sayane poseti maṃ pitāti pitā me kāsirājā “mā naṃ kumāraṃ rajo vā ussāvo vā”ti jātakālato paṭṭhāya setacchattassa heṭṭhā sirisayane sayāpetvā mahantena parivārena maṃ poseti.

Here, 'obtained with difficulty' means obtained with hardship, with trouble, through long-term aspiration. 'Noble-born' means endowed with high birth. 'Radiant' means endowed with both bodily radiance and the radiance of wisdom. 'My father, holding a white parasol, nurtures me on a couch': this means my father, the king of Kāsi, thinking, “Let no dust or dew touch the prince,” has nurtured me from birth with a great retinue, having me lie on a splendid couch beneath a white parasol.

51. Niddāyamāno sayanavare pabujjhitvā ahaṃ olokento paṇḍaraṃ setacchattaṃ addasaṃ. Yenāhaṃ nirayaṃ gatoti yena setacchattena tato tatiye attabhāve ahaṃ nirayaṃ gato, setacchattasīsena rajjaṃ vadati.

51. While sleeping on an excellent couch, I awoke and, looking around, saw the white parasol. 'It was because of this that I had gone to hell': because of that white parasol, in the third existence from then, I had gone to hell. By 'white parasol' he speaks of kingship.

52. Saha diṭṭhassa me chattanti taṃ setacchattaṃ diṭṭhassa diṭṭhavato me saha tena dassanena, dassanasamakālamevāti attho. Tāso uppajji bheravoti suparividitādīnavattā bhayānako cittutrāso udapādi. Vinicchayaṃ samāpanno, kathāhaṃ imaṃ muñcissanti kathaṃ nu kho ahaṃ imaṃ rajjaṃ kāḷakaṇṇiṃ muñceyyanti evaṃ vicāraṇaṃ āpajjiṃ.

52. 'Along with the sight of the parasol': for me who saw that white parasol, this means along with that sight, at the very moment of seeing it. 'Terror arose, dreadful': a frightening mental terror arose because its danger was well understood. 'Having come to a decision, how shall I escape this?': I began to reflect, 'How indeed shall I free myself from this accursed kingship?'

53. Pubbasālohitā mayhanti pubbe ekasmiṃ attabhāve mama mātubhūtapubbā tasmiṃ chatte adhivatthā devatā mayhaṃ atthakāminī hitesinī. Sā maṃ disvāna dukkhitaṃ, tīsu ṭhānesu yojayīti sā devatā maṃ tathā [P 0.0219] cetodukkhena dukkhitaṃ disvā mūgapakkhabadhirabhāvasaṅkhātesu tīsu rajjadukkhato nikkhamanakāraṇesu yojesi.

53. 'My former blood relative': a deity who had formerly been my mother in a previous existence dwelt in that parasol, wishing for my welfare and benefit. 'Seeing me distressed, she guided me in three ways': that deity, seeing me thus distressed with mental suffering, engaged me in the three means of escape from the suffering of kingship, namely, the states of being mute, crippled, and deaf.

54. Paṇḍiccayanti paṇḍiccaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Mā vibhāvayāti mā pakāsehi. Bālamatoti bāloti ñāto. Sabboti sakalo antojano ceva bahijano ca. Ocināyatūti nīharathetaṃ [V 0.0199] kāḷakaṇṇinti avajānātu. Evaṃ tava attho bhavissatīti evaṃ yathāvuttanayena avajānitabbabhāve sati tuyhaṃ gehato nikkhamanena hitaṃ pāramiparipūraṇaṃ bhavissati.

54. 'By wisdom' (paṇḍiccāya): or the reading is just 'wisdom' (paṇḍiccaṃ). 'Do not reveal': do not disclose. 'As a fool': known as a fool. 'All': the entire household as well as outsiders. 'Let him cast out': let him expel this ill-omened one, let him scorn him. 'Thus your welfare will be': thus, when you are to be despised in the aforesaid manner, your welfare—the fulfillment of the perfections—will be accomplished by your leaving the home.

55. Tetaṃ [M 0.0212] vacananti te etaṃ tīṇi aṅgāni adhiṭṭhāhīti vacanaṃ. Atthakāmāsi me ammāti amma devate, mama atthakāmā asi. Hitakāmāti tasseva pariyāyavacanaṃ. Atthoti vā ettha sukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Hitanti tassa kāraṇabhūtaṃ puññaṃ.

55. 'That statement of yours': this refers to the statement, 'Resolve on these three factors.' 'You are one who desires my welfare, mother': O mother goddess, you desire my welfare. 'Desiring my benefit': a synonym for that. Or, 'welfare' here should be understood as happiness. 'Benefit': the merit that is the cause of that.

56. Sāgareva thalaṃ labhinti coragehe vatāhaṃ jāto, ahu me mahāvatānatthoti sokasāgare osīdanto tassā devatāya ahaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā sāgare osīdanto viya thalaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ alabhiṃ, rajjakulato nikkhamanopāyaṃ alabhinti attho. Tayo aṅge adhiṭṭhahinti yāva gehato nikkhamiṃ, tāva tīṇi aṅgāni kāraṇāni adhiṭṭhahiṃ.

56. 'Like gaining land from the ocean': sinking in an ocean of grief, thinking, 'Alas, I have been born in a thieves' den! It is a great misfortune for me!', upon hearing the deity’s words, like one sinking in the ocean who finds solid ground, I gained a firm footing. The meaning is that I found a means of escape from the royal family. 'I resolved on the three factors': until I left the home, I was resolved on those three factors, or reasons.

57. Idāni tāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “mūgo ahosi”nti gāthamāha. Tattha pakkhoti pīṭhasappi. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

57. Now, to show these in their actual form, he spoke the verse beginning: 'I was mute.' Therein, 'pakkho' means a cripple. The rest is easily understood.

Evaṃ pana mahāsatte devatāya dinnanaye ṭhatvā jātavassato paṭṭhāya mūgādibhāvena attānaṃ dassente mātāpitaro dhātiādayo ca “mūgānaṃ hanupariyosānaṃ nāma evarūpaṃ na hoti, badhirānaṃ kaṇṇasotaṃ nāma evarūpaṃ na hoti, pīṭhasappīnaṃ hatthapādā nāma evarūpā na honti, bhavitabbamettha kāraṇena, vīmaṃsissāma na”nti cintetvā “khīrena tāva vīmaṃsissāmā”ti sakaladivasaṃ khīraṃ na denti. So sussantopi khīratthāya saddaṃ na karoti.

Thus, when the great being, abiding by the counsel given by the deity, began to show himself as if mute and so on from the year of his birth, his parents, nurses, and others thought: 'For mutes, the jaw is not shaped like this; for the deaf, the ear canal is not like this; for cripples, the hands and feet are not like this. There must be some reason here; let us investigate.' Thinking thus, they decided, 'First, let us test him with milk,' and so they did not give him milk for a whole day. Even though he was parched, he made no sound for milk.

Athassa mātā “putto me chāto, khīramassa dethā”ti khīraṃ dāpesi. Evaṃ antarantarā khīraṃ adatvā ekasaṃvaccharaṃ vīmaṃsantāpi antaraṃ na passiṃsu. Tato “kumārakā nāma pūvakhajjakaṃ piyāyanti, phalāphalaṃ piyāyanti, kīḷanabhaṇḍakaṃ piyāyanti, bhojanaṃ piyāyantī”ti tāni tāni palobhanīyāni upanetvā vīmaṃsanavasena palobhentā yāva pañcavassakālā antaraṃ na passiṃsu. Atha naṃ “dārakā nāma [P 0.0220] aggito bhāyanti, mattahatthito bhāyanti, sappato bhāyanti, ukkhittāsikapurisato bhāyanti, tehi vīmaṃsissāmā”ti yathā tehissa anattho na jāyati, tathā purimameva saṃvidahitvā atibhayānakākārena upagacchante kāresuṃ.

Then his mother, thinking, 'My son is hungry, give him milk,' had milk given to him. Even when they tested him by withholding milk from time to time for a whole year, they saw no flaw in him. Then they thought, 'Young boys delight in cakes and sweets, they delight in various fruits, they delight in toys, they delight in food.' So they brought various tempting things to test and entice him, but even up to the age of five, they saw no flaw in him. Then they thought, 'Children are afraid of fire, of rutting elephants, of snakes, and of men with drawn swords—we will test him with these.' So they arranged beforehand that no harm would come to him, and then they had people approach him in an exceedingly frightening manner.

Mahāsatto [M 0.0213][V 0.0200] nirayabhayaṃ āvajjetvā “ito sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena nirayo bhāyitabbo”ti niccalova hoti. Evampi vīmaṃsitvā antaraṃ na passantā puna “dārakā nāma samajjatthikā hontī”ti samajjaṃ kāretvāpi mahāsattaṃ sāṇiyā parikkhipitvā ajānantasseva catūsu passesu saṅkhasaddehi bherisaddehi ca sahasā ekaninnādaṃ kāretvāpi andhakāre ghaṭehi dīpaṃ upanetvā sahasā ālokaṃ dassetvāpi sakalasarīraṃ phāṇitena makkhetvā bahumakkhike ṭhāne nipajjāpetvāpi nhāpanādīni akatvā uccārapassāvamatthake nipannaṃ ajjhupekkhitvāpi tattha ca palipannaṃ sayamānaṃ parihāsehi akkosanehi ca ghaṭṭetvāpi heṭṭhāmañce aggikapallaṃ katvā uṇhasantāpena pīḷetvāpīti evaṃ nānāvidhehi upāyehi vīmaṃsantāpissa antaraṃ na passiṃsu.

The great being, reflecting on the fear of hell, remained steadfast, thinking, 'Hell is to be feared a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times more than this.' Having tested him in this way and finding no flaw, they again thought, 'Children are fond of festivals.' So they arranged a festival, surrounded the great being with a curtain, and then, as if he were unaware, they suddenly made a single loud noise on all four sides with conch shells and drums. They also brought lamps into the darkness and suddenly showed him light. They smeared his entire body with molasses and made him lie down in a place with many flies. They neglected to bathe him and left him lying in his own urine and feces. They assailed him with jests and insults as he lay there smeared in filth. They placed a pot of hot coals under his bed and tormented him with scorching heat. Thus, though they tested him with various methods, they still found no flaw in him.

Mahāsatto hi sabbattha nirayabhayameva āvajjetvā adhiṭṭhānaṃ avikopento niccalova ahosi. Evaṃ pannarasavassāni vīmaṃsitvā atha soḷasavassakāle “pīṭhasappino vā hontu mūgabadhirā vā rajanīyesu arajjantā dussanīyesu adussantā nāma natthīti nāṭakānissa paccupaṭṭhapetvā vīmaṃsissāmā”ti kumāraṃ gandhodakena nhāpetvā devaputtaṃ viya alaṅkaritvā devavimānakappaṃ pupphagandhadāmādīhi ekāmodapamodaṃ pāsādaṃ āropetvā uttamarūpadharā bhāvavilāsasampannā devaccharāpaṭibhāgā itthiyo upaṭṭhapesuṃ – “gacchatha naccādīhi kumāraṃ abhiramāpethā”ti. Tā upagantvā tathā kātuṃ vāyamiṃsu. So buddhisampannatāya “imā me sarīrasamphassaṃ mā vindiṃsū”ti assāsapassāse nirundhi. Tā tassa sarīrasamphassaṃ avindantiyo “thaddhasarīro esa, nāyaṃ manusso, yakkho bhavissatī”ti pakkamiṃsu.

The great being, reflecting only on the fear of hell in all circumstances, remained steadfast and did not waver in his resolve. After testing him for fifteen years, at the age of sixteen they thought: 'There is no one, not even a cripple or a deaf-mute, who is not aroused by the arousing and repelled by the repulsive. We will test him by presenting dancers to him.' Having bathed the prince with fragrant water and adorned him like a celestial youth, they led him to a palace like a celestial mansion, filled with flowers, garlands, and perfumes, a place of great delight. There, they presented women of supreme beauty, skilled in charm and grace, resembling celestial nymphs, instructing them: 'Go and entertain the prince with dancing and so on.' They approached and attempted to do so. But he, endowed with wisdom, restrained his breathing, thinking, 'Let them not feel my body move.' When they touched him and found his body rigid, they concluded, 'His body is stiff; he is no human—he must be a yakkha,' and departed.

Evaṃ soḷasa vassāni soḷasahi mahāvīmaṃsāhi anekāhi ca khuddakavīmaṃsāhi pariggaṇhituṃ asakkuṇitvā mātāpitaro “tāta, temiyakumāra, mayaṃ tava amūgādibhāvaṃ jānāma, na hi tesaṃ evarūpāni mukhakaṇṇasotapādāni honti, tvaṃ amhehi [P 0.0221] patthetvā laddhaputtako, mā no nāsehi, sakalajambudīpe rājūnaṃ santikā garahato mocehī”ti saha visuṃ visuñca anekavāraṃ yāciṃsu. So tehi evaṃ yāciyamānopi asuṇanto viya hutvā nipajji.

When for sixteen years they were unable to find any flaw in him with sixteen great tests and many minor tests, his parents pleaded with him together and separately many times, saying: 'Dear Prince Temiya, we know you are not really mute and so on. Truly, the faces, ears, and feet of such people are not like yours. You are a son we obtained through prayer; do not destroy us. Free us from the blame we would receive from all the kings in Jambudīpa.' But though they pleaded with him thus, he lay down as if not hearing them.

58. Atha [M 0.0214] rājā mahāsattassa ubho pāde kaṇṇasote jivhaṃ ubho ca hatthe kusalehi purisehi vīmaṃsāpetvā “yadipi apīṭhasappiādīnaṃ viyassa pādādayo, tathāpi ayaṃ pīṭhasappi mūgabadhiro maññe, īdise kāḷakaṇṇipurise imasmiṃ gehe vasante tayo antarāyā paññāyanti [V 0.0201] jīvitassa vā chattassa vā mahesiyā vā”ti lakkhaṇapāṭhakehi idāni kathitaṃ. Jātadivase pana “tumhākaṃ domanassapariharaṇatthaṃ ‘dhaññapuññalakkhaṇo’ti vutta”nti amaccehi ārocitaṃ sutvā antarāyabhayena bhīto “gacchatha naṃ avamaṅgalarathe nipajjāpetvā pacchimadvārena nīharāpetvā āmakasusāne nikhaṇathā”ti āṇāpesi. Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto haṭṭho udaggo ahosi – “cirassaṃ vata me manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ “tato me hatthapāde cā”tiādi.

58. Then the king had the great being's two feet, ears, tongue, and both hands examined by experts. He thought: 'Although his feet and other limbs are like those of one who is not a cripple, I still think he is a cripple, mute, and deaf. With such an ill-omened person living in this house, three dangers are apparent: to my life, to the royal parasol, or to the chief queen,' as the interpreters of signs had now stated. Although on the day of his birth the ministers had announced, 'To dispel your grief, he was called "One with signs of fortune and merit,"' the king was now terrified by the danger and ordered: 'Go, lay him on an inauspicious cart, take him out through the western gate, and bury him in the raw charnel ground.' Hearing this, the great being was delighted and elated, thinking, 'At last, my wish will reach its culmination!' Hence it is said: 'Then my hands and feet,' etc.

Tattha maddiyāti maddanavasena vīmaṃsitvā. Anūnatanti hatthādīhi avikalataṃ. Nindisunti “evaṃ anūnāvayavopi samāno mūgādi viya dissamāno “rajjaṃ kāretuṃ abhabbo, kāḷakaṇṇipuriso aya”nti garahiṃsu. “Niddisu”ntipi pāṭho, vadiṃsūti attho.

Therein, 'maddiyā' means having tested by way of pressing. 'Anūnataṃ' means completeness, being without deficiency in limbs and so on. 'Nindisuṃ' means they censured him, saying: 'Although he is complete in his limbs, since he appears to be mute and so on, he is unfit to rule; this is an ill-omened person.' There is also the reading 'niddisuṃ,' meaning 'they said.'

59. Chaḍḍanaṃ anumodisunti rājadassanatthaṃ āgatā sabbepi janapadavāsino senāpatipurohitappamukhā rājapurisā te sabbepi ekamanā samānacittā hutvā antarāyapariharaṇatthaṃ raññā āṇattā bhūmiyaṃ nikhaṇanavasena mama chaḍḍanaṃ mukhasaṅkocaṃ akatvā abhimukhabhāvena sādhu suṭṭhu idaṃ kattabbamevāti anumodiṃsu.

59. 'They approved of the abandonment' means: all the country-dwellers and the royal officials headed by the commander-in-chief and the royal chaplain, who had come for an audience with the king—all of them, being of one mind and united in thought, approved of my abandonment by being buried in the ground, which was commanded by the king to avert danger. They did so without making a grimace, but with an open countenance, saying: 'Good, very good! This must indeed be done.'

60. So me attho samijjhathāti yassatthāya yadatthaṃ tato mūgādibhāvādhiṭṭhānavasena dukkaracaraṇaṃ ciṇṇaṃ caritaṃ, so attho mama samijjhati. Tesaṃ mama mātāpituādīnaṃ matiṃ adhippāyaṃ sutvā so ahaṃ mama adhippāyasamijjhanena haṭṭho anupadhāretvā bhūmiyaṃ nikhaṇanānujānanena saṃviggamānasova ahosinti vacanasesena sambandho veditabbo.

60. 'So me attho samijjhathāti' means: 'May that purpose of mine succeed!' The purpose for which I had undertaken the difficult practice by resolving to be in the state of a mute and so on—that purpose of mine is succeeding. Having heard the intention of my parents and others, I was delighted by the fulfillment of my wish. And without deliberation, I was as if with an agitated mind on account of the permission to bury me in the ground—the connection is to be understood with the remaining words.

61. Evaṃ [P 0.0222] kumārassa bhūmiyaṃ nikhaṇane raññā āṇatte candādevī taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “deva, tumhehi mayhaṃ varo dinno, mayā [M 0.0215] ca gahitakaṃ katvā ṭhapito, taṃ me idāni dethā”ti. “Gaṇha, devī”ti. “Puttassa me rajjaṃ dethā”ti. “Putto te kāḷakaṇṇī, na sakkā dātu”nti. “Tena hi, deva, yāvajīvaṃ adento satta vassāni dethā”ti. “Tampi na sakkā”ti. “Cha vassāni, pañcacattāritīṇidveekaṃ vassaṃ, satta māse, chapañcacattārotayodveekaṃ māsaṃaddhamāsaṃsattāhaṃ dethā”ti. Sādhu gaṇhāti.

61. Thus, when the king had commanded that the prince be buried in the ground, Queen Candādevī, having heard of this matter, approached the king and said: 'Your Majesty, you gave me a boon, which I accepted and have kept in reserve. Now grant it to me.' 'Take it, Queen.' 'Give the kingdom to my son.' 'Your son is inauspicious; it cannot be given.' 'Then, Your Majesty, if you will not give it for life, give it for seven years.' 'That too is not possible.' 'Then for six years, five, four, three, two, one year; for seven months, six, five, four, three, two, one month; for half a month; for seven days—give it.' 'Very well, take it.'

Sā puttaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā “temiyakumārassa idaṃ rajja”nti nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā puttaṃ hatthikkhandhaṃ āropetvā setacchattaṃ matthake kārāpetvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā [V 0.0202] āgataṃ alaṅkatasirisayane nipajjāpetvā sabbarattiṃ yāci – “tāta temiya, taṃ nissāya soḷasa vassāni niddaṃ alabhitvā rodamānāya me akkhīni uppakkāni, sokena hadayaṃ bhijjati viya, tava apīṭhasappiādibhāvaṃ jānāmi, mā maṃ anāthaṃ karī”ti. Iminā niyāmena cha divase yāci. Chaṭṭhe divase rājā sunandaṃ nāma sārathiṃ pakkosāpetvā “sve pātova avamaṅgalarathena kumāraṃ nīharitvā āmakasusāne bhūmiyaṃ nikhaṇitvā pathavivaḍḍhanakakammaṃ katvā ehī”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā devī “tāta, kāsirājā taṃ sve āmakasusāne nikhaṇituṃ āṇāpesi. Sve maraṇaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti āha.

Having had her son adorned, she had a drum beaten through the city, proclaiming: 'This kingdom belongs to Prince Temiya!' She had the city decorated, had her son mounted on the back of an elephant, had a white parasol held over his head, and after he had been paraded around the city, she had him laid down on a beautifully adorned royal couch. All night long she pleaded: 'Dear Temiya, on your account for sixteen years I have not slept. My eyes are swollen from weeping, and my heart feels as if it is breaking with grief. I know that you are not a cripple or mute. Do not make me helpless!' In this way she pleaded for six days. On the sixth day, the king summoned a charioteer named Sunanda and said: 'Tomorrow at dawn, take the prince out in an inauspicious chariot, bury him in the charnel ground for raw corpses, perform the rite of leveling the earth, and come back.'
