Hearing this, the queen said: 'Dear one, the king of Kāsi has ordered you to be buried in the charnel ground tomorrow. Tomorrow you will meet your death.'

Mahāsatto taṃ sutvā “temiya, soḷasa vassāni tayā kato vāyāmo matthakaṃ patto”ti haṭṭho udaggo ahosi. Mātuyā panassa hadayaṃ bhijjanākāraṃ viya ahosi. Atha tassā rattiyā accayena pātova sārathi rathaṃ ādāya dvāre ṭhapetvā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā “devi, mā mayhaṃ kujjhi, rañño āṇā”ti puttaṃ āliṅgitvā nipannaṃ deviṃ piṭṭhihatthena apanetvā kumāraṃ ukkhipitvā pāsādā otari. Devī uraṃ paharitvā mahāsaddena paridevitvā mahātale ohīyi.

Hearing this, the Great Being was happy and elated, thinking: 'Temiya, the effort you have made for sixteen years has reached its culmination.' But his mother’s heart was as if breaking. Then, at the end of that night, at dawn, the charioteer brought the chariot and placed it at the gate. He entered the royal chamber and said: 'Queen, do not be angry with me; it is the king’s command.' Pushing aside with the back of his hand the queen who lay embracing her son, he lifted up the prince and descended from the palace. The queen struck her breast, wailed loudly, and collapsed on the great floor.

Atha naṃ mahāsatto oloketvā “mayi akathente mātu soko balavā bhavissatī”ti kathetukāmo hutvāpi “sace kathessāmi soḷasa vassāni kato [P 0.0223] vāyāmo mogho bhavissati, akathento panāhaṃ attano ca mātāpitūnañca paccayo bhavissāmī”ti adhivāsesi. Sārathi “mahāsattaṃ rathaṃ āropetvā pacchimadvārābhimukhaṃ [M 0.0216] rathaṃ pesessāmī”ti pācīnadvārābhimukhaṃ pesesi. Ratho nagarā nikkhamitvā devatānubhāvena tiyojanaṭṭhānaṃ gato. Mahāsatto suṭṭhutaraṃ tuṭṭhacitto ahosi. Tattha vanaghaṭaṃ sārathissa āmakasusānaṃ viya upaṭṭhāsi. So “idaṃ ṭhānaṃ sundara”nti rathaṃ okkamāpetvā maggapasse ṭhapetvā rathā oruyha mahāsattassa ābharaṇabhaṇḍaṃ omuñcitvā bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā ṭhapetvā kudālaṃ ādāya avidūre āvāṭaṃ khaṇituṃ ārabhi. Tena vuttaṃ “nhāpetvā anulimpitvā”tiādi.

Then the Great Being, looking at her, thought: 'If I do not speak, my mother’s grief will become very strong.' Though he wished to speak, he endured, thinking: 'If I speak, the effort of sixteen years will be in vain. But by not speaking, I will become a support for myself and for my parents.' The charioteer thought, 'I will place the Great Being in the chariot and drive it toward the western gate,' but he drove it toward the eastern gate. The chariot left the city and, by the power of the devas, traveled a distance of three yojanas. The Great Being was extremely pleased. There, a forest thicket appeared to the charioteer like a charnel ground for raw corpses. Thinking, 'This place is suitable,' he stopped the chariot and placed it by the side of the road. Dismounting from the chariot, he removed the Great Being’s ornaments, made a bundle of them and set it aside, and taking a spade, he began to dig a pit nearby. Therefore it was said: 'Having bathed and anointed,' and so on.

Tattha nhāpetvāti soḷasahi gandhodakaghaṭehi nhāpetvā. Anulimpitvāti surabhivilepanena vilimpetvā. Veṭhetvā rājaveṭhananti kāsirājūnaṃ paveṇiyāgataṃ rājamakuṭaṃ sīse paṭimuñcitvā. Abhisiñcitvāti tasmiṃ rājakule rājābhisekaniyāmena abhisiñcitvā. Chattena kāresuṃ puraṃ padakkhiṇanti setacchattena dhāriyamānena maṃ nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ kāresuṃ.

Herein, 'having bathed' means having bathed him with sixteen pots of fragrant water. 'Having anointed' means having anointed him with fragrant unguent. 'Having wrapped with the royal head-wrap' means having placed on his head the royal crown that had come down through the lineage of the kings of Kāsi. 'Having consecrated' means having consecrated him according to the custom of royal consecration in that royal family. 'They had the city circumambulated under the parasol' means: they had me circumambulate the city while a white parasol was being held over me.

62. Sattāhaṃ dhārayitvānāti mayhaṃ mātu candādeviyā varalābhanavasena laddhaṃ sattāhaṃ mama setacchattaṃ [V 0.0203] dhārayitvā. Uggate ravimaṇḍaleti tato punadivase sūriyamaṇḍale uggatamatte avamaṅgalarathena maṃ nagarato nīharitvā bhūmiyaṃ nikhaṇanatthaṃ sārathi sunando vanamupagacchi.

62. 'Having held for seven days' means: having held the white parasol over me for the seven days obtained by means of the boon gained by my mother, Queen Candādevī. 'When the sun’s disk had risen' means: on the very next day, as soon as the sun’s disk had risen, the charioteer Sunanda took me out of the city in an inauspicious chariot and went to the forest for the purpose of burying me in the ground.

63. Sajjassanti sannaddho assaṃ, yuge yojitassaṃ me rathaṃ maggato ukkamāpanavasena ekokāse katvā. Hatthamuccitoti muccitahattho, rathapācanato muttahatthoti attho. Atha vā hatthamuccitoti hatthamutto mama hatthato muccitvāti attho. Kāsunti āvāṭaṃ. Nikhātunti nikhaṇituṃ.

63. 'A ready horse' means a harnessed horse. 'And my yoked chariot' means: having placed my chariot aside in one spot by having it moved off the road. 'Hand-released' means one whose hand is released, that is, one whose hand is free from the chariot-goad. Or else, 'hand-released' means the rein has been released, having slipped from my hand. 'A pit' means a hole. 'To bury' means to dig.

64-5. Idāni yadatthaṃ mayā soḷasa vassāni mūgavatādiadhiṭṭhānena dukkaracariyā [P 0.0224] adhiṭṭhitā, taṃ dassetuṃ “adhiṭṭhitamadhiṭṭhāna”nti gāthādvayamāha.

64–65. Now, to show for what purpose he undertook the difficult practice for sixteen years with the resolution to act like a mute and so on, he spoke the two verses beginning: 'The resolution was resolved upon.'

Tattha tajjento vividhakāraṇāti dvimāsikakālato paṭṭhāya yāva soḷasasaṃvaccharā thaññapaṭisedhanādīhi vividhehi nānappakārehi kāraṇehi tajjayanto bhayaviddhaṃsanavasena viheṭhiyamāno. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Herein, 'threatening with various reasons' means: being harassed from the time he was two months old up to his sixteenth year; being threatened with various and diverse reasons, such as the denial of breast milk, in order to shatter his composure. The rest is easily understood.

Atha [M 0.0217] mahāsatto sunande kāsuṃ khaṇante “ayaṃ me vāyāmakālo”ti uṭṭhāya attano hatthapāde sambāhitvā rathā otarituṃ me balaṃ atthīti ñatvā cittaṃ uppādesi. Tāvadevassa pādapatiṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ vātapuṇṇabhastacammaṃ viya uggantvā rathassa pacchimantaṃ āhacca aṭṭhāsi. So otaritvā katipaye vāre aparāparaṃ caṅkamitvā “yojanasatampi gantuṃ me balaṃ atthī”ti ñatvā rathaṃ pacchimante gahetvā kumārakānaṃ kīḷanayānakaṃ viya ukkhipitvā “sace sārathi mayā saddhiṃ paṭivirujjheyya, atthi me paṭivirujjhituṃ bala”nti sallakkhetvā pasādhanatthāya cittaṃ uppādesi. Taṅkhaṇaññeva sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā vissakammaṃ āṇāpesi – “gaccha kāsirājaputtaṃ alaṅkarohī”ti. So “sādhū”ti vatvā dibbehi ca mānusehi ca alaṅkārehi sakkaṃ viya taṃ alaṅkari. So devarājalīḷāya sārathissa khaṇanokāsaṃ gantvā āvāṭatīre ṭhatvā –

Then, while Sunanda was digging the pit, the Great Being thought, 'This is the time for my effort.' Rising up, he massaged his own hands and feet, and knowing he had the strength to get down from the chariot, he made a resolve. At that very moment, the place where his feet rested swelled up like a leather bellows full of wind and stood firm, striking the rear of the chariot. Having descended, he paced back and forth a few times. Realizing, 'I have the strength to go even a hundred yojanas,' he took the chariot by its rear end and lifted it up like a prince's toy cart. Reflecting, 'If the charioteer should oppose me, I have the strength to oppose him,' he made a resolve to be adorned. At that instant, Sakka’s abode showed a sign of heat. Sakka, understanding the reason, commanded Vissakamma: 'Go, adorn the prince of Kāsi.' Saying, 'Very well,' Vissakamma adorned him with divine and human ornaments so that he resembled Sakka himself. Then, with the majesty of the king of the devas, he went to the place where the charioteer was digging and stood on the edge of the pit:

“Kinnu santaramānova, kāsuṃ khaṇasi sārathi;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃ kāsuyā karissasī”ti. (jā. 2.22.3) –

“Why, O charioteer, do you dig this pit in such a hurry? I ask you, my friend, please tell me: what will you do with this pit?”

Āha.

He said:

Tena [V 0.0204] uddhaṃ anoloketvāva –

The charioteer, without even looking up, replied:

“Rañño mūgo ca pakkho ca, putto jāto acetaso;

Somhi raññā samajjhiṭṭho, puttaṃ me nikhaṇaṃ vane”ti. (jā. 2.22.4) –

“The king has a son who was born mute, crippled, and witless. I have been instructed by the king: ‘Bury my son in the forest.’”

Vutte mahāsatto –

When this was said, the Great Being replied:

“Na [P 0.0225] badhiro na mūgosmi, na pakkho na ca vīkalo;

Adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā, maṃ ce tvaṃ nikhaṇaṃ vane.

“I am not deaf, nor am I mute; I am not crippled or deformed. O charioteer, you would be doing an unrighteous deed if you were to bury me in this forest.

“Ūrū bāhuñca me passa, bhāsitañca suṇohi me;

Adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā, maṃ ce tvaṃ nikhaṇaṃ vane”ti. (jā. 2.22.5-6) –

“Behold my thighs and my arms, and listen to my speech. O charioteer, you would be doing an unrighteous deed if you were to bury me in this forest.”

Vatvā puna tena āvāṭakhaṇanaṃ pahāya uddhaṃ oloketvā tassa rūpasampattiṃ disvā “manusso vā devo vā”ti ajānantena –

When this was said, the charioteer stopped digging the pit. Looking up and seeing the perfection of his form, not knowing whether he was a human or a deva, he asked:

“Devatā nusi gandhabbo, adu sakko purindado;

Ko vā tvaṃ kassa vā putto, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ maya”nti. (jā. 2.22.7) –

“Are you a deva, or a gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka, the Giver to the city? Who are you, and whose son? How are we to know you?”

Vutte –

To this, he replied:

“Namhi [M 0.0218] devo na gandhabbo, nāpi sakko purindado;

Kāsirañño ahaṃ putto, yaṃ kāsuyā nikhaññasi.

“I am not a deva, nor a gandhabba, nor am I Sakka Purindada. I am the son of the king of Kāsi, the one whom you are about to bury in a pit.

“Tassa rañño ahaṃ putto, yaṃ tvaṃ sammūpajīvasi;

Adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā, maṃ ce tvaṃ nikhaṇaṃ vane.

“I am the son of that king whom you serve for your living. O charioteer, you would be doing an unrighteous deed if you were to bury me in this forest.

“Yassa [V 0.0205] rukkhassa chāyāya, nisīdeyya sayeyya vā;

Na tassa sākhaṃ bhañjeyya, mittadubbho hi pāpako.

“Of the tree in whose shade one might sit or lie, one should not break off a branch, for a betrayer of a friend is an evil person.”

“Yathā rukkho tathā rājā, yathā sākhā tathā ahaṃ;

Yathā chāyūpago poso, evaṃ tvamasi sārathi;

Adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā, maṃ ce tvaṃ nikhaṇaṃ vane”ti. (jā. 2.22.8-11) –

“As the tree, so the king; as the branch, so am I; as a person who resorts to it for shade, so are you, charioteer. You would be acting unrighteously, charioteer, if you were to bury me in the forest.”

Ādinā nayena dhammaṃ desetvā tena nivattanatthaṃ yācito anivattanakāraṇaṃ pabbajjāchandaṃ tassa ca hetu nirayabhayādikaṃ atītabhave attano pavattiṃ vitthārena kathetvā tāya dhammakathāya tāya ca paṭipattiyā tasmimpi pabbajitukāme jāte rañño imaṃ –

Having taught the Dhamma in this way, when he was requested by the king to turn back, he explained his reason for not turning back: his aspiration to go forth and its cause—the fear of hell and the like. He recounted in detail his own conduct in a past existence. Through that Dhamma talk and that practice, the king too became desirous of going forth. He then said this to the king:

“Rathaṃ niyyātayitvāna, anaṇo ehi sārathi;

Anaṇassa hi pabbajjā, etaṃ isīhi vaṇṇita”nti. (jā. 2.22.44) –

“Having returned the chariot, charioteer, come back free from debt. For going forth is for one who is debt-free; this has been praised by the seers.”

Vatvā taṃ vissajjesi.

Having said this, he dismissed him.

So rathaṃ ābharaṇāni ca gahetvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Rājā tāvadeva “mahāsattassa santikaṃ [P 0.0226] gamissāmī”ti nagarato niggacchi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya itthāgārehi nāgarajānapadehi ca. Mahāsattopi kho sārathiṃ uyyojetvā pabbajitukāmo jāto. Tassa cittaṃ ñatvā sakko vissakammaṃ pesesi – “temiyapaṇḍito pabbajitukāmo, tassa assamapadaṃ pabbajitaparikkhāre ca māpehī”ti. So gantvā tiyojanike vanasaṇḍe assamaṃ māpetvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānacaṅkamanapokkharaṇīphalarukkhasampannaṃ katvā sabbe ca pabbajitaparikkhāre māpetvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Bodhisatto taṃ disvā sakkadattiyabhāvaṃ ñatvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā vatthāni apanetvā tāpasavesaṃ [M 0.0219] gahetvā kaṭṭhatthare nisinno aṭṭha samāpattiyo, pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattetvā pabbajjāsukhena assame nisīdi.

Taking the chariot and the ornaments, he went to the king and informed him of the matter. The king immediately thought, “I will go to the Great Being,” and left the city with his fourfold army, together with the women of the harem and the people of the town and countryside. The Great Being, for his part, having dismissed the charioteer, became desirous of going forth. Knowing his mind, Sakka sent Vissakamma, saying, “Temiya the Wise wishes to go forth; create a hermitage and the requisites of a renunciant for him.” He went and built a hermitage in a three-yojana forest grove, complete with places for resting by day and night, a walking path, a pond, and fruit trees. Having created all the requisites of a renunciant, he returned to his own abode. The Bodhisatta, seeing this and recognizing it as a gift from Sakka, entered the leaf-hut, removed his garments, adopted the guise of an ascetic, and sat on a bed of sticks. Having produced the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges, he dwelled in the hermitage in the bliss of renunciation.

Kāsirājāpi sārathinā dassitamaggena gantvā assamaṃ pavisitvā mahāsattena saha samāgantvā katapaṭisanthāro rajjena nimantesi. Temiyapaṇḍito taṃ paṭikkhipitvā anekākāravokāraṃ [V 0.0206] aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttāya ca kāmādīnavapaṭisaṃyuttāya ca dhammiyā kathāya rājānaṃ saṃvejesi. So saṃviggamānaso gharāvāse ukkaṇṭhito pabbajitukāmo hutvā amacce itthāgāre ca pucchi. Tepi pabbajitukāmā ahesuṃ. Atha rājā candādeviṃ ādiṃ katvā soḷasa sahasse orodhe ca amaccādike ca pabbajitukāme ñatvā nagare bheriṃ carāpesi – “ye mama puttassa santike pabbajitukāmā, te pabbajantū”ti. Suvaṇṇakoṭṭhāgārādīni ca vivarāpetvā vissajjāpesi. Nāgarā ca yathāpasāriteyeva āpaṇe vivaṭadvārāneva gehāni ca pahāya rañño santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Rājā mahājanena saddhiṃ mahāsattassa santike pabbaji. Sakkadattiyaṃ tiyojanikaṃ assamapadaṃ paripūri.

The king of Kāsi, following the path shown by the charioteer, entered the hermitage and met with the Great Being. After exchanging friendly greetings, he invited him to accept the kingdom. The wise Temiya declined and instead stirred the king with a Dhamma talk on the numerous drawbacks and dangers of sensual pleasures and on impermanence and the like. Deeply moved, the king grew disenchanted with household life and desired to go forth. He consulted his ministers and the women of his harem, and they too wished to go forth. Then the king, knowing that Queen Candādevī to begin with, the sixteen thousand women of the harem, and his ministers and others wished to go forth, had a proclamation by drum made throughout the city: “Let all who wish to go forth in the presence of my son do so!” He also had the treasuries, including the gold storehouses, opened and their contents given away. The townspeople, leaving their shops just as they were and their homes with doors wide open, went to the king. The king, along with the great multitude, went forth in the presence of the Great Being. The three-yojana hermitage site, a gift of Sakka, was filled to capacity.

Sāmantarājāno “kāsirājā pabbajito”ti sutvā “bārāṇasirajjaṃ gahessāmā”ti nagaraṃ pavisitvā devanagarasadisaṃ nagaraṃ sattaratanabharitaṃ devavimānakappaṃ rājanivesanañca disvā “imaṃ dhanaṃ nissāya bhayena bhavitabba”nti tāvadeva nikkhamitvā pāyāsuṃ. Tesaṃ āgamanaṃ sutvā mahāsatto vanantaṃ gantvā ākāse nisīditvā [P 0.0227] dhammaṃ desesi. Te sabbe saddhiṃ parisāya tassa santike pabbajiṃsu. Evaṃ aparepi aparepīti mahāsamāgamo ahosi. Sabbe phalāphalāni paribhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti. Yo kāmādivitakkaṃ vitakketi, tassa cittaṃ ñatvā mahāsatto tattha gantvā ākāse nisīditvā dhammaṃ deseti.

The neighboring kings, hearing, “The king of Kāsi has gone forth,” thought, “We will seize the kingdom of Bārāṇasī,” and entered the city. But seeing the city like a city of the gods, filled with the seven kinds of gems, and the royal palace like a celestial mansion, they thought, “Because of this wealth, there must be fear,” and they immediately left and departed. Hearing of their arrival, the Great Being went to the edge of the forest, sat in the air, and taught the Dhamma. All of them, along with their retinues, went forth in his presence. Thus others, and still others, came, and a great assembly gathered. All of them, subsisting on fruits, fulfilled the duties of recluses. If anyone entertained a thought of sensual desire or the like, the Great Being, knowing their mind, would go there, sit in the air, and teach them the Dhamma.

So dhammassavanasappāyaṃ labhitvā samāpattiyo abhiññāyo ca nibbatteti. Evaṃ aparopi aparopīti sabbepi jīvitapariyosāne brahmalokaparāyanā ahesuṃ. Tiracchānagatāpi mahāsatte isigaṇepi cittaṃ pasādetvā chasu kāmasaggesu nibbattiṃsu. Mahāsattassa brahmacariyaṃ ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ pavattittha. Tadā chatte adhivatthā devatā uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, sārathi sāriputtatthero, mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni, parisā buddhaparisā, temiyapaṇḍito lokanātho.

That person, having obtained the benefit of hearing the Dhamma, developed the meditative attainments and the higher knowledges. Thus one after another, all of them, at the end of their lives, were destined for the Brahma-world. Even animals, having gained confidence in the Great Being and the host of seers, were reborn in the six sensual heavens. The Great Being’s holy life continued for a very long time. At that time, the deity dwelling in the parasol was Uppalavaṇṇā, the charioteer was the Elder Sāriputta, the parents were members of the great royal families, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Temiya the Wise was the Lord of the World.

Tassa [M 0.0220] adhiṭṭhānapāramī idha matthakaṃ pattā, sesapāramiyopi yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbā. Tathā māsajātakālato paṭṭhāya nirayabhayaṃ pāpabhīrutā rajjajigucchā nekkhammanimittaṃ mūgādibhāvādhiṭṭhānaṃ tattha ca virodhippaccayasamodhānepi niccalabhāvoti evamādayo guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Here his perfection of determination reached its culmination; the remaining perfections should be identified as appropriate. Likewise, the power of his virtues should be explained, such as: from the time he was one month old, his fear of hell, his dread of evil, his repugnance for kingship, the sign of renunciation, his determination to be mute and so on, and his unshakeable nature even when confronted with opposing conditions.

Temiyacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the conduct of Temiya.

Adhiṭṭhānapāramī niṭṭhitā.

The Perfection of Determination is finished.

7. Kapirājacariyāvaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Conduct of the Monkey King

67. Sattame [V 0.0207] yadā ahaṃ kapi āsinti yasmiṃ kāle ahaṃ kapiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vuddhimanvāya nāgabalo thāmasampanno assapotakappamāṇo mahāsarīro kapi homi. Nadīkūle darīsayeti ekissā nadiyā tīre ekasmiṃ darībhāge yadā vāsaṃ kappemīti attho.

67. In the seventh account: When I was a monkey. This means at the time when I was born in the monkey womb and, having grown up, I was a monkey possessing the strength of an elephant, endowed with stamina, about the size of a colt, and with a large body. On a riverbank, in a mountain cleft. This means: when I made my dwelling on the bank of a river in a part of a mountain cleft.

Tadā kira bodhisatto yūthapariharaṇaṃ akatvā ekacaro hutvā vihāsi. Tassā pana nadiyā vemajjhe eko dīpako nānappakārehi ambapanasādīhi phalarukkhehi sampanno. Bodhisatto [P 0.0228] thāmajavasampannatāya nadiyā orimatīrato uppatitvā dīpakassa pana nadiyā ca majjhe eko piṭṭhipāsāṇo atthi, tasmiṃ patati. Tato uppatitvā tasmiṃ dīpake patati. So tattha nānappakārāni phalāphalāni khāditvā sāyaṃ teneva upāyena paccāgantvā attano vasanaṭṭhāne vasitvā punadivasepi tatheva karoti. Iminā niyāmena vāsaṃ kappesi.

At that time, it is said, the Bodhisatta lived as a solitary wanderer, not leading a troop. In the middle of that river was an island endowed with various kinds of fruit trees such as mango and jackfruit. The Bodhisatta, being endowed with strength and speed, would leap from the near bank of the river and land on a flat rock that was midway between the bank and the island. Leaping from there, he would land on that island. Having eaten various kinds of fruits there, in the evening he would return by the same means, dwell in his own living place, and on the next day do the same. In this way he made his dwelling.

Tasmiṃ pana kāle eko kumbhīlo sapajāpatiko tassaṃ nadiyaṃ vasati. Tassa bhariyā bodhisattaṃ aparāparaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā tassa hadayamaṃse dohaḷaṃ uppādetvā kumbhīlaṃ āha – “mayhaṃ kho, ayyaputta, imassa vānarassa hadayamaṃse dohaḷo uppanno”ti. So “sādhu, bhadde, lacchasī”ti vatvā “ajja taṃ sāyaṃ dīpakato āgacchantameva gaṇhissāmī”ti gantvā piṭṭhipāsāṇe nipajji. Bodhisatto taṃ divasaṃ gocaraṃ caritvā [M 0.0221] sāyanhasamaye dīpake ṭhitova pāsāṇaṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ pāsāṇo idāni uccataro khāyati, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti cintesi. Mahāsattassa hi udakappamāṇañca pāsāṇappamāṇañca suvavatthāpitameva hoti. Tenassa etadahosi – “ajja imissā nadiyā udakaṃ neva hāyati, atha ca panāyaṃ pāsāṇo mahā hutvā paññāyati, kacci nu kho ettha mayhaṃ gahaṇatthāya kumbhīlo nipanno”ti?

Now at that time, a crocodile and his mate lived in that river. Seeing the Bodhisatta going back and forth, his wife conceived a craving for his heart-flesh and said to the crocodile: “Noble husband, a craving has arisen in me for this monkey’s heart-flesh.” He said: “Good, my dear, you shall get it.” And thinking, “Today I will seize him in the evening as he is coming from the island,” he went and lay on the flat rock. The Bodhisatta, having roamed for food that day, stood on the island in the evening and looked at the rock. He thought: “This rock appears higher now. What could be the reason?” For the Great Being had the measure of the water and the measure of the rock well established. Therefore it occurred to him: “Today the water in this river has not gone down, and yet this rock appears large. Could it be that a crocodile is lying here in order to catch me?”

So “vīmaṃsissāmi tāva na”nti tattheva ṭhatvā pāsāṇena saddhiṃ kathento viya “bho, pāsāṇā”ti vatvā paṭivacanaṃ alabhanto yāvatatiyaṃ “bho, pāsāṇā”ti āha. Pāsāṇo paṭivacanaṃ na deti. Punapi bodhisatto “kiṃ, bho pāsāṇa, ajja mayhaṃ paṭivacanaṃ na desī”ti [P 0.0229] āha. Kumbhīlo “addhā ayaṃ pāsāṇo aññesu divasesu vānarindassa paṭivacanaṃ deti maññe, ajja pana mayā ottharitattā na deti, handāhaṃ dassāmissa paṭivacana”nti cintetvā “kiṃ vānarindā”ti āha. “Kosi tva”nti? “Ahaṃ kumbhīlo”ti[V 0.0208]. “Kimatthaṃ ettha nipannosī”ti? “Tava hadayaṃ patthayamāno”ti. Bodhisatto cintesi – “añño me gamanamaggo natthi, paṭiruddhaṃ vata me gamana”nti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Thinking, “First I will investigate it,” he stood right there and, as if conversing with the rock, he said, “O rock!” Not receiving a reply, he said, “O rock!” a second and a third time. The rock gave no answer. Again the Bodhisatta said: “Why, O rock, do you not give me an answer today?” The crocodile thought: “Surely this rock must give a reply to the king of the monkeys on other days, but today it does not because it is covered by me. Well now, I will give him a reply.” So he said: “What is it, king of the monkeys?” “Who are you?” “I am a crocodile.” “For what reason are you lying here?” “Desiring your heart.” The Bodhisatta thought: “There is no other path for me to take. Alas, my way is blocked!” Therefore it was said:

“Pīḷito susumārena, gamanaṃ na labhāmahaṃ”.

“Afflicted by the crocodile, I cannot find a way to go.”

68.

68.

“Yamhokāse ahaṃ ṭhatvā, orā pāraṃ patāmahaṃ;

Tatthacchi sattuvadhako, kumbhīlo luddadassano”ti.

“From the place where I stand and leap from the near to the far shore, there sits the murderous enemy, the crocodile of cruel appearance.”

Tattha “pīḷito susumārenā”ti addhagāthāya vuttamevatthaṃ. “Yamhokāse”ti gāthāya pākaṭaṃ karoti. Tattha yamhokāseti yasmiṃ nadīmajjhe ṭhitapiṭṭhipāsāṇasaṅkhāte padese ṭhatvā. Orāti dīpakasaṅkhātā oratīrā. Pāranti tadā mama vasanaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ nadiyā paratīraṃ. Patāmahanti uppatitvā patāmi ahaṃ. Tatthacchīti tasmiṃ piṭṭhipāsāṇappadese sattubhūto vadhako ekanteneva ghātako paccatthiko luddadassano ghorarūpo bhayānakadassano nisīdi.

Here, the meaning of the half-verse 'Afflicted by the crocodile' is just what was said. He makes it clear with the verse beginning 'From the place where.' Therein, 'from the place where' means: having stood in the spot in the middle of the river known as the flat-backed rock. 'The near shore' is the near shore designated as the island. 'The far shore' is the far shore of the river, which was then my dwelling place. 'I leap' means: having leapt up, I land. 'There sits' means: in that place on the flat-backed rock sat the one who had become an enemy, a slayer, a definite murderer, an adversary, of cruel appearance, of frightful form, of terrifying appearance.

Atha mahāsatto cintesi – “añño me gamanamaggo natthi, ajja mayā kumbhīlo vañcetabbo, evañhi ayañca mahatā pāpato mayā parimocito siyā, mayhañca jīvitaṃ laddha”nti. So kumbhīlaṃ āha – “samma, kumbhīla, ahaṃ tuyhaṃ upari patissāmī”ti. Kumbhīlo [M 0.0222] “vānarinda, papañcaṃ akatvā ito āgacchāhī”ti āha. Mahāsatto “ahaṃ āgacchāmi, tvaṃ pana attano mukhaṃ vivaritvā maṃ tava santikaṃ āgatakāle gaṇhāhī”ti avoca. Kumbhīlānañca mukhe vivaṭe akkhīni nimmīlanti. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ asallakkhento mukhaṃ vivari. Athassa akkhīni nimmīliṃsu. So mukhaṃ vivaritvā [P 0.0230] sabbaso nimmīlitakkhī hutvā nipajji. Mahāsatto tassa tathābhāvaṃ ñatvā dīpakato uppatito gantvā kumbhīlassa matthakaṃ akkamitvā tato uppatanto vijjulatā viya vijjotamāno paratīre aṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then the Great Being thought: 'There is no other path for me to take. Today I must deceive the crocodile. For in this way he might be freed by me from a great evil, and my own life would be obtained.' So he said to the crocodile: 'Friend crocodile, I will fall upon you.' The crocodile said: 'King of the monkeys, come here without making a diversion.' The Great Being said: 'I am coming. But you, open your mouth and catch me when I come into your presence.' Now, when crocodiles open their mouths, their eyes close. He, not noticing this fact, opened his mouth. Then his eyes closed. Having opened his mouth, he lay down with his eyes completely closed. The Great Being, knowing his state, leapt up from the island, went and trod on the crocodile’s head, and then, leaping from there, he stood on the far shore, flashing like a streak of lightning. Therefore it was said:

69.

69.

“So maṃ asaṃsi ehīti, ahampemīti taṃ vadiṃ;

Tassa matthakamakkamma, parakūle patiṭṭhahi”nti.

“He told me, ‘Come!’ and I told him, ‘I am coming!’ Having trodden upon his head, I stood firm on the far shore.”

Tattha asaṃsīti abhāsi. Ahampemīti ahampi āgacchāmīti taṃ kathesiṃ.

Therein, `asaṃsi` means he spoke. `Ahampemi` means: 'I too am coming,' thus I said to him.

Yasmā [V 0.0209] pana taṃ dīpakaṃ ambajambupanasādiphalarukkhasaṇḍamaṇḍitaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ nivāsayoggañca, “āgacchāmī”ti pana paṭiññāya dinnattā saccaṃ anurakkhanto mahāsattopi “āgamissāmevā”ti tathā akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

And because that island was adorned with groves of fruit trees such as mango, rose-apple, and jackfruit, and was delightful and fit for dwelling, and because a promise, 'I am coming,' had been given, the Great Being, protecting the truth, acted thus, thinking, 'I will indeed come.' Therefore it was said:

70.

70.

“Na tassa alikaṃ bhaṇitaṃ, yathā vācaṃ akāsaha”nti.

“No falsehood was spoken by me; as I spoke, so I did.”

Yasmā cetaṃ saccānurakkhaṇaṃ attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā kataṃ, tasmā āha –

And because this protection of truth was done by abandoning his own life, therefore he said:

“Saccena me samo natthi, esā me saccapāramī”ti.

“In truth there is no equal to me; this is my perfection of truth.”

Kumbhīlo pana taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā “iminā vānarindena atiaccherakaṃ kata”nti cintetvā “bho vānarinda, imasmiṃ loke catūhi dhammehi samannāgato puggalo amitte abhibhavati, te sabbepi tuyhaṃ abbhantare atthi maññe”ti āha –

Then the crocodile, seeing that marvel, thought, “This king of the monkeys has done something truly wonderful.” He then said, “O king of the monkeys, in this world a person endowed with four qualities overcomes his enemies. I think all of them are present within you.”

“Yassete caturo dhammā, vānarinda, yathā tava;

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, diṭṭhaṃ so ativattatī”ti. (jā. 1.2.147);

“One who has these four qualities, O king of the monkeys, just as you do—truth, wisdom, fortitude, and relinquishment—that one overcomes his enemy.” (Jā 1.2.147)

Tattha yassāti yassa kassaci puggalassa. Eteti idāni vattabbe paccakkhato dasseti. Caturo dhammāti cattāro guṇā. Saccanti vacīsaccaṃ, “mama [M 0.0223] santikaṃ āgamissāmī”ti vatvā musāvādaṃ akatvā āgato evāti etaṃ te vacīsaccaṃ. Dhammoti vicāraṇapaññā, “evaṃ kate idaṃ nāma bhavissatī”ti pavattā te esā vicāraṇapaññā. Dhitīti abbocchinnaṃ vīriyaṃ vuccati, etampi te atthi. Cāgoti attapariccāgo, tvaṃ attānaṃ pariccajitvā mama santikaṃ āgato, yaṃ panāhaṃ gaṇhituṃ nāsakkhiṃ, mayhamevesa doso[P 0.0231]. Diṭṭhanti paccāmittaṃ. So ativattatīti yassa puggalassa yathā tava evaṃ ete cattāro dhammā atthi, so yathā maṃ tvaṃ ajja atikkanto, tatheva attano paccāmittaṃ atikkamati abhibhavatīti.

Therein, `yassa` means: of any person. `Ete` (these) points directly to what is now to be said. `Caturo dhammā` means: four qualities. `Sacca` means truthfulness of speech; since you said, 'I will come into your presence,' and came without speaking falsely, this is your truthfulness of speech. `Dhamma` means investigative wisdom; that investigative wisdom of yours which proceeded by thinking, 'If this is done, such will be the result.' `Dhiti` is said to be uninterrupted energy; this too you have. `Cāga` is self-sacrifice; you sacrificed yourself and came into my presence, but that I was unable to catch you is my own fault. `Diṭṭhaṃ` means an adversary. `So ativattati` means: any person who has these four qualities as you do, just as you have overcome me today, so too does he overcome and vanquish his own adversary.

Evaṃ kumbhīlo bodhisattaṃ pasaṃsitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gato. Tadā kumbhīlo devadatto ahosi, tassa bhariyā ciñcamāṇavikā, kapirājā pana lokanātho.

Thus, having praised the Bodhisatta, the crocodile went to his dwelling place. At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, his wife was Ciñcamāṇavikā, and the monkey king was the Protector of the World.

Tassa [V 0.0210] idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā udakassa pāsāṇassa ca pamāṇavavatthānena idāni pāsāṇo uccataro khāyatīti pariggaṇhanavasena pāsāṇassa upari susumārassa nipannabhāvajānanaṃ, pāsāṇena kathanāpadesena tassatthassa nicchayagamanaṃ, susumārassa upari akkamitvā sahasā paratīre patiṭṭhānavasena sīghakāritāya tassa mahatā pāpato parimocanaṃ, attano jīvitarakkhaṇaṃ, saccavācānurakkhaṇañcāti evamādayo guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Here too the remaining perfections should be determined in the same way as explained below. Likewise, the following displays of the power of his virtues should be analyzed: his knowing that the crocodile was lying on the rock by way of grasping, 'the rock appears higher now,' through having established the measure of the water and the rock; his arriving at certainty about the matter under the pretext of speaking with the rock; and, by means of his swift action in stepping on the crocodile and suddenly establishing a footing on the far shore, his freeing of the crocodile from a great evil, the protection of his own life, and the protection of his truthful speech.

Kapirājacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Conduct of the Monkey King is finished.

8. Saccatāpasacariyāvaṇṇanā

8. The Exposition on the Conduct of the Ascetic of Truth

Aṭṭhame tāpaso saccasavhayoti saccasaddena avhātabbo saccanāmako tāpaso yadā yasmiṃ kāle homi, tadā. Saccena lokaṃ pālesinti attano avisaṃvādibhāvena sattalokaṃ jambudīpe tattha tattha sattanikāyaṃ pāpato nānāvidhā anatthato ca rakkhiṃ. Samaggaṃ janamakāsahanti tattha tattha kalahaviggahavivādāpannaṃ mahājanaṃ kalahe ādīnavaṃ dassetvā sāmaggiyaṃ ānisaṃsakathanena samaggaṃ avivadamānaṃ sammodamānaṃ ahamakāsiṃ.

In the eighth: 'an ascetic named Sacca.' This means: when, at which time, I was an ascetic to be addressed by the word 'Sacca,' that is, an ascetic named Sacca, then... 'By truth I protected the world' means: by my own truthfulness I protected the world of beings, the various communities of beings here and there in Jambudīpa, from evil and from various kinds of harm. 'I made the people harmonious' means: having shown the danger in quarreling and explained the benefit in harmony to the great populace who had fallen into quarrels, strife, and disputes here and there, I made them harmonious, not disputing, and rejoicing together.

Tadā [M 0.0224] hi bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ aññatarasmiṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbatti. Tassa “sacco”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā nacirasseva sabbasippānaṃ nipphattiṃ patto. Ācariyena anuññāto bārāṇasiṃ paccāgantvā mātāpitaro vanditvā tehi abhinandiyamāno tesaṃ cittānurakkhaṇatthaṃ [P 0.0232] katipāhaṃ tesaṃ santike vasi. Atha naṃ mātāpitaro patirūpena dārena saṃyojetukāmā sabbaṃ vibhavajātaṃ ācikkhitvā gharāvāsena nimantesuṃ.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a great brahmin family in Bārāṇasī. They gave him the name 'Sacca.' When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā and, having studied the arts under a world-renowned teacher, he soon attained mastery of all the arts. Having received his teacher’s permission, he returned to Bārāṇasī, paid homage to his parents, and, being welcomed by them, he stayed with them for a few days to gratify them. Then his parents, desiring to unite him with a suitable wife, pointed out all their accumulated wealth and invited him to the household life.

Mahāsatto nekkhammajjhāsayo attano nekkhammapāramiṃ paribrūhetukāmo gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ pabbajjāya ānisaṃsañca nānappakārato kathetvā mātāpitūnaṃ assumukhānaṃ rodamānānaṃ aparimāṇaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ anantaṃ yasaṃ mahantañca ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ pahāya mahānāgova ayasaṅkhalikaṃ gharabandhanaṃ chindanto nikkhamitvā himavantappadesaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vanamūlaphalāphalehi [V 0.0211] yāpento nacirasseva aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷayamāno samāpattivihārena viharati.

The Great Being, whose disposition was inclined to renunciation and who wished to fulfill his perfection of renunciation, explained in various ways to his weeping, tear-faced parents the danger in the household life and the benefit in the going forth. Having abandoned an immeasurable mass of wealth, endless fame, and a great circle of relatives, severing the bond of the household like a great elephant breaking an iron chain, he went forth. He entered the region of the Himalayas and undertook the going forth of a seer. Sustaining himself on roots and fruits of the forest, before long he produced the eight attainments and the five direct knowledges. He dwelt enjoying the sport of jhāna, abiding in the attainment.

So ekadivasaṃ dibbacakkhunā lokaṃ olokento addasa sakalajambudīpe manusse yebhuyyena pāṇātipātādidasaakusalakammapathapasute kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ aññamaññaṃ vivādāpanne. Disvā evaṃ cintesi – “na kho pana metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yadidaṃ ime satte evaṃ pāpapasute vivādāpanne ca disvā ajjhupekkhaṇaṃ. Ahañhi ‘satte saṃsārapaṅkato uddharitvā nibbānathale patiṭṭhapessāmī’ti mahāsambodhiyānaṃ paṭipanno, tasmā taṃ paṭiññaṃ avisaṃvādento yaṃnūnāhaṃ manussapathaṃ gantvā te te satte pāpato oramāpeyyaṃ, vivādañca nesaṃ vūpasameyya”nti.

One day, surveying the world with the divine eye, he saw that for the most part the people in the whole of Jambudīpa were intent on the ten unwholesome courses of action beginning with the destruction of life, and that, with sensual pleasures as the source and sensual pleasures as the cause, they had fallen into disputes with one another. Having seen this, he thought: 'It is not proper for me to look on with equanimity after seeing these beings so intent on evil and fallen into disputes. For I have entered upon the vehicle to great, perfect enlightenment with the resolve, "I will lift beings out of the mire of saṃsāra and establish them on the firm ground of Nibbāna." Therefore, being true to that promise, let me go to the world of humans, make those beings desist from evil, and pacify their disputes.'

Evaṃ pana cintetvā mahāsatto mahākaruṇāya samussāhito santaṃ samāpattisukhaṃ pahāya iddhiyā tattha tattha gantvā tesaṃ cittānukūlaṃ dhammaṃ desento kalahaviggahavivādāpanne satte diṭṭhadhammikañca samparāyikañca virodhe ādīnavaṃ dassetvā aññamaññaṃ samagge sahite akāsi. Anekākāravokārañca pāpe ādīnavaṃ vibhāvento tato satte vivecetvā ekacce dasasu kusalakammapathadhammesu patiṭṭhāpesi. Ekacce pabbājetvā [M 0.0225] sīlasaṃvare indriyaguttiyaṃ satisampajaññe pavivekavāse jhānābhiññāsu ca yathārahaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Having thus reflected, the Great Being, spurred on by great compassion, abandoned the bliss of serene attainment and, going here and there by psychic power, taught the Dhamma that was suitable to their minds. To beings who had fallen into quarrels, strife, and disputes, he showed the danger in conflict both in the present life and in future lives, and he made them harmonious and united with one another. Explaining the danger in evil in its many aspects and details, he separated beings from it and established some in the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action. Having given the going forth to others, he established them, as was fit, in moral restraint, restraint of the sense faculties, mindfulness and clear comprehension, a secluded dwelling, and in the jhānas and direct knowledges. Therefore it was said:

71.

71.

“Punāparaṃ [P 0.0233] yadā homi, tāpaso saccasavhayo;

Saccena lokaṃ pālesiṃ, samaggaṃ janamakāsaha”nti.

"Again, when I was an ascetic named Sacca, I protected the world with truth; I made the people harmonious."

Idhāpi mahāpurisassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā guṇānubhāvā ca vibhāvetabbāti.

Here too, the remaining perfections of the Great Man should be determined in the same way as stated above. Likewise, the majestic power of his virtues should be discerned.

Saccatāpasacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Conduct of the Ascetic Sacca is finished.

9. Vaṭṭapotakacariyāvaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition on the Conduct of the Quail Chick

72. Navame magadhe vaṭṭapotakotiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – magadharaṭṭhe aññatarasmiṃ araññappadese [V 0.0212] vaṭṭakayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā aciranikkhantatāya taruṇo maṃsapesibhūto, tato eva ajātapakkho vaṭṭakacchāpako yadā ahaṃ kulāvakeyeva homi.

72. In the ninth, in regard to the verse beginning 'A quail chick in Magadha,' this is the meaning in brief: In the country of Magadha, in a certain forest region, having been reborn as a quail and having broken the eggshell, being a tender lump of flesh because I had just emerged, and thus a quail chick with wings not yet grown—when I was still just in the nest.

73. Mukhatuṇḍakenāharitvāti mayhaṃ mātā attano mukhatuṇḍakena kālena kālaṃ gocaraṃ āharitvā maṃ poseti. Tassā phassena jīvāmīti parisedanatthañceva paribhāvanatthañca sammadeva kālena kālaṃ mamaṃ adhisayanavasena phusantiyā tassā mama mātuyā sarīrasamphassena jīvāmi viharāmi attabhāvaṃ pavattemi. Natthi me kāyikaṃ balanti mayhaṃ pana atitaruṇatāya kāyasannissitaṃ balaṃ natthi.

73. She nourishes me, having brought food with her beak: this means my mother brought food from time to time with her own beak and nourished me. I live by her touch: this means I live, I dwell, I maintain my existence through the bodily contact with my mother, who touches me properly from time to time by lying over me, both for the purpose of warming me and for cherishing me. I have no bodily strength: this means that because of my extreme youth, I have no strength based in the body.

74. Saṃvacchareti saṃvacchare saṃvacchare. Gimhasamayeti gimhakāle. Sukkharukkhasākhānaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭanasamuppannena agginā tasmiṃ padese davaḍāho padippati pajjalati, so tathā padīpito. Upagacchati amhākanti mayhaṃ mātāpitūnañcāti amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānappadesaṃ attano patiṭṭhānassa asuddhassāpi suddhabhāvakaraṇena pāvanato pāvakoti ca gatamagge indhanassa bhasmabhāvāvahanato kaṇhavattanīti ca laddhanāmo aggi vanarukkhagacche dahanto kālena kālaṃ upagacchati.

74. Yearly: means year after year. In the summer season: means in the summer time. A forest fire, produced by the friction of dry tree branches against one another, ignites and blazes in that region. Thus ignited, it approaches us: it approaches the region of our dwelling place, that is, of my mother, father, and me. The fire, which has received the names 'purifier' (pāvaka) because it purifies by making clean even its impure standing place, and 'black-pathed' (kaṇhavattanī) because it reduces the fuel on its path to ash, approaches from time to time, burning the trees and thickets of the forest.

75. Evaṃ [M 0.0226] upagamanato tadāpi saddāyantoti “dhamadhama”iti evaṃ saddaṃ karonto, anuravadassanañhetaṃ dāvaggino. Mahāsikhīti pabbatakūṭasadisānaṃ indhanānaṃ vasena mahatiyo [P 0.0234] sikhā etassāti mahāsikhī. Anupubbena anukkamena taṃ araññappadesaṃ jhāpento dahanto aggi mama samīpaṭṭhānaṃ upāgami.

75. Thus, as it approached, it was making a sound: making a sound like 'dhamadhama,' for this shows the roaring of a forest fire. Great-crested: it has great crests of flame on account of fuel resembling mountain peaks, thus it is 'great-crested' (mahāsikhī). Gradually: in sequence, the fire, burning and consuming that forest region, approached my vicinity.

76. Aggivegabhayāti vegena āgacchato aggino bhayena bhītā. Tasitāti cittutrāsasamuṭṭhitena kāyassa chambhitattena ca utrāsā. Mātāpitāti mātāpitaro. Attānaṃ parimocayunti agginā anupaddutaṭṭhānagamanena attano sotthibhāvamakaṃsu. Mahāsatto hi tadā mahāgeṇḍukappamāṇo mahāsarīro ahosi. Taṃ mātāpitaro kenaci upāyena gahetvā gantuṃ asakkuṇantā attasinehena ca abhibhuyyamānā puttasinehaṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyiṃsu.

76. Frightened by the fear of the fire's speed: frightened by the fear of the fire approaching with speed. Terrified: terrified because of the body's rigidity that arose from mental terror. Mother and father. They freed themselves: they made themselves safe by going to a place not afflicted by the fire. For the Great Being at that time was the size of a large ball and had a large body. His parents, unable to take him away by any means and being overwhelmed by self-love, abandoned their love for their son and fled.

77. Pāde pakkhe pajahāmīti attano ubho pāde ubho pakkhe ca bhūmiyaṃ ākāse ca gamanasajje karonto pasāremi iriyāmi vāyamāmi. “Paṭīhāmī”tipi pāṭho, vehāsagamanayogge kātuṃ īhāmīti attho. “Patīhāmī”tipi paṭhanti. Tassattho – pāde pakkhe ca [V 0.0213] pati visuṃ īhāmi, gamanatthaṃ vāyamāmi, taṃ pana vāyāmakaraṇatthameva. Kasmā? Yasmā natthi me kāyikaṃ balaṃ. Sohaṃ agatiko tatthāti so ahaṃ evaṃbhūto pādapakkhavekallena gamanavirahito mātāpitūnaṃ apagamanena vā appaṭisaraṇo, tattha dāvaggiupaddute vane, tasmiṃ vā kulāvake ṭhitova evaṃ idāni vattabbākārena tadā cintesiṃ. Dutiyañcettha ahanti nipātamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

77. I stretch out my feet and wings: I stretch out both my feet and both my wings, preparing them for movement on the ground and in the air; I move, I strive. There is also the reading paṭīhāmi, meaning 'I strive to make myself fit for travel in the sky.' They also read patīhāmi, which means: I strive separately with feet and wings, I exert myself for the sake of movement; but that exertion is merely for the sake of making the effort. Why? Because I have no bodily strength. Thus, I am helpless there: I, being such—deprived of movement due to the deficiency of my feet and wings, and without refuge after my parents' departure—stood there in that forest afflicted by the forest fire, or in that nest, and then reflected in the manner now to be described. And here the second 'I' (ahaṃ) should be seen as a mere particle.

78.

78.

Idāni tadā attano cintitākāraṃ dassetuṃ “yesāha”ntiādimāha;

Now, to show the nature of his own thought at that time, he spoke the verse beginning, "Those to whom I..."

Tattha yesāhaṃ upadhāveyyaṃ, bhīto tasitavedhitoti maraṇabhayena bhīto tato eva cittutrāsena tasito sarīrakampanena vedhito yesamahaṃ pakkhantaraṃ etarahi dāvaggiupadduto jaladuggaṃ viya maññamāno pavisituṃ upadhāveyyaṃ te mama mātāpitaro maṃ ekakaṃ eva ohāya jahitvā pakkantā. Kathaṃ me ajja kātaveti kathaṃ nu kho mayā ajja kātabbaṃ, paṭipajjitabbanti attho.

Therein, 'Those to whom I would run for refuge, frightened, terrified, and trembling': this means frightened by the fear of death, terrified by the mental agitation arising from that, and trembling with bodily shaking. Those to whom I, now afflicted by the forest fire, would run to enter their protection, regarding it as a stronghold of water—those parents of mine have departed, having left and abandoned me all alone. 'What should I do today?': the meaning is, 'What indeed should be done by me today? What course should be undertaken?'

Evaṃ [M 0.0227] mahāsatto itikattabbatāsammūḷho hutvā ṭhito puna cintesi – “imasmiṃ loke sīlaguṇo nāma atthi, saccaguṇo nāma atthi, atīte pāramiyo pūretvā bodhitale nisīditvā abhisambuddhā sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanasampannā saccānudayakāruññakhantisamannāgatā [P 0.0235] sabbasattesu samappavattamettābhāvanā sabbaññubuddhā nāma atthi, tehi ca paṭividdho ekantaniyyānaguṇo dhammo atthi, mayi cāpi ekaṃ saccaṃ atthi. Saṃvijjamāno eko sabhāvadhammo paññāyati, tasmā atītabuddhe ceva tehi paṭividdhaguṇe ca āvajjetvā mayi vijjamānaṃ saccaṃ sabhāvadhammaṃ gahetvā saccakiriyaṃ katvā aggiṃ paṭikkamāpetvā ajja mayā attano ceva idha vāsīnaṃ sesapāṇīnañca sotthibhāvaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Evaṃ pana cintetvā mahāsatto attano ānubhāve ṭhatvā yathācintitaṃ paṭipajji. Tena vuttaṃ –

Thus the Great Being, standing there bewildered as to what should be done, reflected again: 'In this world there exists the quality of moral virtue, there exists the quality of truth. In the past, having fulfilled the perfections and seated at the site of enlightenment, there have existed All-Knowing Buddhas—endowed with morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; possessed of truth, compassion, and patience; and who developed loving-kindness extending equally to all beings. And there exists the Dhamma penetrated by them, which possesses the quality of leading exclusively to deliverance. In me, too, there is a certain truth. A certain existing intrinsic principle is discernible. Therefore, by adverting to the past Buddhas and the qualities they penetrated, and by taking hold of the truth—the intrinsic principle existing in me—I will make an asseveration of truth. By this, having made the fire recede, it is fitting for me today to bring about the well-being of myself and of the other living beings dwelling here.' Having reflected thus, the Great Being, standing firm in his own power, acted as he had resolved. Hence it was said:

79.

79.

“Atthi loke sīlaguṇo, saccaṃ soceyyanuddayā;

Tena saccena kāhāmi, saccakiriyamuttamaṃ.

'In the world there is the quality of moral virtue, truth, purity, and compassion. By that truth, I will make a supreme asseveration of truth.'

80.

80.

“Āvajjetvā dhammabalaṃ, saritvā pubbake jine;

Saccabalamavassāya, saccakiriyamakāsaha”nti.

"Having adverted to the power of the Dhamma, recalling the former Conquerors, relying on the power of truth, I made an asseveration of truth."

81. Tattha [V 0.0214] mahāsatto atīte parinibbutānaṃ buddhānaṃ guṇe āvajjetvā attani vijjamānaṃ saccasabhāvaṃ ārabbha yaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā tadā saccakiriyamakāsi, taṃ dassetuṃ “santi pakkhā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

81. There, the Great Being, adverting to the qualities of the Buddhas who had attained final Nibbāna in the past and taking as his object the intrinsic nature of truth within himself, spoke a verse and then made an asseveration of truth. To show this, it is said: "There are wings," and so on.

Tattha santi pakkhā apatanāti mayhaṃ pakkhā nāma atthi upalabbhanti, no ca kho sakkā etehi uppatituṃ ākāsena gantunti apatanā. Santi pādā avañcanāti pādāpi me atthi, tehi pana vañcituṃ padavāragamanena gantuṃ na sakkāti avañcanā. Mātāpitā ca nikkhantāti ye maṃ aññattha neyyuṃ, tepi maraṇabhayena mama mātāpitaro nikkhantā. Jātavedāti aggiṃ ālapati. So hi jātova vediyati, dhūmajāluṭṭhānena paññāyati, tasmā “jātavedo”ti vuccati. Paṭikkamāti paṭigaccha nivattāti jātavedaṃ āṇāpeti.

Herein, There are wings, but they cannot fly means: I have wings, they exist, but it is not possible to fly up and go through the sky with them; thus 'they cannot fly.' There are feet, but they cannot walk means: I also have feet, but it is not possible to proceed with them, to go step by step; thus 'they cannot walk.' My mother and father have departed means: those who would have carried me elsewhere, my mother and father, have departed out of fear of death. Jātaveda: he addresses the fire. For it is known as soon as it is born, it is recognized by the rising smoke and flame; therefore it is called 'Jātaveda.' Retreat! means: 'Go back, turn away!'; thus he commands Jātaveda.

Iti [M 0.0228] mahāsatto “sace mayhaṃ pakkhānaṃ atthibhāvo, te ca pasāretvā ākāse apatanabhāvo, pādānaṃ atthibhāvo, te ca ukkhipitvā avañcanabhāvo, mātāpitūnaṃ maṃ kulāvakeyeva chaḍḍetvā palātabhāvo ca saccasabhāvabhūto [P 0.0236] eva, jātaveda, etena saccena tvaṃ ito paṭikkamā”ti kulāvake nipannova saccakiriyaṃ akāsi. Tassa saha saccakiriyāya soḷasakarīsamatte ṭhāne jātavedo paṭikkami. Paṭikkamanto ca na jhāyamānova araññaṃ gato, udake pana opilāpitaukkā viya tattheva nibbāyi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Thus the Great Being, while still lying in the nest, made an asseveration of truth: 'If the fact that I have wings, and that having spread them I cannot fly in the sky; the fact that I have feet, and that having lifted them I cannot walk; and the fact that my parents have abandoned me in the nest and fled—if these are indeed true in their intrinsic nature, then, O Jātaveda, by this truth, you retreat from here!' Simultaneously with his asseveration of truth, the fire retreated over a space of sixteen karīsas. As it retreated, it passed through the forest without burning it and was extinguished right there, like a firebrand plunged into water. Hence it was said:

82.

82.

“Saha sacce kate mayhaṃ, mahāpajjalito sikhī;

Vajjesi soḷasakarīsāni, udakaṃ patvā yathā sikhī”ti.

"'When I made my asseveration of truth, the great blazing fire avoided a space of sixteen karīsas, like a fire that has reached water.'"

Sā panesā bodhisattassa vaṭṭakayoniyaṃ tasmiṃ samaye buddhaguṇānaṃ āvajjanapubbikā saccakiriyā anaññasādhāraṇāti āha “saccena me samo natthi, esā me saccapāramī”ti. Teneva hi tassa ṭhānassa sakalepi imasmiṃ kappe agginā anabhibhavanīyattā taṃ kappaṭṭhiyapāṭihāriyaṃ nāma jātaṃ.

Now, this asseveration of truth of the Bodhisatta in the quail existence at that time, preceded by adverting to the qualities of the Buddhas, was unique. Thus he said: 'There is none equal to me in truth; this is my perfection of truth.' Indeed, because of that very circumstance, since that place could not be overcome by fire for this entire aeon, it came to be known as the 'aeon-lasting miracle'.

Evaṃ mahāsatto saccakiriyavasena attano tattha vāsīnaṃ sattānañca sotthiṃ katvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus the great being, by means of an asseveration of truth, secured the well-being of himself and the beings dwelling there, and at the end of his life, he passed on according to his kamma.

Tadā mātāpitaro etarahi mātāpitaro ahesuṃ, vaṭṭakarājā pana lokanātho.

The parents at that time were the parents of the present day; but the king of the quails was the Protector of the World.

Tassa [V 0.0215] heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sesapāramiyopi yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbā. Tathā dāvaggimhi tathā bheravākārena avattharitvā āgacchante tasmiṃ vaye ekako hutvāpi sāradaṃ anāpajjitvā saccādidhammaguṇe buddhaguṇe ca anussaritvā attano eva ānubhāvaṃ nissāya saccakiriyāya tattha vāsīnampi sattānaṃ sotthibhāvāpādanādayo ānubhāvā vibhāvetabbā.

His remaining perfections should also be determined appropriately in the way previously stated. Likewise, his powerful effects should be explained: how, in the forest fire that was advancing and overwhelming in such a terrifying manner, even though he was alone at that tender age, he did not become timid; and how, by recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma such as truth and the qualities of the Buddhas, and by relying on his own power, through an asseveration of truth he brought about such results as the well-being of the beings dwelling there.

Vaṭṭapotakacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Conduct of the Young Quail is finished.

10. Maccharājacariyāvaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Conduct of the Fish-King

83. Dasame [M 0.0229] yadā homi, maccharājā mahāsareti atīte macchayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā kosalaraṭṭhe sāvatthiyaṃ jetavane pokkharaṇiṭṭhāne [P 0.0237] valligahanaparikkhitte ekasmiṃ mahāsare macchānaṃ catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi rañjanato yadā ahaṃ rājā homi, macchagaṇaparivuto tattha paṭivasāmi tadā. Uṇheti uṇhakāle gimhasamaye. Sūriyasantāpeti ādiccasantāpena. Sare udaka khīyathāti tasmiṃ sare udakaṃ khīyittha chijjittha. Tasmiñhi raṭṭhe tadā devo na vassi, sassāni milāyiṃsu, vāpiādīsu udakaṃ parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ agamāsi, macchakacchapā kalalagahanaṃ pavisiṃsu. Tasmimpi sare macchā kaddamagahanaṃ pavisitvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne nilīyiṃsu.

83. In the tenth: When I was the fish-king in the great lake: in the past, having been reborn from a fish-womb in the country of Kosala, at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, in the place of a lotus pond surrounded by a thicket of creepers, in a certain great lake—when I was king there because I delighted the fish with the four bases of sympathy, I dwelt there surrounded by a shoal of fish. Hot means in the hot season, in summertime. Scorched by the sun means by the heat of the sun. The water in the lake dwindled means in that lake the water dwindled and was depleted. For in that country at that time the deva did not rain, the crops withered, and the water in reservoirs and so on went to exhaustion, to utter depletion; fish and turtles entered the muddy thicket. In that lake too, the fish entered the muddy thicket and hid in various places.

84. Tatoti tato udakaparikkhayato aparabhāge. Kulalasenakāti kulalāceva senā ca. Bhakkhayanti divārattiṃ, macche upanisīdiyāti tattha tattha kalalapiṭṭhe upanisīditvā kalalagahanaṃ pavisitvā nipanne macche kākā vā itare vā divā ceva rattiñca kaṇayaggasadisehi tuṇḍehi koṭṭetvā koṭṭetvā nīharitvā vipphandamāne bhakkhayanti.

84. Then: that is, afterwards, after the water was depleted. Kites and hawks: that is, kites and hawks. They devour them day and night, settling near: having settled on the mudflats here and there, crows or other birds of prey devour by day and by night the wriggling fish that are lying in the muddy thicket, pecking at them again and again with beaks like the points of darts and pulling them out.

85. Atha mahāsatto macchānaṃ taṃ byasanaṃ disvā mahākaruṇāya samussāhitahadayo “ṭhapetvā maṃ ime mama ñātake imasmā dukkhā mocetuṃ samattho nāma añño natthi, kena nu kho ahaṃ upāyena te ito dukkhato moceyya”nti cintento “yaṃnūnāhaṃ pubbakehi mahesīhi āciṇṇasamāciṇṇaṃ mayi ca saṃvijjamānaṃ saccadhammaṃ nissāya saccakiriyaṃ katvā devaṃ vassāpetvā mama ñātisaṅghassa jīvitadānaṃ dadeyyaṃ, tena ca sakalassāpi āhārūpajīvino sattalokassa mahāupakāro sampādito mayā”ti nicchayaṃ katvā devaṃ vassāpetuṃ saccakiriyaṃ akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “evaṃ cintesaha”ntiādi.

85. Then the Great Being, seeing that disaster of the fish, his heart stirred by great compassion, thought: 'Apart from me, there is no one else capable of freeing these kinsmen of mine from this suffering. By what means, I wonder, could I free them from this suffering?' Thinking thus, he made a determination: 'Let me now, relying on the true Dhamma—practiced and thoroughly practiced by the great seers of the past and existing in me—perform an act of truth, make the deva rain, and give the gift of life to my community of kinsmen. And by this, a great benefit will have been rendered by me to the entire world of beings that subsists on food.' Having made this determination, he performed an act of truth to make the deva rain. Therefore it was said: 'Thus I thought,' and so on.

Tattha [V 0.0216] saha ñātīhi pīḷitoti mayhaṃ ñātīhi saddhiṃ tena udakaparikkhayena pīḷito. Sahāti vā nipātamattaṃ. Mahākāruṇikatāya tena byasanena dukkhitehi ñātīhi kāraṇabhūtehi pīḷito, ñātisaṅghadukkhadukkhitoti attho.

Herein, afflicted together with my kinsfolk means: afflicted along with my kinsfolk by that depletion of water. Or, together is a mere particle. He was afflicted because of his great compassion for his kinsmen who were suffering from that disaster; the meaning is that he was afflicted by the suffering of the community of his kinsmen.

86. Dhammatthanti [M 0.0230] dhammabhūtaṃ atthaṃ, dhammato vā anapetaṃ atthaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Saccaṃ. Addasapassayanti mayhaṃ ñātīnañca apassayaṃ addasaṃ. Atikkhayanti mahāvināsaṃ.

86. A matter of Dhamma: a matter that is Dhamma itself, or a matter not deviating from Dhamma. What is that? Truth. I saw a refuge: I saw a refuge for myself and my kinsmen. Great destruction: great ruin.

87. Saddhammanti sataṃ sādhūnaṃ buddhādīnaṃ [P 0.0238] ekassāpi pāṇino ahiṃsanasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ. Anussaritvā. Paramatthaṃ vicintayanti taṃ kho pana paramatthaṃ saccaṃ aviparītasabhāvaṃ katvā cintayanto. Yaṃ loke dhuvasassatanti yadetaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ ekassāpi pāṇino ahiṃsanaṃ, taṃ sabbakālaṃ tathabhāvena dhuvaṃ sassataṃ vicintayaṃ saccakiriyaṃ akāsinti sambandho.

87. The true Dhamma: the Dhamma of the good and virtuous, such as the Buddhas and others, which is designated as the non-harming of even a single living being. Having recollected. Contemplating the ultimate meaning: contemplating that ultimate meaning, taking it as true and of an unperverted nature. What in the world is firm and eternal: contemplating that this non-harming of even a single living being by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples is always firm and eternal in its very nature, he performed an act of truth. This is the connection.

88. Idāni taṃ dhammaṃ mahāsatto attani vijjamānaṃ gahetvā saccavacanaṃ payojetukāmo kālavaṇṇaṃ kaddamaṃ dvidhā viyūhitvā añjanarukkhasāraghaṭikavaṇṇamahāsarīro sudhotalohitakamaṇisadisāni akkhīni ummīletvā ākāsaṃ ullokento “yato sarāmi attāna”nti gāthamāha.

88. Now the Great Being, wishing to utter a statement of truth by taking that Dhamma existing within himself, parted the black-colored mud in two. With his great body the color of a lump of the heartwood of the añjana tree, he opened his eyes, which were like well-washed red gems, and looking up at the sky, he spoke the verse beginning: 'Since I remember myself...'

Tattha yato sarāmi attānanti yato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ attānaṃ sarāmi anussarāmi. Yato pattosmi viññutanti yato paṭṭhāya tāsu tāsu itikattabbatāsu viññutaṃ vijānanabhāvaṃ pattosmi, uddhaṃ ārohanavasena ito yāva mayhaṃ kāyavacīkammānaṃ anussaraṇasamatthatā viññutappatti eva, etthantare samānajātikānaṃ khādanaṭṭhāne nibbattopi taṇḍulakaṇappamāṇampi macchaṃ mayā na khāditapubbaṃ, aññampi kañci pāṇaṃ sañcicca hiṃsitaṃ bādhitaṃ nābhijānāmi, pageva jīvitā voropitaṃ.

Herein, since I remember myself means: from the time I remember myself, designated as my individual existence. Since I attained understanding means: from the time I attained understanding—the state of knowing—in regard to various duties. From that time onwards, as far back as I am able to recollect my bodily and verbal actions—this is the attainment of understanding. During this entire interval, though born in a place where those of the same species are eaten, I do not recall ever having eaten a fish even the size of a broken grain of rice, nor do I know of having intentionally harmed or oppressed any other living being, much less of having deprived one of life.

89. Etena saccavajjenāti “yadetaṃ mayā kassaci pāṇassa ahiṃsanaṃ vuttaṃ, sace etaṃ saccaṃ tathaṃ aviparītaṃ, etena saccavacanena pajjunno megho abhivassatu, ñātisaṅghaṃ me dukkhā pamocetū”ti vatvā puna attano paricārikaceṭakaṃ āṇāpento viya pajjunnaṃ devarājānaṃ ālapanto “abhitthanayā”ti gāthamāha.

89. By this utterance of truth: 'If this that has been spoken by me—the non-harming of any living being—is true, factual, and not otherwise, then by this statement of truth let the cloud Pajjunna rain down and free my community of kinsmen from suffering.' Having spoken thus, then, addressing Pajjunna the deva-king as if commanding his own attendant servant, he spoke the verse beginning: 'Thunder forth!'

Tattha abhitthanaya pajjunnāti pajjunno vuccati megho, ayaṃ pana meghavasena laddhanāmaṃ vassavalāhakadevarājānaṃ [V 0.0217] ālapati. Ayaṃ hissa adhippāyo [M 0.0231] – devo nāma anabhitthanayanto vijjulatā anicchārento pavassantopi na sobhati, tasmā tvaṃ abhitthanayanto vijjulatā nicchārento vassāpehīti. Nidhiṃ kākassa nāsayāti kākā kalalaṃ pavisitvā ṭhite macche tuṇḍena koṭṭetvā nīharitvā khādanti[P 0.0239], tasmā tesaṃ antokalale macchā “nidhī”ti vuccanti. Taṃ kākasaṅghassa nidhiṃ devaṃ vassāpento udakena paṭicchādetvā nāsehi. Kākaṃ sokāya randhehīti kākasaṅgho imasmiṃ mahāsare udakena puṇṇe macche alabhamāno socissati, taṃ kākagaṇaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaddamaṃ pūrento sokāya randhehi, sokassatthāya pana vassāpayatha, yathā antonijjhānalakkhaṇaṃ sokaṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃ karohīti attho. Macche sokā pamocayāti mama ñātake sabbeva macche imamhā maraṇasokā pamocehi. “Mañca sokā pamocayā”ti (jā. 1.1.75) jātake paṭhanti. Tattha ca-kāro sampiṇḍanattho, mañca mama ñātake cāti sabbeva maraṇasokā pamocehi (jā. aṭṭha. 1.1.75). Macchānañhi anudakabhāvena paccatthikānaṃ ghāsabhāvaṃ gacchāmāti mahāmaraṇasoko, mahāsattassa pana tesaṃ anayabyasanaṃ paṭicca karuṇāyato karuṇāpatirūpamukhena sokasambhavo veditabbo.

Herein, Thunder forth, Pajjunna!: Pajjunna is said to be the cloud, but this one addresses the rain-cloud deva-king who has obtained his name on account of the cloud. This is his intention: a deva, indeed, does not look splendid if he rains without thundering and without flashing lightning. Therefore, you, thundering and flashing lightning, make it rain! Destroy the crow's treasure: crows enter the mud, peck with their beaks at the fish staying there, pull them out, and eat them. Therefore the fish inside the mud are called their 'treasure.' By causing rain to fall, cover that treasure of the flock of crows with water and destroy it. Deliver the crow to grief: when this great lake is filled with water, the flock of crows, not getting any fish, will grieve. You, by filling this mud, deliver that flock of crows to grief. That is, make it rain for the sake of their grief, so that they experience grief characterized by inner burning; do so—this is the meaning. Free the fish from grief: free all my kinsmen, the fish, from this grief of death. And free me from grief: so they recite in the Jātaka. Here the particle ca has a collective sense: 'me and my kinsmen,' meaning free all from the grief of death. For the fish, there is the great grief of death, thinking: 'Due to the lack of water, we are becoming food for our enemies.' For the Great Being, however, the arising of grief should be understood as a counterpart to compassion, which arises on account of their misfortune and disaster.

Evaṃ bodhisatto attano paricārikaceṭakaṃ āṇāpento viya pajjunnaṃ ālapitvā sakale kosalaraṭṭhe mahāvassaṃ vassāpesi. Mahāsattassa hi sīlatejena saccakiriyāya samakālameva sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So “kiṃ nu kho”ti āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā vassavalāhakadevarājānaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, mahāpuriso maccharājā ñātīnaṃ maraṇasokena vassāpanaṃ icchati, sakalaṃ kosalaraṭṭhaṃ ekameghaṃ katvā vassāpehī”ti āha.

Thus the Bodhisatta, addressing Pajjunna as if commanding his own attendant servant, caused a great rain to fall over the entire country of Kosala. For, by the power of the Great Being’s virtue, at the very same time as his act of truth, Sakka’s stone seat, the Paṇḍukambalasilā, showed a sign of heat. He, reflecting, 'What can this be?' and discerning the reason, had the rain-cloud deva-king summoned and said: 'My dear, the great being, the fish-king, desires rain because of his kinsmen's grief of death. Make it rain over the entire country of Kosala, making it a single cloud.'

So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā ekaṃ valāhakaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā meghagītaṃ gāyanto pācīnalokadhātuabhimukho pakkhandi. Pācīnadisābhāge khalamaṇḍalamattaṃ ekaṃ meghamaṇḍalaṃ uṭṭhāya satapaṭalaṃ sahassapaṭalaṃ hutvā abhitthanayantaṃ vijjulatā nicchārentaṃ adhomukhaṭhapitaudakakumbhākārena vissandamānaṃ sakalaṃ kosalaraṭṭhaṃ mahoghena [M 0.0232] ajjhotthari. Devo acchinnadhāraṃ vassanto muhutteneva taṃ mahāsaraṃ pūresi. Macchā maraṇabhayato mucciṃsu. Kākādayo [P 0.0240] apatiṭṭhā ahesuṃ. Na kevalaṃ macchā eva, manussāpi vividhasassāni sampādentā catuppadādayopīti sabbepi vassūpajīvino kāyikacetasikadukkhato mucciṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

He, assenting with 'Good!', put on one cloud as a lower garment, draped another over himself, and singing the cloud-song, he set out towards the eastern world-sphere. In the eastern quarter, a single cloud-mass the size of a threshing floor arose, became a hundred-layered, a thousand-layered cloud, and thundering, flashing lightning, and pouring down in the manner of an overturned water pot, it inundated the entire country of Kosala with a great flood. The deva, raining with an unbroken stream, filled that great lake in just a moment. The fish were freed from the fear of death. The crows and others were left without a foothold. Not only the fish, but also humans producing various crops, and quadrupeds and so on—all beings subsisting on rain were freed from bodily and mental suffering. Therefore it is said:

90.

90.

“Saha kate saccavare, pajjunno abhigajjiya;

Thalaṃ ninnañca pūrento, khaṇena abhivassathā”ti.

"As soon as the excellent statement of truth was made, Pajjunna thundered loudly; filling high ground and low, he rained down in an instant."

Tattha [V 0.0218] khaṇena abhivassathāti adandhāyitvā saccakiriyakhaṇeneva abhivassi.

Herein, he rained down in an instant means: he rained without delay, at the very moment of the act of truth.

91. Katvā vīriyamuttamanti deve avassante kiṃ kātabbanti kosajjaṃ anāpajjitvā ñātatthacariyāsampādanamukhena mahato sattanikāyassa hitasukhanipphādanaṃ uttamaṃ vīriyaṃ katvā. Saccatejabalassito mama saccānubhāvabalasannissito hutvā tadā mahāmeghaṃ vassāpesiṃ. Yasmā cetadevaṃ, tasmā “saccena me samo natthi, esā me saccapāramī”ti mahāmaccharājakāle attano saccapāramiyā anaññasādhāraṇabhāvaṃ dassesi dhammarājā.

91. “Having exerted supreme effort”: when the deva did not send rain, instead of succumbing to indolence, he exerted the highest effort by accomplishing the welfare of his kinsmen, thereby producing the welfare and happiness for a great host of beings. “Relying on the power of truth”: being supported by the power of my truth’s might, “I then caused the great cloud to rain.” Because this is so, the King of Dhamma declared, “There is none equal to me in truth, this is my perfection of truth,” thus showing the unique nature of his perfection of truth during the time of the great fish king.

Evaṃ mahāsatto mahākaruṇāya samussāhitahadayo sakalaraṭṭhe mahāvassaṃ vassāpanavasena mahājanaṃ maraṇadukkhato mocetvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus the Great Being, his heart stirred by great compassion, caused a great rain to fall over the entire country, thereby freeing the populace from the suffering of death. At the end of his life, he passed on according to his kamma.

Tadā pajjunno ānandatthero ahosi, macchagaṇā buddhaparisā, maccharājā lokanātho.

At that time, Pajjunna was the Venerable Ānanda, the shoal of fish was the Buddha’s assembly, and the fish king was the Protector of the World.

Tassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sesapāramiyopi niddhāretabbā. Tathā attano samānajātikānaṃ khādanaṭṭhāne macchayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā taṇḍulakaṇamattampi macchaṃ ādiṃ katvā kassacipi pāṇino akhādanaṃ, tiṭṭhatu khādanaṃ ekasattassapi aviheṭhanaṃ, tathā saccakaraṇena devassa vassāpanaṃ, udake parikkhīṇe kalalagahane nimujjanavasena attanā anubhavamānaṃ dukkhaṃ vīrabhāvena agaṇetvā ñātisaṅghasseva taṃ dukkhaṃ attano hadaye katvā asahantassa sabbabhāvena karuṇāyanā, tathā ca paṭipattīti evamādayo guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

His remaining perfections should be determined in the same way as stated above. Likewise, one should discern his powerful virtues, such as these: having been reborn in a fish-womb where those of the same species are eaten, he did not eat any living being, not even a fish the size of a broken grain of rice. Let alone eating them, he did not harm even a single being. Also, by making an asseveration of truth, he caused the deva to rain. When the water was exhausted, through his valor he did not count as hardship the suffering he experienced while sinking into the thick mud, but took the suffering of his community of kinsmen into his own heart; unable to bear it, he was filled with compassion in every way. Such was his practice. These and other powerful virtues should be discerned.

Maccharājacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Conduct of the Fish King is finished.

11. Kaṇhadīpāyanacariyāvaṇṇanā

11. The Explanation of the Conduct of Kaṇhadīpāyana

92. Ekādasame [M 0.0233][P 0.0241] kaṇhadīpāyano isīti evaṃnāmako tāpaso. Bodhisatto hi tadā dīpāyano nāma attano sahāyaṃ maṇḍabyatāpasaṃ sūle uttāsitaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tassa sīlaguṇena taṃ avijahanto tiyāmarattiṃ sūlaṃ nissāya ṭhito tassa sarīrato paggharitvā patitapatitehi lohitabindūhi sukkhehi kāḷavaṇṇasarīratāya “kaṇhadīpāyano”ti pākaṭo ahosi. Paropaññāsavassānīti sādhikāni paññāsavassāni, accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Anabhirato cariṃ [V 0.0219] ahanti pantasenāsanesu ceva adhikusaladhammesu ca anabhirativāsaṃ vasanto ahaṃ brahmacariyaṃ acariṃ. Pabbajitvā sattāhameva hi tadā mahāsatto abhirato brahmacariyaṃ cari. Tato paraṃ anabhirativāsaṃ vasi.

92. In the eleventh, “the rishi Kaṇhadīpāyana” means an ascetic so named. For at that time the Bodhisatta, who was named Dīpāyana, approached his friend, the ascetic Maṇḍabya, who had been impaled on a stake. Not abandoning him on account of his virtue, he stood by the stake for the three watches of the night. He became known as “Kaṇhadīpāyana” because his body became dark-colored from the dried drops of blood that trickled down and fell from the other’s body. “Over fifty years” means more than fifty years; this is a usage indicating an absolute connection. “I lived the holy life discontentedly” means: I lived the holy life while dwelling discontentedly with both remote lodgings and with higher wholesome states. For after going forth, the Great Being lived the holy life with delight for only seven days. After that, he dwelt in discontent.

Kasmā pana mahāpuriso anekasatasahassesu attabhāvesu nekkhammajjhāsayo brahmacariyavāsaṃ abhiramitvā idha taṃ nābhirami? Puthujjanabhāvassa cañcalabhāvato. Kasmā ca puna na agāraṃ ajjhāvasīti? Paṭhamaṃ nekkhammajjhāsayena kāmesu dosaṃ disvā pabbaji. Athassa ayonisomanasikārena anabhirati uppajji. So taṃ vinodetumasakkontopi kammañca phalañca saddahitvā tāva mahantaṃ vibhavaṃ pahāya agārasmā nikkhamanto yaṃ pajahi, puna tadatthameva nivatto, “eḷamūgo capalo vatāyaṃ kaṇhadīpāyano”ti imaṃ apavādaṃ jigucchanto attano hirottappabhedabhayena. Api ca pabbajjāpuññaṃ nāmetaṃ viññūhi buddhādīhi pasatthaṃ, tehi ca anuṭṭhitaṃ, tasmāpi sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena assumukho rodamānopi brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasi, na taṃ vissajjesi. Vuttañcetaṃ –

But why did the Great Man, who in many hundreds of thousands of existences had an inclination for renunciation and delighted in the holy life, not delight in it here? Because of the fickle nature of the state of a worldling. And why, again, did he not return to the household life? First, with an inclination for renunciation, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures and went forth. Then discontent arose in him through unwise attention. Though unable to dispel it, he had faith in kamma and its fruit. Having abandoned such great wealth when he went forth from the household life, he was tempted to turn back for that very same thing, but loathing the reproach, “This Kaṇhadīpāyana is indeed a dumb sheep and fickle!” and fearing the loss of his moral shame and dread, he did not. Moreover, this merit of going forth is praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas, and has been undertaken by them. Therefore, even with suffering and grief, with a tearful face and weeping, he lived the holy life and did not relinquish it. And this was said:

“Saddhāya nikkhamma puna nivatto, so eḷamūgo capalo vatāyaṃ;

Etassa vādassa jigucchamāno, akāmako carāmi brahmacariyaṃ;

Viññuppasatthañca [P 0.0242] satañca ṭhānaṃ, evampahaṃ puññakaro bhavāmī”ti. (jā. 1.10.66);

“Having gone forth in faith, he turns back again—this one is truly a dumb sheep and fickle! Loathing such talk, I live the holy life, though unwillingly. It is praised by the wise and is the state of the good; thus may I become a maker of merit.”

93. Na [M 0.0234] koci etaṃ jānātīti etaṃ mama anabhiratimanaṃ brahmacariyavāse abhirativirahitacittaṃ koci manussabhūto na jānāti. Kasmā? Ahañhi kassaci nācikkhiṃ mama mānase citte arati carati pavattatīti kassacipi na kathesiṃ, tasmā na koci manussabhūto etaṃ jānātīti.

93. “No one knows this” means: no human being knows this discontented mind of mine, this mind devoid of delight in the holy life. Why? Because I have not declared to anyone, I have not told anyone, “Discontent moves and proceeds in my mind and heart.” Therefore no human being knows this.

94.

94.

“Sabrahmacārī [P 0.0243] maṇḍabyo, sahāyo me mahāisi;

Pubbakammasamāyutto, sūlamāropanaṃ labhi.

“Maṇḍabya, my fellow in the holy life, my companion, the great rishi, in consequence of a past kamma, received impalement upon a stake.”

.

.

Sabrahmacārīti tāpasapabbajjāya samānasikkhatāya sabrahmacārī. Maṇḍabyoti evaṃnāmako. Sahāyoti gihikāle pabbajitakāle ca daḷhamittatāya piyasahāyo. Mahāisīti mahānubhāvo isi. Pubbakammasamāyutto, sūlamāropanaṃ labhīti katokāsena attano pubbakammena yutto sūlāropanaṃ labhi, sūlaṃ uttāsitoti.

“Fellow in the holy life”: one who shares the holy life because of the same training in the ascetic’s going-forth. “Maṇḍabya”: so named. “Companion”: a dear companion because of their firm friendship both as a householder and after going forth. “Great rishi”: a rishi of great power. “In consequence of a past kamma, he received impalement upon a stake”: connected with his own past kamma that had found its opportunity, he received impalement on a stake; that is, he was impaled on a stake.

Tatrāyaṃ [V 0.0220] anupubbikathā – atīte vaṃsaraṭṭhe kosambiyaṃ kosambiko nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto aññatarasmiṃ nigame asītikoṭivibhavassa brāhmaṇamahāsālassa putto hutvā nibbatti, nāmena dīpāyano nāma. Tādisasseva brāhmaṇamahāsālassa putto brāhmaṇakumāro tassa piyasahāyo ahosi, nāmena maṇḍabyo nāma. Te ubhopi aparabhāge mātāpitūnaṃ accayena kāmesu dosaṃ disvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā kāme pahāya ñātimittaparijanassa rodantassa paridevantassa nikkhamitvā himavantappadese assamaṃ katvā pabbajitvā uñchācariyāya vanamūlaphalāhārena yāpento paropaṇṇāsavassāni vasiṃsu, kāmacchandaṃ vikkhambhetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, te jhānamattampi na nibbattesuṃ.

Here is the story in sequence. In the past, in the country of the Vaṃsas, a king named Kosambika reigned in Kosambī. At that time the Bodhisatta was born in a certain market town as the son of a brahmin of great wealth who possessed a fortune of eighty crores; his name was Dīpāyana. A brahmin youth who was the son of a similar brahmin of great wealth was his dear companion; his name was Maṇḍabya. Later, after the passing of their parents, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, they gave great alms, abandoned sensual pleasures, and went forth from amidst their weeping and lamenting kinsmen, friends, and servants. Having built a hermitage in the Himalayan region, they went forth and lived for over fifty years, sustaining themselves by gleaning and on the roots and fruits of the forest. Yet they were unable to suppress sensual desire and did not generate even a mere jhāna.

Te loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadacārikaṃ carantā [P 0.0244] kāsiraṭṭhaṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Tatrekasmiṃ nigame dīpāyanassa gihisahāyo maṇḍabyo nāma paṭivasati. Te ubhopi tassa santikaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu. So te disvā attamano paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahi. Te tattha tīṇi cattāri vassāni vasitvā taṃ āpucchitvā cārikaṃ carantā bārāṇasisamīpe atimuttakasusāne vasiṃsu. Tattha dīpāyano [M 0.0235] yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā puna tasmiṃ nigame maṇḍabyassa attano sahāyassa santikaṃ gato. Maṇḍabyatāpaso tattheva vasi.

While wandering through the countryside to obtain salt and sour foods, they arrived at the Kāsī country. In a certain market town there, a householder friend of Dīpāyana named Maṇḍabya was living. Both ascetics approached him. Pleased to see them, he had a leaf-hut built and attended to them with the four requisites. They lived there for three or four years, then took leave of him and, wandering on tour, they came to dwell near Bārāṇasī in the Atimuttaka cemetery. After staying there as long as he liked, Dīpāyana went again to that market town to his friend, Maṇḍabya. The ascetic Maṇḍabya remained where he was.

Athekadivasaṃ eko coro antonagare corikaṃ katvā dhanasāraṃ ādāya nikkhanto paṭibuddhehi gehasāmikehi nagarārakkhakamanussehi ca anubaddho niddhamanena nikkhamitvā vegena susānaṃ pavisitvā tāpasassa paṇṇasāladvāre bhaṇḍikaṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyi. Manussā bhaṇḍikaṃ disvā “are duṭṭhajaṭila, rattiṃ, corikaṃ katvā divā tāpasavesena carasī”ti tajjetvā pothetvā taṃ ādāya rañño dassayiṃsu. Rājā anupaparikkhitvāva “sūle uttāsethā”ti āha. Taṃ susānaṃ netvā khadirasūle āropayiṃsu. Tāpasassa sarīre sūlaṃ na pavisati. Tato nimbasūlaṃ āhariṃsu, tampi na pavisati. Tato ayasūlaṃ āhariṃsu, tampi na pavisati. Tāpaso “kiṃ nu kho me pubbakamma”nti cintesi. Tassa jātissarañāṇaṃ uppajji. Tena pubbakammaṃ addasa – so kira purimattabhāve vaḍḍhakīputto hutvā pitu rukkhatacchanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā ekaṃ makkhikaṃ gahetvā koviḷārasakalikāya sūlena viya vijjhi. Tassa taṃ pāpaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne okāsaṃ labhi. So “na sakkā ito pāpato muccitu”nti ñatvā rājapurise āha – “sace maṃ sūle uttāsetukāmattha, koviḷārasūlaṃ āharathā”ti. Te tathā katvā taṃ sūle uttāsetvā ārakkhaṃ datvā pakkamiṃsu.

Then one day a thief, having committed a theft in the inner city and taken a valuable treasure, was leaving when he was pursued by the awakened householders and the city guards. Escaping through a drain, he quickly entered the cemetery and, throwing the bundle at the door of the ascetic’s leaf-hut, he fled. Seeing the bundle, the people threatened and beat the ascetic, scolding him: “Hey, you wicked matted-hair ascetic! At night you commit theft and by day you wander in the guise of an ascetic!” They seized him and presented him to the king.
