Without any investigation, the king ordered: “Impale him on a stake!” They took him to the cemetery and tried to impale him on an acacia stake, but it did not pierce his body. Then they brought a neem stake, but that too did not pierce him. Next, they brought an iron stake, but that too did not pierce him. The ascetic thought: “What past kamma of mine can this be?” Then knowledge of his past lives arose in him. With it he saw his past kamma: it seems that in a previous existence he had been a carpenter’s son and, going to his father’s wood-cutting place, he had caught a fly and pierced it with a koviḷāra splinter as if with a stake. That evil kamma of his found its opportunity on this occasion. Knowing, “It is not possible to be freed from this evil kamma,” he told the king’s men: “If you wish to impale me, bring a koviḷāra stake.” They did so, impaled him on it, posted a guard, and departed.

Tadā [V 0.0221] kaṇhadīpāyano “ciradiṭṭho me sahāyo”ti maṇḍabyassa santikaṃ āgacchanto taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito “kiṃ, samma, kārakosī”ti pucchitvā “akārakomhī”ti vutte “attano manopadosaṃ rakkhituṃ sakkhi na sakkhī”ti pucchi. “Samma, yehi ahaṃ gahito, neva tesaṃ na rañño upari mayhaṃ manopadoso [P 0.0245] atthī”ti. “Evaṃ sante tādisassa sīlavato chāyā mayhaṃ sukhā”ti vatvā kaṇhadīpāyano sūlaṃ nissāya nisīdi. Ārakkhakapurisā taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “anisāmetvā me kata”nti vegena tattha gantvā “kasmā, bhante, tvaṃ sūlaṃ nissāya nisinnosī”ti dīpāyanaṃ pucchi. “Mahārāja, imaṃ tāpasaṃ rakkhanto nisinnosmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ imassa kārakabhāvaṃ ñatvā evaṃ karosī”ti. So kammassa avisodhitabhāvaṃ ācikkhi. Athassa dīpāyano “raññā nāma nisammakārinā bhavitabbaṃ.

At that time, Kaṇhadīpāyana, thinking, “My friend is seen after a long time,” was coming to Maṇḍabya when he heard of this event. He went to that place, stood to one side, and asked, “Friend, are you the perpetrator?” When he replied, “I am not the perpetrator,” he asked, “Were you able to guard your mind against corruption?” He replied, “Friend, I have no mental corruption towards those who seized me, nor towards the king.” “If that is so, the shadow of such a virtuous one is pleasant to me,” said Kaṇhadīpāyana and sat down leaning against the stake. The guards reported this to the king. The king, thinking, “I have acted without investigation,” hurried there and asked Dīpāyana, “Why, venerable sir, are you sitting leaning against the stake?” “Great king, I am sitting here protecting this ascetic.” “But do you do this knowing he is the perpetrator?” He explained the unpurified nature of his kamma. Then Dīpāyana said to him, “A king should be one who acts with due consideration.

“Alaso [M 0.0236] gihī kāmabhogī na sādhu, asaññato pabbajito na sādhu;

Rājā na sādhu anisammakārī, yo paṇḍito kodhano taṃ na sādhū”ti. (jā. 1.4.127; 1.5.4; 1.10.153; 1.15.229) –

“A lazy householder enjoying sensual pleasures is not good; an unrestrained renunciant is not good; a king who acts without due consideration is not good; a wise person who is angry—that is not good.”

Ādīni vatvā dhammaṃ desesi.

Having said this and more, he taught the Dhamma.

Rājā maṇḍabyatāpasassa niddosabhāvaṃ ñatvā “sūlaṃ harathā”ti āṇāpesi. Sūlaṃ harantā harituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Maṇḍabyo āha – “mahārāja, ahaṃ pubbe katakammadosena evarūpaṃ ayasaṃ patto, mama sarīrato sūlaṃ harituṃ na sakkā, sacepi mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ dātukāmo, kakacena imaṃ sūlaṃ cammasamaṃ katvā chindāpehī”ti. Rājā tathā kāresi. Sūlaṃ antoyeva ahosi, na kañci pīḷaṃ janesi. Tadā kira sukhumaṃ sakalikahīraṃ gahetvā makkhikāya vaccamaggaṃ pavesesi, taṃ tassa anto eva ahosi. So tena kāraṇena amaritvā, attano āyukkhayeneva mari, tasmā ayampi na matoti. Rājā tāpase vanditvā khamāpetvā ubhopi uyyāneyeva vasāpento paṭijaggi. Tato paṭṭhāya so āṇimaṇḍabyo nāma jāto. So rājānaṃ upanissāya tattheva vasi. Dīpāyano pana tassa vaṇaṃ phāsukaṃ karitvā attano gihisahāyamaṇḍabyena kāritaṃ paṇṇasālameva gato. Tena vuttaṃ –

The king, recognizing the innocence of the ascetic Maṇḍabya, ordered, “Remove the stake.” When they tried to remove it, they were unable to do so. Maṇḍabya said: “Great king, it is due to the fault of a kamma I performed in the past that I have met with such disgrace. It is not possible to remove the stake from my body. If you wish to grant me my life, have this stake cut level with my skin with a saw.” The king had this done. The stake remained inside but caused him no pain. It is said that once, in a past life, he had inserted a fine thorn-splinter into a fly's rectum, and it remained inside it. For that reason, the fly did not die but perished only at the exhaustion of its lifespan. Therefore, this one, too, did not die. The king paid homage to the ascetics, begged their forgiveness, and provided for both of them, having them dwell in the park. From then on, he became known as Āṇi-Maṇḍabya. He stayed there under the king's patronage. Dīpāyana, however, after tending to his wound until it was comfortable, went to the leaf-hut that had been built by his householder friend, Maṇḍabya. Hence it was said:

95.

95.

“Tamahaṃ [V 0.0222] upaṭṭhahitvāna, ārogyamanupāpayiṃ;

Āpucchitvāna āgañchiṃ, yaṃ mayhaṃ sakamassama”nti.

“Having attended upon him, I brought him back to health; then taking my leave I came to my own hermitage.”

Tattha āpucchitvānāti mayhaṃ sahāyaṃ maṇḍabyatāpasaṃ āpucchitvā. Yaṃ mayhaṃ sakamassamanti yaṃ taṃ mayhaṃ gihisahāyena maṇḍabyabrāhmaṇena kāritaṃ sakaṃ mama santakaṃ assamapadaṃ paṇṇasālā, taṃ upāgañchiṃ.

Herein, having taken leave means: having taken leave of my friend, the ascetic Maṇḍabya. To my own hermitage means: I went to that hermitage site with its leaf-hut, which was my own possession, built for me by my householder friend, the brahmin Maṇḍabya.

96. Taṃ pana paṇṇasālaṃ pavisantaṃ disvā sahāyassa ārocesuṃ. So sutvāva tuṭṭhacitto saputtadāro bahugandhamālaphāṇitādīni ādāya paṇṇasālaṃ [M 0.0237] gantvā dīpāyanaṃ vanditvā pāde dhovitvā pānakaṃ pāyetvā āṇimaṇḍabyassa pavattiṃ suṇanto nisīdi. Athassa putto yaññadattakumāro nāma caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ geṇḍukena kīḷi. Tattha cekasmiṃ vammike āsiviso vasati. Kumārena bhūmiyaṃ pahatageṇḍuko gantvā vammikabile āsivisassa matthake pati. Kumāro ajānanto bile hatthaṃ pavesesi.

96. Seeing him entering the leaf-hut, they informed his friend. As soon as he heard, he was delighted and, taking his wife and son along with many perfumes, garlands, molasses, and other things, he went to the leaf-hut. He paid homage to Dīpāyana, washed his feet, gave him a drink, and sat down to listen to the story of Āṇimaṇḍabya. Meanwhile, his son, the boy Yaññadatta, was playing with a ball at the end of the walking path. In an anthill there lived a venomous snake. The ball, struck by the boy, went into the hole of the anthill and fell on the snake’s head. Not knowing this, the boy put his hand into the hole.

Atha naṃ kuddho āsiviso hatthe ḍaṃsi. So visavegena mucchito tattheva pati. Athassa mātāpitaro sappena daṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā kumāraṃ ukkhipitvā tāpasassa pādamūle nipajjāpetvā “bhante, osadhena vā mantena vā puttakaṃ no nīrogaṃ karothā”ti āhaṃsu. So “ahaṃ osadhaṃ na jānāmi, nāhaṃ vejjakammaṃ karissāmi, pabbajitomhī”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, imasmiṃ kumārake mettaṃ katvā saccakiriyaṃ karothā”ti. Tāpaso “sādhu saccakiriyaṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā yaññadattassa sīse hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā saccakiriyaṃ [P 0.0246] akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “sahāyo brāhmaṇo mayha”ntiādi.

Then the enraged venomous snake bit him on the hand. Overcome by the force of the poison, he fainted and fell right there. His parents, realizing he had been bitten by a snake, lifted the boy up, laid him at the ascetic’s feet, and said: “Venerable sir, please make our son well with medicine or a charm.” He replied: “I do not know any medicine, nor will I practice the physician’s art; I am a renunciant.” “In that case, venerable sir, please extend loving-kindness to this boy and perform an act of truth.” The ascetic said, “Very well, I will perform an act of truth,” and placing his hand on Yaññadatta’s head, he performed the act of truth. Hence it was said: “My friend the brahmin,” and so on.

Tattha āgañchuṃ pāhunāgatanti atithiabhigamanaṃ abhigamiṃsu.

Herein, ‘guests came’ means: they arrived as visitors.

97. Vaṭṭamanukkhipanti khipanavaṭṭasaṇṭhānatāya “vaṭṭa”nti laddhanāmaṃ geṇḍukaṃ anukkhipanto, geṇḍukakīḷaṃ kīḷantoti attho. Āsivisamakopayīti bhūmiyaṃ paṭihato hutvā vammikabilagatena geṇḍukena tattha ṭhitaṃ kaṇhasappaṃ sīse paharitvā rosesi.

97. ‘Tossing the ball’ means: tossing up a ball, which is called a vaṭṭa (round object) because it is a round object for throwing; the meaning is, he was playing a ball game. ‘He provoked the venomous snake’ means: the ball, after bouncing off the ground and entering the anthill hole, struck the black snake that was dwelling there on its head and angered it.

98. Vaṭṭagataṃ maggaṃ, anvesantoti tena vaṭṭena gataṃ maggaṃ gavesanto. Āsivisassa hatthena, uttamaṅgaṃ parāmasīti vammikabilaṃ pavesitena attano hatthena āsīvisassa sīsaṃ phusi.

98. ‘Seeking the path the ball had taken’ means: searching for the path that the ball had gone. ‘With his hand he touched the head of the venomous snake’ means: with his own hand, which he had inserted into the anthill hole, he touched the head of the venomous snake.

99. Visabalassitoti [V 0.0223] visabalanissito attano visavegaṃ nissāya uppajjanakasappo. Aḍaṃsi dārakaṃ khaṇeti tasmiṃ parāmasitakkhaṇe eva taṃ brāhmaṇakumāraṃ ḍaṃsi.

99. ‘Relying on the power of its venom’ means: a snake that depends on the power of its venom, that relies on the force of its own poison. ‘It bit the boy in that instant’ means: it bit the brahmin boy at the very moment it was touched.

100. Sahadaṭṭhoti ḍaṃsena saheva, daṭṭhasamakālameva. Āsivisenāti ghoravisena. Tenāti tena dārakassa visavegena mucchitassa [M 0.0238] bhūmiyaṃ patanena ahaṃ dukkhito ahosiṃ. Mama vāhasi taṃ dukkhanti taṃ dārakassa mātāpitūnañca dukkhaṃ mama vāhasi, mayhaṃ sarīre viya mama karuṇāya vāhesi.

100. ‘As soon as he was bitten’ means: simultaneously with the bite, at the very same time he was bitten. ‘By the venomous snake’ means: by the one with dreadful poison. ‘By that’ means: I was afflicted with sorrow by the boy’s fainting from the force of the poison and falling to the ground. ‘You bore that suffering for me’ means: you bore for me that suffering of the boy and his parents; through my compassion, you bore it as if upon my own body.

101. Tyāhanti te tassa dārakassa mātāpitaro ahaṃ “mā socatha, mā paridevathā”tiādinā nayena samassāsetvā. Sokasalliteti sokasallavante. Agganti seṭṭhaṃ tato eva varaṃ uttamaṃ saccakiriyaṃ akāsiṃ.

101. ‘Them I’ means: I, having consoled them, the parents of that boy, in this way, “Do not grieve, do not lament,” and so on. ‘Pierced by the dart of sorrow’ means: those possessing the dart of sorrow. ‘The foremost’ means: I performed the foremost, that is, the best, the superior, the highest act of truth.

102. Idāni taṃ saccakiriyaṃ sarūpena dassetuṃ “sattāhamevā”ti gāthamāha.

102. Now, to state the act of truth itself, he spoke the verse beginning: “For seven days only…”

Tattha sattāhamevāti pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya satta ahāni eva. Pasannacittoti kammaphalasaddhāya pasannamānaso. Puññatthikoti puññena atthiko, dhammacchandayutto. Athāparaṃ yaṃ caritanti atha tasmā sattāhā uttari yaṃ mama brahmacariyacaraṇaṃ.

Herein, ‘for seven days only’ means: for just seven days from the day I went forth. ‘With a confident mind’ means: with a mind made confident by faith in the fruit of kamma. ‘Desiring merit’ means: one who has need of merit, endowed with zeal for the Dhamma. ‘And what was practiced after’ means: then, beyond those seven days, whatever was my practice of the holy life.

103. Akāmakovāhīti pabbajjaṃ anicchanto eva. Etena saccena suvatthi hotūti sace atirekapaññāsavassāni anabhirativāsaṃ vasantena mayā kassaci ajānāpitabhāvo sacco, etena saccena yaññadattakumārassa sotthi hotu, jīvitaṃ paṭilabhatūti.

103. ‘Unwillingly I lived it’ means: not desiring the going forth at all. ‘By this truth may there be well-being’ means: If it is true that for over fifty years I have lived this life without delight and have not made this known to anyone, then by this truth may there be well-being for the boy Yaññadatta; may he regain his life.

Evaṃ [P 0.0247] pana mahāsattena saccakiriyāya katāya yaññadattassa sarīrato visaṃ bhassitvā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Kumāro akkhīni ummīletvā mātāpitaro oloketvā “amma, tātā”ti vatvā vuṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

When the Great Being thus performed the act of truth, the poison fell away from Yaññadatta's body and entered the earth. The boy opened his eyes, looked at his parents, said, “Mother, father!” and rose up. Therefore, it is said:

104.

104.

“Saha sacce kate mayhaṃ, visavegena vedhito;

Abujjhitvāna vuṭṭhāsi, arogo cāsi māṇavo”ti.

“As soon as my act of truth was made, he who was afflicted by the poison’s force awoke and stood up; the young man was healthy.”

Tassattho – mama saccakaraṇena saha samānakālameva tato pubbe visavegena vedhito kampito [V 0.0224] visaññibhāvena abujjhitvā ṭhito vigatavisattā paṭiladdhasañño sahasā vuṭṭhāsi. So māṇavo kumāro visavegābhāvena arogo ca ahosīti.

Its meaning is: Simultaneously with my performance of the act of truth, he who had previously been afflicted and trembling from the force of the poison, and was standing there unconscious, suddenly stood up, his consciousness regained as the poison was gone. And that young man, that boy, became healthy due to the absence of the poison’s force.

Idāni satthā tassā attano saccakiriyāya paramatthapāramibhāvaṃ dassento “saccena me samo natthi, esā me saccapāramī”ti āha. Taṃ uttānatthameva[M 0.0239]. Jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (jā. aṭṭha. 4.10.62) pana “mahāsattassa saccakiriyāya kumārassa thanappadesato uddhaṃ visaṃ bhassitvā vigataṃ. Dārakassa pitu saccakiriyāya kaṭito uddhaṃ, mātu saccakiriyāya avasiṭṭhasarīrato visaṃ bhassitvā vigata”nti āgataṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

Now the Teacher, showing that this act of truth of his was a perfection of the ultimate meaning, said, “None is equal to me in truth—this is my perfection of truth.” This has a plain meaning. However, in the Jātaka commentary it is said: “By the Great Being's act of truth, the poison vanished, having fallen away from the boy's chest upwards. By his father's act of truth, the poison from the waist upwards vanished; by his mother's act of truth, the poison fell away from the rest of the body and vanished.” As it is said:

“Yasmā dānaṃ nābhinandiṃ kadāci, disvānahaṃ atithiṃ vāsakāle;

Na cāpi me appiyataṃ aveduṃ, bahussutā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca;

Akāmako vāpi ahaṃ dadāmi, etena saccena suvatthi hotu;

Hataṃ visaṃ jīvatu yaññadatto.

“Because I never took delight in giving, even when seeing a guest at mealtime; and learned ascetics and brahmins have never found me disagreeable; and though unwilling, still I give: by this truth, may there be well-being! May the poison be destroyed, may Yaññadatta live!”

“Āsīviso tāta pahūtatejo, yo taṃ adaṃsī patarā udicca;

Tasmiñca me appiyatāya ajja, pitari ca te natthi koci viseso;

Etena saccena suvatthi hotu, hataṃ visaṃ jīvatu yaññadatto”ti.

“Dear one, that venomous snake of great power that bit you, rising up from a fissure—for me, in my displeasure, there is no difference today between it and your father. By this truth, may there be well-being! May the poison be destroyed, may Yaññadatta live!”

Tattha vāsakāleti vasanatthāya gehaṃ āgatakāle. Na cāpi [P 0.0248] me appiyataṃ avedunti bahussutāpi samaṇabrāhmaṇā ayaṃ neva dānaṃ abhinandati, na amheti imaṃ mama appiyabhāvaṃ neva jāniṃsu. Ahañhi te piyacakkhūhiyeva olokemīti dīpeti. Etena saccenāti sace ahaṃ dadamānopi vipākaṃ asaddahitvā attano anicchāya demi, anicchabhāvañca me pare na jānanti, etena saccena suvatthi hotūti attho. Itaragāthāya, tātāti puttaṃ ālapati. Pahūtatejoti balavaviso. Patarāti padarā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Udiccāti uddhaṃ gantvā, vammikabilato uṭṭhahitvāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta yaññadatta, tasmiñca āsivise tava ca pitari appiyabhāvena mayhaṃ koci viseso natthi, tañca pana appiyabhāvaṃ ṭhapetvā ajja mayā na koci jānāpitapubbo, sace etaṃ saccaṃ, etena saccena suvatthi hotūti.

Herein, vāsakāle means at the time of coming to a house for the purpose of lodging. As to Na cāpi me appiyataṃ aveduṃ: even the learned ascetics and brahmins did not know this displeasure of mine, thinking, ‘This one rejoices neither in the gift nor in us.’ It shows: ‘For I look upon them only with affectionate eyes.’ As to Etena saccena: The meaning is: ‘If, though giving, I give with my own unwillingness, not having faith in the result, and others do not know of my unwillingness, by this truth may there be well-being!’ In the other verse, tāta is an address to the son. Pahūtatejo means having powerful venom. Patarā means padarā (a fissure), or this is the reading. Udicca means having gone upwards; the meaning is having risen up from an anthill-hole. This is what is said: ‘Dear Yaññadatta, for me, in my displeasure, there is no difference between that venomous snake and your father. But apart from that displeasure, I have never before informed anyone of it. If this is true, by this truth may there be well-being!’

Evaṃ [M 0.0240] bodhisatto kumāre aroge jāte tassa pitaraṃ “dānaṃ dadantena nāma kammañca phalañca [V 0.0225] saddahitvā dātabba”nti kammaphalasaddhāya nivesetvā sayaṃ anabhiratiṃ vinodetvā jhānābhiññāyo uppādetvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokaparāyano ahosi.

Thus, when the boy became healthy, the Bodhisatta established his father in faith in kamma and its fruit, saying: “Indeed, when giving a gift, one should give it having faith in the deed and its fruit.” Having dispelled his own discontent, he developed the jhānas and the supernormal knowledges, and at the end of his life, he was destined for the Brahma-world.

Tadā maṇḍabyo ānandatthero ahosi, tassa bhariyā visākhā, putto rāhulatthero, āṇimaṇḍabyo sāriputtatthero, kaṇhadīpāyano lokanātho.

At that time, Maṇḍabya was the Elder Ānanda, his wife was Visākhā, the son was the Elder Rāhula, Āṇimaṇḍabya was the Elder Sāriputta, and Kaṇhadīpāyana was the Lord of the World.

Tassa idha pāḷiyā āruḷhā saccapāramī, sesā ca pāramiyo heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva niddhāretabbā. Tathā anavasesamahābhogapariccāgādayo guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Here, his perfection of truth is established in the Pāli text, and the remaining perfections should be determined in the same way as stated below. Similarly, the qualities and power such as the complete relinquishment of great wealth and so on should be explained.

Kaṇhadīpāyanacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Conduct of Kaṇhadīpāyana is finished.

12. Mahāsutasomacariyāvaṇṇanā

12. The Explanation of the Conduct of Mahāsutasoma

105. Dvādasame sutasomo mahīpatīti evaṃnāmo khattiyo. Mahāsatto hi tadā kururaṭṭhe indapatthanagare korabyassa rañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. Taṃ sutavittatāya candasamānasommavaravaṇṇatāya ca “sutasomo”ti sañjāniṃsu. Taṃ vayappattaṃ sabbasippanipphattippattaṃ mātāpitaro [P 0.0249] rajje abhisiñciṃsu. Gahito porisādenāti purisānaṃ manussānaṃ adanato khādanato “porisādo”ti laddhanāmena bārāṇasiraññā devatābalikammatthaṃ gahito.

105. In the twelfth (cariya), he was a khattiya named Sutasoma, a great ruler. For at that time the Great Being was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of King Korabya in the city of Indapattha in the Kuru country. Because of his learning and wealth and his moon-like, gentle, and excellent complexion, they named him ‘Sutasoma.’ When he came of age and had attained proficiency in all crafts, his mother and father consecrated him in the kingdom. He was captured by Porisāda—that is, by the king of Bārāṇasī, who had acquired the name ‘Porisāda’ from eating men, that is, human beings—for the purpose of a sacrificial offering to a deity.

Bārāṇasirājā hi tadā maṃsaṃ vinā abhuñjanto aññaṃ maṃsaṃ alabhantena bhattakārakena manussamaṃsaṃ khādāpito rasataṇhāya baddho hutvā manusse ghātetvā manussamaṃsaṃ khādanto “porisādo”ti laddhanāmo amaccapārisajjappamukhehi nāgarehi negamajānapadehi ca ussāhitena kāḷahatthinā nāma attano senāpatinā “deva, yadi rajjena atthiko manussamaṃsakhādanato viramāhī”ti vutto “rajjaṃ pajahantopi manussamaṃsakhādanato na oramissāmī”ti vatvā tehi raṭṭhā pabbājito [M 0.0241] araññaṃ pavisitvā ekasmiṃ nigrodharukkhamūle vasanto khāṇuppahārena pāde jātassa vaṇassa phāsubhāvāya “sakalajambudīpe ekasatakhattiyānaṃ galalohitena balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti devatāya āyācanaṃ katvā sattāhaṃ anāhāratāya vaṇe phāsuke jāte “devatānubhāvena me sotthi ahosī”ti saññāya “devatāya balikammatthaṃ rājāno [V 0.0226] ānessāmī”ti gacchanto atītabhave sahāyabhūtena yakkhena samāgantvā tena dinnamantabalena adhikatarathāmajavaparakkamasasampanno hutvā sattāhabbhantareyeva satarājāno ānetvā attano vasananigrodharukkhe olambetvā balikammakaraṇasajjo ahosi.

For at that time the king of Bārāṇasī, who would not eat without meat, was made to eat human flesh by his cook when no other meat was available. Bound by craving for the taste, he started killing people and eating human flesh, thereby acquiring the name ‘Porisāda.’ When, urged on by his ministers, courtiers, and the people of the city, towns, and countryside, his own general named Kāḷahatthi said to him: ‘Your majesty, if you want the kingdom, you must stop eating human flesh,’ he replied: ‘Even if I have to give up the kingdom, I will not stop eating human flesh.’ Thus he was banished from the country by them. He entered the forest and while dwelling at the foot of a banyan tree, a wound arose on his foot from being struck by a stump. For the sake of the wound’s healing, he made a plea to a deity: ‘I will make a sacrificial offering with the throat-blood of one hundred khattiyas from all over Jambudīpa.’ After he had been without food for seven days, the wound healed. With the thought, ‘I have become well through the power of the deity,’ he resolved, ‘I will bring kings for the deity’s sacrificial offering.’ As he was going, he met a yakkha who had been his companion in a past existence. Endowed with superior strength, speed, and power through a mantra given by him, within just seven days he brought a hundred kings, hung them on the banyan tree where he lived, and became ready to perform the sacrificial offering.

Atha tasmiṃ rukkhe adhivatthā devatā taṃ balikammaṃ anicchantī “upāyena naṃ nisedhessāmī”ti pabbajitarūpena tassa attānaṃ dassetvā tena anubaddho tiyojanaṃ gantvā puna attano dibbarūpameva dassetvā “tvaṃ musāvādī tayā ‘sakalajambudīpe rājāno ānetvā balikammaṃ karissāmī’ti paṭissutaṃ. Idāni ye vā te vā dubbalarājāno ānesi. Jambudīpe jeṭṭhakaṃ sutasomarājānaṃ sace nānessasi, na me te balikammena attho”ti āha.

Then the deity dwelling in that tree, not wanting that sacrificial offering, thought, ‘I will stop him by a stratagem.’ She showed herself to him in the form of an ascetic and, being followed by him, went for three yojanas. Then she showed her own divine form again and said: ‘You are a liar! It was promised by you: “I will bring kings from all over Jambudīpa and make a sacrificial offering.” Now you have brought just any weak kings. If you do not bring King Sutasoma, the chief in Jambudīpa, I have no use for your sacrificial offering.’”

So “diṭṭhā me attano devatā”ti tusitvā “sāmi, mā cintayi, ahaṃ ajjeva sutasomaṃ ānessāmī”ti vatvā vegena migājinauyyānaṃ gantvā asaṃvihitāya ārakkhāya pokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā paduminipattena sīsaṃ paṭicchādetvā aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ [P 0.0250] antouyyānagateyeva balavapaccūse samantā tiyojanaṃ ārakkhaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Mahāsatto pātova alaṅkatahatthikkhandhavaragato caturaṅginiyā senāya nagarato nikkhami. Tadā takkasilato nando nāma brāhmaṇo catasso satārahagāthāyo gahetvā vīsayojanasataṃ maggaṃ atikkamma taṃ nagaraṃ patto rājānaṃ pācīnadvārena nikkhamantaṃ disvā hatthaṃ ukkhipitvā “jayatu bhavaṃ, mahārājā”ti vatvā jayāpesi.

Pleased that ‘I have seen my own deity,’ he said: ‘Master, do not worry, I will bring Sutasoma this very day.’ He went swiftly to the Migājina Park and, as the guard was not yet arranged, he descended into the lotus pond, covered his head with a lotus leaf, and stood there. Just after he had entered the inner park, at bright dawn, they set a guard all around for three yojanas. The Great Being, early in the morning, having mounted a splendid elephant, went out from the city with the fourfold army. Then a brahmin named Nanda from Takkasilā, having procured four stanzas worth a hundred thousand each and having traversed a road of two thousand yojanas, reached that city. Seeing the king coming out by the eastern gate, he raised his hand and wished him victory, saying: ‘May your majesty be victorious, O great king!’

Rājā hatthinā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kuto nu, tvaṃ brāhmaṇa, āgacchasi, kimicchasi, kiṃ te dajja”nti āha. Brāhmaṇo “tumhe ‘sutavittakā’ti sutvā catasso satārahagāthāyo ādāya tumhākaṃ desetuṃ āgatomhī”ti āha. Mahāsatto tuṭṭhamānaso hutvā “ahaṃ uyyānaṃ [M 0.0242] gantvā nhāyitvā āgantvā sossāmi, tvaṃ mā ukkaṇṭhī”ti vatvā “gacchatha brāhmaṇassa asukagehe nivāsaṃ ghāsacchādanañca saṃvidahathā”ti āṇāpetvā uyyānaṃ pavisitvā mahantaṃ ārakkhaṃ saṃvidhāya oḷārikāni ābharaṇāni omuñcitvā massukammaṃ kāretvā ubbaṭṭitasarīro pokkharaṇiyā rājavibhavena nhāyitvā paccuttaritvā udakaggahaṇasāṭake nivāsetvā aṭṭhāsi.

The king approached him on his elephant and said: ‘Whence, brahmin, have you come? What do you wish for? What may I give you?’ The brahmin said: ‘Having heard that you are renowned for learning, I have come bringing four stanzas, each worth a hundred thousand, to teach to you.’ The Great Being, with a pleased mind, said: ‘I will go to the park, bathe, and return to listen. Do not be anxious.’ Then he commanded: ‘Go and arrange lodging, food, and clothing for the brahmin in such-and-such a house.’ He entered the park, arranged for a great guard, took off his heavy ornaments, had his beard attended to, and with his body anointed, he bathed in the lotus pond with royal splendor. Having come out, he put on a bathing cloth and stood there.

Athassa gandhamālālaṅkāre upahariṃsu. Porisādo “alaṅkatakāle rājā bhāriko bhavissati, sallahukakāleyeva naṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti nadanto khaggaṃ parivattento “ahamasmi porisādo”ti nāmaṃ sāvetvā udakā nikkhami. Tassa saddaṃ sutvā hatthārohādayo hatthiādito bhassiṃsu. Balakāyo dūre ṭhito tatova palāyi. Itaro attano āvudhāni chaḍḍetvā urena nipajji. Porisādo [V 0.0227] rājānaṃ ukkhipitvā khandhe nisīdāpetvā sammukhaṭṭhāneyeva aṭṭhārasahatthaṃ pākāraṃ laṅghitvā purato pagalitamadamattavaravāraṇe kumbhe akkamitvā pabbatakūṭāni viya pātento vātajavānipi assaratanāni piṭṭhiyaṃ akkamitvā pātento rathasīse akkamitvā pātento bhamarikaṃ bhamanto viya nīlakāni nigrodhapattāni maddanto viya ekavegeneva tiyojanamaggaṃ gantvā kañci anubandhantaṃ [P 0.0251] adisvā saṇikaṃ gacchanto sutasomassa kesehi udakabindūni attano upari patantāni “assubindūnī”ti saññāya “kimidaṃ sutasomopi maraṇaṃ anusocanto rodatī”ti āha.

Then they brought him perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. Porisāda thought: ‘When he is adorned, the king will be heavy; I will seize him while he is still light.’ Roaring, brandishing his sword, and announcing his name, ‘I am Porisāda,’ he came out of the water. Hearing his cry, the elephant-drivers and others fell from their elephants and other mounts. The army, standing at a distance, fled from that very spot. The others, having thrown down their weapons, lay prostrate on their chests. Porisāda lifted the king, set him on his shoulder, and right from where he stood, leaped over the eighteen-cubit wall. Trampling on the foreheads of the excellent, intoxicated elephants with rut flowing and felling them like mountain peaks; trampling on the backs of the jewel-like horses, even those swift as the wind, and felling them; trampling on the tops of the chariots and felling them; as if whirling in a whirlwind, as if crushing dark-blue banyan leaves, he went a distance of three yojanas in a single rush. Seeing no one pursuing him and going slowly, when drops of water from Sutasoma’s hair fell upon him, he perceived them as teardrops and said: ‘What is this? Is Sutasoma also lamenting his death and weeping?’

Mahāsatto “nāhaṃ maraṇato anusocāmi, kuto rodanā, api ca kho saṅgaraṃ katvā saccāpanaṃ nāma paṇḍitānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ, taṃ na nipphajjatī”ti anusocāmi. Kassapadasabalena desitā catasso satārahagāthāyo ādāya takkasilato āgatassa brāhmaṇassa āgantukavattaṃ kāretvā “nhāyitvā āgantvā suṇissāmi, yāva mamāgamanā āgamehī”ti saṅgaraṃ katvā uyyānaṃ gato, tvañca tā gāthāyo sotuṃ adatvā maṃ gaṇhīti. Tena vuttaṃ –

The Great Being said: ‘I do not lament on account of death—whence could there be weeping? Rather, I lament that this is not being accomplished: the keeping of a promise, which is the custom of the wise. For a brahmin who came from Takkasilā, bringing four stanzas worth a hundred thousand each taught by Kassapa of the Ten Powers, I had the duties to a visitor performed and went to the park after making this promise: “I will bathe, return, and listen; wait until my arrival.” But you seized me without allowing me to hear those stanzas.’ Therefore it was said:

“Gahito porisādena, brāhmaṇe saṅgaraṃ sari”nti.

“Seized by Porisāda, he remembered his promise to the brahmin.”

Tattha brāhmaṇe saṅgaraṃ sarinti nandabrāhmaṇe attanā kataṃ paṭiññaṃ anussariṃ.

Therein, 'he remembered his promise to the brahmin' means: I remembered the pledge made by myself to the brahmin Nanda.

106. Āvuṇitvā [M 0.0243] karattaleti tattha tattha uyyānādīsu gantvā attano balena ānītānaṃ ekasatakhattiyānaṃ hatthatale chiddaṃ katvā rukkhe lambanatthaṃ rajjuṃ paṭimuñcitvā. Etesaṃ pamilāpetvāti ete ekasatakhattiye jīvaggāhaṃ gahetvā uddhaṃpāde adhosire katvā paṇhiyā sīsaṃ paharanto bhamaṇavasena hatthatale āvuṇitvā rukkhe ālambanavasena sabbaso āhārūpacchedena ca sabbathā pamilāpetvā visosetvā khedāpetvāti attho. Yaññattheti balikammatthe sādhetabbe. Upanayī mamanti maṃ upanesi.

106. 'Having pierced the palm of the hand' (āvuṇitvā karattaleti) means that after going to various gardens and other places, he brought back one hundred and one warriors by his own strength, made holes in the palms of their hands, and tied ropes through them to hang them from trees. 'Having exhausted them' (etesaṃ pamilāpetvāti) means he seized these one hundred and one warriors alive, turned them upside down with their feet up and heads down, and struck their heads with his heels, piercing their palms and hanging them from trees; he completely exhausted them in every way by cutting off their food, thus drying them out and causing them suffering. 'For the sake of the sacrifice' (yaññattheti) means for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrificial rite. 'He brought me' (upanayī mamanti) means he led me.

107. Tathā upanīyamāno pana mahāsatto porisādena “kiṃ tvaṃ maraṇato bhāyasī”ti vutte “nāhaṃ maraṇato bhāyāmi, tassa pana brāhmaṇassa mayā kato saṅgaro na parimocito”ti anusocāmi. “Sace maṃ vissajjessasi, taṃ dhammaṃ sutvā tassa ca sakkārasammānaṃ katvā puna āgamissāmī”ti. “Nāhamidaṃ saddahāmi, yaṃ tvaṃ mayā vissajjito gantvā puna mama hatthaṃ āgamissāsī”ti. “Samma porisāda, mayā saddhiṃ ekācariyakule sikkhito sahāyo hutvā [V 0.0228] ‘ahaṃ jīvitahetupi na musā kathemī’ti kiṃ na saddahasī”ti? Kiñcāpi me etena vācāmattakena –

107. Then, as he was being led away, the Great Being, when asked by Porisāda, “Are you afraid of death?” replied, “I do not fear death, but I grieve that the promise I made to that brahmin has not been fulfilled. If you release me, I will listen to that teaching, properly honor him, and then return.” “I do not believe this, that you, once released by me, would return to my hand.” “Friend Porisāda, having been trained in the same teacher's family with me as a companion, why do you not believe that ‘I would not speak falsely even for the sake of my life’?” Though by me only these words were spoken—

“Asiñca [P 0.0252] sattiñca parāmasāmi, sapathampi te samma ahaṃ karomi;

Tayā pamutto anaṇo bhavitvā, saccānurakkhī punarāvajissa”nti. (jā. 2.21.407) –

“I touch the sword and the spear, and I make an oath to you, friend; freed by you, being without debt, as a guardian of truth, I will return.”

Mahāsattena imāya gāthāya vuttāya porisādo “ayaṃ sutasomo ‘khattiyehi akattabbaṃ sapathaṃ karomī’ti vadati, gantvā anāgacchantopi mama hatthato na muccissatī”ti cintetvā –

—when the Great Being had spoken this verse, Porisāda thought, “This Sutasoma says, ‘I will make an oath that should not be made by warriors.’ Even if he goes and does not return, he will not escape from my hand,” and reflecting thus—

“Yo te kato saṅgaro brāhmaṇena, raṭṭhe sake issariye ṭhitena;

Taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇa sappadāya, saccānurakkhī punarāvajassū”ti. (jā. 2.21.408) –

“The promise that you, established in your own sovereign kingdom, made with the brahmin; having fulfilled that promise for the brahmin, as a guardian of truth, you must return.”

Vissajjesi.

—he released him.

Mahāsatto [M 0.0244] rāhumukhā mutto cando viya nāgabalo thāmasampanno khippameva taṃ nagaraṃ sampāpuṇi. Senāpissa “sutasomarājā paṇḍito, porisādaṃ dametvā sīhamukhā pamuttamattavaravāraṇo viya āgamissatī”ti ca “rājānaṃ porisādassa datvā āgatā”ti garahabhayena ca bahinagareyeva niviṭṭhā taṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā paccuggantvā vanditvā “kaccittha, mahārāja, porisādena na kilamito”ti paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “porisādena mayhaṃ mātāpitūhipi dukkaraṃ kataṃ, tathārūpo nāma caṇḍo sāhasiko mamaṃ saddahitvā maṃ vissajjesī”ti vutte rājānaṃ alaṅkaritvā hatthikkhandhaṃ āropetvā parivāretvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Taṃ disvā sabbe nāgarā tusiṃsu.

The Great Being, freed from the mouth of Rāhu like the moon, with the strength of an elephant, powerful and strong, quickly reached that city. His army, thinking, "King Sutasoma is wise; having tamed Porisāda, he will return like a noble elephant released from a lion’s jaws," and fearing blame—"They have given the king to Porisāda and come back"—encamped just outside the city. Seeing him approaching from afar, they went to meet him, paid homage, and after exchanging courtesies, inquired, "Great king, we hope you were not troubled by Porisāda." When he said, "Porisāda did for me what was difficult even for my parents, yet such a fierce and violent man trusted me and released me," they adorned the king, mounted him on an elephant's back, surrounded him, and entered the city. Seeing him, all the citizens rejoiced.

Sopi dhammasoṇḍatāya mātāpitaropi anupasaṅkamitvā nivesanaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇaṃ pakkosāpetvā tassa mahantaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ katvā dhammagarutāya sayaṃ nīcāsane nisīditvā “tumhehi mayhaṃ ābhatā satārahagāthā suṇomi ācariyā”ti āha. Brāhmaṇo mahāsattena yācitakāle gandhehi hatthe ubbaṭṭetvā pasibbakato manoramaṃ potthakaṃ nīharitvā ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā “tena hi[P 0.0253], mahārāja, suṇohī”ti potthakaṃ vācento gāthā abhāsi –

Due to his deep reverence for the Dhamma, he did not even visit his parents but went straight to his residence. He summoned the brahmin, showed him great honor and respect, and out of reverence for the Dhamma, sat himself on a low seat. He said, "Teacher, I will listen to the verses worth a hundred that you have brought for me." At the request of the Great Being, the brahmin anointed his hands with perfumes, took out a beautiful book from his bag, held it with both hands, and said, "Then, great king, listen." Reciting from the book, he spoke the verses:

“Sakideva [V 0.0229] sutasoma, sabbhi hoti samāgamo;

Sā naṃ saṅgati pāleti, nāsabbhi bahusaṅgamo.

"O Sutasoma, an encounter with the good, even once, is what matters; that association protects one, not frequent association with the bad."

“Sabbhireva samāsetha, sabbhi kubbetha santhavaṃ;

Sataṃ saddhammamaññāya, seyyo hoti na pāpiyo.

"Associate only with the good; keep company with the virtuous. Knowing the true Dhamma of the good, one becomes better, not worse."

“Jīranti ve rājarathā sucittā, atho sarīrampi jaraṃ upeti;

Satañca dhammo na jaraṃ upeti, santo have sabbhi pavedayanti.

"Even well-adorned royal chariots wear out, and the body too comes to old age; but the Dhamma of the good does not age; the good, indeed, make it known to the good."

“Nabhañca dūre pathavī ca dūre, pāraṃ samuddassa tadāhu dūre;

Tato have dūrataraṃ vadanti, satañca dhammo asatañca rājā”ti. (jā. 2.21.411-414, 445-448);

"The sky is far, the earth is far, the far shore of the ocean is said to be far. But further indeed than that, they say, is the Dhamma of the good and that of the wicked, O King."

Tā [M 0.0245] sutvā mahāsatto “saphalaṃ me āgamana”nti tuṭṭhacitto “imā gāthā neva sāvakabhāsitā, na isibhāsitā, na kavibhāsitā, na devabhāsitā, sabbaññunāva bhāsitā. Kiṃ nu kho aggha”nti cintento “imaṃ sakalampi cakkavāḷaṃ yāva brahmalokā sattaratanapuṇṇaṃ katvā dinnepi neva anucchavikaṃ kataṃ nāma hoti, ahaṃ kho panassa tiyojanasatike kururaṭṭhe sattayojanike indapatthanagare rajjaṃ dātuṃ pahomi. Rajjaṃ kātuṃ panassa bhāgyaṃ natthi, tathā hissa aṅgalakkhaṇānusārena appānubhāvatā dissati, tasmā dinnampi rajjaṃ na imasmiṃ tiṭṭhatī”ti cintetvā “ācariya, tumhe aññesaṃ khattiyānaṃ imā gāthāyo desetvā kiṃ labhathā”ti pucchi. “Ekekāya sataṃ sataṃ, mahārāja, teneva satārahagāthā nāma jātā”ti. Athassa mahāsatto “tvaṃ ācariya, attanā gahetvā vicaraṇabhaṇḍassa agghaṃ na jānāsī”ti.

Hearing this, the Great Being, delighted in heart, thought, "My coming has been fruitful." He reflected, "These verses are neither spoken by disciples, nor by seers, nor by poets, nor by gods—they are spoken by the Omniscient One. What, then, is their worth?" Pondering further, he thought, "Even if this entire world-system were filled with the seven treasures up to the Brahma-world and given, it would not be a fitting price. Yet, I can offer him kingship over the city of Indapatta, which is seven yojanas in size, in the Kuru country that spans three hundred yojanas. However, he has no good fortune to rule, for according to the marks on his body, his lack of power is evident. Thus, even if kingship were given, it would not remain with him." Having considered this, he asked, "Teacher, when you teach these verses to other nobles, what do you receive?" "A hundred for each verse, great king. Hence, they are called the 'verses worth a hundred.'" Then the Great Being said, "Teacher, you do not know the value of the merchandise you carry yourself."

“Sahassiyā [P 0.0254] imā gāthā, nayimā gāthā satārahā;

Cattāri tvaṃ sahassāni, khippaṃ gaṇhāhi brāhmaṇā”ti. (jā. 2.21.415);

"These verses are worth a thousand, not a hundred. Quickly take four thousand, Brahmin."

Cattāri sahassāni dāpetvā ekañca sukhayānakaṃ datvā mahatā sakkārasammāneneva taṃ uyyojetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā “ahaṃ brāhmaṇena ābhataṃ saddhammaratanaṃ pūjetvā tassa ca sakkārasammānaṃ katvā āgamissāmīti porisādassa paṭiññaṃ datvā āgato. Tattha yaṃ brāhmaṇassa [V 0.0230] kattabbaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ taṃ kataṃ, idāni porisādassa santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti vutvā “tena hi, tāta sutasoma, kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathesi, caturaṅginiyā senāya coraṃ gaṇhissāma, mā gaccha corassa santika”nti yāciṃsu. Soḷasasahassā nāṭakitthiyo sesaparijanāpi “amhe anāthe katvā kuhiṃ gacchasi devā”ti parideviṃsu. “Punapi kira rājā corassa santikaṃ gamissatī”ti ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi.

Having had four thousand given, along with one comfortable vehicle, and having sent him off with great honor and respect, he paid homage to his parents and said, "I came here having given a promise to Porisāda that I would worship the precious Dhamma brought by the brahmin, honor him, and then return. What needed to be done for the brahmin has been done; now I shall go to Porisāda." They pleaded, "Dear Sutasoma, what is this you are saying? We will capture the thief with a fourfold army; do not go to the thief!" Sixteen thousand dancing women and the rest of the retinue lamented, "Leaving us helpless, where are you going, Your Majesty?" A great uproar arose: "Is the king really going to the thief again?"

Mahāsatto “paṭiññāya saccāpanaṃ nāma sādhūnaṃ sappurisānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ, sopi mamaṃ saddahitvā vissajjesi, tasmā gamissāmiyevā”ti mātāpitaro vanditvā sesajanaṃ anusāsetvā assumukhena nānappakāraṃ paridevantena itthāgārādinā janena anugato nagarā nikkhamma taṃ janaṃ nivattetuṃ magge daṇḍakena tiriyaṃ lekhaṃ katvā “imaṃ mama lekhaṃ mā atikkamiṃsū”ti [M 0.0246] vatvā agamāsi. Mahājano tejavato mahāsattassa āṇaṃ atikkamituṃ asakkonto mahāsaddena kanditvā roditvā nivatti. Bodhisatto āgatamaggeneva tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “apucchi maṃ porisādo”tiādi.

The Great Being thought, "Keeping a promise is the practice of the virtuous and the good; he too, having faith in me, released me. Therefore, I must indeed go." Having paid homage to his parents and instructed the rest of the people, he departed from the city, followed by the people from the women's quarters and others, weeping and lamenting in various ways with tearful faces. To make the people turn back, he drew a line across the road with a stick and said, "Let no one cross this line of mine." Then he went on his way. The great multitude, unable to disobey the command of the powerful Great Being, cried out loudly, wept, and turned back. The Bodhisatta proceeded along the path by which he had come and approached him. Thus it was said: "Porisāda questioned me," and so on.

Tattha kiṃ tvaṃ icchasi nisajjanti tvaṃ attano nagaraṃ gantuṃ mama hatthato nissajjanaṃ kiṃ icchasi, tvaṃ “mayā takkasilādīsu ciraparicito saccavādī cā”ti vadasi, tasmā yathā mati te kāhāmi, yathāruci te karissāmi. Yadi me tvaṃ punehisīti sace puna tvaṃ ekaṃseneva mama santikaṃ āgamissasi.

Herein, 'What do you desire, sitting?' means, 'Do you desire release from my hand to go to your own city?' You say, "I have long been familiar in Takkasilā and other places, and I am truthful." Therefore, I will do according to your judgment, I will do as you please. 'If you come to me again' means, if you will indeed come back to my presence.

108. Paṇhe āgamanaṃ mamāti pageva mama āgamanaṃ tassa [P 0.0255] porisādassa paṭissuṇitvā pātova āgamissāmīti paṭissavaṃ katvā. Rajjaṃ niyyātayiṃ tadāti tadā porisādassa santikaṃ gantukāmo “idaṃ vo rajjaṃ paṭipajjathā”ti mātāpitūnaṃ tiyojanasatikaṃ rajjaṃ niyyātesiṃ.

108. Here, 'my coming concerning the question' (paṇhe āgamanaṃ mama) means, having already promised my coming to that Porisāda, having made a vow, 'I will come in the morning.' 'Then I handed over the kingdom' (rajjaṃ niyyātayiṃ tadā) means, at that time, desiring to go into the presence of Porisāda, I handed over the kingdom, extending three hundred yojanas, to my parents, saying, 'Accept this kingdom.'

109. Kasmā pana rajjaṃ niyyātayinti? Anussaritvā sataṃ dhammanti yasmā pana paṭiññāya saccāpanaṃ nāma sataṃ sādhūnaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ paveṇī kulavaṃso, tasmā taṃ saccapāramitādhammaṃ pubbakaṃ porāṇaṃ jinehi buddhādīhi sevitaṃ anussaritvā saccaṃ anurakkhanto tassa brāhmaṇassa dhanaṃ datvā attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā porisādaṃ upāgamiṃ.

109. But why did he hand over the kingdom? Because of 'remembering the Dhamma of the good.' Since the fulfillment of a promise is indeed the tradition and lineage of the good, the virtuous, and the great Bodhisattas, therefore, remembering that former and ancient Dhamma of the perfection of truth practiced by the Jinas, the Buddhas and others, and protecting the truth, having given wealth to that brahmin and having sacrificed my own life, I approached Porisāda.

110. Natthi me saṃsayo tatthāti tasmiṃ porisādassa santikaṃ gamane “ayaṃ maṃ kiṃ nu [V 0.0231] kho ghātessati, udāhu no”ti mayhaṃ saṃsayo natthi. “Caṇḍo sāhasiko mayā saddhiṃ ekasatakhattiye devatāya balikammakaraṇasajjo ekanteneva ghātessatī”ti jānanto eva kevalaṃ saccavācaṃ anurakkhanto attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā taṃ upāgamiṃ. Yasmā cetadevaṃ, tasmā saccena me samo natthi, esā me paramatthabhāvappattā saccapāramīti.

110. 'I have no doubt about that.' This means, in going to the presence of that Porisāda, I had no such doubt as, 'Will he kill me, or will he not?' Knowing full well, 'This fierce and violent one, ready to make a sacrificial offering to the deity with me and one hundred other Khattiyas, will certainly kill me,' it was only while protecting my word of truth and sacrificing my own life that I approached him. Because this is so, there is none equal to me in truth; this is my perfection of truth, which has reached the ultimate state.

Upāgate pana mahāsatte vikasitapuṇḍarīkapadumasassirikamassa mukhaṃ disvā “ayaṃ vigatamaraṇabhayo hutvā āgato, kissa nu kho esa ānubhāvo”ti cintento “tassa maññe dhammassa sutattā ayaṃ evaṃ tejavā [M 0.0247] nibbhayo ca jāto, ahampi taṃ sutvā tejavā nibbhayo ca bhavissāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā porisādo mahāsattaṃ āha – “suṇoma satārahagāthāyo yāsaṃ savanatthaṃ tvaṃ attano nagaraṃ gato”ti.

When the Great Being arrived, seeing his face, which was as splendid as a blooming white lotus, Porisāda thought, 'This one has come without fear of death. What could be the power behind this?' Concluding, 'I believe it is from having heard the Dhamma that he has become so radiant and fearless. I too, having heard it, will become radiant and fearless,' Porisāda made this resolution and said to the Great Being: 'Let us hear those verses worthy of the good, for the sake of hearing which you went to your city.'

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “ayaṃ porisādo pāpadhammo, imaṃ thokaṃ niggahetvā lajjāpetvā kathessāmī”ti –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta thought: 'This Porisāda is of a wicked nature. Having subdued and shamed him a little, I will speak.'

“Adhammikassa luddassa, niccaṃ lohitapāṇino;

Natthi saccaṃ kuto dhammo, kiṃ sutena karissasī”ti. (jā. 2.21.427) –

For the unrighteous and cruel one, ever with blood-stained hands, there is no truth. Whence then is Dhamma? What will you do with learning?

Vatvā puna tena suṭṭhutaraṃ sañjātasavanādarena –

After he had spoken, Porisāda, in whom a much greater reverence for listening had arisen, replied:

“Sutvā dhammaṃ vijānanti, narā kalyāṇapāpakaṃ;

Api gāthā suṇitvāna, dhamme me ramate mano”ti. (jā. 2.21.444) –

Having heard the Dhamma, people understand good and evil; even having heard a single verse, my mind delights in the Dhamma.

Vutte [P 0.0256] “ayaṃ ativiya sañjātādaro sotukāmo, handassa kathessāmī”ti cintetvā “tena hi samma, sādhukaṃ suṇohi manasikarohī”ti vatvā nandabrāhmaṇena kathitaniyāmeneva gāthānaṃ sakkaccaṃ thutiṃ katvā chakāmāvacaradevaloke ekakolāhalaṃ katvā devatāsu sādhukāraṃ dadamānāsu mahāsatto porisādassa –

When this was said, the Great Being thought, 'He has become extremely respectful and is desirous of hearing; well then, I shall teach him.' He then said, 'In that case, friend, listen well and pay close attention.' Then, having praised the verses respectfully in the very manner instructed by the brahmin Nanda, and having caused a single uproar in the six desire-realm deva worlds as the deities shouted their approval, the Great Being spoke to Porisāda:

“Sakideva [V 0.0232] mahārāja, sabbhi hoti samāgamo;

Sā naṃ saṅgati pāleti, nāsabbhi bahusaṅgamo.

Just once, great king, does association with the good occur; that association protects one, not frequent association with the wicked.

“Sabbhireva samāsetha, sabbhi kubbetha santhavaṃ;

Sataṃ saddhammamaññāya, seyyo hoti na pāpiyo.

Associate only with the good; keep company with the virtuous. Knowing the true Dhamma of the good, one becomes better, not worse.

“Jīranti ve rājarathā sucittā, attho sarīrampi jaraṃ upeti;

Satañca dhammo na jaraṃ upeti, santo have sabbhi pavedayanti.

The king's splendid chariots indeed wear out, and the body too approaches old age; but the Dhamma of the good does not approach old age—thus do the good declare it to the good.

“Nabhañca dūre pathavī ca dūre, pāraṃ samuddassa tadāhu dūre;

Tato have dūrataraṃ vadanti, satañca dhammo asatañca rājā”ti. (jā. 2.21.411-414) –

The sky is far, and the earth is far; the far shore of the ocean, they say, is far. But farther still than that, they say, is the Dhamma of the good and that of the wicked, O king.

Dhammaṃ [M 0.0248] kathesi. Tassa tena sukathitattā ceva attano ca puññānubhāvena gāthā suṇantasseva sakalasarīraṃ pañcavaṇṇāya pītiyā paripūri. So bodhisatte muducitto hutvā “samma sutasoma, dātabbayuttakaṃ hiraññādiṃ na passāmi, ekekāya gāthāya ekekaṃ varaṃ dassāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ mahāsatto “tvaṃ attanopi hitāni ajānanto parassa kiṃ nāma varaṃ dassasī”ti apasādetvā puna tena “varaṃ gaṇhathā”ti yācito sabbapaṭhamaṃ “ahaṃ cirakālaṃ taṃ arogaṃ passeyya”nti varaṃ yāci. So “ayaṃ idāni me vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khāditukāmassa mahānatthakarassa mayhameva jīvitamicchatī”ti tuṭṭhamānaso vañcetvā varassa gahitabhāvaṃ ajānanto adāsi. Mahāsatto hi upāyakusalatāya tassa ciraṃ jīvitukāmatāpadesena attano jīvitaṃ yāci. Atha “parosataṃ khattiyānaṃ jīvitaṃ dehī”ti dutiyaṃ varaṃ, tesaṃ sake raṭṭhe paṭipādanaṃ tatiyaṃ varaṃ, manussamaṃsakhādanato viramaṇaṃ catutthaṃ varaṃ yāci. So [P 0.0257] tīṇi varāni datvā catutthaṃ varaṃ adātukāmo “aññaṃ varaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vatvāpi mahāsattena nippīḷiyamāno tampi adāsiyeva.

He taught the Dhamma. Both because of how well it was spoken by him and by the power of his own merit, even as he listened to the verses, his entire body was filled with five-hued rapture. With a softened heart towards the Bodhisatta, he said, 'Friend Sutasoma, I see no suitable gold or other gift to give you; for each single verse, I will grant you a single boon.' Then the Great Being, rebuking him, said, 'You, who do not even know what is for your own welfare, what boon could you possibly grant another?' But when requested again by him, 'Accept a boon,' he first asked for the boon, 'May I see you in good health for a long time.' Delighted, he thought, 'This man desires a long life for me, who was intent on killing him and eating his flesh and am a great cause of ruin!' And so, being deceived and not understanding the nature of the boon he had accepted, he granted it. For the Great Being, through his skill in means, asked for his own life under the pretext of desiring a long life for Porisāda. Then he asked for a second boon: 'Grant life to the more than one hundred Khattiyas'; for a third boon, their restoration to their own kingdoms; and for a fourth boon, abstention from eating human flesh. Having granted the first three boons, though he was unwilling to grant the fourth and said, 'Take another boon,' being pressured by the Great Being, he granted that one as well.

Atha bodhisatto porisādaṃ nibbisevanaṃ katvā teneva rājāno mocāpetvā bhūmiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā dārakānaṃ kaṇṇato suttavaṭṭi viya saṇikaṃ rajjuyo nīharitvā porisādena ekaṃ tacaṃ āharāpetvā pāsāṇena ghaṃsitvā saccakiriyaṃ katvā tesaṃ hatthatalāni makkhesi. Taṅkhaṇaṃ eva phāsukaṃ ahosi. Dvīhatīhaṃ tattheva vasitvā te aroge kāretvā tehi saddhiṃ abhijjanakasabhāvaṃ [V 0.0233] mittasanthavaṃ kāretvā tehi saddhiṃ taṃ bārāṇasiṃ netvā rajje patiṭṭhāpetvā “appamattā hothā”ti te rājāno attano attano nagaraṃ pesetvā indapatthanagarato āgatāya attano caturaṅginiyā senāya parivuto attano nagaraṃ gato tuṭṭhapamuditena nāgarajanena samparivāriyamāno antepuraṃ pavisitvā mātāpitaro vanditvā mahātalaṃ abhiruhi.

Then the Bodhisatta, having made the man-eater renounce his practice, had the kings released and laid them on the ground. As one would draw a thread from a child’s ear, he gently removed the ropes. He had the man-eater bring a strip of bark, ground it with a stone, performed an act of truth, and anointed their palms. Instantly, they were healed. After staying there for two or three days and restoring them to health, he established an unbreakable friendship and intimacy among them. He then escorted them to Bārāṇasī and reinstated them in their kingdoms. Saying, “Be vigilant,” he sent each king back to his own city. Then, surrounded by his fourfold army that had come from Indapatta, he returned to his own city, accompanied by the delighted and rejoicing citizens. Entering the inner palace, he paid homage to his parents and ascended to the great upper chamber.

Atha mahāsatto cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ mahādānāni pavattento sīlāni paripūrento uposathaṃ upavasanto pāramiyo anubrūhesi. Tepi rājāno mahāsattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā āyupariyosāne saggapuraṃ pūrayiṃsu.

Then the Great Being, having established six alms-halls, daily dispensed great gifts, fulfilled the moral precepts, observed the uposatha, and cultivated the perfections. Those kings, too, abiding by the Great Being's advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and at the end of their lives, they filled the city of the gods.

Tadā porisādo [M 0.0249] aṅgulimālatthero ahosi, kāḷahatthiamacco sāriputtatthero, nandabrāhmaṇo ānandatthero, rukkhadevatā mahākassapatthero, rājāno buddhaparisā, mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni, sutasomamahārājā lokanātho.

At that time, the man-eater Porisāda was the Elder Aṅgulimāla, the minister Kāḷahatthi was the Elder Sāriputta, the brahmin Nanda was the Elder Ānanda, the tree deity was the Elder Mahākassapa, the kings were the Buddha's assembly, the parents were the great royal families, and King Sutasoma was the Protector of the World.

Tassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sesapāramiyopi niddhāretabbā. Tathā alīnasattucariyāvaṇṇanāya (cariyā aṭṭha. 2.74 ādayo) viya mahāsattassa guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

His remaining perfections should be determined in the same way as stated before. Likewise, the virtues and power of the Great Being should be expounded as in the commentary on the conduct of Alīnasattu (Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary 2.74 ff.).

Mahāsutasomacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the commentary on the conduct of the Great Sutasoma.

Saccapāramī niṭṭhitā.

The Perfection of Truth is concluded.

13. Suvaṇṇasāmacariyāvaṇṇanā

13. The Commentary on the Conduct of Suvaṇṇasāma

111. Terasame [P 0.0258] sāmo yadā vane āsinti himavantasmiṃ migasammatāya nāma nadiyā tīre mahati araññe sāmo nāma tāpasakumāro yadā ahosi. Sakkena abhinimmitoti sakkassa devānamindassa upadesasampattiyā jātattā sakkena nibbattito janito. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – atīte bārāṇasito avidūre nadiyā tīre eko nesādagāmo ahosi. Tattha jeṭṭhanesādassa putto jāto. Tassa “dukūlo”ti nāmamakaṃsu. Tassā eva nadiyā paratīrepi eko nesādagāmo ahosi. Tattha jeṭṭhanesādassa dhītā jātā. Tassā “pārikā”ti nāmamakaṃsu. Te ubhopi brahmalokato āgatā suddhasattā. Tesaṃ vayappattānaṃ anicchamānānaṃyeva āvāhavivāhaṃ [V 0.0234] kariṃsu. Te ubhopi kilesasamuddaṃ anotaritvā brahmāno viya ekato vasiṃsu. Na ca kiñci nesādakammaṃ karonti.

111. In the thirteenth Cariyā, the words 'When Sāma was in the forest' refer to the time when the ascetic youth named Sāma dwelt in a great wilderness in the Himālaya, on the bank of the river called Migasammatā. The phrase 'created by Sakka' means that he was brought into being and born through the successful instruction of Sakka, king of the gods. Herein is the sequential narrative: In the past, not far from Bārāṇasī, there was a village of hunters on a riverbank. There, a son was born to the chief hunter, and they named him Dukūla. On the opposite bank of that same river, there was another village of hunters. There, a daughter was born to the chief hunter, and they named her Pārikā. Both of them were pure beings who had come from the Brahmā world. When they came of age, they were joined in marriage, though they themselves were unwilling. Without descending into the ocean of defilements, they both lived together like Brahmās and did not engage in any work of a hunter.

Atha dukūlaṃ mātāpitaro “tāta, tvaṃ nesādakammaṃ na karosi, neva gharāvāsaṃ icchasi, kiṃ nāma karissasī”ti āhaṃsu. So “tumhesu anujānantesu pabbajissāmī”ti āha. “Tena hi pabbajāhī”ti. Dvepi janā himavantaṃ pavisitvā yasmiṃ ṭhāne migasammatā nāma nadī himavantato otaritvā gaṅgaṃ pattā, taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā gaṅgaṃ pahāya migasammatābhimukhā abhiruhiṃsu. Tadā [M 0.0250] sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā vissakammunā tasmiṃ ṭhāne assamaṃ māpesi. Te tattha gantvā pabbajitvā sakkadattiye assame kāmāvacaramettaṃ bhāvetvā paṭivasiṃsu. Sakkopi tesaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchati.

Then Dukūla’s parents said to him, “My dear son, you do not do the work of a hunter, nor do you desire the household life. What will you do?” He replied, “If you give your permission, I will go forth.” They said, “Then go forth.” The two of them entered the Himālaya and went to the place where the river Migasammatā, descending from the Himālaya, meets the Gaṅgā. Leaving the Gaṅgā, they ascended towards the Migasammatā. At that time, Sakka’s celestial palace showed signs of heat. Knowing the reason, Sakka had Vissakamma create a hermitage in that place. They went there, went forth, and dwelt in the hermitage given by Sakka, cultivating loving-kindness pertaining to the sense-sphere. Sakka also came to attend to them.

So ekadivasaṃ “tesaṃ cakkhū parihāyissantī”ti ñatvā upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, vo cakkhūnaṃ antarāyo paññāyati, paṭijagganakaṃ puttaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, jānāmi tumhākaṃ suddhacittataṃ, tasmā pārikāya utunikāle nābhiṃ hatthena parāmaseyyātha[P 0.0259], evaṃ vo putto jāyissati, so vo upaṭṭhahissatī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Dukūlapaṇḍito taṃ kāraṇaṃ pārikāya ācikkhitvā tassā utunikāle nābhiṃ parāmasi. Tadā bodhisatto devalokā cavitvā tassā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, sā dasamāsaccayena suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Tenevassa “suvaṇṇasāmo”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Taṃ aparabhāge vaḍḍhitvā soḷasavassuddesikampi mātāpitaro rakkhantā assame nisīdāpetvā sayameva vanamūlaphalāphalatthāya gacchanti.

One day, knowing that their eyesight would fail, Sakka approached them and said, “Venerable sirs, a danger to your eyes is foreseen. It is fitting that you should have a son to care for you. I know the purity of your minds; therefore, during Pārikā’s fertile season, you should touch her navel with your hand. In this way a son will be born to you, and he will attend to you.” Having said this, he departed. The wise Dukūla explained this to Pārikā and, during her fertile season, he touched her navel. At that moment, the Bodhisatta passed away from the world of the gods and took conception in her womb. At the end of ten months, she gave birth to a son the color of gold. For that reason, they gave him the name Suvaṇṇasāma. Later, when he had grown to be about sixteen years of age, his parents, seeking to protect him, would have him remain in the hermitage while they themselves went to gather wild roots and fruits.

Athekadivasaṃ vane phalāphalaṃ ādāya nivattitvā assamapadato avidūre meghe uṭṭhite rukkhamūlaṃ pavisitvā vammikamatthake ṭhitānaṃ sarīrato sedagandhamissake udake tasmiṃ vammikabile ṭhitassa āsivisassa nāsāpuṭaṃ paviṭṭhe āsiviso kujjhitvā nāsāvātena pahari. Dve andhā hutvā paridevamānā viraviṃsu. Atha mahāsatto “mama mātāpitaro aticirāyanti, kā nu kho tesaṃ pavattī”ti paṭimaggaṃ gantvā saddamakāsi. Te tassa saddaṃ sañjānitvā paṭisaddaṃ katvā puttasinehena “tāta sāma, idha paripantho atthi, mā āgamī”ti vatvā saddānusārena sayameva samāgamiṃsu. So “kena vo kāraṇena cakkhūni vinaṭṭhānī”ti pucchitvā “tāta, mayaṃ na jānāma, deve vassante rukkhamūle vammikamatthake ṭhitā, atha na passāmā”ti vuttamatte eva aññāsi “tattha āsivisena bhavitabbaṃ, tena kuddhena nāsāvāto vissaṭṭho bhavissatī”ti.

Then one day, having gathered fruits in the forest and returned, not far from the hermitage, when a cloud arose, they entered the foot of a tree. While they were standing on the top of an anthill, water from their bodies mixed with the scent of sweat entered the nostrils of a venomous snake dwelling in that anthill. The snake, enraged, struck with its breath. Both became blind and lamented loudly. Then the Great Being thought, "My parents are taking too long; what could be happening to them?" He went along the path and made a sound. Recognizing his voice, they responded, and out of love for their son, said, "Dear Sāma, there is danger here, do not come!" But following the sound, they themselves met him. He asked, "For what reason have you lost your eyesight?" They replied, "Dear son, we do not know. While it was raining, we were standing on the top of an anthill under a tree, and then we could not see." Hearing this, he understood, "There must have been a venomous snake there, and it must have released its angry breath."

Atha [V 0.0235] “mā cintayittha, ahaṃ vo paṭijaggissāmī”ti mātāpitaro assamaṃ netvā tesaṃ rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādisañcaraṇaṭṭhāne rajjuke bandhi. Tato paṭṭhāya te assame ṭhapetvā vanamūlaphalāphalāni āharati, pātova vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sammajjati, pānīyaṃ āharati, paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpeti, dantakaṭṭhamukhodakāni [M 0.0251] datvā madhuraphalāphalaṃ deti. Tehi mukhe vikkhālite sayaṃ paribhuñjitvā mātāpitaro vanditvā tesaṃ avidūreyeva acchati – “kiṃ nu kho ime āṇāpentī”ti. Visesena ca mettaṃ bahulamakāsi, tenassa sattā appaṭikkūlā ahesuṃ[P 0.0260]. Yathā cassa sattā, evaṃ sattānaṃ so bodhisatto appaṭikkūlo. Evaṃ so divase divase phalāphalatthāya araññaṃ gacchantopi āgacchantopi migagaṇaparivuto eva ahosi. Sīhabyagghādivipakkhasattāpi tena saddhiṃ ativiya vissatthā, mettānubhāvena panassa vasanaṭṭhāne aññamaññaṃ tiracchānagatā muducittataṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Iti so sabbattha mettānubhāvena abhīrū anutrāsī brahmā viya avero vihāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “pavane sīhabyagghe ca, mettāyamupanāmayi”ntiādi.

Then, saying, "Do not worry, I will take care of you," he led his parents to the hermitage and tied ropes in the places where they would move about during the day and night. From then on, keeping them in the hermitage, he would bring roots and fruits from the forest, sweep their dwelling place in the morning, fetch drinking water, prepare what was to be eaten, give them tooth-sticks and water for washing their mouths, and offer sweet fruits. After they had rinsed their mouths and he himself had eaten, he would pay respects to his parents and stay not far from them, thinking, "What might they command?" He especially cultivated abundant loving-kindness, so beings became non-hostile towards him. Just as beings were towards him, so too was the Bodhisatta non-hostile towards beings. Thus, day after day, whether going to the forest for fruits or returning, he was always surrounded by herds of deer. Even naturally hostile creatures like lions and tigers became very trusting of him. Due to the power of his loving-kindness, in his dwelling place, the animals attained gentle hearts towards one another. Thus, through the power of loving-kindness everywhere, he lived fearless, untroubled, and free from enmity like a Brahmā. Therefore, it is said: "In the forest, to lions and tigers, he brought loving-kindness," and so on.

Tattha mettāyamupanāmayinti ma-kāro padasandhikaro, mettābhāvanāya kurūrakammante sīhabyagghepi phari, pageva sesasatteti adhippāyo. Atha vā mettā ayati pavattati etenāti mettāyo, mettābhāvanā. Taṃ mettāyaṃ upanāmayiṃ sattesu anodhiso upanesiṃ. “Sīhabyagghehī”tipi pāṭho. Tassattho – na kevalamahameva, atha kho pavane sīhabyagghehi, yasmiṃ mahāvane tadā ahaṃ viharāmi, tattha sīhabyagghehi saddhiṃ ahaṃ sattesu mettaṃ upanāmesiṃ. Sīhabyagghāpi hi tadā mamānubhāvena sattesu mettacittataṃ paṭilabhiṃsu, pageva itare sattāti dasseti.

Here, in "mettāyamupanāmayi," the letter "ma" is a euphonic link. The meaning is that through the cultivation of loving-kindness, he pervaded even fierce-natured lions and tigers, what to say of other beings. Alternatively, "mettāyo" is that by which loving-kindness (mettā) extends or proceeds, thus it refers to the cultivation of loving-kindness. That loving-kindness I brought, I brought it to beings without distinction. The reading "sīhabyagghehī" also exists. Its meaning is: Not only I, but in the forest in which I then lived, I, together with the lions and tigers, extended loving-kindness to beings. For by my influence, even the lions and tigers at that time attained a mind of loving-kindness towards beings, what to say of other creatures—this is what it shows.

112. Pasadamigavarāhehīti pasadamigehi ceva vanasūkarehi ca. Parivāretvāti etehi attānaṃ parivāritaṃ katvā tasmiṃ araññe vasiṃ.

112. `Pasadamigavarāhehīti` refers to both spotted deer and wild boars. `Parivāretvāti` means: having made myself surrounded by these, I dwelt in that forest.

113. Idāni tadā attano mettābhāvanāya laddhaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ matthakappattiñcassa dassetuṃ “na maṃ koci uttasatī”ti osānagāthamāha. Tassattho – sasabiḷārādiko bhīrukajātikopi koci satto maṃ na uttasati na ubbijjeti. Ahampi kassaci sīhabyagghāditiracchānato yakkhādiamanussato luddalohitapāṇimanussatoti kutocipi na bhāyāmi. Kasmā? Yasmā mettābalenupatthaddho cirakālaṃ bhāvitāya mettāpāramitāyānubhāvena upatthambhito tasmiṃ pavane mahāaraññe tadā ramāmi abhiramāmīti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

113. Now, to reveal the benefit he gained from his cultivation of loving-kindness and the pinnacle of its attainment, he speaks the concluding verse: "No one is frightened of me." Its meaning is—no creature, not even one of a timid nature such as a hare or a cat, is frightened of me or alarmed by me. Nor do I fear anything—whether from beasts such as lions and tigers, from non-human beings such as yakkhas, or from cruel, bloody-handed humans. Why? Because, fortified by the power of loving-kindness, supported by the power of the long-cultivated perfection of loving-kindness, I then delighted and rejoiced in that great forest wilderness. The rest is easily understood.

Evaṃ [M 0.0252][V 0.0236] pana mahāsatto sabbasatte mettāyanto mātāpitaro ca sādhukaṃ paṭijagganto ekadivasaṃ araññato madhuraphalāphalaṃ āharitvā assame ṭhapetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā “pānīyaṃ [P 0.0261] ādāya āgamissāmī”ti migagaṇaparivuto dve mige ekato katvā tesaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ pānīyaghaṭaṃ ṭhapetvā hatthena gahetvā nadītitthaṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ samaye bārāṇasiyaṃ pīḷiyakkho nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. So migamaṃsalobhena mātaraṃ rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā sannaddhapañcāvudho himavantaṃ pavisitvā mige vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā caranto migasammataṃ nadiṃ patvā anupubbena sāmassa pānīyagahaṇatitthaṃ patto. Migapadavalañjaṃ disvā gacchanto taṃ tathā gacchantaṃ disvā “mayā ettakaṃ kālaṃ evaṃ vicaranto manusso na diṭṭhapubbo, devo nu kho esa nāgo nu kho, sacāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchissāmi, sahasā pakkameyyāti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ etaṃ vijjhitvā dubbalaṃ katvā puccheyya”nti cintetvā mahāsattaṃ nhatvā vākacīraṃ nivāsetvā ajinacammaṃ ekaṃsaṃ karitvā pānīyaghaṭaṃ pūretvā ukkhipitvā vāmaṃsakūṭe ṭhapanakāle “idāni taṃ vijjhituṃ samayo”ti visapītena sarena dakkhiṇapasse vijjhi. Saro vāmapassena nikkhami. Tassa viddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā migagaṇo bhīto palāyi.

Then the Great Being, extending loving-kindness to all beings and diligently caring for his parents, one day brought sweet fruits from the forest and placed them in the hermitage. After paying respects to his parents, he said, 'I will fetch water and return.' Surrounded by a herd of deer, he placed two deer side by side, set a water pot on their backs, and holding it with his hand, went to the watering place on the river. At that time, King Pīḷiyakkha ruled in Benares. Driven by a craving for deer meat, he entrusted the kingdom to his mother, armed himself with the five weapons, entered the Himalayas, and wandered about, killing deer and eating their flesh. He came to the river frequented by deer and, in due course, reached the watering place where Sāma drew water. Seeing deer tracks, he followed them and saw him walking in that way. He thought, 'In all my time wandering like this, I have never before seen such a man. Is he a god or a nāga? If I approach and question him, he might suddenly flee. What if I were to shoot him, weaken him, and then ask?' Having so thought, just as the Great Being—after bathing, putting on his bark garment, and draping a deerskin over one shoulder—had filled the water pot and was lifting it to place on his left shoulder, the king shot him in the right side with a poisoned arrow. The arrow exited through his left side. Realizing he had been shot, the herd of deer fled in fear.

Sāmapaṇḍito pana viddhopi pānīyaghaṭaṃ yathā vā tathā vā anavasumbhetvā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā saṇikaṃ otāretvā vālukaṃ byūhitvā ṭhapetvā disaṃ vavatthapetvā mātāpitūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānadisābhāgena sīsaṃ katvā nipajjitvā mukhena lohitaṃ chaḍḍetvā “mama koci verī nāma natthi, mamapi katthaci veraṃ nāma natthī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

But Sāma the wise, though wounded, did not let the water pot fall this way or that. Establishing mindfulness, he slowly lowered it, arranged the sand, and set it down. Determining the direction, he lay down with his head toward the place where his parents dwelt, and spitting blood from his mouth, he said, 'I have no enemy whatsoever, nor do I have enmity for anyone anywhere,' and then uttered this verse:

“Ko nu maṃ usunā vijjhi, pamattaṃ udahārakaṃ;

Khattiyo brāhmaṇo vesso, ko maṃ viddhā nilīyatī”ti. (jā. 2.22.296);

"Who now has shot me with an arrow, a heedless water-carrier? A noble, a brahmin, or a merchant—who, having shot me, hides?"

Taṃ [P 0.0262] sutvā rājā “ayaṃ mayā vijjhitvā pathaviyaṃ pātitopi neva maṃ akkosati na paribhāsati, mama hadayamaṃsaṃ sambāhanto viya piyavacanena samudācarati, gamissāmissa santika”nti cintetvā upasaṅkamitvā attānaṃ attanā ca viddhabhāvaṃ āvikatvā “ko vā tvaṃ kassa vā putto”ti mahāsattaṃ pucchi.

Hearing this, the king thought, 'Though I shot him and made him fall to the earth, he neither curses nor insults me. Instead, he speaks kindly, as if massaging the very flesh of my heart. I will go to him.' Having so thought, he approached him, revealed who he was and that he himself had shot him, and asked the Great Being, 'Who are you, and whose son are you?'

So [M 0.0253] “sāmo nāmāhaṃ dukūlapaṇḍitassa nāma nesādaisino putto, kissa pana maṃ vijjhī”ti āha. So paṭhamaṃ “migasaññāyā”ti musāvādaṃ vatvā “ahaṃ imaṃ niraparādhaṃ akāraṇena [V 0.0237] vijjhi”nti anusocitvā yathābhūtaṃ āvikatvā tassa mātāpitūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitvā tattha gantvā tesaṃ attānaṃ āvikatvā tehi katapaṭisanthāro “sāmo mayā viddho”ti vatvā te paridevante sokasamāpanne “yaṃ sāmena kattabbaṃ paricārikakammaṃ, taṃ katvā ahaṃ vo upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti samassāsetvā sāmassa santikaṃ ānesi. Te tattha gantvā nānappakāraṃ paridevitvā tassa ure hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā “puttassa me sarīre usumā vattateva, visavegena visaññitaṃ āpanno bhavissatīti nibbisabhāvatthāya saccakiriyaṃ karissāmā”ti cintetvā –

“I am known as Sāma, the son of the ascetic named Dukūlapaṇḍita. Why then did you shoot me?” he said. At first, the king spoke a falsehood, saying, “Thinking it was a deer,” but then he lamented, “I have shot this innocent one without reason.” Then, having revealed the truth, he asked for the dwelling place of Sāma's parents. Going there, he disclosed himself to them. Having been welcomed by them, when he said, “Sāma has been shot by me,” they wailed, overcome by grief. To console them, he said, “I will attend to you by performing all the duties of service that Sāma would have done.” He brought them to Sāma’s side. They went there and wailed in various ways. Placing their hands on his chest, they thought, “Warmth still remains in my son’s body. He must have become unconscious due to the force of the poison. To counteract the poison, we shall perform an act of truth.”

“Yaṃ kiñcitthi kataṃ puññaṃ, mayhañceva pitucca te;

Sabbena tena kusalena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatū”ti. (jā. 2.22.388) –

"Whatever merit has been made by me, and by your father, too; by all that is wholesome, may Sāma’s poison be destroyed!"

Mātarā,

By the mother.

“Yaṃ kiñcitthi kataṃ puññaṃ, mayhañceva mātucca te;

Sabbena tena kusalena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatū”ti. (jā. 2.22.396) –

"Whatever merit has been made by me, and by your mother, too; by all that is wholesome, may Sāma’s poison be destroyed!"

Pitarā,

By the father.

“Pabbatyāhaṃ gandhamādane, cirarattanivāsinī;

Na me piyataro koci, añño sāmena vijjati;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatū”ti. (jā. 2.22.398) –

"On Mount Gandhamādana I dwell, a long-time resident. No one is dearer to me than Sāma; by this utterance of truth, may Sāma’s poison be destroyed!"

Devatāya ca saccakiriyāya katāya mahāsatto khippaṃ vuṭṭhāsi. Padumapattapalāse udakabindu viya vinivaṭṭetvā ābādho vigato. Viddhaṭṭhānaṃ arogaṃ pākatikameva ahosi. Mātāpitūnaṃ cakkhūni uppajjiṃsu. Iti [P 0.0263] mahāsattassa arogatā, mātāpitūnañca cakkhupaṭilābho, aruṇuggamanaṃ, tesaṃ catunnampi assameyeva avaṭṭhānanti sabbaṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva ahosi.

And when the act of truth had been performed by the deity, the Great Being quickly arose. The affliction vanished, rolling away like a drop of water from a lotus leaf. The wound became healthy, just as it was naturally. The eyes of his parents arose. Thus, the Great Being's recovery to health, his parents' regaining of their sight, the rising of the dawn, and the establishment of all four of them in the hermitage—all this happened in a single moment.

Atha [V 0.0238] mahāsatto raññā saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “dhammaṃ cara, mahārājā”tiādinā (jā. 2.22.411-412) dhammaṃ desetvā uttarimpi ovaditvā pañca sīlāni adāsi[M 0.0254]. So tassa ovādaṃ sirasā paṭiggahetvā vanditvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyano ahosi. Bodhisattopi saddhiṃ mātāpitūhi abhiññāsamāpattiyo nibbattetvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Then the Great Being, having exchanged greetings with the king, taught him the Dhamma, beginning with “Practice the Dhamma, great king.” He further advised him and gave him the five precepts. The king, having accepted his advice with his head, paid homage and went to Benares, where he performed meritorious deeds such as generosity and became destined for a heavenly realm. The Bodhisatta, together with his parents, developed the supernormal knowledges and meditative attainments. At the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

Tadā rājā ānandatthero ahosi, devadhītā uppalavaṇṇā, sakko anuruddho, pitā mahākassapatthero, mātā bhaddakāpilānī, sāmapaṇḍito lokanātho.

At that time, the king was the Elder Ānanda, the goddess was Uppalavaṇṇā, Sakka was the Elder Anuruddha, the father was the Elder Mahākassapa, the mother was Bhaddakāpilānī, and Sāma the wise was the Protector of the World.

Tassa heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva sesapāramiyo niddhāretabbā. Tathā visapītena sallena dakkhiṇapassena pavisitvā vāmapassato vinivijjhanavasena viddhopi kiñci kāyavikāraṃ akatvā udakaghaṭassa bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipanaṃ, vadhake aññātepi ñāte viya cittavikārābhāvo, piyavacanena samudācāro, mātāpituupaṭṭhānapuññato mayhaṃ parihānīti anusocanamattaṃ, aroge jāte rañño kāruññaṃ mettañca upaṭṭhāpetvā dhammadesanā, ovādadānanti evamādayo guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

The remaining perfections should be determined in the same way as stated previously. Likewise, even when pierced by a poisoned arrow, which entered from the right side and exited from the left, without showing any bodily contortion, placing the water pot on the ground; the absence of any mental agitation, treating the assailant as if known even when he was unknown; behaving with kind words; lamenting only that his merit from attending to his parents would decline; establishing compassion and loving-kindness in the king when he became well, and giving a Dhamma discourse and advice—such displays of virtuous power should be elucidated.

Suvaṇṇasāmacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The description of the conduct of Suvaṇṇasāma is concluded.

14. Ekarājacariyāvaṇṇanā

14. The Commentary on the Ekarāja Cariyā

114. Cuddasame ekarājāti vissutoti ekarājāti iminā anvatthanāmena jambudīpatale pākaṭo.

114. In the fourteenth, “renowned as Ekarāja”: by this meaningful name, Ekarāja, he was famous throughout Jambudīpa.

Mahāsatto hi tadā bārāṇasirañño putto hutvā nibbatti. Vayappatto sabbasippanipphattiṃ patto hutvā pitu accayena rajjaṃ kārento kusalasīlācārasaddhāsutādianaññasādhāraṇaguṇavisesayogena [P 0.0264] pāramiparibhāvanena ca jambudīpatale adutiyattā padhānabhāvena ca “ekarājā”ti pakāsanāmo ahosi. Paramaṃ sīlaṃ adhiṭṭhāyāti suparisuddhakāyikavācasikasaṃvarasaṅkhātañceva suparisuddhamanosamācārasaṅkhātañca paramaṃ uttamaṃ dasakusalakammapathasīlaṃ [V 0.0239] samādānavasena ca avītikkamanavasena ca adhiṭṭhahitvā anuṭṭhahitvā. Pasāsāmi mahāmahinti tiyojanasatike kāsiraṭṭhe mahatiṃ mahiṃ anusāsāmi rajjaṃ kāremi.

At that time, the Great Being was born as the son of the king of Bārāṇasī. Having reached maturity and attained proficiency in all arts, upon his father’s passing, while ruling the kingdom, he became known by the proclaimed name “Ekarāja” (Sole King). This was due to his association with distinguished and incomparable qualities such as virtue, good conduct, faith, and learning, and through the cultivation of the perfections, by which he was without a second and preeminent in Jambudīpa. “Having firmly resolved upon the highest virtue”: that is, having resolved upon and practiced, by way of undertaking and not transgressing, the supreme, excellent virtue of the ten wholesome courses of action, which is defined as supremely purified bodily and verbal restraint and supremely purified mental conduct. “I rule the great earth”: thus, I instruct the great earth, governing the Kāsi kingdom spanning three hundred leagues.

115. Dasakusalakammapatheti [M 0.0255] pāṇātipātāveramaṇi yāva sammādiṭṭhīti etasmiṃ dasavidhe kusalakammapathe, ete vā anavasesato samādāya vattāmi. Catūhi saṅgahavatthūhīti dānaṃ piyavacanaṃ atthacariyā samānattatāti imehi catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi saṅgaṇhanakāraṇehi yadā ekarājāti vissuto homi, tadā yathārahaṃ mahājanaṃ saṅgaṇhāmīti sambandho.

115. “In the tenfold wholesome path of action”: I abide in this tenfold path of wholesome action, from abstaining from killing living beings up to right view, having undertaken it completely and without exception. “By the four bases of sympathy”—giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and equality—by these four bases of sympathy, which are causes for gathering others, when I became renowned as Ekarāja, I then gathered the great populace as was fitting. This is the connection.

116. Evanti dasakusalakammapathasīlaparipūraṇaṃ catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi mahājanasaṅgaṇhananti yathāvuttena iminā ākārena appamattassa. Idhaloke parattha cāti imasmiṃ loke yaṃ appamajjanaṃ, tattha diṭṭhadhammike atthe, paraloke yaṃ appamajjanaṃ tattha samparāyike atthe appamattassa me satoti attho. Dabbasenoti evaṃnāmako kosalarājā. Upagantvāti caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā abbhuyyānavasena mama rajjaṃ upagantvā. Acchindanto puraṃ mamāti mama bārāṇasinagaraṃ balakkārena gaṇhanto.

116. “Thus”: this refers to the fulfillment of the virtue of the ten wholesome courses of action and the gathering of the multitude through the four bases of sympathy. In this manner described, for one who is heedful. “Here in this world and in the next”: in this world, heedfulness is for the sake of benefits visible in this life; in the next world, heedfulness is for the sake of benefits in the future life. This is the meaning of “of me who is heedful.” “Dabbaseno”: a Kosala king of this name. “Upagantvā” (having approached): having marshaled a fourfold army and approached my kingdom by way of invasion. “Acchindanto puraṃ mama” (seizing my city): seizing my city of Bārāṇasī by force.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – mahāsatto hi tadā nagarassa catūsu dvāresu catasso majjhe ekaṃ nivesanadvāre ekanti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā kapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ rakkhati, uposathakammaṃ karoti, khantimettānuddayasampanno aṅke nisinnaṃ puttaṃ paritosayamāno viya sabbasatte paritosayamāno dhammena rajjaṃ kāreti. Tasseko amacco antepuraṃ padussitvā aparabhāge pākaṭova jāto. Amaccā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā pariggaṇhanto taṃ attanā paccakkhato ñatvā taṃ amaccaṃ pakkosāpetvā “andhabāla, ayuttaṃ te kataṃ, na tvaṃ mama vijite vasituṃ arahasi, attano dhanañca [P 0.0265] puttadārañca gahetvā aññattha yāhī”ti raṭṭhā pabbājesi.

Herein is the sequential story: at that time, the Great Being had six alms halls built—four at the four gates of the city, one in the middle, and one at the gate of his residence—and gave alms to the poor, the needy, and others.
