He observed the moral precepts, performed the Uposatha duties, and, being endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, he ruled righteously, delighting all beings as if delighting a son seated on his lap. One of his ministers corrupted the inner quarters of the palace, and this later became public. The ministers reported it to the king. The king, investigating and knowing it for himself firsthand, summoned that minister and said, “Blind fool, you have done what is improper. You do not deserve to live in my domain. Take your wealth, children, and wife, and go elsewhere!” Thus, he banished him from the kingdom.

So kosalajanapadaṃ gantvā dabbasenaṃ nāma kosalarājānaṃ upaṭṭhahanto anukkamena tassa vissāsiko hutvā ekadivasaṃ taṃ rājānaṃ āha – “deva, bārāṇasirajjaṃ nimmakkhikamadhupaṭalasadisaṃ, atimuduko rājā, sukheneva taṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhituṃ sakkosī”ti. Dabbaseno bārāṇasirañño mahānubhāvatāya tassa vacanaṃ asaddahanto manusse pesetvā [M 0.0256] kāsiraṭṭhe gāmaghātādīni kāretvā tesaṃ corānaṃ bodhisattena dhanaṃ datvā vissajjitabhāvaṃ sutvā “ativiya dhammiko rājā”ti ñatvā “bārāṇasirajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti balavāhanaṃ ādāya niyyāsi[V 0.0240]. Atha bārāṇasirañño mahāyodhā “kosalarājā āgacchatī”ti sutvā “amhākaṃ rajjasīmaṃ anokkamantameva naṃ pothetvā gaṇhāmā”ti attano rañño vadiṃsu.

He went to the Kosala country and, while attending upon the Kosalan king named Dabbasena, he gradually became his confidant. One day he said to that king: “Your Majesty, the kingdom of Bārāṇasī is like a honeycomb free of flies; the king is very mild. You can seize that kingdom with ease.” Dabbasena, not believing his words due to the great power of the king of Bārāṇasī, sent men to the Kāsi country and had them commit village raids and other such acts. When he heard that the Bodhisatta had given wealth to those thieves and dismissed them, he realized, “The king is exceedingly righteous.” Thinking, “I will seize the kingdom of Bārāṇasī,” he set out with his army and transport. Then, the great warriors of the king of Bārāṇasī, hearing that the Kosalan king was coming, said to their own king: “Let us crush and capture him before he even crosses our kingdom’s border.”

Bodhisatto “tātā, maṃ nissāya aññesaṃ kilamanakiccaṃ natthi, rajjatthikā rajjaṃ gaṇhantu, mā gamitthā”ti nivāresi. Kosalarājā janapadamajjhaṃ pāvisi. Mahāyodhā punapi rañño tatheva vadiṃsu. Rājā purimanayeneva nivāresi. Dabbaseno bahinagare ṭhatvā “rajjaṃ vā detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti ekarājassa sāsanaṃ pesesi. Ekarājā “natthi mayā yuddhaṃ, rajjaṃ gaṇhātū”ti paṭisāsanaṃ pesesi. Punapi mahāyodhā “deva, na mayaṃ kosalarañño nagaraṃ pavisituṃ dema, bahinagareyeva naṃ pothetvā gaṇhāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā purimanayeneva nivāretvā nagaradvārāni avāpurāpetvā mahātale pallaṅkamajjhe nisīdi. Dabbaseno mahantena balavāhanena nagaraṃ pavisitvā ekampi paṭisattuṃ apassanto sabbarajjaṃ hatthagataṃ katvā rājanivesanaṃ gantvā mahātalaṃ āruyha niraparādhaṃ bodhisattaṃ gaṇhāpetvā āvāṭe nikhaṇāpesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

The Bodhisatta said, "My dear ones, there is no need for others to exert themselves on my account. Let those who desire the kingdom take it; do not go." Thus he restrained them. The Kosala king entered the middle of the country. The great warriors again spoke to the king in the same way. The king restrained them as before. Dabbasena, standing outside the city, sent a message to Ekarāja, saying, "Either give up the kingdom or fight." Ekarāja sent back a message, saying, "I will not fight; let him take the kingdom." Again, the great warriors said, "Your Majesty, we will not allow the Kosala king to enter the city. Let us strike him down outside the city and seize him." The king restrained them as before, had the city gates opened, and sat on a throne in the middle of the great hall. Dabbasena entered the city with a great army and many vehicles. Seeing no opponent at all, he took control of the entire kingdom, went to the royal residence, ascended to the great hall, and had the innocent Bodhisatta seized and buried in a pit. Thus it is said:

“Dabbaseno upagantvā, acchindanto puraṃ mama.

"Dabbasena, having approached, seized my city.

117.

117.

“Rājūpajīve nigame, sabalaṭṭhe saraṭṭhake;

Sabbaṃ hatthagataṃ katvā, kāsuyā nikhaṇī mama”nti.

"Having brought under his hand all those dependent on the king, the towns, the army, and the country, he buried me in a pit."

Tattha rājūpajīveti amaccapārisajjabrāhmaṇagahapatiādike rājānaṃ upanissāya jīvante. Nigameti negame. Sabalaṭṭheti senāpariyāpannatāya bale tiṭṭhantīti balaṭṭhā, hatthārohādayo, balaṭṭhehi sahāti sabalaṭṭhe. Saraṭṭhaketi [P 0.0266] sajanapade, rājūpajīve nigame ca aññañca sabbaṃ hatthagataṃ katvā. Kāsuyā nikhaṇī mamanti sabalavāhanaṃ sakalaṃ mama rajjaṃ gahetvā mampi galappamāṇe āvāṭe nikhaṇāpesi. Jātakepi –

Therein, 'rājūpajīve' refers to ministers, courtiers, brahmins, householders, and the like, who live in dependence on the king. 'Nigame' means the market towns. 'Sabalaṭṭhe' means those who stand in the army, such as elephant riders and others; thus, 'sabalaṭṭhe' means together with the army. 'Saraṭṭhake' means with the country. [This is all part of] having brought everything under his hand: those who live by the king, the market towns, and all else. 'Kāsuyā nikhaṇī mamanti' means having seized my entire kingdom along with its army and vehicles, he had me buried in a pit up to my neck. In the Jātaka as well:

“Anuttare [M 0.0257] kāmaguṇe samiddhe, bhutvāna pubbe vasi ekarājā;

So dāni dugge narakamhi khitto, nappajjahe vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇa”nti. (jā. 1.4.9) –

"Formerly, King Ekarāja lived having enjoyed supreme, flourishing sensual pleasures; now he is cast into a dreadful hell, yet he does not relinquish his former beauty and strength."

Āvāṭe [V 0.0241] khittabhāvo āgato. Jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (jā. aṭṭha. 3.4.9) pana “sikkāya pakkhipāpetvā uttarummāre heṭṭhāsīsakaṃ olambesī”ti vuttaṃ.

The state of being thrown into a pit has been mentioned. In the Jātaka commentary, however, it is said: "Having had him placed in a net basket, they hung him head downwards from the northern lintel."

Mahāsatto corarājānaṃ ārabbha mettaṃ bhāvetvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā kāsuto uggantvā ākāse pallaṅkena nisīdi. Tena vuttaṃ –

The great being, developing loving-kindness towards the robber king, performed the preliminary work for the kasiṇa meditation, produced the jhānas and the higher knowledges, rose up from the pit, and sat cross-legged in the sky. Thus it was said:

118.

118.

“Amaccamaṇḍalaṃ rajjaṃ, phītaṃ antepuraṃ mama;

Acchinditvāna gahitaṃ, piyaputtaṃva passaha”nti.

"Though he seized and took my circle of ministers, my kingdom, and my prosperous inner palace, I regarded him as a beloved son."

Tattha amaccamaṇḍalanti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ rājakicce raññā amā saha vattantīti amaccā, saddhiṃ vā tesaṃ maṇḍalaṃ samūhaṃ. Phītanti balavāhanena nagarajanapadādīhi samiddhaṃ rajjaṃ. Itthāgāradāsidāsaparijanehi ceva vatthābharaṇādiupabhogūpakaraṇehi ca samiddhaṃ mama antepurañca acchinditvā gahitakaṃ gaṇhantaṃ amittarājānaṃ yāya attano piyaputtaṃva passiṃ ahaṃ, tāya evaṃbhūtāya mettāya me samo sakalaloke natthi, tasmā evaṃbhūtā esā me mettāpāramī paramatthapāramibhāvaṃ pattāti adhippāyo.

Therein, 'amaccamaṇḍala' means ministers who are with the king in various royal duties, or their assembly, their group. 'Phīta' refers to a prosperous kingdom, thriving with an army, vehicles, cities, and rural areas. The enemy king seized and took my inner palace, which was flourishing with women's quarters, male and female servants, attendants, and replete with garments, ornaments, and other articles of enjoyment and use; yet I regarded him as my own dear son. Because of such loving-kindness, there is no one in the entire world equal to me. Therefore, this perfection of loving-kindness of mine has reached the state of an ultimate perfection—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ pana mahāsatte taṃ corarājānaṃ ārabbha mettaṃ pharitvā ākāse pallaṅkena nisinne tassa sarīre dāho uppajji. So “ḍayhāmi ḍayhāmī”ti bhūmiyaṃ aparāparaṃ parivattati. “Kimeta”nti vutte, mahārāja, tumhe niraparādhaṃ dhammikarājānaṃ āvāṭe nikhaṇāpayitthāti. “Tena hi vegena gantvā taṃ uddharathā”ti āha. Purisā gantvā taṃ rājānaṃ ākāse pallaṅkena nisinnaṃ disvā āgantvā [P 0.0267] dabbasenassa ārocesuṃ. So vegena gantvā vanditvā khamāpetvā “tumhākaṃ rajjaṃ tumheva kāretha, ahaṃ vo core paṭibāhessāmī”ti vatvā tassa duṭṭhāmaccassa rājāṇaṃ kāretvā pakkāmi. Bodhisattopi rajjaṃ amaccānaṃ niyyātetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā mahājanaṃ sīlādiguṇesu patiṭṭhāpetvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokaparāyano [M 0.0258] ahosi.

Then, as the great being sat cross-legged in the air, suffusing that robber king with loving-kindness, a burning sensation arose in the robber king's body. He rolled back and forth on the ground, crying, "I am burning, I am burning!" When it was asked, "What is this?", the reply was, "Great king, you had an innocent and righteous king buried in a pit." "Then quickly go and lift him out," the king commanded. The men went and saw that king sitting cross-legged in the air. They returned and reported this to Dabbasena. He hurried there, paid homage, begged for forgiveness, and said, "You yourself should rule your kingdom. I will keep the robbers away for you." Having made that wicked minister king, he departed. The Bodhisatta, after entrusting the kingdom to his ministers, went forth into the ascetic life. He established the people in virtues such as morality and, at the end of his life, was destined for the Brahma world.

Tadā dabbaseno ānandatthero ahosi, ekarājā lokanātho.

At that time, Dabbasena was the Elder Ānanda, and Ekarāja was the Lord of the World.

Tassa divase divase chasu dānasālāsu chasatasahassavissajjanena paccatthikarañño sakalarajjapariccāgena ca dānapāramī, niccasīlauposathakammavasena pabbajitassa anavasesasīlasaṃvaravasena ca sīlapāramī, pabbajjāvasena jhānādhigamavasena ca nekkhammapāramī, sattānaṃ [V 0.0242] hitāhitavicāraṇavasena dānasīlādisaṃvidahanavasena ca paññāpāramī, dānādipuññasambhārassa abbhussahanavasena kāmavitakkādivinodanavasena ca vīriyapāramī, duṭṭhāmaccassa dabbasenarañño ca aparādhasahanavasena khantipāramī, yathāpaṭiññaṃ dānādinā avisaṃvādanavasena ca saccapāramī, dānādīnaṃ acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānavasena adhiṭṭhānapāramī, paccatthikepi ekantena hitūpasaṃhāravasena mettājhānanibbattanena ca mettāpāramī, duṭṭhāmaccena dabbasenena ca katāparādhe hitesīhi attano amaccādīhi nibbattite upakāre ca ajjhupekkhaṇena rajjasukhappattakāle paccatthikaraññā narake khittakāle samānacittatāya ca upekkhāpāramī veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

His perfection of generosity should be understood from his daily distribution of six hundred thousand in the six alms halls, and from his renunciation of the entire kingdom to the hostile king. His perfection of morality, from his constant observance of the precepts and Uposatha duties, and from the complete moral restraint of one gone forth. His perfection of renunciation, from his going forth and his attainment of meditative absorption. His perfection of wisdom, from his discernment of the welfare and harm of beings, and from his arranging of generosity, virtue, and so forth. His perfection of energy, from his energetic undertaking of the accumulation of merit through generosity and the like, and from his dispelling of thoughts of sensual desire and so forth. His perfection of patience, from his endurance of the offenses of the wicked minister and of King Dabbasena. His perfection of truthfulness, from his not deviating from his pledges regarding generosity and the like. His perfection of determination, from his unwavering undertaking and resolve regarding generosity and other virtues. His perfection of loving-kindness, from his bringing about of welfare absolutely even for enemies, and from his generation of the loving-kindness meditation. His perfection of equanimity, from his looking on with equanimity at the offenses committed by the wicked minister and by Dabbasena, and at the help rendered by his own ministers and others wishing his welfare, and from his maintaining an even mind both when attaining royal happiness and when cast into a pit by a hostile king. For this has been said:

“Panujja dukkhena sukhaṃ janinda, sukhena vā dukkhamasayhasāhi;

Ubhayattha santo abhinibbutattā, sukhe ca dukkhe ca bhavanti tulyā”ti. (jā. 1.4.12);

“Having dispelled happiness with suffering, O lord of men, or suffering with happiness, O invincible one; being peaceful in both, having attained complete extinguishment, they are equal in happiness and suffering.”

Yasmā panettha mettāpāramī atisayavatī, tasmā tadatthadīpanatthaṃ sā eva pāḷi āruḷhā. Tathā idha mahāsattassa sabbasattesu orasaputte viya samānukampatādayo guṇavisesā niddhāretabbāti.

Since the perfection of loving-kindness is pre-eminent here, therefore that very Pāli text is cited to elucidate its meaning. Likewise, in this context, the special qualities of the Great Being, such as equal compassion toward all beings as if they were his own children, should be understood.

Ekarājacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Conduct of Ekarāja is completed.

Mettāpāramī niṭṭhitā.

The perfection of loving-kindness is completed.

15. Mahālomahaṃsacariyāvaṇṇanā

15. The Account of the Conduct of Mahālomahaṃsa

119. Pannarasame [M 0.0259][P 0.0268] “susāne seyyaṃ kappemī”ti etthāyaṃ anupubbikathā –

119. In the fifteenth, regarding “I make my bed in the charnel ground,” herein is the introductory story:

Mahāsatto hi tadā mahati uḷārabhoge kule nibbattitvā vuddhimanvāya disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike garuvāsaṃ vasanto sabbasippānaṃ nipphattiṃ patvā kulagharaṃ āgantvā mātāpitūnaṃ accayena ñātakehi “kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapehī”ti yāciyamānopi aniccatāmanasikāramukhena sabbabhavesu abhivaḍḍhamānasaṃvego kāye ca asubhasaññaṃ paṭilabhitvā gharāvāsapalibodhādhibhūtaṃ [V 0.0243] kilesagahanaṃ anogāhetvāva cirakālasamparicitaṃ nekkhammajjhāsayaṃ upabrūhayamāno mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya pabbajitukāmo hutvā puna cintesi – “sacāhaṃ pabbajissāmi, guṇasambhāvanāpākaṭo bhavissāmī”ti.

At that time, the Great Being was born into a great family of abundant wealth. Growing up, he lived as a pupil under a teacher famous in all directions, and having attained proficiency in all crafts, he returned to his family home. After the demise of his parents, though urged by his relatives, “Establish the household,” yet, by way of reflecting on impermanence, his sense of urgency regarding all states of existence ever increased. He also gained the perception of foulness in the body. Without plunging into the thicket of defilements overcome by the impediments of household life, he developed his long-familiar inclination towards renunciation. Wishing to abandon his great mass of wealth and go forth, he thought again: “If I go forth, my virtues will become manifest.”

So lābhasakkāraṃ jigucchanto pabbajjaṃ anupagantvā “pahomi cāhaṃ lābhālābhādīsu nibbikāro hotu”nti attānaṃ takkento “visesato paraparibhavasahanādipaṭipadaṃ pūrento upekkhāpāramiṃ matthakaṃ pāpessāmī”ti nivatthavattheneva gehato nikkhamitvā paramasallekhavuttikopi abalabalo amandamando viya paresaṃ acittakarūpena hīḷitaparibhūto hutvā gāmanigamarājadhānīsu ekarattivāseneva vicarati. Yattha pana mahantaṃ paribhavaṃ paṭilabhati, tattha cirampi vasati. So nivatthavatthe jiṇṇe pilotikakhaṇḍena tasmimpi jiṇṇe kenaci dinnaṃ aggaṇhanto hirikopīnapaṭicchādanamatteneva carati. Evaṃ gacchante kāle ekaṃ nigamagāmaṃ agamāsi.

He, disgusted with gain and homage, without undertaking the going forth, considered himself: “Am I able to be undisturbed by gain and loss and so forth?” “Especially by fulfilling the practice of enduring others’ contempt and the like, I shall bring the perfection of equanimity to its summit,” he thought. Thus, having gone forth from home with just the clothes he was wearing, though living a life of supreme austerity, he was like one very weak, like one very dull-witted, being despised and scorned by others in a disregarded manner. He wandered, staying only one night in villages, market towns, and royal cities. But where he received great contempt, there he stayed even longer. When the clothes he was wearing became worn out, and when even that piece of rag became worn out, not accepting anything given by anyone, he wandered with just enough to cover his private parts for modesty. While time was passing thus, he came to a market town and village.

Tattha gāmadārakā dhuttajātikā vedhaverā keci rājavallabhānaṃ puttanattudāsādayo ca uddhatā unnaḷā capalā mukharā vikiṇṇavācā kālena kālaṃ kīḷābahulā vicaranti. Duggate mahallake purise ca itthiyo ca gacchante disvā bhasmapuṭena piṭṭhiyaṃ ākiranti, ketakīpaṇṇaṃ kacchantare olambenti, tena vippakārena parivattetvā olokente [P 0.0269] yathāvajjakīḷitaṃ dassetvā upahasanti. Mahāpuriso tasmiṃ nigame te evaṃ vicarante dhuttadārake disvā “laddho vata dāni me upekkhāpāramiyā paripūraṇūpāyo”ti [M 0.0260] cintetvā tattha vihāsi. Taṃ te dhuttadārakā passitvā vippakāraṃ kātuṃ ārabhanti.

There, village boys, of mischievous nature, reckless, some sons, grandsons, slaves, and so forth, of the king’s favorites, were arrogant, unruly, fickle, garrulous, and loose-tongued, wandering about, frequently indulging in games. Seeing poor old men and women going by, they would scatter ash on their backs with a handful, hang ketaki leaves under their armpits, and by such pranks, when they turned around to look, they would show them an improper gesture and mock them. The Great Being, in that town, saw those mischievous boys behaving thus and thought, “Indeed, now I have found a means for the fulfillment of the perfection of equanimity.” So he remained there. Those mischievous boys, seeing him, began to play pranks on him.

Mahāsatto taṃ asahanto viya ca tehi bhāyanto viya ca uṭṭhahitvā gacchati. Te taṃ anubandhanti. So tehi anubandhiyamāno “ettha natthi koci paṭivattā”ti susānaṃ gantvā aṭṭhikaṃ sīsūpadhānaṃ katvā sayati. Dhuttadārakāpi tattha gantvā oṭṭhubhanādikaṃ nānappakāraṃ vippakāraṃ katvā pakkamanti. Evaṃ te divase divase karonti eva. Ye pana viññū purisā, te evaṃ karonte passanti. Te te paṭibāhitvā “ayaṃ mahānubhāvo tapassī mahāyogī”ti ca ñatvā uḷāraṃ sakkārasammānaṃ karonti. Mahāsatto pana sabbattha ekasadisova hoti majjhattabhūto. Tena vuttaṃ “susāne seyyaṃ kappemī”tiādi.

The Great Being, as if unable to endure them and as if fearing them, rose and departed. They followed him. Being pursued by them, thinking, “There is no one here to turn them back,” he went to the charnel ground, making a bone his head-rest, and lay down. The mischievous boys also went there and, having inflicted various kinds of mischief, such as spitting, they departed. Thus they did this day after day. But those wise men who saw them acting thus, rebuked them. Knowing that “this ascetic is of great power, a great yogi,” they paid him great honor and respect. The Great Being, however, was everywhere alike, being of equable mind. Therefore it is said: “I make my bed in the charnel ground,” and so forth.

Tattha susāne seyyaṃ kappemi, chavaṭṭhikaṃ upanidhāyāti āmakasusāne chaḍḍitakaḷevarato soṇasiṅgālādīhi tahiṃ tahiṃ vikkhittesu aṭṭhikesu ekaṃ aṭṭhikaṃ sīsūpadhānaṃ katvā sucimhi ca [V 0.0244] asucimhi ca samānacittatāya tasmiṃ susāne seyyaṃ kappemi, sayāmīti attho. Gāmaṇḍalāti gāmadārakā. Rūpaṃ dassentinappakanti yathāvajjakīḷitāya oṭṭhubhanaupahasanaummihanādīhi kaṇṇasote salākappavesanādīhi ca atikakkhaḷaṃ anappakaṃ nānappakāraṃ rūpaṃ vikāraṃ karonti.

There, “I make my bed in the charnel ground, making a corpse-bone a head-rest”—thus, in the raw charnel ground, from the discarded corpses, among the bones scattered here and there by dogs, jackals, and so forth, making one bone a head-rest, by having an equal mind towards the clean and the unclean, I make my bed in that charnel ground, I lie down—this is the meaning. “Gāmaṇḍalā” means “village boys.” “They show forms, not a little”—that is, by means of improper play, by spitting, mocking, making faces, sticking reeds into the ears, and so forth, they make very harsh, abundant, various kinds of mischief.

120. Apareti tesu eva gāmadārakesu ekacce. Upāyanānūpanentīti “ayaṃ imesu paribhavavasena evarūpaṃ vippakāraṃ karontesu na kiñci vikāraṃ dasseti, sammānane nu kho kīdiso”ti pariggaṇhantā vividhaṃ bahuṃ gandhamālaṃ bhojanaṃ aññāni ca upāyanāni paṇṇākārāni upanenti upaharanti. Aparehi vā tehi anācāragāmadārakehi aññe viññū manussā “ayaṃ imesaṃ evaṃ vividhampi vippakāraṃ karontānaṃ na kuppati, aññadatthu khantimettānuddayaṃyeva tesu upaṭṭhapeti, aho acchariyapuriso”ti haṭṭhā “bahu vatimehi etasmiṃ vippaṭipajjantehi [P 0.0270] apuññaṃ pasuta”nti saṃviggamānasāva hutvā bahuṃ gandhamālaṃ vividhaṃ bhojanaṃ aññāni ca upāyanāni upanenti upaharanti.

120. “Apare” means “some” among those very village boys. “They bring offerings”—thinking, “When these (boys) act in such a mischievous way by means of contempt, he shows no change; how then would he be when honored?”—thus testing him, they bring and offer various abundant perfumes, garlands, food, and other gifts and presents. Alternatively, 'others' refers to wise people, different from those ill-behaved village boys, who think: “Even when these others treat him with such varied mischief, he does not get angry. On the contrary, he establishes only patience, loving-kindness, and compassion towards them. What a marvelous person!” Delighted, and being with minds agitated thinking: “Indeed, much demerit has been produced by these (boys) acting wrongly towards him,” they bring and offer abundant perfumes, various foods, and other gifts.

121. Ye [M 0.0261] me dukkhaṃ upaharantīti ye gāmadārakā mayhaṃ sarīradukkhaṃ upaharanti upanenti. “Upadahantī”tipi pāṭho, uppādentīti attho. Ye ca denti sukhaṃ mamāti ye ca viññū manussā mama mayhaṃ sukhaṃ denti, mālāgandhabhojanādisukhūpakaraṇehi mama sukhaṃ upaharanti. Sabbesaṃ samako homīti katthacipi vikārānuppattiyā samānacittatāya vividhānampi tesaṃ janānaṃ samako ekasadiso homi bhavāmi. Dayā kopo na vijjatīti yasmā mayhaṃ upakārake mettacittatāsaṅkhātā dayā, apakārake manopadosasaṅkhāto kopopi na vijjati, tasmā sabbesaṃ samako homīti dasseti.

121. “Those who inflict suffering on me” means those village boys who bring and inflict bodily suffering upon me. “Upadahantī” is also a reading, meaning “they produce” or “they cause.” “And those who give me happiness” means those wise people who give me happiness, who offer me comfort with garlands, perfumes, food, and so forth, as means of happiness. “I am the same to all” means that by the non-arising of any change, by having an equal mind, I am the same, one and the same, to all those various people. “Compassion and anger do not exist” means that because towards benefactors, compassion, which is reckoned as a mind of loving-kindness, does not exist for me, and towards wrongdoers, anger, which is reckoned as mental aversion, also does not exist, therefore it is shown that I am the same to all.

122. Idāni bhagavā tadā upakārīsu apakārīsu ca sattesu samupacitañāṇasambhārassa attano samānacittatā vikārābhāvo yā ca lokadhammesu anupalittatā ahosi, taṃ dassetuṃ “sukhadukkhe tulābhūto”ti osānagāthamāha.

122. Now, to show his own equanimity towards beings who had helped or harmed him, his unperturbed state, and his unstained state amidst worldly conditions, the Blessed One, for whom the store of knowledge had been accumulated, then spoke this concluding verse: “Balanced in pleasure and pain.”

Tattha sukhadukkheti sukhe ca dukkhe ca. Tulābhūtoti samakaṃ gahitatulā viya onatiunnatiapanatiṃ vajjetvā majjhattabhūto, sukhadukkhaggahaṇeneva cettha taṃnimittabhāvato lābhālābhāpi gahitāti veditabbaṃ. Yasesūti kittīsu. Ayasesūti nindāsu. Sabbatthāti sabbesu sukhādīsu lokadhammesu. Iti bhagavā tadā sabbasattesu sabbalokadhammesu ca anaññasādhāraṇaṃ [V 0.0245] attano majjhattabhāvaṃ kittetvā tena tasmiṃ attabhāve attano upekkhāpāramiyā sikhāppattabhāvaṃ vibhāvento “esā me upekkhāpāramī”ti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

Therein, ‘in happiness and suffering’ means in happiness and in suffering. ‘Balanced’ means like a scale held evenly, avoiding inclination, rising, or falling, being in the middle. Here, by the inclusion of happiness and suffering, it should be understood that gain and loss are also included because they are caused by them. ‘In fame’ means in praise. ‘In disgrace’ means in blame. ‘In all’ means in all worldly conditions such as happiness and so on. Thus, the Blessed One, having proclaimed his unique and uncommon neutrality toward all beings and all worldly conditions, then, by that very state in that existence, revealed his attainment of the peak of the perfection of equanimity. He concluded the teaching by declaring, ‘This is my perfection of equanimity.’”

Idhāpi mahāsattassa paṭhamaṃ dānapāramī nāma visesato sabbavibhavapariccāgo “ye keci imaṃ sarīraṃ gahetvā yaṃkiñci attano icchitaṃ karontū”ti anapekkhabhāvena attano attabhāvapariccāgo ca dānapāramī, hīnādikassa sabbassa akattabbassa akaraṇaṃ sīlapāramī, kāmassādavimukhassa gehato nikkhantassa sato kāye asubhasaññānubrūhanā nekkhammapāramī, sambodhisambhārānaṃ upakāradhammapariggahaṇe tappaṭipakkhappahāne ca kosallaṃ aviparītato dhammasabhāvacintanā ca paññāpāramī[P 0.0271], kāmavitakkādivinodanaṃ dukkhādhivāsanavīriyañca vīriyapāramī, sabbāpi adhivāsanakhanti khantipāramī, vacīsaccaṃ samādānāvisaṃvādanena viratisaccañca saccapāramī[M 0.0262], anavajjadhamme acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānapāramī, anodhiso sabbasattesu mettānuddayabhāvo mettāpāramī, upekkhāpāramī panassa yathāvuttavaseneva veditabbāti dasa pāramiyo labbhanti. Upekkhāpāramī cettha atisayavatīti katvā sāyeva desanaṃ āruḷhā. Tathā idha mahāsattassa mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ mahantañca ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ pahāya mahābhinikkhamanasadisaṃ gehato nikkhamanaṃ, tathā nikkhamitvā lābhasakkāraṃ jigucchato paresaṃ sambhāvanaṃ pariharitukāmassa pabbajjāliṅgaṃ aggahetvā citteneva anavasesaṃ pabbajjāguṇe adhiṭṭhahitvā paramasukhavihāro, paramappicchatā, pavivekābhirati, upekkhaṇādhippāyena attano kāyajīvitanirapekkhā, parehi attano upari katavippakārādhivāsanaṃ, ukkaṃsagatasallekhavutti, bodhisambhārapaṭipakkhānaṃ kilesānaṃ tanubhāvena khīṇāsavānaṃ viya paresaṃ upakārāpakāresu nibbikārabhāvahetubhūtena sabbattha majjhattabhāvena samuṭṭhāpito lokadhammehi anupalepo, sabbapāramīnaṃ muddhabhūtāya upekkhāpāramiyā sikhāppattīti evamādayo guṇānubhāvā vibhāvetabbāti.

Here too, for the Great Being, the perfection of giving is, firstly, the relinquishment of all possessions, and the relinquishment of his own self through complete detachment, thinking, ‘Let anyone who takes hold of this body do whatever they wish with it.’ The perfection of virtue is abstaining from all that should not be done, whether minor or otherwise. The perfection of renunciation is the cultivation of the perception of foulness in the body by one who, being mindful, has left the household life, turning away from the taste of sensual pleasures. The perfection of wisdom is skill in acquiring qualities that aid the requisites of enlightenment and in abandoning their opposites, along with correctly reflecting on the true nature of phenomena without perversion. The perfection of energy is the dispelling of sensual thoughts and so on, and the energy in enduring suffering. The perfection of patience is the forbearance to endure all. The perfection of truthfulness is verbal truth, and the truth of abstention by not being false to one's undertakings. The perfection of determination is unwavering resolve in blameless qualities. The perfection of loving-kindness is a state of boundless goodwill and compassion toward all beings. The perfection of equanimity, however, should be understood as previously described. Thus, the ten perfections are attained. Here, the perfection of equanimity is considered pre-eminent, and it is this that has ascended into the teaching. Likewise, here, the Great Being’s abandonment of a great mass of wealth and an extensive retinue of relatives, and his departure from the household life, resembled a great renunciation. Having left, as one who loathed gain and honor and wished to avoid the respect of others, without taking up the outward signs of monastic life, through his mind alone, he fully resolved upon the qualities of renunciation—dwelling in supreme bliss, supreme contentment, delight in seclusion, indifference to his own body and life with the intention of equanimity, enduring ill-treatment done by others, and practicing a refined and elevated mode of life; unstainedness by worldly phenomena, produced by an impartiality in all situations which is the cause of an unperturbed state—like that of the arahants—towards the help and harm of others, due to the attenuation of defilements hostile to the requisites of enlightenment; and the attainment of the peak of the perfection of equanimity, which is the crown of all perfections—such are the virtues and powers to be elucidated.

Mahālomahaṃsacariyāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Conduct of Mahālomahaṃsa is completed.

Upekkhāpāramī niṭṭhitā.

The Perfection of Equanimity is completed.

Tatiyavaggassa atthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the third chapter is completed.

Uddānagāthāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Summary Verses

“Yudhañjayo”tiādikā [V 0.0246] uddānagāthā. Tattha bhisenāti bhisāpadesena mahākañcanacariyaṃ (cariyā. 3.34 ādayo) dasseti. Soṇanandoti iminā soṇapaṇḍitacariyaṃ (cariyā. 3.42 ādayo ) dasseti. Tathā mūgapakkhoti mūgapakkhāpadesena temiyapaṇḍitacariyaṃ (cariyā. 3.48 ādayo) dasseti. Upekkhāpāramisīsena mahālomahaṃsacariyaṃ (cariyā. 3.119 ādayo) dasseti. Āsi iti vuṭṭhaṃ mahesināti yathā, sāriputta, tuyhaṃ etarahi desitaṃ, iti evaṃ iminā vidhānena mahantānaṃ dānapāramiādīnaṃ bodhisambhārānaṃ esanato mahesinā tadā bodhisattabhūtena [P 0.0272] mayā vuṭṭhaṃ ciṇṇaṃ caritaṃ paṭipannaṃ āsi ahosīti attho[M 0.0263]. Idāni pāramiparipūraṇavasena cirakālappavattitaṃ idha vuttaṃ avuttañca attano dukkarakiriyaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā yadatthaṃ sā pavattitā, tañca saṅkhepeneva dassetuṃ “evaṃ bahubbidha”nti gāthamāha.

The summary verse begins with ‘Yudhañjayo.’ Therein, ‘bhisena’ indicates the conduct of Mahākañcana by means of the reference to ‘bhisā’ (lotus stalk). ‘Soṇanando’ indicates the conduct of the wise Soṇa. Similarly, ‘mūgapakkha’ indicates the conduct of the wise Temiya by means of the reference to ‘mūgapakkha’ (the mute and crippled). By means of the heading ‘Perfection of Equanimity,’ it indicates the conduct of Mahālomahaṃsa. The meaning of ‘Thus was it lived by the Great Seer’ is as follows: ‘Just as, Sāriputta, it is now taught to you, in this very manner, so was it lived, practiced, followed, and adhered to by me, the Great Seer, who was then a Bodhisatta, while seeking the great requisites of enlightenment, such as the perfection of giving and so on.’ Now, having brought together his own difficult deeds, both those mentioned here and those not mentioned, which were long-practiced for the fulfillment of the perfections, and in order to show briefly the purpose for which they were practiced, he spoke the verse beginning, ‘Thus, in many ways...’

Tattha evanti iminā vuttanayena. Bahubbidhaṃ dukkhanti akittipaṇḍitādikāle kārapaṇṇādiāhāratāya tañca yācakassa datvā āhārūpacchedādinā ca bahuvidhaṃ nānappakāraṃ dukkhaṃ. Tathā kururājādikāle sakkasampattisadisā sampattī ca bahubbidhā. Bhavābhaveti khuddake ceva mahante ca bhave. Bhavābhave vā vuddhihāniyo anubhavitvā bahuvidhehi dukkhehi avihaññamāno bahuvidhāhi ca sampattīhi anākaḍḍhiyamāno pāramiparipūraṇapasuto eva hutvā tadanurūpaṃ paṭipattiṃ paṭipanno uttamaṃ anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ sabbaññutaṃ patto, adhigatosmīti attho.

Herein, 'thus' means in the manner stated. 'Manifold suffering' refers to the many forms of diverse hardship, such as during the time of Akitti the wise, when he sustained himself on leaves and roots; and after giving that food to a beggar, he experienced the cutting off of sustenance and other sufferings. Similarly, during the time of King Kuru, his prosperity was of many kinds, comparable to the prosperity of Sakka. 'In various existences' refers to both minor and major states of being. Having experienced growth and decline in existence after existence, not tormented by manifold sufferings and not drawn in by manifold prosperities, he was solely devoted to fulfilling the perfections. Having undertaken a practice in accordance with that, he attained the supreme, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, omniscience—the meaning is, 'I have attained it.'

Idāni yāsaṃ pāramīnaṃ paripūraṇatthaṃ esā dukkaracariyā ciraṃ pavattitā, tāsaṃ anavasesato paripuṇṇabhāvaṃ tena ca pattabbaphalassa attanā adhigatabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “datvā dātabbakaṃ dānaṃ, sīlaṃ pūretvā asesato”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Now, to show the complete fulfillment of those perfections for which this difficult practice was undertaken for a long time, and to demonstrate his own attainment of the fruit attainable thereby, it was said: 'Having given the gift that should be given, having fulfilled morality completely,' and so on.

Tattha datvā dātabbakaṃ dānanti tadā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhituṃ aggayānapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannena mahābodhisattena dātabbaṃ deyyadhammaṃ bāhiraṃ rajjādiṃ abbhantaraṃ attapariccāgoti pañca mahāpariccāgapariyosānaṃ dānapāramidānaupapāramidānaparamatthapāramippabhedaṃ [V 0.0247] dānaṃ anavasesato sampādetvāti attho. Tattha akittibrāhmaṇakāle (cariyā. 1.1 ādayo; jā. 1.13.83 ādayo) saṅkhabrāhmaṇakāleti (cariyā. 1.11 ādayo; jā. 1.10.39 ādayo) evamādīsu idha āgatesu anāgatesu ca visayhaseṭṭhikāle (jā. 1.4.157 ādayo) velāmakāleti (a. ni. 9.20) evamādīsupi dānapāramiyā mahāpurisassa pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa sasapaṇḍitakāle –

Therein, 'having given the gift that should be given' means that the Great Bodhisatta, who was then practicing the foremost path to attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, completely fulfilled without remainder the giving that should be given—the object of giving, external things like kingdoms, and internal self-sacrifice—which culminates in the five great sacrifices and is differentiated as the perfection of giving, the upa-perfection of giving, and the ultimate perfection of giving. In this context, during the time of the Brahmin Akitti (Cariyā. 1.1 ff.; Jā. 1.13.83 ff.), the time of the Brahmin Saṅkha (Cariyā. 1.11 ff.; Jā. 1.10.39 ff.), and in such instances mentioned here and not mentioned, such as the time of the merchant Visayha (Jā. 1.4.157 ff.) or the time of Velāma (A.N. 9.20), there is no limit to the measure of the Great Man's having fulfilled the perfection of giving. But certainly, during the time of the wise hare—

“Bhikkhāya [P 0.0273] upagataṃ disvā, sakattānaṃ pariccajiṃ;

Dānena me samo natthi, esā me dānapāramī”ti. (cariyā. 1. tassuddāna) –

'Having seen one who had come for alms, I relinquished my own self; there is none equal to me in giving, this is my perfection of giving.'

Evaṃ [M 0.0264] attapariccāgaṃ karontassa dānapāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Itaresu pana yathārahaṃ pāramiupapāramiyo veditabbā.

Thus, for one making such a self-sacrifice, the perfection of giving is called the ultimate perfection. But in the other cases, the perfections and upa-perfections should be understood as appropriate.

Sīlaṃ pūretvā asesatoti tathā anavasesato kāyiko saṃvaro, vācasiko saṃvaro, kāyikavācasiko saṃvaro, indriyasaṃvaro, bhojane mattaññutā, suvisuddhājīvatāti evamādikaṃ bodhisattasīlaṃ sampādentena sīlapāramisīlaupapāramisīlaparamatthapāramippabhedaṃ pūretabbaṃ sabbaṃ sīlaṃ pūretvā sammadeva sampādetvā. Idhāpi sīlavanāgarājakāle (cariyā. 2.1 ādayo; jā. 1.1.72) campeyyanāgarājakāleti (cariyā. 2.20 ādayo; jā. 1.15.240 ādayo) evamādīsu idha āgatesu, anāgatesu ca mahākapikāle (cariyā. 3.67 ādayo; jā. 1.7.83 ādayo; 1.16.178 ādayo) chaddantakāleti (jā. 1.16.97 ādayo) evamādīsu mahāsattassa sīlapāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa saṅkhapālakāle –

'Having fulfilled virtue completely' means that the Bodhisatta, by completing all such kinds of Bodhisatta virtue—bodily restraint, verbal restraint, bodily and verbal restraint, restraint of the senses, moderation in eating, and purity of livelihood—without any remainder, properly fulfilled all virtue differentiated as the perfection of virtue, the upa-perfection of virtue, and the ultimate perfection of virtue. Here too, in the time of the virtuous Nāga king (Cariyā. 2.1 ff.; Jā. 1.1.72), in the time of the Nāga king Campeyya (Cariyā. 2.20 ff.; Jā. 1.15.240 ff.), and in such instances mentioned here and not mentioned, such as in the time of the Great Monkey (Cariyā. 3.67 ff.; Jā. 1.7.83 ff.; 1.16.178 ff.) and in the time of Chaddanta (Jā. 1.16.97 ff.), there is no limit to the measure of the Great Being's having fulfilled the perfection of virtue. However, in the time of Saṅkhapāla—

“Sūlehi vinivijjhante, koṭṭayantepi sattibhi;

Bhojaputte na kuppāmi, esā me sīlapāramī”ti. (cariyā. 2.91) –

'Though pierced with stakes, and struck with spears, I am not angry with the Bhoja prince—this is my perfection of virtue.'

Evaṃ attapariccāgaṃ karontassa sīlapāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Itaresu pana yathārahaṃ pāramiupapāramiyo veditabbā.

Thus, for one making such a self-sacrifice, the perfection of virtue is called the ultimate perfection. But in the other cases, the perfections and upa-perfections should be understood as appropriate.

Nekkhamme [V 0.0248] pāramiṃ gantvāti tathā tividhepi mahābhinikkhamane pāramiṃ paramukkaṃsaṃ gantvā. Tattha yudhañjayakāle (cariyā. 3.1 ādayo; jā. 1.11.73 ādayo) somanassakumārakāleti (cariyā. 3.7 ādayo; jā. 1.15.211 ādayo) evamādīsu idha āgatesu, anāgatesu ca hatthipālakumārakāle (jā. 1.15.337 ādayo) maghadevakāleti (ma. ni. 2.308 ādayo; jā. 1.1.9) evamādīsu mahārajjaṃ pahāya nekkhammapāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa cūḷasutasomakāle –

“Having gone to the perfection of renunciation” means having reached the highest excellence in the threefold great renunciation. In this context, during times such as the reign of Yudhañjaya (Cariyā. 3.1, etc.; Jā. 1.11.73, etc.), the life as Prince Somanassa (Cariyā. 3.7, etc.; Jā. 1.15.211, etc.), and similar instances mentioned here and not mentioned—such as the life as the youth Hatthipāla (Jā. 1.15.337, etc.) and the reign of King Maghadeva (Ma. Ni. 2.308, etc.; Jā. 1.1.9)—there is no limit to the measure of those existences in which the perfection of renunciation was fulfilled by abandoning great kingdoms. However, in the case of Cūḷasutasoma—

“Mahārajjaṃ hatthagataṃ, kheḷapiṇḍaṃva chaḍḍayiṃ;

Cajato na hoti lagganaṃ, esā me nekkhammapāramī”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; jā. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā);

“I discarded the great kingdom that had come into my hands, like a lump of spittle. For one who relinquishes, there is no attachment—this is my perfection of renunciation.”

Evaṃ nissaṅgatāya rajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā nikkhamantassa nekkhammapāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Itaresu pana yathārahaṃ pāramiupapāramiyo veditabbā.

Thus, for one going forth after having renounced the kingdom without attachment, the perfection of renunciation became what is called the ultimate perfection. In the other cases, however, the perfections and upa-perfections should be understood as is appropriate.

Paṇḍite [M 0.0265] paripucchitvāti kiṃ kusalaṃ kiṃ akusalaṃ kiṃ sāvajjaṃ kiṃ anavajjantiādinā kusalādidhammavibhāgaṃ kammakammaphalavibhāgaṃ sattānaṃ upakārāvahaṃ anavajjakammāyatanasippāyatanavijjāṭṭhānādiṃ [P 0.0274] paṇḍite sappaññe paripucchitvā. Etena paññāpāramiṃ dasseti. Tattha vidhurapaṇḍitakāle (jā. 2.22.1346 ādayo) mahāgovindapaṇḍitakāle (dī. ni. 2.293 ādayo; cariyā 1.37 ādayo) kudālapaṇḍitakāle (jā. 1.1.70) arakapaṇḍitakāle (jā. 1.2.37 ādayo) bodhiparibbājakakāle mahosadhapaṇḍitakāleti (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) evamādīsu paññāpāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa senakapaṇḍitakāle –

“Having inquired from the wise” means having inquired from the wise and discerning ones concerning what is wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, and so on—the divisions of wholesome and other qualities, the divisions of kamma and its results, blameless spheres of action, spheres of skill, and foundations of knowledge that are beneficial to beings. By this, the perfection of wisdom is shown. In that context, during the time of Vidhura the Wise (Jā. 2.22.1346, etc.), Mahāgovinda the Wise (Dī. Ni. 2.293, etc.; Cariyā. 1.37, etc.), Kudāla the Wise (Jā. 1.1.70), Araka the Wise (Jā. 1.2.37, etc.), the time of the Bodhi-Paribbājaka, and Mahosadha the Wise (Jā. 2.22.590, etc.), and so on—there is no measure to the fulfilled states of the perfection of wisdom. However, especially during the time of Senaka the Wise—

“Paññāya vicinantohaṃ, brāhmaṇaṃ mocayiṃ dukhā;

Paññāya me samo natthi, esā me paññāpāramī”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; jā. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakkathā) –

“Investigating with wisdom, I freed a brahmin from suffering. There is none equal to me in wisdom; this is my perfection of wisdom.”

Antobhastagataṃ sappaṃ dassentassa paññāpāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Vīriyaṃ katvāna uttamanti [V 0.0249] sammāsambodhiṃ pāpetuṃ samatthatāya uttamaṃ padhānaṃ vīriyanti vividhampi vīriyapāramiṃ katvā uppādetvā. Tattha mahāsīlavarājakāle (jā. 1.1.51) pañcāvudhakumārakāle (jā. 1.1.55) mahāvānarindakāleti (jā. 1.1.57) evamādīsu vīriyapāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa mahājanakakāle –

In showing the snake that had entered the bag, his perfection of wisdom became what is called the ultimate perfection. ‘Having made supreme effort’ means having made and brought forth the perfection of energy in its various forms—the supreme, principal effort due to its capacity to lead to perfect self-enlightenment. In this regard, during the time of the Great Virtuous King (Jā. 1.1.51), the time of Prince Pañcāvudha (Jā. 1.1.55), the time of the Great Monkey King (Jā. 1.1.57), and so on, there is no measure for the number of existences in which the perfection of energy was fulfilled. But particularly in the time of Mahājanaka—

“Atīradassī jalamajjhe, hatā sabbeva mānusā;

Cittassa aññathā natthi, esā me vīriyapāramī”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; jā. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā) –

“Though seeing no shore in the midst of the ocean, while all other people perished, there was no change in my mind; this is my perfection of energy.”

Evaṃ mahāsamuddaṃ tarantassa vīriyapāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for one crossing the great ocean, the perfection of energy became what is called the ultimate perfection.

Khantiyā pāramiṃ gantvāti adhivāsanakhantiādi khantiparamukkaṃsabhāvaṃ pāpento khantiyā pāramiṃ paramakoṭiṃ gantvā, khantipāramiṃ sampādetvāti attho. Tattha mahākapikāle (cariyā. 3.67 ādayo; jā. 1.7.83 ādayo) mahiṃsarājakāle (jā. 1.3.82 ādayo) rurumigarājakāle (jā. 1.13.117 ādayo) dhammadevaputtakāleti (jā. 1.11.26 ādayo) evamādīsu khantipāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa khantivādikāle –

‘Having gone to the perfection of patience’ means: attaining the state of supreme excellence in patience, such as the patience of endurance, and having reached the ultimate limit of the perfection of patience, thereby fulfilling the perfection of patience. In this regard, during the time of the Great Monkey (Cariyā. 3.67 ff.; Jā. 1.7.83 ff.), the time of King Mahiṃsa (Jā. 1.3.82 ff.), the time of the Ruru Deer King (Jā. 1.13.117 ff.), and the time of the devaputta Dhammadeva (Jā. 1.11.26 ff.), and so on, there is no measure for the number of existences in which the perfection of patience was fulfilled. But particularly in the time of the Khantivādī—

“Acetanaṃ [M 0.0266] va koṭṭente, tiṇhena pharasunā mamaṃ;

Kāsirāje na kuppāmi, esā me khantipāramī”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; jā. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā) –

“While they chop me with a sharp axe as if I were an insentient thing, I am not angry with the King of Kāsi; this is my perfection of patience.”

Evaṃ acetanabhāvena viya mahādukkhaṃ anubhavantassa khantipāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him experiencing great suffering as if in a state of insentience, the perfection of patience became what is called the ultimate perfection.

Katvā daḷhamadhiṭṭhānanti kusalasamādānādhiṭṭhānaṃ tassa tassa pāramisamādānassa tadupakārakasamādānassa ca adhiṭṭhānaṃ daḷhataraṃ asithilaṃ katvā, taṃ taṃ vatasamādānaṃ [P 0.0275] anivattibhāvena adhiṭṭhahitvāti attho. Tattha jotipālakāle (ma. ni. 2.282 ādayo) sarabhaṅgakāle (jā. 2.17.50 ādayo) nemikāleti (cariyā. 1.40 ādayo; jā.2.22.421 ādayo) evamādīsu [V 0.0250] adhiṭṭhānapāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa temiyakumārakāle –

‘Having made a firm resolution’ means: having made a very firm and unyielding resolution—a resolution to undertake what is wholesome, to undertake each perfection, and to undertake what is conducive thereto—and having resolved upon each observance with a state of not turning back. In this regard, during the time of Jotipāla (M.N. 2.282 ff.), the time of Sarabhaṅga (Jā. 2.17.50 ff.), and the time of Nemi (Cariyā. 1.40 ff.; Jā. 2.22.421 ff.), and so on, there is no measure for the number of existences in which the perfection of resolution was fulfilled. But particularly in the time of Prince Temiya—

“Mātāpitā na me dessā, attā me na ca dessiyo;

Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ, tasmā vatamadhiṭṭhahi”nti. (cariyā. 3.65) –

“My mother and father are not hateful to me, nor is my self hateful to me; but omniscience is dear to me, therefore I have undertaken this vow.”

Evaṃ jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā vataṃ adhiṭṭhahantassa adhiṭṭhānapāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him who resolved upon his vow even to the point of abandoning his life, the perfection of resolution became what is called the ultimate perfection.

Saccavācānurakkhiyāti saccavācaṃ anurakkhitvā jīvitantarāyepi anariyavohāraṃ gūthaṃ viya jigucchanto pariharitvā sabbaso avisaṃvādibhāvaṃ rakkhitvā. Tattha kapirājakāle (cariyā. 3.67 ādayo) saccatāpasakāle maccharājakāleti evamādīsu saccapāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa mahāsutasomakāle –

‘By guarding truthful speech’ means: having protected truthful speech, shunning and avoiding ignoble speech as if it were excrement even when life is in danger, and having guarded a state of utter truthfulness. In this regard, during the time of the Monkey King (Cariyā. 3.67 ff.), the time of the Truth-Ascetic, and the time of the Fish King, and so on, there is no measure for the number of existences in which the perfection of truth was fulfilled. But particularly in the time of Mahāsutasoma:

“Saccavācaṃ anurakkhanto, cajitvā mama jīvitaṃ;

Mocesiṃ ekasataṃ khattiye, esā me saccapāramī”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; jā. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā) –

“Guarding my truthful speech, I gave up my own life and freed one hundred nobles; this is my perfection of truth.”

Evaṃ jīvitaṃ cajitvā saccaṃ anurakkhantassa saccapāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him who guarded the truth even to the point of giving up his life, the perfection of truth became what is called the ultimate perfection.

Mettāya [M 0.0267] pāramiṃ gantvāti sabbasattesu anodhiso hitūpasaṃhāralakkhaṇāya mettāya pāramiṃ paramukkaṃsataṃ patvā. Tattha cūḷadhammapālakāle (jā. 1.5.44 ādayo) mahāsīlavarājakāle (jā. 1.1.51) sāmapaṇḍitakāleti (cariyā. 3.111 ādayo; jā. 2.22.296 ādayo) evamādīsu mettāpāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa suvaṇṇasāmakāle –

‘Having gone to the perfection of loving-kindness’ means having attained the highest excellence, the perfection of loving-kindness, which is characterized by promoting the welfare of all beings without distinction. In this regard, during the time of Cūḷadhammapāla (Jā. 1.5.44 ff.), the Great Virtuous King (Jā. 1.1.51), and the wise Sāma (Cariyā. 3.111 ff.; Jā. 2.22.296 ff.), and so on, there is no measure for the number of existences in which the perfection of loving-kindness was fulfilled. But particularly in the time of Suvaṇṇasāma—

“Na maṃ koci uttasati, napihaṃ bhāyāmi kassaci;

Mettābalenupatthaddho, ramāmi pavane tadā”ti. (cariyā. 3.113) –

“No one is afraid of me, nor do I fear anyone; supported by the power of loving-kindness, I delight in the forest.”

Evaṃ jīvitampi anoloketvā mettāyantassa mettāpāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā.

Thus, for him who practiced loving-kindness without any regard for his own life, the perfection of loving-kindness became what is called the ultimate perfection.

Sammānanāvamānaneti sakkaccaṃ pūjāsakkārādinā sammānane oṭṭhubhanādinā avamānane ca [V 0.0251] sabbattha lokadhamme samako samacitto nibbikāro hutvā uttamaṃ anuttaraṃ labbaññutaṃ adhigatosmīti attho. Tattha mahāvānarindakāle (jā. 1.1.57) kāsirājakāle khemabrāhmaṇakāle aṭṭhisenaparibbājakakāleti (jā. 1.7.54 ādayo) evamādīsu upekkhāpāramiyā pūritattabhāvānaṃ [P 0.0276] parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa mahālomahaṃsakāle –

‘In honor and dishonor’ means: having become equal, even-minded, and unperturbed amidst all worldly conditions—whether in the case of honor through respectful worship and hospitality, or in the case of dishonor through spitting and the like; this is the meaning through which the supreme, unsurpassed omniscience is attained. In this regard, during the time of the Great Monkey King (Jā. 1.1.57), the King of Kāsi, the brahmin Khema, and the ascetic Aṭṭhisena (Jā. 1.7.54 ff.), and so on, there is no measure for the number of existences in which the perfection of equanimity was fulfilled. But particularly in the time of Mahālomahaṃsa—

“Susāne seyyaṃ kappemi, chavaṭṭhikaṃ upanidhāyahaṃ;

Gāmaṇḍalā upāgantvā, rūpaṃ dassentinappaka”nti. (cariyā. 3.119) –

“I make my bed in the charnel ground, using a corpse’s bone for a pillow. Village children approach and perform all sorts of acts before me.”

Evaṃ gāmadārakesu oṭṭhubhanādīhi ceva mālāgandhūpahārādīhi ca sukhadukkhaṃ uppādentesupi upekkhaṃ anativattantassa upekkhāpāramī paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Iti bhagavā –

Thus, even when village children caused him pleasure and pain by spitting and so on, or by offering garlands, perfumes, and gifts, his equanimity did not waver; the perfection of equanimity became the ultimate perfection. Thus the Blessed One said:

“Evaṃ bahubbidhaṃ dukkhaṃ, sampattī ca bahubbidhā;

Bhavābhave anubhavitvā, patto sambodhimuttama”nti. –

“Thus manifold is suffering, and manifold are attainments; having experienced these in existence after existence, he attained supreme enlightenment.”

Sammāsambodhiṃ adhigantuṃ imasmiṃ bhaddakappe attanā kataṃ dukkaracariyaṃ saṅkhepeneva vatvā puna –

In order to attain perfect enlightenment in this auspicious aeon, having briefly recounted the arduous practices undertaken by himself, he further said:

“Datvā dātabbakaṃ dānaṃ, sīlaṃ pūretvā asesato;

Nekkhamme pāramiṃ gantvā, patto sambodhimuttamaṃ.

“Having given the gifts that should be given, fulfilling virtue completely, having reached perfection in renunciation, he attained supreme enlightenment.

“Paṇḍite [M 0.0268] paripucchitvā, vīriyaṃ katvāna muttamaṃ;

Khantiyā pāramiṃ gantvā, patto sambodhimuttamaṃ.

“Having questioned the wise, having made supreme effort, having gone to the perfection of patience, he attained the supreme enlightenment.”

“Katvā daḷhamadhiṭṭhānaṃ, saccavācānurakkhiya;

Mettāya pāramiṃ gantvā, patto sambodhimuttamaṃ.

“Having made a firm determination, having guarded truthful speech, having gone to the perfection of loving-kindness, he attained the supreme enlightenment.”

“Lābhālābhe yasāyase, sammānanāvamānane;

Sabbattha samako hutvā, patto sambodhimuttama”nti. –

“In gain and loss, fame and disrepute, honor and dishonor; having become equal in all circumstances, he attained the supreme enlightenment.”

Attanā sammadeva paripūritā dasa pāramiyo dasseti.

He shows the ten perfections that he himself had fully perfected.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

A Miscellaneous Discourse

Imasmiṃ [M 0.0269][V 0.0252] pana ṭhāne ṭhatvā mahābodhiyānapaṭipattiyaṃ ussāhajātānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ bodhisambhāresu nānappakārakosallatthaṃ sabbapāramīsu pakiṇṇakakathā kathetabbā.

Now, at this point, a miscellaneous discourse on all the perfections should be given for the noble sons who have generated enthusiasm for the practice of the vehicle of great enlightenment, for the sake of their skill in the various requisites for enlightenment.

Tatridaṃ pañhakammaṃ – kā panetā pāramiyo? Kenaṭṭhena pāramiyo? Katividhā cetā? Ko tāsaṃ kamo? Kāni lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni? Ko paccayo? Ko saṃkileso? Kiṃ vodānaṃ? Ko paṭipakkho? Kā paṭipatti? Ko vibhāgo? Ko saṅgaho? Ko sampādanūpāyo? Kittakena kālena sampādanaṃ? Ko ānisaṃso? Kiṃ cetāsaṃ phalanti?

Herein is the set of questions: What are these perfections? In what sense are they perfections? How many kinds are they? What is their order? What are their characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes? What is their condition? What is their defilement? What is their purification? What is their opponent? What is their practice? What is their division? What is their grouping? What is the means of their accomplishment? In how much time is their accomplishment? What is their benefit? What is their result?

Tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ – kā panetā pāramiyoti? Taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīhi [P 0.0277] anupahatā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā dānādayo guṇā pāramiyo.

Herein is the answer: What are these perfections? The qualities such as generosity and so forth, uncorrupted by craving, conceit, and views, and encompassed by compassion and skill in means, are the perfections.

Kenaṭṭhena pāramiyoti? Dānasīlādiguṇavisesayogena sattuttamatāya paramā mahāsattā bodhisattā, tesaṃ bhāvo kammaṃ vā pāramī, dānādikiriyā. Atha vā paratīti paramo, dānādiguṇānaṃ pūrako pālako cāti bodhisatto, paramassa ayaṃ, paramassa vā bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramī, dānādikiriyāva. Atha vā paraṃ sattaṃ attani mavati bandhati guṇavisesayogena, paraṃ vā adhikataraṃ majjati sujjhati saṃkilesamalato, paraṃ vā seṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ visesena mayati gacchati, paraṃ vā lokaṃ pamāṇabhūtena ñāṇavisesena idhalokaṃ viya munāti paricchindati, paraṃ vā ativiya sīlādiguṇagaṇaṃ attano santāne minoti pakkhipati, paraṃ vā attabhūtato dhammakāyato aññaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ vā tadanatthakaraṃ kilesacoragaṇaṃ mināti hiṃsatīti paramo, mahāsatto. Paramassa ayantiādi vuttanayena yojetabbaṃ. Pāre vā nibbāne majjati sujjhati satte ca sodheti, tattha vā satte mavati bandhati yojeti, taṃ vā mayati gacchati gameti ca, munāti vā taṃ yāthāvato[M 0.0270], tattha vā satte minoti pakkhipati, kilesārayo [V 0.0253] vā sattānaṃ tattha mināti hiṃsatīti pāramī, mahāpuriso. Tassa bhāvo kammaṃ vā pāramitā, dānādikiriyāva. Iminā nayena pāramīsaddattho veditabbo.

In what sense are they perfections? The great beings, the Bodhisattas, are supreme by virtue of being the best of beings through their association with special qualities such as generosity and virtue; their state or action is a perfection, namely, the practice of giving and so forth. Or, one who crosses over is supreme (paramo); the Bodhisatta is the fulfiller and protector of virtues like generosity. This belongs to the supreme, or is the state or action of the supreme, namely, the practice of giving and so forth. Or, he binds other beings to himself through the excellence of his qualities; or he cleanses others more thoroughly from the stains of defilements; or he especially goes to the supreme, the excellent Nibbāna; or he knows and defines the other world with the special knowledge that serves as a standard, just as this world; or he places the supreme multitude of virtues like morality into his own continuum; or he injures and harms the other, the opposing and harmful hordes of thieves which are the defilements—thus, he is supreme, a great being. This, beginning with 'this belongs to the supreme,' should be connected in the manner stated. Or, on the other shore, Nibbāna, he is purified and purifies beings; or he binds and unites beings there; or he goes to it and makes others go to it; or he knows it as it truly is; or he places beings there; or he injures and harms the enemies, the defilements, of beings there—thus he is one who reaches the far shore (pāramī), a great person. His state or action is a perfection (pāramitā), namely, the practice of giving and so forth. In this way, the meaning of the term 'perfection' should be understood.

Katividhāti? Saṅkhepato dasavidhā. Tā pana pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato āgatāyeva. Yathāha –

How many kinds are there? In brief, there are ten kinds. These, however, appear in the Pāli texts in their own form, as it is said:

“Vicinanto tadā dakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, anuciṇṇaṃ mahāpatha”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.116) –

“Then, investigating, I saw first the perfection of generosity, the great path trodden by the great sages of the past.”

Ādi. Yathā cāha – “kati nu kho, bhante, buddhakārakā dhammā? Dasa kho, sāriputta, buddhakārakā dhammā. Katame dasa? Dānaṃ kho, sāriputta, buddhakārako dhammo, sīlaṃ, nekkhammaṃ, paññā, vīriyaṃ, khanti, saccaṃ, adhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettā, upekkhā buddhakārako dhammo. Ime kho, sāriputta, dasa buddhakārakā dhammā”ti. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvā sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

And as it is said: “How many, venerable sir, are the qualities that make a Buddha? There are, Sāriputta, ten qualities that make a Buddha. Which ten? Generosity, Sāriputta, is a quality that makes a Buddha; so too are virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity. These, Sāriputta, are the ten qualities that make a Buddha.” This was spoken by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:

“Dānaṃ [P 0.0278] sīlañca nekkhammaṃ, paññā vīriyena pañcamaṃ;

Khanti saccamadhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettupekkhāti te dasā”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 1.76 thokaṃ visadisaṃ);

“Generosity, virtue, and renunciation, wisdom with energy as the fifth; patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these are the ten.”

Keci pana “chabbidhā”ti vadanti. Taṃ etāsaṃ saṅgahavasena vuttaṃ. So pana saṅgaho parato āvi bhavissati.

Some, however, say they are sixfold. That is said by way of grouping them. But that grouping will become clear later.

Ko tāsaṃ kamoti? Ettha kamoti desanākkamo, so ca paṭhamasamādānahetuko, samādānaṃ pavicayahetukaṃ, iti yathā ādimhi pavicitā samādinnā ca, tathā desitā. Tattha dānaṃ sīlassa bahūpakāraṃ sukarañcāti taṃ ādimhi vuttaṃ. Dānaṃ sīlapariggahitaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsanti dānānantaraṃ sīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlaṃ nekkhammapariggahitaṃ, nekkhammaṃ paññāpariggahitaṃ, paññā vīriyapariggahitā, vīriyaṃ khantipariggahitaṃ, khanti saccapariggahitā, saccaṃ adhiṭṭhānapariggahitaṃ, adhiṭṭhānaṃ mettāpariggahitaṃ, mettā [M 0.0271] upekkhāpariggahitā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsāti mettānantaramupekkhā vuttā. Upekkhā pana karuṇāpariggahitā karuṇā ca upekkhāpariggahitāti veditabbā. “Kathaṃ pana mahākāruṇikā bodhisattā sattesu upekkhakā hontī”ti? “Upekkhitabbayuttesu kañci kālaṃ upekkhakā honti[V 0.0254], na pana sabbattha sabbadā cā”ti keci. Apare pana – “na sattesu upekkhakā, sattakatesu pana vippakāresu upekkhakā hontī”ti.

What is their order? Here, 'order' refers to the sequence of teaching, which is caused by the initial undertaking, and the undertaking is caused by investigation. Thus, as they were investigated and undertaken at the beginning, so were they taught. In this context, generosity is very beneficial for virtue and easy to practice, hence it is mentioned first. Generosity, when embraced by virtue, yields great fruit and great benefit—thus virtue is mentioned after generosity. Virtue is embraced by renunciation, renunciation by wisdom, wisdom by energy, energy by patience, patience by truthfulness, truthfulness by determination, determination by loving-kindness, and loving-kindness, when embraced by equanimity, yields great fruit and great benefit—thus equanimity is mentioned after loving-kindness. However, it should be understood that equanimity is embraced by compassion, and compassion is embraced by equanimity. “But how can the greatly compassionate Bodhisattas be equanimous towards beings?” “Toward those for whom equanimity is appropriate, they are equanimous for a time, but not always and everywhere,” say some. Others say, “They are not equanimous towards beings, but toward the misdeeds committed by beings, they are equanimous.”

Aparo nayo – pacurajanesupi pavattiyā sabbasattasādhāraṇattā appaphalattā sukarattā ca ādimhi dānaṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlena dāyakapaṭiggāhakasuddhito parānuggahaṃ vatvā parapīḷānivattivacanato kiriyadhammaṃ vatvā akiriyadhammavacanato bhogasampattihetuṃ vatvā bhavasampattihetuvacanato ca dānassa anantaraṃ sīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Nekkhammena sīlasampattisiddhito kāyavacīsucaritaṃ vatvā manosucaritavacanato visuddhasīlassa sukheneva jhānasamijjhanato kammāparādhappahānena payogasuddhiṃ vatvā kilesāparādhappahānena āsayasuddhivacanato vītikkamappahānena cittassa pariyuṭṭhānappahānavacanato ca sīlassa [P 0.0279] anantaraṃ nekkhammaṃ vuttaṃ. Paññāya nekkhammassa siddhiparisuddhito jhānābhāvena paññābhāvavacanato “samādhipadaṭṭhānā hi paññā, paññāpaccupaṭṭhāno ca samādhi”. Samathanimittaṃ vatvā upekkhānimittavacanato parahitajjhānena parahitakaraṇūpāyakosallavacanato ca nekkhammassa anantaraṃ paññā vuttā. Vīriyārambhena paññākiccasiddhito sattasuññatādhammanijjhānakkhantiṃ vatvā sattahitāya ārambhassa acchariyatāvacanato upekkhānimittaṃ vatvā paggahanimittavacanato nisammakāritaṃ vatvā uṭṭhānavacanato ca “nisammakārino hi uṭṭhānaṃ phalavisesamāvahatī”ti paññāya anantaraṃ vīriyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Another method: generosity is taught first because of its prevalence even among many people, because it is common to all beings, because it yields little fruit, and because it is easy to perform. After generosity, virtue is taught because of the purification of giver and recipient through virtue; by speaking of benefiting others and then of abstaining from harming others; by speaking of active and non-active principles; and by speaking of it as the cause of attaining wealth and the cause of attaining existence. Following virtue, renunciation is taught because virtue is perfected by it; by speaking of good conduct in body and speech and then of good conduct in mind; from the easy attainment of jhāna for one with purified virtue; by speaking of purity of application through abandoning offenses of action and of purity of intention through abandoning offenses of defilement; and by speaking of abandoning transgression and abandoning mental obsession. After renunciation, wisdom is taught because renunciation is fulfilled and purified by it; by speaking of the absence of wisdom in the absence of jhāna, for 'wisdom has concentration as its proximate cause, and concentration has wisdom as its manifestation'; by speaking of the sign of tranquility and the sign of equanimity; and by speaking of skill in the means for benefiting others through the jhāna that benefits others. Following wisdom, energy is taught because the tasks of wisdom are accomplished through it; by speaking of the endurance of reflecting on phenomena as empty of a being; by speaking of the wonder of striving for the welfare of beings; by speaking of the sign of equanimity and the sign of exertion; and by speaking of acting with consideration and then of effort, because it is said, 'For those who act with discernment, effort yields special fruits.'

Vīriyena titikkhāsiddhito “vīriyavā hi āraddhavīriyattā sattasaṅkhārehi upanītaṃ dukkhaṃ abhibhuyya viharati”. Vīriyassa titikkhālaṅkārabhāvato “vīriyavato hi titikkhā sobhati”. Paggahanimittaṃ vatvā samathanimittavacanato accārambhena uddhaccadosappahānavacanato “dhammanijjhānakkhantiyā hi uddhaccadoso pahīyati”. Vīriyavato sātaccakaraṇavacanato “khantibahulo hi anuddhato sātaccakārī hoti”. Appamādavato [M 0.0272] parahitakiriyārambhe paccupakārataṇhābhāvavacanato “yāthāvato dhammanijjhāne hi sati taṇhā na hoti”. Parahitārambhe paramepi parakatadukkhasahanatāvacanato ca vīriyassa anantaraṃ khanti vuttā. Saccena khantiyā cirādhiṭṭhānato apakārino apakārakhantiṃ vatvā tadupakārakaraṇe avisaṃvādavacanato khantiyā apavādavācāvikampanena bhūtavāditāya avijahanavacanato sattasuññatādhammanijjhānakkhantiṃ vatvā tadupabrūhitañāṇasaccavacanato ca khantiyā anantaraṃ saccaṃ vuttaṃ.

After energy, patience is taught because endurance is achieved through energy, for 'the energetic one, being resolute in energy, overcomes the suffering brought on by conditioned things and dwells'; and because endurance is the ornament of energy, for 'endurance adorns the energetic one.' It is also taught by speaking of the sign of exertion and then the sign of tranquility; by speaking of abandoning the fault of restlessness through excessive striving, for 'the fault of restlessness is abandoned through the endurance of reflecting on the Dhamma'; by speaking of the energetic one’s continuous practice, for 'one rich in endurance is unagitated and continuously practicing'; by speaking of the absence of craving for reciprocal benefit when initiating actions for the benefit of others for the heedful one, for 'when there is true reflection on the Dhamma, craving does not arise'; and by speaking of enduring suffering inflicted by others even when striving for their highest welfare. After patience, truthfulness is taught because endurance is long-established through truth; by speaking of enduring harm from wrongdoers and of non-deception in benefiting them; by speaking of not abandoning truthful speech when endurance is shaken by slanderous words; and by speaking of the endurance of reflecting on phenomena as empty of a being and of the truth of knowledge augmented by that.

Adhiṭṭhānena [V 0.0255] saccasiddhito “acalādhiṭṭhānassa hi virati sijjhati”. Avisaṃvāditaṃ vatvā tattha acalabhāvavacanato “saccasandho hi dānādīsu paṭiññānurūpaṃ niccalova [P 0.0280] pavattati”. Ñāṇasaccaṃ vatvā sambhāresu pavattiniṭṭhāpanavacanato “yathābhūtañāṇavā hi bodhisambhāre adhiṭṭhāti, te ca niṭṭhāpeti paṭipakkhehi akampiyabhāvato”ti saccassa anantaraṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Mettāya parahitakaraṇasamādānādhiṭṭhānasiddhito adhiṭṭhānaṃ vatvā hitūpasaṃhāravacanato “bodhisambhāre hi adhitiṭṭhamāno mettāvihārī hoti”. Acalādhiṭṭhānassa samādānāvikopanena samādānasambhavato ca adhiṭṭhānassa anantaraṃ mettā vuttā. Upekkhāya mettāvisuddhito sattesu hitūpasaṃhāraṃ vatvā tadaparādhesu udāsīnatāvacanato mettābhāvanaṃ vatvā tannissandabhāvanāvacanato hitakāmasattepi upekkhakoti acchariyaguṇatāvacanato ca mettāya anantaraṃ upekkhā vuttāti evametāsaṃ kamo veditabbo.

Because truth is accomplished by determination—for 'for one with unwavering determination, restraint is achieved'; because, having spoken of non-deception, it speaks of immovability therein—for 'one bound by truth remains steadfast in giving and other acts, unwavering in accordance with their pledge'; and because, having spoken of the truth of knowledge, it speaks of bringing the requisites to completion—for 'one endowed with true knowledge resolves upon the requisites of enlightenment and brings them to completion, unshaken by opposing forces'—thus, after truth, determination is spoken of. After determination, loving-kindness is spoken of. This is because determination is accomplished through the undertaking of benefiting others with loving-kindness; because, having spoken of determination, it speaks of bringing about benefit—for 'one who resolves upon the requisites of enlightenment abides in loving-kindness'; and also because for one with unwavering determination, the undertaking arises without being shaken. After loving-kindness, equanimity is spoken of. This is because loving-kindness is purified by equanimity; because, having spoken of bringing about benefit for beings, it speaks of neutrality towards their faults; because, having spoken of the cultivation of loving-kindness, it speaks of the cultivation of its result; and because of the marvelous quality of being equanimous even towards beings for whom one wishes well. Thus, the sequence of these should be understood.

Kāni lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānīti ettha avisesena tāva sabbāpi pāramiyo parānuggahalakkhaṇā, paresaṃ upakārakaraṇarasā, avikampanarasā vā, hitesitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, buddhattapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, mahākaruṇāpadaṭṭhānā, karuṇūpāyakosallapadaṭṭhānā vā.

What are their characteristics, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? Here, in general, all the perfections have the characteristic of benefiting others, the function of assisting others or of being unwavering, the manifestation of desiring the welfare of others or of Buddhahood, and the proximate cause of great compassion or of compassion and skill in means.

Visesena pana yasmā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā attūpakaraṇapariccāgacetanā dānapāramitā, karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ kāyavacīsucaritaṃ atthato akattabbaviratikattabbakaraṇacetanādayo ca sīlapāramitā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamo kāmabhavehi nikkhamanacittuppādo nekkhammapāramitā, karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito dhammānaṃ sāmaññavisesalakkhaṇāvabodho paññāpāramitā[M 0.0273]. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito kāyacittehi parahitārambho vīriyapāramitā, karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ sattasaṅkhārāparādhasahanaṃ adosappadhāno tadākārappavattacittuppādo khantipāramitā, karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ viraticetanādibhedaṃ avisaṃvādanaṃ saccapāramitā, karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānaṃ tadākārappavatto cittuppādo adhiṭṭhānapāramitā, karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito lokassa hitasukhūpasaṃhāro [P 0.0281] atthato abyāpādo mettāpāramitā, karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā anunayapaṭighaviddhaṃsanī iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu sattasaṅkhāresu samappavatti upekkhāpāramitā.

Specifically, since the intention to relinquish one's own requisites, embraced by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā); since the wholesome conduct of body and speech, embraced by compassion and skillful means—which in essence is the intention to refrain from what should not be done and to do what should be done, and so on—is the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramitā); since the arising of the mind to depart from sensual and other forms of existence, preceded by seeing the danger therein and embraced by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of renunciation (nekkhammapāramitā); since the understanding of the general and specific characteristics of phenomena, embraced by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramitā); since the exertion for the welfare of others through body and mind, embraced by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of energy (vīriyapāramitā); since the endurance of offenses from beings and conditioned things, which is chiefly non-aversion and the arising of a mind that proceeds in that manner, embraced by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of patience (khantipāramitā); since non-deception, which has divisions such as the intention to abstain, embraced by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of truthfulness (saccapāramitā); since unwavering resolve, which is the arising of a mind that proceeds in that manner, embraced by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of determination (adhiṭṭhānapāramitā); since bringing welfare and happiness to the world, which in essence is non-ill will, embraced by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of loving-kindness (mettāpāramitā); and since proceeding equally towards desirable and undesirable beings and conditioned things, which destroys attraction and repulsion, embraced by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of equanimity (upekkhāpāramitā).

Tasmā pariccāgalakkhaṇā dānapāramī, deyyadhamme lobhaviddhaṃsanarasā, anāsattipaccupaṭṭhānā, bhavavibhavasampattipaccupaṭṭhānā vā, pariccajitabbavatthupadaṭṭhānā. Sīlanalakkhaṇā [V 0.0256] sīlapāramī, samādhānalakkhaṇā patiṭṭhānalakkhaṇā cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dussīlyaviddhaṃsanarasā, anavajjarasā vā, soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānā, hirottappapadaṭṭhānā. Kāmato ca bhavato ca nikkhamanalakkhaṇā nekkhammapāramī, tadādīnavavibhāvanarasā, tato eva vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, saṃvegapadaṭṭhānā. Yathāsabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā paññāpāramī, akkhalitapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā vā kusalissāsakhittausupaṭivedho viya, visayobhāsanarasā padīpo viya, asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā araññagatasudesiko viya, samādhipadaṭṭhānā, catusaccapadaṭṭhānā vā. Ussāhalakkhaṇā vīriyapāramī, upatthambhanarasā, asaṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhānā, vīriyārambhavatthupadaṭṭhānā, saṃvegapadaṭṭhānā vā. Khamanalakkhaṇā khantipāramī, iṭṭhāniṭṭhasahanarasā, adhivāsanapaccupaṭṭhānā, avirodhapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, yathābhūtadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Avisaṃvādanalakkhaṇā saccapāramī, yathāsabhāvavibhāvanarasā, sādhutāpaccupaṭṭhānā, soraccapadaṭṭhānā. Bodhisambhāresu adhiṭṭhānalakkhaṇā adhiṭṭhānapāramī, tesaṃ paṭipakkhābhibhavanarasā, tattha acalatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, bodhisambhārapadaṭṭhānā. Hitākārappavattilakkhaṇā mettāpāramī, hitūpasaṃhārarasā, āghātavinayanarasā vā, sommabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ manāpabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Majjhattākārappavattilakkhaṇā upekkhāpāramī, samabhāvadassanarasā, paṭighānunayavūpasamapaccupaṭṭhānā, kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇapadaṭṭhānā.

Therefore, the perfection of giving (dānapāramī) is characterized by relinquishment, its function is to destroy greed for things to be given, its manifestation is non-attachment or the attainment of prosperity and abundance, and its proximate cause is the object to be relinquished. The perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī) is characterized by morality—it is said to be characterized by composure and by being a foundation. Its function is to destroy immorality or its function is blamelessness, its manifestation is purity, and its proximate cause is shame and moral dread. The perfection of renunciation (nekkhammapāramī) is characterized by withdrawal from sensual pleasures and existence, its function is to reveal their dangers, its manifestation is turning away from them, and its proximate cause is a sense of spiritual urgency. The perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī) is characterized by penetrating the true nature of things, or by unerring penetration like that of an arrow shot by a skilled archer; its function is to illuminate its object like a lamp; its manifestation is non-delusion, like a good guide to one who has entered a forest; and its proximate cause is concentration or the four noble truths. The perfection of energy (vīriyapāramī) is characterized by exertion, its function is to support, its manifestation is non-collapse, and its proximate cause is a basis for arousing effort or a sense of spiritual urgency. The perfection of patience (khantipāramī) is characterized by endurance, its function is to bear the pleasant and unpleasant, its manifestation is forbearance or non-opposition, and its proximate cause is seeing things as they truly are. The perfection of truthfulness (saccapāramī) is characterized by non-deception, its function is to reveal things as they are, its manifestation is rectitude, and its proximate cause is gentleness. The perfection of determination (adhiṭṭhānapāramī) is characterized by resolve regarding the requisites for awakening, its function is to overcome their opposites, its manifestation is unshakability in that regard, and its proximate cause is the requisites for awakening. The perfection of loving-kindness (mettāpāramī) is characterized by promoting the welfare of others, its function is to provide benefit or to remove resentment, its manifestation is amiability, and its proximate cause is seeing the agreeable aspects in beings. The perfection of equanimity (upekkhāpāramī) is characterized by promoting a balanced attitude, its function is to see things impartially, its manifestation is the quieting of aversion and attraction, and its proximate cause is reflection on ownership of kamma.

Ettha [M 0.0274] ca karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitatā dānādīnaṃ pariccāgādilakkhaṇassa visesanabhāvena vattabbā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitāni hi dānādīni bodhisattasantāne pavattāni dānādipāramiyo nāma honti.

Herein, being encompassed by compassion and skillful means should be stated as the distinguishing factor for the characteristic of relinquishment and so on, of giving and so on. For giving and the others, when occurring in the mental continuum of a bodhisattva and encompassed by compassion and skillful means, are called the perfections of giving and so on.

Ko [P 0.0282] paccayoti? Abhinīhāro tāva pāramīnaṃ paccayo. Yo hi ayaṃ –

What is the condition? Firstly, aspiration is a condition for the perfections. For it is this:

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā;

Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā, abhinīhāro samijjhatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59) –

"Human existence, possession of the male gender, the cause, seeing the Teacher; going forth, attainment of qualities, a meritorious foundation, and inclination; when these eight factors come together, the aspiration succeeds." (Bu. Va. 2.59)

Evaṃ vutto aṭṭhadhammasamodhānasampādito “tiṇṇo tāreyyaṃ mutto moceyyaṃ danto dameyyaṃ santo sameyyaṃ assattho assāseyyaṃ parinibbuto parinibbāpeyyaṃ suddho sodheyyaṃ buddho bodheyya”ntiādinayappavatto abhinīhāro. So avisesena sabbapāramīnaṃ paccayo. Tappavattiyā [V 0.0257] hi uddhaṃ pāramīnaṃ pavicayupaṭṭhānasamādānādhiṭṭhānanipphattiyo mahāpurisānaṃ sambhavanti.

The aspiration, thus described as being accomplished through the convergence of these eight factors, proceeds in this way: "Having crossed, I shall help others cross; freed, I shall free others; tamed, I shall tame others; calmed, I shall calm others; comforted, I shall comfort others; fully extinguished, I shall lead others to full extinguishment; purified, I shall purify others; awakened, I shall awaken others." This, in general, is the condition for all perfections. For it is through its operation that the investigation, establishment, undertaking, determination, and accomplishment of the perfections arise for great beings.

Tattha manussattanti manussattabhāvo. Manussattabhāveyeva hi ṭhatvā buddhattaṃ patthentassa patthanā samijjhati, na nāgasupaṇṇādijātīsu ṭhitassa. Kasmāti ce? Buddhabhāvassa ananucchavikabhāvato.

Herein, "human existence" means the state of being human. For it is only when established in the human state that the aspiration of one who aspires to Buddhahood succeeds, not for one established in births as a nāga, supaṇṇa, or the like. If you ask why, it is because the state of a Buddha is not suitable for them.

Liṅgasampattīti manussattabhāve ṭhitassāpi purisasseva patthanā samijjhati, na itthiyā na paṇḍakanapuṃsakaubhatobyañjanakānaṃ vā samijjhati. Kasmāti ce? Yathāvuttakāraṇato lakkhaṇapāripūriyā abhāvato ca. Vuttañcetaṃ – “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ itthī arahaṃ assa sammāsambuddho”ti (a. ni. 1.279; vibha. 809) vitthāro. Tasmā manussajātikassāpi itthiliṅge ṭhitassa paṇḍakādīnaṃ vā patthanā na samijjhati.

"Accomplishment of gender" means that, even while in the human state, the aspiration succeeds only for a male, not for a female, nor for a eunuch, one of indeterminate sex, or a hermaphrodite. Why is that? Because of the reasons stated and due to the lack of the complete characteristics. And this was said: "Monks, this is impossible, it cannot happen, that a woman could be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha" (A. i. 28)—and so on in detail. Therefore, even for one of human birth abiding in the female gender, or for eunuchs and the like, the aspiration does not succeed.

Hetūti upanissayasampatti. Manussapurisassāpi hi upanissayasampannasseva hetusampattiyā patthanā samijjhati, na itarassa.

"Cause" means the accomplishment of supporting conditions. For even a human male, an aspiration succeeds only for one endowed with the accomplishment of supporting conditions, not for another.
