Satthāradassananti [M 0.0275] satthusammukhībhāvo. Dharamānakabuddhasseva hi santike patthentassa patthanā samijjhati, parinibbute pana bhagavati cetiyassa santike vā bodhimūle vā paṭimāya vā paccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ vā santike patthanā na samijjhati. Kasmā? Adhikārassa balavabhāvābhāvato. Buddhānaṃ eva pana santike patthanā samijjhati, ajjhāsayassa uḷārabhāvena tadadhikārassa balavabhāvāpattito.

"Seeing the Teacher" means being in the Teacher’s presence. An aspiration succeeds only for one who makes the resolve in the presence of a living Buddha. But when the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, an aspiration does not succeed near a shrine, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, before an image, or in the presence of Paccekabuddhas or a Buddha's disciples. Why? Because of the absence of a powerful qualification. However, an aspiration does succeed in the presence of Buddhas, due to the magnificence of their disposition and the attainment of a powerful qualification thereby.

Pabbajjāti buddhassa bhagavato santike patthentassāpi kammakiriyavādīsu tāpasesu vā [P 0.0283] bhikkhūsu vā pabbajitasseva patthanā samijjhati, no gihiliṅge ṭhitassa. Kasmā? Buddhabhāvassa ananucchavikabhāvato. Pabbajitā eva hi mahābodhisattā sammāsambodhiṃ adhigacchanti, na gahaṭṭhabhūtā, tasmā paṇidhānakāle ca pabbajjāliṅgaṃ eva hi yuttarūpaṃ kiñca guṇasampattiadhiṭṭhānabhāvato.

"Going forth" means that the aspiration, even of one aspiring in the presence of the Blessed One, the Buddha, succeeds only for one who has gone forth among ascetics who are proponents of action or among monks, not for one remaining in the householder's guise. Why? Because that is unsuitable for the state of Buddhahood. For it is only great Bodhisattvas who have gone forth who attain perfect enlightenment, not those who remain householders. Therefore, at the time of making the aspiration, the outward sign of one who has gone forth is indeed fitting, and moreover, because it is the foundation for the accomplishment of virtues.

Guṇasampattīti abhiññādiguṇasampadā. Pabbajitassāpi hi aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino pañcābhiññasseva patthanā samijjhati, na yathāvuttaguṇasampattiyā virahitassa. Kasmā? Pāramipavicayassa [V 0.0258] asamatthabhāvato, upanissayasampattiyā abhiññāsampattiyā ca samannāgatattā mahāpurisā katābhinīhārā sayameva pāramī pavicetuṃ samatthā honti.

"Accomplishment of qualities" means the accomplishment of qualities such as the higher knowledges. Even for a renunciate who has attained the eight meditative attainments, the aspiration succeeds only for one who possesses the five higher knowledges, not for one lacking the aforementioned accomplishment of qualities. Why? Because one would be incapable of investigating the perfections; for great beings who have made their aspiration are themselves capable of investigating the perfections, being endowed with the accomplishment of supporting conditions and the accomplishment of higher knowledges.

Adhikāroti adhiko upakāro. Yathāvuttaguṇasampannopi hi yo attano jīvitampi buddhānaṃ pariccajitvā tasmiṃ kāle adhikaṃ upakāraṃ karoti, tasseva abhinīhāro samijjhati, na itarassa.

"Great service" means superior help. Even one endowed with the aforementioned qualities, who sacrifices even his own life for the Buddhas and renders superior help at that time—only his aspiration succeeds, not that of another.

Chandatāti kattukāmatākusalacchando. Yassa hi yathāvuttadhammasamannāgatassa buddhakārakadhammānaṃ atthāya mahanto chando mahatī patthanā mahatī kattukāmatā atthi, tasseva samijjhati, na itarassa.

"Zeal" means the wholesome zeal which is the desire to act. For one endowed with the aforementioned qualities, who has great zeal, great aspiration, and great desire to act for the sake of the qualities that make a Buddha—only for such a one does it succeed, not for another.

Tatridaṃ chandamahantatāya opammaṃ – yo sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ ekodakībhūtaṃ attano bāhubaleneva uttaritvā pāraṃ gantuṃ samattho, so buddhattaṃ [M 0.0276] pāpuṇātīti sutvā taṃ dukkarato adahanto “ahaṃ taṃ uttaritvā pāraṃ gamissāmī”ti chandajāto hoti, na tattha saṅkocaṃ āpajjati. Tathā yo sakalacakkavāḷaṃ vītaccikānaṃ vigatadhūmānaṃ aṅgārānaṃ pūraṃ pādehi akkamanto atikkamitvā parabhāgaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho…pe… na tattha saṅkocaṃ āpajjati. Tathā yo sakalacakkavāḷaṃ sattisūlehi sunisitaphalehi nirantaraṃ ākiṇṇaṃ pādehi akkamanto atikkamitvā…pe… na tattha saṅkocaṃ āpajjati. Tathā yo sakalacakkavāḷaṃ nirantaraṃ ghanaveḷugumbasañchannaṃ kaṇṭakalatāvanagahanaṃ vinivijjhitvā parabhāgaṃ gantuṃ samattho…pe… na tattha saṅkocaṃ āpajjati. Tathā yo “cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni satasahassañca kappe niraye paccitvā buddhattaṃ [P 0.0284] pattabba”nti sutvā taṃ dukkarato adahanto “ahaṃ tattha paccitvā buddhattaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti chandajāto hoti, na tattha saṅkocaṃ āpajjatīti evamādinā nayena ettha chandassa mahantabhāvo veditabbo.

Here is a simile to illustrate the greatness of zeal: Hearing that one who could cross to the far shore with the strength of his own arms, should the entire world-system become a single mass of water, would attain Buddhahood, he, undaunted by the difficulty, thinks, "I will cross it and get to the far shore," and zeal arises in him; he does not shrink back from it. Similarly, one who could tread with his feet upon the entire world-system filled with flameless, smokeless coals and cross to the other side… does not shrink back. Likewise, one who could tread with his feet upon the entire world-system densely strewn with spears with well-sharpened points and cross beyond… does not shrink back. Likewise, one who could penetrate the entire world-system, continuously covered with thick bamboo clumps and a thicket of thorny creepers, and reach the other side… does not shrink back. Likewise, hearing, "After burning in hell for four incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons, Buddhahood is to be attained," he, undaunted by the difficulty, thinks, "I will burn there and attain Buddhahood," and zeal arises in him; he does not shrink back from it. In this way, the greatness of zeal should be understood.

Evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato panāyaṃ abhinīhāro atthato tesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ aṅgānaṃ samodhānena tathāpavatto cittuppādoti veditabbo. So sammadeva sammāsambodhiyā paṇidhānalakkhaṇo. “Aho vatāhaṃ anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjheyyaṃ, sabbasattānaṃ hitasukhaṃ nipphādeyya”nti evamādipatthanāraso, bodhisambhārahetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, mahākaruṇāpadaṭṭhāno, upanissayasampattipadaṭṭhāno vā. Acinteyyaṃ buddhabhūmiṃ aparimāṇaṃ sattalokahitañca ārabbha pavattiyā [V 0.0259] sabbabuddhakārakadhammamūlabhūto paramabhaddako paramakalyāṇo aparimeyyappabhāvo puññavisesoti daṭṭhabbo.

This aspiration, thus endowed with eight factors, should be understood in its meaning as the arising of a thought that has thus come about through the convergence of those eight factors. It has the characteristic of a resolution for supreme perfect enlightenment. Its function is the aspiration: "Oh, may I awaken to unsurpassed supreme perfect enlightenment and accomplish the welfare and happiness of all beings!" Its manifestation is its being a cause for the requisites of enlightenment. Its proximate cause is great compassion, or the accomplishment of supporting conditions. Having arisen in relation to the inconceivable Buddha-domain and the immeasurable welfare of the world of beings, it should be seen as the root of all qualities that make a Buddha, supremely auspicious, supremely excellent, of immeasurable power, and a special kind of merit.

Yassa ca uppattiyā saheva mahāpuriso mahābodhiyānapaṭipattiṃ otiṇṇo nāma hoti niyatabhāvasamadhigamanato tato anivattanasabhāvattā bodhisattoti samaññaṃ paṭilabhati, sabbabhāvena sammāsambodhiyaṃ samāsattamānasatā bodhisambhārasikkhāsamatthatā cassa santiṭṭhati. Yathāvuttābhinīhārasamijjhanena hi mahāpurisā sabbaññutaññāṇādhigamanapubbaliṅgena sayambhuñāṇena sammadeva sabbapāramiyo pavicinitvā samādāya anukkamena paripūrenti. Tathā katamahābhinīhāro hi sumedhapaṇḍito paṭipajji. Yathāha –

And indeed, from whose very arising the Great Being is called one who has entered upon the practice for Great Enlightenment—because of the attainment of a fixed state and because of his nature of not turning back from it, he obtains the designation of a Bodhisattva. And his mind stands firm, fully attached to supreme perfect enlightenment in every way, and he is capable of the training in the requisites for enlightenment. For it is by the success of the aspiration as described that Great Beings, with the preliminary sign of the attainment of omniscience, by means of their self-arisen wisdom, rightly discern and undertake all the perfections and gradually fulfill them. Thus did the wise Sumedha, who had made the great aspiration, practice. As it is said:

“Handa [M 0.0277] buddhakare dhamme, vicināmi ito cito;

Uddhaṃ adho dasa disā, yāvatā dhammadhātuyā;

Vicinanto tadā dakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapārami”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.115-116) –

"Come, I will examine the qualities that make one a Buddha, searching here and there; upwards, downwards, and in the ten directions, as far as the Dhamma-element extends; searching then, I saw the first perfection, generosity."

Vitthāro. Tassa ca abhinīhārassa cattāro paccayā cattāro hetū cattāri ca balāni veditabbāni.

In detail. And for that aspiration, four conditions, four causes, and four strengths should be understood.

Tattha katame cattāro paccayā? Idha mahāpuriso passati tathāgataṃ mahatā buddhānubhāvena acchariyabbhutaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ karontaṃ. Tassa taṃ nissāya taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā mahābodhiyaṃ cittaṃ santiṭṭhati – “mahānubhāvā vatāyaṃ dhammadhātu, yassā suppaṭividdhattā bhagavā evaṃ acchariyabbhutadhammo acinteyyānubhāvo cā”ti[P 0.0285]. So tameva mahānubhāvadassanaṃ nissāya taṃ paccayaṃ katvā sambodhiyaṃ adhimuccanto tattha cittaṃ ṭhapeti. Ayaṃ paṭhamo paccayo mahābhinīhārāya.

Herein, what are the four conditions? In this case, a Great Being sees the Tathāgata performing a marvelous and astonishing miracle with great Buddha-power. Relying on that, making that the object, his mind settles on great enlightenment—thinking, "Truly, this Dhamma-element is of great power, such that the Blessed One, having fully penetrated it, is so marvelous and astonishing in nature, and of inconceivable power." Relying on that very vision of great power, making that the condition, he resolves upon enlightenment and establishes his mind there. This is the first condition for the great aspiration.

Na heva kho passati tathāgatassa yathāvuttaṃ mahānubhāvataṃ, api ca kho suṇāti “ediso ca ediso ca bhagavā”ti. So taṃ nissāya taṃ paccayaṃ katvā sambodhiyaṃ adhimuccanto tattha cittaṃ ṭhapeti. Ayaṃ dutiyo paccayo mahābhinīhārāya.

He does not see the Tathāgata's great power as described, but he hears, "Such and such is the Blessed One." Relying on that and making that a condition, he resolves upon enlightenment and fixes his mind there. This is the second condition for the great aspiration.

Na heva kho passati tathāgatassa yathāvuttaṃ mahānubhāvataṃ, napi taṃ parato suṇāti, api [V 0.0260] ca kho tathāgatassa dhammaṃ desentassa “dasabalasamannāgato, bhikkhave, tathāgato”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.21-22) buddhānubhāvapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammaṃ suṇāti. So taṃ nissāya taṃ paccayaṃ katvā sambodhiyaṃ adhimuccanto tattha cittaṃ ṭhapeti. Ayaṃ tatiyo paccayo mahābhinīhārāya.

He does not see the Tathāgata's great power as described, nor does he hear it from another, yet he hears the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata—such as, "Monks, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers," and so on—connected with the Buddha's power. Relying on that and making that a condition, he resolves upon enlightenment and fixes his mind there. This is the third condition for the great aspiration.

Na heva kho passati tathāgatassa yathāvuttaṃ mahānubhāvataṃ, napi taṃ parato suṇāti, napi tathāgatassa dhammaṃ suṇāti, api ca kho uḷārajjhāsayo kalyāṇādhimuttiko “ahametaṃ buddhavaṃsaṃ buddhatantiṃ buddhapaveṇiṃ buddhadhammataṃ paripālessāmī”ti yāvadeva dhammaṃ eva sakkaronto garukaronto mānento pūjento dhammaṃ apacāyamāno taṃ nissāya taṃ paccayaṃ katvā sambodhiyaṃ adhimuccanto tattha cittaṃ ṭhapeti. Ayaṃ catuttho paccayo mahābhinīhārāya.

He does not see the Tathāgata’s great power as described, nor does he hear it from others, nor does he hear the Dhamma from the Tathāgata, yet he has lofty aspirations and wholesome inclinations, thinking, "I will maintain this lineage of Buddhas, the tradition of Buddhas, the succession of Buddhas, and the nature of Buddhahood." Simply by honoring, respecting, esteeming, and revering the Dhamma, showing deference to the Dhamma, he relies on that and makes it a condition, resolves upon enlightenment, and fixes his mind there. This is the fourth condition for the great aspiration.

Tattha [M 0.0278] katame cattāro hetū mahābhinīhārāya? Idha mahāpuriso pakatiyā upanissayasampannova hoti purimakesu buddhesu katādhikāro. Ayaṃ paṭhamo hetu mahābhinīhārāya. Puna caparaṃ mahāpuriso pakatiyā karuṇājjhāsayo hoti karuṇādhimutto sattānaṃ dukkhaṃ apanetukāmo api ca attano kāyajīvitaṃ pariccajitvā. Ayaṃ dutiyo hetu mahābhinīhārāya. Puna caparaṃ mahāpuriso sakalatopi vaṭṭadukkhato sattahitāya ca dukkaracariyato sucirampi kālaṃ ghaṭento vāyamanto anibbinno hoti anutrāsī yāva icchitatthanipphatti. Ayaṃ tatiyo hetu mahābhinīhārāya. Puna caparaṃ mahāpuriso kalyāṇamittasannissito hoti, yo [P 0.0286] ahitato nivāreti, hite patiṭṭhapeti. Ayaṃ catuttho hetu mahābhinīhārāya.

Herein, what are the four causes for the great aspiration? Here, a Great Being is naturally endowed with supporting conditions and has performed special service in the presence of past Buddhas. This is the first cause for the great aspiration. Furthermore, a Great Being is naturally of a compassionate disposition, inclined to compassion, desiring to remove the suffering of beings, even giving up his own body and life. This is the second cause for the great aspiration. Furthermore, a Great Being, striving and making effort for a very long time for the welfare of beings by means of difficult practice, is not weary of all the suffering of the round of existence, nor is he frightened, until the accomplishment of the desired aim. This is the third cause for the great aspiration. Furthermore, a Great Being relies on virtuous friends, who restrain him from what is unbeneficial and establish him in what is beneficial. This is the fourth cause for the great aspiration.

Tatrāyaṃ mahāpurisassa upanissayasampadā – ekantenevassa yathā ajjhāsayo sambodhininno hoti sambodhipoṇo sambodhipabbhāro, tathā sattānaṃ hitacariyā. Yato cānena purimabuddhānaṃ santike sambodhiyā paṇidhānaṃ kataṃ hoti manasā vācāya ca “ahampi ediso sammāsambuddho hutvā sammadeva sattānaṃ hitasukhaṃ nipphādeyya”nti. Evaṃ sampannūpanissayassa panassa imāni upanissayasampattiyā liṅgāni bhavanti yehi samannāgatassa sāvakabodhisattehi ca paccekabodhisattehi ca mahāviseso mahantaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati indriyato paṭipattito kosallato ca. Idha upanissayasampanno mahāpuriso yathā visadindriyo hoti visadañāṇo, na tathā itare. Parahitāya paṭipanno hoti, na attahitāya. Tathā hi so yathā bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya [V 0.0261] lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ paṭipajjati, na tathā itare. Tattha ca kosallaṃ āvahati ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānena ṭhānāṭhānakusalatāya ca.

Herein is the Great Being’s perfection of decisive support: his disposition is entirely inclined, leaning, and tending towards enlightenment, just as his conduct is for the welfare of beings. For he has made the aspiration for enlightenment in the presence of past Buddhas, mentally and verbally, thinking, “May I too become such a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One and rightly bring about the welfare and happiness of beings.” For one whose decisive support is thus perfected, these are the signs of his attainment of decisive support, by which a great distinction, a great difference, is discerned between him and disciple Bodhisattas and Paccekabodhisattas, in terms of faculties, practice, and skill. Here, the Great Being endowed with decisive support is one whose faculties are clear, whose knowledge is clear—not so for others. He practices for the welfare of others, not for his own. Indeed, he conducts himself for the welfare and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans—not so for others. And in this, he brings skill through ready wit and through expertise in what is possible and impossible.

Tathā mahāpuriso pakatiyā dānajjhāsayo hoti dānābhirato, sati deyyadhamme deti eva, na dānato saṅkocaṃ āpajjati, satataṃ samitaṃ saṃvibhāgasīlo hoti, pamuditova deti ādarajāto, na udāsīnacitto, mahantampi dānaṃ datvā na ca dānena santuṭṭho hoti, pageva appaṃ, paresañca ussāhaṃ janento dāne vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, dānapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammakathaṃ karoti, aññe ca paresaṃ dente disvā attamano [M 0.0279] hoti, bhayaṭṭhānesu ca paresaṃ abhayaṃ detīti evamādīni dānajjhāsayassa mahāpurisassa dānapāramiyā liṅgāni.

Similarly, the Great Being is naturally inclined to generosity and delights in giving. When there is a gift to be given, he gives it; he does not shrink back from giving. He is constantly and continuously disposed to sharing, and he gives with joy and respect, not with indifference. Even after giving a great gift, he is not satisfied with that giving, let alone a small one. He inspires others to generosity, praises giving, and speaks on the Dhamma connected with giving. Seeing others give, he is delighted. In places of fear, he gives safety to others. Such are the signs of the Great Being’s inclination to generosity, the perfection of giving.

Tathā pāṇātipātādīhi pāpadhammehi hirīyati ottappati, sattānaṃ aviheṭhanajātiko hoti sorato sukhasīlo asaṭho amāyāvī ujujātiko suvaco sovacassakaraṇīyehi dhammehi samannāgato [P 0.0287] mudujātiko atthaddho anatimānī, parasantakaṃ nādiyati antamaso tiṇasalākaṃ upādāya, attano hatthe nikkhittaṃ iṇaṃ vā gahetvā paraṃ na visaṃvādeti, parasmiṃ vā attano santake byāmūḷhe vissarite vā taṃ saññāpetvā paṭipādeti yathā taṃ na parahatthagataṃ hoti, aloluppo hoti, parapariggahesu pāpakaṃ cittampi na uppādeti, itthibyasanādīni dūrato parivajjeti, saccavādī saccasandho bhinnānaṃ sandhātā sahitānaṃ anuppadātā, piyavādī mihitapubbaṅgamo pubbabhāsī atthavādī dhammavādī anabhijjhālu abyāpannacitto aviparītadassano, kammassakatañāṇena saccānulomikañāṇena kataññū katavedī vuddhāpacāyī suvisuddhājīvo dhammakāmo parepi dhamme samādapetā sabbena sabbaṃ akiccato satte nivāretā kiccesu patiṭṭhapetā attanā ca tattha kicce yogaṃ āpajjitā, katvā vā pana sayaṃ akattabbaṃ sīghaññeva tato paṭivirato hotīti evamādīni sīlajjhāsayassa mahāpurisassa sīlapāramiyā liṅgāni.

Similarly, he is ashamed and afraid of evil qualities such as the destruction of life. He is naturally non-violent towards beings, gentle, of pleasant conduct, not deceitful, not fraudulent, straightforward, easy to instruct, endowed with qualities that make him easy to admonish, gentle, not stubborn, and not conceited. He does not take what belongs to others, not even a blade of grass. If he takes a debt placed in his hands, he does not deceive another. Or if others are confused or forgetful regarding their own possessions, he makes them understand and returns it properly, so that it does not fall into another’s hands. He is not greedy, nor does he harbor evil thoughts about others’ possessions. He avoids misconduct with women and so forth from afar. He speaks truthfully, is trustworthy, reconciles those who are divided, and promotes unity among those who are united. He speaks kindly, with a smile preceding his words, speaks first, speaks meaningfully, speaks on the Dhamma, is free from covetousness, has a mind free from ill will, and has right view. He has the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, has knowledge in accordance with the truths, is grateful and appreciative, respects elders, lives a very pure life, loves the Dhamma, encourages others to undertake the Dhamma, altogether restrains beings from what is unskillful, establishes them in what is skillful, and himself applies himself to those duties. If he has done what should not be done, he quickly refrains from it. Such are the signs of the Great Being’s inclination to virtue, the perfection of virtue.

Tathā mandakileso hoti mandanīvaraṇo, pavivekajjhāsayo avikkhepabahulo, na tassa pāpakā vitakkā cittaṃ anvāssavanti, vivekagatassa cassa appakasireneva cittaṃ samādhiyati, amittapakkhepi tuvaṭaṃ mettacittatā santiṭṭhati, pageva itarasmiṃ, satimā ca hoti cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi saritā anussaritā, medhāvī ca hoti dhammojapaññāya samannāgato, nipako ca hoti tāsu tāsu itikattabbatāsu, āraddhavīriyo ca hoti sattānaṃ hitakiriyāsu, khantibalasamannāgato ca hoti sabbasaho, acalādhiṭṭhāno ca hoti daḷhasamādāno[V 0.0262], ajjhupekkhako ca hoti upekkhāṭhānīyesu dhammesūti evamādīni mahāpurisassa nekkhammajjhāsayādīnaṃ vasena nekkhammapāramiādīnaṃ liṅgāni veditabbāni.

Similarly, he has weak defilements and weak hindrances. He is inclined to seclusion and is abundant in non-distraction. Evil thoughts do not flow into his mind. For one who has gone to seclusion, his mind is easily concentrated. Even towards hostile factions, his mind of loving-kindness is swiftly established—how much more so towards others. He is mindful, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago. He is intelligent, endowed with wisdom that masters the Dhamma. He is skillful in various duties. He is energetic in acting for the welfare of beings. He is endowed with the strength of patience, enduring all. He is unwavering in resolve, firm in commitment. He is one who looks on with equanimity regarding things that warrant equanimity. Such are to be known as the signs of the Great Being’s perfections, such as the perfection of renunciation, based on his inclination towards renunciation and so forth.

Evametehi [M 0.0280] bodhisambhāraliṅgehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa yaṃ vuttaṃ “mahābhinīhārāya kalyāṇamittasannissayo hetū”ti. Tatridaṃ saṅkhepato kalyāṇamittalakkhaṇaṃ – idha kalyāṇamitto saddhāsampanno hoti sīlasampanno sutasampanno cāgasampanno vīriyasampanno satisampanno [P 0.0288] samādhisampanno paññāsampanno. Tattha saddhāsampattiyā saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ kammaphalañca, tena sammāsambodhiyā hetubhūtaṃ sattesu hitesitaṃ na pariccajati, sīlasampattiyā sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo garu bhāvanīyo codako pāpagarahī vattā vacanakkhamo, sutasampattiyā sattānaṃ hitasukhāvahaṃ gambhīraṃ dhammakathaṃ kattā hoti, cāgasampattiyā appiccho hoti santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho, vīriyasampattiyā āraddhavīriyo hoti sattānaṃ hitapaṭipattiyaṃ, satisampattiyā upaṭṭhitasati hoti anavajjadhammesu, samādhisampattiyā avikkhitto hoti samāhitacitto, paññāsampattiyā aviparītaṃ pajānāti, so satiyā kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesamāno paññāya sattānaṃ hitāhitaṃ yathābhūtaṃ jānitvā samādhinā tattha ekaggacitto hutvā vīriyena ahitā satte nisedhetvā hite niyojeti. Tenāha –

Thus, for the Great Being endowed with these characteristics of the requisites for enlightenment, it is said: 'Association with good friends is the cause for the great aspiration.' Here, in brief, are the characteristics of a good friend: a good friend is endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Regarding the accomplishment of faith, he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata and in the fruit of kamma; therefore, he does not abandon the desire for the welfare of beings, which is the cause for perfect enlightenment. Regarding the accomplishment of virtue, he is dear to beings, agreeable, respected, worthy of reverence, an admonisher, a critic of evil, a speaker, and patient in speech. Regarding the accomplishment of learning, he is one who delivers profound Dhamma talks that bring welfare and happiness to beings. Regarding the accomplishment of generosity, he is of few desires, content, secluded, and unentangled. Regarding the accomplishment of energy, he is energetic in the practice for the welfare of beings. Regarding the accomplishment of mindfulness, he is established in mindfulness regarding blameless qualities. Regarding the accomplishment of concentration, he is undistracted and composed in mind. Regarding the accomplishment of wisdom, he understands without perversion. He, investigating the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states with mindfulness, and knowing the welfare and harm of beings as it actually is with wisdom, having become one-pointed in mind with concentration, and restraining beings from what is harmful with energy, guides them towards welfare. Therefore, it is said—

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no caṭṭhāne niyojako”ti. (a. ni. 7.37; netti. 113) –

“Dear, respected, worthy of reverence, a speaker and patient in speech; one who delivers a profound talk, and does not engage one in what is inappropriate.” (AN 7.37; Netti. 113)

Evaṃ guṇasamannāgatañca kalyāṇamittaṃ upanissāya mahāpuriso attano upanissayasampattiṃ sammadeva pariyodapeti. Suvisuddhāsayapayogo ca hutvā catūhi balehi samannāgato na cireneva aṭṭhaṅge samodhānetvā mahābhinīhāraṃ karonto bodhisattabhāve patiṭṭhahati anivattidhammo niyato sambodhiparāyano.

The Great Being, relying on such a good friend endowed with qualities, rightly purifies his own attainment of decisive support. And being one whose application of intention is very pure, and endowed with the four powers, not long after uniting the eight factors and making the great aspiration, he becomes established in the Bodhisattva state, of irreversible nature, destined for enlightenment.

Tassimāni cattāri balāni. Ajjhattikabalaṃ yā sammāsambodhiyaṃ attasannissayā dhammagāravena abhiruci ekantaninnajjhāsayatā, yāya mahāpuriso attādhipati lajjāpassayo abhinīhārasampanno ca hutvā pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇāti. Bāhirabalaṃ yā sammāsambodhiyaṃ parasannissayā abhiruci ekantaninnajjhāsayatā, yāya mahāpuriso [M 0.0281] lokādhipati mānāpassayo abhinīhārasampanno [P 0.0289] ca hutvā pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇāti. Upanissayabalaṃ [V 0.0263] yā sammāsambodhiyaṃ upanissayasampattiyā abhiruci ekantaninnajjhāsayatā, yāya mahāpuriso tikkhindriyo visadadhātuko satisannissayo abhinīhārasampanno ca hutvā pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇāti. Payogabalaṃ yā sammāsambodhiyaṃ tajjā payogasampadā sakkaccakāritā sātaccakāritā, yāya mahāpuriso visuddhapayogo nirantarakārī abhinīhārasampanno ca hutvā pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇāti.

These are the four powers. The internal power is the delight and one-pointed inclination towards perfect enlightenment through reliance on oneself, with reverence for the Dhamma. By this, the Great Being, with self as his master, supported by shame, and endowed with aspiration, fulfills the perfections and attains perfect enlightenment. The external power is the delight and one-pointed inclination towards perfect enlightenment through reliance on others. By this, the Great Being, with the world as his master, supported by pride, and endowed with aspiration, fulfills the perfections and attains perfect enlightenment. The power of decisive support is the delight and one-pointed inclination towards perfect enlightenment through the accomplishment of decisive support. By this, the Great Being, with keen faculties, a clear element, reliance on mindfulness, and endowed with aspiration, fulfills the perfections and attains perfect enlightenment. The power of application is the delight and one-pointed inclination towards perfect enlightenment through the accomplishment of appropriate application, acting with care and continually. By this, the Great Being, with purified application, acting without ceasing, and endowed with aspiration, fulfills the perfections and attains perfect enlightenment.

Evamayaṃ catūhi paccayehi catūhi hetūhi catūhi ca balehi sampannasamudāgamo aṭṭhaṅgasamodhānasampādito abhinīhāro pāramīnaṃ paccayo mūlakāraṇabhāvato. Yassa ca pavattiyā mahāpurise cattāro acchariyā abbhutā dhammā patiṭṭhahanti, sabbasattanikāyaṃ attano orasaputtaṃ viya piyacittena pariggaṇhāti. Na cassa cittaṃ puttasaṃkilesavasena saṃkilissati. Sattānaṃ hitasukhāvaho cassa ajjhāsayo payogo ca hoti. Attano ca buddhakārakadhammā uparūpari vaḍḍhanti paripaccanti ca. Yato ca mahāpuriso uḷāratamena puññābhisandena kusalābhisandena pavattiyā paccayena sukhassāhārena samannāgato sattānaṃ dakkhiṇeyyo uttamagāravaṭṭhānaṃ asadisaṃ puññakkhettañca hoti. Evamanekaguṇo anekānisaṃso mahābhinīhāro pāramīnaṃ paccayoti veditabbo.

Thus this aspiration, accomplished through the eightfold harmonious combination, and endowed with four conditions, four causes, and four powers, is a condition for the perfections, being the root cause. And in the course of its arising, four marvelous and wonderful qualities become established in the Great Being: he embraces all beings with a loving heart as if they were his own legitimate children. His mind is not defiled by the defilement of affection for children. His intention and application are for the welfare and happiness of beings. And the qualities that lead to Buddhahood grow and mature in him more and more. Moreover, the Great Being, being endowed with a most noble current of merit and a wholesome current, and with the condition of its arising as nourishment for happiness, becomes worthy of offerings to beings, the supreme object of reverence, and an incomparable field of merit. Thus, the great aspiration should be understood as a condition for the perfections, possessing many virtues and countless benefits.

Yathā ca abhinīhāro, evaṃ mahākaruṇā upāyakosallañca. Tattha upāyakosallaṃ nāma dānādīnaṃ bodhisambhārabhāvassa nimittabhūtā paññā, yāhi mahākaruṇūpāyakosallatāhi mahāpurisānaṃ attasukhanirapekkhatā nirantaraṃ parahitakaraṇapasutatā sudukkarehipi mahābodhisattacaritehi visādābhāvo pasādasambuddhidassanasavanānussaraṇakālesupi sattānaṃ hitasukhappaṭilābhahetubhāvo ca sampajjati. Tathā hissa paññāya buddhabhāvasiddhi, karuṇāya buddhakammasiddhi, paññāya sayaṃ tarati, karuṇāya pare tāreti, paññāya paradukkhaṃ parijānāti, karuṇāya paradukkhapatikāraṃ ārabhati, paññāya ca dukkhe nibbindati, karuṇāya [M 0.0282] dukkhaṃ sampaṭicchati, tathā paññāya nibbānābhimukho hoti, karuṇāya vaṭṭaṃ pāpuṇāti, tathā karuṇāya saṃsārābhimukho hoti, paññāya tatra nābhiramati, paññāya ca sabbattha virajjati, karuṇānugatattā na ca na sabbesaṃ anuggahāya pavatto, karuṇāya sabbepi anukampati, paññānugatattā [P 0.0290] na ca na sabbattha virattacitto, paññāya ca ahaṃkāramamaṃkārābhāvo, karuṇāya ālasiyadīnatābhāvo, tathā paññākaruṇāhi yathākkamaṃ attaparanāthatā dhīravīrabhāvo, anattantapaaparantapatā, attahitaparahitanipphatti, nibbhayābhiṃsanakabhāvo, dhammādhipatilokādhipatitā, kataññupubbakāribhāvo, mohataṇhāvigamo, vijjācaraṇasiddhi, balavesārajjanipphattīti [V 0.0264] sabbassāpi pāramitāphalassa visesena upāyabhāvato paññākaruṇā pāramīnaṃ paccayo. Idañca dvayaṃ pāramīnaṃ viya paṇidhānassāpi paccayo.

Just as with aspiration, so too with great compassion and skill in means. Herein, skill in means refers to the wisdom that serves as the sign of the requisites of enlightenment, such as giving, etc. Through this great compassion and skill in means, the Great Beings, indifferent to their own happiness, are constantly devoted to the welfare of others. Even in the face of the most difficult deeds in the great bodhisattva's conduct, they remain free from discouragement, and they become a cause for beings to attain welfare and happiness even when seeing, hearing, or recollecting the Buddha with serene faith. Thus, through wisdom, the attainment of Buddhahood is accomplished; through compassion, the work of a Buddha is accomplished. By wisdom, one crosses over oneself; by compassion, one causes others to cross over. By wisdom, one fully understands the suffering of others; by compassion, one undertakes to counteract that suffering. By wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with suffering; by compassion, one accepts suffering. By wisdom, one is oriented towards Nibbāna; by compassion, one reaches the round of existence. By compassion, one is oriented towards saṃsāra; by wisdom, one does not delight in it. By wisdom, one becomes dispassionate towards all things; yet, being accompanied by compassion, one does not fail to proceed to help all beings. By compassion, one has pity for all; yet, being accompanied by wisdom, one's mind does not fail to be dispassionate towards all things. By wisdom, there is the absence of 'I' and 'mine'; by compassion, there is the absence of laziness and dejection. Thus, through wisdom and compassion, in due order, one attains the state of being a refuge for oneself and others, the state of being wise and heroic, not tormenting oneself or others, the fulfillment of one’s own welfare and that of others, the state of fearlessness and of inspiring awe, sovereignty over the Dhamma and the world, the state of being grateful and a benefactor, the dispelling of delusion and craving, the accomplishment of true knowledge and conduct, and the attainment of the powers and confidences. Because wisdom and compassion serve as the special means for the fruit of all the perfections, they are a condition for the perfections. Moreover, these two are a condition for aspiration, just as they are for the perfections.

Tathā ussāhaummaṅgaavatthānahitacariyā ca pāramīnaṃ paccayāti veditabbā, yā buddhabhāvassa uppattiṭṭhānatāya buddhabhūmiyoti vuccanti. Tattha ussāho nāma bodhisambhārānaṃ abbhussahanavīriyaṃ. Ummaṅgo nāma bodhisambhāresu upāyakosallabhūtā paññā. Avatthānaṃ nāma adhiṭṭhānaṃ acalādhiṭṭhānatā. Hitacariyā nāma mettābhāvanā karuṇābhāvanā ca.

Similarly, effort, wisdom, steadfastness, and conduct beneficial to others are to be understood as conditions for the perfections, which are called the 'Buddha-grounds' because they serve as the basis for the arising of Buddhahood. Herein, effort refers to the energy of striving for the requisites of enlightenment. Wisdom refers to the wisdom that is skill in means regarding the requisites of enlightenment. Steadfastness refers to determination, unshakable determination. Conduct beneficial to others refers to the cultivation of loving-kindness and compassion.

Tathā nekkhammapavivekaalobhādosāmohanissaraṇappabhedā cha ajjhāsayā. Nekkhammajjhāsayā hi bodhisattā honti kāmesu gharāvāse ca dosadassāvino, tathā pavivekajjhāsayā saṅgaṇikāya dosadassāvino, alobhajjhāsayā lobhe dosadassāvino, adosajjhāsayā dose dosadassāvino, amohajjhāsayā mohe dosadassāvino, nissaraṇajjhāsayā sabbabhavesu dosadassāvinoti. Tasmā ete bodhisattānaṃ cha ajjhāsayā dānādīnaṃ pāramīnaṃ paccayāti veditabbā. Na hi lobhādīsu ādīnavadassanena alobhādīnaṃ adhikabhāvena ca vinā dānādipāramiyo sambhavanti, alobhādīnañhi adhikabhāvena pariccāgādininnacittatā alobhajjhāsayāditāti veditabbā.

Similarly, there are six inclinations: renunciation, seclusion, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, and deliverance. For Bodhisattas with an inclination towards renunciation, they see the faults in sensual pleasures and household life. Similarly, those with an inclination towards seclusion see the faults in association. Those with an inclination towards non-greed see the faults in greed. Those with an inclination towards non-hatred see the faults in hatred. Those with an inclination towards non-delusion see the faults in delusion. Those with an inclination towards deliverance see the faults in all states of existence. Therefore, these six inclinations of Bodhisattas should be understood as conditions for the perfections, such as giving, etc. For without seeing the dangers in greed and so forth, and without the predominance of non-greed and so forth, the perfections like giving cannot arise. For it should be understood that the mind inclined towards relinquishment and so forth, due to the predominance of non-greed and so forth, is the inclination towards non-greed, etc.

Yathā [M 0.0283] cete evaṃ dānajjhāsayatādayopi bodhiyā carantānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ dānādipāramīnaṃ paccayo. Dānajjhāsayatāya hi bodhisattā tappaṭipakkhe macchere dosadassāvino hutvā sammadeva dānapāramiṃ paripūrenti. Sīlajjhāsayatāya dussīlye dosadassāvino hutvā sammadeva sīlapāramiṃ paripūrenti. Nekkhammajjhāsayatāya kāmesu gharāvāse ca[P 0.0291], yathābhūtañāṇajjhāsayatāya aññāṇe vicikicchāya ca, vīriyajjhāsayatāya kosajje, khantiyajjhāsayatāya akkhantiyaṃ, saccajjhāsayatāya visaṃvāde, adhiṭṭhānajjhāsayatāya anadhiṭṭhāne, mettājjhāsayatāya byāpāde, upekkhājjhāsayatāya lokadhammesu ādīnavadassāvino hutvā sammadeva nekkhammādipāramiyo paripūrenti. Dānajjhāsayatādayo dānādipāramīnaṃ nipphattikāraṇattā paccayo.

Just as these are, so too are the inclinations towards giving and so forth a condition for the perfections of giving and so forth for Bodhisattas who practice for enlightenment. For by the inclination towards giving, Bodhisattas, seeing the fault in its opposite, stinginess, rightly fulfill the perfection of giving. By the inclination towards virtue, seeing the fault in misconduct, they rightly fulfill the perfection of virtue. By the inclination towards renunciation, seeing the fault in sensual pleasures and household life; by the inclination towards true knowledge, seeing the fault in ignorance and doubt; by the inclination towards energy, seeing the fault in laziness; by the inclination towards patience, seeing the fault in impatience; by the inclination towards truthfulness, seeing the fault in falsehood; by the inclination towards determination, seeing the fault in indecision; by the inclination towards loving-kindness, seeing the fault in ill will; by the inclination towards equanimity, seeing the danger in worldly conditions—they rightly fulfill the perfections of renunciation and so forth. The inclinations towards giving and so forth are a condition because they are the cause for the accomplishment of the perfections of giving and so forth.

Tathā apariccāgapariccāgādīsu yathākkamaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsapaccavekkhaṇā dānādipāramīnaṃ paccayo. Tatthāyaṃ paccavekkhaṇāvidhikhettavatthuhiraññasuvaṇṇagomahiṃsadāsidāsaputtadārādipariggahabyāsattacittānaṃ sattānaṃ khettādīnaṃ vatthukāmabhāvena bahupatthanīyabhāvato rājacorādisādhāraṇabhāvato [V 0.0265] vivādādhiṭṭhānato sapattakaraṇato nissārato paṭilābhaparipālanesu paraviheṭhanahetuto vināsanimittañca sokādianekavihitabyasanāvahato tadāsattinidānañca maccheramalapariyuṭṭhitacittānaṃ apāyūpapattihetubhāvatoti evaṃ vividhavipulānatthāvahāni pariggahavatthūni nāma. Tesaṃ pariccāgoyeva eko sotthibhāvoti pariccāge appamādo karaṇīyo.

Similarly, reflecting on the disadvantages and advantages, in due order, with regard to non-relinquishment, relinquishment, and so forth, is a condition for the perfections of giving and so forth. Herein, this reflection is as follows: For beings whose minds are engrossed in possessions such as fields, building sites, gold, silver, cattle, buffaloes, male and female slaves, sons, wives, and so forth, these fields and so forth, being objects of sensual pleasure, are highly desirable, common to kings, thieves, and others, grounds for disputes, causes of animosity, without substance, a cause of harming others in acquiring and maintaining them, and a sign of ruin, bringing various calamities such as sorrow; and being the origin of attachment to them, they are the cause of rebirth in woeful states for those whose minds are assailed by the stain of stinginess. Thus, objects of possession bring manifold and extensive harm. Their relinquishment alone is the state of well-being. Therefore, one should be heedful in relinquishment.

Api ca yācako yācamāno attano guyhassa ācikkhanato “mayhaṃ vissāsiko”ti ca, “pahāya gamanīyamattano santakaṃ gahetvā paralokaṃ yāhīti mayhaṃ upadesako”ti ca, “āditte viya agāre maraṇagginā āditte loke tato mayhaṃ santakassa apavāhakasahāyo”ti ca, “apavāhitassa cassa ajhāpananikkhepaṭṭhānabhūto”ti ca dānasaṅkhāte kalyāṇakammasmiṃ sahāyabhāvato sabbasampattīnaṃ aggabhūtāya paramadullabhāya buddhabhūmiyā sampattihetubhāvato ca “paramo kalyāṇamitto”ti ca paccavekkhitabbaṃ.

Moreover, the beggar who asks should be regarded as one who, by revealing his private need, is 'my confidant'; and as an advisor who says, 'Relinquishing what must be left behind, take your own possessions with you to the next world'; and as a companion who helps one remove one's possessions from the world that is ablaze with the fire of death, like a house on fire; and as a secure place to deposit what has been removed. Furthermore, because of his companionship in the meritorious act known as giving, and because it is a cause for attaining the state of Buddhahood—the highest of all attainments and supremely rare—one should reflect, 'He is a supreme spiritual friend.'

Tathā [M 0.0284] “uḷāre kammani anenāhaṃ sambhāvito, tasmā sā sambhāvanā avitathā kātabbā”ti ca, “ekantabheditāya jīvitassa ayācitenāpi mayā dātabbaṃ, pageva yācitenā”ti ca, “uḷārajjhāsayehi gavesitvāpi dātabbato sayamevāgato mama puññenā”ti ca “yācakassa dānāpadesena mayhamevāyamanuggaho”ti ca, “ahaṃ viya ayaṃ sabbopi loko mayā anuggahetabbo”ti ca, “asati yācake kathaṃ [P 0.0292] mayhaṃ dānapāramī pūreyyā”ti ca, “yācakānameva catthāya mayā sabbo pariggahetabbo”ti ca, “maṃ ayācitvāva mama santakaṃ yācakā kadā sayameva gaṇheyyu”nti ca, “kathamahaṃ yācakānaṃ piyo cassaṃ manāpo”ti ca, “kathaṃ vā te mayhaṃ piyā cassu manāpā”ti ca, “kathaṃ vāhaṃ dadamāno datvāpi ca attamano cassaṃ pamudito pītisomanassajāto”ti ca, “kathaṃ vā me yācakā bhaveyyuṃ uḷāro ca dānajjhāsayo”ti ca, “kathaṃ vāhamayācito eva yācakānaṃ hadayamaññāya dadeyya”nti ca, “sati dhane yācake ca apariccāgo mahatī mayhaṃ vañcanā”ti ca, “kathaṃ vāhaṃ attano aṅgāni jīvitaṃ vāpi yācakānaṃ pariccajeyya”nti ca pariccāganinnatā upaṭṭhapetabbā. Api ca “attho nāmāyaṃ nirapekkhaṃ dāyakamanugacchati, yathā taṃ nirapekkhaṃ khepakaṃ kiṭako”ti ca atthe nirapekkhatāya cittaṃ uppādetabbaṃ.

Similarly, one should reflect: 'By this noble act, I am honored; therefore, that honor should be made true,' and 'Given that life is utterly perishable, I must give even without being asked, how much more so when asked,' and 'Since it should be given even when sought by those with noble aspirations, he has come by himself through my merit,' and 'By the pretext of giving to the beggar, this is indeed a favor to me,' and 'This entire world should be helped by me, just as I would help myself,' and 'If there were no beggars, how could my perfection of giving be fulfilled?' and 'For the sake of beggars alone should all my possessions be acquired,' and 'When will beggars take what is mine by themselves without even asking me?' and 'How can I become dear and pleasing to beggars?' and 'How can they become dear and pleasing to me?' and 'How can I, while giving and after giving, be content, delighted, joyous, and filled with happiness and gladness?' and 'How might I have beggars, and a noble inclination to give?' and 'How can I, without being asked, know the hearts of beggars and give?' and 'When there is wealth and a beggar, not relinquishing is a great self-deception,' and 'How can I give up my own limbs or even my life for beggars?'—such an inclination towards relinquishment should be established. Moreover, one should reflect: 'This benefit indeed follows the giver who is without expectation, just as a pebble follows the one who flicks it without expectation'—thus, the mind should be developed towards being without expectation for the result.

Yācamāno pana yadi piyapuggalo hoti, “piyo maṃ yācatī”ti somanassaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Atha udāsīnapuggalo hoti, “ayaṃ maṃ yācamāno addhā iminā pariccāgena mitto [V 0.0266] hotī”ti somanassaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Dadantopi hi yācakānaṃ piyo hotīti. Atha pana verī puggalo yācati, “paccatthiko maṃ yācati, ayaṃ maṃ yācamāno addhā iminā pariccāgena verī piyo mitto hotī”ti visesena somanassaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Evaṃ piyapuggale viya majjhattaveripuggalesupi mettāpubbaṅgamaṃ karuṇaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāva dātabbaṃ.

When a beloved person asks, one should generate joy, thinking, "A beloved person is asking me." If it is a neutral person, one should generate joy, thinking, "This person asking me will surely become a friend through this act of giving." For one who gives becomes dear to those who ask. But if an enemy asks, one should generate even greater joy, thinking, "My adversary is asking me; surely, through this act of giving, this enemy will become a beloved friend." Thus, just as with a beloved person, having established compassion preceded by loving-kindness, one should give even to neutral and hostile individuals.

Sace panassa cirakālaparibhāvitattā lobhassa deyyadhammavisayā lobhadhammā uppajjeyyuṃ, tena bodhisattapaṭiññena iti paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ “nanu tayā sappurisasambodhāya abhinīhāraṃ karontena sabbasattānaṃ upakāratthāya ayaṃ kāyo nissaṭṭho tappariccāgamayañca puññaṃ, tattha nāma [M 0.0285] te bāhirepi vatthusmiṃ abhisaṅgappavatti hatthisinānasadisī hoti, tasmā tayā na katthaci saṅgo uppādetabbo. Seyyathāpi nāma mahato bhesajjarukkhassa tiṭṭhato mūlaṃ mūlatthikā haranti, papaṭikaṃ tacaṃ khandhaṃ viṭapaṃ sāraṃ sākhaṃ palāsaṃ pupphaṃ phalaṃ phalatthikā haranti, na tassa rukkhassa ‘mayhaṃ santakaṃ ete harantī’ti vitakkasamudācāro [P 0.0293] hoti, evameva sabbalokahitāya ussukkamāpajjantena mayā mahādukkhe akataññuke niccāsucimhi kāye paresaṃ upakārāya viniyujjamāne aṇumattopi micchāvitakko na uppādetabbo. Ko vā ettha viseso ajjhattikabāhiresu mahābhūtesu ekantabhedanavikiraṇaviddhaṃsanadhammesu, kevalaṃ pana sammohavijambhitametaṃ, yadidaṃ etaṃ mama esohamasmi eso me attāti abhiniveso. Tasmā bāhiresu viya ajjhattikesupi karacaraṇanayanādīsu maṃsādīsu ca anapekkhena hutvā ‘taṃ tadatthikā harantū’ti nissaṭṭhacittena bhavitabba”nti.

However, if, due to long habituation, states of greed concerning the object to be given should arise, then that one with the resolve of a Bodhisatta should reflect thus: 'Did you not, when undertaking the striving for perfect enlightenment, relinquish this body for the benefit of all beings and the merit consisting of that relinquishing? Yet, in that case, your attachment to even external objects becomes like an elephant's bath. Therefore, you should not allow attachment to arise anywhere. Just as when a great medicinal tree is standing, those who need its root take its root; those who need its bark, trunk, branches, heartwood, limbs, leaves, flowers, or fruit take them; and that tree does not have the thought, "They are taking what belongs to me." Even so, as I become eager for the welfare of the whole world, I should not allow even the slightest wrong thought to arise when offering this body—which is subject to great suffering, ungrateful, and ever impure—for the benefit of others. What difference, indeed, is there between internal and external great elements, which are of a nature to be utterly broken up, scattered, and destroyed? This, namely the clinging that "This is mine, this I am, this is my self," is merely a manifestation of delusion. Therefore, just as with external things, one should be without concern even for internal things—hands, feet, eyes, and so on, and flesh and so on—and one should be with a mind relinquished, thinking, "Let those who need them take them."'

Evaṃ paṭisañcikkhato cassa sambodhāya pahitattassa kāyajīvitesu nirapekkhassa appakasireneva kāyavacīmanokammāni suvisuddhāni honti. So suvisuddhakāyavacīmanokammanto visuddhājīvo ñāyapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhito apāyupāyakosallasamannāgamena bhiyyosomattāya deyyadhammapariccāgena abhayadānasaddhammadānehi ca sabbasatte anuggaṇhituṃ samattho hotīti ayaṃ tāva dānapāramiyaṃ paccavekkhaṇānayo.

By reflecting thus, one whose mind is directed towards enlightenment and is indifferent to body and life will effortlessly purify bodily, verbal, and mental actions. With purified bodily, verbal, and mental actions and purified livelihood, established in righteous practice, endowed with skill in what is the way and what is not the way, one becomes capable of helping all beings to a greater extent through the relinquishing of gifts, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dhamma. This, then, is the method of reviewing the perfection of giving.

Sīlapāramiyaṃ pana evaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ – idañhi sīlaṃ nāma gaṅgodakādīhi visodhetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa dosamalassa vikkhālanajalaṃ, haricandanādīhi vinetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa rāgādipariḷāhassa vinayanaṃ, hāramakuṭakuṇḍalādīhi pacurajanālaṅkārehi asādhāraṇo sādhūnaṃ alaṅkāraviseso, sabbadisāvāyanato akittimo sabbakālānurūpo ca surabhigandho, khattiyamahāsālādīhi devatāhi ca vandanīyādibhāvāvahanato paramo vasīkaraṇamanto, cātumahārājikādidevalokārohaṇasopānapanti[V 0.0267], jhānābhiññānaṃ adhigamūpāyo, nibbānamahānagarassa sampāpakamaggo, sāvakabodhipaccekabodhisammāsambodhīnaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūmi, yaṃ yaṃ vā panicchitaṃ patthitaṃ, tassa tassa samijjhanūpāyabhāvato cintāmaṇikapparukkhādike ca atiseti.

Now, the perfection of virtue should be reflected upon thus: This virtue is the water for washing away the stain of hatred, which cannot be cleansed by the waters of the Ganges or other rivers. It is the allaying of the burning fever of lust and other torments, which cannot be remedied by sandalwood paste or other means. It is a unique adornment of the virtuous, unmatched by the abundant decorations of many people, like necklaces, crowns, or earrings. It is a natural fragrance, wafting in all directions, suitable for all times. By bringing about a state of being worthy of veneration by nobles, great householders, and deities, it is the supreme spell of mastery. It is a flight of stairs for ascending to the heavens, beginning with the realm of the Four Great Kings. It is a means to the attainment of jhānas and higher knowledges. It is the path that leads to the great city of Nibbāna. It is the ground of establishment for the enlightenment of disciples, solitary Buddhas, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas. Inasmuch as it is the means for the fulfillment of whatever is desired and wished for, it even surpasses the wish-fulfilling gem and the wish-granting tree.

Vuttañcetaṃ [M 0.0286] bhagavatā – “ijjhati, bhikkhave, sīlavato cetopaṇidhivisuddhattā”ti (dī. ni. 3.337; a. ni. 8.35). Aparampi vuttaṃ – “ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo ca assaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cā’ti, sīlesvevassa [P 0.0294] paripūrakārī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.65). Tathā “avippaṭisāratthāni kho, ānanda, kusalāni sīlānī”ti (a. ni. 11.1). “Pañcime, gahapatayo, ānisaṃsā sīlavato sīlasampadāyā”tiādisuttānañca (dī. ni. 2.150; 3.316; a. ni. 5.213; mahāva. 285) vasena sīlassa guṇā paccavekkhitabbā. Tathā aggikkhandhopamasuttādīnaṃ (a. ni. 7.72) vasena sīlavirahe ādīnavā. Pītisomanassanimittato attānuvādaparāpavādadaṇḍaduggatibhayābhāvato viññūhi pāsaṃsabhāvato avippaṭisārahetuto sotthiṭṭhānato atijanasāpateyyādhipateyyāyurūpaṭṭhānabandhumittasampattīnaṃ atisayanato ca sīlaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Sīlavato hi attano sīlasampadāhetu mahantaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppajjati – “kataṃ vata mayā kusalaṃ, kataṃ kalyāṇaṃ, kataṃ bhīruttāṇa”nti.

This was spoken by the Blessed One: 'Monks, the aspiration of one with virtue succeeds because of purity of intention' (Dī. Ni. 3.337; A. Ni. 8.35). Furthermore, it was said: 'If a monk, monks, should wish, "May I be dear to my fellow practitioners, beloved, respected, and esteemed," he should be a perfect fulfiller of the virtues' (Ma. Ni. 1.65). Likewise, 'Indeed, Ānanda, wholesome virtues are for the purpose of freedom from remorse' (A. Ni. 11.1). 'Householders, there are these five benefits for one with virtue, accomplished in virtue' — and so on, as found in the suttas (Dī. Ni. 2.150; 3.316; A. Ni. 5.213; Mahāva. 285) — the qualities of virtue should be contemplated. Similarly, through the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta and others (A. Ni. 7.72), the disadvantages of lacking virtue should be considered. Virtue should be contemplated as a source of joy and gladness, as the absence of fear of self-reproach, blame from others, punishment, and a bad destination, as being praised by the wise, as the cause for non-remorse, as a foundation of safety, and as surpassing the accomplishments of human wealth, sovereignty, longevity, beauty, status, and the abundance of relatives and friends. For a virtuous one, due to their accomplishment in virtue, great joy and gladness arise: 'Truly, I have done a wholesome deed, I have done a meritorious deed, I have done what is a refuge from fear.'

Tathā sīlavato attā na upavadati, na pare viññū, daṇḍaduggatibhayānaṃ sambhavo eva natthi. “Sīlavā purisapuggalo kalyāṇadhammo”ti viññūnaṃ pāsaṃso hoti. Tathā sīlavato yvāyaṃ “kataṃ vata mayā pāpaṃ, kataṃ luddakaṃ, kataṃ kibbisa”nti dussīlassa vippaṭisāro uppajjati, so na hoti. Sīlañca nāmetaṃ appamādādhiṭṭhānato bhogabyasanādiparihāramukhena mahato atthassa sādhanato maṅgalabhāvato ca paramaṃ sotthiṭṭhānaṃ, nihīnajaccopi sīlavā khattiyamahāsālādīnaṃ pūjanīyo hotīti kulasampattiṃ atiseti sīlasampadā, “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja? Idha te assa dāso kammakaro”tiādivacanañcettha (dī. ni. 1.186) sādhakaṃ. Corādīhi asādhāraṇato paralokānugamanato mahapphalabhāvato samathādiguṇādhiṭṭhānato ca bāhiradhanaṃ atiseti sīlaṃ. Paramassa cittissariyassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato khattiyādīnaṃ issariyaṃ atiseti sīlaṃ. Sīlanimittañhi taṃtaṃsattanikāyesu sattānaṃ issariyaṃ, vassasatadīghappamāṇato jīvitato ekāhampi sīlavato jīvitassa visiṭṭhatāvacanato sati ca jīvite sikkhānikkhipanassa maraṇatāvacanato sīlaṃ jīvitato visiṭṭhataraṃ[M 0.0287][V 0.0268]. Verīnampi manuññabhāvāvahanato jarārogavipattīhi anabhibhavanīyato ca rūpasampattiṃ atiseti sīlaṃ. Pāsādahammiyādiṭṭhānavisese rājayuvarājasenāpatiādiṭṭhānavisese ca atiseti sīlaṃ sukhavisesādhiṭṭhānabhāvato. Sabhāvasiniddhe santikāvacarepi bandhujane mittajane ca atiseti ekantahitasampādanato [P 0.0295] paralokānugamanato ca “na taṃ mātāpitā kayirā”tiādivacanañcettha (dha. pa. 43) sādhakaṃ. Tathā hatthiassarathapattibalakāyehi mantāgadasotthānappayogehi ca durārakkhaṃ attānaṃ ārakkhābhāvena sīlameva visiṭṭhataraṃ attādhīnato aparādhīnato mahāvisayato ca. Tenevāha – “dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāri”ntiādi (jā. 1.10.102). Evamanekaguṇasamannāgataṃ sīlanti paccavekkhantassa aparipuṇṇā ceva sīlasampadā pāripūriṃ gacchati aparisuddhā ca pārisuddhiṃ.

Thus, the virtuous person does not reproach themselves, nor do other wise ones reproach them. There is simply no arising of the fear of punishment and of a bad destination. 'A virtuous individual is one of excellent qualities'—such is the praise of the wise. For the virtuous, there arises no remorse such as, 'I have done evil, I have acted cruelly, I have committed sin,' the kind of remorse which torments the unvirtuous. Moreover, virtue, because it is founded on heedfulness, because it averts the loss of wealth and other misfortunes, because it accomplishes great benefit, and because it is auspicious, is the supreme foundation of security. Even a person of low birth, if virtuous, is worthy of honor from great nobles and brahmins—thus the accomplishment of virtue surpasses the accomplishment of lineage. As it is said: 'What do you think, great king? Suppose you had a slave or a worker...' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.186)—this illustrates the point. Virtue surpasses external wealth because it is not shared with thieves and others, it accompanies one to the next life, it yields great fruit, and it serves as the foundation for qualities like tranquility. Virtue surpasses the sovereignty of kings and others because it is the foundation of supreme mastery over the mind. For virtue is the mark of sovereignty among beings in the various classes of beings. Because it is said that even a single day of a virtuous person's life is more excellent than a life a hundred years long, and because, while one is alive, the laying down of the training is said to be death, virtue is more excellent than life itself. Virtue surpasses physical beauty because it brings about a pleasing state even in enemies and because it cannot be overcome by the misfortunes of old age and sickness. Virtue surpasses special places such as palaces and mansions, and special positions such as king, crown prince, and general, because it is the foundation of a special happiness. Virtue surpasses even naturally affectionate and nearby relatives and friends because it accomplishes one's exclusive welfare and accompanies one to the next life. And the saying, 'Not what a mother or father might do...' (Dhammapada 43) is a proof of this. Furthermore, virtue itself is more excellent for protecting the self, which is difficult to protect, than are the forces of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, or the use of spells, medicines, and blessings, because it is dependent on oneself, not on others, and because of its vast scope. Therefore it was said: 'The Dhamma indeed protects one who lives by the Dhamma...' (Jātaka 1.10.102). For one who reflects thus on virtue as being endowed with these many qualities, an incomplete accomplishment of virtue reaches fulfillment, and an impure one reaches purity.

Sace panassa dīgharattaṃ paricayena sīlapaṭipakkhā dhammā dosādayo antarantarā uppajjeyyuṃ, tena bodhisattapaṭiññena evaṃ paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ – nanu tayā sambodhāya paṇidhānaṃ kataṃ, sīlavikalena ca na sakkā lokiyāpi sampattiyo pāpuṇituṃ, pageva lokuttarā, sabbasampattīnaṃ pana aggabhūtāya sammāsambodhiyā adhiṭṭhānabhūtena sīlena paramukkaṃsagatena bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā “kikīva aṇḍa”ntiādinā (visuddhi. 1.19; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7) vuttanayena sammā sīlaṃ rakkhantena suṭṭhutaraṃ tayā pesalena bhavitabbaṃ.

But if, through long familiarity, qualities opposed to virtue, such as aversion, should arise from time to time, then one who has made the bodhisatta promise should reflect thus: 'Have you not made a resolve for full enlightenment? With deficient virtue, it is not possible to attain even worldly accomplishments, let alone supramundane ones. Furthermore, for perfect self-enlightenment, which is the chief of all accomplishments, the virtue that is its foundation must be brought to the highest excellence. Therefore, in the manner spoken of as 'like a pheasant its egg,' guarding your virtue well, you must be even more amiable.'

Api ca tayā dhammadesanāya yānattaye sattānaṃ avatāraṇaparipācanāni kātabbāni, sīlavikalassa ca vacanaṃ na paccetabbaṃ hoti, asappāyāhāravicārassa viya vejjassa tikicchanaṃ, tasmā kathāhaṃ saddheyyo hutvā sattānaṃ avatāraṇaparipācanāni kareyyanti sabhāvaparisuddhasīlena bhavitabbaṃ. Kiñca jhānādiguṇavisesayogena me sattānaṃ upakārakaraṇasamatthatā paññāpāramiādiparipūraṇañca, jhānādayo ca guṇā sīlapārisuddhiṃ vinā na sambhavantīti sammadeva sīlaṃ parisodhetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, by teaching the Dhamma, you must accomplish the guiding and maturing of beings in the three vehicles. And the word of one deficient in virtue is not to be trusted, like the treatment by a physician who himself partakes of unsuitable food. Therefore, one must be of naturally pure virtue, thinking, 'How can I, being trustworthy, accomplish the guiding and maturing of beings?' Moreover, my ability to benefit beings comes through the application of special qualities such as jhāna, as does the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom and so on. And since jhāna and other such qualities are not possible without purity of virtue, virtue must be thoroughly purified.

Tathā “sambādho gharāvāso rajopatho”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.191; saṃ. ni. 2.154; ma. ni. 1.291; 2.10) gharāvāse, “aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.234; pāci. 175) “mātāpi puttena vivadatī”tiādinā [M 0.0288] (ma. ni. 1.178) ca kāmesu, “seyyathāpi puriso iṇaṃ ādāya kammante payojeyyā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.218) kāmacchandādīsu ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamā vuttavipariyāyena “abbhokāso pabbajjā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.191; saṃ. ni. 2.154) pabbajjādīsu [V 0.0269] ānisaṃsapaṭisaṅkhāvasena nekkhammapāramiyaṃ paccavekkhaṇā veditabbā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana dukkhakkhandha- (ma. ni. 1.163 ādayo) āsivisopamasuttā- (saṃ. ni. 4.238) divasena veditabbo.

Likewise, the reviewing of the perfection of renunciation is to be understood as follows. It is preceded by seeing the drawbacks in household life, as in 'Household life is confining, a path of dust,' and so on; in sensual pleasures, as in 'Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton,' and 'Even a mother quarrels with her son,' and so on; and in sensual desire and so on, as in 'Just as a man, having taken a loan, would engage in work,' and so on. Conversely, it is the contemplation of the benefits in the going forth and so on, as in 'The going forth is the open air,' and so on. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is to be understood by way of discourses such as the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta and the Āsivisopama Sutta.

Tathā [P 0.0296] “paññāya vinā dānādayo dhammā na visujjhanti, yathāsakaṃ byāpārasamatthā ca na hontī”ti paññāguṇā manasikātabbā. Yatheva hi jīvitena vinā sarīrayantaṃ na sobhati, na ca attano kiriyāsu paṭipattisamatthaṃ hoti, yathā ca cakkhādīni indriyāni viññāṇena vinā yathāsakaṃ visayesu kiccaṃ kātuṃ nappahonti, evaṃ saddhādīni indriyāni paññāya vinā sakiccapaṭipattiyaṃ asamatthānīti pariccāgādipaṭipattiyaṃ paññā padhānakāraṇaṃ. Ummīlitapaññācakkhukā hi mahābodhisattā attano aṅgapaccaṅgānipi datvā anattukkaṃsakā aparavambhakā ca honti, bhesajjarukkhā viya vikapparahitā kālattayepi somanassajātā. Paññāvasena hi upāyakosallayogato pariccāgo parahitappavattiyā dānapāramibhāvaṃ upeti. Attatthañhi dānaṃ vaḍḍhisadisaṃ hoti.

Thus, "Without wisdom, virtues such as generosity do not become purified, nor are they capable of their respective functions." The qualities of wisdom should be reflected upon. Just as a bodily frame without life does not shine, nor is it capable of acting in its own functions, and just as faculties like the eye cannot fulfill their respective functions regarding their objects without consciousness, so too faculties like faith are incapable of acting in their own functions without wisdom. Therefore, wisdom is the primary cause for practices such as giving. For the great bodhisattvas, whose eyes of wisdom are opened, even after giving away their own limbs, they neither exalt themselves nor disparage others. Like medicinal trees, they remain free of discrimination and are joyful in all three times. Through wisdom and the application of skillful means, giving that leads to the welfare of others attains the state of the perfection of generosity. For, giving for one's own benefit is like interest.

Tathā paññāya abhāvena taṇhādisaṃkilesāviyogato sīlassa visuddhi eva na sambhavati, kuto sabbaññuguṇādhiṭṭhānabhāvo. Paññavā eva ca gharāvāse kāmaguṇesu saṃsāre ca ādīnavaṃ pabbajjāya jhānasamāpattiyaṃ nibbāne ca ānisaṃsaṃ suṭṭhu sallakkhento pabbajitvā jhānasamāpattiyo nibbattetvā nibbānābhimukho pare ca tattha patiṭṭhāpeti. Vīriyañca paññāvirahitaṃ yathicchitamatthaṃ na sādheti durārambhabhāvato. Varameva hi anārambho durārambhato, paññāsahitena pana vīriyena na kiñci duradhigamaṃ upāyapaṭipattito. Tathā paññavā eva parāpakārādīnaṃ adhivāsakajātiko hoti, na duppañño. Paññāvirahitassa ca parehi upanītā apakārā khantiyā paṭipakkhameva anubrūhenti, paññavato pana te khantisampattiyā paribrūhanavasena assā thirabhāvāya saṃvattanti. Paññavā eva tīṇipi saccāni [M 0.0289] nesaṃ kāraṇāni paṭipakkhe ca yathābhūtaṃ jānitvā paresaṃ avisaṃvādako hoti.

Thus, without wisdom, the purity of virtue is not possible due to non-separation from defilements like craving—how much less the state of being the foundation for the qualities of an omniscient one! Moreover, only the wise, having thoroughly considered the dangers in household life, sensual pleasures, and saṃsāra, as well as the benefits of renunciation, meditative attainments, and Nibbāna, go forth from home. They generate meditative attainments and, turning toward Nibbāna, establish others there as well. And energy devoid of wisdom does not achieve its desired goal, because it is a wrong undertaking. Indeed, non-undertaking is better than wrong undertaking; but with energy accompanied by wisdom, nothing is hard to achieve, due to skillful practice. Likewise, only the wise are naturally patient with harm from others, not the unwise. For one lacking wisdom, the harms inflicted by others only augment what is contrary to patience; but for the wise, those very harms, by way of increasing the accomplishment of patience, conduce to its stability. Only the wise, having truly understood the three truths, their causes, and their counteractions, are not deceptive to others.

Tathā paññābalena attānaṃ upatthambhetvā dhitisampadāya sabbapāramīsu acalasamādānādhiṭṭhāno hoti. Paññavā eva ca piyamajjhattaverivibhāgaṃ akatvā sabbattha hitūpasaṃhārakusalo hoti. Tathā paññāvasena lābhālābhādilokadhammasannipāte nibbikāratāya majjhatto hoti. Evaṃ sabbāsaṃ pāramīnaṃ paññāva pārisuddhihetūti paññāguṇā paccavekkhitabbā. Api ca paññāya vinā na [P 0.0297] dassanasampatti, antarena ca diṭṭhisampadaṃ na sīlasampadā[V 0.0270], sīladiṭṭhisampadāvirahitassa na samādhisampadā, asamāhitena ca na sakkā attahitamattampi sādhetuṃ, pageva ukkaṃsagataṃ parahitanti parahitāya paṭipannena “nanu tayā sakkaccaṃ paññāya parivuddhiyaṃ āyogo karaṇīyo”ti bodhisattena attā ovaditabbo. Paññānubhāvena hi mahāsatto caturadhiṭṭhānādhiṭṭhito catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi lokaṃ anuggaṇhanto satte niyyānamagge avatāreti, indriyāni ca nesaṃ paripāceti.

Thus, by the power of wisdom, one supports oneself and, through the accomplishment of steadfastness, becomes established with an unwavering resolution and undertaking in all perfections. The wise one, without making distinctions between the dear, the neutral, and the hostile, becomes skilled in promoting welfare everywhere. Moreover, through wisdom, one remains equanimous in the face of the confluence of worldly conditions such as gain and loss, being unperturbed. In this way, wisdom alone is the cause of the purification of all perfections—thus, the qualities of wisdom should be contemplated. Furthermore, without wisdom, there is no accomplishment of vision; without the accomplishment of right view, there is no accomplishment of virtue; for one devoid of the accomplishment of virtue and right view, there is no accomplishment of concentration; and one who is unconcentrated cannot even achieve one's own welfare, much less the supreme welfare of others. Therefore, the Bodhisatta should admonish himself, saying: "Surely, you should diligently apply yourself to the increase of wisdom." For by the power of wisdom, the Great Being, established in the four resolutions, favors the world through the four bases of sympathy, guiding beings onto the path of liberation and maturing their faculties.

Tathā paññābalena khandhāyatanādīsu pavicayabahulopavattinivattiyo yāthāvato parijānanto dānādayo guṇe visesanibbedhabhāgiyabhāvaṃ nayanto bodhisattasikkhāya paripūrakārī hotīti evamādinā anekākāravokāre paññāguṇe vavatthapetvā paññāpāramī anubrūhetabbā.

Thus, through the power of wisdom, by frequently investigating and thereby thoroughly understanding the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, sense bases, and so forth as they actually are, and by leading virtues such as generosity to a state conducive to distinction and penetration, one becomes a fulfiller of the bodhisattva training. In this way, having ascertained the qualities of wisdom in their diverse aspects and divisions, the perfection of wisdom should be developed.

Tathā dissamānānipi lokiyāni kammāni nihīnavīriyena pāpuṇituṃ asakkuṇeyyāni, agaṇitakhedena pana āraddhavīriyena duradhigamaṃ nāma natthi. Nihīnavīriyo hi “saṃsāramahoghato sabbasatte santāressāmī”ti ārabhitumeva na sakkuṇāti. Majjhimo ārabhitvā antarā vosānamāpajjati. Ukkaṭṭhavīriyo pana attasukhanirapekkho ārambhapāramimadhigacchatīti vīriyasampatti paccavekkhitabbā. Api ca “yassa attano eva saṃsārapaṅkato samuddharaṇatthamārambho, tassāpi na vīriyassa sithilabhāve manorathānaṃ matthakappatti sakkā sambhāvetuṃ, pageva sadevakassa lokassa samuddharaṇatthaṃ katābhinīhārenā”ti [M 0.0290] ca “rāgādīnaṃ dosagaṇānaṃ mattamahāgajānaṃ viya dunnivārabhāvato tannidānānañca kammasamādānānaṃ ukkhittāsikavadhakasadisabhāvato tannimittānañca duggatīnaṃ sabbadā vivaṭamukhabhāvato, tattha niyojakānañca pāpamittānaṃ sadā sannihitabhāvato tadovādakāritāya ca bālassa puthujjanabhāvassa satisambhave yuttaṃ sayameva saṃsāradukkhato nissaritunti micchāvitakkā vīriyānubhāvena dūrībhavantī”ti ca “yadi pana sambodhi attādhīnena vīriyena sakkā samadhigantuṃ, kimettha dukkara”nti ca evamādinā nayena vīriyaguṇā paccavekkhitabbā.

Likewise, even worldly deeds that are seen cannot be accomplished with weak effort; but for one with resolute effort who disregards fatigue, there is nothing that is hard to achieve. For one with feeble effort cannot even begin with the thought, "I will deliver all beings from the great flood of saṃsāra." A person of moderate effort begins, but gives up midway. But one with supreme effort, indifferent to personal pleasure, attains the perfection of endeavor—thus, the accomplishment of effort should be reflected upon. Moreover, "Even for one whose endeavor is only to free themselves from the mire of saṃsāra, the attainment of the summit of their desires cannot be expected when effort is slack, let alone for one who has resolved to liberate the world with its gods." And, "Because the groups of defilements, such as passion, are hard to restrain, like great intoxicated elephants; and because the undertakings of actions caused by them are like a killer with a raised sword; and because the woeful states resulting from them always have their mouths open; and because evil friends who direct one there are always near; and given the possibility of the state of a foolish ordinary person acting on their advice—wrong thoughts such as, ‘It is fitting to escape from the suffering of saṃsāra by myself alone,’ are driven far away by the power of effort." And, "If enlightenment can be attained through effort dependent on oneself, what here is difficult?" In this way, the qualities of effort should be contemplated.

Tathā [P 0.0298] khanti nāmāyaṃ niravasesaguṇapaṭipakkhassa kodhassa vidhamanato guṇasampādane sādhūnamappaṭihatamāyudhaṃ, parābhibhavasamatthānaṃ alaṅkāro, samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ balasampadā, kodhaggivinayanaudakadhārā, kalyāṇassa kittisaddassa sañjātideso, pāpapuggalānaṃ vacīvisavūpasamakaro mantāgado, saṃvare ṭhitānaṃ paramā dhīrapakati, gambhīrāsayatāya sāgaro, dosamahāsāgarassa velā, apāyadvārassa pidahanakavāṭaṃ, devabrahmalokānaṃ ārohaṇasopānaṃ, sabbaguṇānaṃ adhivāsanabhūmi, uttamā kāyavacīmanovisuddhīti manasikātabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be contemplated that patience, by its subduing of anger—the opponent of all virtues without remainder—is the unhindered weapon of good people in accomplishing virtues, the adornment of those capable of overcoming others, the wealth of strength of ascetics and brahmins, the stream of water that extinguishes the fire of anger, the birthplace of a good reputation, the mantra-medicine that calms the verbal poison of evil individuals, the supreme steadfast nature of those established in restraint, an ocean due to its profound disposition, the shore of the great ocean of aversion, the bolt that shuts the door to the lower realms, the staircase for ascending to the worlds of devas and brahmas, the foundation for all virtues, and the supreme purity of body, speech, and mind.

Api [V 0.0271] ca “ete sattā khantisampattiyā abhāvato idhaloke tappanti, paraloke ca tapanīyadhammānuyogato”ti ca “yadipi parāpakāranimittaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, tassa pana dukkhassa khettabhūto attabhāvo bījabhūtañca kammaṃ mayāva abhisaṅkhata”nti ca “tassa ca dukkhassa āṇaṇyakāraṇameta”nti ca “apakārake asati kathaṃ mayhaṃ khantisampadā sambhavatī”ti ca “yadipāyaṃ etarahi apakārako, ayaṃ nāma pubbe anena mayhaṃ upakāro kato”ti ca “apakāro eva vā khantinimittatāya upakāro”ti ca “sabbepime sattā mayhaṃ puttasadisā, puttakatāparādhesu ca ko kujjhissatī”ti ca “yena kodhapisācāvesena ayaṃ mayhaṃ aparajjhati, svāyaṃ kodhabhūtāveso mayā vinetabbo”ti ca, “yena apakārena idaṃ mayhaṃ dukkhaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa ahampi nimitta”nti ca, “yehi dhammehi apakāro kato, yattha ca kato, sabbepi te tasmiṃ eva khaṇe niruddhā kassidāni kena kopo kātabbo”ti [M 0.0291] ca, “anattatāya sabbadhammānaṃ ko kassa aparajjhatī”ti ca paccavekkhantena khantisampadā anubrūhetabbā.

Moreover, the accomplishment of patience should be developed by reflecting thus: "These beings suffer in this world due to the lack of the accomplishment of patience, and in the next world due to engaging in practices that cause torment." "And even if suffering arises on account of harm from others, I myself have produced the field for that suffering—my personal existence—and its seed—my kamma." "And this is the reason for becoming free from debt regarding that suffering." "If there were no wrongdoer, how could the accomplishment of patience be possible for me?" "Even if this person is a wrongdoer now, surely this person has helped me in the past." "Or, the harm itself is a help, as it is the condition for patience." "All these beings are like my own children—who would get angry at the offenses of their own children?" "This person wrongs me due to possession by the demon of anger; that possession by the anger-demon must be subdued by me." "Of the harm by which this suffering has arisen in me, I too am a condition." "Those phenomena by which the harm was done, and where it was done, all have ceased in that very moment. Now, towards whom should anger be made, and by whom?" "Due to the not-self nature of all phenomena, who wrongs whom?"

Yadi panassa dīgharattaṃ paricayena parāpakāranimittako kodho cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭheyya, tena iti paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ – “khanti nāmesā parāpakārassa paṭipakkhapaṭipattīnaṃ paccupakārakāraṇa”nti ca “apakāro ca mayhaṃ dukkhūpanisā saddhāti dukkhuppādanena saddhāya sabbaloke [P 0.0299] anabhiratisaññāya ca paccayo”ti ca, “indriyapakati hesā yadidaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhavisayasamāyogo. Tattha aniṭṭhavisayasamāyogo mayhaṃ na siyāti taṃ kutettha labbhā”ti ca “kodhavasiko satto kodhena ummatto vikkhittacitto, tattha kiṃ paccapakārenā”ti ca “sabbepime sattā sammāsambuddhena orasaputtā viya paripālitā, tasmā na tattha mayā cittakopo kātabbo”ti ca, “aparādhake ca sati guṇe guṇavati mayā kopo na kātabbo”ti ca, “asati guṇe visesena karuṇāyitabbo”ti ca “kopena ca mayhaṃ guṇayasā nihīyantī”ti ca, “kujjhanena mayhaṃ dubbaṇṇadukkhaseyyādayo sapattakantā āgacchantī”ti ca, “kodho ca nāmāyaṃ sabbāhitakārako sabbahitavināsako balavā paccatthiko”ti ca, “sati ca khantiyā na koci paccatthiko”ti ca, “aparādhakena aparādhanimittaṃ yaṃ āyatiṃ laddhabbaṃ dukkhaṃ sati ca khantiyā mayhaṃ tadabhāvo”ti ca, “cintanena kujjhantena ca mayā paccatthikoyeva anuvattito hotī”ti ca, “kodhe ca mayā khantiyā abhibhūte tassa dāsabhūto paccatthiko sammadeva abhibhūto hotī”ti ca, “kodhanimittaṃ khantiguṇapariccāgo mayhaṃ na yutto”ti ca, “sati ca kodhe guṇavirodhapaccanīkadhamme kathaṃ me sīlādidhammā pāripūriṃ gaccheyyuṃ, asati ca tesu kathāhaṃ sattānaṃ [V 0.0272] upakārabahulo paṭiññānurūpaṃ uttamaṃ sampattiṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti ca, “khantiyā ca sati bahiddhā vikkhepābhāvato samāhitassa sabbe saṅkhārā aniccato dukkhato sabbe dhammā anattato nibbānañca asaṅkhatāmatasantapaṇītatādibhāvato nijjhānaṃ khamanti buddhadhammā ca acinteyyāparimeyyappabhāvā”ti.

If, however, through long familiarity, anger arising from the harm of others takes hold of his mind, he should reflect thus: "Patience is the cause of helping in return, which is the practice that counteracts harm from others." "And the harm done to me is a proximate cause for suffering; by producing suffering, it is a condition for faith and for the perception of non-delight in the whole world." "This is the nature of the faculties: contact with pleasant and unpleasant objects. That contact with unpleasant objects should not be for me—whence could that be obtained?" "A person overcome by anger is deranged and mentally disturbed—what use is retaliation?" "All these beings are cared for by the Perfectly Enlightened One as his own true sons; therefore, I should not harbor anger toward them." "When an offender is virtuous, I should not be angry." "If they lack virtue, they are especially to be shown compassion." "By anger, my virtue and reputation decline." "By getting angry, ugliness, painful sleep, and other things desired by my enemies, come to me." "And this anger is a doer of all that is unbeneficial, a destroyer of all that is beneficial, a powerful enemy." "With patience, there is no enemy." "Whatever suffering the offender is to receive in the future on account of the offense, with patience, I am free of it." "By thinking and getting angry, I am only following my enemy." "When anger is conquered by me through patience, the enemy, who is a slave to it, is truly conquered." "It is not fitting for me to abandon the virtue of patience on account of anger." "With anger present—a state hostile and opposed to virtue—how can my qualities like morality and so on reach fulfillment? And without them, how can I, being of great help to beings, attain the supreme accomplishment in accordance with my vow?" "And with patience, due to the absence of external distraction, for one who is concentrated, all formations are fit for contemplation as impermanent and suffering; all phenomena as not-self; and Nibbāna as unconditioned, deathless, peaceful, and sublime; and the qualities of a Buddha are of inconceivable and immeasurable power."

Tato ca anulomiyaṃ khantiyaṃ ṭhito kevalā ime attattaniyabhāvarahitā dhammamattā yathāsakaṃ paccayehi uppajjanti vayanti, na kutoci āgacchanti, na kuhiñci gacchanti, na ca katthaci patiṭṭhitā, na cettha koci kassaci byāpāroti [M 0.0292] ahaṃkāramamaṃkārānadhiṭṭhānatā nijjhānaṃ khamati, yena bodhisatto bodhiyā niyato anāvattidhammo hotīti evamādinā khantipāramiyā paccavekkhaṇā veditabbā.

And then, established in conformity-patience, the contemplation of non-adherence to I-making and my-making becomes acceptable: that these are merely phenomena, devoid of self and what pertains to a self, arising and ceasing according to their respective conditions; they come from nowhere, go nowhere, nor are they established anywhere, and herein there is no agent of anyone over anyone. By this, the bodhisatta becomes fixed on enlightenment, of a nature not to turn back. In such ways should the reflection on the perfection of patience be understood.

Tathā saccena vinā sīlādīnaṃ asambhavato paṭiññānurūpaṃ paṭipattiyā abhāvato ca, saccadhammātikkame ca sabbapāpadhammānaṃ samosaraṇato asaccasandhassa apaccayikabhāvato [P 0.0300] āyatiñca anādeyyavacanatāvahanato sampannasaccassa ca, sabbaguṇādhiṭṭhānabhāvato saccādhiṭṭhānena sabbabodhisambhārānaṃ pārisuddhipāripūrisāmatthiyato sabhāvadhammāvisaṃvādanena sabbabodhisambhārakiccakaraṇato bodhisattapaṭipattiyā ca, parinipphattitotiādinā saccapāramiyā sampattiyo paccavekkhitabbā.

Likewise, because without truth, virtues such as morality cannot exist, and there is no practice in accordance with one's avowals; and because when the principle of truth is transgressed, all evil states converge; because an untruthful person is untrustworthy, and in the future this leads to their speech being unreliable; and because one perfected in truth becomes the foundation of all good qualities; because through the establishment in truth there is the capacity for the purity and fulfillment of all the requisites for enlightenment; because by not deviating from the true nature of things the duties of all the requisites for enlightenment are performed, and the practice of a Bodhisatta is brought to complete fulfillment—thus, in these and other ways, should the accomplishments of the perfection of truth be reflected upon.

Tathā dānādīsu daḷhasamādānaṃ taṃpaṭipakkhasannipāte ca nesaṃ acalādhiṭṭhānaṃ tattha ca dhīravīrabhāvaṃ vinā na dānādisambhārā sambodhinimittā sambhavantītiādinā adhiṭṭhāne guṇā paccavekkhitabbā.
