Similarly, the qualities of determination should be reflected upon in this and other ways: 'Without firm resolve in giving and other virtues, without unshaken steadfastness in them when adversities arise, and without courage and heroism therein, the accumulations of giving and so forth cannot become conducive to perfect enlightenment.'

Tathā “attahitamatte avatiṭṭhantenāpi sattesu hitacittataṃ vinā na sakkā idhalokaparalokasampattiyo pāpuṇituṃ, pageva sabbasatte nibbānasampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetukāmenā”ti ca, “pacchā sabbasattānaṃ lokuttarasampattiṃ ākaṅkhantena idāni lokiyasampattiākaṅkhā yuttarūpā”ti ca, “idāni āsayamattena paresaṃ hitasukhūpasaṃhāraṃ kātuṃ asakkonto kadā payogena taṃ sādhessāmī”ti ca, “idāni mayā hitasukhūpasaṃhārena saṃvaḍḍhitā pacchā dhammasaṃvibhāgasahāyā mayhaṃ bhavissantī”ti ca, “etehi vinā na mayhaṃ bodhisambhārā sambhavanti, tasmā sabbabuddhaguṇavibhūtinipphattikāraṇattā mayhaṃ ete paramaṃ puññakkhettaṃ anuttaraṃ kusalāyatanaṃ uttamaṃ gāravaṭṭhāna”nti ca, savisesaṃ sattesu sabbesu hitajjhāsayatā paccupaṭṭhapetabbā[V 0.0273], kiñca karuṇādhiṭṭhānatopi sabbasattesu mettā anubrūhetabbā. Vimariyādīkatena hi cetasā sattesu hitasukhūpasaṃhāraniratassa tesaṃ ahitadukkhāpanayanakāmatā balavatī uppajjati daḷhamūlā. Karuṇā ca sabbesaṃ buddhakārakadhammānaṃ ādi caraṇaṃ patiṭṭhā mūlaṃ mukhaṃ pamukhanti evamādinā mettāya guṇā paccavekkhitabbā.

"Even if one dwells solely on their own welfare, without a mind inclined toward the benefit of beings, it is impossible to attain success in this world or the next—how much more so for one who wishes to establish all beings in the attainment of Nibbāna." "Moreover, for one who later aspires to the supramundane attainment of all beings, it is fitting now to aspire for worldly success." "Now, if one is unable to bring happiness and welfare to others with mere inclination, when will one accomplish it through effort?" "Now, those nurtured by me with happiness and welfare will later become my companions in sharing the Dhamma." "Without these, my requisites for enlightenment (bodhisambhārā) cannot be fulfilled. Therefore, because they are the cause for accomplishing the majesty of all the Buddha’s qualities, for me, they are the supreme field of merit, the unsurpassed foundation of goodness, and the highest object of reverence." Thus, a distinct attitude of wishing for the welfare of all beings should be established. Moreover, founded upon compassion, loving-kindness (mettā) should be further cultivated toward all beings. For when the mind is boundless and devoted to bringing welfare and happiness to beings, a strong and deeply rooted desire arises to remove their harm and suffering. And compassion is the beginning, the conduct, the foundation, the root, the face, and the foremost of all the qualities that make a Buddha. Thus, in these and other ways, one should reflect on the virtues of loving-kindness.

Tathā “upekkhāya abhāve sattehi katā vippakārā cittassa vikāraṃ uppādeyyuṃ, sati ca cittavikāre dānādīnaṃ sambhārānaṃ sambhavo eva natthī”ti [M 0.0293] ca, “mettāsinehena sinehite citte upekkhāya vinā sambhārānaṃ pārisuddhi na hotī”ti [P 0.0301] ca, “anupekkhako sambhāresu puññasambhāraṃ tabbipākañca sattahitatthaṃ pariṇāmetuṃ na sakkotī”ti ca, “upekkhāya abhāve deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakānaṃ vibhāgaṃ akatvā pariccajituṃ na sakkotī”ti ca, “upekkhārahitena jīvitaparikkhārānaṃ jīvitassa ca antarāyaṃ amanasikaritvā sīlavisodhanaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotī”ti ca, tathā upekkhāvasena aratiratisahasseva nekkhammabalasiddhito upapattito ikkhaṇavasena sabbasambhārakiccanipphattito accāraddhassa vīriyassa anupekkhaṇe padhānakiccākaraṇato upekkhato eva titikkhānijjhānasambhavato upekkhāvasena sattasaṅkhārānaṃ avisaṃvādanato lokadhammānaṃ ajjhupekkhaṇena samādinnadhammesu acalādhiṭṭhānasiddhito parāpakārādīsu anābhogavaseneva mettāvihāranipphattitoti sabbabodhisambhārānaṃ samādānādhiṭṭhānapāripūrinipphattiyo upekkhānubhāvena sampajjantīti evamādinā nayena upekkhāpāramī paccavekkhitabbā. Evaṃ apariccāgapariccāgādīsu yathākkamaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsapaccavekkhaṇā dānādipāramīnaṃ paccayoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Similarly, one should reflect: 'Without equanimity, wrongs done by beings would cause a disturbance of mind; and when the mind is disturbed, the accumulation of meritorious deeds like generosity cannot arise.' 'Moreover, without equanimity, even a mind imbued with loving-kindness cannot achieve the purity of accumulated merits.' 'One who lacks equanimity cannot dedicate the accumulation of meritorious deeds and their results for the welfare of beings.' 'Without equanimity, one cannot relinquish offerings without discriminating between recipients.' 'Devoid of equanimity, one cannot purify virtue without considering threats to life and its necessities.' Likewise, because through equanimity, aversion and attachment are overcome, leading to the accomplishment of the power of renunciation; because by observing the arising of phenomena, all activities related to the accumulations are fulfilled; because when excessive effort is not regarded with equanimity, the primary task is not accomplished; because forbearance and contemplation arise from equanimity; because through equanimity, one is not deceived by the formations of beings; because through equanimously regarding worldly conditions, steadfast resolve in the adopted principles is achieved; and because through non-engagement with harm from others, the abiding in loving-kindness is fulfilled—thus all the undertakings, determinations, fulfillments, and accomplishments of the requisites for enlightenment are fulfilled by the power of equanimity. In this and other ways, the perfection of equanimity should be contemplated. Thus, it should be understood that reflecting in due order on the dangers and benefits of things such as non-relinquishment and relinquishment is the condition for the perfections of giving and so forth.

Tathā saparikkhārā pañcadasa caraṇadhammā pañca ca abhiññāyo. Tattha caraṇadhammā nāma sīlasaṃvaro, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, jāgariyānuyogo, satta saddhammā, cattāri jhānāni ca. Tesu sīlādīnaṃ catunnaṃ terasāpi dhutadhammā appicchatādayo ca parikkhārā. Saddhammesu saddhāya buddhadhammasaṅghasīlacāgadevatūpasamānussatilūkhapuggalaparivajjana- siniddhapuggalasevanapasādanīyadhammapaccavekkhaṇatadadhimuttatā parikkhāro. Hirottappānaṃ akusalādīnavapaccavekkhaṇaapāyādīnavapaccavekkhaṇakusaladhammūpatthambhana- bhāvapaccavekkhaṇahirottapparahitapuggalaparivajjanahirottappasampannapuggalasenatadadhimuttatā. Bāhusaccassa pubbayogaparipucchaka- bhāvasaddhammābhiyogaanavajjavijjāṭṭhānādiparicayaparipakkindriyatākilesadūrībhāvaappassuta- parivajjanabahussutasevanatadadhimuttatā. Vīriyassa apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇa- [P 0.0302] gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇadhammamahattapaccavekkhaṇathinamiddhavinodanakusītapuggalaparivajjana- āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanasammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇatadadhimuttatā[V 0.0274]. Satiyā satisampajaññamuṭṭhassatipuggalaparivajjanaupaṭṭhitassatipuggalasevanatadadhimuttatā. [M 0.0294] Paññāya paripucchakabhāravatthuvisadakiriyāindriyasamattapaṭipādanaduppaññapuggala- parivajjanapaññavantapuggalasevanagambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇatadadhimuttatā. Catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ sīlādicatukkaṃ aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu pubbabhāgabhāvanā āvajjanādivasībhāvakaraṇañca parikkhāro. Tattha sīlādīhi payogasuddhiyā sattānaṃ abhayadāne āsayasuddhiyā āmisadāne ubhayasuddhiyā dhammadāne samattho hotītiādinā caraṇādīnaṃ dānādisambhārānaṃ paccayabhāvo yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbo. Ativitthārabhayena na niddhārayimhāti. Evaṃ sampatticakkādayopi dānādīnaṃ paccayoti veditabbā.

Thus, the fifteen practices of conduct and the five higher knowledges are complete with their requisites. Herein, the practices of conduct are: restraint by virtue, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven good qualities, and the four jhānas. Among these, for the first four—virtue and so on—the thirteen ascetic practices and qualities like having few desires are the requisites. For the good qualities, faith has as its requisite the recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, deities, and peace, as well as avoiding coarse individuals, associating with refined individuals, reflecting on inspiring qualities, and devotion to them. Moral shame and fear of wrongdoing have as their requisites reflecting on the danger of the unwholesome, the perils of the lower realms, reflecting on the state of being a support for wholesome qualities, avoiding those devoid of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, associating with those endowed with them, and devotion to them. For extensive learning, the requisites are prior practice, being one who questions, dedication to the true Dhamma, familiarity with blameless fields of knowledge and so on, maturity of faculties, distance from defilements, avoiding the unlearned, associating with the learned, and devotion to them. For energy, the requisites are reflecting on the fear of the lower realms, the path of progress, the greatness of the Dhamma, dispelling sloth and torpor, avoiding the lazy, associating with the energetic, reflecting on the right efforts, and devotion to it. For mindfulness, the requisites are mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding those with lost mindfulness, associating with those with established mindfulness, and devotion to it. For wisdom, the requisites are being one who questions, clarifying the subject matter, bringing about a balance of the faculties, avoiding the unwise, associating with the wise, reflecting on the conduct of profound knowledge, and devotion to it. For the four jhānas, the requisites are the fourfold beginning with virtue, preliminary development on the thirty-eight objects, and the making of mastery in adverting and so on. Herein, through purity of application with virtue and so on, one becomes capable of giving fearlessness to beings; through purity of intention, of giving material gifts; and through purity of both, of giving the gift of Dhamma. In this way, the conditionality of the practices of conduct and so on for the provisions of generosity and the like should be determined accordingly. Due to fear of excessive elaboration, we have not elaborated. Thus, the wheels of success and so on should also be understood as conditions for generosity and the like.

Ko saṃkilesoti? Avisesena taṇhādīhi parāmaṭṭhabhāvo pāramīnaṃ saṃkileso, visesena pana deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakavikappā dānapāramiyā saṃkileso. Sattakālavikappā sīlapāramiyā, kāmabhavatadupasamesu abhiratianabhirativikappā nekkhammapāramiyā, ahaṃ mamāti vikappā paññāpāramiyā, līnuddhaccavikappā vīriyapāramiyā, attaparavikappā khantipāramiyā, adiṭṭhādīsu diṭṭhādivikappā saccapāramiyā, bodhisambhāratabbipakkhesu dosaguṇavikappā adhiṭṭhānapāramiyā, hitāhitavikappā mettāpāramiyā, iṭṭhāniṭṭhavikappā upekkhāpāramiyā saṃkilesoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

What is defilement? Generally, the state of being affected by craving and the like is the defilement of the perfections. Specifically, for the perfection of giving, it is deliberation concerning the gift and the recipient. For the perfection of virtue, it is deliberation concerning the seven occasions. For the perfection of renunciation, it is deliberation regarding delight and non-delight in sensual existence and its subsiding. For the perfection of wisdom, it is deliberation of 'I' and 'mine.' For the perfection of energy, it is deliberation due to sloth and restlessness. For the perfection of patience, it is deliberation between self and others. For the perfection of truthfulness, it is deliberation regarding the seen and unseen and so on. For the perfection of determination, it is deliberation concerning faults and virtues regarding the requisites for enlightenment and their opposites. For the perfection of loving-kindness, it is deliberation between benefit and non-benefit. For the perfection of equanimity, it is deliberation between the liked and disliked. These should be seen as defilements.

Kiṃ vodānanti? Taṇhādīhi anupaghāto yathāvuttavikappaviraho ca etāsaṃ vodānanti veditabbaṃ. Anupahatā hi taṇhāmānadiṭṭhikodhūpanāhamakkhapaḷāsaissāmacchariya- māyāsāṭheyyathambhasārambhamadappamādādīhi kilesehi deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakavikappādirahitā ca dānādipāramiyo parisuddhā pabhassarā bhavantīti.

What is purification? It should be understood that for these perfections, purification is non-affliction by craving and the like, and freedom from the aforementioned deliberations. For, when the perfections of giving and so on are uncorrupted by defilements such as craving, conceit, views, anger, hostility, denigration, dominance, envy, miserliness, deceit, dishonesty, stubbornness, competitiveness, intoxication, negligence, and others, and are free from deliberations concerning the gift, the recipient, and so on, they become utterly pure and radiant.

Ko paṭipakkhoti? Avisesena sabbepi saṃkilesā sabbepi [P 0.0303] akusalā dhammā etāsaṃ paṭipakkho, visesena pana pubbe vuttā maccherādayoti veditabbā. Api ca deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakadānaphalesu alobhādosāmohaguṇayogato lobhadosamohapaṭipakkhaṃ dānaṃ, kāyādidosavaṅkāpagamato lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ sīlaṃ, kāmasukhaparūpaghātaattakilamathaparivajjanato dosattayapaṭipakkhaṃ nekkhammaṃ, lobhādīnaṃ andhīkaraṇato ñāṇassa ca anandhīkaraṇato lobhādipaṭipakkhā paññā[M 0.0295], alīnānuddhatañāyārambhavasena lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ vīriyaṃ, iṭṭhāniṭṭhasuññatānaṃ khamanato lobhādipaṭipakkhā khanti, satipi paresaṃ upakāre apakāre ca yathābhūtappavattiyā [V 0.0275] lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ saccaṃ, lokadhamme abhibhuyya yathāsamādinnesu sambhāresu acalanato lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, nīvaraṇavivekato lobhādipaṭipakkhā mettā, iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu anunayapaṭighaviddhaṃsanato samappavattito ca lobhādipaṭipakkhā upekkhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

What is the antithesis? Generally, all defilements and all unwholesome states are the antithesis to these perfections. Specifically, the previously mentioned faults such as stinginess and so on should be understood as such. Moreover, giving is the antithesis to greed, hatred, and delusion, as it arises from the qualities of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion in relation to the gift, the recipient, and the fruits of giving. Virtue is the antithesis to greed and the like, as it arises from the removal of crookedness in body and so on. Renunciation is the antithesis to the three faults, as it arises from the avoidance of sensual pleasures, harming others, and self-mortification. Wisdom is the antithesis to greed and the like, as it arises from their being a cause of blindness and from knowledge being a cause of non-blindness. Energy is the antithesis to greed and the like, as it arises by way of undertaking what is proper without indolence or agitation. Patience is the antithesis to greed and the like, as it arises from enduring the liked and disliked as empty. Truthfulness is the antithesis to greed and the like, as it arises from acting according to reality, even when there is help or harm from others. Determination is the antithesis to greed and the like, as it arises from being unwavering in the requisites undertaken as they are, having overcome worldly conditions. Loving-kindness is the antithesis to greed and the like, as it arises from seclusion from the hindrances. Equanimity, as the antithesis to greed and the like, should be understood as arising from the destruction of favoring and opposing in liked and disliked things, and from balanced functioning.

Kā paṭipattīti? Dānapāramiyā tāva sukhūpakaraṇasarīrajīvitapariccāgena bhayāpanudanena dhammopadesena ca bahudhā sattānaṃ anuggahakaraṇaṃ paṭipatti. Tattha āmisadānaṃ abhayadānaṃ dhammadānanti dātabbavatthuvasena tividhaṃ dānaṃ. Tesu bodhisattassa dātabbavatthu ajjhattikaṃ bāhiranti duvidhaṃ. Tattha bāhiraṃ annaṃ pānaṃ vatthaṃ yānaṃ mālāgandhavilepanaṃ seyyāvasathapadīpeyyanti dasavidhaṃ. Annādīnaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyādivibhāgena anekavidhaṃ. Tathā rūpārammaṇaṃ yāva dhammārammaṇanti ārammaṇato chabbidhaṃ. Rūpārammaṇādīnañca nīlādivibhāgena anekavidhaṃ. Tathā maṇikanakarajatamuttāpavāḷādi, khettavatthuārāmādi, dāsidāsagomahiṃsādi nānāvidhavittūpakaraṇavasena anekavidhaṃ.

What is the practice? First, regarding the perfection of giving, the practice is to benefit beings in many ways: by relinquishing requisites for comfort, body, and life; by dispelling fear; and by teaching the Dhamma. Herein, gifts are of three kinds based on the object to be given: the gift of material things, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dhamma. For a bodhisatta, the objects to be given are twofold: internal and external. Among these, external gifts are of ten kinds: food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps. Food and the like are further divided into many kinds, such as hard and soft foods. Similarly, from the perspective of sense objects, gifts are of six kinds: from forms up to mental objects. Forms and the other objects are further divided into many kinds, such as blue and other colors. Likewise, there are many kinds of wealth and requisites—such as jewels, gold, silver, pearls, coral, fields, land, parks, male and female slaves, cattle, and buffaloes.

Tattha mahāpuriso bāhiraṃ vatthuṃ dento “yo yena atthiko, taṃ tassa deti, dento ca tassa atthiko”ti sayameva jānanto ayācitopi deti pageva yācito. Muttacāgo deti, no amuttacāgo, pariyattaṃ deti, no apariyattaṃ sati deyyadhamme. Na paccupakārasannissito [P 0.0304] deti. Asati deyyadhamme hi pariyatte saṃvibhāgārahaṃ saṃvibhajati. Na ca deti parūpaghātāvahaṃ satthavisamajjādikaṃ, nāpi kīḷanakaṃ yaṃ anatthūpasaṃhitaṃ pamādāvahañca. Na ca gilānassa yācakassa pānabhojanādiasappāyaṃ pamāṇarahitaṃ vā deti, pamāṇayuttaṃ pana sappāyameva deti.

There, the great person, giving external things, knows by himself, "Whoever is in need of something, he gives that to him, and in giving, he is one who is concerned for that person's welfare," and gives even without being asked, all the more when asked. He gives with open-handed generosity, not constricted generosity. He gives what is sufficient, not what is insufficient, when there is a gift to be given. He does not give expecting a return favor. When a sufficient gift is not available, he shares what is fit for sharing. And he does not give things that bring harm to others, such as weapons, poisons, or intoxicants; nor does he give playthings that are associated with what is unbeneficial and that bring about negligence. Nor does he give a sick beggar drink, food, and the like that is unsuitable, or without measure; but he gives only what is suitable and in proper measure.

Tathā yācito gahaṭṭhānaṃ gahaṭṭhānucchavikaṃ deti, pabbajitānaṃ pabbajitānucchavikaṃ deti, mātāpitaro ñātisālohitā mittāmaccā puttadāradāsakammakarāti etesu kassaci pīḷaṃ ajanento deti, na ca uḷāraṃ deyyadhammaṃ paṭijānitvā lūkhaṃ deti, na ca lābhasakkārasilokasannissito deti, na ca paccupakārasannissito deti, na ca phalapāṭikaṅkhī deti [M 0.0296] aññatra sammāsambodhiyā, na ca yācake deyyadhammaṃ vā jigucchanto deti, na ca asaññatānaṃ yācakānaṃ akkosakarosakānampi apaviddhaṃ dānaṃ deti, aññadatthu pasannacitto anukampanto sakkaccameva deti, na ca kotūhalamaṅgaliko hutvā deti, kammaphalameva pana saddahanto deti, napi yācake payirupāsanādīhi parikilesetvā deti, aparikilesanto eva pana deti, na ca paresaṃ vañcanādhippāyo bhedanādhippāyo vā dānaṃ deti, asaṃkiliṭṭhacitto eva deti, napi pharusavāco bhākuṭimukho dānaṃ deti, piyavādī pana pubbabhāsī mitavacano hutvā deti[V 0.0276], yasmiñca deyyadhamme uḷāramanuññatāya vā ciraparicayena vā gedhasabhāvatāya vā lobhadhammo adhimatto hoti, jānanto bodhisatto taṃ khippameva paṭivinodetvā yācake pariyesitvāpi deti, yañca deyyavatthu parittaṃ yācakopi paccupaṭṭhito, taṃ acintetvāpi attānaṃ bādhetvā dento yācakaṃ sammāneti yathā taṃ akittipaṇḍito. Na ca mahāpuriso attano puttadāradāsakammakaraporise yācito te asaññāpite domanassappatte yācakānaṃ deti, sammadeva pana saññāpite somanassappatte deti. Dento ca yakkharakkhasapisācādīnaṃ vā manussānaṃ kurūrakammantānaṃ vā jānanto na deti, tathā rajjampi tādisānaṃ na deti. Ye lokassa ahitāya dukkhāya anatthāya paṭipajjanti, ye pana dhammikā dhammena lokaṃ pālenti, tesaṃ deti. Evaṃ tāva bāhiradāne paṭipatti veditabbā.

Similarly, when asked, he gives to householders what is suitable for householders, and to renunciants what is suitable for renunciants. He gives without causing distress to parents, relatives, blood relatives, friends, associates, children, wife, servants, or workers. He does not promise a superior gift and then give an inferior one. He does not give motivated by gain, honor, or fame. He does not give expecting a return favor, nor does he give in anticipation of any fruit other than supreme enlightenment. He does not give while feeling disgust toward the gift or the recipient. He does not give discarded things even to unrestrained beggars who are abusive or rude. Instead, with a serene and compassionate mind, he gives attentively and respectfully. He does not give out of festivity or for auspiciousness, but with faith in the fruit of kamma. He does not trouble recipients with excessive formalities before giving, but gives without causing them distress. He does not give with the intent to deceive or divide others, but with an undefiled mind. He does not give with harsh words or a scowling face, but with kind speech, speaking first, and with gentle words. If the Bodhisatta knows that he has excessive greed for a particular gift—whether due to its excellence, long familiarity, or natural attachment—he quickly overcomes it and even seeks out recipients to give it away. Even if the gift is meager and the recipient is present, he does not hesitate, even while inconveniencing himself, but gives, honoring the recipient as Akitti the wise did. A great man, when asked for his own children, wife, servants, or workers, does not give them to beggars if they are unpersuaded and displeased; rather, he gives them only when they have been well persuaded and are pleased. And in giving, he does not knowingly give to yakkhas, rakkhasas, pisācas, or to humans of cruel deeds; similarly, he does not give sovereignty to such beings. He does not give to those who act for the harm, suffering, and misfortune of the world; rather, he gives to those who are righteous and protect the world according to the Dhamma. Thus, the practice of external giving should be understood.

Ajjhattikadānaṃ [P 0.0305] pana dvīhi ākārehi veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Yathā nāma koci puriso ghāsacchādanahetu attānaṃ parassa nissajjati, vidheyyabhāvaṃ upagacchati dāsabyaṃ, evameva mahāpuriso sambodhihetu nirāmisacitto sattānaṃ anuttaraṃ hitasukhaṃ icchanto attano dānapāramiṃ paripūretukāmo attānaṃ parassa nissajjati, vidheyyabhāvaṃ upagacchati yathākāmakaraṇīyataṃ. Karacaraṇanayanādiaṅgapaccaṅgaṃ tena tena atthikānaṃ akampito anolīno anuppadeti, na tattha sajjati na saṅkocaṃ āpajjati yathā taṃ bāhiravatthusmiṃ, tathā hi mahāpuriso dvīhi ākārehi bāhiravatthuṃ pariccajati yathāsukhaṃ paribhogāya vā yācakānaṃ tesaṃ manorathaṃ paripūrento, attano vasībhāvāya vā, tattha [M 0.0297] sabbena sabbaṃ muttacāgo, evamahaṃ nissaṅgabhāvanāya sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissāmīti. Evaṃ ajjhattikavatthusminti veditabbaṃ.

The internal gift, however, should be understood in two ways. How? Just as a person, for the sake of food and clothing, might surrender themselves to another, accepting servitude and becoming submissive, even so, the Great Being—with a mind free from materialism, wishing for the unsurpassed welfare and happiness of beings, and desiring to perfect the pāramī of giving—surrenders himself to others, accepting submissiveness and becoming subject to their doing as they please. Without wavering or clinging, he bestows hands, feet, eyes, and other major and minor limbs to those who ask for them, not becoming attached to them, not shrinking back, just as with external objects. For the Great Being relinquishes external objects in two ways: either for the comfortable enjoyment of supplicants, fulfilling their wishes, or for his own mastery, thinking, "By this complete relinquishment, I will attain enlightenment through the development of non-attachment." So too should it be understood in the case of internal objects.

Tattha yaṃ ajjhattikavatthu dīyamānaṃ yācakassa ekanteneva hitāya saṃvattati, taṃ deti, na itaraṃ. Na ca mahāpuriso mārassa mārakāyikānaṃ devatānaṃ vā vihiṃsādhippāyānaṃ attano attabhāvaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgāni vā jānamāno deti “mā tesaṃ anattho ahosī”ti. Yathā ca mārakāyikānaṃ, evaṃ tehi anvāviṭṭhānampi na deti, napi ummattakānaṃ. Itaresaṃ pana yāciyamāno samanantarameva deti, tādisāya yācanāya dullabhabhāvato tādisassa ca dānassa dukkarabhāvato.

Here, when giving an internal object, one gives only what will truly benefit the supplicant, not otherwise. Nor does the Great Being knowingly give his own person, or his major and minor limbs, to Māra, or to deities of Māra's retinue, or to those who intend harm, thinking, 'May it not bring them misfortune.' Just as he does not give to those of Māra's retinue, so too he does not give to those possessed by them, nor to the insane. But when asked by others, he gives immediately, since such a request is rare and such giving is difficult to do.

Abhayadānaṃ pana rājato corato aggito udakato veripuggalato sīhabyagghādivāḷamigato nāgayakkharakkhasapisācādito sattānaṃ bhaye paccupaṭṭhite tato parittāṇabhāvena veditabbaṃ.

The gift of fearlessness, however, should be understood as providing protection to beings when danger arises from kings, thieves, fire, water, hostile individuals, lions, tigers, or other wild beasts, or from nāgas, yakkhas, ogres, and goblins.

Dhammadānaṃ [V 0.0277] pana asaṃkiliṭṭhacittassa aviparītā dhammadesanā, opāyiko hitassa upadeso diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthavasena yena sāsane anotiṇṇānaṃ avatāraṇaṃ otiṇṇānaṃ paripācanaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ nayo – saṅkhepato tāva dānakathā sīlakathā saggakathā kāmānaṃ ādīnavo saṃkileso ca nekkhamme ānisaṃso. Vitthārato pana sāvakabodhiyaṃ adhimuttacittānaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ sīlasaṃvaro indriyesu guttadvāratā bhojane mattaññutā jāgariyānuyogo satta saddhammā aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu kammakaraṇavasena samathānuyogo [P 0.0306] rūpakāyādīsu vipassanābhinivesesu yathārahaṃ abhinivesamukhena vipassanānuyogo, tathā visuddhipaṭipadā sammattagahaṇaṃ tisso vijjā cha abhiññā catasso paṭisambhidā sāvakabodhīti etesaṃ guṇasaṃkittanavasena yathārahaṃ tattha tattha patiṭṭhāpanā pariyodapanā ca. Tathā paccekabodhiyaṃ sammāsambodhiyañca adhimuttānaṃ sattānaṃ yathārahaṃ dānādipāramīnaṃ sabhāvarasalakkhaṇādisaṃkittanamukhena tīsupi avatthāsu tesaṃ buddhānaṃ mahānubhāvatāvibhāvanena yānadvaye patiṭṭhāpanā pariyodapanā ca. Evaṃ mahāpuriso sattānaṃ dhammadānaṃ deti.

The gift of Dhamma, indeed, is the undeviating teaching of Dhamma by one with an untainted mind; it is beneficial guidance for welfare in this life, in the next, and for the ultimate goal. It serves as a means for those not yet entered into the Dispensation to enter, and for those already entered to mature. Herein, the method is as follows: briefly, there is the talk on generosity, the talk on virtue, the talk on heaven, the danger and defilement in sensual pleasures, and the benefits of renunciation. In detail, for those with minds inclined to the disciple’s enlightenment, it includes going for refuge, restraint in virtue, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven noble qualities, the practice of serenity by working with the thirty-eight meditation objects, the practice of insight through the method of appropriately applying the mind to objects such as the physical body, and likewise the path of purification, right grasp, the three true knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the four analytical knowledges—this is the disciple’s enlightenment. By summarizing these qualities, one establishes and purifies beings in them wherever suitable. Similarly, for beings inclined to the solitary enlightenment or the perfect enlightenment, it includes, as appropriate, summarizing the perfections such as generosity—their intrinsic nature, function, characteristics, and so forth. By explaining the great power of the Buddhas in all three states, one establishes and purifies beings in the two vehicles. Thus does the Great Being give the gift of Dhamma to beings.

Tathā [M 0.0298] mahāpuriso sattānaṃ āmisadānaṃ dento “imināhaṃ dānena sattānaṃ āyuvaṇṇasukhabalapaṭibhānādisampattiñca ramaṇīyaṃ aggaphalasampattiñca nipphādeyya”nti annadānaṃ deti, tathā sattānaṃ kāmakilesapipāsāvūpasamāya pānaṃ deti, tathā suvaṇṇavaṇṇatāya hirottappālaṅkārassa ca nipphattiyā vatthāni deti, tathā iddhividhassa ceva nibbānasukhassa ca nipphattiyā yānaṃ deti, tathā sīlagandhanipphattiyā gandhaṃ deti, tathā buddhaguṇasobhānipphattiyā mālāvilepanaṃ deti, bodhimaṇḍāsananipphattiyā āsanaṃ deti, tathāgataseyyānipphattiyā seyyaṃ deti, saraṇabhāvanipphattiyā āvasathaṃ deti, pañcacakkhupaṭilābhāya padīpeyyaṃ deti, byāmappabhānipphattiyā rūpadānaṃ deti, brahmassaranipphattiyā saddadānaṃ deti, sabbalokassa piyabhāvāya rasadānaṃ deti, buddhasukhumālabhāvāya phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ deti, ajarāmarabhāvāya bhesajjadānaṃ deti, kilesadāsabyavimocanatthaṃ dāsānaṃ bhujissatādānaṃ deti, saddhammābhiratiyā anavajjakhiḍḍāratihetudānaṃ deti, sabbepi satte ariyāya jātiyā attano puttabhāvūpanayanāya puttadānaṃ deti, sakalassapi lokassa patibhāvūpagamanāya dāradānaṃ deti, subhalakkhaṇasampattiyā suvaṇṇamaṇimuttāpavāḷādidānaṃ, anubyañjanasampattiyā nānāvidhavibhūsanadānaṃ, saddhammakosādhigamāya vittakosadānaṃ, dhammarājabhāvāya rajjadānaṃ, jhānādisampattiyā ārāmuyyānataḷākavanadānaṃ, cakkaṅkitehi pādehi bodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamanāya caraṇadānaṃ, caturoghanittharaṇāya sattānaṃ saddhammahatthadānatthaṃ hatthadānaṃ, saddhindriyādipaṭilābhāya [P 0.0307] kaṇṇanāsādidānaṃ, samantacakkhupaṭilābhāya cakkhudānaṃ, “dassanasavanānussaraṇapāricariyādīsu sabbakālaṃ [V 0.0278] sabbasattānaṃ hitasukhāvaho, sabbalokena ca upajīvitabbo me kāyo bhaveyyā”ti maṃsalohitādidānaṃ, “sabbalokuttamo bhaveyya”nti uttamaṅgadānaṃ deti.

Thus, the Great Being, while giving material gifts to beings, gives food with the thought: 'By this gift, may I bring about for beings the attainment of long life, beauty, happiness, strength, intelligence, and other excellences, as well as the supreme attainment of the highest fruit.' In the same way, he gives drink to quench the thirst of beings for sensual pleasures and defilements. He gives clothing to bring about a golden complexion and the adornment of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing. He gives vehicles to attain psychic powers and the bliss of Nibbāna. He gives fragrances to develop the fragrance of virtue. He gives garlands and ointments to develop the splendor of the Buddha's qualities. He gives seats to attain the seat of enlightenment. He gives beds to attain the resting place of the Tathāgata. He gives dwellings to develop the state of refuge. He gives lamps to gain the five eyes. He gives forms to develop a radiant light of a fathom's length. He gives sounds to attain the voice of Brahmā. He gives tastes to become dear to the whole world. He gives tactile objects to attain the subtle delicacy of a Buddha. He gives medicine to attain freedom from aging and death. He gives the gift of manumission to slaves to free them from the slavery of defilements. He gives the gift of innocent playthings as a cause for delight in the true Dhamma. He gives children to lead all beings to the noble state of being his own children. He gives spouses to attain lordship over the entire world. He gives gold, jewels, pearls, corals, and so forth to attain the perfection of auspicious marks. He gives various ornaments to perfect the minor characteristics. He gives treasuries of wealth to attain the treasury of the true Dhamma. He gives kingdoms to attain the state of a Dhamma king. He gives parks, gardens, lakes, and groves to attain the excellences of jhāna and so on. He gives the gift of feet to approach the seat of enlightenment with feet marked by wheels. He gives the gift of hands in order to give the hand of the true Dhamma to beings for crossing the four floods. He gives ears, noses, and so forth to gain the faculties of faith and others. He gives eyes to gain the all-seeing eye. He gives flesh, blood, and so forth with the thought: 'May my body bring welfare and happiness to all beings at all times through seeing, hearing, recollecting, serving, and so forth, and may it be a source of sustenance for the whole world.' He gives the gift of his head to become the foremost in all the world.

Evaṃ dadanto ca na anesanāya deti, na ca paropaghātena, na bhayena, na lajjāya, na dakkhiṇeyyarosanena, na paṇīte sati lūkhaṃ, na attukkaṃsanena, na paravambhanena, na phalābhisaṅkhāya, na yācakajigucchāya, na acittīkārena deti, atha kho sakkaccaṃ deti, sahatthena deti, kālena deti, cittīkatvā deti, avibhāgena deti. Tīsu kālesu somanassito deti, tato [M 0.0299] eva ca datvā na pacchānutāpī hoti. Na paṭiggāhakavasena mānāvamānaṃ karoti, paṭiggāhakānaṃ piyasamudācāro hoti vadaññū yācayogo saparivāradāyako. Annadānañhi dento “taṃ saparivāraṃ katvā dassāmī”ti vatthādīhi saddhiṃ deti. Tathā vatthadānaṃ dento “taṃ saparivāraṃ katvā dassāmī”ti annādīhi saddhiṃ deti. Yānadānādīsupi eseva nayo.

Giving in this way, one does not give through improper seeking, nor to harm others, nor out of fear, nor out of shame, nor out of resentment toward those worthy of offerings, nor giving what is coarse when something choice is available, nor for self-praise, nor to belittle others, nor with the thought of recompense, nor out of disgust for the supplicant, nor disrespectfully. Instead, one gives attentively, with one's own hand, at the proper time, respectfully, and impartially. One is joyful at three times when giving, and after having given, does not feel regret. One does not show respect or disrespect based on the recipient; one is of pleasant conduct towards recipients, generous, approachable to supplicants, and a giver of gifts with their accompaniments. When giving food, one thinks, 'I will give this along with its accompaniments,' and so gives it together with clothing and so forth. Similarly, when giving clothing, one thinks, 'I will give this along with its accompaniments,' and so gives it together with food and so forth. The same principle applies to the giving of vehicles and other such things.

Tathā rūpadānaṃ dento itarārammaṇānipi tassa parivāraṃ katvā deti, evaṃ sesesupi. Tattha rūpadānaṃ nāma nīlapītalohitaodātādivaṇṇāsu pupphavatthadhātūsu aññataraṃ labhitvā rūpavasena ābhujitvā “rūpadānaṃ dassāmi, rūpadānaṃ mayha”nti cintetvā tādise dakkhiṇeyye dānaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti savatthukaṃ katvā. Etaṃ rūpadānaṃ nāma.

Similarly, when giving a gift of form, one also gives other sense-objects, making them its accompaniment; and so it is with the rest. Here, a gift of form means obtaining any one of the blue, yellow, red, white, or other colored flowers, cloths, or minerals, and having considered it as form, thinking, "I will give a gift of form, this gift of form is mine." One establishes such a gift for a worthy recipient, making it have a physical basis. This is called a gift of form.

Saddadānaṃ pana bherisaddādivasena veditabbaṃ. Tattha saddaṃ kandamūlāni viya uppāṭetvā nīluppalahatthakaṃ viya ca hatthe ṭhapetvā dātuṃ na sakkā, savatthukaṃ pana katvā dento saddadānaṃ deti nāma. Tasmā yadā “saddadānaṃ dassāmī”ti bherimudiṅgādīsu aññatarena tūriyena tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ upahāraṃ karoti kāreti ca, “saddadānaṃ me”ti bheriādīni ṭhapeti ṭhapāpeti ca. Dhammakathikānaṃ pana sarabhesajjaṃ telaphāṇitādiṃ deti, dhammassavanaṃ ghoseti, sarabhaññaṃ bhaṇati, dhammakathaṃ katheti, upanisinnakakathaṃ [P 0.0308] anumodanakathañca karoti kāreti ca, tadā saddadānaṃ nāma hoti.

The gift of sound, however, should be understood in terms of drum sounds and so forth. Here, it is not possible to give sound by uprooting it like roots and tubers, or by placing it in the hand like a handful of blue lotuses. However, when one gives it by providing it with a physical basis, one is said to give a gift of sound. Therefore, when one thinks, "I will give a gift of sound," and offers or causes to be offered a tribute to the Three Jewels with any musical instrument such as a large or small drum; and when one establishes or causes to be established large drums and so forth, thinking, "This is my gift of sound," then it is called a gift of sound. Moreover, when one gives throat medicine like oil and molasses to Dhamma speakers, proclaims the hearing of the Dhamma, recites melodiously, delivers a Dhamma talk, and performs or causes to be performed talks while seated nearby and talks of appreciation, then it is called a gift of sound.

Tathā gandhadānaṃ mūlagandhādīsu aññataraṃ rajanīyaṃ gandhavatthuṃ piṃsitameva vā gandhaṃ yaṃkiñci labhitvā gandhavasena ābhujitvā “gandhadānaṃ dassāmi, gandhadānaṃ mayha”nti buddharatanādīnaṃ pūjaṃ karoti kāreti ca, gandhapūjanatthāya agarucandanādike gandhavatthuke pariccajati. Idaṃ gandhadānaṃ.

Similarly, the gift of fragrance is when, having obtained any desirable fragrant object from among root-fragrances and so on, or any ground fragrance, and having considered it as fragrance, one thinks, 'I will give the gift of fragrance, this gift of fragrance is mine,' and performs or causes to be performed worship of the Buddha Jewel and others, or relinquishes fragrant substances like aloe and sandalwood for the purpose of fragrant worship. This is the gift of fragrance.

Tathā [V 0.0279] mūlarasādīsu yaṃkiñci rajanīyaṃ rasavatthuṃ labhitvā rasavasena ābhujitvā “rasadānaṃ dassāmi, rasadānaṃ mayha”nti dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ deti, rasavatthumeva vā dhaññagavādikaṃ pariccajati. Idaṃ rasadānaṃ.

Similarly, having obtained any desirable flavor-substance among root-flavors and so forth, and considering it as flavor, one offers it to those worthy of offerings, thinking, "I will give a gift of flavor; this gift of flavor is mine." Or, one relinquishes the flavor-producing substance itself, such as grain, cattle, and so forth. This is the gift of flavor.

Tathā phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ mañcapīṭhādivasena attharaṇapāvuraṇādivasena ca veditabbaṃ. Yadā hi mañcapīṭhabhisibimbohanādikaṃ nivāsanapārupanādikaṃ vā sukhasamphassaṃ [M 0.0300] rajanīyaṃ anavajjaṃ phoṭṭhabbavatthuṃ labhitvā phoṭṭhabbavasena ābhujitvā “phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ dassāmi, phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ mayha”nti dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ deti. Yathāvuttaṃ phoṭṭhabbavatthuṃ labhitvā pariccajati, idaṃ phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ.

Similarly, the gift of tangible things should be understood in terms of things like beds and chairs, and in terms of coverings and garments. For when one obtains a pleasant to the touch, desirable, and blameless tangible object—such as a bed, chair, bolster, pillow, and so forth, or an under-robe, upper-robe, and so forth—and, considering it as a tangible thing, offers it to worthy recipients with the thought, "I will give a gift of tangible things, this gift of tangible things is mine." Having obtained the tangible object as described, one relinquishes it; this is the gift of tangible things.

Dhammadānaṃ pana dhammārammaṇassa adhippetattā ojapānajīvitavasena veditabbaṃ. Ojādīsu hi aññataraṃ rajanīyaṃ vatthuṃ labhitvā dhammārammaṇavasena ābhujitvā “dhammadānaṃ dassāmi, dhammadānaṃ mayha”nti sappinavanītādiojadānaṃ deti. Ambapānādiaṭṭhavidhapānadānaṃ deti, jīvitadānanti ābhujitvā salākabhattapakkhikabhattādīni deti, aphāsukabhāvena abhibhūtānaṃ byādhitānaṃ vejje paccupaṭṭhāpeti, jālaṃ phālāpeti, kuminaṃ viddhaṃsāpeti, sakuṇapañjaraṃ viddhaṃsāpeti, bandhanena baddhānaṃ sattānaṃ bandhanamokkhaṃ kāreti, māghātabheriṃ carāpeti, aññāni ca sattānaṃ jīvitaparittāṇatthaṃ evarūpāni kammāni karoti kārāpeti ca. Idaṃ dhammadānaṃ nāma.

The gift of mental phenomena, however, should be understood in terms of sustenance, drink, and life, as it pertains to a mental object. For when one obtains any desirable object among sustenance and the like, and considering it as a mental object, thinking, "I will give the gift of mental phenomena, this gift of mental phenomena is mine," one gives a gift of sustenance such as ghee, fresh butter, and so on. One gives a gift of the eight kinds of drinks, such as mango juice. Considering it as the gift of life, one gives meals such as ticket-food or fortnightly food. For those overcome by discomfort or afflicted by illness, one arranges for a physician to attend to them. One has a net torn, a snare destroyed, or a birdcage destroyed. One arranges for the release of beings bound by fetters. One has the drum of non-killing sounded, and performs or causes to be performed other such deeds for the protection of beings' lives. This is called the gift of mental phenomena.

Sabbametaṃ yathāvuttaṃ dānasampadaṃ sakalalokahitasukhāya pariṇāmeti. Attano ca sammāsambodhiyā akuppāya vimuttiyā aparikkhayassa chandassa aparikkhayassa vīriyassa aparikkhayassa samādhissa aparikkhayassa paṭibhānassa aparikkhayassa ñāṇassa aparikkhayāya vimuttiyā pariṇāmeti[P 0.0309]. Imañca dānapāramiṃ paṭipajjantena mahāsattena jīvite aniccasaññā paccupaṭṭhāpetabbā tathā bhogesu, bahusādhāraṇatā ca nesaṃ manasikātabbā, sattesu ca mahākaruṇā satataṃ samitaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetabbā. Evañhi bhoge gahetabbasāraṃ gaṇhanto ādittato viya agārato sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ attānañca bahi nīharanto na kiñci seseti, na katthaci vibhāgaṃ karoti, aññadatthu nirapekkho nissajjati eva. Ayaṃ tāva dānapāramiyā paṭipattikkamo.

One dedicates all this aforesaid accomplishment of giving to the welfare and happiness of the entire world. And one dedicates it to one's own unshakable liberation in supreme enlightenment, to undiminishing aspiration, undiminishing energy, undiminishing concentration, undiminishing eloquence, undiminishing knowledge, and undiminishing liberation. While practicing this perfection of giving, the great being should establish the perception of impermanence regarding life and possessions, should consider their nature of being common to many, and should constantly and continuously establish great compassion for all beings. Thus, taking the essence that should be taken from wealth, as if rescuing all one's property and oneself from a burning house, one brings everything out, leaving nothing behind, making no distinctions anywhere, but rather, being without attachment, one simply relinquishes. This, for now, is the way of practicing the perfection of giving.

Sīlapāramiyā pana ayaṃ paṭipattikkamo – yasmā sabbaññusīlālaṅkārehi satte alaṅkaritukāmena mahāpurisena ādito attano eva tāva sīlaṃ visodhetabbaṃ. Tattha ca catūhi ākārehi [V 0.0280] sīlaṃ visujjhati – ajjhāsayavisuddhito, samādānato, avītikkamanato, sati ca vītikkame puna paṭipākatikakaraṇato. Visuddhāsayatāya hi ekacco [M 0.0301] attādhipati hutvā pāpajigucchanasabhāvo ajjhattaṃ hiridhammaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā suparisuddhasamācāro hoti. Tathā parato samādāne sati ekacco lokādhipati hutvā pāpato uttasanto ottappadhammaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā suparisuddhasamācāro hoti. Iti ubhayathāpi ete avītikkamanato sīle patiṭṭhahanti. Atha pana kadāci satisammosena sīlassa khaṇḍādibhāvo siyā. Tāyayeva yathāvuttāya hirottappasampattiyā khippameva naṃ vuṭṭhānādinā paṭipākatikaṃ karoti.

The practice of the perfection of virtue proceeds as follows: a Great Being, desiring to adorn beings with the ornaments of the virtues of an omniscient one, must first purify his own virtue. Virtue is purified in four ways: by purity of intention, by undertaking, by non-transgression, and, in case of transgression, by restoring it to its original condition. For one who is pure in intention, having self-mastery and a nature disgusted by evil, establishes inwardly the quality of conscience (hiri) and thus maintains perfectly pure conduct. Similarly, another, having undertaken virtue out of regard for the world, being fearful of evil, establishes the quality of moral dread (ottappa) and thus maintains perfectly pure conduct. Thus, in both cases, they are established in virtue by not transgressing. But if ever, due to a lapse of mindfulness, the virtue becomes broken or flawed, then, through the very same accomplishment of conscience and moral dread as described, one quickly makes it whole again by means of rehabilitation and so forth.

Tayidaṃ sīlaṃ vārittaṃ, cārittanti duvidhaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ bodhisattassa vārittasīle paṭipattikkamo – sabbasattesu tathā dayāpannacittena bhavitabbaṃ, yathā supinantenapi na āghāto uppajjeyya. Parūpakāraniratatāya parasantako alagaddo viya na parāmasitabbo. Sace pabbajito hoti, abrahmacariyatopi ārācārī hoti sattavidhamethunasaṃyogavirahito, pageva paradāragamanato. Sace pana apabbajito gahaṭṭho samāno paresaṃ dāresu sadā pāpakaṃ cittampi na uppādeti. Kathento ca saccaṃ hitaṃ piyaṃ vacanaṃ parimitameva ca kālena dhammiṃ kathaṃ bhāsitā hoti, sabbattha anabhijjhālu abyāpannacitto aviparītadassano kammassakatañāṇena ca samannāgato sammaggatesu sammāpaṭipannesu niviṭṭhasaddho [P 0.0310] hoti niviṭṭhapemo.

This virtue is twofold: that of restraint and that of practice. Herein, this is the Bodhisattva's course of practice in the virtue of restraint: One should cultivate a mind of such compassion toward all beings that not even in a dream does aversion arise. Being intent on benefiting others, one should not touch another's possessions, as if they were a venomous snake. If one is a monastic, one abstains from unchastity, being free from the seven kinds of sexual union, how much more so from adultery. But if one is a layperson, being a householder, one never generates even an evil thought toward the wives of others. When speaking, one should speak what is true, beneficial, and pleasant, and should give a talk on the Dhamma only at the proper time and in moderation. In all things, one should be without covetousness and ill will, possess right view, be endowed with the knowledge of ownership of kamma, and have established faith and affection toward those who have gone rightly and are practicing rightly.

Iti caturāpāyavaṭṭadukkhānaṃ pathabhūtehi akusalakammapathehi akusaladhammehi ca oramitvā saggamokkhānaṃ pathabhūtesu kusalakammapathesu patiṭṭhitassa mahāpurisassa parisuddhāsayapayogatāya yathābhipatthitā sattānaṃ hitasukhūpasaṃhitā manorathā sīghaṃ sīghaṃ abhinipphajjanti, pāramiyo paripūrenti. Evaṃbhūto hi ayaṃ. Tattha hiṃsānivattiyā sabbasattānaṃ abhayadānaṃ deti, appakasireneva mettābhāvanaṃ sampādeti, ekādasa mettānisaṃse adhigacchati, appābādho hoti appātaṅko, dīghāyuko sukhabahulo lakkhaṇavisese pāpuṇāti, dosavāsanañca samucchindati.

Thus, having turned away from the unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome states that are the path to the suffering of the round in the four woeful states, and being established on the wholesome courses of action that are the path to heaven and liberation, the great being, through purity of intention and effort, quickly and rapidly fulfills the wishes of beings connected with their welfare and happiness, and perfects the perfections. For such indeed is this one. Here, by abstaining from harming, he gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings. With little effort, he accomplishes the development of loving-kindness and attains the eleven benefits of loving-kindness. He becomes one with little illness and little affliction, long-lived, full of happiness, and attains special marks. And he eradicates the latent tendency of aversion.

Tathā adinnādānanivattiyā corādīhi asādhāraṇe bhoge adhigacchati. Parehi anāsaṅkanīyo piyo manāpo vissasanīyo vibhavasampattīsu alaggacitto pariccāgasīlo lobhavāsanañca samucchindati.

Similarly, by abstaining from taking what is not given, he acquires wealth not shared with thieves and the like. He is not suspected by others; he is dear and agreeable, trustworthy, with a mind unattached to material possessions, generous by nature, and he utterly eradicates the latent tendency of greed.

Abrahmacariyanivattiyā [M 0.0302] alolo hoti santakāyacitto, sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo aparisaṅkanīyo[V 0.0281], kalyāṇo cassa kittisaddo abbhuggacchati, alaggacitto hoti mātugāmesu aluddhāsayo, nekkhammabahulo lakkhaṇavisese adhigacchati, lobhavāsanañca samucchindati.

By abstaining from unchastity, he is free from craving, with tranquil body and mind. He is dear and agreeable to beings, inspiring no suspicion. A good reputation arises for him. His mind is unattached to women, his intentions ungreedy. He abounds in renunciation, attains special characteristics, and completely uproots the latent tendency of greed.

Musāvādanivattiyā sattānaṃ pamāṇabhūto hoti paccayiko theto ādeyyavacano, devatānaṃ piyo manāpo, surabhigandhamukho ārakkhitakāyavacīsamācāro, lakkhaṇavisese ca adhigacchati, kilesavāsanañca samucchindati.

By abstaining from false speech, he becomes a standard for beings, reliable, trustworthy, steadfast, and one whose word is to be heeded. He is dear and agreeable to devas, his mouth emits a fragrant scent, his bodily and verbal conduct is guarded, he attains special characteristics, and he completely uproots the latent tendency of the defilements.

Pesuññanivattiyā parūpakkamehipi abhejjakāyo hoti abhejjaparivāro, saddhammesu ca abhejjanakasaddho, daḷhamitto bhavantaraparicitānaṃ viya sattānaṃ ekantapiyo asaṃkilesabahulo.

By abstaining from divisive speech, he has a body unbreakable even by the hostile actions of others, and an unbreakable retinue. He has unwavering faith in the True Dhamma. He is a firm friend to beings, exceedingly dear to them as if acquainted in former existences, and abounding in freedom from defilement.

Pharusavācānivattiyā sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo sukhasīlo madhuravacano sambhāvanīyo, aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato cassa saro nibbattati.

By abstaining from harsh speech, he is dear and agreeable to beings, of pleasant disposition, sweet-spoken, and esteemed. And his voice arises endowed with eight qualities.

Samphappalāpanivattiyā sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo garu bhāvanīyo ca ādeyyavacano parimitālāpo. Mahesakkho ca hoti mahānubhāvo, ṭhānuppattikena paṭibhānena pañhānaṃ byākaraṇakusalo, buddhabhūmiyañca ekāya eva vācāya anekabhāsānaṃ sattānaṃ anekesaṃ pañhānaṃ byākaraṇasamattho hoti.

By abstaining from idle chatter, he is dear and agreeable to beings, respected, worthy of veneration, one whose word is to be heeded, and speaks moderately. He becomes of great power and great might, skilled in answering questions with spontaneous insight. And on the stage of Buddhahood, with a single utterance, he is able to answer the many questions of beings of many languages.

Anabhijjhālutāya icchitalābhī hoti, uḷāresu ca bhogesu ruciṃ paṭilabhati, khattiyamahāsālādīnaṃ [P 0.0311] sammato hoti, paccatthikehi anabhibhavanīyo, indriyavekallaṃ na pāpuṇāti, appaṭipuggalo ca hoti.

By being free from covetousness, he obtains desired gains and finds delight in excellent possessions. He is esteemed by great khattiya nobles and others, is unvanquishable by enemies, does not experience impairment of the faculties, and has no rival.

Abyāpādena piyadassano hoti, sattānaṃ sambhāvanīyo parahitābhinanditāya ca satte appakasireneva pasādeti, alūkhasabhāvo ca hoti mettāvihārī, mahesakkho ca hoti mahānubhāvo.

By being free from ill will, he is pleasing to behold and esteemed by beings. By rejoicing in the welfare of others, he easily gladdens them. He is of gentle nature, abiding in loving-kindness, and becomes of great power and great might.

Micchādassanābhāvena kalyāṇe sahāye paṭilabhati, sīsacchedampi pāpuṇanto pāpakammaṃ na karoti, kammassakatādassanato akotūhalamaṅgaliko ca hoti, saddhamme cassa saddhā patiṭṭhitā hoti mūlajātā, saddahati ca tathāgatānaṃ bodhiṃ, samayantaresu nābhiramati ukkāraṭṭhāne [M 0.0303] viya rājahaṃso[V 0.0282], lakkhaṇattayaparijānanakusalo hoti, ante ca anāvaraṇañāṇalābhī, yāva bodhiṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sattanikāye ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho ca hoti, uḷāruḷārā sampattiyo pāpuṇāti. Iti hidaṃ sīlaṃ nāma sabbasampattīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, sabbabuddhaguṇānaṃ pabhavabhūmi, sabbabuddhakārakadhammānaṃ ādi caraṇaṃ mukhaṃ pamukhanti bahumānanaṃ uppādetvā kāyavacīsaṃyame indriyadamane ājīvavisuddhiyaṃ paccayaparibhogesu ca satisampajaññabalena appamattena lābhasakkārasilokaṃ mittamukhapaccatthikaṃ viya sallakkhetvā “kikīva aṇḍa”ntiādinā (visuddhi. 1.19; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7) vuttanayena sakkaccaṃ sīlaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva vārittasīle paṭipattikkamo.

By the absence of wrong views, one gains virtuous friends. Even at the cost of one’s head, one does not commit evil deeds. Seeing that deeds are one's own, one is free from superstitious practices and reliance on omens. Faith in the True Dhamma becomes deeply rooted. One believes in the enlightenment of the Tathāgatas. One does not delight in other doctrines, like a royal swan avoids a dung heap. One becomes skilled in understanding the three characteristics of existence. In the end, one attains unobstructed knowledge. Until reaching enlightenment, one becomes supreme among beings in each realm and attains the most splendid attainments. Thus, this virtue is the foundation of all attainments, the ground from which all Buddha-qualities arise, the beginning, conduct, and foremost and chief among all qualities that lead to Buddhahood. Having developed deep reverence, one should carefully cultivate virtue through restraint of body and speech, mastery of the senses, purity of livelihood, and, with the strength of mindfulness and clear comprehension, diligently considering gain, honor, and fame as an enemy with the face of a friend in the use of the requisites, as described in the example of the kiki bird’s egg (Visuddhimagga 1.19; Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.7). This, then, is the practice regarding the virtue of avoidance.

Cārittasīle pana paṭipatti evaṃ veditabbā – idha bodhisatto kalyāṇamittānaṃ garuṭṭhāniyānaṃ abhivādanaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ añjalikammaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ kālena kālaṃ kattā hoti, tathā tesaṃ kālena kālaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ kattā hoti, gilānānaṃ kāyaveyyāvaṭikaṃ. Subhāsitapadāni sutvā sādhukāraṃ kattā hoti, guṇavantānaṃ guṇe vaṇṇetā paresaṃ apakāre khantā, upakāre anussaritā, puññāni anumoditā, attano puññāni sammāsambodhiyā pariṇāmetā, sabbakālaṃ appamādavihārī kusalesu dhammesu, sati ca accaye accayato disvā tādisānaṃ sahadhammikānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ āvikattā, uttari ca sammāpaṭipattiṃ sammadeva paripūretā.

Now, the practice regarding the virtue of conduct should be understood thus: Here, the Bodhisatta is one who, from time to time, performs acts of reverence, such as greeting, rising up to meet, saluting with joined palms, and proper courtesy toward spiritual friends who are worthy of respect. So too, he attends to them from time to to time, providing bodily assistance to the sick. Having heard well-spoken words, he applauds. He praises the virtues of the virtuous, is patient with offenses from others, remembers kindnesses done to him, rejoices in the merits of others, and dedicates his own merits to perfect enlightenment. At all times, he dwells diligently in wholesome states. And seeing a transgression as a transgression, he reveals it as it is to such fellow practitioners. Furthermore, he perfectly fulfills the right practice in the right way.

Tathā attano anurūpāsu atthūpasaṃhitāsu sattānaṃ itikattabbatāsu dakkho analaso sahāyabhāvaṃ upagacchati. Uppannesu ca sattānaṃ byādhiādidukkhesu yathārahaṃ [P 0.0312] patikāravidhāyako. Ñātibhogādibyasanapatitesu sokāpanodano ullumpanasabhāvāvaṭṭhito hutvā niggahārahānaṃ dhammeneva niggaṇhanako yāvadeva akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā kusale patiṭṭhāpanāya. Paggahārahānaṃ dhammeneva paggaṇhanako. Yāni purimakānaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ uḷāratamāni paramadukkarāni acinteyyānubhāvāni sattānaṃ ekantahitasukhāvahāni caritāni, yehi nesaṃ bodhisambhārā sammadeva paripākaṃ agamaṃsu, tāni sutvā anubbiggo anutrāso tepi [M 0.0304] mahāpurisā manussā eva, kamena pana sikkhāpāripūriyā bhāvitattabhāvā tādisāya uḷāratamāya ānubhāvasampattiyā bodhisambhāresu ukkaṃsapāramippattā ahesuṃ, tasmā mayāpi sīlādisikkhāsu sammadeva tathā paṭipajjitabbaṃ, yāya paṭipattiyā ahampi anukkamena sikkhaṃ paripūretvā ekantato taṃ padaṃ anupāpuṇissāmīti saddhāpurecārikaṃ vīriyaṃ avissajjento sammadeva sīlesu paripūrakārī hoti.

Likewise, he skillfully and tirelessly undertakes to be a helper in the duties of beings that are suitable for him and beneficial. When suffering such as sickness arises for beings, he provides a remedy as is appropriate. For those who have fallen into misfortune regarding relatives, wealth, and so on, he removes their sorrow, being established in a nature of rescuing them. He censures those deserving of censure only in accordance with the Dhamma, for the sole purpose of raising them from the unwholesome and establishing them in the wholesome. He supports those deserving of support only in accordance with the Dhamma. Having heard of the conducts of the great Bodhisattas of the past—which were most sublime, extremely difficult to do, of inconceivable power, and brought exclusive welfare and happiness to beings, and by which their requisites for enlightenment rightly came to maturity—he is without agitation and without fear, thinking: 'Those great beings were also just humans, but by gradually fulfilling the training, they developed themselves and, through such a most sublime accomplishment of power, reached the highest perfection in the requisites for enlightenment. Therefore, I too must practice rightly in the trainings of virtue and so on, so that by this practice I too, having gradually fulfilled the training, may certainly attain that state.' Not abandoning energy preceded by faith, he becomes one who rightly fulfills the virtues.

Tathā [V 0.0283] paṭicchannakalyāṇo hoti vivaṭāparādho, appiccho santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho dukkhasaho aparitassanajātiko anuddhato anunnaḷo acapalo amukharo avikiṇṇavāco santindriyo santamānaso kuhanādimicchājīvarahito ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu āraddhavīriyo pahitatto kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkho, appamattakampi kāye jīvite vā apekkhaṃ nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti, pageva adhimattaṃ. Sabbepi dussīlyahetubhūte kodhūpanāhādike upakkilese pajahati vinodeti. Appamattakena ca visesādhigamena aparituṭṭho hoti, na saṅkocaṃ āpajjati, uparūpari visesādhigamāya vāyamati.

Similarly, he is hidden in good qualities and open about his faults, having few desires, content, secluded, unsociable, enduring of suffering, not of a nature to be agitated, not arrogant, not insolent, not fickle, not garrulous, not of scattered speech, with tranquil senses, with a tranquil mind, free from wrong livelihood such as deceit, complete in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, undertaking and training in the precepts, aroused in energy, resolute, indifferent to body and life, not enduring even a little attachment to body or life, but abandoning and dispelling it, how much more so a great deal. He abandons and dispels all defilements that are causes of immorality, such as anger and resentment. And he is not content with a small measure of special attainment; he does not shrink back, but strives for ever higher attainment.

Yena yathāladdhā sampatti hānabhāgiyā vā ṭhitibhāgiyā vā na hoti, tathā mahāpuriso andhānaṃ pariṇāyako hoti, maggaṃ ācikkhati, badhirānaṃ hatthamuddāya saññaṃ deti, atthamanuggāheti, tathā mūgānaṃ. Pīṭhasappikānaṃ pīṭhaṃ deti yānaṃ deti vāheti vā. Assaddhānaṃ saddhāpaṭilābhāya vāyamati, kusītānaṃ ussāhajananāya, muṭṭhassatīnaṃ satisamāyogāya, vibbhantacittānaṃ samādhisampadāya, duppaññānaṃ paññādhigamāya vāyamati. Kāmacchandapariyuṭṭhitānaṃ [P 0.0313] kāmacchandapaṭivinodanāya vāyamati. Byāpādathinamiddhauddhaccakukkuccavicikicchāpariyuṭṭhitānaṃ vicikicchāvinodanāya vāyamati. Kāmavitakkādiapakatānaṃ kāmavitakkādimicchāvitakkavinodanāya vāyamati. Pubbakārīnaṃ sattānaṃ kataññutaṃ nissāya pubbabhāsī piyavādī saṅgāhako sadisena adhikena vā paccupakārena sammānetā hoti.

So that the attainment he has gained does not become subject to decline or stagnation, the great person is a leader for the blind, pointing out the path; to the deaf, he gives a hand signal, helping them understand the meaning; likewise to the mute. To those who are crippled, he gives a seat, a vehicle, or carries them. He strives for the acquisition of faith by the faithless, for the generation of energy in the lazy, for the association with mindfulness by the unmindful, for the attainment of concentration by the bewildered of mind, for the acquisition of wisdom by the unwise. He strives for the removal of sensual desire in those overcome by sensual desire. He strives for the removal of doubt in those overcome by ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. He strives for the removal of wrong thoughts, such as sensual thoughts, in those who have not done away with them. Relying on gratitude to beings who have previously helped him, he is first to speak, a speaker of endearing words, a helper, and one who honors them appropriately with a similar or greater return.

Āpadāsu [M 0.0305] sahāyakiccaṃ anutiṭṭhati. Tesaṃ tesañca sattānaṃ pakatisabhāvañca parijānitvā yehi yathā saṃvasitabbaṃ hoti, tehi tathā saṃvasati. Yesu ca yathā paṭipajjitabbaṃ hoti, tesu tathā paṭipajjati. Tañca kho akusalato vuṭṭhāpetvā kusale patiṭṭhāpanavasena, na aññathā. Paracittānurakkhaṇā hi bodhisattānaṃ yāvadeva kusalābhivaḍḍhiyā. Tathā hitajjhāsayenāpi paro na hiṃsitabbo, na bhaṇḍitabbo, na maṅkubhāvamāpādetabbo, na parassa kukkuccaṃ uppādetabbaṃ, na niggahaṭṭhāne na codetabbo, na nīcataraṃ paṭipannassa attā uccatare ṭhapetabbo, na ca paresu sabbena sabbaṃ asevinā bhavitabbaṃ, na atisevinā bhavitabbaṃ, na akālasevinā.

In times of trouble, he performs the duty of a friend. Having fully understood the natural dispositions of those various beings, he associates with them in whatever way is appropriate. He conducts himself toward them in whatever manner is suitable. And that, by removing them from the unwholesome and establishing them in the wholesome—not otherwise. For protecting the minds of others is for the Bodhisattvas solely for the sake of increasing wholesome qualities. Likewise, even with a benevolent intention, another should not be harmed, nor reviled, nor caused to be dismayed, nor should remorse be aroused in another. One should not reprove them on grounds for censure, nor should one set oneself as higher than one who behaves in a lower manner. And one should not be entirely unassociated with others, nor overly associated, nor associated at the wrong time.

Sevitabbayutte pana satte desakālānurūpaṃ sevati. Na ca paresaṃ purato piye vigarahati, appiye [V 0.0284] vā pasaṃsati. Na avissaṭṭhavissāsī hoti. Na dhammikaṃ upanimantanaṃ paṭikkhipati. Na saññattiṃ upagacchati, nādhikaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti. Saddhāsampanne saddhānisaṃsakathāya sampahaṃsati. Sīlasutacāgapaññāsampanne paññāsampannakathāya sampahaṃsati. Sace pana bodhisatto abhiññābalappatto hoti, pamādāpanne satte abhiññābalena yathārahaṃ nirayādike dassento saṃvejetvā assaddhādike saddhādīsu patiṭṭhāpeti. Sāsane otāreti. Saddhādiguṇasampanne paripāceti. Evamayaṃ mahāpurisassa cārittabhūto aparimāṇo puññābhisando kusalābhisando uparūpari abhivaḍḍhatīti veditabbaṃ.

Moreover, when associating with beings fit to be associated with, he associates with them in a manner appropriate to the time and place. And he does not, in front of others, criticize those who are dear, nor praise those who are disliked. He is not unduly trusting. He does not refuse a proper invitation. He does not make a request, nor accept too much. He makes those endowed with faith exceedingly glad by speaking on the benefits of faith. He makes those endowed with virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom exceedingly glad by speaking on the endowment of wisdom. But if the Bodhisatta has attained the power of higher knowledge, by showing hells and the like as is fitting with the power of higher knowledge, and having aroused a sense of urgency in those beings fallen into heedlessness, he establishes the faithless and the like in faith and other virtuous qualities. He leads them into the Teaching. He brings to maturity those endowed with faith and other qualities. Thus, it should be understood that this immeasurable flow of merit, this flow of the wholesome, which is the characteristic conduct of a great being, grows ever upwards.

Api ca yā sā “kiṃ sīlaṃ kenaṭṭhena sīla”ntiādinā pucchaṃ katvā “pāṇātipātādīhi viramantassa vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanādayo dhammā sīla”ntiādinā nayena nānappakārato sīlassa vitthārakathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.6 ādayo) vuttā, sā sabbāpi idha āharitvā vattabbā. Kevalañhi [P 0.0314] tattha sāvakabodhisattavasena sīlakathā āgatā, idha mahābodhisattavasena karuṇūpāyakosallapubbaṅgamaṃ katvā vattabbāti ayameva viseso. Yato idaṃ sīlaṃ mahāpuriso yathā na attano duggatiyaṃ parikkilesavimuttiyā sugatiyampi, na rajjasampattiyā, na cakkavatti, na deva, na sakka, na māra, na brahmasampattiyā pariṇāmeti, tathā na attano tevijjatāya, na chaḷabhiññatāya[M 0.0306], na catuppaṭisambhidādhigamāya, na sāvakabodhiyā, na paccekabodhiyā, pariṇāmeti, atha kho sabbaññubhāvena sabbasattānaṃ anuttarasīlālaṅkārasampādanatthameva pariṇāmetīti. Ayaṃ sīlapāramiyā paṭipattikkamo.

Furthermore, the detailed explanation of virtue from the Visuddhimagga (beginning with Vism. I, 6)—which proceeds by asking, 'What is virtue? For what purpose is virtue?' and answering, 'Virtue is the volitions and other mental states of one who abstains from killing living beings and so on, or of one who fulfills the practice of duties'—all this should be brought here and stated. However, there is this distinction: there, the discussion of virtue is presented in terms of a disciple aspiring to enlightenment, whereas here it must be stated in terms of a Great Bodhisatta, with compassion and skillful means as its precursor. For this virtue, the great being dedicates it neither to his own liberation from defilements, nor to a bad destination, nor even to a good destination; nor to the attainment of kingship, universal sovereignty, divinity, or the state of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā. Nor does he dedicate it to his own attainment of the threefold knowledge, the six higher powers, the four analytical knowledges, the enlightenment of a disciple, or the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. Rather, he dedicates it solely for the state of omniscience, for the sake of providing all beings with the unsurpassed adornment of virtue. This is the course of practice for the perfection of virtue.

Tathā yasmā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamā kāmehi ca bhavehi ca nikkhamanavasena pavattā kusalacittuppatti nekkhammapāramī, tasmā sakalasaṃkilesanivāsanaṭṭhānatāya puttadārādīhi mahāsambādhatāya kasivāṇijjādinānāvidhakammantādhiṭṭhānabyākulatāya ca gharāvāsassa nekkhammasukhādīnaṃ anokāsataṃ, kāmānañca satthadhārālaggamadhubindu viya ca avaliyhamānā parittassādā vipulānatthānubandhāti ca, vijjulatobhāsena gahetabbanaccaṃ viya parittakālūpalabbhā, ummattakālaṅkāro viya viparītasaññāya anubhavitabbā, karīsāvacchādanā viya patikārabhūtā, udakatemitaṅguliyā tanūdakapānaṃ viya atittikarā, chātajjhattabhojanaṃ viya sābādhā, baḷisāmisaṃ viya byasanasannipātakāraṇaṃ, aggisantāpo viya kālattayepi dukkhuppattihetubhūtā, makkaṭalepo viya bandhanimittaṃ, ghātakāvacchādanā viya anatthacchādanā, sapattagāmavāso viya bhayaṭṭhānabhūtā, paccatthikaposako [V 0.0285] viya kilesamārādīnaṃ āmisabhūtā, chaṇasampattiyo viya vipariṇāmadukkhā, koṭaraggi viya antodāhakā, purāṇakūpāvalambībīraṇamadhupiṇḍaṃ viya anekādīnavā, loṇūdakapānaṃ viya pipāsāhetubhūtā, surāmerayaṃ viya nīcajanasevitā, appassādatāya aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamātiādinā [P 0.0315] (ma. ni. 1.234; 2.42; pāci. 417; mahāni. 3; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 147) ca nayena ādīnavaṃ sallakkhetvā tabbipariyāyena nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ passantena nekkhammapavivekaupasamasukhādīsu ninnapoṇapabbhāracittena nekkhammapāramiyaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Yasmā pana nekkhammaṃ pabbajjāmūlakaṃ, tasmā pabbajjā tāva anuṭṭhātabbā. Pabbajjamanutiṭṭhantena ca mahāsattena asati buddhuppāde kammavādīnaṃ kiriyavādīnaṃ tāpasaparibbājakānaṃ pabbajjā anuṭṭhātabbā.

So too, since the perfection of renunciation is the arising of wholesome consciousness—encompassed by compassion and skillful means, preceded by seeing the dangers, and proceeding by way of departure from sensual pleasures and states of existence—one should undertake the perfection of renunciation. This should be done after having reflected on the dangers of the household life: its being a dwelling for all defilements, its great confinement with children, spouses, and the like, and its turmoil from being the basis for various activities such as agriculture and commerce, thus affording no opportunity for the happiness of renunciation and so on. And one should reflect on the dangers of sensual pleasures: that they have but little taste and are followed by great harm, like licking a drop of honey on a razor's edge; that they are obtainable for only a short time, like a dance seen in a flash of lightning; that they are to be experienced with a perverted perception, like the adornments of a madman; that they are a mere remedy, like a covering of dung; that they are unsatisfying, like drinking a little water from a moistened finger; that they are accompanied by affliction, like eating when tormented by hunger; that they are a cause for a conjunction of calamities, like bait on a hook; that they are a cause for the arising of suffering in all three periods of time, like the heat of a fire; that they are a cause of bondage, like monkey-lime; that they conceal what is harmful, like a disguise for an executioner; that they are a place of fear, like living in a hostile village; that they are bait for the defilements, Māra, and so on, like one who nourishes an enemy; that they are suffering due to change, like festival-time fortunes; that they burn from within, like a fire in a hollow tree; that they have many dangers, like a honeycomb hanging from a grass rope in an old well; that they are a cause of thirst, like drinking salt water; that they are frequented by base people, like liquor and spirits; and that they are like a skeleton, due to their having little satisfaction—all according to the method described in the suttas. And, having seen in contrast the benefits of renunciation, one should undertake the perfection of renunciation with a mind inclined, bent, and sloping towards the happiness of renunciation, seclusion, and peace. Since renunciation is rooted in going forth, the going forth must first be undertaken. And when a great being undertakes the going forth in a period when no Buddha has arisen, he should undertake the going forth of those ascetics and wanderers who are proponents of action and of the efficacy of deeds.

Uppannesu pana sammāsambuddhesu tesaṃ sāsane eva pabbajitabbaṃ. Pabbajitvā ca yathāvutte sīle patiṭṭhitena tassā eva hi sīlapāramiyā vodāpanatthaṃ dhutaguṇā samādātabbā. Samādinnadhutadhammā hi mahāpurisā sammadeva te [M 0.0307] pariharantā appicchāsantuṭṭhāsallekhapavivekaasaṃsaggavīriyārambhasubharatādi- guṇasalilavikkhālitakilesamalatāya anavajjasīlavataguṇaparisuddhasabbasamācārā porāṇe ariyavaṃsattaye patiṭṭhitā catutthaṃ bhāvanārāmatāsaṅkhātaṃ ariyavaṃsaṃ adhigantuṃ cattārīsāya ārammaṇesu yathārahaṃ upacārappanābhedaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharanti. Evaṃ hissa sammadeva nekkhammapāramī paripūritā hoti.

When, however, Fully Enlightened Ones have arisen, one should go forth in their Dispensation. Having gone forth, and being established in the precepts as described, one should undertake the ascetic qualities to purify the perfection of virtue. For great beings who have undertaken the ascetic practices, maintaining them rightly, being of few desires, content, devoted to expunging defilements, solitude, non-association, energetic in effort, ease of support, and so on, the stains of defilements are washed away by the water of these good qualities. With all their behavior purified by blameless conduct and virtuous qualities, established in the three ancient noble lineages, they enter and dwell in the jhānas—distinguished as access and absorption—according to suitability among the forty objects, to attain the fourth noble lineage, known as delight in development. Thus, indeed, is their perfection of renunciation rightly fulfilled.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne terasahi dhutadhammehi saddhiṃ dasa kasiṇāni, dasa asubhāni, dasānussatiyo, cattāro brahmavihārā, cattāro āruppā, ekā saññā, ekaṃ vavatthānanti cattārīsāya samādhibhāvanāya kammaṭṭhānāni bhāvanāvidhānañca vitthārato vattabbāni. Taṃ panetaṃ sabbaṃ yasmā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.22 ādayo, 47, 55) sabbākārato vitthāretvā vuttaṃ, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Kevalañhi tattha sāvakabodhisattassa vasena vuttaṃ, idha mahābodhisattassa vasena karuṇūpāyakosallapubbaṅgamaṃ katvā vattabbanti ayameva visesoti. Evamettha nekkhammapāramiyā paṭipattikkamo veditabbo.

In this context, along with the thirteen ascetic practices, the ten kasiṇas, the ten foul objects, the ten recollections, the four divine abodes, the four formless attainments, one perception, and one analysis—these forty subjects of meditation for the cultivation of concentration, along with the method of practice, should be explained in detail. However, since all this has been comprehensively explained in the Visuddhimagga, it should be understood according to the method given there. For there, it was taught with reference to a disciple-bodhisatta, whereas here it is to be taught with reference to a great Bodhisatta, having compassion and skillful means as its precursor—this is the only difference. Thus, the order of practice for the perfection of renunciation should be understood here.

Tathā paññāpāramiṃ sampādetukāmena yasmā paññā āloko viya andhakārena mohena saha na vattati, tasmā mohakāraṇāni tāva bodhisattena parivajjetabbāni. Tatthimāni [P 0.0316] mohakāraṇāni – arati tandi vijambhitā ālasiyaṃ gaṇasaṅgaṇikārāmatā niddāsīlatā anicchayasīlatā ñāṇasmiṃ akutūhalatā micchādhimāno aparipucchakatā kāyassa na sammāparihāro [V 0.0286] asamāhitacittatā duppaññānaṃ puggalānaṃ sevanā paññavantānaṃ apayirupāsanā attaparibhavo micchāvikappo viparītābhiniveso kāyadaḷhibahulatā asaṃvegasīlatā pañca nīvaraṇāni. Saṅkhepato ye vā pana dhamme āsevato anuppannā paññā nuppajjati, uppannā parihāyati. Iti imāni sammohakāraṇāni parivajjentena bāhusacce jhānādīsu ca yogo karaṇīyo.

Similarly, a Bodhisatta who wishes to perfect the perfection of wisdom should first avoid the causes of delusion. For wisdom, like light, does not coexist with delusion, which is like darkness. These are the causes of delusion: discontent, sloth, yawning, laziness, fondness for company, delight in socializing, habitual sleepiness, habitual indecision, lack of enthusiasm for knowledge, wrong conceit, failure to inquire, improper care of the body, an uncollected mind, associating with unwise persons, not attending on wise persons, self-contempt, wrong thinking, distorted adherence, excessive corpulence, lack of urgency, and the five hindrances. In brief, whatever qualities, when cultivated, prevent unarisen wisdom from arising or cause arisen wisdom to decline—avoiding these causes of delusion, one should apply oneself to extensive learning, jhāna, and the like.

Tatthāyaṃ bāhusaccassa visayavibhāgo – pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo cattāri saccāni bāvīsatindriyāni dvādasapadiko paṭiccasamuppādo tathā satipaṭṭhānādayo kusalādidhammappakārabhedā ca, yāni ca loke anavajjāni vijjāṭṭhānāni, ye ca sattānaṃ hitasukhavidhānayoggā [M 0.0308] byākaraṇavisesā, iti evaṃ pakāraṃ sakalameva sutavisayaṃ upāyakosallapubbaṅgamāya paññāya satiyā vīriyena ca sādhukaṃ uggahaṇasavanadhāraṇaparicayaparipucchāhi ogāhetvā tattha ca paresaṃ patiṭṭhāpanena sutamayā paññā nibbattetabbā.

Here is the classification of the scope of extensive learning: the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the twelve-linked dependent origination, as well as the foundations of mindfulness and other various types of distinctions of skillful and unskillful qualities. Also included are the blameless fields of knowledge in the world, and those special explanations suitable for arranging the benefit and happiness of beings. Thus, this entire scope of learning should be thoroughly mastered through learning, listening, retention, familiarity, and inquiry, preceded by skillful means, wisdom, mindfulness, and effort. And by establishing others in this knowledge, the wisdom born of learning should be generated.

Tathā sattānaṃ itikattabbatāsu ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānabhūtā āyāpāyaupāyakosallabhūtā ca paññā hitesitaṃ nissāya tattha tattha yathārahaṃ pavattetabbā. Tathā khandhādīnaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ ākāraparivitakkanamukhena te nijjhānaṃ khamāpentena cintāmayā paññā nibbattetabbā. Khandhādīnaṃyeva pana salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇapariggahaṇavasena lokiyapariññā nibbattentena pubbabhāgabhāvanāpaññā sampādetabbā. Evañhi nāmarūpamattamidaṃ yathārahaṃ paccayehi uppajjati ceva nirujjhati ca, na ettha koci kattā vā kāretā vā, hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccaṃ, udayabbayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhaṃ, avasavattanaṭṭhena anattāti ajjhattikadhamme bāhirakadhamme ca nibbisesaṃ parijānanto tattha āsaṅgaṃ pajahanto pare ca tattha taṃ jahāpento kevalaṃ karuṇāvaseneva yāva na buddhaguṇā [P 0.0317] hatthatalaṃ āgacchanti, tāva yānattaye satte avatāraṇaparipācanehi patiṭṭhapento jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattiyo abhiññāyo ca lokiyā vasībhāvaṃ pāpento paññāya matthakaṃ pāpuṇāti.

Thus, wisdom—which consists of ready wit arising in response to what should be done for beings, and of skill in the means for their progress and decline—should be applied in various situations as is appropriate, based on the desire for their welfare. Likewise, wisdom born of reflection should be developed by patiently reflecting upon the aggregates and other real phenomena by way of analyzing their characteristics. Moreover, mundane full understanding should be accomplished through the preliminary development of wisdom by comprehending the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates and so on. For in this way, one fully understands without remainder that this is mere name-and-form, which arises and ceases according to conditions—that there is no doer or instigator here. One sees that internally and externally, phenomena are impermanent in the sense of ceasing after arising, suffering in the sense of being oppressed by rise and fall, and non-self in the sense of being ungovernable. Abandoning attachment to these phenomena and helping others to abandon it as well, one establishes beings in the three vehicles through guidance and maturation—solely through compassion—until the qualities of a Buddha become as clear as the palm of one's hand. By mastering the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, attainments, and mundane higher knowledges, one reaches the pinnacle of wisdom.

Tattha yā imā iddhividhañāṇaṃ dibbasotadhātuñāṇaṃ cetopariyañāṇaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ yathākammupagañāṇaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇanti saparibhaṇḍā pañcalokiyaabhiññāsaṅkhātā bhāvanāpaññā, yā ca khandhāyatanadhātuindriyasaccapaṭiccasamuppādādibhedesu bhūmibhūtesu dhammesu uggahaparipucchāvasena ñāṇaparicayaṃ katvā sīlavisuddhicittavisuddhīti [V 0.0287] mūlabhūtāsu imāsu dvīsu visuddhīsu patiṭṭhāya diṭṭhivisuddhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhimaggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi- paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiñāṇadassanavisuddhīti sarīrabhūtā imā pañca visuddhiyo sampādentena bhāvetabbā lokiyalokuttarabhedā bhāvanāpaññā, tāsaṃ sampādanavidhānaṃ yasmā “tattha ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotītiādikaṃ iddhivikubbanaṃ kātukāmena ādikammikena yoginā”tiādinā “khandhāti rūpakkhandho vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho viññāṇakkhandho”tiādinā ca visayavibhāgena saddhiṃ [M 0.0309] visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.430 ādayo) sabbākārato vitthāretvā vuttaṃ, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.
