In brief. In detail, however, all accomplishments proclaimed in the entire word of the Buddha are solely dependent on right effort. Therefore, the Blessed One, having enjoined the undertaking of energy, said, “This is the instruction of the Buddhas.”

Tatrāyaṃ [V 0.0302] saṅkhepattho – yvāyaṃ sabbasaṃkilesamūlabhāvato sabbānatthavidhāyakanti kosajjaṃ bhayato tappaṭipakkhato catūhi yogehi anupaddavabhāvasādhanato vīriyārambhañca khemato disvā adhisīlasikkhādisampādanavasena vīriyassa ārambho sammappadhānānuyogo, tattha yaṃ sammadeva niyojana, “āraddhavīriyā hothā”ti, esā buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ anusāsanī anusiṭṭhi ovādoti. Sesagāthāsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

Herein, this is the concise meaning: Having seen laziness as a danger—because it is the root of all defilements and productive of all harm—and the undertaking of energy as safety—because it is the opposite of that and because it accomplishes a state free from affliction through the four exertions—the undertaking of energy by way of accomplishing the training in higher virtue and so forth is the application to right effort. Therein, the proper injunction, “Be resolute in energy!”—this is the instruction, teaching, and advice of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. The meaning of the remaining verses should also be understood by this same method.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – vivādanti viruddhavādaṃ, chavivādavatthuvasena vivadananti attho. Avivādanti vivādapaṭipakkhaṃ mettāvacīkammaṃ, mettābhāvanaṃ vā. Atha vā avivādanti avivādahetubhūtaṃ chabbidhaṃ sāraṇīyadhammaṃ. Samaggāti avaggā, kāyena ceva cittena ca sahitā aviramitā aviyuttāti attho. Sakhilāti sakkīlā mudusīlā, aññamaññamhi muduhadayāti attho. Esā buddhānusāsanīti ettha sabbena sabbaṃ vivādamanupagamma yadidaṃ chasāraṇīyadhammaparipūraṇavasena samaggavāse niyojanaṃ, esā buddhānaṃ anusiṭṭhīti yojetabbaṃ. Samaggavāsañhi vasamānā sīladiṭṭhisāmaññagatā avivadamānā sukheneva tisso sikkhā paripūressantīti satthā samaggavāse niyojanaṃ attano sāsananti dassesi.

Here, however, is the distinction: “dispute” means they dispute, speaking contradictory things, that is, quarreling on account of the six grounds for dispute. “Non-dispute” means the opposite of dispute: verbal action imbued with loving-kindness, or the cultivation of loving-kindness. Alternatively, “non-dispute” refers to the six qualities conducive to harmony, which are the cause of non-dispute. “Harmonious” means not divided, united in body and mind, unceasing, and inseparable. “Kind” means affable, with gentle conduct, and soft-hearted toward one another. “This is the instruction of the Buddhas”: here, by not engaging in any dispute whatsoever, the injunction to dwell in harmony through the fulfillment of these six qualities conducive to harmony should be construed as, “This is the instruction of the Buddhas.” For those dwelling in harmony, possessing commonality in virtue and view, not disputing, will easily fulfill the threefold training; thus the Teacher showed that the injunction to dwell in harmony is his teaching.

Pamādanti pamajjanaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pamussanaṃ akusalesu ca dhammesu cittavossaggaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “tattha katamo pamādo, kāyaduccarite [P 0.0334] vā vacīduccarite vā manoduccarite vā pañcasu vā kāmaguṇesu cittassa vosaggo vosaggānuppadānaṃ kusalānaṃ vā dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya asakkaccakiriyatā, asātaccakiriyatā, anaṭṭhitakiriyatā, olīnavuttitā, nikkhittachandatā, nikkhittadhuratā anāsevanā abhāvanā abahulīkammaṃ…pe… yo evarūpo pamādo pamajjanā pamajjitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati pamādo”ti (vibha. 846).

“Negligence” means heedlessness, the forgetting of wholesome qualities, and the abandoning of the mind to unwholesome states. As it is said: “Therein, what is negligence? The abandoning and giving up of the mind in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct, or in the five strands of sensual pleasure; or, in the development of wholesome qualities, the lack of earnestness, lack of continuity, lack of steadfastness, sluggishness, abandonment of desire, abandonment of the burden, non-practice, non-development, non-cultivation… whatever kind of negligence, heedlessness, or state of being negligent, this is called negligence.” (Vibhaṅga 846)

Appamādanti appamajjanaṃ. Taṃ pamādassa paṭipakkhato veditabbaṃ. Atthato hi appamādo nāma satiyā avippavāso, “satiyā avippavāso”ti ca [M 0.0326] niccaṃ upaṭṭhitāya satiyā evetaṃ nāmaṃ. Apare pana “satisampajaññappadhānā tathā pavattā cattāro arūpino khandhā appamādo”ti vadanti. Yasmā pana appamādabhāvanā nāma visuṃ ekā bhāvanā natthi. Yā hi kāci puññakiriyā kusalakiriyā, sabbā sā appamādabhāvanātveva veditabbā.

“Diligence” means non-negligence. It should be understood as the opposite of negligence. In essence, diligence is non-separation from mindfulness, and this name is indeed for mindfulness that is constantly present. Others, however, say, “The four immaterial aggregates, when they proceed with mindfulness and clear comprehension as predominant, are diligence.” But there is no separate cultivation called “the cultivation of diligence.” For any meritorious or wholesome action is to be understood as the cultivation of diligence.

Visesato pana vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ kāyikavācasikasaṃvarañca upādāya sabbā sīlabhāvanā, sabbā samādhibhāvanā, sabbā paññābhāvanā, sabbā kusalabhāvanā, anavajjabhāvanā[V 0.0303], appamādabhāvanā. “Appamādo”ti hi idaṃ padaṃ mahantaṃ atthaṃ dīpeti, mahantaṃ atthaṃ pariggahetvā tiṭṭhati, sakalampi tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ āharitvā appamādapadassa atthaṃ katvā kathento dhammakathiko “atitthena pakkhando”ti na vattabbo. Kasmā? Appamādapadassa mahantabhāvato. Tathā hi sammāsambuddho kusinārāyaṃ yamakasālānamantare parinibbānasamaye nipanno abhisambodhito paṭṭhāya pañcacattālīsāya vassesu attanā bhāsitaṃ dhammaṃ ekeneva padena saṅgahetvā dassento “appamādena sampādethā”ti (dī. ni. 2.218) bhikkhūnaṃ ovādamadāsi. Tathā cāha – “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yāni kānici jaṅgamānaṃ pāṇānaṃ padajātāni, sabbāni tāni hatthipade samodhānaṃ gacchanti, hatthipadaṃ tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati yadidaṃ mahantattena, evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye keci kusalā dhammā, sabbe te appamādamūlakā appamādasamosaraṇā, appamādo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.300 thokaṃ visadisaṃ). Tattha appamādabhāvanaṃ sikhāppattaṃ dassento satthā “bhāvethaṭṭhaṅgikaṃ magga”nti āha.

In particular, based on taking refuge which has liberation as its support and on bodily and verbal restraint, there is all development of virtue, all development of concentration, all development of wisdom, all development of wholesome qualities, the development of blamelessness, and the development of diligence. For the word “diligence” illuminates a great meaning; it stands encompassing a great meaning. Even if a Dhamma speaker were to gather the entire Tipiṭaka of the Buddha’s words and explain the meaning of the word “diligence,” he would not be said to have plunged in inadequately. Why? Because of the vastness of the word “diligence.” Thus, at the time of his final passing in Kusinārā, lying between the twin sāl trees, the Perfectly Enlightened One, summarizing the Dhamma he had taught for forty-five years since his supreme enlightenment, gave this advice to the bhikkhus in a single word: “Strive with diligence.” And he also said: “Just as, bhikkhus, the footprints of all walking creatures can be encompassed within the elephant’s footprint, and the elephant's footprint is declared the chief among them for its greatness, so too, bhikkhus, all wholesome qualities are rooted in diligence, converge upon diligence, and diligence is declared the chief among them.” Therein, to show that the development of diligence reaches its peak, the Teacher said: “Develop the Eightfold Path.”

Tassattho – yo esa sīlādikhandhattayasaṅgaho sammādiṭṭhipubbaṅgamo sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃyeva [P 0.0335] aṭṭhannaṃ aṅgānaṃ vasena aṭṭhaṅgiko ariyamaggo, taṃ bhāvetha attano santāne uppādetha. Dassanamaggamatte aṭhatvā upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ uppādanavasena vaḍḍhetha, evaṃ vo appamādabhāvanā sikhāppattā bhavissatīti. Esā buddhānusāsanīti yadidaṃ kusalesu dhammesu appamajjanaṃ, tañca ussukkāpetvā ariyamaggassa bhāvanā esā buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ anusiṭṭhi ovādoti.

Its meaning is this: that which is the Noble Eightfold Path—the collection of the three aggregates beginning with virtue, preceded by right view, and consisting of the eight factors starting with right view—that you should develop, you should bring forth in your own continuum. Not stopping at the path of vision, you should augment it by giving rise to the three higher paths. In this way, your cultivation of diligence will reach its peak. “This is the instruction of the Buddhas” means that this non-negligence in wholesome qualities, and the enthusiastic cultivation of the Noble Path, is the instruction and advice of the Blessed Buddhas.

Iti [M 0.0327] bhagavā arahattanikūṭeneva cariyāpiṭakadesanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Itthaṃ sudantiādīsu itthanti kappe ca satasahassetiādinā (cariyā. 1.1) pakārena. Sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Bhagavāti bhāgyavantatādīhi kāraṇehi bhagavā. Attano pubbacariyanti purimāsu akittipaṇḍitādijātīsu attano paṭipattidukkarakiriyaṃ. Sambhāvayamānoti hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya sammadeva pakāsento. Buddhāpadāniyaṃ nāmāti buddhānaṃ purātanakammaṃ porāṇaṃ dukkarakiriyaṃ adhikicca pavattattā desitattā buddhāpadāniyanti evaṃnāmakaṃ. Dhammapariyāyanti dhammadesanaṃ dhammabhūtaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ. Abhāsitthāti avoca. Yaṃ panettha na vuttaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthattā ca na vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Thus the Blessed One concluded the exposition of the Cariyāpiṭaka with the pinnacle of arahantship. Here, “in this way” refers to the manner described at the beginning of the Cariyāpiṭaka with “Itthaṃ sudanti,” etc., and with phrases like “a hundred thousand eons ago.” “Sudanti” is merely a particle. “Bhagavā” is so called for reasons such as being fortunate. “His own past conduct” refers to his own practice and difficult deeds in previous births, such as that of Akitti the Wise. “Making manifest” means revealing perfectly, like an āmalaka fruit in the palm of the hand. It is called the “Buddhāpadāniya” because it was taught concerning the ancient and difficult deeds of the Buddhas. “Discourse on the Dhamma” means the teaching of the Dhamma or a principle that is the nature of things. “He spoke” means he declared. Whatever is not stated here should be understood as unstated either because it was explained previously or because its meaning is obvious.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Verses

Ettāvatā [V 0.0304] ca –

And thus far:

Visuddhacarito satthā, buddhicariyāya pāragū;

Sabbacariyāsu kusalo, lokācariyo anuttaro.

The Teacher is of pure conduct, a master of the practice of wisdom; skilled in all practices, the unsurpassed teacher of the world.

Yaṃ acchariyadhammānaṃ, sabbamacchariyātigo;

Attano pubbacariyānaṃ, ānubhāvavibhāvanaṃ.

A manifestation of the power of the former conduct of him who has transcended all wonderful things, who has gone beyond all marvels.

Desesi nātho cariyā-piṭakaṃ yañca tādino;

Dhammasaṅgāhakā therā, saṅgāyiṃsu tatheva ca.

The Lord, the Self-Controlled One, taught that Cariyāpiṭaka; and the Elders, compilers of the Dhamma, also recited it in that same way.

Tassa atthaṃ pakāsetuṃ, porāṇaṭṭhakathānayaṃ;

Nissāya yā samāraddhā, atthasaṃvaṇṇanā mayā.

To explain its meaning, this exposition of the meaning has been undertaken by me, relying on the method of the ancient commentaries.

Yā tattha paramatthānaṃ, niddhāretvā yathārahaṃ;

Pakāsanā paramattha-dīpanī nāma nāmato.

Having ascertained the ultimate meanings therein according to their due, this exposition, which illuminates the ultimate meanings, is named by name Paramatthadīpanī.

Sampattā pariniṭṭhānaṃ, anākulavinicchayā;

Sādhikāyaṭṭhavīsāya, pāḷiyā bhāṇavārato.

This work, of unconfused analysis, has reached completion, amounting in size to a little over twenty-eight bhāṇavāras of Pāli text.

Iti taṃ saṅkharontena, yaṃ taṃ adhigataṃ mayā;

Puññaṃ tassānubhāvena, lokanāthassa sāsanaṃ.

By whatever merit has been attained by me in thus composing this, through the power of that merit, may the teaching of the Lord of the World endure.

Ogāhetvā [M 0.0328] visuddhāya, sīlādipaṭipattiyā;

Sabbepi dehino hontu, vimuttirasabhāgino.

Having plunged into the perfectly pure practice of virtue and so on, may all beings share in the taste of liberation.

Ciraṃ [V 0.0305] tiṭṭhatu lokasmiṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsanaṃ;

Tasmiṃ sagāravā niccaṃ, hontu sabbepi pāṇino.

Long may the teaching of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One endure in the world; may all beings always hold it in reverence.

Sammā vassatu kālena, devopi jagatīpati;

Saddhammanirato lokaṃ, dhammeneva pasāsatūti.

May the rains fall in due season, and may the king, the lord of the earth, devoted to the True Dhamma, govern the world righteously.

Iti badaratitthavihāravāsinā ācariyadhammapālena

Thus, by Ācariya Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery,

Katā

was composed

Cariyāpiṭakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka is completed.
